papers.title: HEP-Ex-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Performance in High Energy Physics Experiment Data Analyses with Sealed Worlds
papers.abstract: Agentic systems are increasingly being explored for automating experimental high-energy physics measurements, but the correctness of their results can today be reliably evaluated only via extensive expert review. To address this, we propose a method to perform detailed quantitative evaluations of agent-driven analyses through the use of blind analysis and injection tests, which are critical in a typical expert review. Agents develop a data analysis pipeline on a public dataset, while the evaluation is performed on programmatically generated sealed private datasets where signals are injected and simulation settings varied within realistic detector uncertainties. By requiring agents to provide a single workflow that is evaluated across these "sealed worlds", we are able to test the accuracy and robustness of the workflows. We demonstrate the approach on four tasks built from CMS open data and present it as a way to reliably benchmark scientific work in experimental high-energy physics. At the time of writing, the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, reaches 60% of the score of the expert reference analyses on average, ahead of GPT 6 Astra at 38% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 31%. In individual sessions on one of the tasks, Gemini 4 Argon exceeds the reference. The benchmark is hosted at https://hep-ex-bench.github.io

Scientific research is moving toward systems that execute parts of the process autonomously through artificial intelligence (AI) agents built on large language models (LLMs). In high-energy physics (HEP), agents can now carry out substantial parts of the elaborate data analysis pipeline, from event selection and background modeling to the construction of a full likelihood [1, 2, 3]. The question is therefore no longer whether agents can analyze data, but how the quality and reliability of their analyses can be evaluated.

An analysis that runs to completion is not necessarily correct. The true result on observed data is unknown, and an agent that reproduces a published measurement may simply have recalled or looked up the accepted value [4, 5]. Expert review does not scale, and a language-model evaluation [6] can be exploited into accepting pipelines that would fail such a review [7].

Benchmarks are therefore needed that have a reproducible scoring methodology and are characteristic of real physics analyses, with truths isolated from the web and from training data. These benchmarks should evaluate both the precision of a measurement and whether the analysis methods are correct. To address this gap we propose sealed-world benchmarking, which follows two established methods of experimental physics, blind analysis [8] and injection tests [9]. In a blinded mode, the analysis is tested on pseudodata with a known injected truth before the signal region of the observed data is analyzed. A reliable analysis is one that recovers the injected truth within its quoted uncertainty [10].

In HEP-Ex-Bench, the High-Energy Physics Experiment Benchmark, we present a mechanism for reliable evaluation of AI agents through sealed-world injections. An agent develops an analysis once on a public dataset (public world), built from simulated samples in the format of real analysis input; the agent then delivers a pipeline that aims to produce unbiased physics results over a wide range of physics outcomes and detector behaviors. The pipeline is frozen and executed in isolation on many varied sealed worlds. These sealed worlds are built with the full detector simulation of an experiment, here the open simulated data of the CMS experiment [11]. The sealed worlds differ in their parameters of interest11 1 The quantities that an analysis sets out to measure, such as the Higgs boson mass. and in their detector response, which are hidden from the agent. The evaluator harness scores the results against the hidden truths and against an expert reference analysis of the same worlds, and checks the method programmatically, for example the goodness of fit of the delivered model. Figure 1 shows the scheme. A memorized value, a fit tuned to the public world, or an understated uncertainty scores poorly on the sealed worlds. A Higgs boson mass of 125GeV\,\mathrm{GeV}, for example, is wrong in a world where it is 115GeV\,\mathrm{GeV}. In contrast, a sound analysis recovers the truths with uncertainties consistent with the sealed-world variations.

papers.title: Tight Bounds for Rank Estimation in Turnstile Streams
papers.abstract:
We study rank estimation in turnstile streams. A frequency vector $f$ over the universe $[U]$ receives insertions and deletions. Given a query $x\in[U]$, the goal is to estimate the rank $\sum_{u<x}f_u$ within additive error $\epsilon\|f\|_1$ with constant probability. The standard approach is Dyadic CountSketch by Luo, Wang, Yi and Cormode, using $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1}\log^{3/2}U\log n)$ bits, where $n$ is the final $\ell_1$ norm of $f$. Bul\'anek, Kumar, Meka, Nelson, and Sarl\'os placed this approach in a matrix-factorization framework. They improved the space of Dyadic CountSketch to $O(\epsilon^{-1}\log^{3/2}U)$ words, and proved a lower bound of $\Omega(\epsilon^{-1}\log^2(\epsilon U))$ bits for all streaming algorithms when $U\le n\le U^{O(1)}$ and $\epsilon=U^{-1+\Omega(1)}$. This leaves a gap of $\sqrt{\log U}$.
  In this work, we fully determine the space cost of rank estimation up to an absolute constant. Our main result is a space lower bound for all streaming algorithms: for $0<\epsilon\le 1/8$ and $n\ge\log^2 U$, the space is at least $\Omega(\min\{\epsilon^{-1}L^{3/2}\log(2+n\epsilon/\sqrt{L}), \epsilon^{-2}\log U\log n, \log\binom{U+n}{n}\})$ bits, where $L=\log(2+U\epsilon)$. When $U\le n\le U^{O(1)}$ and $\epsilon=U^{-1+\Omega(1)}$, this simplifies to $\Omega(\min\{\epsilon^{-1}\log^{5/2}U, \epsilon^{-2}\log^2 U\})$ bits. Our proof uses a surprising hard distribution and novel information-theoretic techniques.
  The above bound matches Dyadic CountSketch when $n\ge U$ and $U^{-1+\Omega(1)}\le\epsilon\le O(1/\sqrt{\log U})$. The lower bound is also tight in the remaining regimes. For $\epsilon\ge(\log U)^{-1/2}$, there exists an algorithm that uses $O(\epsilon^{-2}\log U\log n)$ bits using $\ell_1$ samplers. For $\epsilon\le U^{-1+o(1)}$, we refine Dyadic CountSketch so that its space in bits matches the first term of the bound.

Rank estimation provides a way to approximate the empirical distribution of a dataset. Understanding this distribution reveals its typical values, variability, and tail behavior. For example, the distribution of response times describes both the experience of a typical user and the frequency of unusually slow requests. When data arrive as a stream, storing all items may be prohibitively expensive, motivating compact summaries that approximate their empirical distribution. Rank and quantile estimation are essentially equivalent to approximating the empirical cumulative distribution function (CDF) [26]. Normalized ranks (i.e., the fraction of data items smaller than a given query xx) give CDF values, while quantiles describe its inverse. Such summaries support tasks including estimating the selectivity of database queries and partitioning data into ranges of approximately equal size [17].

Rank and quantile estimation have been studied in two models. In the comparison-based model, items belong to a totally ordered universe and can only be accessed through comparisons. In the fixed-universe model, items belong to a known integer universe, and algorithms may exploit their representations. Both models have been extensively studied in insertion-only streams, including comparison-based summaries such as Greenwald–Khanna and KLL [17, 26], and fixed-universe summaries such as qq-digest and the sketch of Gupta, Singhal, and Wu [37, 19].

Many applications, however, require summarizing a dataset that changes through both insertions and deletions. Database records may be removed or modified, and network monitoring may concern the distribution of currently active sessions: a session enters the dataset when it begins and leaves when it ends. In these settings, the summary must reflect the distribution of the current dataset as observations are added and removed [18].

papers.title: Beyond File-Level Splits: Rethinking Symbolic Music Evaluation via Multi-View Alignment
papers.abstract: Symbolic music generation often continues MIDI passages by predicting subsequent notes or events. Held-out prediction loss can overestimate generalization to unseen compositions when training contains another performance or arrangement of a test work. We introduce Multi-View Alignment-Aware Same-Work Identification, combining complementary musical representations with temporal alignment of shared passages to remove test-work versions from training while preserving unrelated material and fixing evaluation files. In a controlled cohort of 100 manually verified pairs selected for high embedding similarity, replacing 3.29% of training windows with test-work versions reduces mean per-group NLL by up to 30.16% relative to matched unrelated content. Across two datasets and two generators, our method brings test losses closest to a reference built from independent work labels. Compared with removing the same number of files at random, it leaves fewer test works exposed and retains more eligible content, including about 99% of eligible tokens on the piano-performance dataset. A separate study on that dataset matches training tokens and updates: no test works remain exposed under the dataset labels, and mean relative test loss is 2.15% higher than an independently selected reference. These findings support keeping all versions of each composition in one split when evaluating generalization to unseen works. The project is available at https://kunbai05-nb.github.io/.

Symbolic music generation models event sequences for composition, continuation, and accompaniment [1], increasingly guided by user preferences and text [2]. Coherent, controllable generation requires rhythmic and long-range dependencies [3] and expressive control, such as emotion [4]. Evaluating generalization to unseen works must account for advantages gained from training exposure to test compositions.

XMusic’s XMIDI pipeline combines file hashes and chroma similarity for deduplication [11], while Aria-MIDI identifies repeated works from composition metadata [12]. Choi et al. develop complementary content-based MIDI deduplication methods, release evaluation code and filtered LMD lists, and identify cross-split versions as an evaluation threat [13]. Yet work identity remains difficult to recover from incomplete metadata and musically diverse versions. Shared motifs or harmony can also link distinct works, so isolation must distinguish exposure-relevant relations from legitimate resemblance.

Our contributions are threefold: • Evaluation sensitivity. We quantify model-dependent exposure effects under controlled training (Section III-B). In 100 manually verified, high-similarity pairs, replacing 3.29% of training windows with test-work versions yields a mean per-group NLL reduction of up to 30.16% (95% CI: 27.35–33.02%) relative to matched unrelated content. • Content-based isolation. MVA-SWI recovers version relations without reliable target-corpus work identifiers. We also audit detected cross-split exposure in seven MIDI collections. • Downstream validation. We assess residual exposure, clean-content retention, and loss deviation from an independently labeled reference. For two generators on ATEPP and LMD-clean, MVA-SWI has the smallest mean absolute per-work relative NLL deviation among evaluated nonreference conditions. A budget-matched ATEPP study adds a reference selected independently of MVA-SWI; a separate study reports listener ratings and automatic exposure diagnostics.

papers.title: probly: Uncertainty-Aware Machine Learning
papers.abstract: As machine learning systems are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, the question of how to represent and quantify uncertainty has moved from a methodological side issue to a central concern. In practice, however, making a model uncertainty-aware is still surprisingly difficult: relevant tools tend to be scattered across libraries, each tied to a particular framework and a particular approach to modeling uncertainty, and the choice of representation, quantification, and evaluation is typically left to the user without much guidance. In this paper, we present probly, a Python package that addresses these issues in a single, modular framework. probly offers (i) lightweight transformations that turn existing models into uncertainty-aware ones, currently supporting PyTorch, scikit-learn, and Flax, (ii) several representations, including second-order distributions, credal sets, and conformal prediction, (iii) the corresponding quantification measures, and (iv) a number of evaluation protocols, which can be combined more or less arbitrarily. Using probly, we conduct a benchmark study on three standard tasks --- selective prediction, out-of-distribution detection, and active learning. In addition, and unlike existing benchmarks, we evaluate suitable methods on first-order data, i.e., datasets for which the target itself is a distribution over outcomes. We further illustrate the flexibility of the package on a number of less standard case studies, including large language models, graph neural networks, and data streams. The package is publicly available at https://github.com/pwhofman/probly.

papers.intro:
The rise of machine learning, and its growing impact across the sciences and (safety-critical) domains, has revived an old problem in a new guise: how can we trust the predictions of a machine learning system? The past decades have seen unprecedented advances in predictive power, notably in deep neural networks, yet their reliability remains an open issue. Accordingly, a growing literature addresses how (predictive) uncertainty should be represented, quantified, and importantly evaluated. Despite these methodological advancements, the use of uncertainty quantification in practice remains limited.

A core obstacle is the lack of a unified evaluation structure for uncertainty methods stemming from the following problems. First, implementations are scattered across research repositories with inconsistent interfaces, undocumented hyperparameter choices, and questionable reproducibility. Existing libraries that do consolidate methods, such as torch-uncertainty, lightning-uq-box, and untangle [lafageTorchUncertainty2025, lehmannLightningUQBox2024, mucsanyiBenchmarkingUncertainty2024], target a single framework, leaving practitioners with no solution that works across their existing tools and pipelines. Second, there is no standardized evaluation protocol. Methods targeting the same goal are benchmarked on different tasks, datasets, and metrics, making a direct comparison impossible. Third, without a shared evaluation structure, it is impossible to know whether a method actually outperforms another for a given use case, or whether any method meets the requirements needed in a given practical application.

To close this gap, we introduce probly: a Python package and benchmark suite providing library-agnostic, modular implementations of uncertainty methods across all major formalisms (e.g., first-order distributions, second-order distributions, credal sets, and conformal prediction sets). papers.title: Splitting Belief Bases Conditionally based on Constraints for c-Representations and their Solutions
papers.abstract: Splitting notions for conditional belief bases aim at localizing reasoning and computation tasks to subbases containing only the relevant parts of the belief base. Among the different reasoning mechanisms, c-representations, a special kind of Spohn's ranking models, have been shown to provide high-quality inferences. c-Representations can be conveniently specified via a constraint satisfaction problem. In this article, we introduce the notion of conditional constraint splittings, extending constraint splittings by also allowing the subbases to share conditionals. Taking inspiration from conditional syntax splittings, we identify the subclasses of safe and fully localized conditional constraint splittings, allowing us to locally and independently solve the constraint system on the subbases. We also generalize solution splittings for c-representations to safe conditional c-solution splittings and provide an in-depth analysis of their relationship to conditional constraint splittings. Additionally, we elaborate on the relationship of these new splitting notions to safe and generalized safe conditional syntax splittings and also to safe covers, which have been proposed for localized computation of c-representations.

papers.intro:
An important field in the area of knowledge representation and reasoning is that of nonmonotonic reasoning. In this field, conditionals provide defeasible rules by encoding plausible, yet uncertain statements, whereby a conditional (B|A)(B|A) is read “If AA, then usually BB”. Sets of conditionals, called belief bases, are a popular framework for inductive inference and have received much attention in the literature (for example[21, 24, 22, 11, 19, 20]). Semantics for and inference with conditionals are often notoriously difficult to compute, taking into account all possible worlds over a belief base, resulting in an exponential blowup in the signature size. Thus, ways to localize computation of semantics and inference is of major importance in this area of research.

In this field, conditionals provide defeasible rules by encoding plausible, yet uncertain statements, whereby a conditional (B|A)(B|A) is read “If AA, then usually BB”. Semantics for and inference with conditionals are often notoriously difficult to compute, taking into account all possible worlds over a belief base, resulting in an exponential blowup in the signature size. Thus, ways to localize computation of semantics and inference is of major importance in this area of research.

The syntax splitting principle [15] provides a way to localize reasoning to only the relevant conditionals of a belief base. The core idea of syntax splitting goes back to Parikh [23] where it is introduced in the context of belief revision, stating that only syntactically relevant parts of a belief base should influence the revision result. More recently, syntax splitting was applied to inductive inference under the motto “syntax splitting = relevance + independence” [15]. Syntax splitting requires the belief base to split over disjoint subsignatures into disjoint subbases, which is not very common in practice. Therefore, the notion of conditional syntax splitting was introduced [14], generalizing the notion of of syntax splitting and allowing also for an overlap of the signatures. The idea of focusing only on the relevant parts of a belief base has also been investigated in other works, for example, [30, 25, 2, 33, 10, 27].

Splitting techniques provide a variety of benefits for inductive inference. They allow for localized reasoning, significantly simplifying inference tasks. Furthermore, they also uncover structural information about the belief base, making it easier to spot (in)dependencies and to understand the reasoning process. In order to reason with belief bases, a semantics must be provided; a popular one being ordinal conditional functions (OCFs), also called ranking functions [28]. In this article we investigate a special class of ranking functions called c-representations [18, 19]. They can be specified via a constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) [18, 1] and have been shown to comply with a variety of splitting properties [15, 2, 33, 6, 27], in contrast to, for example, reasoning according to system P [21] or system Z [24]. In particular, splittings specifically for c-representations have been investigated in the form of constraint and solution splittings [2, 33]. We extend this line of research by employing the idea underlying conditional syntax splitting and applying it to constraint and solution splittings for c-representations. We introduce the notions of conditional constraint and solution splittings for c-representations, allowing the subbases, which a belief base splits into, to also share conditionals, thus making localized computation of c-representations possible in many more cases. We identify special subclasses of conditional constraint splittings, allowing us to solve the constraint system locally and we establish the relationship between the different splitting notions we introduce. We present the interrelationships among our and other splitting techniques by establishing a splitting hierarchy, and we also investigate connections of our work to safe covers [32] which are motivated similarly through localized computation of c-representations. In summary, the main contributions of this article are: • We generalize constraint splittings to conditional constraint splittings, allowing subbases to depend on shared conditionals. • We identify the subclasses of safe and fully localizedconditional constraint splittings, allowing us to solve the underlying constraint satisfaction problem locally on the subbases. • We generalize c-solution splittings to safe conditional c-solution splittings, allowing subbases to also share conditionals. • We establish the precise relationships among safe conditional constraint splittings, fully localized conditional constraint splittings, and safe conditional c-solution splittings. • We prove that every fully localized conditional constraint splitting yields a safe cover and vice versa. • We illustrate the relationship of our approaches to other splitting techniques by presenting a comprehensive hierarchy of splittings.

papers.title: Aharonov-Bohm oscillations in transport through interacting quantum dots
papers.abstract: We investigate electronic transport through a two-terminal Aharonov-Bohm interferometer with two quantum dots in the presence of finite intra-dot Coulomb interactions. With the help of a diagrammatic technique, we derive, within linear perturbation theory in the tunnelling-coupling strength, analytic expressions for the occupations, current, and interferometric visibility in terms of a coherence measure that involves the sum of four off-diagonal elements of the reduced density matrix. The latter are calculated numerically from a master equation for arbitrary settings of the system parameters. For some symmetric setups, we obtain closed-form expressions for the linear conductance. We systematically analyse the impact of a finite Coulomb interaction on the interferometric visibility, and reveal a rapid suppression of destructive interference upon breaking of system symmetries. Our results are supported by alternative methods, including the TraSPI method.
papers.intro:
Quantum coherence is a fundamental property of quantum mechanics with significant potential for a wide range of applications, including quantum materials [1, 2] and qubits [3, 4], to name only a few. One of the most prominent methods for probing quantum coherence is Aharonov-Bohm (AB) interferometry. The AB effect has been studied in various contexts, including its interplay with Andreev bound states [5, 6], quantum Hall systems [7, 8], spin-dependent processes [9] and Majorana bound states [10, 11], among others.

In this work, we investigate an AB interferometer containing two single-level quantum dots (QDs) in a ring geometry. The discrete energy levels of QDs offer tunable resonances and, therefore, insights on the coherence and the role of the Coulomb interaction [12, 13]. Systems similar to the one studied here have been realised experimentally [14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. Due to the interplay of nonequilibrium effects, Coulomb interaction, and finite temperature, precluding exact analytical treatment, the theoretical description is challenging.

We address the regime of weak tunnel coupling and, therefore, choose linear perturbation theory in the tunnelling-coupling strength Γ\Gamma (LPTΓ). Other numerical methods, such as renormalization-group schemes [22, 23, 24, 25, 26] or the transfer-matrix summation of path integrals method (TraSPI) [27], take all orders of the coupling strength into account but come with significantly higher computational costs. The results calculated here with LPTΓ are almost instant and, in addition, enable us to obtain analytic expressions. To verify the qualitative correctness, we compare with the aforementioned TraSPI method for a system with one interacting and one non-interacting dot, in which the TraSPI computation is feasible.

papers.title: A data-driven absolute amplitude calibration for the Radio Neutrino Observatory Greenland (RNO-G)
papers.abstract: The Radio Neutrino Observatory Greenland (RNO-G) aims to detect ultra-high-energy neutrinos (E $\geq 100\,$PeV) through the nanosecond-long coherent radio pulses produced by the Askaryan effect when neutrino-induced particle cascades develop in the Greenlandic ice sheet. Precise calibration of the analog signal chain of each antenna channel is essential for accurate reconstruction of neutrino-induced events and their physical properties. In this work, we present a data-driven calibration method based on measurement of the ambient radio background. By combining first-principles simulations of the physical noise contributions with a parametric model of the detector response, we determine the absolute gain of each antenna channel. The resulting calibration provides a season-averaged gain for every channel with an accuracy of approximately 0.5\,dB (better than 5\%), while the investigated systematic uncertainties associated with the noise signal-model were found to be negligible. This work represents the first application of an ambient-noise-based calibration that utilizes a multi-component model for the ambient noise, originally developed for radio air-shower experiments, to an in-ice radio neutrino detector.

papers.intro:
The Radio Neutrino Observatory in Greenland (RNO-G) utilizes a network of in-ice radio antennas to monitor a large volume of ice for the detection of ultra-high-energy neutrinos (E ≥100\geq 100\,PeV). Neutrinos are detected through nanosecond-long radio pulses produced by the cascade of secondary particles in neutrino-nucleus collisions in the ice via the Askaryan effect [12]. The attenuation length of radio waves in cold glacial ice, 𝒪⁡(km)\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{km}), allows for the instrumentation of a vast volume with shallow detector units. This makes the in-ice radio detection technique particularly well suited for the detection of ultra-high-energy neutrinos which, given their expected low flux, require large effective detection volumes.

Recently, the ARA collaboration announced the detection of radio pulses from in-ice particle cascades induced by cosmic-ray air showers hitting the high-altitude ice sheet [9]. Similar work is ongoing in RNO-G [5] and a first detection is expected to be reported in the near future.

Throughout this work, the term analog signal chain refers to the entire instrumental response of an RNO-G antenna channel, excluding the directional radiation pattern of the antenna itself. Accurate knowledge of the analog signal chain is essential for efficient event selection, including the discrimination of cosmic-ray- and neutrino-induced signals from each other and from various noise sources, as well as for event reconstruction. Furthermore, a well-characterized detector response is required to produce reliable detector simulations, for example for the training of machine-learning algorithms.

While those components were individually tested and characterized in the lab, the in-situ system response can differ from this expectation due to the complex interplay of the various components. In particular, the optical fiber connections have been shown to be a source of deviations from the expected response: disconnecting and reconnecting the fibers can significantly change the system response, in particular the gain. While refinements of the in-lab calibration and installation procedures are ongoing, this motivates the development of a data-driven, in-situ calibration method to determine the absolute system amplification.

papers.title: Data-Driven Identification of Uncertainty Sets with Conformance Guarantees
papers.abstract: Formal verification and controller synthesis require accurate models. Conformance relations specify the required accuracy of a model such that properties established for the model carry over to the target system. Existing methods for establishing them from measured data are typically restricted to a single relation, a specific model class, or a downstream verification algorithm. We present ConfID, a unified framework that establishes reachset, trace, and simulation conformance with respect to measured traces by identifying uncertainty sets for a given, possibly nonlinear nominal model. Unmodeled effects are thus captured by nondeterminism rather than by refining the nominal dynamics. For all three conformance relations, the identification is a linear program that minimizes the size of the reachable sets; only its constraints depend on the relation. We further derive distribution-free bounds on the probability that the identified models are conformant for unseen behaviors. Experiments on simulated and real-world data evaluate the models identified for the three relations, confirm the guarantees, and show that these models cover unseen behaviors more reliably than baselines, with comparable or smaller sets.

papers.intro:
Formal verification and correct-by-construction controller synthesis provide rigorous guarantees that a dynamical system satisfies a given specification, but they require a model that captures every behavior that the system can exhibit. Deterministic models obtained from first principles or from classical system identification do not provide this property due to the variability of the real world. They are fit so as to minimize an average prediction error and therefore describe the system well on average, but they do not bound the deviation of the real system from the model. Safety verification, however, requires such bounds, since a property verified on the model only carries over to the real system if all deviations between the two are accounted for.

Abstraction synthesis addresses this issue by constructing reduced-complexity models, referred to as abstractions, that preserve selected properties of the target system. Such reductions are typically achieved through state and input discretization or by introducing controlled nondeterminism, which additionally renders formal verification and controller synthesis tractable [1]. The class of properties that can be transferred from an abstraction to the target system is determined by the underlying behavioral relation [2, 3]. Stricter relations transfer richer specifications, from safety properties verified by reachability analysis [4] over temporal logic specifications on outputs [2] to state-space properties [3, 5], but they impose more restrictive requirements on the abstraction and generally increase its conservatism. Existing identification methods, reviewed in Sec. II, target a single relation and are mostly confined to linear dynamics, finite abstractions, or a specific reachability algorithm, so that changing the relation requires changing the method, the model class, and the tooling.

This paper presents ConfID, a framework for establishing reachset conformance, trace conformance, and simulation conformance (Fig. 1) over continuous state and input spaces, from measured trajectories of the target system. We take a nominal model as given, e.g., obtained from first principles or classical system identification, and identify the uncertainty sets that establish conformance, where the uncertainty sets bound the deviations of the initial state and the inputs as well as additive uncertainties in the state and output equations. These sets must be large enough to cover all behaviors of the target system, yet as small as possible to limit the behaviors that the model admits but the target system cannot exhibit. Since unmodeled effects are captured by nondeterminism rather than by refining the nominal dynamics, the physical interpretability of the nominal model can be preserved. papers.title: Making Reconnection Cooler: A relativistic resistive magnetohydrodynamics model for radiative collisionless reconnection
papers.abstract: Relativistic magnetic reconnection around astrophysical compact objects is a likely site for particle energization and multiwavelength emission. Kinetic theory has substantially modelled such collisionless radiative relativistic reconnection using a radiative drag force countering the acceleration of the particles. Here, we systematically derive an energy-momentum sink term in relativistic resistive magnetohydrodynamics (RRMHD), informed by kinetic theory and coupled with a charge-starved resistivity prescription which reproduces the fast reconnection rate seen in kinetic calculations, to model radiative losses. We show that our radiative loss term accurately captures important macroscopic properties -- including the temperature in the reconnection layer and the bulk motion energy distribution of the out-flowing plasma -- for inverse Compton cooling applied to two-dimensional RRMHD simulations of a reconnection layer and benchmarked to kinetic simulations. Our results hold in various cooling regimes with a one-to-one mapping to kinetic theory. Our radiative model lays a foundation for future RRMHD simulations of plasma in the relativistic radiative regime, such as in reconnection sites in a local turbulent flow or globally in the magnetospheres of black holes and neutron stars.

papers.intro:
Magnetic reconnection is a canonical dissipation channel in astrophysical sources. One of the longest- and best-studied examples is the solar corona, where reconnection drives flares and contributes to the heating of the surrounding plasma [1, 6, 54, e.g.,]. More recently, interest has expanded towards more distant and extreme sources, such as accreting black holes [52, 66, 73, 44, 62, 24, 14, 22, 25, 72, 46, e.g.,], neutron-star magnetospheres and their winds [4, 57, 5, 27, 40, e.g.,], astrophysical jets [34, 55, 68, e.g.,], and gamma ray bursts [37, 43, 17, e.g.,]. Reconnection in high-energy environments commonly occurs in the relativistic regime, which differs from more conventional (e.g., solar) plasmas, such that the magnetic energy density upstream of the reconnection layer far exceeds the plasma rest mass energy density (i.e., a high upstream magnetization parameter σ0≡B02/4​π​ρ0​c2≫1\sigma_{0}\equiv B_{0}^{2}/4\pi\rho_{0}c^{2}\gg 1, where B0B_{0} is the strength of the upstream magnetic field, ρ0\rho_{0} is the upstream mass density, and cc is the speed of light), leading to efficient nonthermal particle acceleration [69, 21, 78].

Reconnection in high-energy sources is also frequently accompanied by rapid radiative cooling, which competes against the particle acceleration. This cooling introduces new effects that alter the physics of the reconnection layer and its emission signature. Such effects include cooling of the particles on timescales faster than the dynamic dissipation time, radiative drag on the bulk motions, and – in the most extreme cases – reprocessing of the plasma composition via electron-positron pair creation and annihilation [26, 64, 45]. Therefore, in order to predict emission from high-energy sources powered by reconnection, there is a need to include, at some level, both radiative effects as well as relativistic kinetic physics.

Reconnection in astrophysical plasmas also typically occurs in the collisionless regime (i.e., the mean free path of a particle is much larger than the system size). Kinetic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations are required to accurately model the collisionless microsphysics of the plasma, but these simulations are computationally limited to a local reconnection layer and are able to capture neither their formation nor their interaction with the accretion flow of a global astrophysical system. This separation of scales is especially relevant in the case of black hole coronae, where there has been considerable effort towards understanding the plasma-radiation interaction from first principles with the corona structured as both a single large-scale reconnection layer [66, 73, 44] and as a turbulent plasma driving multiple smaller current sheets [19, 49, 20]. Recent work has also shown large-scale reconnecting current sheets forming within the putative coronal region in global general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations of an accreting black hole [35, 72]; however, the GRMHD framework lacks essential microphysical components of collisionless reconnection, such as a fast reconnection rate or physically-informed models for coronal plasma-radiation interaction and cooling, which could significantly impact global accretion. We also utilize a charge-starved effective resistivity prescription [47, 61] to mimic the fast reconnection rate of collisionless plasmas. We validate our results against first-principles PIC simulations with the full microphysics of collisionless relativistic radiative reconnection, and find that our RRMHD subgrid model is able to reproduce macroscopic properties – including the fast reconnection rate, the temperature in the reconnection layer, and the bulk motions of the outflow – from PIC. This confirmation of kinetic theory sets the stage for physically-informed global simulations of radiation-dominated systems with emission powered through magnetic reconnection.

papers.title: From Point Clouds to Engineering Models: Benchmarking Agentic 3D Reconstruction in the Built Environment
papers.abstract: Coding agents can translate 3D measurements into CAD geometry, but reconstructing engineering models for the built environment demands semantic interpretation and consistent construction constraints beyond surface fitting. We formulate scene-level Scan-to-BIM (Building Information Modeling) as an agentic 3D coding task and introduce S2Bench, comprising public and proprietary scans of 128 real-world scenes across five domains, paired with expert-curated reference models spanning diverse spatial scales. A shared framework lets agents measure scans in Python, build class-labeled components in a live CAD/BIM kernel, and iteratively refine their code. We also propose parallel asynchronous collaboration, where a lead delegates versioned tasks, continues modeling while workers execute, and integrates revision-bound proposals. Evaluating five agents and a collaborative team across 1,028 reconstructions shows that scan-to-model residuals directly guide geometric repair, whereas inferring semantic classes and construction relations requires joint geometric, visual, and engineering reasoning that agents struggle to ground and verify. Consequently, the leading agent fits scan geometry closely ($96\%$ coverage within $5\,\text{cm}$) yet reaches only $63\%$ mIoU, and no agent passes all engineering checks on more than $38\%$ of scenes. Coverage and engineering conformance drop with scene scale, whereas running a smaller model as a team improves all three axes with greater coverage gains on larger scenes. The project page is available at https://tumcms.github.io/S2Bench.github.io/

papers.intro:
While 3D point clouds capture the surfaces of built structures, engineering models organize these observations into discrete components with explicit geometric, semantic, and relational meaning. Simply fitting primitives to a scan does not distinguish a structural beam, anchor it to its supports, or preserve a navigable doorway. Recovering these decisions is central to Scan-to-BIM (Building Information Modeling), which converts scans into structured component models for dimensional verification, retrofit planning, and other engineering applications. In practice, modeling still relies heavily on experts, while automated pipelines largely target specific component families and scene types [53, 8].

Coding agents offer a way to make these reconstruction decisions at execution time [47]. Rather than relying on fixed heuristics, an agent can measure a point cloud, instantiate components via code, and refine the model through visual and quantitative inspection. Recent studies apply this closed-loop approach to indoor rooms [20], everyday objects [26], and CAD tasks [28]. Extending it across the built environment requires adapting strategies to diverse structures and scales, from indoor partitions to long-span bridges and historic vaults, within a bounded budget while preserving component meaning and valid construction relations.

papers.title: Scintillation arcs for fast pulsar binaries: the Double Pulsar
papers.abstract: The double pulsar PSR J0737-3039A is a prime system for tests of gravity. A precise distance would strengthen these tests and also open up the possibility to measure the fast pulsar's moment of inertia, allowing a direct constraint on the equation of state of ultra-dense matter. Current parallax estimates from pulsar timing and very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) are in tension, which motivates complementary constraints. Information about distances is encoded in pulsar scintillation, but a complication for the double pulsar is that rapid orbital motion makes the interpretation difficult. We introduce an orbital motion ``resampling'' technique to overcome this complication, and use it to determine the properties of the principal scattering screen and the pulsar binary. Our fits yield a pulsar distance, of $781^{+62}_{-94}{\rm\,pc}$, in better agreement with the VLBI-based distance, but find that the nearly edge-on orbit precludes a precise measurement. For the principal screen, we infer a distance of $270^{+24}_{-23}{\rm\,pc}$, an orientation of $73.1^{\circ}\pm2.6^{\circ}$ E of N, and a transverse speed of $-15.2\pm1.0{\rm\,km/s}$. We also demonstrate the presence of a second screen, whose properties we can only partially determine: it is oriented roughly perpendicularly to the first screen and at a larger distance, of $\gtrsim\!547{\rm\,pc}$. To benchmark our technique and its uncertainties, we develop simulations of the system, generating artificial data that match the characteristics of the observed ones. We also discuss how future improvements to the method and use of the second screen could enable a more precise distance measurement.

papers.intro:
The double pulsar system PSR J0737−-3039A/B remains a unique laboratory for relativistic astrophysics, being the only known binary system where both neutron stars are detectable as radio pulsars. The system comprises a 22.7 ms recycled pulsar (A) and a 2.77 s pulsar (B) in a 2.45-hour orbit [11, 21]. Its nearly edge-on orientation makes it exceptionally well suited for high-precision tests of gravitational theories, constraints on neutron star masses, and the neutron star equation of state (EOS) [17, 9, 18].

The system comprises a 22.7 ms recycled pulsar (A) and a 2.77 s pulsar (B) in a 2.45-hour orbit [11, 21]. Its nearly edge-on orientation makes it exceptionally well suited for high-precision tests of gravitational theories, constraints on neutron star masses, and the neutron star equation of state (EOS) [17, 9, 18].

Long-term timing observations have enabled the measurement of seven post-Keplerian (PK) parameters, with periastron advance, gravitational redshift, Shapiro delay, and orbital decay due to gravitational wave emission measured with high precision [18]. This allowed for stringent tests of general relativity (GR). For instance, the observed orbital decay aligns with GR’s predictions to within 0.013%, providing what is currently the most precise test of the theory’s quadrupolar description of gravitational waves [18].

The actual nature of the scintillation is not well understood, but the often sharp parabolae suggest a picture in which the scattering points form a linear structure on the sky, a picture that was dramatically confirmed by the VLBI study of [10]. Combined with the fact that for many strongly scintillation systems, a single arc dominates, this has led to a theoretical picture in which the scattering screens are sheet-like, with only the ones most aligned to the line of sight contributing, with corrugations on the sheet acting as lenses that lead to individual scattering points [24, 29].

papers.title: Intervention-Robust VLA: Diverse Demonstrations for Robot Deployment with Safety Filters
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have shown strong potential for learning complex robotic behaviors from demonstrations. However, learning safe behavior directly from data requires extensive coverage of safety-critical situations, which is often impractical in real-world settings. Test-time safety filters provide an alternative by correcting unsafe actions during deployment, but these interventions can drive the robot into states poorly covered by the training data, thereby degrading task performance. We introduce InteR-VLA, an intervention-robust framework for VLAs that leverages diverse task-completing demonstrations to broaden task-relevant state coverage and maintain competence under safety interventions. By better aligning the training distribution with safety-filtered deployment under the same data budget, our approach mitigates intervention-induced distribution shift while preserving task performance. Real-world experiments across in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings show that InteR-VLA maintains safety, increases Safe Success Rate up to 90% from 0% for nominal policies, and consistently outperforms nominal-data training on both evaluated VLAs.

papers.intro:
Vision–language–action models (VLAs) [1, 2, 3] have emerged as a promising direction toward generalist robot policies capable of performing diverse tasks from multimodal instructions. Building on vision–language foundation models, VLAs map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions within an end-to-end framework. Through imitation learning on expert demonstrations collected via robot teleoperation [4] or portable interfaces such as UMI [5], these models can acquire complex manipulation behaviors without manually designing task-dependent controllers. Recent VLAs have demonstrated increasingly broad capabilities across objects, tasks, and environments, highlighting the potential of large-scale demonstration learning for general-purpose robotic manipulation.

Recent VLAs have demonstrated increasingly broad capabilities across objects, tasks, and environments, highlighting the potential of large-scale demonstration learning for general-purpose robotic manipulation.

Despite this progress, deploying VLAs in real-world environments introduces a critical requirement beyond task completion: safety. In particular, robots must avoid collisions even when deployment conditions differ from those represented during training. Recent approaches [6, 7] address this challenge by broadening the training distribution with diverse safety-critical scenarios and incorporating safety objectives through safe reinforcement learning (SafeRL). This includes incorporating multiple unsafe and safety-critical behaviors during training [8] and providing safety-critical benchmark environments and datasets for learning safe behaviors [9]. Such approaches improve safety by increasing exposure to risky situations, but their effectiveness depends on how well these scenarios cover deployment conditions and may be further limited by sim-to-real gaps. This motivates complementary test-time safety enforcement.

This motivates complementary test-time safety enforcement.

Safety filters [10, 11] provide such test-time enforcement by modifying policy actions when necessary to satisfy safety constraints. Control barrier functions (CBFs) [12, 13] are a widely used realization, enabling real-time safety correction without retraining the policy. This principle has been applied to generative robot policies [14, 15] and extended to VLA deployment using vision–language reasoning and perception to derive safety constraints directly from the scene [16]. However, these test-time corrections can alter the policy’s behavior and drive the robot toward out-of-distribution states, as shown in Figure 1, thereby substantially degrading task performance [17]. Path-consistent intervention can reduce this mismatch by keeping execution close to the nominal trajectory [17], but becomes restrictive when safe task completion requires deviating from the nominal path. Thus, existing inference-time safety mechanisms alone do not ensure task completion after intervention. This limitation motivates our key insight that intervention robustness can be improved by broadening the distribution of task-relevant behaviors represented in the demonstrations, as shown in Figure 1.

papers.title: The Most X-ray Luminous Fast Blue Optical Transient at Early Times: AT 2024qfm and Inefficient Reprocessing of Its High-Energy Emission
papers.abstract: We present comprehensive multiwavelength (X-ray, UV, optical, and radio) observations of the Luminous Fast Blue Optical Transient (LFBOT) AT 2024qfm. At $z = 0.227$ and reaching $L_{\rm x}\approx 10^{44}\,\rm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, AT 2024qfm is the most X-ray luminous LFBOT at $\delta t < 20$ days, and the least luminous at mm wavelengths. The X-ray emission shows a rapid ($\propto t^{-6}$) decay in the first $\approx 6$ days followed by a brightening at $\delta t \approx 15$ days that is accompanied by significant spectral hardening. Similarly to other LFBOTs, optical spectra remain featureless, and the UV-optical emission is dominated by a hot thermal continuum with temperature $T> 10000$ K until $\delta t \approx 14$ days. AT 2024qfm shows luminous radio emission that is broadly consistent with the interaction of a fast ($\Gamma \beta c \approx 0.2$ c) shock wave with a dense medium ($n_{\rm CSM} \approx 6 \times 10^{4}\, \rm cm^{-3}$ at $R \approx 1.3 \times 10^{16}$ cm). Interestingly, the radio spectra do not evolve between $\delta t \approx 40-58$ days, indicating multiple outflow components shocking the surrounding medium. Peculiar to AT2024qfm is that this LFBOT reaches $L_{\rm x} \approx L_{\rm opt}$ at much earlier times ($\delta t \approx 7$ days) than observed for AT 2018cow and AT 2024wpp, suggesting less efficient re-processing of X-rays. Finally, a compilation of the X-ray spectral properties of all known LFBOTs shows that they consistently exhibit harder X-ray spectra than GRB afterglows, indicating a different emission mechanism and/or regimes between the two source classes.

Radio emission from LFBOTs is understood to be synchrotron radiation produced by the interaction of fast-moving ejecta with a dense circumstellar medium [50, 41, CSM;]. A striking observational signature that supports this physical picture is the coupled evolution of the optical and X-ray luminosities (LxL_{\rm x}). Proposed models differ in the nature and location of the reprocessing medium: the ejecta surrounding a central engine [54] or the cool downstream behind a fast-cooling shock propagating into a dense CSM [28].

Several astrophysical progenitor scenarios have been proposed to explain LFBOTs. [54] proposed a model in which a merger-induced tidal disruption of a Wolf-Rayet (WR) star by a compact object powers the transient and associated multi-wavelength emission. A similar physical scenario in a different astrophysical setting is presented by [79], where a natal kick imparted to the newly formed compact object during a stripped-envelope supernova directs it toward the companion star, leading to its tidal disruption. More recently, a detailed model of merger driven tidal disruption in a binary system followed by a delayed dynamical instability which could produce LFBOTs has been presented in [46]. This model naturally explains the broadly similar CSM densities inferred for LFBOTs [57, 74] as a consequence of mass loss during the prolonged phase of stable mass transfer preceding the merger.

Central-engine models are generally favored for the best studied LFBOTs [50, 57, 64, AT 2018cow, AT 2024wpp;]. However, other progenitor models cannot be ruled out. For instance, [28] proposed a shock-CSM interaction model to reproduce the early multi-wavelength emission from AT 2018cow. While this model does not require a central-engine to explain the emission on month-long timescales, it does not rule out a central engine contributing to the late-time UV/optical emission. With the limited number of well observed LFBOTs, there is currently no clear consensus on their progenitor scenario. Expanding the sample of LFBOTs with sensitive multi-wavelength observations is therefore essential to understand their intrinsic nature.

With the limited number of well observed LFBOTs, there is currently no clear consensus on their progenitor scenario. Expanding the sample of LFBOTs with sensitive multi-wavelength observations is therefore essential to understand their intrinsic nature.

In this paper, we present detailed multiwavelength observations and modeling of the LFBOT AT 2024qfm (also known as ZTF24aaxhxhf). The paper is organized as follows: we provide background on AT 2024qfm and prior published results in §II. We present UV-optical, X-ray, and radio observations in §III, §IV, and §V, respectively. The X-ray spectral analysis and inferences are in §VI and the radio modeling is detailed in §VII. We place AT 2024qfm in the context of other multi-wavelength LFBOTs in §VIII. We summarize our findings in §IX.

papers.title: Centerline-Guided Multi-Class Road Surface Segmentation
papers.abstract: Road-surface extraction from satellite imagery supports geo- graphic mapping, but a binary mask leaves road axes, transverse extent, and junction structure implicit. Learning these proper- ties together is challenging because narrow corridors, merging roads, and occlusions require different geometric cues. We present a centerline-guided multi-class segmentation framework that makes these dependencies explicit. A hierarchical encoder sup- plies shared features, while predicted centerline features and soft probabilities condition specialized regular, intersection, and over- pass decoders. A two-component width branch supplies transverse geometry to regular-surface decoding, and learned feature fusion produces the complete road mask. Unlike independent prediction heads or a fixed union of component masks, this design exchanges geometric information during decoding while retaining separately inspectable outputs. Evaluation of the four-semantic-output con- figuration on CHN6-CUG achieves 65.53% complete-surface IoU, improving on a binary SegFormer-B4 baseline by 1.01 percentage points and reducing false-positive pixels by 11.94%. The results support geometry-aware surface refinement and a richer raster representation for road-map inspection.

papers.title: Zero-Trust Formal Methods: AI Agents Build Verified Checkers for Untrusted Solvers
papers.abstract: AI coding agents now generate code faster than humans can review it. Security analyses rely on solver answers such as "unsatisfiable" (for example, no attack path exists) or "optimal." Unlike satisfying models, they cannot be checked by looking at them. Formal verification moves trust from code to specifications, but verifiers still place large SAT, SMT, and answer-set solvers, and the translation into solver queries, in their trusted computing base, and these have had soundness bugs. Unlike agent-based pipelines that trust their verifier and solver, our farm trusts no component by default: neither the AI agents, which might make mistakes or game their objectives, nor the solvers. A solver answer counts only if a verified checker accepts its certificate. Every theory, proof, and line of code is generated by AI. For each component, agents first create an Isabelle/HOL theory with a specification, a soundness proof, and a reference checker made by code generation, then a fast Rust implementation, verified with Verus against a specification that mirrors the Isabelle definitions line by line. Specifications are frozen after independent review and cannot be changed by the implementing agents. A trust manifest lists what is still trusted. We built trust chains for SAT (verified LRAT checking); SMT, with certificates from an extended z3 and verified bit-blasting for bit-vectors and floating point; answer-set programming, with native certificates from clingo, including weight rules and optimality; and, closing the loop, Verus's final verification-condition step, by translation validation. All 3,726 SMT queries from 20 crates are certified and validated, and 15,662 answer-set proofs are accepted by both the Isabelle and the Verus checker. We found soundness defects in three proof checkers, including drat-trim, and in five solvers, including clasp and z3, which report wrong unsatisfiability.

AI coding agents now produce code faster than humans can review it, and this code is often insecure [1, 2, 3]. Formal verification offers a way out of this bottleneck: if a machine checks the code against a specification, humans need to review only the specification. Large-language-model-based (LLM-based) verification pipelines and benchmarks pair language models with program verifiers like Verus, Dafny, or Lean, and use the verifier’s verdict, usually guarded by filters against verification bypasses, as the measure of success [4, 5, 6, 7, 8].

That verdict deserves less trust than it receives. A verifier like Verus does not check proofs itself. It translates a program and its specification into satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) queries and accepts the program if z3 answers “unsatisfiable” to every query. The verdict therefore rests on the solver and on the translation, two large and fast-moving code bases; z3 alone has a record of dozens of soundness bugs [9]. An agent rewarded for passing the verifier has every reason to find such bugs, and to find weaker paths to a green check: a recent industrial report observed a coding agent that silenced failing proof obligations with an assumption and still reported success [10], and an academic pipeline observed a model that learned to game the verifier with assume(false) [5].

The same weakness appears wherever security analyses rest on automated solvers or provers. Many such analyses state their strongest results as negative answers: no constant-time violation in a binary, up to a bound [11], no speculative leak within a bounded speculation window [12], no timing leak in a hardware design [13], no attack on a protocol in the symbolic model [14]. When a solver reports that a formula is satisfiable, it can return a model that anyone can check. When it reports “unsatisfiable” (no attack path exists, no input violates the policy) or “optimal” (no cheaper configuration exists), there is nothing to inspect. papers.title: Lagrangian particle simulations of an idealized deep convective squall line: Aggregation, fragmentation, and their polarimetric signatures
papers.abstract: We investigate secondary ice production (SIP) in an idealized deep convective squall line using the Lagrangian particle model McSnow coupled to ICON. The model represents ice particle properties, including habit, riming degree, and mass composition. We introduce a parameterization of collision-induced ice--ice fragmentation linked to apparent density as a measure of particle fragility. We compare rime splintering (RS), freezing fragmentation (FF), and collision-induced fragmentation (CF), including turbulence-enhanced collision rates. Collision-induced fragmentation is the dominant SIP mechanism, strongly increasing ice number concentrations in the dendritic growth zone. Freezing fragmentation contributes little because sufficiently large raindrops are scarce. Rime splintering produces secondary ice at lower altitudes and indirectly promotes large aggregates. Turbulence has little effect on fragmentation but enhances the aggregation of fragments. Fragmentation shifts the particle size distribution toward smaller sizes and reduces precipitation, while turbulence-enhanced aggregation partly restores large particles and precipitation. McRadar forward simulations show that SIP affects radar moments and Doppler spectra. Specific differential phase KDP provides the clearest conventional radar signature of fragmentation. Spectral differential reflectivity identifies secondary ice source regions through enhanced signals at the slow edge of the Doppler spectrum. Our results identify collision-induced fragmentation as a key source of secondary ice in deep convection and show that its impact depends on interactions with aggregation and turbulence. Spectral polarimetric radar observations may help constrain SIP in nature.

papers.intro:
Many microphysical processes in deep convective clouds remain incompletely understood. Major challenges include the formation and growth of ice particles, the relative importance of warm-rain versus ice-phase precipitation pathways, the role of turbulence in enhancing collision rates, and the impact of different ice-nucleating processes (Morrison et al., 2020). Additional uncertainty arises from secondary ice production (SIP) mechanisms, such as rime splintering, freezing fragmentation, and collision-induced breakup (Field et al., 2017; Korolev and Leisner, 2020; Phillips et al., 2021). The complexity of these interacting processes, combined with the difficulty of obtaining reliable in situ observations within deep convective updrafts, helps explain why our understanding of cloud microphysics in deep convection remains limited.

The complexity of these interacting processes, combined with the difficulty of obtaining reliable in situ observations within deep convective updrafts, helps explain why our understanding of cloud microphysics in deep convection remains limited.

Numerical simulations provide an essential tool for testing our current process-level understanding. In particular, particle-based models that explicitly represent microphysical processes offer a way to evaluate whether our theoretical description is sufficient to reproduce key features of deep convective systems (Morrison et al., 2020). For example, can such models improve the representation of observed characteristics of a deep convective squall line? Do they require SIP to achieve realistic behavior, and can they provide observable signatures of fragmentation processes that help constrain the underlying mechanisms?

papers.title: Last-Iterate Convergence of Payoff-Gradient Learning in M\"obius Pricing Games
papers.abstract: We prove global last-iterate convergence of payoff-gradient learning in every typewise Riemannian metric, which for scalar actions is the same as typewise mirror descent, with explicit rates, in a class of Bayesian bidding and pricing games that includes first-price auctions, unit-demand pay-as-bid auctions, rank-based generalized first-price auctions, and homogeneous-good price competition with inelastic demand. The result holds for symmetric self-play: all players use a common strategy and apply the same payoff-gradient update at each type. Convergence is from every continuous weakly increasing feasible initial strategy, including pooling, and does not rely on the monotonicity or Minty conditions that underlie existing guarantees in other games. Instead, the class is characterized by two structural properties: a direct payoff effect that is independent of the action, and a payoff difference at the allocation threshold that is affine in the action. These properties reduce the learning dynamics to a singular transport-damping equation for the common strategy, which, under the stated coefficient and metric assumptions, admits a unique viscosity solution. Comparison barriers make the uniform distance to the unique rest point a strict Lyapunov functional and yield convergence rates with optimal algebraic exponents. In allocation games, the rest point is the unique weakly increasing symmetric equilibrium under the stated tie-breaking conditions, and a positive lower slope bound converts strategy-error bounds into explicit approximate-equilibrium guarantees. A projected grid scheme with a slope floor makes the approximation constructive, with error bounds under deterministic perturbations and almost-sure convergence on a fixed grid under martingale gradient noise.

papers.intro:
First-price auctions, procurement, and price competition are central models of price formation and resource allocation under private information. They share one strategic trade-off: a more aggressive bid or price raises the probability of receiving an allocation but lowers the surplus conditional on receiving it. Whether learning reaches equilibrium in these environments matters both for equilibrium computation and for the behavioral foundations of predictions about prices, revenues, and allocations.

First-price auctions, procurement, and price competition are central models of price formation and resource allocation under private information. They share one strategic trade-off: a more aggressive bid or price raises the probability of receiving an allocation but lowers the surplus conditional on receiving it. Whether learning reaches equilibrium in these environments matters both for equilibrium computation and for the behavioral foundations of predictions about prices, revenues, and allocations.

Numerical studies show that learning algorithms approximate Bayes–Nash equilibria with remarkable accuracy in a range of auction environments with continuous types and actions, including settings in which analytical equilibrium characterizations are difficult to obtain (Bichler et al., 2021; Bichler et al., 2025a). The theoretical explanation remains incomplete. The classical sufficient conditions for convergence of gradient methods, monotonicity of the game (Rosen, 1965) and Minty-type variational conditions (Minty, 1962; Mertikopoulos and Zhou, 2019; Cai et al., 2022), fail already in the first-price auction (Bichler et al., 2025c). papers.title: CLASP: Complementary Layer Selection and Profiling for Zero-Shot OOD Detection using Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) detection in medical imaging, yet existing approaches often rely on final-layer confidence or entropy-based layer selection, potentially missing complementary information. We show that low in-distribution (ID) confidence entropy does not reliably predict OOD discrimination. We introduce CLASP (Complementary Layer Selection and Profiling), an ID-only framework that jointly models layer--prompt responses and visual features. CLASP ranks visual encoder layers using Gaussian conditional mutual information and selects a compact subset through anchored spectral selection, without fixing the number of layers. It then combines the selected layer--prompt profiles with PCA-compressed visual embeddings and fits a single shrinkage-regularized Gaussian. OOD scores are computed using squared Mahalanobis distance, without fine-tuning, OOD training data, or test-time adaptation. Across histopathology, chest X-ray, and brain MRI benchmarks with UniMedCLIP and BioMedCLIP, CLASP performs strongly under varied distribution shifts. On MIDOG near-OOD, it achieves 87.54% AUROC with UniMedCLIP, outperforming confidence-based baselines; with BioMedCLIP, it remains competitive but trails visual-only Mahalanobis modeling. Ablations highlight the value of layer--prompt interactions and cross-feature dependencies, while exposing shift-dependent contributions and limitations under semantic shifts.

papers.intro:
Deep learning has demonstrated considerable potential in medical image analysis, including disease classification, segmentation, and computer-aided diagnosis. However, its reliability remains challenged by distribution shifts arising from variations in imaging devices, acquisition protocols, and patient populations. Such shifts can lead to unreliable predictions, even when models exhibit high confidence [30, 8]. Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection seeks to identify inputs that deviate from the in-distribution (ID) population before their predictions are used for clinical decision-making. Vision-language models (VLMs), particularly medical adaptations such as BioMedCLIP and UniMed-CLIP [32, 13], offer a promising direction by enabling zero-shot OOD detection through image–text alignment without requiring additional task-specific classifier training.

Existing VLM-based OOD detection methods typically rely on confidence scores derived from similarities between image representations and textual descriptions of known ID concepts. Maximum Concept Matching (MCM) [21], for instance, estimates confidence using the maximum softmax-normalized image–text similarity. While such approaches predominantly exploit final-layer representations, recent studies have investigated intermediate visual encoder layers and introduced entropy-guided strategies for selecting informative representations [20, 25]. However, their effectiveness can vary substantially across distribution shifts and VLM backbones, with approaches that perform well in one setting often deteriorating in another. These limitations raise three fundamental questions concerning how to select complementary visual layers, preserve their prompt-conditioned information, and jointly exploit visual and textual representations for OOD detection.

Maximum Concept Matching (MCM) [21], for instance, estimates confidence using the maximum softmax-normalized image–text similarity. While such approaches predominantly exploit final-layer representations, recent studies have investigated intermediate visual encoder layers and introduced entropy-guided strategies for selecting informative representations [20, 25]. However, their effectiveness can vary substantially across distribution shifts and VLM backbones, with approaches that perform well in one setting often deteriorating in another. These limitations raise three fundamental questions concerning how to select complementary visual layers, preserve their prompt-conditioned information, and jointly exploit visual and textual representations for OOD detection.

Q1: Can complementary visual layers be selected more effectively than through entropy minimization? Existing entropy-guided approaches favor layers exhibiting concentrated confidence-score distributions on unlabeled ID samples. However, low ID entropy does not necessarily imply strong discrimination against unseen OOD samples. As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), our analysis reveals only a weak association between ID histogram entropy and near-OOD detection performance across candidate layer subsets. Beyond identifying informative layers, determining how many layers to retain is equally important. Fig. 2 illustrates that the preferred number of layers differs across distribution shifts: incorporating additional layers improves near-OOD detection on MIDOG before performance largely stabilizes, whereas fewer layers are preferable for Chest X-ray semantic OOD. These observations motivate a complementarity-aware selection strategy that automatically determines a compact set of visual layers without relying on entropy minimization or a predefined layer budget.

Q2: Does scalar confidence aggregation discard useful layer–prompt information? Conventional confidence-based approaches reduce image–text similarities to a single score, potentially discarding individual responses to different textual descriptions. As illustrated in Fig. 1(b), two images can exhibit identical layer-wise maximum similarities despite substantially different layer–prompt response patterns. Such differences may contain information relevant to identifying distribution shifts that cannot be recovered from the maximum scores alone. This motivates preserving the structured image–text similarity responses, or layer–prompt profiling (LPP) across selected visual layers and ID textual prompts, rather than collapsing them into scalar confidence estimates.

Q3: Can visual and prompt-conditioned representations be jointly exploited for OOD detection? Vision-language models provide two complementary sources of information: visual embeddings encode image characteristics, while image–text similarities capture their alignment with predefined semantic descriptions. Although layer–prompt profiles preserve structured semantic responses, they may not fully capture visual variations that are weakly reflected in the available textual prompts. Conversely, visual embeddings alone do not explicitly represent the relationships between images and ID concepts. This motivates jointly modeling visual features and matched layer–prompt profiles, allowing both representation types to contribute to a unified OOD detection framework across heterogeneous distribution shifts.

Motivated by these observations, we propose CLASP (Complementary Layer Selection and Profiling), a zero-shot OOD detection framework built around three components. First, CLASP employs Gaussian conditional mutual information (CMI) to rank visual encoder layers according to their complementary information relative to an ID-fitted visual reference, followed by anchored spectral admission to automatically determine which layers to retain without a predefined layer budget. Second, the selected layers define a matched layer–prompt profile that preserves their individual image–text similarity responses. Third, CLASP combines this structured profile with compact visual representations from the same selected layers and models their joint distribution using a single multivariate Gaussian with Ledoit–Wolf shrinkage-regularized covariance, fitted exclusively on unlabeled in-distribution (ID) calibration images. During inference, squared Mahalanobis distance from the estimated ID distribution serves as the OOD anomaly score. CLASP requires no VLM fine-tuning, external OOD data, or test-time adaptation. Our main contributions are as follows: • We introduce a complementarity-aware layer-selection strategy that replaces entropy-guided ranking with Gaussian Visual CMI and employs anchored spectral admission to automatically determine a compact subset of visual encoder layers using only unlabeled ID data, without requiring a predefined layer budget. • We propose matched layer–prompt profiling, preserving the structured image–text similarity responses of selected layers instead of reducing them to scalar confidence estimates. Our analysis demonstrates that these response patterns retain information that maximum confidence aggregation discards. • We develop a unified visual–prompt OOD detector that jointly models matched layer–prompt profiles and compact visual representations using an ID-fitted Gaussian. Evaluations across histopathology, chest X-ray, and brain MRI benchmarks with two medical VLMs demonstrate competitive performance across heterogeneous shifts, while ablations and calibration stability experiments characterize the contributions and robustness of the framework.

papers.title: The dimension of optimal plans in multi-marginal optimal transport
papers.abstract: For general cost functions, we determine the maximal dimension on which solutions to the multi-marginal optimal transport problem with absolutely continuous marginals are concentrated. The dimension is obtained via a novel characteristic integer associated with the Hessian of the cost function. Applications are given to important examples of multi-marginal problems like Wasserstein barycenters, Wasserstein cubic splines and Brenier's generalized Euler equations.

The fact that the associated marginals are absolutely continuous relies on a non-obvious surjectivity property of the marginal projections of this kernel (see Proposition 4).

papers.title: Single-Shot Single-Stage Stellarators
papers.abstract: In stellarator design, the plasma and the coils are so geometrically complex that they are usually designed separately, so that a high-performance plasma may be impossible to reproduce with coils that can actually be manufactured and assembled. We present a new method to close this gap. In this framework, the plasma shape is optimized while, for every candidate shape, near-optimal coils that satisfy hard engineering limits are found. Without any manually-tuned weights, the method steers the plasma towards shapes that real coils can produce. Moreover, we demonstrate the first single-shot optimization runs starting from tokamak ``cold-starts''. From a single-shot cold-start, we design a finite-$\beta$ stellarator comparable to reactor-scaled NCSX, as well as a compact aspect-ratio 2.5 and $\langle\beta\rangle=2\%$ quasi-axisymmetric stellarator with one field period and self-consistent bootstrap current. Starting from a boundary derived from W7-X, we design a quasi-isodynamic stellarator with reactor-relevant stability properties. We then use this to warm-start an optimization for a single coil-set solution that produces a high-performance QI stellarator at every pressure value from vacuum to $\langle\beta\rangle=4\%$, addressing directly the ``start-up'' phase of a reactor. The self-consistent free-boundary solutions for these stellarators typically have better coils than a traditional separate-design approach, at comparable or better plasma performance, illustrating that robust single-stage methods are possible and providing a direct route to the design of reactor-scale stellarators.

papers.intro:
The stellarator, a toroidal magnetic confinement device, is a promising candidate for achieving controlled nuclear fusion [84, 44, 71, 39]. Unlike the tokamak, the stellarator relies on a three-dimensional magnetic field produced mostly by external coils, and therefore does not require large plasma currents that can lead to disruptions [14, 43, 82, 45]. This allows for steady-state operation, which is a clear advantage for a future power plant [43, 10]. However, this advantage does not come for free. A generic three-dimensional field does not confine the plasma well. Without the continuous symmetry of the tokamak, the orbits of trapped particles drift out of the plasma, which leads to large transport losses [44, 72] and to the loss of the energetic alpha particles born in deuterium–tritium (D–T) fusion reactions before they can heat the plasma [7, 2]. The confining field must be carefully shaped, and the coils that produce such a field, which are complicated three-dimensional curves, must also be shaped so that they can be built [85, 92, 97, 90].

Recent advances in stellarator optimization have shown that the magnetic field can be shaped with remarkable precision. Quasisymmetry (QS), a property of the field strength that confines collisionless trapped particles, can now be achieved to a very high degree across the plasma volume [65, 67]. Similarly, quasi-isodynamic (QI) configurations, in which the contours of the field strength close poloidally, are being pursued both in research and in industry because of their low bootstrap current and good fast-particle confinement [41, 23, 68]. These results are, however, obtained for the plasma alone. Whether a feasible set of coils can reproduce such a field is a separate question.
