Traditionally, stellarator design is subdivided into two stages. In stage I, the plasma boundary is optimized for physics properties by solving the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) equations of force balance in fixed boundary [49, 65]. In stage II, coils are found that reproduce this boundary [69, 66, 63]. This two-stage procedure has been used for essentially all stellarators built to date, including Wendelstein 7-X [24, 60], Wendelstein 7-AS [80], HSX [5, 3], LHD [53]. The two stages are coupled only through the target plasma boundary. A boundary that is excellent for the plasma properties may be hard to produce with coils of limited length, curvature and clearance, while small, physics-neutral changes of the boundary might make the coil problem much easier. Moreover, the coil problem is an ill-posed magnetostatic inverse problem, and most of its solutions are impractical from an engineering standpoint [54]. The consequences can be severe. Coil complexity and tight tolerances were responsible for most of the cost growth that led to the cancellation of NCSX, and for long delays in the construction of Wendelstein 7-X [86, 60, 15].

Robust joint optimization (single-stage) methods therefore have the capacity to dramatically improve stellarator design. Single-stage methods optimize the plasma boundary and the coils simultaneously. Historically, they have often required “warm-starts” (initializing from a plasma and associated coils that are already highly similar to the desired design point), heavy computation, and the assumption of vacuum stellarators [46, 36, 56, 57, 83, 33]. Single-stage optimization is increasingly used to design real experiments. The Columbia Stellarator eXperiment (CSX) and Electrons and Positrons in an Optimized Stellarator (EPOS) devices were designed with both the fixed-boundary and the Boozer-surface single-stage methods [37], with constraints on the strain of its superconducting tape [8, 9, 52, 34]. Moreover, for some of these methods, the coil degrees of freedom and the plasma boundary degrees of freedom are both optimized over a single cost function, in which the squared flux, the coil engineering penalties and the plasma targets are balanced by weights that are usually tuned by hand. As many as 15–20 such weights are typically used, and there is no a priori knowledge of their optimal values since the class of “good” weights often depend strongly on the particular plasma design. The constrained formulation of the coil problem with an augmented Lagrangian method automatically tunes these weights [32, 31], avoiding manual weight selection and tuning, and coil sets obtained in this way typically outperform published coils in both field accuracy and engineering metrics.

papers.title: Simulation and Rejection of Radon Progeny Backgrounds in nEXO
papers.abstract: Radon-induced backgrounds from $^{214}$Bi decays remain a significant challenge for liquid xenon (LXe) detectors searching for neutrinoless double beta decay ($0\nu\beta\beta$). We present a simulation-based study of the $^{214}$Bi background in nEXO, incorporating a physically motivated model of the transport and implantation of radon progeny into the detector cathode. We show that the spatial distribution of scintillation light provides an additional method for background discrimination for events surviving standard energy, event topology, and fiducial volume selections. A simple discriminator based on the scintillation light detected below the cathode rejects 41% of the remaining $^{214}$Bi backgrounds while retaining 95% of $0\nu\beta\beta$ signal events, and a convolutional neural network classifier improves this rejection to 57% at the same signal efficiency. An updated optical model provides a more accurate estimate of the light collection efficiency below the cathode than used in previous work, increasing the expected $^{214}$Bi-$^{214}$Po (Bi-Po) coincidence-tagging efficiency for bottom-surface $^{214}$Bi decays from less than 1% to approximately 50%. Together, these results demonstrate improved rejection of cathode-implanted $^{214}$Bi backgrounds in nEXO through complementary prompt scintillation-based discrimination and delayed coincidence tagging.

papers.title: SatMend: LLM Agents for Automated Software Repair in Satellite Constellations with Intermittent Ground Contact
papers.abstract: Satellite constellations rely on onboard software to sustain services across cooperating spacecraft. Maintaining this software requires handling related component versions and different failure causes while delivering repairs through intermittent ground contact. Automated software repair in satellite constellations remains underexplored, particularly the coordination of repairs across related versions with verified onboard recovery under intermittent ground contact. To address this gap, we propose SatMend, a software repair method driven by ground-based large language model (LLM) agents. SatMend organizes related versions into persistent sessions to retain diagnostic context and combines source and runtime evidence to select code repair or state recovery actions. It validates each version separately and submits ready candidates during continued repair, allowing ground preparation to overlap with onboard delivery and verification. Experimental results show that across configurations with 16 to 64 satellites, SatMend restores 192 of 224 faulty applications within 600 s, compared with 40 for SWE-agent, 77 for Agentless, 124 for RepairAgent, and 115 for SWE-Search. These results demonstrate SatMend's effectiveness in restoring applications and supporting service continuity in satellite constellations with intermittent ground contact.
papers.intro:
Low Earth orbit satellite constellations rely on onboard software for parameter management, file handling, and data forwarding. Software platforms support onboard data processing [1], while crosslinks enable data distribution among satellites [2]. Reliable software operation therefore supports both individual spacecraft functions and cooperation across a constellation. A component may be deployed on several satellites, with different versions remaining in operation as updates are introduced. A maintenance task can therefore involve multiple related software instances. Crosslinks also support coordinated maintenance: the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) has demonstrated file sharing, software updates, and verification through cooperation among satellites during the extended Starling mission [3]. In Fig. 1, the ground maintenance center sends software updates or commands to restore application state through a gateway satellite. The targets execute these actions and undergo functional checks to confirm application recovery, supporting service continuity across the constellation.

Maintaining these instances requires accounting for both software differences and communication conditions. Versions of the same component share functional context and diagnostic clues, but faults may lie in code, runtime state, or configuration. Telemetry can reveal abnormal behavior [4, 5], but the appropriate recovery action must still be established for each version. Evidence collection and delivery across targets also share intermittent ground contact, while a failed gateway forwarding application may block downstream maintenance. Analysis and testing based on information already available on the ground can continue during disconnection; new target observations, transfers, and acknowledgments depend on contact opportunities. Even after a candidate repair is ready, it must still be transferred, activated, and checked at each target. Its readiness time affects which delivery opportunities remain available. Recovery by a maintenance deadline thus depends on coordinating repair preparation across related versions with contact availability and target execution.

papers.title: OAT3D: A Generative Model for 3D Shape- and Resolution-Free Structural Topology Optimization
papers.abstract: Topology optimization determines how material should be distributed within a design domain to optimize structural performance under prescribed loads, supports, and constraints. The problems are highly nonconvex, and conventional solvers require repeated finite element analyses, making high-resolution 3D topology optimization computationally expensive. Data-driven approaches face an additional bottleneck: generating training datasets requires solving large numbers of these costly problems, so existing work in data-driven topology optimization primarily focuses on 2D problems. Large-scale 3D datasets remain scarce, and existing models remain limited in problem scale and boundary-condition diversity. Here, we introduce Optimize Any Topology-3D (OAT3D), a generative model for high-resolution 3D structural topology optimization. OAT3D introduces a novel sparse problem encoding to represent load and fixity conditions and combines a sparse volumetric variational autoencoder with a conditional diffusion transformer. We construct a dataset of 501,865 optimized topologies, generated using 51,800 GPU-hours and encompassing structures with up to one million elements and substantially more complex loading and support configurations than any existing structural topology optimization dataset. To our knowledge, this is the largest dataset for 3D topology optimization structures. Trained on this dataset, OAT3D generates structures at 512$^3$ resolution and achieves a $44.9\times$ speedup for raw candidate structure generation or $3.65\times$ speedup to reach similar compliance over conventional topology optimization. These contributions expand the scale and diversity of data-driven topology optimization for three-dimensional structural design.

papers.intro:
Topology optimization is a physics-based approach to engineering design that determines how material should be distributed within a prescribed domain to optimize for structural performance objectives, with applications in aerospace engineering (Zhu et al., 2016), civil engineering (Baandrup et al., 2020), biomedical engineering (Sutradhar et al., 2010), and beyond. Rather than only adjusting the dimensions or boundaries of a predefined layout, topology optimization allows the arrangement and connectivity of material to change, so that structural members and internal voids emerge through optimization (Bendsøe & Kikuchi, 1988; Bendsøe et al., 2004). A common formulation minimizes compliance, seeking a stiff material layout under prescribed loads and fixities for a given material-volume budget. Density-based methods enable gradient-based optimization (Sigmund, 2001; Bendsøe et al., 2004). The design is obtained through an iterative coupling between optimization and physical simulation, which can become computationally demanding as the resolution increases, especially in the three-dimensional setting. Furthermore, full optimization must be rerun for every new loading or fixity configuration.

To reduce the cost of solving many distinct design problems, pretrained models learn to predict material layouts from problem conditions rather than running the full iterative topology optimization procedure (Yu et al., 2019; Nie et al., 2021; Giannone et al., 2023; Lutheran et al., 2025). However, these predictors are largely tied to a fixed discretization. Most 3D models are trained on one or a few grid sizes and aspect ratios (Table 1), so a new domain shape or resolution requires retraining a new model with a different size input. This motivates a large-scale generative model that is shape- and resolution-free: a single model, trained on a broad collection of optimized structures, that designs across varied domains, resolutions, and boundary conditions. Since the model must produce topologies that satisfy mechanical constraints, a generative model for optimal structural design requires coupling geometric representation and mechanical conditions. Such a model requires vast training examples that capture material distribution variability across problem specifications, but obtaining a diverse collection of data requires repeatedly solving large linear systems, which limits availability of training data.

OAT3D generates designs for any rectangular domain and resolution that fits within the grid, which is what we mean by shape- and resolution-free. Lastly, we show that the pretrained model can be reused without retraining for downstream design tasks such as joint-count control and lattice replacement.

Our contributions are as follows: • Largest dataset of topology optimized 3D structures. Our dataset contains 501,865 voxelized structures optimized for minimum compliance (maximum stiffness) with randomized mechanical (load and fixity) conditions, prescribed volume fractions from 0.05 to 0.30, and native meshes containing up to approximately one million elements. • Largest generative model for 3D minimum-compliance topology optimization. We develop a conditional generative framework at 5123512^{3} resolution with direct density field tailored to structural design problems. As far as we are aware, this is the largest generative model for three-dimensional minimum-compliance structural topology optimization benefiting from an enormous dataset and recent advances in three-dimensional shape generation. • Guided generation with spatial encoding of mechanical information. Combined load, support, and BNG field embeddings supply both generation stages with spatial and mechanical information as guidance.

papers.title: Fully solid-state all-2D micro-supercapacitors for on-chip energy storage
papers.abstract: Integrating energy storage directly into microelectronic platforms remains a major challenge. Although solid-state micro-supercapacitors (MSCs) have been previously demonstrated, most still rely on liquid or solvent-containing gel electrolytes, which require additional encapsulation and complicate device integration. Here, we demonstrate wafer-scale fabrication of all-2D, fully solid-state MSCs by combining conductive Ti3C2Tz MXene electrodes with a natural vermiculite (VMT) clay solid electrolyte. Both materials are solution-processable and can be independently patterned using microelectronics compatible fabrication techniques, allowing for their integration across 4-inch Si/SiO2 wafers. The resulting devices showcase an active stack of only 28 nm thick, with an areal capacitance of 205 uF/cm2 and volumetric energy density of ~15.5 mWh/cm3. Notably, this work introduces a patterned 2D clay as a solid electrolyte in an on-chip electrochemical energy-storage device, extending the role of layered materials beyond electrodes to ion-conducting components. To investigate device behavior and degradation, we employ non-destructive imaging ellipsometry to map individual layer thicknesses and extract the spatial distribution of MXene conductivity across the chip. This approach reveals localized changes in electrode properties following prolonged electrochemical cycling, providing insight into degradation processes that are difficult to capture using conventional spatially averaged measurements. Together, these results establish a route towards fully solid-state, all-2D energy-storage devices and highlight the potential of solution-processable layered materials for integration into microelectronic systems.

papers.title: Discovery of Two Hyperluminous Infrared Galaxies at $z\sim6$
papers.abstract: Hyperluminous infrared galaxies (HyLIRGs) at cosmic dawn are key to understanding the formation of the first massive galaxies. We report the spectroscopic confirmation of two unlensed HyLIRGs at $z\sim6$ in the COSMOS field, AzTECC63 and S2COS-84, originally selected from single-dish AzTEC and SCUBA-2 surveys. Using ALMA and NOEMA observations, we robustly detected CO and [CII] lines in both galaxies and unambiguously confirmed their redshifts to be $z=6.092$ and $z=5.90$, respectively. Panchromatic SED fitting reveals dust-obscured star formation rates of $\approx1000$ and $\approx2300\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$, ranking them among the most intensely star-forming systems known at $z \gtrsim 6$. High-resolution ALMA observations reveal an extremely compact morphology for S2COS-84, with a dust-continuum effective radius of $\approx0.3$ kpc, implying a star-formation rate surface density above the Eddington limit. The far-infrared SEDs of both galaxies, together with the compact size of S2COS-84, indicate warm dust ($T_{\rm dust} \approx 80$ K) that is likely optically thick at far-infrared wavelengths. Both galaxies exhibit an extreme [CII] deficit, with $L_{\rm [C\,II]}/L_{\rm IR} \approx 10^{-3.7}$, an order of magnitude below that of normal star-forming galaxies. Their molecular gas masses, derived consistently from both [C\,{\sc ii}] and dust, together with their IR-derived SFRs imply short gas depletion times of $\approx$40--60 Myr, making them plausible progenitors of the earliest massive quiescent galaxies found at $z\sim5$.

papers.intro:
Hyperluminous infrared galaxies (HyLIRGs) are the most extreme star-forming systems in the Universe, defined by total infrared luminosities (rest-frame 8–1000 μ\mum) of LIR≥1013​L⊙L_{\rm IR}\geq 10^{13}\,L_{\odot}, an order of magnitude above ultraluminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs; LIR≥1012​L⊙L_{\rm IR}\geq 10^{12}\,L_{\odot}; Sanders and Mirabel 1996; Rowan-Robinson 2000). These luminosities imply vigorous dust-obscured star formation rates (SFRs) above 1000​M⊙​yr−11000\penalty\ M_{\odot}\penalty\ {\rm yr}^{-1} (Kennicutt, 1998). At such rates a galaxy can assemble ∼\sim1011​M⊙10^{11}\,M_{\odot} of stars in only ∼\sim100 Myr. The prototype, IRAS F10214+4724 at z=2.29z=2.29, was identified in the IRAS survey (Rowan-Robinson et al., 1991). Since then, wide-area far-infrared and (sub)millimeter surveys with Herschel, the South Pole Telescope (SPT), and ground-based single-dish facilities have found HyLIRGs mostly at z∼1z\sim 1–4 (Ivison et al., 2019; Berman et al., 2022; Kamieneski et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024, e.g.,), forming the bright tail of the population of dusty star-forming galaxies (Casey et al., 2014, DSFGs; see a review by).

HyLIRGs play a central role in our understanding of how the most massive galaxies form. Their intense, short-lived, dust-enshrouded starbursts make them the leading candidate progenitors of the compact quiescent galaxies seen at z∼2z\sim 2–3 and, eventually, of the massive elliptical galaxies that dominate the centers of present-day galaxy clusters (Toft et al., 2014, e.g.,). HyLIRGs often reside in overdense environments and frequently show signs of major mergers or host obscured active galactic nuclei (Daddi et al., 2009; Capak et al., 2011; Engel et al., 2010; Rowan-Robinson, 2000; Ruiz et al., 2007, AGN; e.g.,). This makes them natural laboratories for studying the joint growth of stellar bulges and supermassive black holes, and the early assembly of protoclusters (Miller et al., 2018; Oteo et al., 2018). JWST has made this connection more pressing by revealing a high abundance of massive quiescent galaxies at z≳3z\gtrsim 3–5 whose stellar populations imply formation epochs at z≳6z\gtrsim 6–10 (Carnall et al., 2023a; Carnall et al., 2023b; Glazebrook et al., 2024; de Graaff et al., 2025; Baker et al., 2025; Sillassen et al., 2026, e.g.,). Explaining these objects requires a population of extremely vigorous starbursts within the first billion years of cosmic history, which is precisely the regime in which HyLIRGs are expected to operate.

Advanced (sub)millimeter interferometers such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) have spectroscopically confirmed distant DSFGs at z>5z>5 and out to the epoch of reionization (Walter et al., 2012; Vieira et al., 2010; Vieira et al., 2013; Riechers et al., 2013; Riechers et al., 2017; Strandet et al., 2017; Zavala et al., 2018; Marrone et al., 2018; Endsley et al., 2022; Fudamoto et al., 2021; Hygate et al., 2023; Rowland et al., 2024, EoR, z∼7z\sim 7; e.g.,), proving these facilities to be powerful “redshift machines” (Vieira et al., 2013; Neri et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022; Cox et al., 2023). Despite this, HyLIRGs at z≳5z\gtrsim 5 remain extremely rare. Only a handful of dusty starbursts with LIR≳1013​L⊙L_{\rm IR}\gtrsim 10^{13}\,L_{\odot} have been confirmed at z≳5z\gtrsim 5, and several of them are gravitationally lensed: for example, the z∼5.3z\sim 5.3–5.7 sources AzTEC-3, GN10, and CRLE (Capak et al., 2011; Riechers et al., 2020; Pavesi et al., 2018), the moderately lensed HFLS3 at z=6.34z=6.34 (Riechers et al., 2013), and the strongly lensed SPT0311−-58 at z=6.90z=6.90 (Strandet et al., 2017; Marrone et al., 2018). Comparably luminous FIR emission is also seen in the host galaxies of some z∼6z\sim 6 quasars (Bertoldi et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2013; Decarli et al., 2018, e.g.,), although the contribution of AGN heating is uncertain. The known HyLIRGs at z∼6z\sim 6 already strain theoretical expectations. Galaxy formation models struggle to reproduce the abundance of the brightest DSFGs only ∼1\sim 1 Gyr after the Big Bang, and their large dust masses challenge models of dust production (Hayward et al., 2013; Michałowski, 2015; Wilkins et al., 2018; Vijayan et al., 2022, e.g.,). Each new z∼6z\sim 6 HyLIRG therefore provides a valuable constraint on the formation pathways of the earliest massive galaxies.

papers.title: Hashing Theorems Modulo Rewrites and Binder Permutation Enables Equivalence Search over 200k Mathlib Theorems
papers.abstract: Like all code, Lean libraries accumulate technical debt and structural deficiencies over the course of their development. A particular concern is duplicate theorems: different parts of a big library can unwittingly contain and prove the same theorem, duplicating maintenance efforts. Tools can help detect redundancy and clean up. For instance, Mathlib's duplicate-declarations linter compares theorem types syntactically after sorting top-level binders and erasing binder information and universe levels. If detecting an equivalence requires unfolding, reorientation, or logical transformations, it escapes this comparison. In this work, we present a method to detect theorems which are equivalent with regard to argument order and currying/uncurrying of dependent types. We implement our method for Lean. By applying it to Mathlib, a library of more than 200k theorems, we demonstrate that it is computationally cheap and scalable. We discuss how our work may enhance efforts to tackle the maintenance burden of Lean libraries.

As Lean grows in popularity, the amount of Lean code significantly increases. Consider Mathlib, which has grown to over 2.2 million lines of Lean. At that size, deprecation and technical debt become central risks to continued library development [3, 21]. Tooling for code maintenance becomes critical. This issue is exacerbated with AI, which enables newer Lean projects to get even bigger even faster, e.g. Anthropic’s formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem (13 million lines) [1, 2] or OpenAI’s Lean certificates for finite-time blow-up of the Navier–Stokes and Euler equations (641,000 lines) [15, 16].

papers.title: TASC: Time-to-Collision Anticipation and Selective Crowd Attention for Non-Holonomic Service Robots
papers.abstract: Service robots that share corridors and lobbies with people must keep moving without endangering them. Reactive planners can stop indefinitely in dense crowds (the freezing robot problem), whereas the attention-based learned navigators that dominate the standard crowd benchmark assume holonomic motion or emit discrete actions unsuited to a differential-drive base. This paper presents TASC, a navigation system for a non-holonomic service robot that integrates an attention-based crowd encoder, an anticipatory collision feature, and a continuous-control policy. We adapt the dual-selection attention module, originally developed for discrete-action value learning, to proximal policy optimization for continuous velocity control, and add a closing-speed time-to-collision feature, a conservative estimate of the time to contact that serves as both an observation and a reward term. The policy is trained on a high-fidelity 3D robot model in NVIDIA Isaac Lab with 10,000 parallel environments, social-force-model pedestrians, and randomized crowd sizes. In 30,000 evaluation episodes, each run to its end, the policy timed out in fewer than 0.5% at every tested crowd density. This liveness comes at a cost: pedestrian collisions rise from 4.5% with five pedestrians to 17.4% with ten. In an ablation with four seeds per variant, policies retrained without the time-to-collision feature succeed 4 to 7 percentage points less often. The policy runs in Gazebo without retraining and on a commercial differential-drive service robot through a ROS 2 package with an inference latency below 10 ms, verified in a hardware-in-the-loop test with virtual pedestrians.
papers.intro:
Service robots are moving out of structured industrial cells and into airports, hospitals, shopping centers, and offices. There, a robot shares the floor with people who neither coordinate with it nor stand still, and navigation becomes a prerequisite for deployment: the robot must reach its goal safely and predictably, without making the people around it uncomfortable.

Service robots are moving out of structured industrial cells and into airports, hospitals, shopping centers, and offices. There, a robot shares the floor with people who neither coordinate with it nor stand still, and navigation becomes a prerequisite for deployment: the robot must reach its goal safely and predictably, without making the people around it uncomfortable.

Classical planners handle this setting poorly because they treat people as moving obstacles, not as agents who react to the robot. In dense crowds, the result is unnecessary detours or a complete stop, known as the freezing robot problem [2]. Deep reinforcement learning instead learns interaction behavior directly, without a map [3], and recent architectures encode the relations between agents with graph networks and attention [4, 5, 6].

Two practical gaps separate this line of work from a deployable platform. First, the attention- and graph-based policies of the standard crowd benchmark [4, 5] are trained for a holonomic disk, whereas a service robot usually has a differential-drive base. Second, the methods that model a unicycle either select from a discrete action set [7, 6], which produces a jerky velocity profile, or output continuous commands [8, 9] but do not select among pedestrians. Non-holonomic kinematics, continuous commands, and hardware deployment each exist in prior work, but not together with selective attention (Section II-D). This paper addresses that combination as a system-integration problem rather than as an isolated algorithm. The target platform is MiPA (My Intelligent Personal Assistant), a commercial differential-drive service robot from NEURA Robotics [10]. We refer to the integrated system as TASC (Time-to-collision Anticipation and Selective Crowd attention).

papers.title: DeclareViT: Decoupling Early Classification from Feature Refinement with Exit Query for Efficient ViTs
papers.abstract: Vision Transformers achieve remarkable recognition performance but incur substantial computational cost during inference, limiting their use in latency- and compute-constrained deployment scenarios. Early-exit inference offers a promising solution by allowing easy samples to terminate at intermediate layers. However, existing approaches typically couple early classification with the shared backbone, requiring intermediate representations to support both early classification and subsequent feature refinement. Under joint training, the corresponding optimization objectives jointly update shared backbone parameters, which can lead to conflicting gradient directions. Motivated by this observation, we introduce DeclareViT, a framework that decouples early classification from feature refinement. Each exit uses a dedicated query to read intermediate features through one-way cross-attention without modifying the backbone token stream. The query branches are optimized for early classification while the backbone and final classifier remain frozen. Across ViT, DeiT, and Swin on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, and Food-101, DeclareViT consistently establishes a state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-off: It achieves 1.58 times to 2.57 times multiply-accumulate (MAC)-based speed-up with only a 0.39-1.91 percentage-point accuracy drop. Wall-clock measurements on CPU and GPU further demonstrate practical inference acceleration. Code is available at https://github.com/TUDa-HWAI/DeclareViT.

papers.title: Multiphase Gas in the Ram-Pressure-Stripped Elliptical Galaxy NGC 1404
papers.abstract: Galaxy groups and low-mass galaxy clusters are major sites of environment-driven galaxy evolution. NGC 1404 is an X-ray-bright early-type galaxy traveling through the intracluster medium of the nearby low-mass Fornax Cluster, and it hosts off-center warm ionized gas. With minimal ongoing stellar feedback and negligible active galactic nucleus feedback, NGC 1404 provides an ideal laboratory for constraining the impact of environmental processes on the thermodynamics of the interstellar medium. We analyzed VLT/MUSE, 506 ks Chandra ACIS, and 119 ks XMM-Newton RGS observations to quantify gas motions in both the hot and warm phases of NGC 1404. We probed the kinematics of the warm gas by deriving the velocity structure function (VSF) from MUSE H$\alpha$ integral-field spectroscopy. To measure the kinematics of the hot gas, we derived the power spectrum of X-ray surface brightness fluctuations from the Chandra data, and independently constrained galaxy-scale hot gas motions by measuring Fe XVII resonant scattering and turbulent line broadening with RGS. Our RGS spectral analysis gives a three-dimensional Mach number of $0.48^{+0.22}_{-0.14}$, consistent with the power-spectrum results from Chandra for the same extraction region, and corresponding to a turbulent-to-thermal energy density ratio of $\sim0.13$. The warm-gas VSF follows the expectation for Kolmogorov turbulence and is broadly consistent with the hot-gas kinematics. The off-center warm gas in NGC 1404 may have formed through radiative cooling of the hot interstellar medium, triggered by the uplift of low-entropy hot gas during ram pressure stripping. Our study suggests that ram pressure stripping can drive substantial gas motions and reshape the thermodynamic state of the interstellar medium of cluster member galaxies.

papers.intro:
A galaxy’s environment has long been recognized as a key factor in driving its evolution (Blanton and Moustakas, 2009), particularly for those residing in groups and clusters (Su et al., 2014; Jain et al., 2025). In addition to inhabiting regions of enhanced galaxy density, member galaxies move through the intracluster or intragroup medium (ICM/IGrM) – a diffuse, X-ray-emitting, ionized plasma. One of the most prominent environmental processes is ram pressure stripping (RPS), in which the drag exerted by the ambient ICM removes gas from a galaxy as it moves through it (Gunn and Gott III, 1972), effectively displacing its interstellar medium (ISM). Observationally, this process is often characterized by a stripped tail extending downstream and, particularly for early-type galaxies (ETGs), a cold front that marks the boundary between the galaxy’s cooler, denser ISM and the surrounding hotter ICM. Such features have been widely used to probe the microphysics of the ICM/IGrM over a broad dynamical range, including viscosity and magnetic fields, which are important for using galaxy clusters as cosmological probes (Su et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2025). Meanwhile, infall and stripping processes can significantly modify the galaxy properties, including driving turbulence in the ISM of member galaxies.

A large fraction of the galaxies found in groups and clusters are ETGs, whose ISM is dominated by hot, X-ray-emitting gas. In addition, some of them harbor substantial multiphase gas reservoirs including warm ionized (Heckman et al., 1989; Hatch et al., 2007; Werner et al., 2014; Tremblay et al., 2018; Olivares et al., 2019) and molecular gas (Edge, 2001; Salome and Combes, 2003; Lim and Ao, 2008). The origin and kinematics of the multiphase gas in ETGs have been studied extensively in the context of mechanical feedback from central supermassive black holes (SMBHs), particularly in brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) (Fabian et al., 2003; Li and Bryan, 2014; Russell et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020; Olivares et al., 2019). One origin of the cooler gas may be radiative cooling and condensation of the hot atmosphere, potentially through thermal instabilities (Field, 1965; Balbus, 1986). In a stably stratified atmosphere, buoyant motions can oppose the nonlinear development of condensates, motivating comparisons between the cooling and dynamical timescales of the gas to probe the conditions favorable for multiphase condensation (McCourt et al., 2012; Sharma et al., 2012; Voit et al., 2017).

VLT/MUSE features broad spectral coverage with superb spectral and spatial resolution and a large field of view, enabling detailed and robust studies of warm ionized gas, which are not achievable with previous IFU surveys, e.g., SAURON (Bacon et al., 2001), CALIFA (Sánchez et al., 2012; Walcher et al., 2014), SAMI (Croom et al., 2012; Bryant et al., 2015), and MaNGA (Bundy et al., 2014). A few filamentary systems, however, exhibit off-center warm nebulae, with no emission-line gas detected at the galaxy centers. The diverse morphology of warm nebulae in non-BCG ETGs may reflect multiple channels for multiphase gas formation in them.

papers.title: ReqSeek: Transformer-Based Automatic Requirements Identification for Building Large Requirements Datasets
papers.abstract: Large, diverse, and high-quality datasets are significant for advancing AI in requirements engineering, yet automated identification of requirements from Software Requirement Specifications (SRS) remains a challenge. Automatic Requirements Identification (ARI) methods demonstrate limited generalization to unseen documents across heterogeneous SRSs. This work presents ReqSeek, a transformer-based, domain-agnostic ARI model for recognizing ISO 29148-style requirements in SRS documents, supporting dataset construction. We curated the Automatic Requirements Identification Dataset (ARID), comprising 2,396 training instances from 23 heterogeneous SRSs, and fine-tuned four transformer architectures. RoBERTa was selected as the base model for ReqSeek and achieved 95% precision, recall, F1, and F0.89 on the held-out evaluation set. Exploratory human-model benchmarking showed performance comparable to humans while requiring substantially less prediction time than manual annotation. Post-hoc evaluation on out-of-domain (OoD) SRSs provided evidence of requirement identification beyond ARID. Robustness analysis demonstrated ReqSeek's insensitivity to minor linguistic variations while maintaining sensitivity to major ISO 29148-style violations. We applied ReqSeek to construct the Software Requirements Dataset (SwaRD), identifying 10,201 ISO 29148-style requirements from 231 industrial SRSs. SwaRD aligns with textual and semantic properties of human-curated datasets while exceeding them in scale and domain diversity. Our results suggest that transformer-based ARI can provide precise and generalizable requirements identification.

papers.intro:
The lack of large-scale datasets for advancing requirements engineering research is a commonly highlighted problem (Ferrari et al., 2017; Alhoshan et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024; Zarour et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2023). This limitation is not due to the unavailability of Software Requirements Specifications (SRS), but rather to the difficulty of extracting requirements from them (Li et al., 2024; Izhar et al., 2025). This challenge stems from the complexity of SRS documents (Falkner et al., 2019), which are often non-machine-readable and intermix requirements with supplementary descriptions. As a result, requirement identification is practical only for a limited number of documents when performed manually. Consequently, assembling a requirements dataset from multiple SRS documents with diverse formats is highly time-consuming and labor-intensive, particularly when requirements content must be precisely separated from non-requirements to preserve dataset quality. Addressing this gap is therefore imperative.

This emphasis on ISO 29148-style requirements builds on existing ARI research (Falkner et al., 2019; Abualhaija et al., 2019; Ivanov et al., 2022). ISO 29148 provides syntactic and semantic guidance for writing explicit, verifiable system obligations or provisions, making ISO 29148-style requirements practically important for requirements specification, verification, and traceability (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, 2018). Prior ARI studies have commonly operationalized the identification of ISO 29148-style requirements as binary classification, distinguishing binding (1) requirements from (2) auxiliary content such as explanations, examples, or references (Winkler and Vogelsang, 2016). These studies applied ARI to support downstream activities such as minimizing oversight risk (Falkner et al., 2019), facilitating risk assessments (Bashir et al., 2023; Winkler and Vogelsang, 2016), and enabling traceability and validation for software reuse (Hayes et al., 2014; Abualhaija et al., 2019). Thus, ISO 29148-style requirements provide a well-established and practically relevant target for studying ARI across projects and domains.

Thus, ISO 29148-style requirements provide a well-established and practically relevant target for studying ARI across projects and domains.

Building on this view of ARI, we investigate whether requirements can be precisely distinguished from auxiliary content across heterogeneous SRS documents to support the automatic construction of requirements datasets. While binary ARI supports scalable extraction of requirements from SRSs, we propose a ternary formulation that further divides auxiliary content into two subcategories: (2.1) system-related auxiliary content, which encompasses algorithms, architecture, or design, and (2.2) contextual auxiliary content, which provides background information. This more fine-grained formulation captures richer distinctions within auxiliary content, thereby supporting the construction of more informative requirements datasets for downstream AI tasks.

papers.title: py4radiation: a framework for generating heating/cooling functions and ion fractions from custom radiation fields for astrophysical simulations
papers.abstract: Modelling multiphase gas in and around galaxies is key to understanding the baryon cycle in galaxy evolution. Modern simulation codes rely on heating/cooling functions and ion fractions to capture the thermodynamics and chemistry of such gases, but coupling all physical factors remains challenging. We present a new Python-based, parallelised package that acts as an integration framework, connecting well-established astrophysical codes and models to produce self-consistent heating/cooling functions and ion fractions from custom ionising UV/X-ray backgrounds. The package returns multi-dimensional tables that can be readily coupled to hydrodynamic and post-processing codes to study radiative processes and extract observables, as we demonstrate with static cloud simulations. Our simulation suite studies the thermodynamic history of a static circumgalactic cloud with smoothed edges subjected to meta-galactic and starburst heating. We find that the clouds experience damped pulsations regulated by strong cooling-driven inflows and heating-driven outflows that constantly overshoot pressure equilibrium. Meta-galactic heating is weak and produces a confined and dense cloud, while starburst heating is strong and sustains large clouds only a little smaller than those obtained with the standard $10^4\,\rm K$ cooling floor. Starburst radiative heating acts as a damping agent, thereby reducing mixing. py4radiation comes with extensive documentation and a sample catalogue of heating/cooling functions and ion tables for a selected set of input meta-galactic and starburst spectral energy distributions. The code is publicly available and can be easily expanded.

papers.intro:
Studying the role of UV/X-ray radiation fields on interstellar and circumgalactic media is key to understanding the cycle of matter and energy in galaxies (Haardt and Madau, 2012; Tumlinson et al., 2017; Faucher-Giguère and Oh, 2023; Wiersma et al., 2009). Feedback processes, either from starbursts (SB) or active galactic nuclei (AGN), result in the formation of large-scale galactic winds, which transport gas, dust, and metals from the interstellar medium (ISM) out to the circumgalactic (CGM) and intergalactic media (IGM) (Veilleux et al., 2005; Veilleux et al., 2020). The detailed physics and chemistry of the multi-phase, outflowing gas as well as the metal ion populations are regulated by several processes, such as the mechanical launching of the wind itself via energy and momentum inputs from SB and AGNs (Chevalier and Clegg, 1985; Veilleux et al., 2005; Faucher-Giguère and Quataert, 2012), the mass loading and entrainment efficiencies of cold gas and dust into the hot flow (Gronke and Oh, 2018; Chen and Oh, 2024), the generation of turbulence (Fielding et al., 2020), the thermal balance regulated by radiative processes (both heating and cooling) (Banda-Barragán et al., 2021; Faucher-Giguère and Oh, 2023; Antipov et al., 2025), and the magnetic stresses exerted by global magnetic fields (Banda-Barragán et al., 2018; Hidalgo-Pineda et al., 2024; Casavecchia et al., 2024). Micro-physical processes also play an important role, such as cold-cloud coagulation (Gronke and Oh, 2023), shattering (Sparre et al., 2019), thermal conduction (Brüggen and Scannapieco, 2016), self-gravity (Li et al., 2020), and hydrodynamic shielding of dense gas (Forbes and Lin, 2019; Villares et al., 2024).

Among the above, radiative processes are of particular interest as they control the thermodynamic state of the gas, both at the wind launching site in the ISM and at several distances along the CGM and IGM of the host galaxies (Wiersma et al., 2009; Oppenheimer and Schaye, 2013; Di Federico et al., 2026). Naturally, UV radiation fields are stronger close to their sources (either AGNs or SBs) and weaker farther away, so the conditions of gas in close proximity to the ionising sources are different from those experienced by gas far away from the sources (Haardt and Madau, 2012; Zhu and Springel, 2024). In this paper, we focus our attention on SB feedback processes regulated by star formation. In such cases, the gas metallicity, the evolutionary stage of the SB (its age), and the initial mass function (IMF) can also play a significant role in determining the shape and strength of the resulting SB UV field (Leitherer et al., 1999). To account for the physical properties of the central SB, its age, and the gas metallicity, it is essential to compute heating and cooling rates as well as ion fractions in a self-consistent manner, i.e. by considering suitable spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of the central SB as well as appropriately calculated flux densities at different distances from the SB source. Such a treatment is relevant not only for accurately modelling the thermodynamic and ionisation structure of multiphase gas, but also for predicting synthetic observables, such as emission- and absorption-line signatures (de la Cruz et al., 2021; Casavecchia et al., 2024; Villarruel et al., 2026), that can be compared with observations of galactic outflows at different redshifts (McClure-Griffiths et al., 2013; Sugahara et al., 2019).

Several astrophysical packages have been developed throughout the years to model the physics and chemistry of gas near ionising sources. In particular, Starburst99 (Sb99; Leitherer et al. 1999) and Cloudy (Ferland et al., 2013) can be used in tandem to produce self-consistent ion fractions and radiative heating and cooling rates. On the one hand, Sb99 has been extensively used to compute the SEDs associated with SB feedback processes. Sb99 takes the IMF, the gas metallicity, and SB conditions (instantaneous or continuous SF models) to calculate the distribution of SB luminosity as a function of wavelength and SB age. On the other hand, the Cloudy code allows users to synthesise the detailed chemistry, ion fractions, and radiative heating and cooling rates of plasmas subjected to different photo-ionising UV fields. Thus, the appropriately normalised and distance-adjusted UV flux densities from Sb99 can be used as inputs for the Cloudy code. Unfortunately, publicly available and user-friendly pipelines to combine both tools are scarce in the literature, with the Perl-based CIAOLoop11 1 https://github.com/brittonsmith/cloudy_cooling_tools code (Smith et al., 2008) being a notable exception.

It aims to facilitate the generation of heating and cooling coefficients together with ion fraction tables, consistent with input meta-galactic UV/X-ray or SB UV radiation fields. The details of the Python code are presented in section 2, usage examples as well as sample radiative heating/cooling coefficients and ion fractions can be found in sections 3 and 4. Lastly, we discuss the limitations and future code development in section 5. Jointly with the code, we also release a sample catalogue of tabulated heating/cooling rates and ion fractions for a sample set of meta-galactic and SB conditions, which can be directly downloaded by users.

papers.title: A Tributary of Tucana III? The Sutlej Stellar Stream in DELVE DR3
papers.abstract: We present the first analysis of the Sutlej stellar stream using deep DECam photometry from the third data release of the DECam Local Volume Exploration Survey (DELVE DR3). Sutlej was discovered in Gaia DR3 as two parallel branches of old, metal-poor stars in projection near the SMC. Our DELVE DR3 sample reaches $\sim$2.5-3.5 mag below the main-sequence turnoff of Sutlej, and with a main-sequence matched filter built from an isochrone fit to Sutlej, we recover both previously identified branches, and find additional structure between them and at the periphery of the stream, occupying a region of $\sim$11$^\circ$ $\times$ 7$^\circ$ scattered at $\sim$23-33 kpc. We investigate this region by separating it into four segments that have Sutlej-like properties. The isochrone is also consistent with the nearby ultra-faint satellite Tucana III (Tuc III), and the two systems have similar distances and proper motions. $N$-body simulations of a Tuc III-like satellite show that, once the passage of a massive LMC is accounted for, Tuc III's preceding pericentric passage was deep enough to strip most of the progenitor. The encounter with the LMC then spreads the debris across the Sutlej field at the observed distances and proper motions, though the models do not recreate the observed discrete overdensities. We find that Sutlej is compatible with a Tuc III origin.

papers.intro:
Few tracers map the Milky Way’s dark matter as directly as stellar streams, the tidal debris stripped from dwarf galaxies and globular clusters [17, e.g.,]. Streams trace the Galactic potential along their orbits, and can be used to constrain the mass and shape of the dark matter halo [56, 60, 61, 44, 19, 18, 16]. Many streams are thin and dynamically cold, and are thus sensitive to small-scale perturbations. A close passage by a dark matter subhalo can leave a gap, create a spur, or modulate the density along a stream [53, 55, 21, 37, 35, 15], which makes streams one of the few probes of low-mass subhalos at, or below, the threshold of galaxy formation. Streams that pass near the LMC show indications of past interactions in misalignment between their tracks and proper motions [36, 93], and these offsets have been used to measure the mass of the LMC [36, 100, 92].

Stream discovery has accelerated with each generation of wide-field imaging. Isochrone filtering of photometry from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey [103, SDSS;], the VLT Survey Telescope ATLAS [90, VST ATLAS;], the Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System [25, Pan-STARRS;], and the Dark Energy Survey [28, DES;] revealed dozens of streams [83, 11, 48, 59, 13, 91, e.g.,]. Gaia astrometry [41] has made it possible to discover streams in phase space [70, 69, 54] and to measure proper motions that separate faint members from the surrounding stellar halo [86, 58, 93]. Spectroscopic surveys such as the Southern Stellar Stream Spectroscopic Survey [64, 63, 67, S5;] and the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument [2, 77, DESI;] have measured radial velocities and metallicities for many streams. Nearly 100 streams are now known [74, 17], but many are traced only by the bright giants that Gaia can measure, and their full extent remains poorly constrained.

The Sutlej stream was discovered by Nidever [82, hereafter N24] in Gaia DR3 [43]. N24 combined Gaia proper motions with metallicities, effective temperatures, and surface gravities derived by Andrae et al. [3] from the Gaia XP spectra of 175 million stars [29]. In the vicinity of the SMC, N24 identified an old, metal-poor population with coherent proper motion. N24 characterized Sutlej as two nearly parallel branches, each ∼\sim8∘×0.6∘{}^{\circ}\times 0.6^{\circ}, separated by ∼\sim2.5∘, with a total stellar mass of ∼\sim33,000 M⊙ and a distance of ∼\sim32 kpc. Because Gaia reaches only G≈21G\approx 21, at 32 kpc N24 sampled only Sutlej’s red giant branch and horizontal branch. With deeper photometry that reaches below the main-sequence turnoff, we can map Sutlej’s structure and extent with many more stars and approximate its distance from the main sequence.

Sutlej resides in a region crowded with old, metal-poor substructure. The ultra-faint satellites Tucana III (Tuc III) and Tucana IV (Tuc IV) lie within ∼\sim5∘ of the N24 footprint [33], and the Indus stream was identified nearby in DES [91]. The SMC Northern Overdensity (SMCNOD), a ∼\sim6∘×2∘{}^{\circ}\times 2^{\circ} structure ∼\sim8∘ north of the SMC also found in DES [84], lies at the distance of the SMC (∼\sim62 kpc) and contains both intermediate-age and older, more metal-poor stars, most likely stripped from the SMC by the LMC [73]. Tuc III in particular is at a comparable distance to Sutlej (∼\sim25 kpc; Drlica-Wagner et al. 33) and is itself being tidally disrupted, which raises the possibility that the two are related. Tuc III was discovered in the second year of DES data [33] with tidal features that were later traced as a ∼\sim5∘ stream spanning both sides of the core [91]. Spectroscopy confirmed a metal-poor stellar population ([Fe/H]≈−2.4\,\approx-2.4), an unresolved velocity dispersion, and a velocity gradient along the tails [94, 65]. Shipp et al. [91] also measured a distance gradient of 0.16±0.060.16\pm 0.06 mag deg-1 along the stream, with distance increasing toward the end nearer Sutlej on the sky, so that it spans ∼\sim4 kpc in distance, consistent with a radial orbit. Its Gaia proper motion has been measured for both the core and the tails [93], and modeling of its orbit indicates a recent close passage with the LMC, which has measurably perturbed the stream [38, 92].

Because DELVE reaches well below the main-sequence turnoff, where stream members vastly outnumber those on the giant branch accessible to Gaia, it is sensitive to faint and extended structure that could not be detected in the discovery data. We use these data to recover the N24 branches and search for extensions beyond them, to measure the distance to each part of the stream independently from its main sequence and from standard candles, and to investigate whether Sutlej is associated with the other old, metal-poor substructure in the region, in particular Tuc III.

We use these data to recover the N24 branches and search for extensions beyond them, to measure the distance to each part of the stream independently from its main sequence and from standard candles, and to investigate whether Sutlej is associated with the other old, metal-poor substructure in the region, in particular Tuc III.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section II we describe the DES, DELVE, and Gaia datasets and the selection of our stellar sample. In Section III we apply a matched filter, divide the stream into four segments, and measure each segment’s distance from Hess diagrams and from standard candles. In Section IV we test whether Sutlej could be tidal debris from Tuc III with restricted NN-body simulations, and we summarize our conclusions in Section V. Appendix C discusses the river for which the stream is named.

papers.title: No Evidence of Cold Trapping in the Dayside Atmosphere of WASP-33 b
papers.abstract: Ultra-hot Jupiters allow simultaneous measurements of volatile molecules and refractory metals, providing constraints on atmospheric chemistry and refractory-element sequestration. We reanalyze the previously published Gemini-N/IGRINS-2 dayside emission spectra of WASP-33~b, extending the analysis to neutral refractory species. Using cross-correlation (CC) and likelihood-based (LL) detection methods, we recover the strongest species detection signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) from CO ($\rm CC~S/N=5.29,\ LL~S/N=5.62$). \ion{Mg}{1} ($\rm CC~S/N=3.88,\ LL~S/N=4.73$) and OH ($\rm CC~S/N=3.88,\ LL~S/N=3.89$) are recovered at lower significance in both metrics. H$_2$O remains marginal, appearing only in the cross-correlation analysis ($\rm CC~S/N=3.24$), while \ion{Ti}{1} ($\rm LL~S/N=3.70$) and \ion{Ca}{1} ($\rm LL~S/N=2.98$) show tentative signals. We do not detect \ion{Fe}{1}, \ion{Si}{1}, and \ion{V}{1} in this dataset. A chemical-equilibrium retrieval with a flexible Bezier-spline pressure--temperature profile yields ${\rm C/O}=0.65^{+0.09}_{-0.10}$ and $[{\rm M/H}]=-0.48^{+0.24}_{-0.18}$, and a refractory-to-volatile ratio of $[R/V]_{\rm p}=-0.15^{+0.24}_{-0.23}$. The corresponding stellar-normalized value is $[R/V]_{\rm p/ \star}=0.37^{+0.38}_{-0.36}$, but this value is sensitive to the stellar oxygen abundance. We find that the atmospheric Ti/Mg and Ca/Mg ratios of WASP-33~b are consistent with their respective stellar values within 68\% confidence. This is in contrast to other ultra-hot Jupiters with lower equilibrium temperatures that often show depleted Ti abundances compared to other metals, indicative of cold-trapping. This would suggest that even the nightside of WASP-33~b is too hot for significant condensation and sequestration to occur. Comparison with disk-chemistry models remains exploratory because the carbon-to-refractory posterior overlaps several formation scenarios.

papers.intro:
Atmospheric elemental abundances provide a means of tracing the formation and migration histories of hot Jupiters. The carbon-to-oxygen ratio (C/O) and overall metallicity depend on where a planet accreted gas and solids relative to major condensation fronts such as the H2O, CO2, and CO snow lines [59, 54]. However, C/O alone is degenerate because similar values can arise from different combinations of gas accretion, solid accretion, and elemental sequestration [52, 84, 13]. Refractory elements provide an additional constraint by tracing the rocky material incorporated into the planetary atmosphere.

Ultra-hot Jupiters (UHJs; Teq ≥\geq2000 K) are especially useful for this test. Their high atmospheric temperatures keep refractory species in the gas phase, enabling simultaneous measurements of volatile molecules and refractory metals [52]. These conditions also reduce the likelihood of high-altitude condensate clouds and therefore lead to relatively clear spectra for transmission and emission observations. High-resolution spectroscopy of UHJs has simultaneously detected refractory metals (e.g., Fe, Mg, Ca) and volatile molecules such as CO, H2O, and OH [72, 78, 6, 93, 75, 37]. Abundance constraints obtained from such detections provide important constraints on both atmospheric chemistry and possible formation scenarios.

Refractory species also provide a test of atmospheric cold trapping. In a tidally locked hot Jupiter, the dayside can be hot enough to keep metals in the gas phase, while the nightside or deeper atmosphere may still be cool enough for condensates to form and rain out [63]. If condensates settle before being transported back to the dayside, the observable atmosphere can become depleted in the corresponding refractory element. Ti is an especially sensitive diagnostic because it is easier to condense than Fe, Mg, and Si: Ti condenses at Tcond∼1600T_{\rm cond}\sim 1600 K, compared with Tcond∼1350T_{\rm cond}\sim 1350–1400 K for Fe, Mg, and Si. Ti can be removed through Ti oxides and CaTiO3 condensates [50, 51]. Observationally, the UHJ WASP-76 b shows a sharp depletion of elements with Tcond>1550T_{\rm cond}>1550 K, interpreted as nightside cold trapping [67]. The slightly hotter UHJ WASP-121 b also shows evidence for Ti depletion from both low- and high-resolution spectroscopy [34, 78, 71, 66]. Meanwhile, hotter UHJs such as WASP-189 b, HAT-P-70 b, and MASCARA-1 b show detectable Ti-bearing species, although partial Ti depletion may still occur depending on nightside temperature, heat redistribution, ionization, and vertical mixing [75, 65, 31, 82, 37]. Overall, a comparative retrieval of six UHJs similarly found Ti-bearing species to be underabundant in most planets in the sample, potentially due to a combination of nightside rain-out and ionization, with Ti and TiO constrained only for the hottest target, WASP-189 b [27].

WASP-33 b is a prototypical UHJ orbiting a δ\delta Scuti A-type star every 1.22 days [16]. With a dayside temperature exceeding 2700 K [94, 86], it resides well within a regime where molecules can thermally dissociate and refractory elements are expected to be fully vaporized and part of the gas phase. Previous high-resolution spectroscopic observations have revealed the presence of CO, OH, and H2O [58, 90, 85, 26, e.g.,] and neutral refractory gases (Fe I, V I, Ti I, Si I) [57, 17, 19, 18, 33, e.g.,] in its dayside atmosphere. In addition to dayside observations, transit observations with various spectrographs have revealed the presence of ionized Ca in its atmosphere [89, 91]. Some studies have also suggested evidence for nightside thermal emission of H2O [92] and reported a detection of CO absorption [55]. Recently, Choi et al. [15, hereafter, C25] used the upgraded Immersion GRating INfrared Spectrograph 2 [45, 60, IGRINS-2;] at Gemini-North to detect multiple volatile species in WASP-33 b’s dayside emission spectra. This study also demonstrated the instrument’s improved throughput and extended K-band coverage, both of which increase CO sensitivity.

papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation in the Agentic Era: Tradition, Present, and Prospect
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) couples frozen language models with external, updatable knowledge, so that generation is grounded in retrieved evidence rather than in parametric memory alone. This work maps RAG in the agentic era by joining them on a single lifecycle axis, from offline indexing through pre-retrieval, retrieval, post-retrieval, and orchestration over these stages. It treats indexing and orchestration as first-class components and agentic workflows as a paradigm of their own, and it covers the agentic work that has appeared since those reviews. Beyond these components, it covers evaluation, applications, and the questions that remain open for future exploration. From tradition to present and beyond, this work systematically reviews RAG from a perspective of the agentic era.

papers.intro:
Language models (LMs) have become remarkably capable, yet adapting them to the virtually infinite world knowledge is still non-trivial. Once training ends, what a model knows is frozen into its parameters, and it can be incomplete, incorrect, or out of date. A model cannot answer questions about knowledge it was not trained on: a client’s files, a product catalogue, yesterday’s news. Teaching it that knowledge by fine-tuning is often not an option at all: it needs the weights, and a black-box model does not expose them. Even with the weights, the run scales with the data and degrades what the model could already do [1]. Nor does the model fail quietly: it invents answers [2], it cannot point to the passage that supports a right answer, and it cannot make full use of its context [3]. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has therefore become the default way to adapt a model to knowledge that does not live in its parameters.

RAG couples a frozen language model, the generator, with external knowledge, held in corpora that can be updated and that a retriever searches: given a query, it retrieves relevant evidence and conditions generation on both the query and that evidence. Lewis et al. [4] introduced the term with a dense retriever and a sequence-to-sequence generator on knowledge-intensive tasks, and it has since spread to nearly every setting where an LM answers from external text.

One question cuts across all five: who decides the control flow. In a pipeline the designer fixes it in advance, loops included; in an agent the model chooses at run time whether to retrieve, what to retrieve, and how often. The stages are the same in both cases, but in the second none of them is scheduled ahead of time. Because these systems differ in who decides rather than in which stage they alter, we discuss agentic RAG separately.

papers.title: Combining Physical Layer Security and Symmetric Encryption to Secure Rate-Splitting Multiple Access
papers.abstract: The demand for increased spectral efficiency (SE) in downlink multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) systems has led to the development of various multiple access techniques. Among these, rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) can improve SE over space division multiple access (SDMA) and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) by splitting each user's data into common and private parts. The common parts from all users are then encoded into a single common message, which is transmitted alongside the private messages using an RSMA-specific precoder. Recent results showed that the precoder can be modified to enable physical layer security (PLS) by integrating secrecy rate constraints into the design. However, this approach only secures the private messages, while the common part of each user remains unprotected. To address this limitation, we propose a hybrid-PLS RSMA scheme that symmetrically encrypts all user data and embeds key information within the PLS-secured private messages. Additionally, the RSMA precoder is adapted to ensure that the private messages are sufficiently sized to carry the key information. The precoder design is formulated as a non-convex SE maximization problem and solved using successive convex approximation (SCA). Analytical and numerical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed hybrid-PLS RSMA can significantly improve SE compared to partially secure RSMA and secure SDMA, when complete user data security is required.

papers.intro:
Future mobile communication systems require high SE to accommodate the growing number of devices and the rising demand from data-intensive applications such as XR (XR) or edge computing. MU-MIMO techniques address this by serving multiple users on the same time-frequency resource by leveraging the spatial dimension through multiple antennas. Widely studied MU-MIMO methods include SDMA and NOMA, which adopt different strategies for handling interference. In SDMA, the receiver treats any interference as noise, whereas NOMA uses superposition coding at the transmitter and SIC (SIC) at the receiver to sequentially decode and subtract interference. In terms of performance, either SDMA or NOMA may provide higher SE depending on factors such as user count, antenna configuration or channel conditions [1].

Future mobile communication systems require high SE to accommodate the growing number of devices and the rising demand from data-intensive applications such as XR (XR) or edge computing. MU-MIMO techniques address this by serving multiple users on the same time-frequency resource by leveraging the spatial dimension through multiple antennas. Widely studied MU-MIMO methods include SDMA and NOMA, which adopt different strategies for handling interference. In SDMA, the receiver treats any interference as noise, whereas NOMA uses superposition coding at the transmitter and SIC (SIC) at the receiver to sequentially decode and subtract interference. In terms of performance, either SDMA or NOMA may provide higher SE depending on factors such as user count, antenna configuration or channel conditions [1].

To further enhance SE, the recently proposed RSMA framework [1] integrates both strategies within several unified architectures, such as downlink linearly precoded 1-layer RSMA (referred to simply as RSMA hereafter). At the transmitter, RSMA splits the message of each user into a common part and a private part. The common parts from all users are then combined into a single common message, which is jointly precoded and transmitted alongside the private messages. At the receiver, each user first decodes and subtracts the common message via SIC to reduce interference. The private message is then decoded while treating any remaining interference as noise. This way, RSMA unifies SDMA and NOMA to achieve equal or higher SE in all scenarios [1].

Another key aspect of future communication systems is PLS, which prevents unauthorized decoding by degrading an attacker’s physical channel [2]. This idea can also be applied to RSMA, as demonstrated in [3], where a secure RSMA mmWave system was proposed to enhance confidentiality against an external ED (ED) with unknown CSI (CSI). This system transmits the common message on spatial paths overlapping between users, while private messages use non-overlapping paths. Consequently, security degrades if an attacker also overlaps with one or more of these paths, making it strongly dependent on the positions of the users and the ED. An alternative strategy is to introduce additional noise to degrade the channel of an external attacker. papers.title: Fast Gradient-Based Framework for Spatial and Length Optimization of Geothermal Borehole Fields
papers.abstract: Common analytical design tools for Borehole Heat Exchanger (BHE) fields size the total drilling length for a given layout but do not optimize the positions of the boreholes. We introduce a framework (OptiGeoS) for the simultaneous, gradient-based optimization of the borehole length and the continuous borehole positions under groundwater advection. It couples the Moving Finite Line Source model with local BHE equations and evaluates the temporal convolutions by Fast Fourier Transforms. The gradients with respect to the length and the positions are computed analytically. A flow-dependent Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation confines each borehole to its own cell, which enforces the spatial separation and provides advection-informed layouts. Under purely conductive conditions, the fluid temperature extremes of the forward model for a single borehole lie between those of EED and GHEtool, which differ by $0.32\,\mathrm{K}$. For a field of 120 boreholes, the hourly outlet temperature agrees with that of EED with an RMSE of $0.28\,\mathrm{K}$, while the peak temperatures deviate by up to $2\,\mathrm{K}$. For 25 boreholes simulated hourly over 20 years, one forward simulation takes less than $0.5\,\mathrm{s}$ and a full optimization about $8\,\mathrm{min}$ on a laptop CPU. In a case study with groundwater advection, the optimized layout requires $16.2\,\%$ less borehole length than a fixed grid. It reduces the length increase caused by the advected thermal plume from $20.9\,\%$ to $1.4\,\%$.

papers.intro:
Heat is the largest energy end use and accounts for almost half of global final energy consumption International Energy Agency [2021b]. Its decarbonization is part of the transition toward carbon neutrality International Energy Agency [2021a]. Ground Source Heat Pumps (GSHPs) are an efficient, low-carbon alternative to fossil-fuel-based heating and cooling systems Bayer et al. [2012], Yang et al. [2010]. Using the stable temperature of the shallow subsurface, GSHPs can provide base-load heating and cooling for individual buildings and for district heating and cooling networks Buffa et al. [2019]. Borehole Heat Exchangers (BHEs) exchange the heat between the heat pump and the ground. The deployment of BHE fields is limited by their high initial capital cost. The ground heat exchangers account for more than 30%30\,\% of the total cost of a GSHP system and are the largest contributor to its cost premium over conventional systems Liu et al. [2019]. Over-sizing the total drilling length by a few percent therefore increases the cost of the ground heat exchangers by about the same fraction. Design tools should minimize the total drilling length while keeping the subsurface thermally sustainable.

Analytical models for BHE fields are reviewed in Li and Lai [2015], Kuntuarova et al. [2024]. Cimmino et al. [2013, Sec. 4] developed a method based on the Finite Line Source that computes thermal response functions for boreholes that are not regularly spaced. This removed the dependence on pre-calculated libraries and allowed the analysis of non-grid layouts. Building on this, Rose et al. [2026, Sec. 2.2] introduced a framework that constructs both short- and long-term g-functions Cimmino and Bernier [2014a]. It is tailored to the thermal interactions of parallel-connected BHE systems. Common design tools use only part of this flexibility. Sizing tools such as Earth Energy Designer (EED) Sanner and Hellström [1997] and GHEtool Peere and Blanke [2022] determine the required borehole length for a given layout. GHEtool also accepts custom borehole positions, but neither tool optimizes the positions together with the length. To our knowledge, neither tool accounts for groundwater advection, although advection shifts the thermal plumes downstream and changes the long-term performance [Tye-Gingras and Gosselin, 2014, Sec. 4.2].

None of these studies optimizes the borehole length. Advection can be included analytically by the Moving Finite Line Source (MFLS) Molina-Giraldo et al. [2011b], Tye-Gingras and Gosselin [2014], which we use here. Numerical simulators based on finite element methods, such as FEFLOW Diersch [2014] or OpenGeoSys Bilke et al. However, a single simulation of a BHE field over several decades is computationally expensive, and an optimization requires many such simulations. These suites also often lack automated optimization routines.

papers.title: SuSi-RAG: A Hybrid Graph RAG for Equipment Maintenance
papers.abstract: In the manufacturing domain, equipment maintenance tasks depend on expert knowledge. Their documentation is often stored in heterogeneous formats and sources. The enhancement of LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is promising for bridging the scattered knowledge, but traditional vector-based RAG shows weaknesses with two characteristics which are common in real maintenance queries: complex causal chains and cross-domain synthesis. To address this, we propose SuSi-RAG, a hybrid Graph RAG solution, that matches a user query and each maintenance record using subgraph similarity. This work shows an in-use system: SuSi-RAG has run on an active Bosch production line for more than eight months, handling 10,664 question-answer interactions and demonstrates upper bound answer accuracy of 96.25% (confirmed error rate 3.75%). In a proof-of-concept, SuSi-RAG improves top-1 retrieval accuracy from 61.5% to 96.2% and expert-rated answer quality from 44.9% to 84.1% against a vector-based baseline. We present an integrated operational feedback loop to update SuSi-RAG.

papers.intro:
More than a decade of Industry 4.0 [1] brought benefits for manufacturing [2], but also increasingly complex shopfloor equipment and industrial machinery with interconnected soft- and hardware. Efficient and high-quality maintenance of this equipment is economically critical for manufacturing companies [3], yet, the required expertise is scarce as experienced engineers possess valuable expert knowledge, while inexperienced personnel needs support in difficult tasks. One exemplary maintenance task is triggered by this question: Station ST1 is experiencing continuous product welding scrap. Even after replacing the electrodes, the issue persists. What are the next steps in the troubleshooting process? Keyword-based retrieval often fails here as it might retrieve documents related to electrode maintenance, despite that this step was already unsuccessfully attempted. A sophisticated approach is needed to follow a causal chain, e.g., welding scrap to position offset to gripper status to cylinder failure, and harmonize information across mechanical, process and control domains. Complex causal chains (C1) and cross-domain synthesis (C2) are two common challenges at large manufacturing companies such as Bosch. We illustrate the challenges in Figure 1.

Complex causal chains (C1) and cross-domain synthesis (C2) are two common challenges at large manufacturing companies such as Bosch. We illustrate the challenges in Figure 1.

Semantic technologies, such as ontologies and knowledge graphs (KGs), have proven effective across industrial applications [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Graph structures enable multi-hop search for causal chains (C1) and maintenance knowledge can be parsed to graph structure with the help of ontologies and KGs. Yet, accessing this knowledge in practice is tedious and non-trivial as no sufficiently accurate solution exists for our scenario. A promising direction are hybrid architectures of graph- and LLM-based components (e.g., [9], [10]). Hence, we ask the following research question: How can we combine operational data and domain knowledge in a RAG-based solution to answer real maintenance queries and does such a solution prove helpful in production use? Unlike existing KG integration approaches for RAG systems, we propose with SuSi-RAG a domain-tailored retrieval method to this question. While user queries and maintenance documents are represented as maintenance graphs, a similarity score with expert-weighted entity types and a proportionality harmonization of incomplete queries selects the most relevant records. A balancing step with two common methods ensures robustness and selects the final output candidate. In contrast to most similar studies, the evaluation of our industry- and application-oriented work is two-fold: a controlled proof-of-concept (PoC) and an in-use analysis on a real production line. Our contributions are: • A subgraph-similarity retrieval mechanism for maintenance events with expert-weighted entities, a harmonization of only partial queries, separated pattern and textual handling to improve search relevance of retrieved items. • An in-use analysis of the implemented, deployed solution for a timeframe of eight months on a selected active Bosch production line with 10,664 interactions and expert-confirmed error rate. In addition, a feedback loop mechanism is presented. • Insights from Practice on parameter configurations for reproducibility, and lessons-learned from the deployment to obtain reliable shopfloor results. • A quantitative comparison of SuSi-RAG against a vector-based RAG with favourable results: SuSi-RAG nearly doubles the performance, increasing retrieval accuracy from 61.5% to 96.2% and expert-rated answer quality from 44.9% to 84.1%. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Next, we discuss related research and identify the research gap on our scenario in Section II. In Section III, we introduce the Intelligent Equipment Maintenance Use Case at Bosch and explain the two main challenges with exemplary maintenance questions. In Section IV, we clarify why a hybrid Graph RAG design is needed, and subsequently, describe ontology, KG and SuSi-RAG with each module in detail. In Section V, we provide configuration settings and evaluate SuSi-RAG in a two-fold manner, with a quantitative PoC analysis and a continuous in-use analysis of the solution to address. We close this section by discussing the limitations of our approach. In Section VI, we present our lessons learned, and, conclude our work in Section VII with an outlook on future steps.

papers.title: Learning Multimodal Representations from Partially Paired, Small-Scale Data
papers.abstract: Modeling multimodal data from partially paired samples is critical for advancing domains like biomedicine, where vast unimodal datasets and foundation models exist but paired data remains scarce. Existing fusion methods rely on large-scale paired datasets, limiting their use in scenarios with incomplete pairing. We introduce CAMEO, an adversarial learning-based modality fusion framework that integrates modalities from small, partially paired datasets. Combining any pre-trained unimodal encoder with a cross-modal latent alignment mechanism, CAMEO learns shared representations requiring only minimal paired samples. Evaluated on computational pathology tasks such as niche classification and cell type composition prediction, CAMEO achieves superior data efficiency, outperforming contrastive approaches like CLIP in low paired-data regimes, and highlighting the benefits of adversarial alignment when paired annotations are scarce. To facilitate further research, we additionally release a fully annotated HuggingFace dataset comprising three organs and paired image and gene expression modalities. By extending fusion methods to address limited pairing and small-scale datasets, we provide a framework that advances multimodal learning and broadens its applicability to real-world biomedical problems.

papers.intro:
Recent advances in spatial transcriptomics and histopathology (HP) imaging have advanced our understanding of tissue organization by providing complementary views of cellular states (Larsson et al., 2021; Palla et al., 2022; Fischer et al., 2023). While spatial transcriptomics captures gene expression with spatial information, HP imaging reveals tissue morphology and cellular organization at high resolution. The integration of these modalities promises deeper insights into tissue architecture and cellular interactions.
