While spatial transcriptomics captures gene expression with spatial information, HP imaging reveals tissue morphology and cellular organization at high resolution. The integration of these modalities promises deeper insights into tissue architecture and cellular interactions.

Foundation models have emerged as powerful tools for analyzing biomedical modalities (Szałata et al., 2024). These models leverage self-supervised learning on large, unimodal datasets (Richter et al., 2024). Models like scGPT (Cui et al., 2024a) and Geneformer (Cui et al., 2024b) learn gene-gene dependencies from gene expression data (i.e., quantitative transcriptomic profiles) through masked language modeling. This type of model is applicable to various cell- and gene-level downstream tasks, including cell annotation and gene function prediction. Vision models like UNI (Chen et al., 2024) and CTransPath (Wang et al., 2022) learn morphological patterns from H&E-stained whole-slide images using a contrastive objective. However, these approaches do not utilize the potentially complementary information present in multiple modalities. While multimodal models have been successfully applied in domains such as language and vision (Radford et al., 2021), they typically require large-scale paired datasets, limiting their applicability to domains where paired data is scarce.

We introduce CAMEO (Fig. 1), an adversarial modality fusion framework, as an alternative to contrastive and naive concatenation approaches. In biomedical settings where paired samples are scarce, CAMEO’s adversarial mechanism provides robust performance with minimal paired data requirements. Our cross-tissue analysis reveals the complementary strengths of different fusion strategies, with adversarial alignment offering superior robustness when paired data is limited, while also highlighting the importance of systematically evaluating encoder combinations regardless of fusion approach.

papers.title: Tri-DNO: Trilateral Diffusion Noise Optimization for 3D Human Object Interaction
papers.abstract:
Generating realistic 3D human object interactions (HOI) is essential for applications, such as augmented or virtual reality (AR/VR) or character animation of interactive entertainment. A particular challenge lies in the faithful generation of hand grasps in human object interaction scenes, where even minor geometric inconsistencies, such as insufficient contact or interpenetration, can significantly compromise realism. While diffusion-based generative models have shown promising results in HOI synthesis, ensuring physically plausible hand-object interactions remains challenging.
  We present Tri-DNO, a diffusion noise optimization strategy to sample from a pretrained multimodal HOI diffusion model, improving hand-object contact. Rather than modifying or retraining the generative model, our approach iteratively optimizes the initial noise of the diffusion generator, thereby generating firm hand object contact, while mitigating penetration and keeping the hand position realistic. Experiments on the GRAB dataset demonstrate improvements over the baseline in grasp quality without additional model training or increased computational cost compared to existing methods. We further demonstrate the applicability of our approach to practical media production scenarios.

papers.title: LLM-Guided Compositional Continual Learning for Robot Manipulation with Gated Low-Rank Experts
papers.abstract: General-purpose manipulation robots must acquire new skills over time without forgetting prior ones or retraining from scratch. We present a continual learning framework that represents each skill as a dedicated expert sub- network in a Progressive Neural Network (PNN). New tasks reuse prior knowledge through low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules on lateral connections controlled by learnable per-parent gates, enabling explicit attenuation of individual transfer paths while reducing the parameter cost of dense PNN laterals. For long-horizon deployment, a frozen local large language model decomposes natural-language instructions into sub-tasks, routes them to suitable experts, and requests a new expert only when the library is insufficient. Using a shared task-space action interface, we evaluate the framework on twelve MetaWorld tasks and in a Sawyer-to-Panda-to-UR5e cross-embodiment transfer experiment, showing improved task success relative to learning from scratch when demonstrations are limited. Real-robot manipulation experiments further demonstrate that the proposed framework supports compositional execution and expert orchestration.
papers.intro:
Robots operating in unstructured environments must acquire new manipulation skills throughout their lifetime without losing previously learned ones. This requirement is difficult to satisfy with the dominant paradigm of training a single monolithic policy across all tasks. When new tasks are added, previously acquired knowledge can be partially or completely overwritten, leading to catastrophic forgetting [1]. Continual learning (CL) addresses this problem by enabling incremental skill acquisition while preserving earlier capabilities. However, forgetting is not the only limitation of monolithic policies [2]. Because different skills are entangled within the same set of parameters, it is difficult to identify which part of the network is responsible for a particular behavior or to quantify how much a new skill reuses prior knowledge. In safety-critical robotics [3], this lack of transparency limits inspection, verification, and selective deployment of individual competencies.

We address these issues by learning each skill as a dedicated expert that is preserved after training and composed only when needed, as shown in Fig. 1. Our architecture is based on a Progressive Neural Network (PNN) [4], where every task is assigned a new column, or sub-network, that is frozen once learned. This prevents parameter overwriting in previously learned columns. To enable forward knowledge transfer with a lower per-connection parameter cost than dense lateral connections, prior knowledge is reused through LoRA-style low-rank lateral adapters [5]. Each adapter is modulated by a learnable per-parent gate, allowing the new column to draw selectively from relevant prior experts while suppressing unhelpful ones. This design reduces the quadratic parameter growth of vanilla PNNs, mitigates negative knowledge transfer, and exposes transfer as a measurable quantity. Depending on the experiment, experts are trained either with soft actor-critic (SAC) augmented by behavior cloning or from demonstrations using conditional flow matching [6].

papers.title: Statistics of Fundamental Fourier Coefficients of Cusp Forms
papers.abstract:
We study sign changes of Fourier coefficients of elliptic and Siegel modular forms in considerable generality. For any $N \geq 1$ and an arbitrary non-zero elliptic cusp form $f\in S_\kappa (\Gamma_1(N))$ ($\kappa \in \frac{1}{2} \mathbb{Z}$) with real Fourier coefficients, we show that a positive proportion of its non-zero Fourier coefficients change sign if $\kappa \geq 1$ is integral. If $\kappa \geq 1/2$ is half-integral, we get an almost optimal result.
  As applications, we establish quantitative sign-change results for `fundamental' Fourier coefficients of Siegel cusp forms of arbitrary degree $n$. These improve the previous best known results on the number of non-zero fundamental Fourier coefficients, even in degree $n=1$.

papers.title: Via a New LP Relaxation: Stronger Performance Guarantees for WSEPT, and an LP-Based Proof of Kawaguchi & Kyan
papers.abstract: We present a new linear programming relaxation for minimizing the total weighted completion time on identical parallel machines. Its right-hand side is supermodular, so the relaxation can be solved by a greedy algorithm. We show that the WSPT rule is within a factor $\frac{1}{2}(1 + \sqrt{2})$ of the optimal LP value. This bounds the integrality gap of the relaxation and gives a short, LP-based proof of the tight bound of Kawaguchi and Kyan on the performance of WSPT. We then turn to the stochastic version of the problem, in which processing times are independent random variables whose squared coefficients of variation are at most~$\Delta$. A variance-corrected version of the new LP relaxation is valid for all non-anticipatory policies, and we show that WSEPT is within a factor $1 + (1 + \Delta)/(3 + \sqrt{7 + 2 \Delta})$ of it for $\Delta \ge 1$, for any number of machines. This is $O(\sqrt\Delta)$, whereas all previous guarantees for this problem grow linearly in $\Delta$. Up to a constant factor, our bound matches the known $\Omega(\sqrt\Delta)$ lower bound for WSEPT. For $\Delta \le 1$, we recover the best known bounds.

We are given jobs N={1,…,n}N=\{1,\ldots,n\}, each with processing time pj>0p_{j}>0 and weight wj>0w_{j}>0, and mm identical machines to process them. papers.title: PVFormer: Proper Velocity Transformer for Stable and Scalable Hyperbolic Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Hyperbolic representations have shown remarkable success on hierarchical and tree-like data, and Transformers have become a central architecture for representation learning. However, a principled construction of hyperbolic Transformers remains challenging because the self-attention layer decomposes into three coupled primitives, transformation, similarity, and aggregation, that should all respect the underlying geometry. Existing hyperbolic Transformer designs are typically built in the Poincar\'e or Lorentz models, where bounded domains, time-like constraints, tangent-space detours, or projection steps make it difficult to keep the full block intrinsic and scalable. To address this gap, we propose PVFormer, to the best of our knowledge, the first Transformer architecture that operates natively in proper velocity (PV) space. The proper velocity model provides an unconstrained representation of hyperbolic geometry, and PVFormer exploits this structure to redesign the Transformer block in PV space. On the transformation side, we use PV homomorphism transformations to update query and value representations. On the similarity side, we generalize Euclidean inner-product attention with a PV Busemann score inspired by Busemann-based hyperbolic learning and a PV point-to-hyperplane key transformation. On the aggregation side, we replace Euclidean averaging with PV midpoint aggregation and further derive a scalable PV linear attention variant for large graphs. Extensive experiments support the effectiveness of PVFormer across graph, text, and vision benchmarks.

papers.intro:
Hyperbolic geometry provides a natural representation for hierarchical and tree-like data because negative curvature offers exponential representation capacity (25, 26, 16, 23, 7). This property has driven successful applications in graphs (21, 43, 42), visual categories (2, 30), and biological sequences (30, 10), and recent work has moved from hyperbolic embeddings toward hyperbolic neural networks that operate within hyperbolic space. However, as emphasized by PVNN (10), the choice of hyperbolic model is central to neural architecture design (30, 10). Poincaré and Lorentz models provide powerful formulations and many closed-form operations, but bounded domains, explicit manifold constraints, tangent-space detours, and projection steps can introduce numerical and implementation difficulties. In particular, Poincaré embeddings that approach the boundary can make computations unstable and cause gradients to vanish (10).

These issues become especially important for Transformers, whose self-attention layer is a coupled pipeline rather than a single similarity function. Each block must transform hidden states into query, key, and value representations, compare queries and keys, and aggregate values (36). Existing hyperbolic attention and Transformer methods make important progress toward this goal, but they often align only part of the pipeline with hyperbolic geometry (18, 42). Euclidean or tangent-space transformations followed by restoration steps preserve feasibility but weaken the link between learned updates and intrinsic geometry (7, 42); distance-based similarities encode proximity but can discard directionality, while tangent-space inner products depend on a base point (18, 42); and log/exp-map or projection-based aggregation can add computational and numerical burden (27). The challenge is therefore not merely to replace the Euclidean dot product, but to realize transformation, similarity, and aggregation in one coherent hyperbolic computational model.

papers.title: Closed-loop Properties of Value Iteration in Continuous Time with Approximation Errors
papers.abstract: Value iteration is an important tool for approximating solutions of infinite-horizon optimal control problems, but in practice it is never carried out exactly: value functions are represented by finite-dimensional approximators, and the iteration is stopped after finitely many steps. This paper analyzes which closed-loop guarantees remain under these limitations for continuous-time nonlinear systems. We consider a value iteration scheme in which each iteration solves a finite-horizon optimal control problem with the previous iterate as terminal cost, and the associated controller applies the optimal input of this problem over each horizon in a sampled-data fashion. We show that if the convergence tolerance and the approximation error are small enough, the controller asymptotically stabilizes the system on sublevel sets of the computed iterate, and provide a suboptimality bound. This condition consists of pointwise inequalities that can be checked for the computed iterate, without establishing convergence of the iteration, and is a first step towards sample-based certification. We further establish inherent robustness of the controller with respect to model errors and recover classical results for the linear-quadratic regulator. Numerical studies on a linear-quadratic problem and on a nonlinear system with known optimal value function are consistent with the guarantees and show that the suboptimality bound is conservative.

papers.intro:
Infinite-horizon optimal control problems characterize the best achievable performance through the optimal value function, which, under suitable assumptions, also serves as a Lyapunov function for the optimally controlled system. Solving the associated Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation is, however, intractable for general nonlinear systems. Approximate dynamic programming (ADP) circumvents this by iteratively updating approximations of the value function or of the policy [1, 2]. Furthermore, in the context of model predictive control (MPC), stability for finite prediction horizons is commonly ensured by terminal costs satisfying a Lyapunov decrease condition [3, 4]. Such terminal costs are hard to construct for nonlinear systems, and approximate value functions are a natural candidate. In discrete time, combining value iteration (VI) with MPC has led to stability and suboptimality guarantees that account for approximation errors and permit shorter prediction horizons [5, 6]. The present analysis provides a continuous-time foundation for such schemes.

Among its two main schemes, policy iteration generally requires an initially stabilizing policy, whereas VI does not, which often constitutes a superfluous requirement in view of the fact that the goal of optimal control is usually to stabilize the system. Accordingly, convergence and stability of VI, including the effect of approximation errors, have been studied extensively [7, 8, 9].

Each of these steps introduces an error, and the controller that is eventually deployed is derived from an imperfect iterate. The central question is therefore not only whether the iterates approach the optimal value function, but what an imperfect iterate guarantees for the closed loop: is the associated controller stabilizing, how robust is it, and how far is its cost from the optimal one?

Most of this theory is formulated in discrete time even though physical systems have continuous-time dynamics, and discretizing a continuous-time system to apply it may not yield the expected results. As the sampling interval shrinks, the cost accumulated over a single transition vanishes, whereas approximation and numerical errors do not. Error conditions stated relative to this cost thus become increasingly restrictive [10]. Moreover, guarantees for the discretized problem need not carry over to the underlying continuous-time system [11, 12]. Continuous-time ADP has been developed both for policy iteration [12, 13] and for VI [14, 15]. In particular, [14] proves convergence of continuous-time VI under a contraction assumption and shows that, with bounded approximation errors, the iterates reach a neighborhood of the optimal value function. Convergence of the iterates and stability of the feedback derived from them are, however, distinct properties: closed-loop guarantees require the approximation and convergence errors to be related to a Lyapunov decrease. For discrete time, such relations have been established in [8, 9, 16]. To the best of our knowledge, no result relates the approximation error and the convergence tolerance of continuous-time VI to the stability, robustness, and suboptimality of the associated controller.

The associated controller for the final iterate is then used in a sampled-data manner with the already mentioned horizon as sampling period [17]. We show that if the convergence tolerance, measured relative to the cost accumulated over the horizon, and the approximation error, measured relative to the minimal cost over one horizon, fulfill a bound, this controller asymptotically stabilizes the system, also between sampling instants, on sublevel sets of the iterate from which its optimal trajectories end in the domain. This condition involves only the last iteration step and can be checked directly, without first establishing convergence of the iteration. We therefore see the present results as a first step towards sample-based certificates for approximate value functions: they identify which quantities must be certified, and relative to which costs. The same condition yields an explicit decrease of the iterate over each horizon and a bound on the closed-loop cost relative to the optimal infinite-horizon cost, which makes the trade-off between approximation accuracy, computational effort, and control performance explicit. papers.title: Search for Axion-like Particles using Blazar Observations with the HAWC Observatory
papers.abstract: Axion-like particles (ALPs) can mix with photons in astrophysical magnetic fields, modifying the propagation of very-high-energy gamma rays from distant blazars and producing an energy-dependent enhancement of the observed flux relative to the standard expectation from absorption on the extragalactic background light (EBL). We search for this signature through a joint likelihood analysis of seven TeV BL Lac objects at redshifts $z = 0.14-0.60$, combining approximately 3,000 days of HAWC observations with published High Energy Spectroscopic System (H.E.S.S.), Major Atmospheric Gamma Imaging Cherenkov Telescopes (MAGIC), and Very Energetic Radiation Imaging Telescope Array System(VERITAS) spectra. We find no statistically significant ALP signal and derive exclusion limits using the $\mathrm{CL}_s$ method. We exclude photon-ALP couplings at the 95% $\mathrm{CL}_s$ level down to $5.5 \times 10^{-12}~\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$ for $m_a \lesssim 4$ neV and $4.6 \times 10^{-12}~\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$ near $m_a \approx 6-9$ neV. The systematic uncertainty on the excluded parameter-space area is $-36.5\%$ to $+32.6\%$, dominated by the choice of EBL model. Because the survival probability oscillates with the coupling, the excluded region is not simply connected, and we quote at each mass the lowest excluded coupling rather than an upper bound. The combined limit is set almost entirely by the highest-redshift detected source, PG 1553+113.

papers.intro:
Axion-like particles (ALPs) are pseudoscalar particles that arise in many extensions of the Standard Model [1, 2], including string theory compactifications [3, 4]. Unlike the quantum chromodynamics (QCD) axion, whose mass and photon coupling are both set by the scale of Peccei-Quinn symmetry breaking [5, 6, 7], ALPs have an independent mass, mam_{a}, and two-photon coupling, ga​γ​γg_{a\gamma\gamma}. They are also viable candidates for cold dark matter [8, 9, 10, 11]. The two-photon coupling induces photon-ALP oscillations in external magnetic fields.

High-energy gamma rays emitted by distant extragalactic sources undergo energy-dependent attenuation via electron-positron pair production (γ​γ→e+​e−\gamma\gamma\rightarrow e^{+}e^{-}) upon interacting with the extragalactic background light (EBL) [12, 13, 14]. The EBL consists of the accumulated radiation from star formation and dust reprocessing over cosmic history. The optical depth, τ⁡(E,z)\tau(E,z), quantifies this attenuation as a function of gamma-ray energy, EE, and source redshift, zz, and depends on both the cosmological distance and the evolution of the EBL. This results in an exponential suppression of the intrinsic flux, ϕint​(E)\phi_{\mathrm{int}}(E): ϕobs​(E)=ϕint​(E)​e−τ⁡(E,z).\phi_{\mathrm{obs}}(E)=\phi_{\mathrm{int}}(E)\,e^{-\tau(E,z)}. (1) This attenuation becomes significant in the very-high-energy (VHE; E≳100E\gtrsim 100 GeV) regime and increases steeply with both energy and redshift.

Gamma rays can oscillate into ALPs when traversing magnetized environments. Because ALPs do not interact with the EBL, they propagate through intergalactic space unattenuated. If these ALPs subsequently reconvert into photons within other magnetized regions (e.g., the Galactic magnetic field; GMF), the net effect is an enhancement of the observed VHE gamma-ray flux relative to the standard EBL attenuation predictions. This phenomenon, referred to as “TeV transparency” [15, 16], is most pronounced at energies where EBL absorption is otherwise severe, so VHE observations provide a sensitive probe of the ALP parameter space. Photon-ALP mixing also produces spectral irregularities, since the conversion probability oscillates with energy [17, 18]. Searches for such irregularities require fine energy resolution over a well-measured spectrum, whereas the present work targets the transparency signature at multi-TeV energies, at which the attenuated flux is smallest and the relative enhancement largest. Several analyses have reported indications that the VHE gamma-ray opacity of the Universe is lower than predicted by EBL models [19, 20], an effect that photon-ALP conversion has been invoked to explain [21, 16], although the significance of these indications has been contested [22]. The present search constrains the ALP parameter space relevant to such interpretations.

While Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes (IACTs) are sensitive over a range from tens of GeV to tens of TeV [23], in practice their spectral measurements of distant blazars are limited to below a few TeV by increasing EBL attenuation [24]. The HAWC Observatory is sensitive from 0.3 TeV to 100 TeV [25] and provides coverage at multi-TeV energies where EBL attenuation is largest. In this work, we perform a joint likelihood fit combining published IACT flux points (described by a Gaussian likelihood) with HAWC data (described by a Poisson likelihood). The IACT flux points constrain the intrinsic blazar energy spectrum, while the HAWC data provide sensitivity to the ALP-induced transparency effect at higher energies. A previous search using the public 3HWC catalog fluxes set limits from a combined sample of seven TeV blazars [26]. The present work analyzes the same seven sources with the full HAWC dataset and its corresponding instrument response function (IRF).

HAWC is located at an altitude of 4,100 m on the Sierra Negra volcano in Puebla, Mexico [27]. The main array comprises 300 water Cherenkov detectors (WCDs), each instrumented with four photomultiplier tubes (PMTs), covering an area of approximately 22,000 m2. Since late 2018 the main array has been surrounded by an outrigger array of 345 smaller WCDs [28, 29]. The outriggers enlarge the instrumented area by approximately a factor of four and improve the reconstruction of showers with cores outside the main array above a few TeV. Outrigger data are not used in the Pass 5 reconstruction employed here. HAWC observes two-thirds of the sky every day with a duty cycle above 93%, enabling long-term monitoring of VHE gamma-ray sources [27].

papers.title: An Intergalactic medium centred parametrisation of the 21-cm power spectrum from the Epoch of Reionization
papers.abstract: The 21-cm signal from the intergalactic medium (IGM) is a key probe of the Epoch of Reionization (EoR). In this work, we present a model of the 21-cm power spectrum centred on the state of the IGM. The framework combines aspects of perturbation and percolation theory to deduce a physically informed parametrisation of the power spectrum. Moreover, it complements classical interpretation methods, centred on modelling the properties of the first ionising sources. We define the IGM parameters driving the shape and amplitude of the 21-cm signal, from the globally averaged volume- and mass-weighted ionisation fractions ($\bar{x}_{HII}$ and $\bar{x}_{HIIm}$), the clustering of sources, through the halo bias ($b_{\mathrm{h}}$), and the characteristic sizes of ionised regions ($R_{i}$) and neutral islands ($R_{n}$). We extend this analysis to model the redshift dependence of the power spectrum, constraining parameters such as the midpoint and duration of reionization. We test the IGM framework on three reionization simulations (C2-Ray, 21cmFAST, and POLAR) with varying cosmologies, astrophysics, and numerical assumptions. The framework constrains the IGM parameter space, recovers the midpoint and duration of the EoR as well as the minimum mass of halos hosting ionising sources $M_{\mathrm{min}}$, and the redshift evolution of the global ionisation fraction, the evolution of ionised and neutral regions (measured with the radial mean free path method by Georgiev et al. (2026b, submitted)). Moreover, the IGM framework lends itself to joint analysis with other EoR probes, such as high-redshift galaxies and quasars and the Cosmic Microwave Background.

papers.intro:
The first billion years of the Universe are a hallmark period, defined by the active formation and growth of the first galaxies. However, the first stars and active galactic nuclei not only affected the formation history of their host galaxies, but also actively shaped the state of the medium between them. The intergalactic medium (IGM), primarily consisting of neutral hydrogen (H i), was re-ionised by the ultraviolet photons from these first ionising sources, leading to a large-scale phase transition we refer to as the Epoch of Reionization (EoR). The EoR is a remarkable process as it is driven by the collective astrophysical properties of the first ionising sources, which themselves are tracers of cosmic structure (Zaroubi, 2013; McQuinn, 2016; Dayal and Ferrara, 2018). A key probe of reionization comes from observations of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), whose measurements of the Thomson optical depth from Planck Collaboration et al. (2020) have constrained a value of τ=0.054±0.007\tau=0.054\pm 0.007, corresponding to a midpoint of reionization of zre∼7.5z_{\mathrm{re}}\sim 7.5 (Cain et al., 2025; Sailer et al., 2026, though see). Moreover, studies of secondary CMB anisotropies such as the patchy kinetic Sunyaev-Zel’dovich effect (pkSZ) (Aghanim et al., 1996; Gruzinov and Hu, 1998) have placed a 2​σ2\sigma upper limit on the duration of reionization of Δ​z<4.1\Delta z<4.1 (Reichardt et al., 2021; Chaubal et al., 2026). Another key parameter of the progress of reionization is the global volume-averaged neutral hydrogen fraction (x¯H i\bar{x}_{\rm\text{H\,{i}}}). This can be probed by studying the spectra of the ionising sources themselves, as emitted Lyα\alpha photons will scatter as they travel across the neutral IGM during the EoR. Few examples of these are the observations of the Gunn-Peterson effect (Gunn and Peterson, 1965) in quasar (QSO) spectra (Fan et al., 2006; Mortlock et al., 2011; Greig et al., 2017; Bañados et al., 2018; Greig et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Becker et al., 2021) as well as studies of dark gaps (Zhu et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2022) and dark pixels (Davies et al., 2026). These studies have provided tight constraints on the final phases of reionization, estimating the end of the EoR to lie in the range zend≈5−5.5z_{\mathrm{end}}\approx 5-5.5 (Bosman et al., 2022). On the other hand, QSO spectra observations have also been shown to be able to constrain the sizes of neutral patches (RnR_{n}), referred to as H i islands (Becker et al., 2015). The advent of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has pushed our understanding of the EoR even further (Naidu et al., 2022; Robertson et al., 2023; Matsuoka et al., 2023; Donnan et al., 2024; Cameron et al., 2023, see), allowing for measurements of the global neutral fraction by studying the Lyα\alpha equivalent width (Tang et al., 2023; Nakane et al., 2024; Jones et al., 2024). Moreover, studies investigating the shape of the UV continuum redward of Lyα\alpha, the Lyα\alpha damping wing, have also placed constraints on x¯H i\bar{x}_{\rm\text{H\,{i}}} and the sizes of ionised regions during the EoR (RiR_{i}) (Curtis-Lake et al., 2023; Umeda et al., 2024; Mason et al., 2026). Furthermore, UV luminosity functions from high-redshift galaxies measured with the Hubble Space Telescope and the JWST have been used to constrain EoR properties (see Bouwens et al., 2021; Whitler et al., 2025; Atek et al., 2026, and references therein). Note, however, that estimates from a selection of ionising sources are sensitive to biasing due to sample variance and the role of their local diversity (see Lu et al., 2024, for a discussion).

One of the most prominent prospective probes of the EoR comes from the state of the IGM itself. This is due to the nature of neutral hydrogen, which can either emit or absorb photons with a rest wavelength of λ=21.106\lambda=21.106 cm (Wouthuysen, 1952; Field, 1957), depending on its hyperfine structure and coupling to the temperature of the IGM. Conversely, ionised hydrogen does not emit a 21-cm signal. Therefore, the temperature and ionisation state of the IGM can be probed directly by the 21-cm signal across a wide range of redshifts and profoundly impact our understanding of cosmology and astrophysics. One detection method consists of measuring the sky-averaged 21-cm signal using single-dish antennae. Such global 21-cm experiments include SARAS (Patra et al., 2015), SARAS2 (Singh et al., 2018), LEDA (Price et al., 2018), and EDGES (Bowman and Rogers, 2010) &\& EDGES 2 (Monsalve et al., 2017) as well as REACH (de Lera Acedo et al., 2022). While the EDGES team have claimed a detection of the signal (Bowman et al., 2018), its distinct and deep absorption profile has not been confirmed by the SARAS3 experiment (see Singh et al., 2022, for an overview). Another prospect is detecting the fluctuations in the 21-cm signal, a key science goal of multiple low-frequency radio interferometers. Examples of such telescopes include the Low-Frequency Array (LOFAR)11 1 www.lofar.org (van Haarlem et al., 2013), the New Extension in Nançay Upgrading LOFAR (NenuFAR) (Zarka et al., 2020), the Hydrogen Epoch of Reionization Array (HERA)22 2 https://reionization.org (DeBoer et al., 2017), the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA)33 3 www.mwatelescope.org (Bowman et al., 2013), and the forthcoming Square Kilometre Array (SKA)44 4 www.skatelescope.org (CD Science Working Group et al., 2026), whose increased sensitivity should also allow us to study tomographic data (Mellema et al., 2015). The power spectrum of the 21-cm signal is the first cornerstone for understanding the EoR (Furlanetto et al., 2006) and a key goal of the aforementioned radio interferometers.

papers.title: Radial mean free path bubble size distribution (RMFP-BSD) from the Epoch of Reionization
papers.abstract: Among the many statistics used to characterise ionised regions during the Epoch of Reionization (EoR), we introduce one which, while closely related to the mean free path bubble size distribution method from Mesinger et al. 2007, is analytically tractable and substantially less dispersive than that method. The radial mean free path (rmfp) method casts six rays along the Cartesian axes in a 3D volume from a random origin to a neutral hydrogen island. This allows us to better quantify the role of overlap during the EoR, identify isolated or interconnected clusters in the simulation, and study the characteristic peak in the ionisation power spectrum, which is important for 21-cm studies of the intergalactic medium. Moreover, we find the method informative about the properties of neutral H I islands during the final phases of the EoR. We also show that applying both methods in tandem can further improve our insight into the morphology of reionization.

papers.intro:
The Epoch of Reionization (EoR) is a key period within the first billion years of the Universe, when the light from the first stars, galaxies, and accreting black holes reionised the neutral intergalactic medium (IGM) (Zaroubi, 2013). Studies of the ionisation morphology can yield critical insight into the first ionising sources and are actively being explored using Lyα\alpha damping wings (Mason et al., 2026), Lyα\alpha emitting galaxies (Hayes and Scarlata, 2023), as well as quasar spectra (Bosman et al., 2022). However, it is the 21-cm signal from the neutral hydrogen in the IGM during the EoR that offers the most direct three-dimensional probe of this process (Giri et al., 2018). Hence, a multitude of methods have been applied to characterise the properties of ionised regions in simulations such as the Friends of Friends (Iliev et al., 2006), Minkowski functionals (Gleser et al., 2006), Spherical-Average (Zahn et al., 2007), Granulometry (Kakiichi et al., 2017), Opening transforms (Busch et al., 2020), Watershed (Lin et al., 2016), and Betti numbers (Giri and Mellema, 2021). Comparative studies such as those of Lin et al. (2016), Kakiichi et al. (2017), and Giri et al. (2018) have examined these methods, each favouring a different approach. Here we adopt the mean free path bubble size distribution method (MFP-BSD, hereafter mfp) (Mesinger and Furlanetto, 2007), which Giri et al. (2018) found to perform best at tracking the progress of reionization and separating different reionization scenarios. In this method, random rays are drawn within an ionised region and traced up to a neutral island. As a result, it samples both very short and very long lines of sight, which broadens the distribution. In this work, we introduce a new method inspired by the mfp that reduces this smearing and, in doing so, introduces a novel summary statistic to the community. We briefly introduce the theory in Sec. 2, applications in Sec. 3, and conclude in Sec. 4.

Hence, a multitude of methods have been applied to characterise the properties of ionised regions in simulations such as the Friends of Friends (Iliev et al., 2006), Minkowski functionals (Gleser et al., 2006), Spherical-Average (Zahn et al., 2007), Granulometry (Kakiichi et al., 2017), Opening transforms (Busch et al., 2020), Watershed (Lin et al., 2016), and Betti numbers (Giri and Mellema, 2021). Comparative studies such as those of Lin et al. (2016), Kakiichi et al. (2017), and Giri et al. (2018) have examined these methods, each favouring a different approach. Here we adopt the mean free path bubble size distribution method (MFP-BSD, hereafter mfp) (Mesinger and Furlanetto, 2007), which Giri et al. (2018) found to perform best at tracking the progress of reionization and separating different reionization scenarios. In this method, random rays are drawn within an ionised region and traced up to a neutral island. As a result, it samples both very short and very long lines of sight, which broadens the distribution. In this work, we introduce a new method inspired by the mfp that reduces this smearing and, in doing so, introduces a novel summary statistic to the community. We briefly introduce the theory in Sec. 2, applications in Sec. 3, and conclude in Sec. 4.

papers.title: TrialAgentBench: Evaluating AI Agents for Clinical-Trial Analysis and Long-Horizon Drug-Development Decisions
papers.abstract: Clinical drug development is a long-horizon, high-stakes process requiring sequential decisions based on information that costs money and time to acquire. AI agents have demonstrated capabilities for scientific analysis, but there is no established way to evaluate them on these decisions, as real trials are expensive, involve people, and never reveal the counterfactual. We introduce TrialAgentBench, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on clinical trial analysis and drug development decision-making using simulated trials where the truth is known, embedded within the data records of a fictional drug sponsor. We publicly release nearly 3,500 tasks, varying from analysing a single trial to managing multi-phase programmes with budget and time constraints. We score each analysis by rerunning its code on new trials, and each programme by the value its decisions achieve. Across 24 closed- and open-weight models, the strongest agents can analyse raw, messy trial records to within 6% of a process-aware analysis, even when an assumption is violated, with 95% confidence intervals containing the true effect 94--95% of the time. Over the prior year, the best model improved from 19% above this analysis, with serious misses on 15% of tasks, to 3.5% and 1%. What limits them is decision-making from evidence under uncertainty: when to correct, what evidence to buy, when to stop. The strongest agents are overly careful, correcting on 83% of tasks with equal recording errors, where it is unnecessary. On drug programmes, the best agent has substantial headroom, reaching 48% of the value an oracle achieves against 58% for a rule-based developer, with others falling 24 to 66% short. Model generations show ongoing improvements in handling data and evidence, with substantial variation. The strongest models can act as competent analysts, but do not yet make reliable long-horizon decisions.

papers.intro:
New medicines are one of the most direct ways that science can improve people’s lives. Every medicine that makes it to patients has the potential to cure a disease, slow its progression, or spare a patient from a worse treatment. The hope is that clinical trials can be made faster, cheaper, and better, so that more medicines can reach patients sooner and with stronger evidence. AI agents could help us get there. The path to developing a new drug is long and costly: including failures, the median cost to develop a drug is US$1.1 billion [1], and most drug candidates that enter clinical trials are never approved [2]. Every decision along the way has to balance time and money against information. A pilot study may lead to a sponsor abandoning a promising drug or designing an underpowered follow-up study [3], and a small, borderline result can just as easily commit a sponsor to years of work. In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a phase 2 study of dexpramipexole that was not powered for efficacy compared two doses in 92 participants in its second part and reached P = 0.046, which its authors said strongly supported further testing. The phase 3 trial that followed enrolled 943 participants and showed no benefit over placebo [4, 5].

Drug development is a multi-phase process, where each step is designed based on the results of the previous one. The results of a safety study determine the regimens tested next, the results of an exploration study determine the most promising candidate to advance, and its estimated effect guides the size of the subsequent confirmation trial, which may take years. Obtaining accurate results requires aligning trial data with the study protocol, handling participant dropout and treatment switching, considering the trial design, and verifying the quality of site records. An analysis that gets these wrong can still produce a precise estimate with a narrow interval. If the effect is overestimated by one standard error, the follow-up trial will be about half the size it needs to be, reducing the chance of detecting a true benefit from 80% to about 54%, so a drug that works may fail after years of development. If the effect is underestimated by one standard error, the follow-up trial will be over twice as large as needed, and the cost may lead a sponsor to abandon a drug that works.

AI agents have demonstrated strong performance in writing code and analysing data. But can we trust them to perform these analyses and make the decisions that depend on them? Real-world data cannot answer this question, because the true effect is never observed. Reanalysing published clinical trials can lead to different conclusions [6], and different analysts can produce different estimates from the same dataset [7]. An evaluation on real data can test whether agents can replicate the original analysis, flaws included, but not whether they can recover the truth. Statisticians have long faced this challenge when developing new methods, and address it by evaluating their methods on simulated data where the true effect is known [8, 9]. Regulators such as the FDA similarly use simulation to evaluate complex clinical trial designs [10].

TrialAgentBench brings this approach to AI agents, for both the analyses and the decisions that depend on them. In TrialEval, an agent is given a completed trial’s documents and raw data records. It must align these records with the documents, analyse them, and save its analysis as a script, which we rerun on new trials. The 420 public tasks cover 17 clinical questions, from childbirth safety to metastatic cancer, across trial designs from individual randomisation to stepped-wedge rollouts and sizes from 52 to 114,000 participants. In TrialDev, an agent manages a drug development programme. Given 3 or 5 candidates, a budget of up to US$314 million, and six years, it must decide which studies to purchase across three phases, from at least 102110^{21} combinations of study designs, read the results as they arrive, and decide when to stop and which drug to advance. Each of the 384 public programmes (3,072 tasks) is built on a simulated population of 64,000 participants. As for a real sponsor, a programme is worth the profit an approved drug generates over its market lifetime, minus the cost of harm, all studies, and each day it runs. We evaluate 24 models on TrialEval and 10 on TrialDev, and release the tasks, harness, replication trials, and an independent verifier.

papers.title: Interface-Engineered Piezoelectricity and Electromechanical Coupling in Two-Dimensional van der Waals Heterostructures
papers.abstract: Interfaces between dissimilar two-dimensional (2D) materials provide a route to engineer electromechanical responses that are not intrinsic to the individual constituent layers. Here, we use high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate 461 van der Waals heterostructures constructed from 57 2D monolayers and establish a materials-design framework linking work-function mismatch, interfacial charge redistribution, dipole formation, and strain-dependent electromechanical response. We find that heterostructure formation generates out-of-plane interfacial dipoles via charge redistribution between the constituent layers, while biaxial in-plane strain systematically modulates them. The resulting heterostructures exhibit two distinct regimes: metallic interfaces with strain-tunable interfacial dipoles and semiconducting heterostructures with well-defined piezoelectric responses. For the latter, Berry-phase (BP) calculations independently validate the charge-density-difference (CDD) approach, which is generally applicable to all representative systems, with piezoelectric coefficients calculated via two methods agreeing to within 10%. Among 24 selected heterostructures, effective biaxial interfacial electromechanical coefficients reach 83.35 pCm-1 . These results demonstrate that the interface can serve as the active element governing electromechanical coupling and provide a computationally guided strategy for designing strain-tunable out-of-plane electromechanical responses in 2D van der Waals heterostructures.

papers.intro:
The discovery of 2D materials has opened new opportunities in nanotechnology because of their remarkable structural, electronic, and mechanical properties. Their atomic-scale thickness, mechanical flexibility, and strong sensitivity to external perturbations make them promising for a wide range of nanoscale applications. Among these materials, graphene played a central role in establishing the field of 2D materials, while subsequent studies have revealed many other monolayers with semiconducting, magnetic, ferroelectric, and piezoelectric properties Dresselhaus and Araujo (2010); Puri and Bhowmick (2018); Sarkar et al. (2020); Naseer et al. (2024); Zelisko et al. (2014).

(2020); Naseer et al. (2024); Zelisko et al. (2014).

In recent years, considerable attention has been devoted to vertically stacking different monolayers to form van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures (HSs) Novoselov et al. (2016). Because weak vdW interactions hold the constituent layers together, they can be combined without the strict lattice-matching requirements of conventional HSs. At the same time, interfacial charge transfer, orbital hybridization, and symmetry breaking can generate properties that are absent in the isolated monolayers. As a result, vdW HSs have emerged as versatile platforms for electronic, optoelectronic, sensing, and energy-harvesting applications Yuan et al. (2020); Chen et al. (2021); Yadav et al. (2025). Several 2D HSs, including PtSe2/PtTe2 Li et al. (2023) and MoS2/PtSe2 Rizu et al. (2025), have already been investigated experimentally.

Among the many functionalities of 2D materials, electromechanical coupling or piezoelectricity is particularly attractive because it enables the direct conversion of mechanical deformation into electrical polarization Blonsky et al. (2015). The piezoelectric effect refers to the generation of an electric response under applied strain or stress and is widely used in sensors, transistors, wearable electronics, and energy-harvesting devices Wang et al. (2006); Ong and Reed (2012). Piezoelectric materials are also being explored for harvesting mechanical energy from ambient sources such as human motion, wind, flowing water, and ocean waves, offering a potential route toward sustainable, self-powered technologies. Piezoelectricity requires the absence of inversion symmetry. Although many bulk crystals are centrosymmetric and therefore nonpiezoelectric, reducing a material to the monolayer limit can alter its symmetry and activate piezoelectric behavior. This possibility was first predicted theoretically and later confirmed experimentally in transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), including MoS2 and WS2 Duerloo et al. (2012); Zhu et al. (2015). These studies established 2D materials as promising candidates for nanoscale piezoelectric and piezotronic applications.

Using high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we systematically investigate 461 van der Waals heterostructures constructed from 57 two-dimensional monolayers to establish how interface formation can be used to engineer out-of-plane electromechanical responses. We consider metal–metal (M–M), metal–semiconductor (M–S), and semiconductor–semiconductor (S–S) heterostructures and examine the relationship between work-function mismatch, interfacial charge redistribution, dipole formation, and the response to biaxial in-plane strain. This analysis reveals two distinct electromechanical regimes. In M–M and M–S heterostructures, interface-induced charge redistribution produces strain-tunable out-of-plane interfacial dipoles, providing an electromechanical response without invoking a conventional bulk polarization in metallic systems. In S–S heterostructures, the interfacial dipole can be expressed as a macroscopic polarization and quantified within the conventional piezoelectric framework. We further validate the charge-density-difference approach against Berry-phase calculations for representative S–S heterostructures. The complete workflow is illustrated in Figure 1. By identifying the interface, rather than the isolated monolayer, as the active element governing the electromechanical response, this work provides a materials-design strategy for developing strain-tunable out-of-plane electromechanical functionality in 2D van der Waals heterostructures.

papers.title: Preliminary evidence for a Universal Magnetic Field Configuration in Disk-Galaxy Halos with POSSUM
papers.abstract: We use the POSSUM catalog with its high density of background RM sources (30-50 per square degree) to extend previous LOFAR work and investigate the sign of galactic halo magnetic fields. We are searching for the universal configuration that arises if halo magnetization originates from a central Cosmic Battery, and is subsequently transported outward by large-scale outflows. Our analysis considers 10 edge-on galaxies in the field of view of the POSSUM survey with angular sizes between 60 and 100. For each such galaxy we collect all available background RM sources in a circular region with a radius of 2? around it. We rescale all galaxy sizes and their associated background RM source distances to a common galaxy size of 100 and stack all these regions together. We divide the stacked configuration of RM sources into the four quadrants on either side of the stacked galaxy axis. The mean RM of background sources is computed in each quadrant, and we obtain a pattern of positive and negative mean RM values around the stacked galaxy. A consistent, systematic RM-gradient pattern emerges inside about 6 stacked galactic radii, as expected in Magnetic Disk-Winds with the axial magnetic field configuration predicted by the Cosmic Battery. The inferred large-scale axial electric current in the halo flows from the center outwards. Beyond 6 galactic radii we observe the reverse mean RM pattern, as expected in the axial Magnetic Black-Hole Jet configuration predicted by the Cosmic Battery. Our work confirms the prediction of the Cosmic Battery, and presents one of the very few known signatures of the magnetic field in the halo and the circumgalactic medium (CGM).

papers.title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment
papers.abstract: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.

papers.intro:
Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models are increasingly transitioning from disembodied cloud services to real-world physical agents, including autonomous robotics, robotic manipulation, and edge cyber-physical systems [38]. As embodied AI systems are granted direct agency over physical actuators and human-adjacent environments, enforcing strict behavioral guardrails is paramount. Current safety paradigms rely almost exclusively on algorithmic alignment – employing techniques such as reinforcement learning and safety fine-tuning to ensure that agents reject hazardous, destructive, or safety policy-violating commands. Consequently, adversarial “jailbreaking” has emerged as a critical concern, prompting extensive study into prompt manipulation and motivating stringent regulatory mandates for safety assurance [1].

Consequently, adversarial “jailbreaking” has emerged as a critical concern, prompting extensive study into prompt manipulation and motivating stringent regulatory mandates for safety assurance [1].

Despite extensive research into prompt- and representation-level jailbreaking, existing safety evaluations share a fundamental, unexamined assumption: the underlying hardware execution is computationally faithful and physically uncompromised [13, 27]. While this assumption largely holds in remote cloud environments, physical tampering becomes a realistic threat as inference shifts toward untrusted edge devices and field-deployed robotics. Most existing software-level defenses focus on filtering input and output tokens or steering latent activations [14, 51], yet physical threats to the edge hardware accelerators powering these robotic platforms remain largely unaddressed. At the same time, mechanistic studies reveal that safety refusal in aligned models is mediated by compact, low-rank subspaces and localized projection matrices [2] suggesting that targeted editing of the model with physical attacks may disrupt safety.

In this paper, we demonstrate that if an adversary with physical access can selectively disrupt memory transactions during these critical computational steps with either transient or persistent faults, the software-level alignment stack collapses entirely, allowing malicious instructions to bypass high-level guardrails and trigger unsafe real-world actions (Figure 1). Particularly, we demonstrate the first physical fault injection attack capable of eliminating refusal in aligned models running on production edge Systems-on-Chip (SoCs). We use a non-invasive Electromagnetic Fault Injection (EMFI) attack and target popular embedded GPU platform – namely NVIDIA Jetson architecture common in modern robotics. Our methodology leverages an autonomous RF side-channel trigger derived from near-field GPU emanations, synchronizing EM pulses directly to safety-critical projection layers during the prompt prefill phase without requiring invasive device modification beyond heatsink removal. By corrupting memory transactions across on-chip LPDDR physical layers (PHY) and off-chip DRAM packages, localized EM pulses flip critical values that are read or written. Crucially, this neutralizes the model’s refusal behavior while maintaining coherence and system stability.

papers.title: Anomalous Field-induced Coherence beyond Single-ion Kondo Physics
papers.abstract: The emergence of coherent heavy quasiparticles in Kondo lattices is generally accompanied by a reduction in electrical resistivity at low temperatures. However, certain strongly correlated metals exhibit anomalously large resistivities that persist to very low temperatures, raising fundamental questions about the mechanisms governing charge transport. Here, we report an unusual magnetic field-induced evolution of electronic transport and thermodynamic properties in a Ce-based heavy fermion compound, Ce$_{2}$Rh$_{3}$Ga$_{5}$. At zero field, Ce$_{2}$Rh$_{3}$Ga$_{5}$ undergoes a magnetic transition at $T$$_{0}$ = 0.45 K and exhibits a strongly enhanced low temperature specific heat coefficient, reaching $C$/$T$ = 2.2 J/mol$_{Ce}$-K$^{2}$, but no discernible coherence in its electrical resistivity. Remarkably, applying a magnetic field produces a large negative magnetoresistance and restores coherent metallic behavior, characterized by low-temperature $T$$^2$ resistivity. Although the field dependence of the electronic specific heat coefficient can be described phenomenologically within a single-ion Kondo framework, the same description fails to account for the strong suppression of the residual resistivity and the overall magnetoresistance. These results point to an additional field-sensitive scattering contribution beyond conventional single-ion Kondo physics. The striking resemblance to the long-standing anomalous magnetotransport behavior of UBe$_{13}$, without the complications introduced by superconductivity, establishes Ce$_{2}$Rh$_{3}$Ga$_{5}$ as a platform for investigating the microscopic origin of anomalous scattering and field-induced coherent transport in strongly correlated electron systems.

papers.intro:
Electrical transport in strongly correlated electron systems is governed by the intricate interplay between localized magnetic moments and itinerant charge carriers [1, 2]. In heavy-fermion compounds based on Ce, Yb, and U, the Kondo interaction produces strong electronic correlations that substantially renormalize the quasiparticle masses and influence their scattering processes [3, 4]. At elevated temperatures, incoherent scattering from local magnetic moments dominates the resistivity, whereas lowering the temperature typically leads to the emergence of a coherent Kondo-lattice state, resulting in a typical resistivity maximum at intermediate temperatures, followed by a pronounced decrease at low temperatures [5, 6, 7]. Applied magnetic fields further modify these processes by suppressing spin-flip scattering and altering the characteristic energy scales of the correlated electronic state [8, 9, 10]. Although such behavior is well understood within the Kondo and heavy-fermion frameworks, the occurrence of exceptionally large low-temperature resistivities and their dramatic suppression by magnetic fields in certain strongly correlated materials remains a challenge [11]. Whether these anomalous transport responses can be explained entirely by conventional Kondo scattering or require additional field-sensitive scattering processes is an important unresolved question.

papers.title: Head Anything: Correspondence-Guided Joint Generation of 3D Heads from Few Images
papers.abstract: Large image-to-3D generators recover detailed heads from a single photograph but treat every image as a new object. For several images of one person, they hallucinate unseen regions independently without using information from the other images. We present Head Anything, which generates detailed head meshes from a few images with changing expressions and viewpoints. Instead of training a multi-image prior, we turn a pretrained single-image generator with a native 3D latent space into a joint generator that denoises all images together. Since global attention between images is hard to learn from scarce 3D head data, lightweight correspondence-attention adapters let every 3D token attend only to its corresponding points in the other images. We obtain correspondences by fitting a neural parametric head model to the generator's own single-image outputs, requiring no ground truth at test time. Training on both ground-truth and fitted correspondences makes the adapters robust to fitting errors. Each mesh stays pixel-aligned with its own image and borrows the unseen regions from all others. On head scans, Head Anything lowers the head Chamfer distance of the best image-to-3D generator by 32% and its cross-frame inconsistency by 47%, and its meshes improve face tracking. Code and models will be released.

Telepresence, games, film production and virtual try-on need the 3D geometry of a person’s head, including the hair, the ears and the back of the head, at a level of detail that today requires a multi-view capture studio [17, 26]. Most images of people, however, come from casual videos or photo collections, such as those in Fig. 1, and depict the head from varying viewpoints and with different expressions. Recovering complete, detailed and mutually consistent meshes from such images would make studio-quality head geometry available from everyday data, with every mesh following its own image and benefiting from what the others reveal.

papers.title: Topological Fairness in Continuous-State Systems
papers.abstract: Since the early days of probabilistic programs, fairness has been used to abstract randomness in software. Intuitively, a fair scheduler reproduces the almost-sure behavior of a random choice based solely on the set of possible outcomes, independent of their (often unknown) distribution. As this abstraction attaches fairness to individual transitions, it becomes ineffective over uncountable state spaces, where every single successor has probability zero. We overcome this limitation by imposing fairness on open sets instead. This leads to the novel notion of topological fairness: every basic open set---with respect to a countable basis of the state-space topology---that lies in the set of possible successors infinitely often must be visited infinitely often. We show that topological fairness carries the intuition from program abstraction to continuous state spaces. For systems with additive stochastic disturbances, almost every trajectory is topologically fair under every control policy. Reasoning over all topologically fair trajectories is therefore a sound proof principle for almost-sure properties of the original system. Unlike in the finite-state case, however, it is not complete: topological fairness cannot capture almost-sure behavior that hinges on the relative likelihoods of disturbance outcomes. Finally, we show that topological fairness supports synthesis directly on the continuous state space. For reach-avoid objectives, we give a nested fixed point over subsets of the state space which, for a broad class of systems, computes the fair winning domain exactly together with a memoryless winning strategy. Our case studies show that this winning domain is substantially larger than the one obtained with currently available techniques, which detour through a finite abstraction and certify a winning domain that depends on the discretization in a non-monotone way.

papers.intro:
In controller synthesis for continuous-state dynamical systems, stochastic disturbances are typically handled in one of two ways. On one hand, a probabilistic model can be used which represents the likelihood of each disturbance realization. Its analysis is precise, but may require numerical transition probabilities and operations over probability distributions. On the other hand, an adversarial model retains only the set of possible disturbance values, i.e., the support of each probabilistic choice, and is hence independent of its often unknown distribution. The adversarial model is often much simpler to analyze, but places no restriction on how disturbances occur over time. Hence, synthesis under an adversarial model may reject a controller because of disturbance realizations that form a probability-zero event under the stochastic model.

Our first main result establishes that topological fairness is indeed a fair model in the sense above. The proof relies on the fact that each fixed basis element has a uniform positive probability of being visited whenever it is enabled, together with a conditional form of the Borel–Cantelli lemma.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Learning machine learning: Investigating the complementarity and biases of strong gravitational lens finding networks on Euclid data
papers.abstract: The Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) strong lens search presents ECLIPSE, the largest catalogue of strong gravitational lens candidates to date, with >15 000 systems identified across 1900 deg2 of sky. It was constructed using five neural networks applied to approximately 68 million galaxies, followed by citizen science and expert visual inspection. In this work, we compare how the independently developed networks use image information to identify their selection of strong lens candidates. The search combines convolutional neural networks and a vision transformer, using the same pool of data but with different image processing and training choices. We investigate why these networks find different systems and what that means for the completeness of our catalogue. We evaluate all networks on a 50 deg2 calibration set and their application to the full DR1 sample. We find that the networks score candidates very differently, and that combining them recovers over 500 lens candidates within our calibration set at an inspection budget of 2000 objects. On the full DR1 sample, we show that individual networks have distinct biases: some networks favour systems with a larger Einstein radius while others are more sensitive to compact configurations. We also investigate network preferences in terms of lens light profile, mass distribution geometry, photometric redshift, and magnitudes. These findings provide a detailed analysis of how neural network selection biases have shaped the Euclid DR1 ECLIPSE catalogue. The results inform how networks should be combined in future Euclid data releases and upcoming wide-field surveys such as LSST or Roman to maximise both completeness and diversity of the recovered lens population.

papers.intro:
Strong gravitational lensing is a phenomenon in our universe where the mass of a foreground galaxy visibly distorts the light of a background source. Understanding these rare systems broadens our capability to study mass distributions in galaxies (Gavazzi et al. 2007; Nightingale et al. 2019; Sonnenfeld 2024; Shajib et al. 2024, e.g.,), observe distant sources (Welch et al. 2022), understand core cosmological parameters such as the Hubble constant (Wong et al. 2020; TDCOSMO Collaboration 2025), and the potential properties of dark matter and dark energy (Vegetti et al. 2024; Li et al. 2024).

The current known strong lens candidates have been identified using a number of methods, from serendipitous discoveries (Walsh et al. 1979, e.g.,), feature extraction methods (Alard 2006; Gavazzi et al. 2014; Joseph et al. 2014, e.g.,), to more modern techniques such as deep learning using neural networks (Euclid Collaboration: Lines et al. 2026a; Storfer et al. 2026, NN; e.g.,). Using these methods across many individual surveys has increased the number of known strong lens candidates from hundreds to thousands over the recent years (Jacobs et al. 2017; Petrillo et al. 2017; Huang et al. 2021, e.g.,). Building on Q1, for the Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1; Euclid Data Release 1 2026), we search for strong lens systems in an area of ∼\sim1900 deg2. To build the DR1 strong lens catalogue, we use five independently developed NN to score and rank all objects. While the use of multiple NN is already established (Savary et al. 2022; Andika et al. 2023; Schuldt et al. 2025; Gonzalez et al. 2025; Herle et al. 2024, e.g.,), with the DR1 search now operating at a much larger scale, understanding the behaviour of these networks becomes more important. Each network differs in architecture, training data input, and training strategy, which means they may be sensitive to different types of lens systems. While the Q1 search already showed that combining networks recovers more candidates than any individual network, it remains unclear what drives these differences. Do the networks find different systems because they respond to different physical properties of the lens, such as Einstein radius, galaxy morphology, or brightness? And if so, does our combination of networks introduce biases into the final catalogue by over-representing certain types of systems?

Furthermore, Euclid Collaboration: Li and others (2026) presents a set of double-source plane lenses, Euclid Collaboration: Ecker et al. (2026) presents an analysis on impact of image processing for neural networks, and Euclid Collaboration: Vincken et al. (2026a) provides a new method for automated creation of segmentation maps for strong lens components. Using these outputs, we investigate whether individual networks show preferences for particular lens properties, where biases lie, and whether the networks are complementary in providing a complete selection for our catalogue.

papers.title: Lyris: Layout-Guided Long Video Generation with Persistent 3D Memory
papers.abstract: Exploring a scene from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough that extends far beyond what was captured, yet remains consistent upon return. Memory-based video generation methods preserve what they have already seen, but have no anchor beyond it, where the camera drifts from its path and a text prompt can name objects but not place them. Layout-conditioned methods provide such an anchor and precise control over what appears where, but rely on layouts that are typically authored by hand. Both limitations arise because, beyond what was captured, nothing anchors the video model unless a human authors one. To overcome both, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework that never leaves the video model without an anchor: a persistent point-cloud memory where the scene has been observed or generated, and a 3D layout that a vision-language model authors where it has not. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse. A layout of one labeled 3D box per object is simple enough for a vision-language model to author (and for a user to edit), yet expressive enough for a video model to follow once rendered along the camera path. We demonstrate walkthroughs of over three minutes and 50 meters from a single photo, passing through doorways into rooms it never shows. When evaluated on minute-long round trips across four datasets, Lyris outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin, reducing camera error by 3.8x and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average.

Virtual touring [61], content creation, and simulation for physical AI [62, 4] benefit from 3D environments that can be explored freely. Creating such environments from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough beyond the captured view, passing through doorways and into unseen rooms. These regions must form a plausible extension of the observed scene and retain their layout and appearance when the camera returns.

Recent video generative models [60, 51, 52] can generate photorealistic clips from an image and a text prompt, but only seconds at a time. Memory-based methods extend them to long rollouts by conditioning each new chunk on the history, through compressed or retrieved past views [86, 41, 57, 29], learned implicit representations [88, 72], or explicitly reconstructed geometry [95, 12, 49]. This memory preserves what has already been seen but offers nothing beyond it. There, the camera path reaches the model only as a pose encoding [57, 90], a far weaker signal than rendered geometry [54, 10], and the camera drifts from its path as unseen regions accumulate. The content of the unseen regions is left to the text prompt, which can name objects and relate them coarsely, but cannot specify where they belong or how one space connects to the next. Layout-conditioned methods instead condition generation on an explicit scene layout, such as untextured geometry, object boxes, or maps [36, 5, 48], and offer precise control over the spatial arrangement of the objects. However, these methods take the layout as an input, typically authored by hand, which does not scale to open-ended exploration.

papers.title: Simulation of the oscillation-induced self-propulsion of an immersed body
papers.abstract: We are studying the dynamics of a rigid body that is immersed in an incompressible fluid and exposed to a periodic forcing. The fundamental question is, whether a non-zero average velocity of the body can result, if it is driven by a zero-average force. Recently we have proven exactly such theoretical guarantees for self-propulsion in the case of forces with average zero. This paper is devoted to the numerical simulation of this phenomenon. The problem is non-trivial, as periodic-in-time solutions must be identified to correctly describe the limit dynamics of this coupled problem. Although the body undergoes oscillations with a substantial amplitude the mean velocity will always be smaller by some orders and close to zero. We will derive several acceleration schemes to identify periodic solutions to flow problems. We show numerically the robustness of our scheme with respect to the physical and numerical parameters.

In this paper, we will describe numerical solution methods for efficiently finding an exact periodic solution for a fluid-solid system. We describe the fluid using the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations and the solid using standard Newtonian mechanics. The main challenge is the very slow convergence of a solution to the periodic limit, which typically behaves like exp(−1/Re)\exp(-1/Re), where R​eRe is the Reynolds number. Since we expect non-zero average motion only for larger Reynolds numbers we cannot take R​eRe too small. We will therefore introduce acceleration schemes that allow us to reach fast convergence towards the periodic solution robustly with respect to the Reynolds number (as long as R​eRe is such that a periodic solution exists). The approach is based on an averaging scheme for finding periodic solutions to flow problem [22].

papers.title: Conceptual Design of a 5 MV High-Voltage System for a Compact Orbitron Fusion Device
papers.abstract: The high-voltage system is a key part of the puzzle toward achieving net-positive fusion power in a compact Orbitron device. This paper presents a conceptual engineering design for a 5 MV, 20 mA, 100 kW HV system for a next-generation Orbitron, serving as an upper-bound design point for the HV system. The MC-TRANS++ 0-D code is used to set the load requirements: a 1 m long, 0.45 m first-wall-radius central cell, 2.5 T on-axis and 10 T mirror-throat fields, and a 5 MV radial potential drop sustaining supersonic rotation ($M = 4.8$). This delivers a triple product of $5.8 \times 10^{21}$ keV s /m3 and $Q_{sci}$ = 8.5. The HV power supply integrates an AC-DC converter, a SiC full-bridge inverter, a CLLC resonant network with an air-core step-up transformer, and feeds a 120-stage parallel-fed series-cascaded rectifier operating at 250 kHz. At full load, this architecture yields an end-to-end efficiency of 85%, much higher than the 60% typical of triode-driven MV-class power supplies. The 5 MV voltage is delivered to a radially nested 50-gap bushing system that interfaces pressurized insulating gas to high vacuum, using brazed alumina spacers with a corrugated profile. The design draws directly on the measured behavior of a previously demonstrated 300 kV prototype, from which six quantitative lessons are extracted and mapped onto the 5 MV design. Electrostatic simulations of the complete assembly at rated voltage show maximum surface fields of 30.3 MV/m on the corona rings, 7.7 MV/m at the cathode triple junction, and average vacuum-gap fields ranging from 5.5 to 40 MV/m. These field strengths remain below breakdown thresholds due to the implementation of triple-junction shielding, insulation corrugation, and axial magnetic insulation at 2.5-10 T. The conceptual system has a form factor of 2.7 meters in diameter and 6.5 meters in length, projected to deliver a net power output of 86-171 kWe.

papers.title: A Novel Multi-Target Approach for simultaneous enhancement of brightness, intensity, and bi-spectral performance of cold neutron sources
papers.abstract:
Increasing the brightness of cold neutron beams is a central objective in modern cold neutron source development, since it largely governs the sample intensity for high-resolution neutron instruments. Raising accelerator beam power is constrained by the target heat-removal limit of 0.5-1 kW/cm2, and increasing the moderator length beyond about 20-30 cm becomes inefficient owing to the finite mean free path of cold neutrons. We propose reversing the conventional design logic: rather than tailoring the cryogenic moderator to a fixed target-premoderator source, we tailor the thermal-neutron source geometry to a high-performance moderator configuration.
  The concept is realized as a staircase moderator assembly of several shorter compressed moderators, each with its own target-premoderator unit, which distributes neutron production among multiple units and thus enables higher accelerator powers while preserving the brightness advantages of compressed moderators. This approach can provide additional brightness and intensity gains relative to a single low-dimensional or conventional voluminous moderator at the desired transverse beam size and may naturally generate bi-spectral neutron beams, thereby extending the dynamic range of neutron instruments.
