papers.title: Redshift-space 3$\times$2pt statistics of galaxy clustering and intrinsic alignments at one-loop order
papers.abstract: Intrinsic alignments of galaxies, long regarded as a systematic in weak lensing, are now recognized as a cosmological probe complementary to galaxy clustering. Exploiting them with spectroscopic surveys requires accurate models in redshift space beyond the linear regime. In this work, we derive the galaxy density--shape cross-power spectrum and shape auto-power spectra at one-loop order in redshift space. We consider two models, one based on the effective field theory (EFT) and the other on the Taruya--Nishimichi--Saito (TNS) prescription. They share the bias expansion but differ in how they treat small-scale velocities along the line of sight. The EFT model expands the effects of these velocities perturbatively and absorbs their sensitivity to small scales into counterterms. We show that, for the sky-projected shape field, this model requires six renormalized bias parameters and two counterterms. Up to order $k^2$, the stochastic terms require two parameters for the cross spectrum and four parameters for the auto spectra. The TNS-based model keeps the one-point velocity dispersion in an unexpanded damping factor and treats it as a single free parameter. We extend our previous linear-bias TNS-based model of the cross spectrum to nonlinear bias and the shape auto spectra. We find that all loop integrals reduce to those already used for shape spectra in real space and galaxy clustering in redshift space, and we evaluate them with FFTLog. We compare both models with power spectra measured from halos in $N$-body simulations and find good agreement on mildly nonlinear scales. These models provide a basis for joint cosmological analyses of galaxy clustering and intrinsic alignments with imaging and spectroscopic galaxy surveys, in which intrinsic alignments are utilized as a cosmological probe.

papers.intro:
Spatial correlations between the unlensed shapes of galaxies, known as intrinsic alignments (IAs), have been studied extensively for their impact on cosmological inference from galaxy surveys (Chisari, 2025). In weak lensing analyses, IAs are a major systematic that can bias cosmological parameter estimates if not properly accounted for Croft and Metzler (2000); Hirata and Seljak (2004) (see Joachimi et al., 2015; Kiessling et al., 2015; Kirk et al., 2015; Troxel and Ishak, 2015; Lamman et al., 2024; Chisari, 2025, for reviews) This has motivated the development of theoretical models of IA across a wide range of scales, such as the linear alignment (Hirata and Seljak, 2004) and nonlinear alignment (Bridle and King, 2007) models, quadratic alignment models based on tidal torquing (Crittenden et al., 2002; Mackey et al., 2002), the tidal alignment and tidal torquing model (Blazek et al., 2015; Blazek et al., 2019), and halo model approaches Schneider and Bridle (2010); Fortuna et al. (2021a); Van Alfen et al. (2024). Observational studies have detected or constrained IA signals in a variety of galaxy samples and surveys (Brown et al., 2002; Mandelbaum et al., 2006; Hirata et al., 2007; Okumura et al., 2009; Okumura and Jing, 2009; Joachimi et al., 2011; Mandelbaum et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2015; Johnston et al., 2019; Georgiou et al., 2019; Fortuna et al., 2021b; Tonegawa and Okumura, 2022; Samuroff et al., 2022; Hervas Peters et al., 2024; Georgiou et al., 2025; Tonegawa et al., 2025; Okumura, 2025; Navarro-Gironés et al., 2026; Siegel et al., 2026). Cosmological hydrodynamical simulations have also been used to investigate the dependence of IA on galaxy properties and to test theoretical models (Tenneti et al., 2015; Chisari et al., 2015; Velliscig et al., 2015; Hilbert et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2021; Samuroff et al., 2021; Delgado et al., 2023; Ferlito et al., 2025; Herle et al., 2026b).

At late times, IAs can also probe cosmic expansion and the growth of structure in the late Universe Chisari and Dvorkin (2013); Taruya and Okumura (2020). The baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) feature in IAs can be used to measure distances (Chisari and Dvorkin, 2013; Okumura et al., 2020; Kurita et al., 2021; van Dompseler et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023; Chan et al., 2026). The Alcock–Paczynski (AP) effect (Alcock and Paczynski, 1979; Matsubara and Suto, 1996) and redshift-space distortions (RSD) provide further information on distances and structure growth (Okumura and Taruya, 2020; Zwetsloot and Chisari, 2022; Inoue et al., 2025; Shim et al., 2025b; Shim et al., 2025a). These signatures have been studied in simulations (Okumura et al., 2020; Kurita et al., 2021; Okumura et al., 2019; Ishikawa et al., 2025), and analyses of actual data have yielded observational constraints (Xu et al., 2023; Okumura and Taruya, 2023; Okumura, 2026; Chan et al., 2026). Combining IAs with velocity measurements from the kinetic Sunyaev–Zel’dovich (kSZ) effect can further improve cosmological constraints (Okumura et al., 2019; van Gemeren and Chisari, 2020; Okumura and Taruya, 2022). The cosmological information from IAs therefore complements that from galaxy clustering and other probes of the late Universe.

Exploiting IAs as a cosmological probe requires accurate theoretical modeling. To include information from mildly nonlinear scales, these models must go beyond the linear alignment model and account for nonlinear gravitational evolution and nonlinear bias. In real space, perturbative descriptions of galaxy and dark matter halo shapes have been developed to incorporate these effects (Blazek et al., 2015; Schmitz et al., 2018; Blazek et al., 2019). The effective field theory (EFT) of IAs provides a systematic framework for this modeling, with predictions for one-loop power spectra and tree-level bispectra (Vlah et al., 2020; Vlah et al., 2021; Chen and Kokron, 2024; Bakx et al., 2025b). Hybrid and field-level approaches have also been developed (Maion et al., 2024; Kokron et al., 2026). NN-body and hydrodynamical simulations have also been used to test perturbative IA models and measure higher-order shape bias (Samuroff et al., 2021; Bakx et al., 2023; Akitsu et al., 2023; Bakx et al., 2025a; Herle et al., 2026a; Vedder et al., 2026). For spectroscopic samples, peculiar velocities affect the galaxy positions inferred from redshifts and thus the three-dimensional IA statistics. Hence, analyses on mildly nonlinear scales require an accurate treatment of nonlinear RSD. For this purpose, models incorporating velocity damping (Okumura et al., 2024) and perturbative treatments of redshift-space IA correlations (Matsubara, 2024a; Matsubara, 2024b; Taruya et al., 2024) have been developed. A model-independent framework for the symmetries of IA statistics in redshift space has also been developed (Akitsu et al., 2026).

papers.title: On the effect of a redshift- and metallicity-dependent top-heavy IMF on high-redshift UV luminosity functions
papers.abstract: JWST observations have revealed a higher-than-expected abundance of bright galaxies at $z \gtrsim 10$. Several scenarios have been proposed to explain this excess, one of which invokes a top-heavy stellar initial mass function (IMF) in the early Universe. In this work, we construct spectral energy distribution (SED) templates based on a redshift- and metallicity-dependent IMF ($z$-$Z$ dependent IMF) motivated by the star-cluster simulations of Chon et al. (2022) and the redshift-dependent IMF model of Steinhardt et al. (2020). We implement these templates in a semi-analytic galaxy model built on a large-box $N$-body simulation to investigate the impact of a top-heavy IMF on the ultraviolet luminosity function (UVLF) of high-redshift galaxies. The adopted $z$-$Z$ dependent IMF enhances the UV luminosity of young stellar populations, particularly at low metallicity, and increases the scatter in the UV luminosity-to-star formation rate conversion factor relative to the Kroupa IMF. Without dust attenuation, both top-heavy IMF models predict a substantially enhanced bright end of the UVLF. However, when dust attenuation is included and calibrated at $z=7$, IMF-dependent metal enrichment and the resulting dust attenuation partly offset the intrinsic UV enhancement. The self-consistent model broadly reproduces the observed UVLF at $z\sim10$, although discrepancies remain at $z\gtrsim12$. For the selected high-redshift UVLF constraints, the best-fitting dust optical depths are 51% and 21% of the fiducial values at $z=9.7$ and $13.04$, respectively, indicating a preference for weaker effective dust attenuation. The highest-redshift comparison does not provide a robust constraint. Our results highlight the importance of accounting for both enhanced stellar UV emission and IMF-dependent metal enrichment and dust attenuation when assessing the impact of a top-heavy IMF on high-redshift galaxies.

papers.intro:
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed a large number of bright galaxies at z≳10z\gtrsim 10 (Castellano et al., 2022; Finkelstein et al., 2022; Donnan et al., 2023; Naidu et al., 2022, e.g.,), including MoM-z14 at zspec=14.44±0.02z_{\mathrm{spec}}=14.44\pm 0.02, the most distant spectroscopically confirmed galaxy to date (Naidu et al., 2026). Before JWST, only a handful of galaxies had been spectroscopically confirmed at z>8z>8 (Zitrin et al., 2015; Hashimoto et al., 2018; Tamura et al., 2019, e.g.,), too few to statistically characterize the early galaxy population. JWST has dramatically expanded the spectroscopic census (Stark et al., 2025), enabling detailed studies of early galaxies, including their stellar populations, star formation histories, and black hole activity. At the same time, the unexpectedly high abundance of bright galaxies poses a challenge to many existing models of galaxy formation and evolution.

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed a large number of bright galaxies at z≳10z\gtrsim 10 (Castellano et al., 2022; Finkelstein et al., 2022; Donnan et al., 2023; Naidu et al., 2022, e.g.,), including MoM-z14 at zspec=14.44±0.02z_{\mathrm{spec}}=14.44\pm 0.02, the most distant spectroscopically confirmed galaxy to date (Naidu et al., 2026). Before JWST, only a handful of galaxies had been spectroscopically confirmed at z>8z>8 (Zitrin et al., 2015; Hashimoto et al., 2018; Tamura et al., 2019, e.g.,), too few to statistically characterize the early galaxy population. JWST has dramatically expanded the spectroscopic census (Stark et al., 2025), enabling detailed studies of early galaxies, including their stellar populations, star formation histories, and black hole activity. At the same time, the unexpectedly high abundance of bright galaxies poses a challenge to many existing models of galaxy formation and evolution.

JWST measurements of the UV luminosity function (UVLF) have consistently found high number densities of UV-bright galaxies at z∼10z\sim 10–12, exceeding many pre-JWST theoretical predictions (Harikane et al., 2023; Harikane et al., 2024b; Harikane et al., 2024a; Bunker et al., 2023; Arrabal Haro et al., 2023; Fujimoto et al., 2024; Carniani et al., 2024; Finkelstein et al., 2024; Whitler et al., 2025; Franco et al., 2025, e.g.,). At higher redshifts, however, the observational picture remains uncertain. While the JADES measurements suggest that the bright-end excess relative to many theoretical models persists at z≳12z\gtrsim 12 (Whitler et al., 2025), wide-area measurements from PANORAMIC and other JWST fields suggest a more rapid decline in the number density of UV-bright galaxies beyond z∼13z\sim 13 (Weibel et al., 2026b; McLeod et al., 2026). Gravitational-lensing surveys further extend UVLF constraints to fainter magnitudes over z∼9z\sim 9–15 (Chemerynska et al., 2026). Thus, although the unexpectedly high abundance of UV-bright galaxies is consistently observed at z∼10z\sim 10–12, the evolution of the UVLF beyond z∼12z\sim 12 remains uncertain.

The physical origin of this bright-end excess remains unclear. Several astrophysical explanations have been proposed, including enhanced star formation efficiency (SFE) at z≳10z\gtrsim 10 due to suppressed feedback in the first galaxies (Inayoshi et al., 2022; Dekel et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2023; Finkelstein et al., 2024; Jeong et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026); reduced dust attenuation resulting from radiation-driven dust removal in galaxies with high Eddington ratios (Fiore et al., 2023; Ferrara et al., 2023; Ferrara, 2024); and large scatter in the relation between UV magnitude (MUV{M_{\text{UV}}}) and halo mass (Mhalo{M_{\text{halo}}}) arising from stochastic star formation histories (Mason et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2023; Mirocha and Furlanetto, 2023; Gelli et al., 2024; Kravtsov and Belokurov, 2024; Yung et al., 2024; Muñoz et al., 2026; Sarkar and Samui, 2026). Other possibilities include additional UV emission from Pop III stars or active galactic nuclei (AGNs) (Harikane et al., 2023; Hegde et al., 2024), and an enhanced LUV{L_{\text{UV}}}/SFR ratio resulting from a top-heavy initial mass function (IMF) at high redshift (Shen et al., 2023; Trinca et al., 2024; Ventura et al., 2024; Cueto et al., 2024; Hutter et al., 2025; Jeong et al., 2025; Durrant et al., 2026). From a cosmological perspective, proposed explanations include enhanced power on ∼1\sim 1 Mpc scales (Padmanabhan and Loeb, 2023; Parashari and Laha, 2023); a blue-tilted primordial power spectrum with positive running (Hirano and Yoshida, 2024; Kobayashi et al., 2026); a modified cosmic time–redshift relation (Melia, 2023; Melia, 2024); accelerated formation of galaxies and galaxy clusters in modified Newtonian dynamics (McGaugh et al., 2024); and a negative cosmological constant (Menci et al., 2024). Furthermore, the consistent detection of this bright-end excess at z∼10z\sim 10–12 in wide-area surveys spanning multiple independent fields suggests that cosmic variance alone cannot explain it (McLeod et al., 2024; Weibel et al., 2026b; Weibel et al., 2026a).

(2026) found that the dust-attenuated UVLFs predicted by COLIBRE systematically fall below observational estimates at the bright end, with the discrepancy increasing toward higher redshifts. Star-cluster-scale simulations predict that the IMF becomes increasingly top-heavy at lower metallicities and higher redshifts (Chon et al., 2021; Chon et al., 2022; Chon et al., 2024). papers.title: VLT, Keck, and Gemini characterization of the temporarily captured flyby 2026 QQ$_8$
papers.abstract: Very Large Telescope, Keck I, and Gemini North photometry of 2026 QQ$_8$ on November 7-21 gives Sloan Digital Sky Survey-equivalent colors $g-r=0.594^{+0.056}_{-0.053}$, $g-i=0.840^{+0.066}_{-0.065}$, and $i-z=-0.104^{+0.067}_{-0.057}$ mag. Apollo 17 basalt slabs 75075,197 and 71055,239 fit the colors (reduced $\chi^2$ of 0.57 and 0.89). The Bus-DeMeo Sq- and K-type templates give reduced $\chi^2=0.87$ and 0.90, respectively. The colors permit both an Sq-like asteroid and exposed lunar basalt. With revised Keck timing uncertainties, 71 positions (August 19-November 21) give an outward acceleration of $(1.363\pm0.090)\times10^{-10}$ au day$^{-2}$ at 1 au, implying an area-to-mass ratio of $(6.02\pm0.40)\times10^{-4}$ m$^2$ kg$^{-1}$ for a unit radiation-pressure coefficient. For pre-encounter analogues, NEOMOD3 assigns source probabilities of 78.8% to the $\nu_6$ resonance and 20.6% to Jupiter's 3:1 resonance. For a sphere with $H=31.37\pm0.34$, the diameter, density, and mass are ($1.44^{+0.28}_{-0.23}$ m, $1.73^{+0.36}_{-0.30}$ g cm$^{-3}$, $2.73^{+1.19}_{-0.82}\times10^3$ kg) for the Sq albedo ($p_V=0.243\pm0.039$), ($1.62^{+0.28}_{-0.24}$ m, $1.54^{+0.29}_{-0.24}$ g cm$^{-3}$, $3.43^{+1.30}_{-0.94}\times10^3$ kg) for NEOMOD3 ($p_V=0.191$), and ($2.49^{+0.42}_{-0.36}$ m, $1.00^{+0.19}_{-0.16}$ g cm$^{-3}$, $8.09^{+3.06}_{-2.22}\times10^3$ kg) for lunar slabs ($p_V=0.081$). With radiation pressure, nominal capture lasts 224.96 days (April 26-December 7). Sun-Earth corotating geocentric longitude advances 0.76 turns, classifying 2026 QQ$_8$ as a temporarily captured flyby. Its three-dimensional corotating path tangent turns 1.33 revolutions. After 10,000 yr, about 800 of 1,000 clones survive in each model, with about 200 colliding with Earth. The paired survival difference (radiation pressure plus gravity minus gravity only) is ~2 percentage points.

papers.intro:
Krisztián Sárneczky discovered 2026 QQ8 on 2026 August 19 with the 0.60 m Schmidt telescope at Piszkéstető, Hungary (station K88) [97]. The Minor Planet Center (MPC) listed it as Sar2901 on the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Confirmation Page. Because the initial orbit allowed an artificial origin, the MPC withdrew the listing on September 2 but kept the astrometry public and requested follow-up under Sar2901 (Minor Planet Electronic Circular [MPEC] 2026-R09) [68].

Krisztián Sárneczky discovered 2026 QQ8 on 2026 August 19 with the 0.60 m Schmidt telescope at Piszkéstető, Hungary (station K88) [97]. The Minor Planet Center (MPC) listed it as Sar2901 on the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Confirmation Page. Because the initial orbit allowed an artificial origin, the MPC withdrew the listing on September 2 but kept the astrometry public and requested follow-up under Sar2901 (Minor Planet Electronic Circular [MPEC] 2026-R09) [68].

David J. Tholen recovered Sar2901 on October 9 at 14:08:38 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) with the University of Hawai‘i 88-inch (2.24 m) telescope on Maunakea (T12). papers.title: The Simons Observatory: Analysis of methods for polarization calibration of multiple instruments
papers.abstract: Cosmic birefringence, the rotation of the CMB linear polarization plane across the Universe, is a powerful test of parity-violating physics beyond the Standard Model. Static isotropic rotation, however, is limited by an instrument's absolute polarization-angle calibration. We present a method for transferring absolute calibration between Simons Observatory (SO) instruments, validated on map-level simulations of the Large Aperture Telescope (LAT) and Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs) with lensed CMB polarization, polarized Galactic foregrounds, correlated instrumental noise, and polarization-angle miscalibration. We develop two pipelines: a joint LAT+SAT likelihood transferring calibration through their overlap, and the Minami-Komatsu foreground-based method, which separates cosmic birefringence from instrumental miscalibration using Galactic dust polarization without an external angle prior. We derive a general variance budget showing that calibration transfer improves sensitivity only when the combined reference and overlap transfer uncertainties remain below the receiving instrument's calibration uncertainty. While transfer does not lower the absolute-angle floor for isotropic $\beta$, it anchors the receiving instrument's multipole range. The relative-angle uncertainty is $\sim 0.1^\circ$ for $\ell_{\max}^{\mathrm{SAT}}=300$, improving to $\sim 0.04^\circ$ at $\ell_{\max}^{\mathrm{SAT}}=600$, subject to SAT beam and transfer-function control. Finally, for $\beta=0.3^\circ$, we show how the LAT's $\ell$-range distinguishes scale-independent dark-energy rotation from scale-dependent axion dark-matter models via $C_\ell^{EB}$.

The cosmic microwave background (CMB) provides a powerful observational window into the early universe, offering precise insights into fundamental physics. One intriguing phenomenon that can be imprinted in the CMB polarization is cosmic birefringence (CB), a frequency-independent rotation of the linear polarization angle of CMB photons as they traverse cosmological distances. The cosmic microwave background (CMB) provides a powerful observational window into the early universe, offering precise insights into fundamental physics. One intriguing phenomenon that can be imprinted in the CMB polarization is cosmic birefringence (CB), a frequency-independent rotation of the linear polarization angle of CMB photons as they traverse cosmological distances. This effect would indicate the existence of parity-violating interactions and new physics beyond the Standard Model [17, 19, 18, 48, 88, 89, 63].

CB manifests as a rotation of the polarization plane across the sky, which could depend on the observed direction [69] or be uniform (isotropic) across the entire sky. Such an isotropic rotation could arise from a slowly time-evolving and nearly homogeneous pseudoscalar field coupled to photons through a Chern-Simons interaction [19, 88]. This type of field is predicted in various theoretical frameworks, including those involving dark energy [19, 40, 93, 41, 20, 90, 43, 42], dark matter [38, 68, 36], early dark energy [80, 33, 41], topological defects [107, 59, 53, 45], and quantum gravity [82, 14, 12]. In many of these models, the field that sources the rotation is that of an axion-like particle (ALP). In this case, the birefringence signal offers an indirect probe of the ALP properties, including mass, coupling strength, and cosmological evolution. Searches for a polarization angle oscillating with observation time rely on relative temporal stability; they are distinct from the scale-dependent E​BEB signatures considered here for fields evolving during CMB polarization generation.

The rotation introduced by isotropic CB mixes the parity-even EE or TT and parity-odd BB modes of the CMB polarization [56, 102], leading to non-zero T​BTB and E​BEB correlations [72, 37], even if the primordial signal lacks them. In particular, among the parity-odd two-point CMB statistics, the E​BEB power spectrum is a more sensitive probe of birefringence than the T​BTB spectrum, owing to its lower cosmic variance [8]. Delensing the BB-mode field further improves the E​BEB-based birefringence sensitivity by reducing the lensing-induced variance [52]. Moreover, if the pseudoscalar field evolves during key epochs such as recombination or reionization, it can subtly alter the shape and amplitude of the E​BEB spectrum [42], increasing the usefulness of this probe in constraining fundamental physics. Reconstructing this angular dependence thus offers a tomographic view of the dynamics of the underlying field [104, 84, 67, 65, 47, 33, 41, 38], while also helping to distinguish it from instrumental effects [113, 60, 57, 8, 103, 79].

Hints of a non-zero isotropic birefringence angle, β\beta, have emerged from several CMB experiments. Analyses of data from Planck [106, 75, 26, 32, 8, 97], the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) [71, 28], and joint Planck-WMAP [31, 34] and Planck-ACT [35] studies, have reported consistent signals of around β≈0.2∘\beta\approx 0.2^{\circ} to 0.3∘0.3^{\circ} at a statistical significance ranging from ∼2​σ{\sim}2\sigma in individual analyses to ∼4.8​σ{\sim}4.8\sigma in the combined ACT and Planck data [35]. Earlier efforts from QUaD [113], WMAP [50], POLARBEAR [4], the South Pole Telescope [16, 44], and SPIDER [5, 114] were inconclusive due to systematic uncertainties. Further studies have tried to quantify possible systematic uncertainties affecting these measurements, such as instrumental polarization angles [27, 6], or the potential intrinsic non-zero E​BEB correlation from Galactic thermal dust [21, 26, 23, 49]. These hints motivate more sensitive tests with ongoing ground-based experiments such as SO [7, 1, 3] and AliCPT [116, 29, 115], the planned LiteBIRD mission [10, 25], and the proposed CMB-HD concept [9], alongside tighter control of systematic uncertainties.

SO is located at 5200 m of altitude in the Atacama desert in northern Chile, targeting fundamental questions in cosmology. It consists of Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs, 0.42 m aperture) optimized for degree-scale polarization, and a Large Aperture Telescope (LAT, 6 m aperture), which will target a variety of science cases. In this work, we develop and validate the methodology needed to extract the CB signal from SO LAT and SAT data, using map-level simulations of both instruments.

These measurements are ultimately limited by the accuracy of the absolute polarization angle calibration, since a global miscalibration is indistinguishable from an isotropic birefringence rotation [58]. Polarization-angle errors also mix EE and BB modes and can contaminate the inferred cosmological polarization signals [91]. Achieving this calibration to the accuracy required for CB is a central experimental challenge. Ground-based experiments have pursued several complementary strategies: artificial polarized sources such as sparse wire grids and drone- or tower-mounted emitters [87, 22, 81, 83, 30], detailed optical modeling of the instrument-induced polarization rotation [62], astrophysical calibrators, most notably the Crab nebula (Tau A), the brightest polarized source in the microwave sky [13, 99], and cross-experiment correlation techniques [98]. Space-based artificial calibrators have also been proposed, notably CalSat, a CubeSat concept designed to provide a common polarized reference source for ground-based and sub-orbital CMB experiments [54, 58]. Each of these has practical limits. Wire-grid and artificial-source calibrations determine the instrument’s internal polarization response, how a known input angle at the source maps to a detector-frame readout, but the orientation of the source itself relative to the sky, and hence of the instrument boresight, must still be surveyed or otherwise independently established; a wire grid alone cannot verify that this geometric link is correct. The absolute angle of Tau A is currently known only to ∼0.3∘{\sim}0.3^{\circ} [13]. An alternative is to self-calibrate the polarization angle by requiring the CMB T​BTB and E​BEB spectra to vanish. However, this procedure also removes an isotropic CB signal, while residual Galactic foregrounds with intrinsic non-zero T​BTB or E​BEB correlations can bias the inferred calibration angle [2, 58].

papers.title: Continuum Pumping Revises Metallicity in the Orion Nebula
papers.abstract: The enrichment of heavy elements in the interstellar medium is central to understanding galaxy evolution. Oxygen, the most abundant element after H and He, provides the principal tracer of gas-phase metallicity, typically measured using nebular emission lines in star-forming regions. However, a long-standing issue-the abundance discrepancy factor (ADF)-produces a $\sim 0.25$ dex offset between metallicities derived from recombination lines (RLs) and collisionally excited lines (CELs). We present deep spectroscopic observations of the Orion Nebula (M42), and use them to assess the contribution of the often neglected continuum pumping process. We find that the continuum pumping effect is at least a factor of two stronger than previously expected. After accounting for the flux contribution from continuum pumping, the RL metallicity is consistent with the CEL metallicity, thus explaining the bulk of the ADF. Reassessing O/H measurements in five literature star-forming regions using the same method, we similarly find a systematic reduction of RL-based metallicities. These results indicate that RL metallicities, which have previously been considered more reliable than CELs, are subject to potentially large bias from continuum pumping. This study provides a foundation to correct this bias and establish accurate element abundance scales throughout cosmic time.

papers.title: Insights on Three Distinct Types of Energetic Particle Flux Variations Ahead of ICME-driven Shocks Observed by ASPEX on board Aditya-L1
papers.abstract: We investigate upstream energetic-ion transport associated with ten interplanetary coronal mass ejection (ICME)-driven shocks observed near 1 au using multidirectional measurements from the Suprathermal and Energetic Particle Spectrometer (STEPS) onboard Aditya-L1. Based on energy-dependent intensity profiles and onset times, the events are classified as dispersed, dispersionless, or mixed. We combine pitch-angle anisotropy, minimum variance analysis, reduced magnetic helicity, two-dimensional Grad-Shafranov reconstruction, quasi-linear transport diagnostics, shock parameters, and energetic-ion spectral fits to characterize each category. The seven dispersed events exhibit energy-dependent arrivals, generally intermittent magnetic-helicity signatures, and larger parallel mean free paths, consistent with less restricted particle propagation. In contrast, the two dispersionless events show nearly simultaneous enhancements across energy channels, extended intervals of enhanced reduced magnetic helicity, and closed magnetic flux contours in Grad-Shafranov reconstructions. They also exhibit shorter parallel mean free paths, higher pitch-angle diffusion coefficients, and comparatively strong shocks. The mixed event transitions from dispersed arrivals to nearly simultaneous enhancements as the shock approaches, accompanied by evolving anisotropy and distinct scattering properties. Spectral indices range from approximately -2.38 to -0.86 for dispersed events and from -0.82 to -0.26 for dispersionless and mixed events, indicating harder spectra in the latter groups. These results reveal systematic associations between energetic-ion transport, magnetic structure, shock conditions, and spectral hardness, suggesting that shock-associated energization and energy-dependent transport jointly shape the observed signatures, while magnetic topology may regulate particle propagation and confinement.

papers.intro:
Solar energetic particle (SEP) events are among the most important manifestations of space weather in the heliosphere [75, 28, 102]. These events are characterized by sudden enhancements in energetic charged particle intensities, spanning energies from a few tens of keV n-1 to several hundreds of MeV n-1 , with durations ranging from a few hours to several days. During major SEP events, particle intensities can exceed quiet-time background levels by many orders of magnitude. SEPs are commonly associated with transient solar eruptive phenomena such as solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs), both of which provide favorable environments for efficient particle acceleration through magnetic reconnection and large-scale shock formation in the solar corona and interplanetary medium [75, 15]. In situ observations throughout the heliosphere routinely detect energetic ions and electrons over broad energy ranges extending from a few keV to hundreds of MeV and, in extreme events, into the relativistic regime [16].

In situ observations throughout the heliosphere routinely detect energetic ions and electrons over broad energy ranges extending from a few keV to hundreds of MeV and, in extreme events, into the relativistic regime [16].

Multiple physical processes have been proposed to explain SEP acceleration. These include particle energization during magnetic reconnection associated with solar flares and jets [44, 52], diffusive shock acceleration, shock drift acceleration at CME-driven shocks propagating through the corona and interplanetary space [42, 90, 16, 50, 40], and acceleration occurring within reconnecting current sheets and evolving post eruptive magnetic structures associated with CMEs [45, 59, 48]. Recent observations from the Aditya Solar Wind Particle Experiment (ASPEX) onboard Aditya-L1 have further shown that interactions between multiple interplanetary CMEs can generate extended interaction regions associated with shock propagation, particle energization, and redistribution of energetic ions in the heliosphere [70]. SEP events are traditionally divided into impulsive and gradual classes based on their temporal evolution, elemental composition, charge states, energy spectra, and associated radio signatures [9, 75]. Gradual SEP events are often observed over extremely broad heliolongitudinal extents, implying efficient acceleration and large-scale particle transport throughout the heliosphere [76, 56, 106, 20, 78, 69, 66, 109, 79, 51, 21, 46].

The transport of energetic particles in the heliosphere is strongly governed by the turbulent interplanetary magnetic field (IMF). During propagation, charged particles undergo both parallel and perpendicular diffusion relative to the ambient magnetic field [41, 24, 62, 74, 89, 81]. Consequently, SEP intensity profiles measured near Earth frequently exhibit substantial spatial and temporal variability arising from the combined effects of acceleration, scattering, magnetic connectivity, and large-scale heliospheric structures [32, 22, 23, 49, 12, 107]. The anisotropy of energetic particles serves as an important diagnostic of these transport processes. Strong anisotropies generally indicate weak pitch-angle scattering and efficient field-aligned streaming, whereas near-isotropic distributions imply enhanced scattering and cross-field diffusion [19].

One of the most intriguing transport-related SEP phenomena is the occurrence of transient intensity modulations such as dropouts and dispersion-less particle variations [63, 29]. These events are characterized by abrupt changes in particle intensities with remarkably sharp temporal boundaries occurring simultaneously across broad energy ranges. Similar dispersion-less intensity modulations have previously been reported for both energetic ions and electrons during impulsive SEP events [4, 8, 77, 13]. Such observations suggest that localized magnetic connectivity and coherent magnetic structures play an important role during particle propagation.

Previous observational and theoretical studies have demonstrated that coherent magnetic structures embedded within solar wind turbulence, including magnetic flux ropes, magnetic islands, current sheets, and magnetic conduit-like structures, can strongly influence energetic particle transport in the heliosphere [7, 6, 10, 96, 97]. These mesoscale magnetic structures can enhance magnetic connectivity, suppress cross-field diffusion, and provide efficient field-aligned transport pathways for energetic particles. Consequently, energetic particle dropouts and dispersion-less flux variations are frequently associated with abrupt changes in magnetic topology and crossings of coherent magnetic structures [14, 96, 97]. In such scenarios, particles can remain confined within localized magnetic flux tubes or magnetic conduits, producing sharp intensity boundaries and nearly simultaneous particle enhancements across broad energy ranges [96, 97].

papers.title: Improved Approximation Algorithms for Multi-Path TSP and Ordered TSP
papers.abstract: In Multi-Path TSP, given a metric and $k$ pairs of vertices $(s_i,t_i)$, where $k$ is part of the input, we seek $s_i$--$t_i$ paths of minimum total length that together visit all vertices. Ratios below $2$ were known only for graphic metrics and special cases such as multiple depots ($s_i=t_i$); in general metrics, the best ratio was $1+2e^{-1/2}\approx2.213$, by a randomized algorithm of B\"ohm, Friggstad, M\"omke and Spoerhase [SODA 2025]. We give a deterministic algorithm with ratio $\frac{5e-2}{3e-2}<1.8833$ relative to a restriction of their LP relaxation, bounding its integrality gap by the same constant. papers.title: Modeling and analysis of a phase-field model for organic solar cells
papers.abstract: We derive and analyze a phase-field model describing the formation of the active layer of organic solar cells. The process combines phase separation of an electron donor (polymer) and an electron acceptor (non-fullerene acceptor) with evaporation of a solvent. Taking the macroscopic motion of the fluid into account, this results in a coupled system of incompressible Navier--Stokes, degenerate multispecies Cahn--Hilliard, and Allen--Cahn equations with cross-diffusion terms. We give a thermodynamically consistent derivation of the system and prove the existence of global-in-time weak solutions without any size constraints on the data. The solutions dissipate the total energy and require an ad-hoc variational formulation of the definition of the diffusion fluxes, which is made necessary by the degeneracy of the mobility matrix.

papers.intro:
Organic photovoltaic cells (OPVs) have emerged as a promising low-cost, sustainable, and flexible alternative to inorganic (e.g., silicon-based) cells [43]. While there are still shortcomings in terms of efficiency and stability [30, 33], the possibility of cost-effective mass production by printing techniques makes them an active area of research [42, 13]. OPVs are typically fabricated by solvent-based thin-film deposition, using methods ranging from spin coating for lab-scale devices to roll-to-roll methods for large-scale production [37]. In each case, an electron donor (polymer) and an electron acceptor (non-fullerene acceptor) are dissolved in at least one solvent to form a homogeneous mixture [27]. The mixture is then coated onto a substrate, creating a thin film. As the solvent evaporates, the donor and acceptor undergo phase separation, a process that halts once the solvent is depleted. This results in a film consisting of donor- and acceptor-rich regions, forming the active layer of the solar cell. The donor–acceptor morphology is highly sensitive to processing conditions, such as blend composition, evaporation rate, and substrate characteristics [10]. In turn, the morphology largely determines device performance [28]. A clear understanding of how processing conditions govern morphology formation is therefore essential for achieving high device efficiency.

Various models addressing different aspects of these phenomena have been proposed. The phase separation of donor and acceptor materials within organic solar cells is described, e.g., in [40, 6] by means of phase-field methods. In these works, evaporation is governed by an outflow boundary condition for the solvent. Ronsin et al. Describing phase separation including hydrodynamic effects requires the formulation of coupled Cahn–Hilliard Navier–Stokes equations. Likewise, evaporation is driven by a free energy, • accounts for hydrodynamic effects through the Navier–Stokes equations, • is thermodynamically consistent, i.e., it satisfies both the first and second laws of thermodynamics. The resulting model takes the form of coupled Cahn–Hilliard, Navier–Stokes, and Allen–Cahn equations.

Analytical problems related to coupled Cahn–Hilliard and Navier–Stokes equations have already been investigated, in particular in the case of single-component fluids without cross-diffusion effects. In [1], the existence of weak solutions to a model developed in [4] is proved. The model employs a diffuse-interface phase-field approach to describe the flow of two viscous incompressible Newtonian fluids, with the phase field evolving according to a Cahn–Hilliard equation. The resulting coupled Cahn–Hilliard Navier–Stokes system is thermodynamically consistent and dissipates the total energy as a consequence. The analysis is extended in [2] to the case of a degenerate mobility. The local-in-time existence of strong solutions for regular energy densities is shown in [5, 39], while the case of less regular energy densities is treated in [21, 22]. The long-time convergence towards a steady state and the propagation of regularity are proved in [3]. A Hele-Shaw Cahn–Hilliard model is studied in [12], which is derived via formal asymptotics from the Navier–Stokes Cahn–Hilliard system presented in [4]. In [19], a phase-field model for tumor growth including viscoelastic effects is presented and studied, which consists of coupled Cahn–Hilliard equations, reaction-diffusion equation, Navier–Stokes equations, and a mechanical force balance. In [14], a phase-field model for tumor growth is introduced, which consists of a coupled Cahn–Hilliard equation for the tumor tissue, a reaction-diffusion-advection equation for the nutrients, and a Brinkman–Stokes-type law for the fluid velocity. The authors prove global-in-time existence of weak solutions for the model with degenerate mobility.

papers.title: Self-similar Inequality Dynamics in Biased Competition for a Conserved Resource
papers.abstract: In many complex systems the redistribution of a conserved resource can generate strong inequality. Important examples are cities exchanging inhabitants, farms competing for farmland, or agents for wealth in saturated markets. Here we model such systems as agents competing for a fixed total resource, and show that coupling agent extinction to a bias favoring richer agents dynamically amplifies this inequality over time. Drawing on an analogy with emulsions, where droplets compete for a conserved quantity, we introduce a dynamical critical resource size that determines an agent's fate. Crucially, this threshold grows in time, continuously raising the bar for survival and further reinforcing inequality. Increasing the bias strength, we find a transition from a continuous resource concentration towards a winner-takes-all outcome. Furthermore, the case of continuous resource concentration is characterized by a self-similar dynamics accompanied by a power-law or exponential increase in inequality, quantified by the Gini coefficient. We derive these results analytically in a mean-field model and compare them to agent-based simulations, showing excellent agreement.

Ever since Pareto’s observation that wealth concentrates in the hands of a few, understanding how inequality emerges has been a defining challenge across the social sciences [30, 43]. During the period known as the Great Acceleration [35], the explosive rise in production and consumption motivated the study of how heterogeneous growth translates into inequality. A first attempt is Gibrat’s law, which states that the absolute growth rate of market participants (agents) is linearly proportional to their sizes [19, 36].

In such saturated systems or fixed pools, agents compete over an approximately conserved resource, so that the growth of one is necessarily coupled to the decline of another.

The absence of net growth does not preclude inequality: on the contrary, even “fair” trades can generate it, provided the total resource being exchanged is conserved. This phenomenon is captured by metaphorical models [10] of random, unbiased asset exchange such as the yard-sale model [13]. These models show that conservative, unbiased exchange alone can lead to wealth condensation generating strong inequality [8], because poorer agents risk a larger fraction of their wealth and random fluctuations tend to concentrate wealth among the rich. Yard-sale models have also been generalized to include wealth redistribution and a bias favoring the wealthier agents. The competition between these two factors leads to a stationary wealth distribution that can undergo a phase transition to a state in which a finite fraction of the wealth condenses onto a single agent [5].

Yard-sale models have also been generalized to include wealth redistribution and a bias favoring the wealthier agents. The competition between these two factors leads to a stationary wealth distribution that can undergo a phase transition to a state in which a finite fraction of the wealth condenses onto a single agent [5].

Far fewer studies have addressed systems that never reach a steady state, where inequality keeps rising [21, 23, 4, 6]. Elaborating on these seminal works, we study biased exchanges of a conserved resource and take a different route: we characterize the evolving resource distribution through a critical size, the time-dependent scale that separates growing agents from shrinking ones. We derive how this scale evolves and connect its dynamics, together with that of the Gini coefficient, to the dynamics of inequality.

During Ostwald ripening, droplets or clusters exchange a conserved quantity and surface tensions drive larger clusters to grow at the expense of smaller ones [41]. The result is a dynamical scaling in which the number of clusters decreases, the typical cluster size grows, and the distribution approaches a self-similar form [12, 28], as described by the Lifshitz-Slyozov-Wagner (LSW) theory [24, 42]. papers.title: Common tiles from fractional tiles for two lattices
papers.abstract: Let $L_1, L_2\subseteq{\mathbb R}^d$ be lattices of the same volume and let $D_1, D_2$ be two bounded fundamental domains for $L_1, L_2$. We show that there is a measurable common tile for $L_1$ and $L_2$ contained in $D_1+D_2$. The main tool is a result of Bowen, Kun and Sabok (2021) which shows how to obtain a measurable perfect matching given a fractional perfect matching in hyperfinite graphings.

papers.title: MH-RAG-DIVE: Dynamic and Cost-Efficient Multi-Hop RAG Evaluation via Tree-Cached Dialogue Simulation
papers.abstract: Quality assessment is essential for determining whether changes to a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system improve or maintain its performance. However, existing evaluation approaches often rely on single-turn or single-hop interactions and therefore do not capture the complexity of multi-hop, multi-turn conversations. We introduce MH-RAG-DIVE, a dynamic interactive user simulation framework designed to evaluate RAG systems in more complex multi-hop and multi-turn settings. The framework extends RAG-DIVE with a Context Discoverer, which identifies documents that can be combined to generate multi-hop questions within an ongoing conversation. To address the high computational cost of dynamic user simulation, we further introduce a Conversation Cacher, which reuses turns from previous evaluation runs while preserving the dynamic nature of the evaluation. We evaluate the framework across six distinct RAG configurations and compare its results with the original RAG-DIVE evaluation and the static, human-created CLAPNQ dataset. Our experiments show consistent performance trends across the evaluation approaches, while the more complex multi-hop and multi-turn setting exposes additional challenges for RAG systems. Furthermore, the Conversation Cacher substantially reduces token consumption, demonstrating its potential to make dynamic evaluation more cost-efficient. Finally, we apply MH-RAG-DIVE to an industrial RAG system with domain-specific data, demonstrating its applicability to real-world evaluation scenarios. Overall, our results show that the proposed approach provides a more complex and cost-efficient framework for evaluating RAG systems. All code and experimental data are publicly available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/Daniel-Innsbruck/MH-RAG-DIVE).

To obtain meaningful evaluations of RAG systems, the experimental setup should reproduce the characteristics of real-world information-seeking, both in the formulation of search queries and in human interactions with the system [10, 2]. These interactions are typically simulated using a question–answer (QA) dataset, which can either be manually created by human experts or automatically generated by an LLM [33, 7]. In practice, however, realistic information-seeking behaviour is difficult to capture because current evaluation methods often employ simplified settings, including single-turn interactions [8, 19, 36] and questions that require information from only a single document [6, 23, 1]. In contrast, real-world applications often require multi-hop reasoning, where answers must be synthesized from information distributed across multiple documents rather than retrieved from a single source [19, 36]. Furthermore, users frequently engage in multi-turn conversations, in which the context established through previous interactions influences subsequent queries and responses [1, 40]. Existing approaches, such as MultiHop-RAG [36], which automatically generates multi-hop QA datasets, and RAG-DIVE [1], which dynamically evaluates RAG systems in a multi-turn setting, already address these requirements individually. However, they do not combine these capabilities. Specifically, existing approaches lack a framework for automatically evaluating RAG systems in a multi-hop, multi-turn setting.

papers.title: A geometric-IEQ approach for curvature-driven flows
papers.abstract: We introduce a geometric invariant energy quadratization (IEQ) formulation for the $L^2$-gradient flow of a class of curvature-dependent energies of closed hypersurfaces, where the energy density depends on the mean curvature and the unit normal. A square-root auxiliary variable converts the geometric energy into a quadratic functional. Combining its evolution equation with a skew-symmetric treatment of surface transport yields a weak formulation whose energy law depends only on the normal velocity and is therefore independent of the chosen tangential motion. We construct monolithic nonlinear parametric finite element methods by coupling a common IEQ discretization with one of two geometric formulations that accommodate either the Barrett-Garcke-N\"urnberg (BGN) tangential velocity or the minimal-deformation-rate (MDR) tangential velocity. Both fully discrete approximations satisfy an unconditional decay estimate for the discrete quadratic energy. We further extend the construction to anisotropic Willmore flow, and to $H^{-1}$-gradient flows. A variety of numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the robustness and accuracy of the introduced methods.

papers.intro:
The motion of interfaces driven by a law for the normal velocity which involves curvature quantities is fundamental in differential geometry and arises in image processing, materials science and models for biological membranes. Two prototypes are mean curvature flow, the L2L^{2}-gradient flow of surface area [30], and the Willmore flow, the L2L^{2}-gradient flow of the surface integral of the squared mean curvature [39]. For either prototype, the L2L^{2}-gradient-flow structure yields a quantitative dissipation law: the time derivative of the driving energy equals the negative squared L2L^{2}-norm of the normal velocity. This dissipation law is the precise geometric structure that a numerical approximation should inherit. The same variational principle admits two natural generalizations. Replacing the isotropic energy with an orientation-dependent energy leads to anisotropic mean curvature or Willmore flows [28, 35], whereas replacing the L2L^{2}-metric with an H−1H^{-1}-metric yields volume conserving geometric evolutions, with surface diffusion as a classical example [34, 14]. The H−1H^{-1}-gradient flow of the Willmore energy has previously been considered in several works [26, 27, 13, 38]. Throughout this paper, we refer to this flow as the “H−1H^{-1} Willmore flow”. The obtained evolution equations range from second- to sixth-order nonlinear geometric PDEs, and their stiffness and strong coupling of geometry and curvature make the construction of robust energy-stable discretizations a central numerical challenge.

Parametric finite element methods (PFEMs) have a long history for approximating curvature-driven interface evolution, see [18, 2, 9, 12, 32, 29, 5, 3, 22]. Dziuk introduced a foundational parametric approximation for mean curvature flow [18]. The BGN approach provides a variational framework that extends naturally to a broad class of geometric flows [6, 9, 11, 10, 12]. It relies on a weak curvature equation which can induce a beneficial tangential motion to yield asymptotically equidistributed curves and conformal polyhedral surfaces in three space dimensions. These properties highlight the importance of a suitable tangential velocity for maintaining mesh quality. Alternative treatments include formulations based on the minimal-deformation-rate (MDR) principle [29, 22], which control mesh deformation and alleviate small-time-step mesh instabilities in BGN schemes, as well as harmonic-map/DeTurck reparametrizations and uniformization strategies [20, 17].

Further constructions have also been developed for anisotropic geometric flows [8, 3, 11]. For Willmore flow, parametric methods with semidiscrete energy stability were developed in early work [19, 10] and, more recently, in [45] with a relaxed MDR tangential velocity. More recently, Bao and Li [4] developed an unconditionally energy-stable fully discrete PFEM for closed planar curves by incorporating an evolution equation for the mean curvature. The scheme in [24] combines this mechanism with a BGN tangential motion. The normal–tangential velocity-splitting technique of [23] separates the curvature-driven normal velocity, which carries the gradient-flow dissipation, from a freely chosen tangential velocity, thereby yielding an energy-stable fully discrete method for Willmore flow of curves and surfaces with arbitrary tangential motion. This development raises a natural question: can the same separation of energy dissipation and mesh motion be achieved systematically for gradient flows of more general surface energies?

These energy-stable methods for Willmore flow [4, 24, 23] share two features. First, they rely on an evolution equation for the mean curvature. Second, the energy stability holds for a modified energy, in which the mean curvature is determined by this evolution equation rather than from the discrete surface. Both features are the hallmarks of the invariant energy quadratization (IEQ) methodology for classical dissipative systems [40, 43], where an auxiliary variable is evolved and the energy stability holds for a modified energy given by this auxiliary variable. On a fixed domain, the IEQ approach introduces an auxiliary variable of the form r=F⁡(u)+Cr=\sqrt{F(u)+C} for a nonlinear energy density FF that is bounded from below. The energy becomes quadratic in rr, while a chain-rule evolution equation couples rr to the original phase variable. Evaluating the nonlinear coefficient explicitly, but using the same coefficient in the two coupled equations, produces the cancellations needed for linear, unconditionally energy-stable time discretizations. The approach has been widely applied and further developed for phase-field and other dissipative systems [41, 44, 25, 33].

papers.title: Quantitative Convergence of the Spherical Brownian Motion collisional particle system for the Maxwellian Landau Equation
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish the quantitative convergence of the spherical Brownian motion (SBM) collisional particle system for the Maxwellian Landau equation via Wasserstein distances. When used as numerical method, it enjoys linear complexity $O(N)$ in particle number $N$, and conserves the momentum and energy almost surely. Moreover, only random grouping and sampling are needed for simulations without further numerical discretization. In the first part, we identify the large particle mean field limit of the system, and the Wasserstein convergence to the limit is justified through a coupling similar to the recent work for the Nanbu type Monte Carlo method \cite{BorghiPareschi2025}. The key difference is that the particles in our coupled shadow system are not i.i.d. due to the perfect matching. In the second part, the convergence of the mean field dynamics to the Landau solution is justified by the relative entropy with a bound $O(\tau^2)$, being $\tau$ the stepsize. This results in an $O(\tau)$ bound for the Wasserstein distance error. A crucial technical tool in the convergence in relative entropy is to provide suitable bounds on the derivatives of the logarithmic density or score function in the mean field dynamics. The combination of these estimates leads to the full convergence of the squared Wasserstein distance with order $O(N^{-1/2}+\tau^2)$ for the numerical scheme in $d=3$.

In this work, we focus on Maxwell molecules, corresponding to γ=0\gamma=0. The conservation of mass, momentum, and kinetic energy, together with entropy dissipation [10] are the important physical properties featured by this model. They also provide important criteria for assessing numerical methods for approximating its solutions.

Typical numerical methods include fast spectral schemes [36] and finite element methods [27, 1]. These approaches often face the difficulty introduced by the nonlocality, nonlinearity and degeneracy of the models. A more convenient way is to seek the particle approximation of the Landau models. Typical stochastic particle approximations to Landau and Landau-type equations include conservative Kac-type diffusion systems [9] and interacting diffusion systems based on the McKean–Vlasov formulation [23]. These belong to the probabilistic models and have been studied recently by several groups, using coupling techniques [25], relative entropy methods [14, 12], and some hierarchy type techniques [22]. These particle systems, however, are not very suitable for numerical simulations because they usually cost O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) per time step if applied as numerical methods. Some existing numerical particle methods include the Monte Carlo collision algorithms [6, 34], and deterministic particle methods based on a regularized entropy [16, 15, 2, 3] and the random batch version [17]. The particle methods based on regularized entropy are numerical methods aiming to approximate the densities and do not keep the particle microscopic collision properties. The Monte Carlo methods in [6, 34] have O⁡(N)O(N) complexity but their approximations are based on the approximation to the Boltzmann equations instead of on the Landau operator directly. The grazing regime is intrinsically the diffusion regime of elastic collision, and some particle systems have been proposed for the Landau and Landau type equations [20, 21] building on this observation. Their advantage is that these methods are direct approximations to Landau collision operator instead of approximating the Boltzmann operator in grazing approximation. We remark that the particle models in [20, 21] look similar to the random batch type methods [29, 30], however they are derived directly from the pairwise collision in the grazing regime, and thus, they are not approximations to the fully-interacting collisional NN particle system.

papers.title: The AMPEL Platform: A Concept for Open-Source Collaboration in Developing In-House Medical Device Software under EU-Regulation
papers.abstract: Clinical decision support systems (CDSS) are expected to enhance medical treatment through automated data analysis, yet a substantial evidence gap persists as to whether they actually improve patient outcomes. It arises due to the black-box nature of commercial products and the constrains of the European medical device regulation (MDR) for such studies: patient outcomes may only be collected through the use of medical device software (MDSW). In-house MDSW under Article 5(5) MDR is a promising solution, allowing healthcare facilities to manufacture and study such software for their own use under reduced requirements. However, the overall limited experience with in-house MDSW development in Europe currently restricts the widespread use of this regulatory approach. While open-source software generally fosters evidence generation, publishing an in-house MDSW as open source would risk a classification as "placement on the market", which the MDR prohibits. The concept presented here builds on experience from developing an in-house CDSS at the University of Leipzig Medical Center, expert discussions, a literature review and a formal legal opinion. A companion online wiki summarizes and regularly updates the results. The current concept outlines a shared open-source codebase, which doesn't constitute a medical device under the MDR. Also, "Data Input" modules must be programmed separately at each site, while still allowing for multicenter collaboration on the codebase. Atypically for open-source projects, this leaves a considerable effort to deploy the software within each site, e.g. each healthcare facility must independently meet the MDR requirements for an in-house MDSW. The AMPEL concept describes a regulatory pathway for the open-source publication and development of in-house MDSW. It underpins the open-source AMPEL platform, which helps healthcare facilities build their own in-house CDSS.

papers.title: The AMPEL Platform: An Open-Source Project for Developing Hospital-Wide Clinical Decision Support Systems under EU-Regulation
papers.abstract: As incentives to digitize more and more aspects of medical healthcare are gaining traction, additional medical data is becoming available. A major goal is to use this data to gain further insights, support medical staff, and ultimately improve patient care. This demands sophisticated solutions that can handle current and future vast amounts of data, all without disrupting well-established workflows of care takers. Additionally, the solution must fulfill the documentation and risk-management obligations of the Medical Device Regulation (MDR), which governs whether a device may be used in patient care in Europe. In this context, we introduce the AMPEL platform, an open-source solution for creating clinical decision support systems (CDSS) that fulfil the requirements of the MDR. Centered around a message broker (Kafka), it adopts an event-driven, distributed architecture, allowing for scaling and efficient processing of medical data as it gets generated. Relying on platform-specific events to implicitly describe the platform's interfaces makes it both extensible and agnostic to the hospital information system in use. With these events being defined in the Protocol Buffers format, medically evaluated algorithms can be independently implemented in a variety of programming languages and easily linked to the platform, extending its analytic capabilities as desired. The platform features a basic UI and alert functionality that can be used to gain medical staff's attention and present analysis results in a traceable and explainable fashion. We further show in a use case how the platform was used to build LAMPE, a CDSS developed and operated at University of Leipzig Medical Center. It demonstrates how the platform solution can be used in a complex and already established environment, while acknowledging current limitations and outlining planned developments to overcome these.

papers.title: In-pixel lock-in readout for wide-field nitrogen-vacancy radio-frequency spectrum analysis
papers.abstract: The growing use of radio-frequency (RF) technologies requires compact, room-temperature sensors that can analyze a wide RF band in real time. Here we present a quantum RF spectrum analyzer based on the gradient-encoded electron spin resonance of a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) ensemble in diamond and read out with a $512\times542$-pixel lock-in camera that demodulates the signal in each pixel. On/off keying the signal under test at the camera's reference frequency lets every pixel extract the spin-resonant photoluminescence modulation. Before digitization, each pixel suppresses the static background and low-frequency noise that limit conventional camera readout. Translating a single permanent magnet tunes the encoded band continuously from 10~MHz to 32~GHz. The magnet position establishes a trade-off between instantaneous bandwidth (up to 4~GHz) and frequency resolution (7--22~MHz), with a 5~ms readout time. The wide-field readout integrates all spectral channels in parallel in a room-temperature sensor head and requires no phase synchronization to the RF carrier. The SNR remains above 70 at an applied power as low as $-32.5$~dBm. The magnetic-field configuration can be adapted to different RF bands without changing the pixel-parallel readout.

papers.intro:
For receivers based on analog-to-digital conversion, intercepting and analyzing rapidly changing radio-frequency (RF) signals over several gigahertz of instantaneous bandwidth is difficult because sampling rate and power consumption limit direct digitization to a few hundred megahertz [1]. Analog alternatives based on microwave photonics [2] or spectral hole burning in rare-earth-doped crystals [3] reach tens of gigahertz, although they sacrifice frequency resolution or require cryogenic operation. Rydberg-atom spectrum analyzers provide high sensitivity from dc to 20 GHz, with instantaneous bandwidth limited to the megahertz scale [4].

Ensembles of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11] enable broadband spectral analysis at room temperature. In a diamond quantum spectrum analyzer [12, 13, 14], a static magnetic-field gradient maps the electron spin resonance (ESR) frequency of each NV center onto position through the Zeeman shift. Similar frequency-to-position encoding has been demonstrated in atomic vapors [15]. An incident microwave field excites only the NV centers resonant with its spectral components, producing a spatially varying photoluminescence (PL) contrast under continuous optical excitation. The camera records this contrast in a single exposure to reconstruct the signal spectrum within the encoded band. The first demonstration achieved 600 MHz instantaneous bandwidth with millisecond refresh rates [12]. Later architectures span tens of gigahertz with improved spectral resolution and dynamic range [13, 14]. The frequency range above 20 GHz overlaps bands used by K- and Ka-band satellite links, 5G millimeter-wave communications, and radar [16, 17]. Wide-field NV imaging can map the near fields of microwave circuits [18].

Optical readout is the main limitation of NV-based microwave spectrum analyzers. The microwave spectrum is encoded as a PL contrast of 10−310^{-3}–10−210^{-2} on a static intensity background. Conventional readout estimates this contrast by subtracting sequentially acquired signal and reference images [19, 20]. The pixel full-well capacity of conventional scientific cameras, typically a few tens of ke- per exposure, limits this differential imaging scheme [21]. Once the pixels are saturated, additional PL intensity does not improve the single-frame signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). The full-well capacity sets the shot-noise floor. Sequential acquisition leaves residual pump-laser intensity fluctuations and fixed-pattern drift after subtraction. This residual noise eventually dominates photon noise during long-term averaging. Lock-in cameras replace sequential image subtraction with direct in-pixel demodulation. Each pixel separates the modulated PL from the static background before digitization, retains the full photon flux for signal detection, and suppresses low-frequency technical noise. In-pixel demodulation has enabled wide-field NV magnetometry with millisecond and sub-millisecond temporal resolution [22, 23, 24], but has not yet been applied to NV-based microwave spectrum analysis.

papers.title: Dual-Stream Event-to-Video Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Event cameras capture brightness changes with high temporal resolution and dynamic range, but converting event streams into videos remains fundamentally ill-posed due to the lack of absolute intensity information. Resolving this ambiguity calls for a brightness reference that complements the intensity changes recorded by events. Inspired by the complementary spatial and temporal processing of the parvocellular and magnocellular pathways in human vision, we propose EvDualDiff, a dual-stream framework that combines a brightness reference from temporal-mapping events with motion-event cues for video reconstruction. Conditioned on both streams, our video diffusion model autoregressively reconstructs long sequences from a single temporal map. Photometric constraints and finetuning on self-generated rollouts reduce accumulated drift. At the hardware level, our approach requires only a minimal light-modulation mechanism on the lens of an event camera. We build this setup and collect a dataset comprising temporal-mapping events, motion events and synchronised ground-truth RGB frames. Experiments on a public benchmark and on our collected EvDual dataset demonstrate that EvDualDiff outperforms existing event-to-video reconstruction methods in fidelity, perceptual quality and video-level realism. The code and dataset will be released.

papers.intro:
Drawing upon the biological mechanisms of human sight, the silicon retina [31] established the conceptual framework for neuromorphic sensors, eventually evolving into what are now widely recognised as event cameras, or Dynamic Vision Sensors (DVS). DVS records relative brightness changes as event streams with high temporal resolution (in the order of μ\mus) and a wide dynamic range (over 120120 dB). DAVIS sensors provide both events and intensity frames, but representative designs have larger pixels and lower resolution than modern event-only DVS [13], which can limit their use in applications requiring high spatial resolution. Here, we study how high-resolution, event-only DVS can acquire a brightness reference without native frame readout or changes to their pixel circuitry. Among the applications of event cameras, event-to-video reconstruction plays a central role, as recovering intensity frames enables compatibility with conventional vision pipelines.

The human visual system processes spatial and temporal information through complementary pathways. This parallel organisation is exemplified by the magnocellular (M) and parvocellular (P) pathways [29], as sketched in Fig. 1(a). Guided by this principle, we propose EvDualDiff, a dual-stream framework that combines temporal-mapping events [3] and motion events from a single sensor for video reconstruction. As Fig. 1(b) shows, a light-modulation device in the lens raises the transmittance from 0%0\% to 100%100\% within a few milliseconds and then keeps it constant. The sweep generates temporal-mapping events that provide a brightness reference, while subsequent motion events capture scene dynamics. In contrast, E2VID+ [43] uses only motion events and produces a nearly blank initial frame and low-contrast reconstructions in Fig. 1(c). To effectively encode the temporal-mapping events, we further design the Time-to-Brightness Encoder, a temporal-mapping-adapted VAE encoder that learns a compact latent representation aligned with the generative prior.

To reconstruct long, temporally dense videos beyond the 1313-frame chunks our model processes, we propose an autoregressive reconstruction strategy. We introduce low-band freezing and colour locking to stabilise brightness, and finetune the control branch on self-generated rollouts to reduce content drift from imperfect references. papers.title: MM-DataLoop: Closing the Data-Side Loop for Recursive Self-Improvement in MLLM Post-Training
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a path toward improving models through repeated evaluation and revision. We study its data side in multimodal language model (MLLM) post-training, where heterogeneous operations and cross-round evidence must be coordinated. MMDataLoop organizes data interventions into five operation families and connects them through an Observe-Diagnose-Plan-Execute-Verify-Reflect cycle with shared rule memory. Across 34 candidate rounds on Qwen3.5-0.8B and five benchmarks, we hold the base initialization, shared training schedule and evaluation protocol fixed while varying data recipes. The five-benchmark mean reaches 63.04 at R33, up 5.32 points from the zero-shot baseline; R29, R32, and R33 form a close top cluster within 0.09 points. In eightcandidate comparisons, guided search reaches the preselected target in six candidates and identifies the top observed candidate, while random arms show higher means and lower dispersion. The selected R29 recipe also scores above two full-pool baselines under the same epoch schedule. Together, these findings establish MM-DataLoop as a traceable workflow and provide an empirical basis for studying how data-side decisions shape outcomes across MLLM post-training recipes.

papers.intro:
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) relies on repeated evaluation and revision. In MLLM post-training, this process can also operate on the training data: benchmark outcomes inform subsequent acquisition, synthesis, denoising, and recipe composition. While much work focuses on model updates or autonomous experiment design, coordinating heterogeneous data operations and carrying evidence from one recipe to the next remains central to the data side of the loop. We study MM-DataLoop as a workflow for doing so with benchmark feedback and recorded experience.

papers.title: On the subtleties of statistical isotropy in cosmic topology
papers.abstract: The cosmological principle assumes homogeneity and isotropy on the largest scales for which the cosmic microwave background (CMB) provides the best testing grounds. Here, an analysis of the statistical isotropy for the CMB in the case of the cubic 3-torus topology is presented. Since the statistical anisotropy in the CMB 3-torus sky maps is very tiny, the analysis requires very large ensembles consisting of 100000 CMB simulations in order to reveal deviations from the isotropy. Orbit sum rules, which also have applications in quantum chaos, are used to describe the anisotropy structures found in the torus ensembles. They relate the length of orbits, which connect a given point on the surface of last scattering with the topological mirror points of the CMB observer, to the anisotropy pattern. It is found that the positions on the surface of last scattering which are closest to mirror observers possess the largest deviations from the statistical isotropy. Furthermore, the anisotropy of the normalised modulus of the gradient of the CMB temperature field is discussed.

papers.intro:
The cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation is almost perfectly statistically isotropic and is one of the strongest pillars of empirical evidence for the cosmological principle which assumes homogeneity and isotropy on the largest scales. In order to achieve this important result, the monopole and the kinematic dipole of the CMB as well as foreground emission have to be subtracted. Since the availability of full-sky CMB surveys, cosmologists ponder the question of a violation of the statistical isotropy. The most recent data are analysed by the Planck team in [1] with respect to the statistical isotropy. A good survey of the diagnostic tools to detect a violation of the statistical isotropy can be found in [2, 3, 4]. One prominent example is the parity asymmetry and the related power asymmetry between even and odd low-multipoles [5]. The parity asymmetry is further investigated in a lot of papers, for example see references in [6] and points to a violation. An analysis of the asymmetry in the Planck data using the Minkowski functionals can be found in [7]. But there are other measures as the correlation matrix Cl​m​l′​m′:=⟨al​m​al′​m′⟩C_{lml^{\prime}m^{\prime}}:=\left<a_{lm}a_{l^{\prime}m^{\prime}}\right> of the spherical expansion coefficients al​ma_{lm} of the CMB temperature fluctuations, which should be diagonal in the case of statistical isotropy, see e. g. [8].

Among the many possibilities for explaining a violation in statistical isotropy are multiply connected manifolds studied in cosmic topology [9, 10, 11, 12], that inherently break this statistical isotropy without the need for modified local physics. This publication deals with the simplest non-trivial topology in the Euclidean space, the 3-torus. This model serves as a testing ground for various diagnostic tools concerning statistical isotropy. For example, [13] introduces the bipolar power spectrum which measures how pairs of different angular scales correlate and thus detects subtle directional patterns. Furthermore, the expected correlation matrix Cl​m​l′​m′C_{lml^{\prime}m^{\prime}} is now calculated for all Euclidean topologies in [14] for orientable manifolds and in [15] for non-orientable manifolds. For the Euclidean orientable case, also the correlation matrix is known for tensor modes [16, 17].

In section 2 the variance σ2​(n^)\sigma^{2}(\hat{n}) of the CMB temperature field and the variance σ12​(n^)\sigma_{1}^{2}(\hat{n}) obtained from its covariant derivative used in our study of the anisotropy are defined. These isotropy measures are applied to the cubic 3-torus ensemble which is defined in section 3. Since the statistical anisotropy proves to be so tiny, torus ensembles consisting of 100 000 members are analysed in section 4 for σ2​(n^)\sigma^{2}(\hat{n}) and σ12​(n^)\sigma_{1}^{2}(\hat{n}). In order to understand the behaviour observed in section 4, we apply orbit sum rules to the ensemble averaging. In the first step, the Sachs-Wolfe approximation is adapted in section 5 by using some simplifying assumptions, while in the next step presented in section 6 the orbit sum rules are applied, which show that the lengths of the orbits, which connect a point on the surface of last scattering with the topological mirror points of the CMB observer, determine the anisotropy structures. papers.title: SAGE-Drive: Benefit-Aware Adaptive Reasoning for Autonomous Driving Planning
papers.abstract: Explicit reasoning enables autonomous vehicles (AVs) to interpret complex traffic interactions and support trajectory planning, but introduces additional computational demands. Determining when explicit reasoning can improve planning accuracy remains a key challenge, as its benefits vary across driving scenarios. To address this challenge, this study proposes Scene-Adaptive Gating of Explicit Reasoning for Driving (SAGE-Drive), a benefit-aware adaptive reasoning framework for autonomous driving planning. First, paired planning outcomes with and without explicit reasoning are analyzed to measure the reasoning benefit, i.e., the reduction in planning error achieved by explicit reasoning, which serves as the supervision label. SAGE-Drive then learns to predict these benefits using geometric features of the initial trajectory planned without reasoning and multimodal scene information, and invokes explicit reasoning only for the scenarios with the highest predicted benefits under a predefined reasoning budget. Experiments on 1,497 paired driving scenarios reveal that explicit reasoning improves planning accuracy in 53.5% of cases while degrading it in 46.5%, yielding a near-zero average benefit. On the test set, with a 20% reasoning budget, SAGE-Drive achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 1.5191 m, compared with 1.5252 m for random selection. At a 35% budget, it achieves an ADE of 1.5148 m, close to the 1.5141 m obtained when reasoning is applied to every scenario. These findings establish the predicted reasoning benefit as an effective criterion for reasoning selection, allowing explicit reasoning to be invoked where it improves planning accuracy at a fraction of its computational cost.
