papers.title: AirVT-15k: A Query-Diverse UAV Video-Text Dataset and Query-Adaptive Evidence Alignment Network for Retrieval
papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle video-text retrieval (UAV-TVR) requires matching language to both scene context and subtle object changes. A harbor-layout query relies on global scene context, whereas a departing-vessel query requires local functional cues and motion states. Existing benchmarks provide diverse aerial descriptions but give limited attention to distinct evidence needs within the same video. We introduce AirVT-15k, a benchmark of 15,504 UAV videos and 155,040 captions, with ten complementary bilingual captions per video describing scenes, object states, and temporal changes. We also propose AirFocus-CST, which selects query-relevant frames and patches, encodes temporal feature differences, and combines coarse-to-fine interaction (CFI) with optimal-transport alignment (OTA). Average mean recall reaches 63.67% on AirVT-15k and 24.41% on CapERA, improving over the strongest baselines by 2.96 and 1.91 percentage points, respectively. The dataset and code are available at https://chenxi000233.github.io/AirVT-15k-site/.
papers.intro:
UAV video–text retrieval supports traffic inspection, port monitoring, and disaster assessment. Queries about the same video can require different visual evidence. A harbor-layout query refers to docks and waterways; a departing-vessel query refers to the vessel’s position relative to its berth and how that position changes over time (Fig. 1). We describe these evidence types as global scene context, local functional cues, and motion states. Wide views, small objects, and subtle motion make their joint representation difficult.

General video–text benchmarks such as MSR-VTT [47] cover diverse content, and aerial resources such as GeoChat [23] support image-level understanding. UAV video benchmarks, including DVTMD [52], extend this setting to aerial video descriptions. Evaluating query-dependent evidence needs also requires captions that describe different aspects of the same clip. We introduce AirVT-15k with 15,504 videos covering aerial scenes, object activities, and temporal changes. Each video has ten complementary bilingual captions, so queries can refer to its surroundings, local objects, or changes over time. Video-level data splits and bidirectional retrieval protocols define the training and evaluation setting.

Retrieval methods address frame aggregation and cross-modal correspondence in different ways. CLIP4Clip [33] aggregates frame representations, X-Pool [14] pools frames conditioned on text, and TCMA [52] aligns sentences with frames and words with patches. UAV retrieval also requires distinguishing activities among videos with similar scenes and object appearances. We propose AirFocus-CST with two components: Query-Guided Multi-Evidence Modeling and Complementary Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Alignment. The first retains global scene context and combines query-guided temporal selection (TS), query-guided spatial refinement (SR), and temporal variation modeling (TV). TS and SR focus on relevant moments and local functional cues; TV encodes frame-feature changes associated with motion states. The second combines Coarse-to-Fine Interaction (CFI) on query-refined features with Optimal-Transport Alignment (OTA) on query-independent visual features. CFI checks sentence–frame, word–frame, and word–patch matches, while OTA jointly allocates word–patch correspondence weights across the video.

papers.title: Data-Driven Nonlinear Observer Design Using the Koopman Generator
papers.abstract: This paper deals with the data-driven design of nonlinear continuous-time observers using the Koopman generator. For systems without inputs, an observer is designed that consists of a linear system part with a nonlinear output injection. Therein, the output injection introduces additional degrees of freedom to ensure an invariant dictionary or a small projection error. Subsequently, this observer is extended to systems with inputs. These results form the basis for a data-driven nonlinear observer design using generator extended dynamic mode decomposition. Probabilistic finite-data error bounds are derived for the observer error w.r.t. the data-driven observer error dynamics and for the corresponding steady-state observation error. Examples of nonlinear systems with invariant and non-invariant dictionaries illustrate the effectiveness of the novel data-driven observer design procedure.

papers.intro:
In recent years data-driven control of unknown dynamical systems has had a tremendous impact on system theory and control. This approach aims at designing controllers based solely on available data without recourse to system modeling and identification (see [11, 4]). This, on the one hand significantly facilitates the controller design and, on the other hand, allows to deal with complex dynamical systems, where a first principle modeling is very involved.

In recent years data-driven control of unknown dynamical systems has had a tremendous impact on system theory and control. This approach aims at designing controllers based solely on available data without recourse to system modeling and identification (see [11, 4]). This, on the one hand significantly facilitates the controller design and, on the other hand, allows to deal with complex dynamical systems, where a first principle modeling is very involved.

Among the existing methods for data-driven control (see, e.g., [17]) the Koopman operator approach has gained increasing interest in the control community (see [18] for an overview). This method offers an alternative view on dynamical systems by describing their dynamics in the space of observables, which can be seen as generalized measurements. Their time evolution is described by the Koopman operator, which is an infinite-dimensional linear map in the space of observables even if the underlying system is nonlinear. Hence, methods from infinite-dimensional linear system theory are applicable for the system analysis. A distinct feature of the Koopman operator is that it can be systematically determined from data by making use of extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD) (see [32]). Similarly, also the Koopman generator, i.e., the infinitesimal generator of the Koopman operator, is attainable from data via generator EDMD (gEDMD) (see [14]). The generator describes the time evolution of the observables by means of a differential equation and thus directly leads to a continuous-time surrogate model. The convergence of the EDMD is verified in the large-data limit in [16]. Since in applications only a finite amount of data is available, finite-data error bounds for the approximation of the Koopman generator are crucial for systematic data-driven control. This was investigated in [23] for gEDMD considering the projected Koopman generator and extended in [26] to obtain probabilistic error bounds for both the finite-data and projection error. Consequently, stability guarantees can be given in the data-driven controller design. This was exploited in [2] for data-driven model predictive control (MPC) and in [28] for state feedback control using tools from linear robust control based on convex optimization. Besides other contributions for data-driven MPC and optimal control in [15, 35, 10], the Koopman-based data-driven control using Lyapunov techniques is presented in [12] and [8] uses feedback linearization.

All these methods consider state feedback control and thus need an observer for output feedback control, which is required for applications. In addition, the open-loop monitoring of nonlinear systems using observers is another important problem. While many results exist for the model-based nonlinear observer design (see [1] for a recent review of observer design techniques), the data-driven observer design for unknown nonlinear systems has received less attention in the literature so far. Existing results use neural networks to learn the unknown nonlinear system dynamics and also the nonlinear mappings for the observer design (see, e.g., [7] for discrete-time and [33] for continuous-time systems). These approaches, however, have to deal with general system nonlinearities in the design. In [30] the Koopman operator framework is applied for the data-driven nonlinear observer design employing a spectral approach in discrete time, while the continuous-time case is treated in [29]. These works demonstrate that the Koopman operator also significantly facilitates the observer design, since for autonomous systems a linear and for non-autonomous systems a bilinear observer results. In particular, the Koopman eigenfunctions are utilized to obtain a Koopman modal system representation leading to a bilinear surrogate model if inputs are taken into account. This forms the basis for the observer design by assuming a finitely bilinearizable system, so that observer design techniques for Lipschitz nonlinear systems can be used. Applications of these results include the power system state estimation in [22] and the estimation of the unsteady flowfield near an actuated airfoil in [9]. In these contributions, however, the approximation error is not taken into account in the design. Furthermore, the application of Koopman eigenfunctions introduces additional technical challenges (see [10] for more details). The recent advances in gEDMD regarding probabilistic finite-data error bounds thus suggest using Koopman generator as a basis for the nonlinear observer design, which, to the best of the author’s knowledge, has not been addressed in the literature so far.

papers.title: Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals
papers.abstract: Looped Transformers iterate a shared block of layers to increase computation without adding parameters, offering stronger performance and test-time scaling. However, this power has so far required training from scratch and yielded only modest gains for LLMs. Finetuning existing models into loops is far cheaper, yet also brings only marginal gains over SFT. We propose LoopRes, an effective, scalable, and simple approach that turns loops into significant and consistent gains for pretrained LLMs. Building on Attention Residuals, LoopRes lets each looped layer attend directly to the outputs of earlier loops. Since these outputs are iterates of the same layers and become harder to tell apart, we give each a trainable loop-aware key that encodes its structural identity. Attending to all earlier loops also lets layers skip intermediate ones, so we restrict each layer to a residual window of the latest W loops, forcing every loop to build incrementally on recent ones. Across 6 pretrained LLMs from 3 model families and 9 benchmarks, LoopRes delivers significant and consistent gains: at 2x compute, it improves Qwen3-1.7B-Base by 29.1% over SFT, more than doubling the gain of the state-of-the-art baseline. The gains hold on larger models up to 30B and across all three families. More importantly, from 1.7B to 8B, LoopRes scales more steeply than SFT as compute grows, reaching a higher ceiling while needing less compute on long outputs. These results establish LoopRes as an effective looping approach, delivering both better performance and better test-time scaling.

papers.title: Personalization of a Commercial Powered Knee Prosthesis Under Clinically Realistic Conditions via Reinforcement Learning: A Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: Personalization of powered prosthesis control to individual user needs remains a significant challenge. To address this challenge, policy iteration with constraint embedded (PICE), a reinforcement learning (RL) tuning approach, has been developed and validated. This feasibility study investigated whether the developed approach can personalize a commercial powered knee prosthesis under clinically realistic conditions. To reduce the time for personalization, tuning was initialized with a policy learned offline from one non-disabled participant walking on a treadmill and was then applied to three other non-disabled participants walking with the knee through a bypass adapter on a 5-meter walkway. All participants reached the goal within 8-18 tuning steps (1.7-4.2 minutes of walking), reducing the knee-kinematic feature error by 64-90% on average. These results support the feasibility of implementing the RL-based tuning approach in clinically realistic conditions with space and equipment constraints.

papers.intro:
For individuals with transfemoral amputation, powered knee prostheses can generate positive mechanical power during gait, which passive knees cannot [1]. Research prototypes have demonstrated clinical benefits in laboratory settings [2], and clinical evaluations of commercial devices have reported improved biomechanical outcomes and favorable user feedback [3], yet these benefits are not fully realized across users [4, 5, 6]. This inconsistency has limited the adoption of powered prostheses in clinical practice and everyday use [3]. A major bottleneck is personalizing the controller to each user [7, 8]. Across robotic lower-limb prostheses, user outcomes depend on how the controller is configured [3, 9, 10]. Commonly used prosthesis control approaches, from finite-state impedance control [11, 2], continuous impedance control [12], hybrid kinematic–impedance control [13], and model-based control [14] to recent learning-based controllers trained in simulation [15], all require per-user customization to achieve clinical benefits [9].

Personalization must account for many user-specific factors and is predominantly performed manually without a standardized procedure. Parameters must be adjusted to each user’s body size and gait style [16, 5]. Some factors also change over time: users re-weight movement goals such as efficiency and stability as environmental risk changes [17, 18], and users adapt their motor control to the device [19], so a configuration tuned once may need to be revisited. In current practice, prosthetists tune the parameters by observing the user across walking trials [11], which is time-consuming and relies on expert knowledge of many interacting parameters: even with a structured starting configuration, 24 of the 140 parameters of a powered knee–ankle prosthesis had to be adjusted for each user, taking up to 5 hours in one such approach [11]. Moreover, clinical evaluations often do not report the tuning procedure or criteria used [3, 5], which makes outcomes difficult to compare across studies.

Moreover, clinical evaluations often do not report the tuning procedure or criteria used [3, 5], which makes outcomes difficult to compare across studies.

Automating tuning toward a prescribed goal could shorten clinic visits, standardize fitting procedures, reduce dependency on subjective expert tuning, which could be biased, and let users benefit more fully from powered prostheses. Such automation is commonly framed as human-in-the-loop optimization (HILO) [8]. Black-box optimizers that search for a single best parameter set, such as covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy and Bayesian optimization, have reduced the metabolic cost of walking with exoskeletons [20, 21], but have not outperformed generic control for prosthesis users [22], likely because users’ motor control and objectives change as they adapt to the device [22, 19]. Another common HILO framework is reinforcement learning (RL) with human-subject testing in the loop, which instead drives the prosthesis motion toward a target profile [23, 15]. Rather than searching for a single optimum, it learns a tuning policy that maps the observed knee-motion error to incremental parameter adjustments [7], which can be reapplied whenever the user’s condition changes. Policy iteration with constraint embedded (PICE) [24] tuned 12 impedance parameters within 45 tuning steps, and the resulting policies remained effective across users and task modifications. RL tuning has since been extended to continuous impedance control [12] and to shaping the user’s thigh motion [25]. RL tuning frameworks such as PICE could therefore serve as a general tuning mechanism, but there are still challenges to be addressed to ensure practical implementation in clinics [7, 24, 12].

papers.title: Assembly-JEPA: Using World Models for Fine-Grained Industrial Image Verification
papers.abstract: Automated verification of industrial assembly processes remains a challenging problem due to substantial visual variability, limited availability of labeled defect data, and the fine-grained nature of many assembly errors. Existing approaches often rely on object detection, CAD models, or supervised classification pipelines, which can struggle to generalize across changing products and assembly configurations. In this work, we propose a novel self-supervised assembly verification framework based on Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs). Starting from the JEPA-based world model LeWorldModel, we investigate how the architecture must be adapted to verify the correctness of fine-grained assembly operations. To this end, we formulate assembly verification as a predictive world modeling task operating on before-and-after observations of assembly processes. Experimental results on industrial assembly tasks demonstrate that the proposed approach reliably detects both fine-grained incorrect assembly states and action-state mismatches, achieving an AUROC of 86.9% on a newly introduced assembly verification dataset. These results indicate that JEPA-based predictive representations constitute a promising foundation for robust and data-efficient industrial assembly verification.

Machine-learning-based vision systems have become an important component of modern manufacturing, supporting quality control, automated optical inspection and process monitoring. Recent surveys report a rapidly growing body of research and industrial applications in deep-learning-based visual inspection [1].

While existing methodologies, such as CNN-based classification (ResNet [2]), object detection (YOLO [3]), or anomaly detection (PaDiM [4], PatchCore [5]), perform remarkably well on standardized benchmarks like MVTec AD [6], recent evaluation studies emphasize that significant challenges remain for real-world industrial deployment [7]. Unlike prior JEPA-based computer vision approaches that primarily use the predictor during training, our method retains both the encoder and predictor during inference. By conditioning the predictor on assembly actions, the model learns expected state transitions between consecutive assembly steps. Verification is then performed by comparing the predicted post-action state with the actually observed state, using the prediction error as an indicator of assembly correctness. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to leverage the complete JEPA, including both encoder and predictor, for industrial assembly verification. papers.title: Alignment under Hard Negative Re-Pairing: Cross-Modal Similarity, Scale and Retrieval
papers.abstract: Do vision and language models represent the world alike? That question hides three: what structure each modality has, whether the two modalities organize images and their captions alike, and whether a model ranks an image's own caption highly. Centered kernel alignment (CKA) and neighborhood agreement answer the second, yet matching and model selection use them as if they identified individual pairs and answered the third. To test this reading, we introduce hard negative re-pairing: every image receives the caption of a similar image, and nothing else changes. Although no image keeps its own caption and annotators judge a majority of the substituted captions wrong, CKA stays higher than under a random re-pairing that keeps 80% of the original pairs. In all 22 image-text models we test, neighborhood agreement loses far less than top-one retrieval, which collapses. The reason is scale: these diagnostics pool over many neighbors, matching and retrieval are decided among the nearest ones, and an exact decomposition shows that near-neighbor pairs contribute almost nothing to CKA. In the matching problems we test, an exact maximizer of CKA would not return the original pairing. On COCO and Flickr30k, the model with the highest diagnostic value retrieves worse on held-out data than the model chosen by validation recall, even where the two correlate positively. What re-pairing removes is the informative part: that share tracks retrieval on both datasets and ranks encoder pairs before alignment training. A diagnostic should be reported with its question and its scale, and tested against hard negative re-pairing.

papers.title: When Modalities (Dis)Agree: How Decomposing Multi-Modal AI Advice Shapes Appropriate Reliance
papers.abstract: Multi-modal AI systems integrate diverse data streams into unified advices, but this fusion conceals how individual modalities contribute to the final output. Consequently, decision-makers cannot observe whether underlying sources aligned or contradicted one another when assessing the provided advice. To test whether revealing this structure supports appropriate reliance, we conducted a pre-registered experiment (N = 240) in which participants evaluated used-car prices with multi-modal AI support. In a 2x2 between-subjects design, we varied the disclosure of modality-level outputs and natural-language explanations, crossed with within-subjects modality agreement. Revealing modality-level outputs increased reliance, while explanations improved decision accuracy independently. However, this occurred only when modalities agreed: visible consensus acted as a persuasive cue that generally amplified adherence, rather than helping participants override errors under conflict. Thus, decomposing multi-modal advice can make AI advice more persuasive without making errors easier to detect.

papers.intro:
Modern AI systems increasingly operate across multiple input modalities simultaneously, processing, for example, images, text, and structured data within a single model (Liang et al., 2024). In most high-stakes domains, the information relevant to a decision is distributed across data types that no single modality fully captures (Baltrušaitis et al., 2018). A radiologist’s judgment draws on imaging, patient history, and lab results (Yildirim et al., 2024); a used-car appraisal depends on photographs, textual descriptions, and technical specifications. Multi-modal AI systems combine information from different modalities, allowing them to use complementary information that may improve the accuracy of the final prediction (Liang et al., 2024; Baltrušaitis et al., 2018). However, this fusion also hides how each modality assessed the case, leaving humans with only the final prediction.

Effective human-AI collaboration depends on accepting a prediction when it is correct and overriding it when it is wrong, so that the human-AI team outperforms either party alone (Lee and See, 2004; Schemmer et al., 2023; Bansal et al., 2021). Doing so requires information about whether a specific prediction can be trusted (Lee and See, 2004; Zhang et al., 2020), but a fused prediction reveals none of the modality-level information that could support the human in doing so. Humans bring their own knowledge and familiarity to different data types, so a buyer assessing a used car may read more from the photographs than from the specifications, or the reverse, depending on what they know about cars. These differences in expertise shape humans’ mental models of how the AI should process information and arrive at a advice (Holstein and Satzger, 2025). Research in perceptual psychology shows that when humans can distinguish separate information sources, they weight them by perceived reliability in a near-optimal accuracy (Ernst and Banks, 2002; Fetsch et al., 2012). Revealing those assessments could therefore provide humans with a basis for deciding when to adhere to the multi-modal AI and when to override it.

papers.title: Design and performance of a top-loading vibrating-sample magnetometer for a helium-flow variable-temperature insert
papers.abstract: We present a custom-built top-loading probe that adds vibrating-sample magnetometry to an existing helium-flow variable-temperature insert without replacing its cryogenic or magnetic-field infrastructure. The modular instrument combines a detachable sealed drive head, a voice-coil resonator operating near 44 Hz, continuous monitoring of the peak vibration amplitude, motorized axial centering, and a compact first-order pickup-coil gradiometer. A numerical flux-linkage calculation reproduces the position and shape of the measured axial response for several vibration amplitudes after multiplication by a common factor of 1.08. Measurements on Ni reference samples demonstrate operation down to 5 K and yield effective geometrical factors between 24.0 V s A$^{-1}$ m$^{-3}$ and 31.4 V s A$^{-1}$ m$^{-3}$. At fixed field, the observed voltage scatter corresponds to moment-equivalent one-standard-deviation repeatabilities of 16.5 nA m$^{2}$ to 27.8 nA m$^{2}$. For a 31.7 nm Ni film measured at 250 K, magnetization curves obtained at three vibration amplitudes approximately collapse after amplitude correction and yield a saturation magnetization of approximately 409 kA m$^{-1}$ after subtraction of the linear high-field background. The results demonstrate a practical retrofit approach for adding bulk and thin-film magnetometry to VTIs with comparable bore and flange constraints.

papers.intro:
Vibrating-sample magnetometry was introduced by Foner in 1959 [1]. In this method, a magnetized sample is vibrated periodically with respect to a set of pickup coils, thereby inducing a voltage that is proportional to its magnetic moment. The original instrument already detected changes in magnetic moment of the order of 10−510^{-5} to 10−6​emu10^{-6}\,\mathrm{emu}. Subsequent developments improved the pickup-coil geometry and reduced the sensitivity to small positioning errors. In particular, a broad saddle point in the axial response was shown to be advantageous [2], and the effects of coil geometry, sample dimensions, and the sample holder on the detected signal were investigated systematically [3, 4, 5, 6].

papers.title: Beyond Outlier Rejection: Transient-Aware Reconstruction of Multi-Stack MRI
papers.abstract: Clinical MRI typically acquires the organ of interest as consecutive stacks of 2D slices in different orientations. Reconstruction methods such as SVRTK and NeSVoR fuse them into one volume and down-weight what does not fit, although in living tissue the change during the scan is often the signal itself and can contain clinically relevant physiological information, such as fetal motion and uterine contraction. We propose an analysis-by-synthesis decomposition that explains every acquired voxel through its exact acquisition geometry as a static anatomy shared by all stacks, a rigid and smooth non-rigid motion per stack, and a sparse transient field per stack for changes during one acquisition only. A robust reweighting keeps such changes out of the anatomy. The model is fitted per subject without training data, with one configuration for all datasets. On a digital phantom with known ground truth, static changes are kept entirely in the anatomy, and the transient field of the stack that saw a transient recovers 68% of it at 12mm radius. From identical inputs, the anatomy predicts held-out stacks better than SVRTK and NeSVoR on uterine (NCC 0.897 against 0.874 and 0.863, 123 patients) and on prostate MRI from unseen sites and scanners (0.847 against 0.795 and 0.757, 85 patients), and on fetal brain MRI as well as SVRTK and better than NeSVoR (0.771 against 0.763 and 0.747, 83 fetuses). The transient fields flag corrupted fetal slices with an AUROC of 0.94 against expert raters. As the input of a frozen anomaly detector trained on healthy subjects only, the anatomy localizes radiologist-delineated uterine lesions better than the SVRTK and NeSVoR volumes (AUROC 0.76 against 0.71 and 0.71, 37 patients).

papers.intro:
Obtaining insights into 3D objects from sparse, noisy and artifacted measurements acquired from different angles and conditions is a common, recurring problem across the disciplines [50], from video observation [16], geophysics [21], remote sensing [45], non-destructive testing [8, 1], archaeology [24] to medical imaging [35]. Typical 3D reconstruction techniques assume the object to be static [44] and focus on down-weighting or eliminating inconsistent measurements [40], acquisition optimization especially in clinical medicine often targets motion-free images by making life comply to the demands of imaging [11]. The observable transient changes, however, carry crucial information themselves: fetal motion informs on neurological status [23], contractile activity reflects muscular tissue health [4] and peristaltic motion is a key biomarker for diagnosis and treatment monitoring in e.g. bowel disease and in-vivo fertilization [14, 10].

Radiological data covers the area of interest in multiple views or ”stacks” of 2D slices in sagittal, coronal and axial orientation, allowing the radiologist to resolve inconsistencies. In areas with substantial motion, with fetal MRI as a prime example, the individual slices are acquired fast to limit motion effects and slice-to-volume-reconstruction (SVR) approaches are used to fuse them into high resolution 3D representations (see Figure 1). Inconsistencies between slices arise from motion, transient physiology such as uterine contractions, characterized as non-rigid, transient changes in shape and signal, and artifacts such as dropouts and aliasing. Beyond medicine, MRI is also used to image porous media or non-metallic materials such as polymers and fibre-reinforced composites [6, 3], where stacks of slices acquired over time face similar inconsistencies. Our experiments, however, are confined to medical data. Current SVR methods (Kuklisova-Murgasova [19], NiftyMIC [9], SVRTK [41], NeSVoR [48]) down-weight or reject inconsistent slices as outliers. Outlier rejection is thereby often binary and unexplained, not distinguishing why a slice doesn’t fit (rigid motion, local deformation, artifact or a physiological event). Comparable vision methods (NeRF in the Wild [22], RobustNeRF [31], HybridGS [18]) also handle transients as distractors to remove, not as phenomena to characterize. On the other hand, dedicated dynamic acquisitions are increasingly added to assess physiology, in turn however not contributing to the anatomical information available. Our approach treats both in a unified framework, reinterpreting a limitation of anatomical MRI, the acquisition of slice-level measurements over a significant time window, as a feature with the acquisition order providing a time axis for free, allowing transient events to be characterized without extra measurements.

We turn the multi-view inconsistencies that conventional reconstruction discards into an explicit, interpretable signal. • Forward model. Per subject, every voxel of every stack is explained through its exact acquisition geometry (scanner affine transform and slice profile). • Decomposition. The model comprises a static anatomy AA shared by all stacks, rigid and smooth non-rigid motion, an intensity model per stack, and a sparse, signed transient field TvT_{v} for changes seen in one stack only. • Attribution instead of rejection. Such changes are attributed to their acquisition time instead of averaged or rejected. Without event labels, the fit yields a transient-free reconstruction, maps of where and when each stack changed, and per-slice transient strengths over time. • Transfer. Developed on fetal MRI with inter-slice motion and uterine MRI with peristalsis, the configuration transfers unchanged to multi-site prostate MRI.

Existing work treats static reconstruction and the detection of inconsistencies as separate problems. Multi-view and SVR methods remove inconsistencies, quality-control methods detect them, and dedicated dynamic acquisitions measure physiology. Multi-view reconstruction. NeRF in the Wild [22] separates a static scene from a per-image transient component by discarding a learned uncertainty at rendering. RobustNeRF [31] treats distractors as outliers of a robust loss, and SpotLessSplats [30], WildGaussians [20] and RobustSplat [12] carry this to 3D Gaussian splatting, with masks or uncertainties derived from residuals or pretrained features. In HybridGS [18] per-image 2D Gaussians model the transients. Transients are considered nuisances, while our goal are time-resolved transient fields as meaningful outputs. Nuisance as signal. Computer vision has often turned artifacts into measurements, recovering depth from defocus [27], motion from blur [7], shape from shadows [36] and hidden scenes from shadows around corners [5]. Closest to our setting, the line-by-line readout of a rolling-shutter camera distorts moving scenes but also encodes their motion, since every image row has its own capture time [2]. Multi-stack MRI has the same structure at a coarser scale, as every slice is acquired at a known time. Dynamic and deformable scenes. D-NeRF [28] represents a moving scene as a canonical configuration and a deformation per instant, Nerfies [25] with an elastic regularizer. HyperNeRF [26] lifts it to higher dimensions for topological changes. All rely on dense frames that each see the whole scene. In multi-stack MRI every slice has its own time, so we keep one smooth deformation per stack and assign what it cannot explain to a sparse transient field. SVR, motion and quality control. SVR fuses stacks of thick 2D slices by alternating slice-to-volume registration with reconstruction. SVR [19] introduced intensity matching and a robust statistical model to remove outliers. NiftyMIC [9] embeds outlier-robust super-resolution in an automated pipeline with brain localization and segmentation. SVRTK [41] adds deformable registration, corrects each slice by a scale and bias and weights residuals by voxel- and slice-level inlier probabilities. NeSVoR [48] represents the volume as an implicit neural field and down-weights inconsistent data through pixel- and slice-level variances, and SVoRT [49] initializes it with transformer-predicted poses. tripleSR [37] fuses pre-aligned orthogonal views of the adult brain with a point-wise coordinate loss, which our forward model extends by the slice profile, motion and transients. Corrupted data are flagged by learned quality control of stacks [33, 47] and volumes [34], or detected to trigger re-acquisition [13, 42]. These approaches need labels or training data. Ours flags corrupted slices as a by-product of the reconstruction. Dedicated dynamic acquisitions quantify uterine contractions [15, 43, 39], adding scan time, while in anatomical stacks the same events are treated as artifacts.

papers.title: Advanced Reactance Method - A Novel Approach for Distance Protection in Presence of Grid-Following Inverter-Based-Resources
papers.abstract:
Renewable Energy Sources and consequently inverter-based resources (IBRs) are increasing worldwide.
  Grid-following (GFL) IBR control is the state-of-the-art.
  GFL IBRs exhibit different fault behavior compared to classical synchronous generators -- particularly in terms of Fault-Ride-Through (FRT) characteristics, which are critical for grid protection relaying.
  Grid protection must work securely, selectively and dependably, regardless of the feeding source.
  As common protection algorithms are designed for fault behavior determined by synchronous generators, their performance is expected to be compromised in the presence of GFL IBRs.
  Distance Protection is a widely used protection algorithm at all voltage levels.
  Literature shows that the FRT behavior of GFL IBRs impacts the Distance Protection relaying adversely.
  This paper proposes the Advanced Reactance Method, a further development of the Classical Reactance Method for Distance Protection in the presence of GFL IBRs.
  The key idea of the proposed method is to make the algorithm independent of the feeding source impedance.
  Therefore, the negative sequence voltage is taken into account along with the negative sequence current.
  This makes the algorithm independent of the FRT behavior of GFL IBRs, even in case of suppression of negative sequence current during unsymmetrical faults.
  Moreover, correct settings for the classical method in the presence of GFL IBRs are presented as a solution for relays without the advanced method.
  The novel algorithm is evaluated against the correctly parameterized Classical Reactance Method and the Distance Protection algorithm.

papers.title: Experimental study of the Reynolds number effect on the mean flow and coherent structures in a 180-degree bent pipe flow using PIV
papers.abstract: In this work, we study the effect of Reynolds number on the flow in a 180{\deg} pipe bend with a curvature of {\gamma} = 0.2. We perform planar particle image velocimetry (PIV) in the symmetry plane of the pipe for bulk Reynolds numbers ReD from 10 000 to 60 000 with water as the working fluid. To remove the refraction at the pipe wall, a hybrid method is employed. A mixture of water, glycerol and sodium iodide is used to match the refractive index of the pipe at its outer interface. The refraction at the inner interface is corrected using reverse ray tracing. The measurements are validated against direct numerical simulations at ReD = 10 000 and 20 000 and against hot-wire data from the literature at 60 000. As the Reynolds number increases, the mean velocity profiles in and downstream of the bend become flatter. Furthermore, a second vortex pair, with the opposite direction of rotation to the Dean vortices, forms further downstream, between bend angles of 116{\deg} and 126{\deg}. A modal decomposition of the planar velocity fields shows that the coherent structures keep their spatial features at all Reynolds numbers. Their Strouhal numbers remain nearly unchanged and show no monotonic trend.

Flows in curved pipes occur in a wide variety of technical and physiological systems, and have been the subject of research for more than a century (Berger et al., 1983; Ito, 1987) with the seminal work of Dean (Dean, 1927; Dean, 1928). Curved-pipe flows are characterised by two independent non-dimensional numbers. These are the bulk Reynolds number R​eD=Ub​D/νRe_{D}=U_{b}D/\nu and the curvature γ=D/(2​Rc)\gamma=D/(2R_{c}). Here, UbU_{b} and DD denote the bulk velocity and the pipe diameter, respectively. The symbols ν\nu and RcR_{c} denote the kinematic viscosity and the radius of curvature of the centreline, respectively. In curved pipe flows, the centrifugal force generates a secondary flow in the form of a counter-rotating pair of Dean vortices (Dean, 1927; Dean, 1928). Further downstream in the bend, the cross-stream flow on the symmetry plane reverses its direction. The reversal is attributed to a second pair of counter-rotating vortices with the opposite direction of rotation to the Dean vortices (Rowe, 1970; Azzola et al., 1986; Anwer et al., 1989; Lee et al., 2007). In earlier measurements and simulations (Anwer et al., 1989; Lai et al., 1991; Moulinec et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2007), this pair was found to form between bend angles of 67.5 °67.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} and 135 °135\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}. In bends with curvatures of 0.250.25 and 0.330.33 compared to 0.20.2 in this study, the pair appears downstream of the bend exit (Sudo et al., 2000; Lupi et al., 2025).

The secondary motion in a bent pipe flow is typically not steady. Tunstall and Harvey (1968) observed in mitred 90 °90\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} bends that the Dean pair was replaced by a single vortex that intermittently flipped its direction of rotation, at frequencies ff corresponding to Strouhal numbers 𝑆𝑡=f​D/Ub\mathit{St}=fD/U_{b} of 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} to 4.5×10−34.5\times 10^{-3}. Brücker (1998) measured an alternating switching of the vortex pair 1.5​D1.5D downstream of a 90 °90\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} bend at 𝑆𝑡≈0.03\mathit{St}\approx 0.03 and 0.120.12, and named it swirl switching. Several unsteady structures were identified in subsequent studies using time-resolved particle image velocimetry (PIV) (Kalpakli and Örlü, 2013; Kalpakli et al., 2013; Hellström et al., 2013; Kalpakli Vester et al., 2015), large-eddy simulation (Rütten et al., 2005; Carlsson et al., 2015; He et al., 2021) and direct numerical simulation (DNS) (Noorani and Schlatter, 2016; Hufnagel et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Lupi et al., 2025). In some of these works, the term swirl switching was used to refer to coherent structures that differ from those described by Brücker (1998) in frequency, in their spatial features and in their location with respect to the bend. Later, Bagheri et al. (2026b) separated these structures into four families of distinct modes depending on their location, symmetry, and generation mechanism. They found a pair of swirl-switching and swirl-breathing modes inside the bend and showed that these modes arise from the local instability of the mean flow. Additionally, two shear-layer modes and a low-frequency axial wave were identified at the downstream straight section of the bend.

In particular, the effect of Reynolds number on the mean velocity profile remains largely unexplored. This has important practical implications, as flow meters and branch connections are calibrated and designed for fully developed pipe flow, and their intended performance is affected by distorted profiles and swirling flows. For the PIV measurement of the flow through a pipe, the pipe must be made of an optically transparent material. However, the images can become distorted as the wall acts as a lens with a varying power depending on the local curvature of the wall and the angle at which the light crosses it. As a result, a regular grid in the symmetry plane appears distorted on the camera sensor. Using a calibration target (Soloff et al., 1997) placed inside the fluid, a mapping can be obtained for image corrections. However, in many applications, placing a calibration target is infeasible. Furthermore, self-calibration using the particle images requires two cameras (Wieneke, 2005). Even when a calibration target is placed inside a straight glass pipe, the mapping deviated by up to 0.27 mm0.27\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m} in the near-wall region (van Doorne and Westerweel, 2007). papers.title: Radial and vertical structure of accretion discs around magnetized stars
papers.abstract: The ubiquity of accretion discs around magnetized stars motivates studies of the structure of these discs, in particular in whether the external magnetic field changes the radial and vertical profiles of pressure, temperature, and other quantities. We study the effects of the magnetic field of a central star on a steady accretion disc under the assumption that the magnetic field of the central star is able to partially penetrate the disc, with a degree of penetration quantified by a single parameter. We construct an analytical model of the interaction between the disc and the star's magnetic field. The equations of motion are modified to take the magnetic field into account. We solve the vertical structure of the disc assuming tabulated opacities and incorporate the magnetic field in order to determine the radial and vertical distributions of the disc parameters. The inner radius of the accretion disc, the viscous stress tensor, and the spin-up torque on the central object follow from the obtained distribution of the magnetic torque. In the limit where the stellar field is expelled from the disc, the inner radius scales with the Alfven radius, whereas when the external field penetrates the disc, the inner radius behaves in a more complex way, remaining within a few corotation radii. The normalized vertical profile depends only weakly on the radius and magnetic field. Nevertheless, the magnetic field can significantly modify the viscous stress tensor, radial structure, spectrum of the disc, and its thermal-equilibrium curves. The publicly available code AlphaDiSC now includes discs around magnetized stars.

papers.intro:
Accretion discs surrounding magnetized stars are found in various astrophysical sources. Changes in the accretion rate are believed to be the underlying cause of phenomena such as bursts in dwarf novae (Livio and Pringle, 1992; Hameury, 2020, e.g.), X-ray transients (King and Ritter, 1998; Lipunova et al., 2022; Çoban and Ertan, 2024, e.g.), and young stellar objects (Bell and Lin, 1994, YSOs, see e.g.). Furthermore, the interaction between the discs and the stars’ magnetospheres plays a critical role in modulating the stars’ spin periods (D’Angelo and Spruit, 2011; Abolmasov et al., 2024; Stierhof et al., 2025, e.g.). Despite the significant amount of analytical work on the interaction between accretion discs around magnetic stars and the stars’ magnetic fields (Ghosh and Lamb, 1979a; Ghosh and Lamb, 1979b; Aly, 1980; Aly and Kuijpers, 1990; Campbell, 1992; Lovelace et al., 1995; Wang, 1995; Wang, 1997; Matt and Pudritz, 2005; Kluźniak and Rappaport, 2007; Begelman et al., 2015; Chashkina et al., 2017; Chashkina et al., 2019, to name a few,), it is often assumed that the influence of the stellar magnetic field is limited to setting the inner disc radius, while the remaining structure and emission properties of the disc remain unchanged from the standard non-magnetic case.

In this paper, we investigate the radial and thermal structure of a stationary accretion disc interacting with a magnetized star. The interaction between the disc and the star’s magnetosphere is a complex problem that has been the focus of extensive research. Two theoretical approaches exist in this regard. The first suggests that the accretion disc behaves as a superconductor; this is justified by the extremely high conductivity for the ionized medium. Consequently, the field is completely expelled from the disc, and the resulting configuration can be approximated by the solution of Aly (1980). The second approach assumes that the external magnetic field penetrates the disc (Ghosh and Lamb, 1979a, e.g. via Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities and turbulent diffusion,), allowing the dipole field to thread the disc, possibly with a screening factor (Aly and Kuijpers, 1990; Campbell, 1992; Wang, 1995; Wang, 1997; Kluźniak and Rappaport, 2007). Some works suggest that the magnetic field penetrates the disc only in a narrow zone near the inner radius (Ghosh et al., 1977; Ghosh and Lamb, 1979a; Ghosh and Lamb, 1979b; Matt and Pudritz, 2005), while others (Lai, 1999, e.g.) suggest wide interaction zone, but that the degree of magnetic field penetration into the disc is determined by the temporal variability of the field.

Some works suggest that the magnetic field penetrates the disc only in a narrow zone near the inner radius (Ghosh et al., 1977; Ghosh and Lamb, 1979a; Ghosh and Lamb, 1979b; Matt and Pudritz, 2005), while others (Lai, 1999, e.g.) suggest wide interaction zone, but that the degree of magnetic field penetration into the disc is determined by the temporal variability of the field.

In this work, we aim to reconcile these somewhat opposing approaches. We assume that the magnetic field can partially penetrate the disc. To quantify this effect, we introduce a parameter, η\eta, defined as the fraction of the stationary vertical component of the dipole magnetic field that penetrates the disc.

papers.title: Fifth-order KdV solitary waves in a nonlinear electrical transmission line
papers.abstract: We report the controlled experimental observation of solitary waves governed by the fifth-order dispersion Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation. To achieve vanishing cubic dispersion, we use a mutual inductive coupling between nearest-neighbor inductors within a nonlinear electrical transmission line. We then experimentally characterize the resulting solitary waves through direct spatiotemporal measurements of the dispersion relation, its oscillatory tail profiles, amplitude-width scaling, and amplitude-velocity relation, finding good agreement with semi-analytical predictions. Collision experiments between two (co- or counter-propagating) solitary waves also show that their self-similar profile persists after interaction, up to a time shift. Dissipation effects are also quantified.

papers.title: Optimization of Piezo Operation for Superconducting TESLA Cavities at EuXFEL
papers.abstract: Superconducting cavities with high-Q factor require precise tuning to match the RF frequency, ensuring stable electromagnetic fields and minimizing RF power consumption. At the European XFEL (EuXFEL) accelerator, TESLA cavities are tuned using slow tuners (step motors) for coarse adjustments and fast tuners (piezoelectric actuators) for fine-tuning and compensating disturbances such as Lorentz Force Detuning (LFD). Piezo actuators, critical to this system, require high-voltage (up to 100V) and high-current (up to 1A) driving signals for effective LFD compensation. However, they are vulnerable to overvoltage, overcurrent, and overheating, and their protection is crucial since replacing damaged piezos in fully assembled modules is infeasible. Additionally, piezo-induced vibrations can affect the machine's stability. Optimizing piezo excitation, by reducing voltage, current, and current slope while ensuring effective LFD compensation, improves equally efficiency, reliability and machine stability. This paper explores the optimization of piezo excitation at EuXFEL, detailing methods and results applicable to other facilities with superconducting cavities as well.

A PI control scheme is used to iteratively adjust the piezo pulse parameters in order to minimize these detuning components: the pulse amplitude compensates for linear detuning, the DC offset corrects static detuning, and the pulse timing addresses curvature-related detuning effects (Fig. 2).

papers.title: Data handling, production, and simulation in the Muon g-2 Experiment at Fermilab
papers.abstract: This paper details the computing strategies of the Muon g-2 Experiment at Fermilab, which measured the muon's anomalous magnetic moment with a precision of 127 ppb by processing over 10 petabytes of detector and simulation data. This paper discusses the computational and operational challenges of data production, data handling, and data analysis of such large datasets. These challenges were overcome by using Fermilab-developed software infrastructure and production tools, making efficient use of resources, and improving the collaboration-developed reconstruction workflow. By overcoming these challenges, the experiment improved the data throughput capacity and reduced the analysis turnaround time by an order of magnitude over the course of its lifetime.

papers.intro:
The Muon g−2g\!-\!2 Experiment conducted a multiyear research program in particle physics hosted at FermilabAguillard and others (2024); D. P. Aguillard et al. (Muon -g2 Collaboration) (2025). During beam data collection, the Muon g−2g\!-\!2 Experiment accumulated about 15,000 files per day, each one 2 GB in size. Over the course of six years of data taking we collected approximately 10 PB of data corresponding to about 10710^{7} files. In addition, physics simulations produced about 2 PB of data. The role of production is to perform the physics reconstruction of all the acquired data and select good quality data. The reconstruction process needed to be highly reproducible and capable of running multiple reconstruction algorithms so that several independent analyses could be performed for cross checks and systematic uncertainty estimations. Each file had to be processed at least twice: first, a pre-production stage determined data-dependent calibrations, and then the full production stage performed the reconstruction. Data quality was assessed and reconstruction performance was validated throughout the processing chain. Given that all the data had to be reconstructed and analyzed, the speed and efficiency of the reconstruction process was of crucial importance and represented a significant computing challenge.

papers.title: Random Feature Neural Networks for Stochastic Optimal Control
papers.abstract: Random feature neural networks (RFNNs) sample their hidden parameters once and train only the output layer. We analyze RFNNs as feedback policies for finite-horizon stochastic control with trajectory-dependent objectives. A policy change alters later states, so the error that matters is the objective error of the induced trajectory rather than a pointwise regression error. We extend the quantitative random-feature approximation theory for PDE solutions and nonlinear regression to feedback control. We investigate the objective error of an RFNN policy through two sources, approximation of the policy by random features and estimation of the objective from finitely many paths. A stability estimate for the controlled trajectory turns a policy error into an objective error. Under bounded actions, a regular benchmark policy and exact empirical minimization, the expected objective gap to the benchmark policy is at most of order $N^{-1/2}+\sqrt{N(1+\log N)/n}$, with $N$ the feature width per output coordinate and $n$ the number of paths. At fixed sample size the two terms trade off in $N$, and balancing them gives $N\asymp\sqrt{n/\log n}$. Across a wide range of examples, estimated gaps generally decrease with width and sample size, and RFNNs show an advantage when simulated paths are limited. We also study Parsimonious Random Feature Learning (PRFL), which grows and prunes the random dictionary during training while training only the output coefficients. At matched retained width and training budget, PRFL improves on a fixed RFNN in the LQ and Heston comparisons, while the fully trained network remains best in those examples.

A common approach is to parameterize the policy and optimize its objective using simulated trajectories. Neural networks provide flexible policy representations for high-dimensional and path-dependent problems [1, 8], but understanding their approximation and statistical properties remains important for assessing the quality of learned policies.

papers.title: Adversarial Attacks Expose Path-Dependent Failures in Discrete Medical Image Tokenizers
papers.abstract: Discrete image tokenizers convert medical images into token sequences that downstream models either decode into an image for a classifier (the reconstruction path), classify directly (the token path), or feed to a generative multimodal model. We ask whether imperceptible input perturbations can break these systems through the tokenizer alone. We evaluate four tokenizers on three imaging modalities and extend the strongest attack to a deployed generative model. Our central finding is path-dependence: the same tokenizer fails in opposite ways depending on how its output is used. A supervised attack collapses diagnostic accuracy on the reconstruction path, with ROC AUC falling to $\leq 0.013$ at $\epsilon=2/255$ on all four tokenizers, while sparing the token path. An unsupervised, label-free attack does the reverse; its damage concentrates in the multi-codebook tokenizers, worst in MedITok, whose token-path AUC falls from 0.919 to 0.239. The same label-free attack transfers to LLaVA-Med, a frozen medical vision-language model built on MedITok, making it report proliferative diabetic retinopathy in a healthy retina or call a malignant lesion benign, without access to the question, answer, or language-model gradients. Harm is driven by how far the attack moves the tokenizer's internal representation, not by how many tokens change: on the learned-codebook tokenizers, a control attack that changes nearly all tokens but moves the representation less leaves every path and answer intact. Domain-specific pretraining does not provide robustness: MedITok has the best clean accuracy yet is the most fragile, more so than UniTok, its general-domain counterpart. None of six candidate defenses repairs every failure mode, and several fail once the attacker optimizes against the defense directly. Medical tokenizer robustness must therefore be evaluated per downstream path, against an adaptive adversary.

Medical imaging is adopting artificial intelligence rapidly, increasingly through generative and multimodal models that read a scan and produce a diagnosis, a report, or an answer to a clinical question (Bannur et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023). Many of these systems, including several built for medical imaging, share one upstream component: a discrete image tokenizer that converts an image into a short sequence of discrete codes (Ma et al., 2025a; Sun et al., 2024). The downstream model consumes these codes in place of pixels, in one of three ways: (a) decoding them back into an image before classifying it (the reconstruction path), (b) classifying the discrete codes directly (the token path), or (c) feeding them to a generative multimodal model that answers questions about the scan (the generative path).

Small, imperceptible pixel changes flip predictions across classification, detection, and segmentation systems and modalities (Finlayson et al., 2019; Madry et al., 2018; Kaviani et al., 2022; Paschali et al., 2018). But existing attacks target the downstream model directly; the tokenizer, now upstream of many and largely open-source with weights and codebooks freely inspectable (Ma et al., 2025a; Sun et al., 2024; Esser et al., 2021), is a distinct and largely unstudied surface (Figure 1).

We red-team this surface across all three downstream paths, evaluating four tokenizers (LlamaGen VQ-16, MedITok, UniTok, Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ)) over three modalities (chest radiography, fundus photography, dermoscopy). Our central finding, path-dependence, is that the same imperceptible perturbation breaks a tokenizer in opposite ways depending on how its output is used: a task-supervised attack collapses the reconstruction path while sparing the token path, and an unsupervised, label-free attack that pushes the tokenizer’s internal features across the boundaries where its token assignments change (a boundary-directed attack) does the reverse. This second attack, computed from the public tokenizer weights alone, propagates to the generative path: it makes a frozen medical vision-language model (LLaVA-Med, vision encoder MedITok) assert that a healthy retina shows proliferative diabetic retinopathy, or that a malignant lesion is benign, without ever seeing the question, the answer, or a gradient from the language model. Our boundary-directed attacks build on the isotropic embedding-displacement attack of Bhagwatkar et al. (2026): we target the quantization boundary directly and separate crossing it from displacing past it. Our primary contribution is not the attack objective itself but the path-dependence analysis it enables across tokenizers, modalities, and downstream uses.

papers.title: MatHarness: Towards Long-Horizon Open-ended AutoResearch for Computational Materials Science
papers.abstract: Materials science research is a non-linear, long-horizon process. Existing scientific agents, however, largely rely on specific task execution or predefined workflows, rendering them brittle in open-ended settings. To bridge this gap, we present MatHarness, an agent harness designed for open-ended, long-horizon computational materials research spanning the complete lifecycle from initial ideation to manuscript writing. MatHarness couples three mechanisms: execution robustness through pre-flight verification, expert-distilled skills, and just-in-time auditing; epistemic adaptability through persistent research artifacts and an evolving scientific mental model; and collective intelligence through a heterogeneous multi-agent round table under targeted human oversight. We evaluate MatHarness on adsorbate-induced surface segregation in Cu-Zn alloys, an open question in methanol-synthesis catalysis. Over a multi-week trajectory consuming roughly 10^3 GPU-hours (50 production DFT relaxations prescreened by 171 machine-learning-potential evaluations) the system revised its plan six times, recovered autonomously from failed calculations, and had an independent auditor overturn one of its own over-attributed claims before publication. Within the sampled metallic dilute-limit models, the validated DFT analysis supports an adsorbate-induced tendency toward greater surface Cu exposure at both composition endpoints, with facet- and coverage-dependent exceptions. These results were compiled into a complete manuscript with human involvement concentrated in specification, approval, and strategic steering gates. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/PrentisAI/pippin.

Computational materials research is an iterative, long-horizon decision process. Rather than executing isolated tasks, researchers must continuously hypothesize mechanisms, construct valid models, troubleshoot non-convergent simulations, and interpret intermediate outputs to determine the next informative experiment. These decisions are deeply coupled, and navigating the vast space of hypotheses and experiments demands continuous, context-aware reasoning in which early mistakes compound over time.

To address these challenges, we introduce MatHarness, an agent harness spanning the full research lifecycle from initial ideation to paper writing. It rests on three design considerations. First, it ensures execution robustness through pre-execution verification with lightweight smoke runs, domain-expert skill abstractions, and just-in-time auditing hooks that intercept intermediate failures before errors compound. Second, it maintains epistemic adaptability by preserving research artifacts and maintaining an evolving scientific mental model, enabling agents to iteratively revise their scientific beliefs. Third, it leverages collective intelligence, deploying a multi-agent round table of heterogeneous foundation models for peer-reviewed ideation, with targeted human oversight at critical checkpoints for scientific rigor and expert alignment. papers.title: DeepDOSReasoner: Physics-Grounded Reasoning for Density-of-States Prediction and Materials Discovery
papers.abstract: Predicting a material's behavior from its atomic structure is a longstanding goal of the physical sciences. The electronic and phonon densities of states (eDOS and phDOS) govern key electronic, optical, vibrational, and thermodynamic properties, yet their calculation using density functional theory (DFT) is costly: about 60% of Materials Project entries lack eDOS and over 80% lack phDOS. Existing crystal-to-spectrum models rely on pooled structural representations and pointwise regression, which blur spectral features and violate total-state conservation. Here we introduce DeepDOSReasoner, a physics-grounded framework that decodes spectra through atom-to-energy source attention and refines the normalized DOS through learned continuity-equation transport, enforcing nonnegativity and total-state conservation by construction. DeepDOSReasoner achieves the highest prediction accuracy across all evaluated metrics for both eDOS and phDOS, recovers element-resolved contributions without supervision, and most reliably identifies rare valence-band (VB) gaps. In a prospective screen of 8,106 uncharted materials validated by new DFT calculations, its predictions remain the most accurate among the methods evaluated, with 25 of its top 50 candidates confirmed as VB-gap materials. Three case studies spanning substituted compounds, photovoltaic chalcogenides, and a high-entropy alloy demonstrate transfer across materials classes. Ablations confirm that both stages are necessary, while the model retains comparable accuracy when trained on only 25% of the data. Predicting spectra in milliseconds enables exhaustive screening; we release predictions filling the missing eDOS for 91,405 and phDOS for 127,768 Materials Project entries. DeepDOSReasoner provides a blueprint for integrating machine learning with physical reasoning toward high-throughput spectral screening and autonomous materials discovery.
papers.intro:
The density of states (DOS) provides a compact bridge between a material’s atomic structure and its physical responses [1, 2]. The electronic DOS (eDOS) governs electronic and optical behavior, while the phonon DOS (phDOS) determines lattice vibrational and thermodynamic properties. Both are one-dimensional spectra defined over a bounded energy or frequency axis and constrained by strict total-state sum rules. Of the two, eDOS prediction is particularly demanding because many performance-relevant properties depend on sharp spectral features: the low-temperature electronic specific heat and Pauli susceptibility on the Fermi-level density of states, near-band-edge optical absorption on the steepness of the band edges, catalytic activity on the near-Fermi-energy states, and thermoelectric and transparent-conductor behavior on narrow gaps below but near the Fermi energy [3]. As a result, downstream discovery workflows for thermoelectrics, photovoltaics, electrocatalysts, superconductors, and transparent conductors depend not only on whether eDOS spectra can be predicted accurately on average, but also on whether their fine spectral structure is faithfully preserved at scale [4]. Density functional theory (DFT) [5, 6] remains the standard route for computing both eDOS and phDOS, but its per-material cost limits coverage. Among the 154,387 inorganic crystal entries in the Materials Project [7], about 60% lack a published eDOS and over 80% lack a phDOS, constraining screening efforts that require full spectral signatures.

Machine learning offers a route to amortize this cost by learning direct mappings from crystal structure to spectrum. Crystal graph neural networks have become reliable surrogates for scalar targets such as formation energy, band gap, and elastic moduli [8, 9, 10], and such surrogates now drive materials discovery at scale [11], but predicting a full DOS spectrum is qualitatively harder. The target is not an unconstrained vector of bin values: it is a nonnegative spectral density whose validity depends on total-state conservation, and whose application-relevant content often lies in sharp, easily blurred features such as band edges, gaps below but near the Fermi energy (i.e., in the valence band) in metallic systems [3], and van Hove singularities [12]. Existing eDOS prediction models [13, 14, 15] fall short in three concrete ways. First, they often predict the band gap and the surrounding spectrum separately and reconcile them only post hoc, which can misalign band edges and introduce spurious in-gap density. Second, pointwise regression losses can yield low per-bin error while still shifting peaks, smoothing van Hove singularities, and drifting from total-state conservation, producing spectra that appear plausible but are physically inconsistent. Third, most models decode the spectrum from a single pooled crystal embedding, obscuring the element-resolved contributions that physically compose the total eDOS [16] and limiting interpretability.

Here we introduce DeepDOSReasoner, a physics-grounded framework for crystal-to-DOS prediction that addresses these shortcomings directly. In Stage I, DeepDOSReasoner encodes the crystal as a graph using an edge-aware Transformer [17, 18] and decodes the eDOS bin by bin through atom-to-energy source attention. This design allows each energy bin to selectively aggregate atom- and element-resolved structural information, rather than reading from a single pooled representation. In Stage II, DeepDOSReasoner treats the normalized DOS as a probability density and refines it through a learned, state-dependent velocity field under a continuity equation with no-flux boundary conditions [19], integrated with a differentiable upwind scheme [20]. By construction, this refinement preserves nonnegativity and total-state conservation throughout its trajectory. In practice, it sharpens band edges and van Hove singularities while resolving the band gap and surrounding spectrum jointly. Thus, DeepDOSReasoner embeds physical consistency directly into the model output rather than imposing it through soft penalties, contributing to a broader effort to couple data-driven learning with principled physical reasoning [21, 22, 23, 24].

papers.title: Metal-Dielectric Bilayer Supported Nanoporous Silver Substrates for Ultrasensitive Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering
papers.abstract: Resolving the chemical footprint of molecules in analytes is of fundamental interest in biosensing and biomedical applications. Surface-enhanced Raman Scattering (SERS) spectroscopy is a powerful tool for non-invasive molecule investigation, and there is a continuous effort to develop highly efficient SERS substrates that can be fabricated at low cost and tuned to the desired spectral range of investigation. Here, we show that the Raman signal of porous silver films can be significantly enhanced by integrating a thin dielectric layer and a metallic backreflector underneath the porous metal film. We call this architecture nanoporous metal on dielectric metal (NPMoDM) and show that it leads to much stronger near-field enhancement in the bulk of the film. Additionally, the spectral band of enhanced sensitivity can be tuned by the thickness of the dielectric layer within the visible spectral range. With rhodamine 6G and para-aminothiophenol as target analytes, we demonstrate SERS detection of substrates incubated with zeptomolar concentrations of the analyte, which corresponds to only few molecules present on a mm2 surface area. Our approach introduces a tunable and scalable (lithography-free) platform for ultrasensitive SERS applications, with a readily accessible surface for analyte functionalization.

papers.title: Useful but Unwieldy: How Software Engineers Perceive the Design of Chain-of-Thought Explanations in Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents (CAs) powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software engineering (SE) workflows. As these CAs take up more tasks and responsibilities, it is imperative for software engineers to understand the CA's rationale behind its' decisions, also known as the chain-of-thought (CoT). During the interaction, some CAs are capable of showing this CoT as a separate message to users with the goal of providing transparency and explainability. However, its effectiveness as an explainable AI (XAI) mechanism for end-users in software engineering has not yet been established in the literature. This motivates us to understand their experiences with the CoT message as an XAI tool through a survey and semi-structured follow-up interviews with 36 software engineers. Through thematic analysis of the survey responses and interview transcripts, we found that CoT message is an indispensable tool for software engineers in terms of transparency, scrutability, and trust towards the CA. However, various instances of CoT messages being overly verbose, containing technical information that does not match the users' expertise, or being perceived by the users as ``detached'' from the conversation because the ``agent is talking to itself'', lead to comprehension difficulties and selective use or abandonment of the tool. We synthesize these insights to inform the design of CoT messages that support software engineers in their explainability needs.

Large language models (LLMs) continue to power many of the tools that humans interact with today (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025; OpenAI et al., 2024, e.g.). More recently, these LLMs serve as the engine that runs agentic tools across specialized domains (Acharya et al., 2025). Current CAs are capable of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning: a series of intermediate reasoning steps that resemble thoughtful consideration and explanation for a decision (Yang et al., 2024) (see Figure 1). These CAs are also capable of exposing these reasoning traces to users as a separate message in the conversation with the goal of improving transparency and explainability. However, the CAs’ advanced capabilities of comprehensive planning and tool invocation (Acharya et al., 2025) may further contribute to the verbosity and complexity of CoT messages. This, in turn, can act as an extraneous cognitive load (Bannert, 2002; Borisov et al., 2026) for users, leading them to miss key details or ignore messages completely (Chou and Hsu, 2021). This problem is particularly critical in SE, because as CAs continue to take more tasks in SE workflows, it is important for software engineers to understand the rationale behind a CA’s decision to ensure safety and security.

papers.title: Forsyth--Glaisher-Type Series for $1/\pi$ Involving Catalan Numbers and Harmonic Numbers
papers.abstract: We develop an elementary method for constructing and evaluating families of Forsyth--Glaisher-type series for $1/\pi$. The approach is based on Newton's generalized binomial theorem, identities for generalized binomial coefficients, and Euler's beta integral, together with properties of the gamma and digamma functions. We establish several parameterized identities involving squares of central binomial coefficients and products of odd integers, from which we derive explicit evaluations in terms of $1/\pi$. By means of transformations connecting generalized binomial coefficients with Catalan numbers, we obtain further families of series involving squares of Catalan numbers. We also derive identities for series involving harmonic and odd harmonic numbers by differentiating suitable parameter-dependent formulas. These results yield evaluations containing both $1/\pi$ and logarithmic terms, particularly $\ln 2$. Our results provide a unified framework for generating and evaluating related binomial and Catalan-type series and reveal connections among central binomial coefficients, Catalan numbers, and harmonic numbers.

papers.title: From Learning Rates to Rotational Schedules: Finite-Horizon Theory on the Sphere
papers.abstract: How should step sizes be scheduled across a finite training horizon? Cosine and warmup-stable-decay (WSD) schedules are widely adopted in large-scale pretraining, yet their effect on optimization also depends on parameter norms. Normalization can make parameter groups scale invariant, so that the loss depends only on their direction, while their norms still affect how fast the parameters rotate. In this work, we formulate schedule design directly in the space of rotational motion. Working within a geodesically convex spherical setting, we derive a last-iterate convergence guarantee for arbitrary rotational schedules that separates their overall scale from their distribution over time. We derive the unique schedule that minimizes this bound and prove that it approaches linear decay as the horizon grows. Empirically, our rotational interpretation and idealized spherical analysis provide useful predictions for LLM pretraining in practice, including schedule comparisons missed by existing analyses. Our analysis predicts schedule ordering across model scales for both vanilla (Adam, Muon) and Hyperball-style (AdamH, MuonH) optimizers. Our Hyperball experiments support the predicted strong performance of linear LR decay and confirm our prediction that WSD underperforms in this setting. Accounting for parameter norm dynamics, we predict instead the strong performance of WSD for Adam and Muon shown in practice. Guided by our theoretical insights, we also derive a new LR schedule for Adam and Muon, which improves over the established cosine and WSD schedules. All in all, these results support the use of rotational dynamics to understand, predict, and ultimately guide scheduling in LLM pretraining.

Rotational dynamics are intertwined with the geometric properties of normalized networks (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015; Ba et al., 2016; van Laarhoven, 2017; Hoffer et al., 2018), which exhibit scale-invariant properties. Under scale invariance, multiplying a parameter group by a positive scalar leaves the network’s function unchanged. Optimization of such groups can therefore be described exactly through rotations of their parameters on the unit sphere (Arora et al., 2018; Li & Arora, 2020; Wan et al., 2021; Roburin et al., 2022; Kodryan et al., 2022). Yet, parameter norms still affect these dynamics: a larger norm reduces the angular motion of the optimization (van Laarhoven, 2017; Kosson et al., 2024). The effective rotation speed per step is therefore determined jointly by the learning rate and parameter norm.

papers.title: How Multi-Timescale Memory Cools Optimization: Theory and Evidence from AdEMAMix
papers.abstract: Augmenting AdamW with multiple momentum timescales improves large language model pretraining, yet the mechanism driving these gains remains poorly understood. We identify an interaction between multi-timescale optimizer memory and the geometry of normalized networks: memory changes parameter norms and thereby controls how fast parameters rotate. Starting from exact norm dynamics under decoupled weight decay, we show that the parameter norm depends on the temporal correlation of the updates, with weight decay controlling how long these correlations influence optimization. We show how an independently weighted slow momentum can substantially increase the norm of parameters, while contributing negligible power to the instantaneous update, therefore acting as an endogenous annealing schedule. We study this mechanism in AdEMAMix for language-model pretraining. Controlled interventions show that this scheduling mechanism has clear practical consequences and is an important factor behind AdEMAMix's advantage over AdamW.

papers.intro:
The rapid scaling of large language models (LLMs) has increasingly relied on practical optimizer heuristics, while a principled understanding of the underlying learning mechanics (Simon et al., 2026) remains an open challenge. Multi-timescale optimizer memory is a recent example. While AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) has long served as the standard optimizer, recent work demonstrates that augmenting it with multiple memory timescales yields significant, consistent gains across large-scale pretraining regimes (Pagliardini et al., 2025; Semenov et al., 2025; Hernández-Cano et al., 2026; Ferbach et al., 2026; Everett & Qiu, 2026). Most notably, AdEMAMix (Pagliardini et al., 2025) equips AdamW with a second, much slower independently weighted exponential moving average (EMA) of past gradients whose timescale and strength evolve over training. Despite recent work relating AdEMAMix to accelerated stochastic methods (Morwani et al., 2025; Ferbach et al., 2026), these perspectives do not explain how its multi-timescale memory alters the training dynamics of modern neural networks. Why such a slow momentum channel consistently benefits large-scale pretraining is therefore an open puzzle.

Prior work establishes that momentum can alter scale-invariant norms and rotational dynamics (Heo et al., 2021; Wan et al., 2021; Kosson et al., 2024). Our focus is on how the temporal structure and timescales of optimizer memory determine this norm trajectory. The key mechanism is the separation between what an optimizer momentum buffer contributes to the update applied now versus what its correlated history leaves behind in the parameter norm.
