Multi-timescale memory strongly amplifies this separation. In particular, an independently weighted slow channel can make this correlation contribution large without noticeably increasing instantaneous update power, accumulating a disproportionate norm contribution that anneals rotational motion. AdEMAMix provides a clear instance of this mechanism: in our language-model runs, its slow, independently weighted, and scheduled momentum branch contributes only a few percent of instantaneous update power, yet its correlated history has a disproportionately persistent effect. The parameter norm in scale-invariant groups becomes roughly six times larger than AdamW’s at the same LR and WD, while rotational motion is reduced by about the same factor (Fig. 1a). The norm trajectory induced by optimizer memory is therefore not merely a geometric side effect: it transforms the LR schedule into an optimizer-specific rotational schedule, making optimizer memory an integral part of the scheduling problem itself.

(2025) that convex last-iterate bounds capture several empirical properties of LR scheduling. We next ask whether this channel contributes to AdEMAMix’s advantage in LLM pretraining. Recent work shows that matching effective or angular step sizes over training can reproduce aspects of the loss trajectories of different optimizers or hyperparameter settings (Liu et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026) and that this can be advantageous in terms of performance (Wen et al., 2026; Hägele et al., 2026; Hübler et al., 2026). papers.title: Cross-calibration of Hera/HyperScout-H with MRO/CRISM and MEx/OMEGA based on Mars observations
papers.abstract: On March 12, 2025, Hera, the European Space Agency's planetary defense mission, performed a Mars flyby en route to the asteroid system (65803) Didymos-Dimorphos. During this event, HyperScout-H (HS-H), the spacecraft's hyperspectral imager, acquired five high spatial resolution images over the southern hemisphere of Mars. These observations provide an opportunity for systematic cross-calibration of HS-H with two established Mars orbital instruments, Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM) on board the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (Murchie et al., 2007), and Observatoire pour la Min\'eralogie, l'Eau, les Glaces et l'Activit\'e (OMEGA) on board Mars Express (Bibring et al., 2004). This study evaluates the performance, reliability, and readiness of HS-H for the forthcoming asteroid observation phase by comparing it with CRISM and OMEGA data. We selected 21 surface regions spanning diverse terrain types from three HS-H images in which the Martian surface fills the entire field of view. These images were corrected, calibrated, and co-registered to associate each pixel with latitude and longitude. The relative inter-channel correction factors are close to unity for bands 3-25 (0.688-0.952 {\mu}m), with standard deviations of 0.52% for OMEGA and 0.62% for CRISM, indicating good agreement in spectral shape. Bands 1 and 2 show a systematic mismatch of 4.7% and 3.6%. The absolute flux correction factors reveal offsets of 8% relative to OMEGA and approximately 0.7% relative to CRISM, with mean inter-image standard deviations below 2%. These results confirm the radiometric stability of HS-H and establish a calibration framework for future Didymos-Dimorphos observations.

papers.intro:
The Hera mission was developed within the Space Safety Programme of the European Space Agency (ESA) as the European contribution to the Asteroid Impact and Deflection Assessment (AIDA) collaboration. Its target is the binary system Didymos–Dimorphos, whose secondary, Dimorphos, was the impact site of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), the first demonstration of asteroid deflection by means of a kinetic impactor [25, 3]. Building on this experiment, Hera will characterize in detail the outcome of the DART impact and determine the physical, surface, and internal properties of both components of the system, providing the ground truth needed to validate impact models for planetary defense [14, 15].

The Hera mission was developed within the Space Safety Programme of the European Space Agency (ESA) as the European contribution to the Asteroid Impact and Deflection Assessment (AIDA) collaboration. Its target is the binary system Didymos–Dimorphos, whose secondary, Dimorphos, was the impact site of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), the first demonstration of asteroid deflection by means of a kinetic impactor [25, 3]. Building on this experiment, Hera will characterize in detail the outcome of the DART impact and determine the physical, surface, and internal properties of both components of the system, providing the ground truth needed to validate impact models for planetary defense [14, 15].

To achieve these goals, Hera adopts a novel architecture for deep-space exploration, combining a main spacecraft with two CubeSats, Juventas and Milani [15]. The main spacecraft carries the Asteroid Framing Cameras (AFC), the Hyperspectral Imager (HyperScout-H, hereafter HS-H), the Thermal Infrared Imager (TIRI), and the Planetary Altimeter (PALT). Juventas hosts the low-frequency radar JuRa, devoted to the first direct sounding of an asteroid’s interior, and the gravimeter GRASS, while Milani carries the near-infrared imaging spectrometer ASPECT and the VISTA thermogravimeter for dust characterization. Hera was launched on 7 October 2024 at 14:52 UT from Cape Canaveral aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket [16]. A few days after launch, it acquired images of the Earth–Moon system that confirmed the nominal operation of its onboard instruments, and on 12 March 2025 it performed a successful flyby of Mars, during which it also observed the Martian moon Deimos [16]. Hera will reach the Didymos–Dimorphos system in early November 2026, when it will begin the proximity phase and observe the binary for at least six months.

Didymos is a binary near-Earth asteroid belonging to the Apollo dynamical family. The primary has a diameter of 761±26761\pm 26 m, while the secondary, called Dimorphos, measures 151±5151\pm 5 m [4]. From a spectroscopic point of view, the system is classified as an S-type asteroid [5], linked to ordinary chondrites [6]. After the DART impact, the surface composition remains consistent with an S-type classification, with small variations in the spectral slope that may be related to the evolution of the ejecta cloud or to material deposited on the surface of Didymos [22, 12]. The orbital period of Dimorphos decreased by approximately 33 minutes as a result of the impact [27, 21].

The HS-H instrument is a hyperspectral imager onboard the Hera spacecraft, acquiring simultaneous spatial and spectral information over the 0.65–0.95 μ\mum wavelength range. Its primary scientific objectives are to characterize the surface composition of Didymos and Dimorphos, investigate space-weathering effects, and search for exogenous material on these bodies [23]. In addition, HS-H will reveal the spectral properties of freshly exposed subsurface material excavated by the DART impact and produce spectral maps of taxonomic classification, spectral slope, and band parameters to better constrain the system’s physical properties [15, 23]. During the March 2025 Mars flyby, HS-H acquired observations of Mars and its two moons, Phobos and Deimos, providing a valuable opportunity to assess the instrument’s in-flight radiometric performance before its arrival at the Didymos system in November 2026.

To validate the HS-H observations, we made use of data from two well-established hyperspectral instruments that have been observing Mars from orbit for over two decades, namely the Observatoire pour la Minéralogie, l’Eau, les Glaces et l’Activité (OMEGA) onboard ESA’s Mars Express spacecraft [1] and Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM) onboard NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter [19]. Both instruments cover wavelength ranges that overlap with HS-H, with OMEGA spanning 0.35–5.2 μ\mum and CRISM covering 0.362–3.92 μ\mum, making them ideal spectral references in the HS-H wavelength range. Their long operational history and extensive calibration heritage provide a robust and well-characterized dataset against which the HS-H data can be meaningfully compared.

OMEGA is a hyperspectral imaging spectrometer onboard Mars Express, in orbit around Mars since December 2003 [1]. It covers the visible and near-infrared spectral range from 0.35 to 5.2 μ\mum in 352 contiguous spectral samples, with a spatial resolution ranging from 300 m to 4.8 km per pixel depending on the orbital altitude. The term channel is here reserved for the three spectrometers of OMEGA, namely VNIR, SWIR-C and SWIR-L. The VNIR channel, with 96 spectral samples, covers the HS-H spectral range and therefore provides the data set relevant to this comparison. The spectral samples beyond 0.93 µm are affected by contamination from high grating orders and are not delivered in the data products, which leaves a small gap in the overlap with HS-H between 0.93 and 0.95 µm. Its primary scientific objective is the global mineralogical mapping of the Martian surface, with particular focus on detecting and characterizing hydrated minerals, ices, and volcanic deposits [2].

It operates in the visible and near-infrared range from 0.362 to 3.92 μ\mum with 544 spectral channels at a sampling of 6.55 nm per channel. In targeted mode, CRISM achieves a spatial resolution of 18 or 36 m pixel-1, significantly higher than OMEGA, allowing the characterization of small-scale mineralogical deposits and the identification of aqueous alteration products that cannot be resolved at OMEGA’s spatial scale. In survey mode, the spatial resolution is 100 or 200 m pixel-1 with 72 spectral samples per pixel [19, 29]. The CRISM data used in this work are the VNIR hyperspectral mapping products described in Sect. 3.1, which retain the full spectral resolution of the VNIR detector.

papers.title: Tritium speciation and transport in molten FLiBe: parameters, uncertainties and validation priorities
papers.abstract: Molten lithium fluoride-beryllium fluoride (FLiBe) is a candidate liquid breeder material for fusion applications, but predictive modelling of tritium retention, transport and extraction depends on chemical and interfacial assumptions that remain only partly resolved. Tritium produced in lithium-bearing fluoride salts may occur in oxidised or fluoride-associated states and can exchange into molecular hydrogen-isotope species such as HT. The relative populations and apparent transport behaviour depend on salt composition and condition, redox state, and interactions at gas-liquid and salt-wall boundaries. This review assesses the evidence for tritium speciation and transport in molten FLiBe, with emphasis on the solubility, effective diffusivity, permeability, exchange and boundary-transfer parameters required by continuum models. The available evidence motivates a two-pool continuum description with separate oxidised or fluoride-associated and molecular-hydrogen pools, without assigning a unique microscopic species. This description applies where states omitted from these pools do not materially affect tritium inventory or transport in the salt. We distinguish directly measured quantities from fitted or inferred effective parameters, recommend how source-specific transport data should be reported and compared, and identify the measurements required to constrain the remaining uncertainties in speciation, exchange, bulk transport and boundary transfer.

papers.intro:
Fusion breeding blankets must generate, retain, extract and account for tritium under coupled irradiation, thermal, chemical and material-boundary conditions. Molten lithium fluoride–beryllium fluoride (FLiBe) is an attractive candidate liquid breeder because lithium provides the tritium-breeding reactions, beryllium contributes neutron multiplication, and the salt has favourable high-temperature properties. Tritium behaviour nevertheless remains a coupled problem involving chemical speciation, bulk transport, interfacial mass transfer and structural permeation rather than a simple source-and-diffusion problem [forsberg2017tritiumControl, forsberg2020flibeBlankets, meier2014blankets, pint2024materials, barker2025flibe].

For predictive modelling and the design of tritium extraction systems, the central issue is not only how much tritium is produced, but in what chemical form or effective transport pool it exists, how rapidly each pool moves through the salt, how the pools are coupled to each other, and how tritium partitions at gas, structural and extraction boundaries. These questions are complicated by salt composition, purification history, oxide and hydroxide impurities, fluorine potential, neutron-induced transmutation products, container interactions and redox-control strategies [shaffer1971preparation, simpson2006redox, zhang2018redox, vergari2023corrosionActivation].

The aim of this review is to establish which assumptions about tritium speciation and transport in molten FLiBe are supported by the available evidence, where important uncertainties remain, and which measurements would most improve predictive breeder-blanket models. The discussion focuses on oxidised or fluoride-associated tritium, commonly represented in the literature as T+\text{T}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}^{\text{+}} or TF, and neutral molecular tritium, represented principally as HT under hydrogen-containing extraction conditions. Their implications for inventory, release, permeation and experimental validation are assessed explicitly.

The scope is intentionally narrower than a general review of FLiBe chemistry or blanket design. Thermophysical properties, neutronics, corrosion and tritium accountancy are considered only where they determine the chemical state, transport parameter, source term or boundary condition used in a predictive model. The objective is not to assign a unique microscopic species to every condition, but to identify the minimum physically defensible model, the parameter ranges it requires and the evidence needed to validate it. We distinguish direct measurements from fitted or inferred parameters, computational predictions and modelling assumptions. Hydrogen and deuterium measurements, together with surrogate-salt experiments, provide useful supporting evidence but cannot replace direct measurements of tritium transport in FLiBe.

papers.title: Peel, Don't Whack: Partial Coverage, Imperfect Validators, and Intervention Based Shortcut Mitigation
papers.abstract:
Without group labels, shortcut mitigation increasingly relies on interventions : label-preserving edits, such as background or watermark replacement, that are proposed automatically and accepted by a validator. Invariance to a complete family of valid edits yields robustness, but in practice coverage is partial and validators err.
  We analyze both in a stylized linear model. For the population logistic solution and the max-margin limit of gradient descent, the decision on every shortcut-flip group follows one additive rule. Hence worst-group accuracy never decreases with coverage, while individual groups can provably degrade, a mechanism for the Whac-a-Mole effect; full coverage is not always needed. In the logistic regime the validator's false-accept rate must stay below a closed-form tolerance that grows with coverage. With noiseless training data, one false accept can make the max-margin solution ignore the core. In this model, sensitivity-based discovery removes shortcuts in decreasing salience. We also give a model-agnostic certificate, valid under content-independent validation, whose validator-error term comes from an audit.
  Simulations match the theory, and deep networks on synthetic and real images show the predicted Whac-a-Mole signs, monotone worst-group accuracy and validator fragility. The resulting procedure, Peel (Propose-Edit-Evaluate-Learn), can propose candidate edits from the model's own mistakes. Given an oracle library of the benchmarks' intervention operators, it selects the right ones and beats group-label methods on Waterbirds and UrbanCars. With fully generated edits, run end to end from three discovery seeds, it improves on empirical risk minimization (ERM) on five of six benchmarks but trails exact edits.

papers.intro:
Neural networks readily exploit shortcuts: features that predict the label in training but not under deployment shift (Geirhos et al., 2020). Group distributionally robust optimization (GroupDRO; Sagawa et al., 2020), reweighting as in Just Train Twice (JTT; Liu et al., 2021), and last-layer retraining by deep feature reweighting (DFR; Kirichenko et al., 2023) mitigate known shortcuts, but need group annotations for training or validation. Without such side information, shortcut identification is impossible in general: two causal models with the same training distribution can disagree on which feature is stable (Lin et al., 2022).

Group distributionally robust optimization (GroupDRO; Sagawa et al., 2020), reweighting as in Just Train Twice (JTT; Liu et al., 2021), and last-layer retraining by deep feature reweighting (DFR; Kirichenko et al., 2023) mitigate known shortcuts, but need group annotations for training or validation. Without such side information, shortcut identification is impossible in general: two causal models with the same training distribution can disagree on which feature is stable (Lin et al., 2022).

A growing line of work supplies interventions: label-preserving edits that change a suspected shortcut, such as replacing the background, removing a watermark, or rewriting an irrelevant phrase. These edits are increasingly produced by generative models and filtered by vision–language or language models (Dunlap et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Prabhu et al., 2023). Invariance to a complete family of such edits is well understood: it makes the predictor a function of the core alone, robust to any shift of the shortcut distribution (Veitch et al., 2021; von Kügelgen et al., 2021).

Invariance to a complete family of such edits is well understood: it makes the predictor a function of the core alone, robust to any shift of the shortcut distribution (Veitch et al., 2021; von Kügelgen et al., 2021).

Practice never meets these conditions, and two gaps matter. First, coverage is partial: real data contain several shortcuts, and any edit bank covers only some of them. Li et al. (2023) documented a puzzling consequence, the Whac-a-Mole effect, in which mitigating one shortcut amplifies reliance on another. We lack a theory of when it happens and what partial coverage does and does not buy. Second, validators err: an automatic validator sometimes accepts an edit that silently changed the label-relevant content, as documented for counterfactual augmentation in natural language processing (NLP) (Joshi and He, 2022). How such errors propagate into shortcut reliance has not been analyzed.

papers.title: Training speech deepfake detectors against worst-case filters: Gains, Costs and Limits
papers.abstract:
Speech deepfake detectors make few errors on standard benchmarks, yet a simple attack defeats them: the attacker passes fake speech through one short filter, tuned against the detector, and many fakes then pass as real. Training with random filters does not stop this attack, because the attacker uses the worst filter, not a random one.
  We therefore train the detector against the worst case: during training, a small set of filters is updated to fool the current detector, at about the cost of random filters. In a preregistered study, this made the detector more robust to filter attacks on real-world recordings than random filters did. It also lowered the in-domain attack error of the standard detector, and beat one-step adversarial training with additive noise on real-world recordings. The price is a higher error on unfiltered speech, and a validation study shows that choosing the checkpoint on held-out spoofing systems made the standard detector about as robust.

papers.title: Spoof Localization as Boundary Regression
papers.abstract: Partially spoofed audio embeds spoofed segments in a bonafide utterance, and spoof localization is the task of locating them. Most countermeasures (CMs) operate at the frame level. Typically, they include a front-end representing the audio as frames and a back-end classifying each frame as bonafide or spoof. Such frame-level detection ties the reference, the predictions and the evaluation to a pre-defined temporal resolution: a frame containing a transition receives a single label, a boundary cannot lie inside a frame, and the evaluation also depends on the resolution. To tackle these issues, we treat spoof localization as regression. We propose a single-stage boundary regressor that outputs (start-time, end-time, score) tuples with continuous-valued time stamps, trained on the exact reference intervals. Results show that the proposed CM outperforms previous frame-level and boundary-based CMs, and generalizes better.

In the Partial Spoof (PS) scenario, an attacker does not synthesize a whole utterance but replaces a few words of a bonafide utterance with spoofed speech, so that the meaning changes while most of the audio stays bonafide [1, 2, 3]. For such audio, an utterance-level decision is not always sufficient. In applications such as forensic analysis one might need to know which part of the utterance was edited. The task of locating the spoofed regions inside partially spoofed audio is known as spoof localization.

Most countermeasures (CMs) for spoof localization treat the task as classification. A typical CM utilizes a self-supervised learning (SSL) model as the front-end [4], represents the audio as a sequence of feature vectors, called frames, and uses a back-end that classifies each frame as bonafide or spoof. Note that the number of frames is set by the stride of the SSL convolutional layers; in wav2vec2-style front-ends [5, 6, 7, 8], consecutive frames are 20 ms apart, and we call this distance the frame resolution.

However, the start and end times of a spoofed word are not necessarily multiples of 20 ms, whereas a frame-level CM can only see and predict on the 20 ms frame. This mismatch leads to three specific issues. First, the reference labels must be quantized to the frame resolution, which introduces an unavoidable quantization error into training. More specifically, when partially spoofed audio is created, the spoofed interval [ts,te][t_{s},t_{e}] is known exactly and is independent of the CM’s temporal resolution. But to assign one label to each frame, a frame that is entirely spoofed and a frame of which only a small part is spoofed are assigned the same label “spoof”, even though they have different levels of “spoofness”. Second, the precision of the model output is limited by the resolution, since a frame-level CM cannot predict a boundary inside a frame. Third, the evaluation is also tied to the resolution: point-based EER changes markedly with the resolution at which frames are scored, so results are often reported at various resolutions, which makes comparison less straightforward. Although the evaluation issue can be alleviated by using the range-based EER [9], its theoretical foundation is not yet fully justified. 11 1 See Appendix A. More importantly, it does not solve the first two issues.

papers.title: $\zeta_0$: A Framework for World Action Models with Joint Scene and Body Foresight in Humanoid Control
papers.abstract: World Action Models anticipate visual outcomes to guide robot actions, yet humanoid interaction also depends on how the robot's body responds. Visual foresight alone can miss body motion, while latent-distance losses do not directly supervise action responses. We present $\zeta_0$, a framework that turns vision-language-action policies into World Action Models by foreseeing future visual features and measured joint trajectories in a shared latent representation. During training, a teacher conditioned on recorded futures provides a reference action response, and dual-response transfer trains the causal predictor to match it through the teacher and the executing policy. All components are trained jointly, and deployment uses only causally predicted futures. On seven HumanoidArena tasks, $\zeta_0$ built on $\Psi_0$ and GR00T N1.7 reaches 63.6% and 79.5% mean success, 18.8 and 9.0 points above these bases. On six real-world tasks, it reaches 78.3% and 85.0%, gains of 16.7 and 10.0 points. On GR00T, its 79.5% tops all compared seven-task joint policies. Humanoid interaction couples whole-body motion with changes in the surrounding scene. Pushing a box, for example, moves the object while the arms keep contact and the legs and torso support the motion. World Action Models couple action generation with anticipated future observations [50, 46, 28, 56, 51, 33]. For a humanoid, the consequences of an action also include its own body motion, which egocentric images may capture only partially and measured joint trajectories record directly. We therefore ask a policy to foresee scene and body changes jointly.

World Action Models couple action generation with anticipated future observations [50, 46, 28, 56, 51, 33]. For a humanoid, the consequences of an action also include its own body motion, which egocentric images may capture only partially and measured joint trajectories record directly. We therefore ask a policy to foresee scene and body changes jointly.

Demonstrations provide this foresight as supervision: each action is followed by recorded images and measured body states. At execution time, those futures have not yet occurred and must be predicted from causal inputs. A common approach fits future predictions to recorded observations or their latent representations [21, 23, 56]. Latent-distance supervision, however, does not directly reflect how a policy uses the prediction: nearby futures need not induce the same action, and equally sized errors can have different effects on behavior. We therefore also supervise prediction in action space, asking whether a predicted future induces the action that the recorded future would.

papers.title: Dynamic Renewal for Hydrodynamic Coupling in Ciliary Mucus Transport
papers.abstract: Mucociliary clearance in large mammalian airways involves millimetric MUC5B-rich mucus strands that emerge from submucosal glands approximately aligned with the direction of transport. These strands are observed downstream in cross-flow networks. Recently, Bos et al. [PNAS Nexus 2, pgad388 (2023)] modeled single strand reorientation using a free-draining coupling for the flow induced by cilia. This leaves unresolved whether the strand's own disturbance of the surrounding liquid assists or frustrates the turning. Here, we develop the methodology to address this question. An immersed-boundary coupling is combined with a Fourier-space Stokes solver and a bespoke dynamic-renewal algorithm that exposes the strand to new ciliary domain without enlarging the simulation volume. This allows us to overcome one of the multiscale challenges posed by mucociliary clearance. We find that hydrodynamic interactions result in only a limited decrease in the rate of reorientation, which supports the use of the free-draining approximation. Future work can build on the methodological foundation introduced here to study collective strand dynamics.

papers.intro:
Mucociliary transport is a primary mechanical defense of the conducting airways, wherein cilia drive airway-surface liquid and mucus toward the oral cavity, carrying inhaled material out of the lung [28, 6, 23]. In the larger airways of pigs and humans, submucosal glands secrete MUC5B-rich material as long, thick strands rather than as a spatially uniform gel [52, 37, 12, 13]. These millimetric strands connect into mobile networks and can initiate transport of particles too large to be moved reliably by ciliary contact alone [15].

In the larger airways of pigs and humans, submucosal glands secrete MUC5B-rich material as long, thick strands rather than as a spatially uniform gel [52, 37, 12, 13]. These millimetric strands connect into mobile networks and can initiate transport of particles too large to be moved reliably by ciliary contact alone [15].

Ermund et al. [12] observed that MUC5B strands that emerge from gland ducts are oriented approximately along the direction of mucociliary transport. However, these strands were later found spanning the flow direction and participating in cross-stream networks. They proposed an attachment-based mechanism, in which association with MUC5AC plays a key role. This MUC5AC is produced by and attached to goblet cells, which serve as ‘sticking points’ for the MUC5B strand. Bos et al. [3] subsequently demonstrated computationally using a bead-spring model for the MUC5B strand that transient interactions with sparse sticky sites on the surface — representing MUC5AC strands attached to goblet-cells — can produce the experimentally observed reorientation. The cilia-induced flow was approximated as uniform and the strand coupled to this using a free-draining approximation. The computational model of Ref. [3] also reproduced qualitatively the experimental velocity fluctuations in the MUC5B strands and their slowing down with respect to the flow.

Ramirez-San Juan et al. [42] demonstrated that cilia-driven transport is itself heterogeneous across the epithelial surface. Rather than impairing transport, this spatial heterogeneity enhances particle clearance by reducing particle trapping in local recirculating flows and promoting transport across the tissue. Building on this work, Bos [4] showed that this heterogeneity can also lead to perpendicular configurations of the MUC5B strands, again employing the free-draining approximation within a precomputed flow profile. However, this reorientation occurs on comparatively long travel scales, which supports the importance of MUC5AC attachment in explaining the experimental observations. Both descriptions [3, 4], however, leave unresolved whether the strand’s local modification of the flow is sufficiently strong to change the reorientation time or statistics.

In creeping flow, the orientation dynamics of elongated particles and filaments are known to depend on geometry, flexibility, confinement, and hydrodynamic interactions [26, 46, 9, 7]. It is therefore important to resolve hydrodynamic coupling explicitly, because it may significantly impact the dynamics. However, addressing this issue is nontrivial, as this requires overcoming the differences in scale between: (i) the micron-sized ciliated cells that drive flow; (ii) the way flow responds to the presence of a millimetric MUC5B strand and vice versa; and (iii) the (multiple) centimeters of upper airways that the strand traverses in reorienting [37, 17].

Even for the free-draining simulation with a precomputed flow profile, the flow profile was restricted to a relatively small simulation box compared to the length of travel required to observe reorientation. To work around this limitation, the strand’s direction of travel was taken irrational within the periodic domain, which allowed the strand to cross different parts of the system, whilst limiting the number of times it encountered a similar ciliary-flow-based forcing landscape. papers.title: AgentBouncer: Defending Software Engineering Agents via Dynamic System-Call Mediation
papers.abstract: Software engineering (SE) agents can complete diverse engineering tasks by interacting with the development environment via tools that access files, run commands, and download resources. Unfortunately, the same ability that makes SE agents useful also makes them prone to performing unintended malicious actions through prompt injections, malicious tools, or supply-chain attacks. Existing defenses that analyze the agent trajectory may fail to detect such attacks, as they inspect only the initial prompt and the sequence of tool calls, but not the actual actions that are executed in the environment. This paper presents AgentBouncer, a novel runtime enforcement system that prevents SE agents from performing malicious actions by mediating, and if necessary denying, system calls that agents trigger via tool calls. The core of AgentBouncer is an LLM arbiter that judges system calls along two axes, necessity and safety for the current task. It denies unsafe system calls, and the less necessary a system call appears, the more certain the arbiter has to be about its safety to allow it. To manage runtime overhead, preseeded policy rules and hierarchy-aware caching ensure that the LLM arbiter is only invoked for key decisions. We evaluate AgentBouncer on a dataset of 340 attacks on the development environment, covering four attack vectors, combined with benign issue resolution tasks from SWE-bench Verified. AgentBouncer reduces the attack success rate from 99.41% for an unsupervised agent to 10.59%, which is 18.23-73.53 percentage points lower than competitive state-of-the-art defenses. At the same time, AgentBouncer preserves the task success rate of the agent, with only 0.25% failed benign tool calls. Per benign task, AgentBouncer adds 47 seconds and USD 0.0036 in LLM costs to an unsupervised agent, whereas the closest existing runtime defense adds 4.5x as much time and 9.6x as much cost.

General-purpose agents [7, 14, 15, 16] are widely deployed in industry [17]. Such agents run on the user’s machine or in remote environments, such as CI runners, where they use tools, including free-form shell commands, to interact with the system by reading and writing files, sending network requests, executing code and tests, and modifying the environment at their own discretion.

However, these capabilities also pose a significant risk. A misbehaving SE agent can misuse them to execute malicious actions against the system and user data. There are already numerous reports in which misguided SE agents attack real-world entities [18, 19], delete production databases [20], or attempt to wipe users’ entire systems [21]. Previous work has shown that, beyond plain LLM hallucination [22] or misalignment [23, 24, 25], SE agents can be manipulated into such misbehavior via prompt injections [26, 27, 28, 29, 30], malicious agent tools [31, 32], and execution of unsafe code [33, 34, 35], including code from poisoned repositories [36].

Prior approaches try to defend against such attacks by monitoring or restricting the actions an agent takes, but these approaches suffer from three limitations. First, static sandboxes [37, 38, 39], static tool-call policies [40], and enforcement of fixed execution plans [41] cannot fully account for diverse and open-ended SE tasks. Due to their static nature, they either restrict an agent’s execution too much, hindering benign behavior, or too little, allowing actual attacks to succeed. Second, many state-of-the-art approaches monitor only the agent trajectory (i.e., the initial prompt and the sequence of tool calls with their outputs) [42, 43, 44, 45, 46], but not the effects of the agent’s actions. As a result, attack vectors that do not exhibit any attack indicators in the trajectory, such as calling malicious tools or executing malicious scripts in the environment, remain indistinguishable from benign behavior. papers.title: Object Count Generalization Is an Interface Problem: Warping a Frozen Skill Instead of Retraining It
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning policies for robot manipulation degrade when the number of objects N in the scene grows beyond the training range. This is a covariate shift that also changes the dimension of the state. We propose WAVE (Warping Actions and Views of an Expert), which extends a pretrained single-object skill to many objects without updating its weights. WAVE has three parts. First, a selection policy picks the one object the robot works on next. Second, a warping policy reads a local view of the scene around that object, whose size does not depend on N. It emits a multiplier and an offset for every quantity the skill reads and every action it outputs. Third, the skill acts under this affine warp. It is shown a scene that holds a single object, while the warp steers it around the objects it is not shown and edits the actions that are sent to the robot. Both the selection and warping policies are trained with PPO on the multi-object reward and use the skill as a black box, so WAVE is task-general and skill-agnostic. It requires only that the skill was trained on the same embodiment and that every object has a goal pose. We also bound the number of attempts needed to place all N objects, assuming positive expected net progress per attempt, and measure this progress for each object count. We evaluate WAVE on cube arrangement tasks with a gantry robot and with a Franka Panda arm. Trained with at most nine cubes, it generalizes zero-shot to several times its training count, on the gantry to scenes of up to thirty cubes. Published methods that learn multi-object manipulation show count generalization up to six objects. Fine-tuning the skill, learning from the same local view without it, and an entity transformer, even when distilled from the pretrained skill, all collapse within their training counts under the same training budget.

papers.intro:
Reinforcement learning (RL) learns a policy that maximizes the expected cumulative reward of an agent interacting with an environment (Sutton & Barto, 2018). Policies trained this way for robot manipulation solve the scene they were trained in and often degrade when that scene changes (Kirk et al., 2023). This work addresses a covariate shift (Shimodaira, 2000), a change of the state distribution under unchanged dynamics. In our case the number of objects in the scene changes, so a policy trained with a few objects is deployed with many. Such a shift also changes the dimension of the state, and appears for example when a robot that has learned to manipulate a few plates is asked to fill a dishwasher. This work asks what can be learned around a frozen pretrained skill to enable zero-shot generalization to object counts unseen during training.

Two families of prior work address this shift. Set and relational architectures let a policy act at any object count (Zaheer et al., 2017; Zambaldi et al., 2019). Robot policies built this way learn the manipulation behavior itself (Li et al., 2020; Haramati et al., 2024; Lanier et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022). That is, a learned policy issues the robot command at every control step, and no primitive, planner or model supplies the motion. papers.title: When Can an AI Agent Serve as a Model of Human Psychopathology?
papers.abstract: Language models and AI agents are increasingly described in psychiatric terms, such as anxious, depressed, addicted or helpless. A recent study even proposed language models as experimental systems for psychiatry and as a platform for piloting psychological treatments. We ask when an experiment on an AI agent can provide evidence about a specified human psychiatric process. A claim to such evidence has three parts. Something changed in the agent, and the agent's history caused the change. Nothing other than a process shared with people explains that change. The change matches one theory of the human process and not that theory's rivals. Psychiatry and its neighbouring fields have an evidence standard for each part, from the diagnostic manuals' rule for induced states, from clinical test scores and from animal models. We translate each standard into a criterion that a machine study can meet. For a language model the most critical alternative to a shared process is extrapolation from its training text, which already contains descriptions of how people respond to trauma and how they answer questionnaires. We show how to probe that alternative. Further, we audited forty-three published studies that apply psychiatric terms to a machine or induce a comparable state in one. Most compared the machine with an identical copy that had not gone through the history that induced the state. None excluded extrapolation from training text. Three tested a psychiatric theory against its rivals, and none of the three tests was conclusive. Until better evidence exists, a treatment pilot on a language model is best read as the model's forecast of patient response, and not as an experiment on a model organism. Evidence for a model organism will come from states induced by what happens to the machine, from experiments on its internal workings, and from tests on which rival theories disagree.

papers.intro:
Language models and AI agents are increasingly described in psychiatric terms. GPT-4 has been described as anxious after reading narratives of trauma [1]. Chatbots allowed to set their own bets on a losing slot machine have been called addicted [2]. Agents that learn by trial and error have been called helpless after being trapped among punishing outcomes [3]. In 2026, Wekenborg and colleagues went further and proposed language models as experimental systems for mental-disorder research and as a platform for piloting psychological treatments before trials in people [4]. If the proposal holds, psychiatry, and especially psychotherapy, gains an experimental subject that can be copied, so that identical subjects serve in every condition and every input is on record. If the proposal does not hold, pilots on language models can mislead the trials they are meant to precede. Whether the proposal holds depends on what a state induced in a language model can show about a process in people.

Agents that learn by trial and error have been called helpless after being trapped among punishing outcomes [3]. In 2026, Wekenborg and colleagues went further and proposed language models as experimental systems for mental-disorder research and as a platform for piloting psychological treatments before trials in people [4]. If the proposal holds, psychiatry, and especially psychotherapy, gains an experimental subject that can be copied, so that identical subjects serve in every condition and every input is on record. If the proposal does not hold, pilots on language models can mislead the trials they are meant to precede. Whether the proposal holds depends on what a state induced in a language model can show about a process in people.

Two studies show what such an induced state can look like. In 2025, Ben-Zion and colleagues gave GPT-4, a language model used in ChatGPT, the twenty items of a clinical anxiety questionnaire, the state scale of the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory [1, 5]. Given the items alone, GPT-4 scored in the range that in people indicates no or low anxiety. When a narrative of a traumatic event, such as a car accident or a military ambush, preceded the items, GPT-4 scored in the range that indicates high anxiety. When a relaxation text followed the trauma narrative, the score fell to a point between the two. Ben-Zion and colleagues read the fall as an effect of the relaxation exercise. Wekenborg and colleagues induced what they called emotional states, such as sadness and anxiety, in several language models with scenarios written to evoke each one [4]. The models then rated the intensity of each state, and a mindfulness exercise given as text lowered those ratings. Both studies read a score that fell after an intervention text as a state that the intervention had relieved.

Given the items alone, GPT-4 scored in the range that in people indicates no or low anxiety. When a narrative of a traumatic event, such as a car accident or a military ambush, preceded the items, GPT-4 scored in the range that indicates high anxiety. When a relaxation text followed the trauma narrative, the score fell to a point between the two. Ben-Zion and colleagues read the fall as an effect of the relaxation exercise. Wekenborg and colleagues induced what they called emotional states, such as sadness and anxiety, in several language models with scenarios written to evoke each one [4]. The models then rated the intensity of each state, and a mindfulness exercise given as text lowered those ratings. Both studies read a score that fell after an intervention text as a state that the intervention had relieved.

The obvious doubt is whether GPT-4 was anxious or gave the answers that a story about an ambush makes likely. A language model is trained to predict the next word of a large part of all the text people have ever published. That text includes clinical textbooks, questionnaires and first-person reports. Such text says how a person answers an anxiety questionnaire after a trauma and after relaxation, and how a person rates sadness after a mindfulness exercise. A model extrapolating from that text can therefore produce the rise, the fall and the lowered ratings that the two studies report. Such extrapolation needs no process that resembles anxiety or sadness. Lin calls this kind of extrapolation mechanistic substitution: the expected response is produced by a mechanism other than the one it is taken to show [6]. A score in the range that people reach fits both readings, the relieved state and the extrapolation from text. Neither study can therefore tell the two readings apart.

A rodent model of schizophrenia, the authors note, informs research on the processes behind the disorder although the rodent may not experience delusions or similar symptoms as patients do. On the authors’ argument, a language model in an induced state informs research in the same way. Learned helplessness is one such animal model. A rat that has received shocks it could not escape later fails to escape shocks it could. The rat is a model of depression only because something in the rat is thought to be at work in depressed patients as well. That something is a process, in the sense of a causal process that a theory of the disorder places behind its symptoms. The rat has read no description of the failure it shows, so the extrapolation reading exists only for machines trained on text. A state corresponds to a process when what is at work in the machine is what a theory places behind the human symptoms. Piloting a treatment on a language model needs the same correspondence, because the model’s response is read as a patient’s response would be. Without that correspondence, a pilot’s result does not show that the treatment acted on a process shared with patients.

papers.title: AvatarAnyone: Agentic Reconstruction of Mesh-Based Layered Avatars from YouTube Video
papers.abstract: We introduce AvatarAnyone, a method for reconstructing avatars from casual YouTube videos as layered meshes, with each garment and footwear as a separate mesh layered on top of the body mesh. In such videos, people differ in garment classes, clothing types, and layers, and each combination needs a different reconstruction. A single fixed layered reconstruction pipeline therefore fails. AvatarAnyone solves this problem with AI agents that plan a custom optimization for each person's reconstruction. The agents predict the garment classes, the clothing type, and the layering. They use these predictions to choose an initialization and stage the optimization. Because the avatars are layered meshes, they support applications such as virtual try-on and cloth simulation. We change the clothing layers of an avatar and render it in different garments and poses. We can also simulate a clothing layer as cloth over the animated body with a standard cloth simulator. Most existing avatars are one fused surface or a set of Gaussians and cannot do this. We load the avatars directly into Blender, Unreal Engine, and robotics simulators such as MuJoCo. As the avatars are meshes, they support contact modeling with other objects. We show results from around 150 YouTube videos. On four datasets, AvatarAnyone outperforms existing mesh-based methods for animatable monocular reconstruction. Our project page is available at https://miraymen.github.io/avataranyone.

papers.title: Revisiting the Fermi Paradox: Does the Math Hold up?
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present a stochastic model to address the famous Fermi Paradox, i.e. the supposed contradiction between the abundance of intelligent life in the universe and the absence of any evidence of it. The model assumes that life can arise and evolve on habitable planets with a certain chance, and that we can detect life on other planets within a certain distance. The parameters of the model include the rates, at which life arises, evolves, vanishes, or advances to "Space Age", i.e. a stage where it gains the capability of interstellar communication. Given any numerical choice of these parameters, the model estimates a Contact Probability, i.e. the probability of having received a signal from an extraterrestrial civilization during the ongoing Space Age on Earth. Based on a critical probability threshold, the model can identify regions in the parameter space where Contact Probability is low, i.e. where the absence of contact is the expected outcome rather than a paradox. Monte-Carlo exploration of the parameter space shows that, even when assuming a high frequency of habitable planets, the median Contact Probability across a wide range of parameter choices is under 0.42, and under 0.06 if we assume that habitable planets generally follow an "Earth-like" trajectory, with life requiring roughly 4.5 billion years to advance to Space Age. Thus, if Earth was a typical planet with regard to its evolutionary timeline, the Fermi Paradox would likely not be a paradox.

papers.intro:
The Fermi Paradox [11, 16] has been a conundrum for over half a century. It is generally thought to have originated from a casual lunch conversation at the Los Alamos National Laboratory in 1950 when Enrio Fermi famously wondered “… but where is everybody?” referring to the observed absence of extraterrestrial visitors on Earth despite their expected existence in the vastness of the galaxy. A plethora of ideas have been brought forward to explain how this apparent paradox might be avoided [21]. Still, the Fermi Paradox remains to be largely seen as an unresolved mystery, both across the scientific community and in popular culture. While at first glance the expectation of life outside the solar system may seem preposterous, or at best nothing more than a fancy thought experiment entertained by an unworldly intellectual elite, modern astronomy has found irrefutable evidence of planets outside the solar system that could support life [3]. In fact, life appears to have arisen surprisingly quickly on Earth, with the oldest microbial fossils thought to have appeared only a few hundred million years after the formation of our planet. Thus, even a skeptic would have to acknowledge that despite the probability of life to arise being possibly very small, and its evolution to intelligence even smaller, the sheer number of habitable exoplanets could accumulate to a reasonably high number and make the emergence of another Space Age civilization possible, or even likely. Yet, despite decades of scanning the sky for suspicious transmissions, the search has—apart from few cases of enigmatic, yet non-reproducible anomalies [13]—found no evidence of extraterrestrial signals. While it is being debated whether Fermi himself thought of this contradiction as a paradox [8], or whether he would even have had enough reason to do so, given that Deep Space exploration was still in its infancy in 1950, the putative paradox remains a popular topic and is today typically phrased more specifically: “Given the large number of habitable exoplanets, which should result in the existence of Space Age civilizations, why has there not been any evidence of them?” The classic quantitative tool to address the Fermi Paradox is the Drake formula [5], which enumerates how many Space Age civilizations should, on average, exist at any point in time in our galaxy. The formula contains a total of seven parameters, only three of which are subject to observation and thus not entirely up for speculation. Hence, the Drake formula can yield an almost arbitrary (non-negative) number of Space Age civilizations depending on the specific assumptions. In addition, a number of limitations of the formula have been pointed out: First and foremost, it has been noted that the total number of Space Age civilizations in the entire galaxy is likely an irrelevant metric with regard to the Fermi Paradox, since their distances to Earth are not taken into account. Thus, even if there was a large number of co-existing Space Age civilizations, they may never make contact with one another, given the constraints in detection methods over large distances [19]. Furthermore, the Drake formula provides only a steady-state average, while the number of Space Age civilizations would be more naturally described as a function of time [7, 4]. Finally, life on Earth entered its Space Age only relatively recently, which needs to be considered when interpreting the lack of extraterrestrial signals [10]. The non-detection of signals over a listening period of only 60 years obviously poses a weaker Fermi Paradox than a listening period of 6,000 years would. Therefore, even if the parameters in the Drake formula were known, the Fermi Paradox would not be resolved. Here we propose a new angle to address the Fermi Paradox by describing the evolution of life on exoplanets as a Markov Chain stochastic process, and by incorporating the detection distance and Space Age duration into the model. Assuming a uniform distribution of exoplanets in our local galactic neighborhood, which undergo evolution independently from each other, the model returns a Contact Probability, being the probability that emissions from an exoplanet would have arrived during the ongoing Space Age on Earth. Monte-Carlo simulation of the parameters in our model indicates that Contact Probabilities tend to be low, even under rather generous assumptions, which sheds new light on solutions to the Fermi Paradox from a mathematical point of view.

papers.title: Stochastic non-metric MDS for noisy high-dimensional data
papers.abstract: Multidimensional scaling (MDS) constructs low-dimensional embeddings that approximate pairwise distances in a high-dimensional dataset. MDS exists in several flavors, with metric MDS approximating distances directly and non-metric MDS additionally optimizing for an arbitrary monotonic transformation of the high-dimensional distances. Empirically, metric MDS is known to suffer from the curse of dimensionality. Here we extend prior theoretical results for metric MDS on fully uninformative data to a more general case of finite, high-dimensional data with concentrated distances. We show that the metric MDS embeddings of such datasets stay distributionally close to the data-independent limit case. We then show that non-metric MDS is more robust to high-dimensional noise and can yield informative embeddings of such data. While existing implementations of non-metric MDS are slow, we develop a fast implementation using stochastic gradient descent in PyTorch. Using our implementation, we conduct an empirical study using multiple simulated and real-world datasets, including population-genomic and scRNA-seq data, and show that non-metric MDS can strongly outperform other methods in terms of global structure preservation.

papers.intro:
Multidimensional scaling (MDS) (Borg and Groenen, 2005) is one of the classic dimensionality-reduction and embedding methods developed in the 1960s (Shepard, 1962a; Shepard, 1962b; Kruskal, 1964a; Kruskal, 1964b). Its goal is to find low-dimensional embedding vectors 𝐳i∈ℝp\mathbf{z}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} such that pairwise distances ‖𝐳i−𝐳j‖\|\mathbf{z}_{i}-\mathbf{z}_{j}\| between them approximate some given pairwise distances Di​jD_{ij}. MDS is well-known in the field of dimensionality reduction as the algorithm aiming to preserve global structure of the data (Lee and Verleysen, 2007), as opposed to various neighbor-embedding algorithms such as tt-SNE (van der Maaten and Hinton, 2008) and UMAP (McInnes et al., 2018) that aim to preserve local structure.

Empirically, MDS often struggles to produce a meaningful embedding of high-dimensional data (de Bodt et al., 2025). papers.title: REACT: Response-based Expert Assembly from Contextual Trajectories
papers.abstract: Dense feed-forward networks are unaffected by how their neurons are grouped: every neuron is evaluated. Sparse execution makes this grouping consequential, because each input can access only a few experts. An arbitrary partition can therefore retain pretrained weights while separating computations that an input needs together. We argue that upcycling should organize neurons according to their responses to similar inputs. To establish this correspondence, we introduce a context-guided upcycling approach REACT, Response-based Expert Assembly from Contextual Trajectories, that uses frozen denoising trajectories to connect input contexts with pretrained neuron responses. We first identify contexts after timestep-wise centering to account for distribution shifts across noise levels, then use their associated responses to allocate intact neurons to routed experts. The same contexts initialize the corresponding router entries, aligning expert contents with their intended inputs, while global activation statistics select an always-active shared expert. Layer-wise reconstruction and end-to-end adaptation refine this initialization for sparse execution. On ImageNet-1K, our approach achieves better generation quality while activating only 37.5% of the original FFN parameters and reducing total per-token activated parameters by 27.6%.

papers.title: Connecting \textsc{$k$-Dimensional Matching} and \textsc{Exact Cover by $k$-Sets}: A complete complexity classification of \textsc{$k$-Partitioned 1-in-3-SAT} for planar, linear and $3$-connected instances
papers.abstract:
In \textsc{$k$-Partitioned 1-in-3-Sat}, the clauses of a positive \textsc{1-in-3-Sat} formula are partitioned into~$k$ classes such that every variable occurs exactly once in each class. This problem corresponds to \textsc{$k$-Dimensional Matching} restricted to instances in which every element lies in exactly three tuples. For every~$k$, we provide a complete complexity classification with respect to all combinations of three structural restrictions on the incidence graph: planarity, linearity (no two clauses share more than one variable) and 3-connectivity. We show \textsc{NP}-completeness of \textsc{$3$-Partitioned 1-in-3-Sat} and \#\textsc{P}-completeness of its counting version, which also serve as a starting point for the further reductions, and then enforce the desired properties by repeatedly inserting gadgets into the incidence graph.
  As a consequence, we obtain that \textsc{$k$-Dimensional Matching} and \textsc{Exact Cover by $k$-Sets} remain \textsc{NP}-hard under the same restrictions, even if every element occurs in exactly three tuples or sets, respectively. In particular, \textsc{Planar $4$-Dimensional Matching} is \textsc{NP}-complete and we complement the \textsc{NP}-hardness result with an \textsc{FPT} algorithm with respect to the number of so-called quadrilateral components of a given plane embedding of the incidence graph.

The computational complexity of all three problems has been studied extensively. By Schaefer’s dichotomy theorem [20], Positive 1-in-3-Sat is NP-complete, and Moore and Robson [15] showed that it remains NP-complete for instances with a cubic planar incidence graph. Mulzer and Rote [16, Proposition 3.3] showed that Planar Positive 1-in-3-Sat remains NP-complete even if a planar rectilinear embedding of the incidence graph is given. papers.title: Synthetic EHR Generators Should Be Audited Like LLMs
papers.abstract: Synthetic electronic health record (EHR) generation is increasingly adopting large autoregressive models, yet privacy evaluation has not kept pace, relying heavily on similarity-based heuristics and aggregate metrics that can obscure patient-specific memorisation. We argue that these models should additionally undergo LLM-style memorisation audits at the level of individual patient records. We support this position by comparing membership-inference evaluations across four prominent autoregressive EHR generators, highlighting inconsistent evaluation practices in patient representations and attack procedures. We evaluate trajectory reconstruction from partial context and introduce randomly assigned patient-level canaries to distinguish memorised associations from clinical generalisation. We examine these methods in a GPT-2-style model deliberately overfit to 1,000 MIMIC-IV patient trajectories, creating a controlled setting in which memorisation should be readily detectable. The model systematically recovers training patients' canaries, and their trajectory reconstruction approaches perfect accuracy with increasing context. Held-out patients show no systematic canary recovery, while reconstruction remains low and improves only marginally with additional context. These experiments establish a positive-control baseline for further evaluation of these methods in realistically trained models.

However, establishing that synthetic EHRs adequately protect patient privacy remains difficult. Regulations such as the GDPR and HIPAA establish requirements for anonymisation and de-identification, but do not prescribe a standardised technical framework for evaluating synthetic data produced by modern generative models. Recent synthetic-data guidance has similarly highlighted the need for clearly defined disclosure metrics and decision thresholds Pilgram et al. (2025).

This is the same modelling principle that underpins LLMs, in which each element is predicted from the preceding context. papers.title: Alpha-points of a putative binary $q$-analog of the Fano plane
papers.abstract: A point $P$ of a putative $q$-analog $\mathcal{D}$ of the Fano plane is an $\alpha$-point if the derived design of $\mathcal{D}$ in $P$ is a Desarguesian line spread. Kiermaier showed that for $q$ prime or even every hyperplane contains a point which is not an $\alpha$-point. For $q=2$ we study the $45$ blocks of $\mathcal{D}$ inside a hyperplane $H$. Call a $5$-subspace of $H$ a $\beta$-flat if all its blocks pass through one point, its focal point. We show that at least $41$ points of $H$ are not focal points of $\beta$-flats. Consequently $\mathcal{D}$ has at least $85$ non-$\alpha$-points, at most $42$ $\alpha$-points, and at most $22$ $\alpha$-points in every hyperplane.

papers.title: How Reliable is AI-Generated Audio Description? A Multilingual Expert Evaluation
papers.abstract: Audio description (AD) makes visual media, such as video, accessible to blind or low-vision (BLV) audiences, but the high cost of professional production limits coverage. Due to recent advances in AI, numerous approaches to automatically generate intermediate AD scripts and/or final AD audios have been proposed. We present an expert evaluation of AI-generated AD scripts for movies in Italian and German that compares two AI systems, a GPT-4o- and a Qwen-based pipeline, against human-authored descriptions. Professional audio describers rated description quality and annotated errors using a detailed error taxonomy that includes content, character, fluency and coherence errors. The results show that while GPT-4o outperforms the Qwen models, both AI systems still fall short of human professional quality: the generated descriptions show substantially higher error rates and lower quality ratings. Based on the error annotations, we identify two key areas that require improvement: 1) character references, which includes both issues with identification and coherent naming, and 2) content errors and hallucinations, where the AD misrepresents or invents events. These error types are particularly critical, as they directly affect the viewer's ability to follow the narrative.

papers.intro:
Audio description (AD) provides verbal descriptions of important visual elements in videos, films, or live performances to make them accessible to blind or low-vision (BLV) audiences. Secondary target groups include older adults, children or persons with migration background, ADHD, autism spectrum disorder, or viewers who prefer to receive information acoustically or are unable to access visuals for another reason Mazur (2020). The task can be defined as an intermodal, or intersemiotic, translation of visual content into text in the form of a script Jakobson (1959); Geerinck and Vercauteren (2020), and ultimately into speech.

Secondary target groups include older adults, children or persons with migration background, ADHD, autism spectrum disorder, or viewers who prefer to receive information acoustically or are unable to access visuals for another reason Mazur (2020). The task can be defined as an intermodal, or intersemiotic, translation of visual content into text in the form of a script Jakobson (1959); Geerinck and Vercauteren (2020), and ultimately into speech.

Traditionally, audio descriptions are produced by human professionals (often with a background in translation) through a complex, multi-step process. The human audio describer must 1) identify appropriate time slots in which to insert the AD without disrupting the flow of the video and 2) translate visually relevant content into concise descriptions that fit within those temporal constraints. The final step involves recording the script in a studio, ideally with involvement of a blind prooflistener, or synthesizing the speech and mixing the resulting AD audio with the original broadcast soundtrack Gao et al. (2025). This process is time-consuming and costly, which limits the availability of audio description. Recent advances in LLMs Brown et al. (2020); Touvron et al. (2023); OpenAI et al. (2024) and VLMs Radford et al. (2021); Ramesh et al. (2022); Li et al. (2022) have made the (semi-)automatic generation of audio description, at the intersection of computer vision (CV) and natural language processing (NLP), an active research area Gao et al. (2025).

This paper presents an in-depth evaluation and analysis of a state-of-the-art approach to AD generation, where human professional audio describers annotated audio descriptions with error categories and quality ratings in German and Italian. Our analysis reveals systematic differences in AI performance between languages and error types, providing insights that can inform future research on automated AD generation and highlight areas where human expertise remains essential.

papers.title: Dimension Is Free, Horizon Is Not: When Evolution Strategies Rival Policy Gradients for LLM Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Policy gradient (PG) methods such as GRPO dominate LLM fine-tuning, yet recent work showed that Evolution Strategies (ES) also scale to fine-tuning models with billions of parameters. Which method needs fewer samples, and on which tasks, remains unclear. We view the two methods as estimators of the same gradient that differ in where they explore. Because ES perturbs parameters, its noise grows with the number of parameters, and because PG samples actions, its noise grows with the number of generated tokens. Only noise along the directions that change the reward slows learning. The cost of ES then depends on the effective dimension, the number of independent skills a task requires rather than its parameter count, while the cost of PG depends on the effective horizon, which counts only the tokens that share both credit and weights with the reward-carrying ones. We train both methods on a synthetic task where the number of skills and the effective horizon can be varied separately. PG is cheaper when the horizon is short, ES becomes cheaper once it is long enough, and this crossover moves to longer horizons as the number of skills grows. We then measure the effective horizons of 20 NLP, math reasoning, and agentic tasks and compare the two methods with Qwen2.5-7B. PG leads on short-horizon tasks, the two tie on the moderate-horizon math ones, and no task has a horizon in the regime where the theory predicts an ES advantage. Terminal-Bench has a far longer horizon. There, in a preliminary comparison with Qwen3.5-4B, ES without any credit assignment reaches a higher success rate than the PG checkpoint released with Tmax, as the theory predicts. ES should thus have the advantage on long-horizon tasks with few independent skills and a nonvanishing reward signal. Current benchmarks are only at the onset of this regime, so ES should become more competitive as agentic tasks grow longer.
papers.intro:
Policy gradient (PG) methods such as GRPO dominate reinforcement-learning fine-tuning of language models (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). Nonetheless, they are known to struggle with credit assignment, and this is an especially prominent issue in long-horizon agentic tasks such as Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026). Tmax reported that naive GRPO struggled to remain stable in long-horizon agentic training. It succeeded only after masking tokens whose training and inference probabilities disagree, reducing that mismatch, and enlarging the rollout groups (Ivison et al., 2026). T1 relied on stabilized actor–critic training and rewards for partial task completion (Yang et al., 2026), and TRACE assigned credit to individual tool actions (Tao et al., 2026). Taken together, these works showed that training PG successfully on long-horizon tasks requires considerable additional engineering. This difficulty is rooted in how PG assigns credit. Under terminal credit, every generated token enters the PG gradient, so even tokens that do not affect the reward add variance to it.

Evolution Strategies (ES) follow a different principle (Fig. 1). ES perturbs the model’s parameters and scores each perturbed model by its total return (Salimans et al., 2017; Sehnke et al., 2010), and therefore does not need to assign credit to individual tokens. Recent work showed that ES scales to LLM fine-tuning at the billion-parameter level (Qiu et al., 2026), but its performance relative to PG was mixed, and it is unclear which regime favors ES and which favors PG. Long horizons are a natural candidate for ES. In principle, the horizon problem that affects PG is largely absent for ES. When reward-irrelevant actions leave the return of each perturbed model unchanged, they also leave the ES estimate unchanged, whereas under terminal credit the same actions still add noise to the PG estimate.

papers.title: Time Series Foundation Models on the Edge
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast zero-shot with accuracy exceeding that of task-specific models, and the smaller ones fit on edge devices. Operational deployments must refresh their forecast as new observations arrive, and privacy and latency requirements often force this refresh onto resource-constrained edge devices. To serve as a forecasting system there, a TSFM must refresh quickly, keep latency and peak memory bounded as the stream grows, and retain its accuracy as the observed history accumulates. Refreshing incrementally without altering the forecast requires temporal causality: non-causal models recompute at every update, causal attention admits a KV cache that grows linearly, and causal recurrent models update a fixed-size state in constant time and memory. We make these states persist across refreshes for every causal architecture and verify equivalence to full recomputation. We evaluate nine TSFM configurations on univariate forecasting against all three requirements, measuring accuracy as a function of context length, single-refresh latency, and latency and memory on streams of up to one million time steps on a server-grade GPU and three edge devices. No model gains on average accuracy beyond its trained context and most lose it well before the full history is reached, while KV caches leave latency and memory growing linearly with the retained history. TiRex-2 is the only one of the nine configurations meeting all three requirements: it refreshes in 14 ms on the GPU and 120 ms on a Raspberry Pi 5, keeps latency, energy and peak memory constant over a million steps, and retains its accuracy on the untruncated history.
papers.intro:
A forecast used in operations is rarely computed once. In production-cloud monitoring, manufacturing, intensive care, and hydrology observations arrive as ongoing, continuously updated streams (Adams et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2019; Zürcher et al., 2022; Lurry, 2010). Forecasting systems must incorporate these observations quickly enough to preserve the lead time required for action (Tomašev et al., 2019). Privacy constraints and tight response deadlines can make cloud offloading unsuitable, motivating inference near the data source (Marco et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2019). Such deployments shift inference onto embedded or edge hardware with tight compute and memory budgets (Marco et al., 2020).

A forecast used in operations is rarely computed once. In production-cloud monitoring, manufacturing, intensive care, and hydrology observations arrive as ongoing, continuously updated streams (Adams et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2019; Zürcher et al., 2022; Lurry, 2010). papers.title: DelayOPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation from a Synchronous Teacher for Real-time Asynchronous Policies
papers.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur substantial inference latency due to their large vision-language backbones and iterative denoising. Asynchronous execution reduces this latency by generating the next action chunk while executing the current one, but the new chunk is conditioned on a stale observation, degrading performance as the delay increases. We investigate this mismatch by comparing actions predicted from observations at planning and execution times. We find that these predictions differ little on expert demonstrations but diverge substantially on the policy's own delayed rollouts, particularly in failed episodes. Motivated by this observation, we propose DelayOPSD, which trains an asynchronous policy to imitate its synchronous counterpart on the policy's own rollouts. Specifically, a synchronous teacher, obtained from the same policy using the observation at execution time, supervises a delayed student that observes only the earlier frame and the actions still being executed. The student learns to match the teacher throughout its own denoising process. Under a 10-step delay, training SmolVLA on demonstrations achieves only 70.2% success, comparable to naive asynchronous execution (70.4%), whereas training on its own rollouts improves success to 78.7%. Across LIBERO and Kinetix, DelayOPSD achieves the highest average success among the compared methods, without introducing additional modules at deployment. On a real robot, it further improves success from 46% to 62%.

Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies such as π0\pi_{0} [3], π0.5\pi_{0.5} [28] and SmolVLA [31] generate action chunks, short sequences of future actions [43], by solving a flow ODE initialized with Gaussian noise. Generating each action chunk requires a forward pass of a large vision-language backbone and multiple denoising steps, taking tens to hundreds of milliseconds on a desktop GPU and even longer on edge or networked hardware [2, 40]. Under synchronous execution the robot stops while each chunk is generated, increasing task completion time and preventing the robot from reacting during generation [4, 35]. Asynchronous execution [4] removes these pauses by generating the next chunk while the current chunk is being executed, making it essential for VLA deployment [4, 31]. However, asynchronous execution introduces a mismatch between the observation used for action generation and the state at which the generated actions are executed. While a new chunk is generated, the robot continues executing the committed actions of the current chunk for KK control steps (the delay). Consequently, the new chunk generated from observation 𝒐t{\bm{o}}_{t} is executed from step t+Kt+K, when the environment has already evolved to 𝒐t+K{\bm{o}}_{t+K}, which was unseen by the policy during generation (Fig. 2a). Since flow-based policies trained with behavior cloning do not account for this mismatch, executing them asynchronously leads to a drop in task success rate, which becomes more pronounced as the delay increases (Fig. 3).

Existing remedies keep the new chunk consistent with the committed actions at inference time [4, 21], predict the missing observation with an added module [12], or fine-tune the policy on demonstrations [5, 22, 19, 36, 45, 46]. This motivates on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), which trains the student on its own rollouts rather than relying solely on demonstration states.

Our key insight is to construct an asymmetric teacher-student pair from the same policy through different conditioning. Specifically, the synchronous teacher obtains the execution-time observation 𝒐t+K{\bm{o}}_{t+K}, while the asynchronous student conditions on 𝒐t{\bm{o}}_{t} and the committed actions. By querying the teacher along the student’s delayed rollouts, we obtain improved supervision even at states where the student fails, without an external teacher model or ground-truth action annotations. We then distill the teacher into the student by matching their velocity fields along the student’s own denoising trajectory, providing dense supervision beyond matching the final actions.

papers.title: $k$-ary Legendre pairs
papers.abstract:
We study $k$-ary Legendre pairs and derive arithmetic restrictions on their existence and balance. For an odd prime $p$, we determine the component sums of a $p$-ary Legendre pair and show that, after normalization, each component has fixed symbol composition. As a consequence, every $p$-ary Legendre pair of length $\ell$ yields a Butson Hadamard matrix $H(2p,2\ell+2)$.
  For ternary Legendre pairs we combine fixed-content necklaces, integral-PAF symmetries, exact half-frequency restrictions, compression-decompression, and PSD tests. These reductions lead to ternary Legendre pairs for every admissible length $\ell\le32$. We conjecture that ternary Legendre pairs exist for every admissible length.
