papers.intro:
The amplitude envelope and instantaneous phase provide complementary descriptions of an oscillatory signal and are well-established attributes for interpreting seismic traces. Both arise naturally from the analytic signal, in which a trace and its Hilbert transform form the real and imaginary components of a complex-valued representation. Expressing the signal in polar form separates the magnitude of the oscillation from its position within the oscillatory cycle, allowing its energetic and structural information to be examined independently. For two-dimensional signals, this construction is generalised by the monogenic signal, introduced by Felsberg and Sommer (2001), which replaces the Hilbert transform with the vector-valued Riesz transform. The key feature of the monogenic signal is that it supplements local amplitude and phase with a local orientation attribute that describes the predominant direction of oscillation.

The monogenic signal was originally motivated by the need to demodulate different aspects of spatially varying patterns, with applications including local orientation estimation, edge detection, image analysis, and denoising (Felsberg and Sommer, 2001). Since its introduction, this decomposition has supported applications across a range of fields. In cardiac imaging, for example, Alessandrini et al. (2013) used monogenic phase to track deformation of the heart muscle independently of variations in image intensity and contrast between frames. The amplitude envelope, by contrast, describes variations in the strength of a pattern independently of its oscillations. Mäteling and Schröder (2022) used this information to investigate how the amplitudes of structures in different regions of a turbulent flow vary together. The complementary roles of amplitude and phase are also evident in guided-wave imaging, where envelopes allow the strengths of different wavelength components to be compared (Flynn et al., 2013), while spatial variations in phase provide estimates of local wavelength following mode filtering (Spytek et al., 2021).

Unlike conventional seismic sensors, which measure particle motion at discrete locations, DAS channels record axial strain or strain rate averaged over a finite gauge length, such that the recorded response depends on the spatial wavelength of the wavefield and on the projection of the associated deformation onto the fibre direction (Dean et al., 2017; Kennett, 2022). Therefore, DAS measurements represent a directional and spatially averaged response of the seismic wavefield. More fundamentally, Muir and Zhan (2022) advocated treating a DAS array as a sampling of an underlying spatial wavefield rather than as a collection of individual channels.

We apply the analysis jointly to distance along the fibre and time coordinates, treating the data as two-dimensional oscillatory fields. In regions where the wavefield is locally dominated by a coherent arrival forming a ridge, the monogenic envelope and phase describe the local amplitude and phase of the arrival, while the monogenic orientation describes the direction normal to the ridge in distance–time space. The ridge direction, obtained from this orientation, defines the local slope and directly relates to the apparent slowness of the arrival along the fibre.

papers.title: Mixed-State Magnetotransport Below $T_c$ in Type-II Superconducting NbN Thin Films
papers.abstract: The transport properties of type-II superconductors in the mixed state below the superconducting transition temperature, $T_c$, remain difficult to interpret because superconducting and dissipative processes coexist in the presence of a magnetic field. To investigate this regime in NbN thin films, we measured the field-dependent sheet resistance ($R^M_{xx}$) and Hall resistance ($R^M_{xy}$) below $T_c$ in Van der Pauw geometry for 4-nm-thick NbN films on sapphire and silicon substrates at driving currents of 1 mA and 2 mA. By combining the longitudinal response with the antisymmetrized Hall signal, we use a phenomenological current-partition model to estimate the dissipative and superconducting current contributions. From this analysis, we estimate the field-dependent superconducting current together with the Hall-derived effective dissipative carrier density and mobility. We also observe an even-in-field transverse signal whose magnitude depends strongly on the driving current. We discuss this signal as a possible mixed-state response involving the magnetic and supercurrent texture of Abrikosov vortices, vortex dynamics, and Cooper-pair current redistribution. The present measurements do not uniquely distinguish vortex, condensate, or combined contributions. The model provides a practical way to compare the longitudinal and transverse mixed-state responses without implying a direct spatial separation of the two current channels.

papers.intro:
Detecting single photons is a key requirement in numerous areas of science and technology, including quantum and fundamental research [4, 14], optical communication [26, 8, 43], long-range optical sensing[45, 48, 13, 27], spectroscopy [9, 21, 15] and astronomy [44]. The need to detect extremely weak photons has driven the development of several single photon-detectors, such as silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) [12], single photon avalanche detectors (SPADs) [11], and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) [30], each offering advantages in specific wavelength ranges. Among these SNSPDs emerged as a leading technology because of high detection efficiency, low dark-count rate, low timing jitter, fast reset time and broadband sensitivity [10, 46]. Recent advancements have pushed SNSPD performance to near unity detection efficiency in the near infrared and telecom spectral range. Fiber-coupled SNSPDs have recorded system detection efficiencies of 98.0 ±\pm 0.5 % at 1550 nm and 99.5−2.07+0.599.5^{+0.5}_{-2.07} % at 1350 nm, while waveguide-integrated SNSPDs have achieved efficiencies above 99% at 1550 nm [41, 31, 6, 22].

Despite the excellent performance of SNSPDs in the visible, near infrared, and telecom regimes, the microscopic origin of the detection event remains incompletely understood. At the device level, SNSPD detection is described as a sequence of photon absorption, followed by local suppression of the superconducting state and formation of a dissipative region in the nanowire, and electrical detection of the resulting voltage pulse [10]. However, the physical origin of this dissipative region remains under active discussion, and is interpreted using hotspot-based models, while vortex-based models emphasize the possible role of vortex entry, motion and vortex assisted switching of nanowire into a resistive state [35, 33, 5, 42, 7].

To understand how a current biased superconducting nanowire evolves into a dissipative state, it is important to examine the superconducting properties of the underlying material. Type-II superconducting Niobium Nitride (NbN) is one of the most widely used materials for SNSPDs because of its high critical temperatures (TcT_{c}) of around 16 K, high critical current densities (JcJ_{c}) [10, 18]. These are of interest for a variety of superconducting devices, ranging from hot-electron bolometer mixers [29, 32] to micro resonators [17], magnetometers [25] and SNSPDs [10, 37]. In these devices, the superconducting state is controlled by three main critical parameters: temperature, current density, and magnetic field. While SNSPD operation mainly relies on the current criticality, with the nanowire biased close to JcJ_{c}, magnetic-field-dependent transport provides a controlled way to examine how vortex formation, field-induced dissipation, and the magnetic suppression of superconductivity in NbN below TcT_{c} occurs. Previous studies have used magnetic field to study vortex dynamics and tune the performance of NbN-SNSPD through I-V characteristics and count rate measurements [5, 7, 23]. However, direct magnetotransport and Hall measurements below-TcT_{c} in structured NbN films remain limited, particularly for understanding field-induced dissipation and vortex-related transport.

papers.title: Tight Query Depth of Recursive Randomized Greedy MIS
papers.abstract: The randomized greedy maximal independent set (RGMIS) algorithm processes vertices in a uniformly random order and greedily constructs an MIS. Its recursive formulation decides whether a vertex belongs to this MIS by querying lower-ranked neighbors in increasing rank order, stopping when a neighbor in the MIS is found. We prove that, on every $n$-vertex graph, this recursive algorithm has $O(\log n)$ query depth with high probability, even without memoization. The bound holds simultaneously for all starting vertices and is asymptotically tight even on bipartite graphs. The proof combines a bound on the total expected number of query paths with an exposure argument: paths with many two-edge shortcuts are unlikely, while the remaining paths admit sufficiently many applications of a two-hop probability bound.

papers.intro:
A maximal independent set (MIS) of a graph is an inclusion-wise maximal set of pairwise nonadjacent vertices. Computing an MIS is a central symmetry-breaking problem in graph algorithms, with fundamental roles in parallel, distributed, and sublinear computation [13, 17, 1, 7, 23, 20, 15, 6, 16, 11, 10, 12, 14].

A maximal independent set (MIS) of a graph is an inclusion-wise maximal set of pairwise nonadjacent vertices. Computing an MIS is a central symmetry-breaking problem in graph algorithms, with fundamental roles in parallel, distributed, and sublinear computation [13, 17, 1, 7, 23, 20, 15, 6, 16, 11, 10, 12, 14].

Among the simplest and most extensively studied approaches to computing an MIS is the randomized greedy MIS (RGMIS) algorithm. The algorithm samples a uniformly random permutation π\pi of the vertices and processes them in this order, adding a vertex if none of its previously processed neighbors has already been selected. Although sequential in its description, RGMIS admits a natural parallel execution. The parallel depth of this execution has been studied since the 1980s, first on random graphs [9, 7, 8], and later on arbitrary graphs under a uniformly random permutation. Blelloch, Fineman, and Shun proved an O⁡(log2⁡n)O(\log^{2}n) high-probability bound on the parallel depth [6], while Fischer and Noever subsequently established the tight Θ⁡(log⁡n)\Theta(\log n) bound [10].

papers.title: FASCIA: Seeing Beneath the Surface with Queryable, Personalized Anatomy in Any Pose
papers.abstract: We present FASCIA (*Functional Anatomical Structures and Composition via Implicit Atlas*), a Momentum Human Rig (MHR)-anchored framework that predicts and poses a person's internal anatomy from their external body shape and skeletal proportions. FASCIA maps a single 290-structure population template onto each individual through a smooth, invertible warp. As people with the same shape can differ internally, a body-dependent Gaussian prior predicts both average warp coordinates and their inter-subject variability. The warp deforms a learned base template into bones, muscles, organs, and fat depots. Extending MHR skinning into the interior enables direct supervision of this model across four automatically labeled CT cohorts and one whole-body MRI cohort. On 82 held-out CT scans, FASCIA reaches a mean volumetric Dice (volume agreement) of 0.48 on named bones and 0.63 on muscles, keeps the majority of bones and muscles in one piece, and yields calibrated voxel probabilities. On 33 held-out whole-body MRI subjects, FASCIA's pointwise field improves tissue overlap over HIT across all compartments, predicts between-person differences in whole-body adipose percentage ($R^2 = 0.88$ vs. $0.38$ in women and $0.54$ vs. $-0.01$ in men), and recovers segment centers of mass within 1.1 mm. Because it needs only an MHR fit, FASCIA can be driven from images, video, or any system that outputs MHR. This opens the door to fitting individualized calibrated musculoskeletal digital twins to video motion data.
papers.intro:
Markerless motion capture measures clinical kinematics from multiview and monocular video (Kanko et al., 2021; Uhlrich et al., 2023; Cotton et al., 2023; Cimorelli et al., 2024; Peiffer et al., 2026; Cotton et al., 2026), yet computing accurate joint moments, muscle forces, and tissue-level biomarkers requires knowing how mass and tissue are distributed beneath the skin. Standard musculoskeletal pipelines (Delp et al., 2007; Werling et al., 2023) scale generic template models by segment length and initialize segment masses and inertias from template defaults—often derived from male cohorts—or regression tables built on small historical samples (de Leva, 1996; Dumas et al., 2007), whereas subject-specific inertias capture true body-composition variability and alter inverse-dynamics joint moments (Akhundov et al., 2022; Gambietz et al., 2026). With rapid advances in mesh-based human recovery from images and video, learning from medical imaging where internal tissues lie relative to a body mesh opens a direct path to more accurate biomechanical analysis grounded in modern computer vision.

A growing body of work predicts internal anatomy from the outer surface. Parametric hulls such as SMPL (Loper et al., 2015) enclose total volume, and OSSO (Keller et al., 2022), SKEL (Keller et al., 2023), and BOSS (Shetty et al., 2023) place discrete bones and organs inside the skin. HIT (Keller et al., 2024), the closest prior work, classifies points inside an SMPL mesh from whole-body magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) into bone, subcutaneous fat, lean tissue merged with visceral fat, or empty space, but compresses predicted tissue volumes toward the cohort mean rather than capturing individual variability. In addition, the HIT MRI dataset provides only five coarse tissue masks without raw scans for relabeling. Alternatively, public computed tomography (CT) datasets (Jimenez-del-Toro et al., 2016; Gutschmayer et al., 2025; Fischer, 2023; Hinge et al., 2026) processed with automated segmentation methods (Wasserthal et al., 2023; Shiyam Sundar et al., 2022; McKay et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2026) can resolve labels for individual bones, muscles, and organs. Leveraging these datasets, however, introduces a key supervision challenge because individual scans frequently provide only partial coverage of the body and each automated segmenter labels only its own subset of structures.

We introduce FASCIA (Functional Anatomical Structures and Composition via Implicit Atlas), anchored to the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) (Ferguson et al., 2025) (Figure 1), which supplies joint angles θ\theta, body shape β\beta, and bone scales ss, from which we form a compact shape-and-scale code zz. In canonical rest space, FASCIA deforms a 290-structure population template onto each person through a smooth, invertible 3D warp ψα\psi_{\alpha}. This warp morphs bone and soft-tissue geometry while keeping thin curved bones such as ribs, scapulae, and clavicles in one piece where a pointwise neural field fragments them. Because people with the same exterior still differ internally, a body-dependent Gaussian prior predicts both the mean warp and variability around it for spatial and volumetric uncertainty. Extending MHR’s skinning into the 3D interior forms a forward posing map Φ\Phi that pushes canonical points into posed CT and MRI scans to supervise training against the extracted tissue labels.

A deformable anatomical template and body-dependent Gaussian warp prior conditioned on MHR shape and scale that predict individualized, posed anatomy with calibrated voxel probabilities and sample-based spatial and volumetric uncertainties. 2. A forward volumetric posing map and partial-label objective trained jointly across five heterogeneously labeled CT and MRI datasets without unposing scans, paired with closed-form mass calibration for personalized body-segment inertial parameters (BSIPs). 3. papers.title: High-rate accumulation of ${8.9\times10^9}$ positrons using a linac-driven buffer-gas trap combined with a SiC remoderator
papers.abstract: We report the accumulation of $(8.9 \pm 0.9)\times10^9$ positrons in less than 35 minutes in a Penning--Malmberg trap connected to the GBAR electron-linac-based positron source. To our knowledge, this exceeds the largest previously reported trapped-positron population by more than a factor of two and was achieved at an 18-fold higher average accumulation rate of $4.5\times10^6$~e$^+$/s. The accumulated positron clouds are intended for the creation of dense positronium targets to produce keV-antihydrogen beams by charge exchange with antiprotons delivered by the CERN AD/ELENA facility. The system combines a low-energy electron linac, a modified Surko-type buffer-gas trap enhanced by a silicon carbide remoderator, and a high-field Penning--Malmberg trap operated as a positron accumulator. Time-resolved annihilation measurements provide insight into the capture and cooling dynamics, while comparisons of CO$_2$ and SF$_6$ show that the trapping signal reaches saturation at lower gas pressures with SF$_6$. Measurements show that the SiC-remoderator-based trapping scheme more than doubles the trapping efficiency, contributing to a more than threefold increase in the positron accumulation rate compared with the original configuration.

GBAR has successfully demonstrated the production of H¯\mathrm{\overline{H}} through the first of these reactions [1]. Producing H¯+\mathrm{\overline{H}}^{+}through these two reactions requires a high positronium density and therefore far more positrons than can practically be supplied by conventional 22Na sources. To overcome this limitation, the GBAR collaboration has developed a high-flux positron source based on a low-energy (9 MeV) electron linear accelerator [7]. In the first version of the installation, the positrons produced by the source were moderated, cooled in a Surko-type buffer-gas trap, and subsequently accumulated in a Penning–Malmberg trap at a rate of 1.3×1061.3\times 10^{6} e+/s, reaching 1.4 billion in 18 minutes [6]. The apparatus described in the present work is an improved version of the GBAR positron beamline.

The principal improvement over the system described in Ref. [6] is a modified buffer-gas-trap configuration incorporating a silicon carbide (SiC) remoderator. This scheme was first demonstrated by us in the GBAR positron beamline in 2021 [19, 5] and has been used in the production setup since 2023. A similar approach was subsequently reported by Michishio et al. [21]. In the new scheme the conventional nitrogen-gas-based capture stage is replaced by implantation following remoderation in a single-crystal silicon-carbide (SiC) wafer. This modification [18], together with the optimization of the transfer of particles to the high-field trap, increased the accumulation rate by a factor of approximately 3.5, from (1.3±0.2)×106(1.3\pm 0.2)\times 10^{6} e+/s to (4.5±0.5)×106(4.5\pm 0.5)\times 10^{6} e+/s. papers.title: TriSegAgent: Context-Efficient 3D Annotation with MLLMs via Tri-Planes
papers.abstract: Interactive segmentation models turn a few clicks into a segmentation prediction across domains, so annotators only decide where the prediction still needs correction. Annotation thus becomes a loop of inspecting the prediction and clicking again. Each step of this loop is a visual judgment, which suits general-purpose multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents. In this work, we focus on letting these agents run this loop on 3D volumes. However, the MLLM in such an agent takes only 2D images as input, so the agent must observe the 3D volume in 2D. Since the loop calls the MLLM many times, this observation must be token-compact enough to keep every call cheap, yet informative enough to show error regions in the 3D prediction. We meet both needs with tri-planes, the three orthogonal planes that cross at one point in the volume. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that tri-planes are context-efficient yet keep sufficient detail to show error regions in the 3D prediction. Building on tri-planes, we introduce TriSegAgent, an MLLM agent that refines the 3D prediction iteratively. Within the agent, the MLLM only judges the prediction on tri-planes, while a visual harness turns each judgment into a 3D action in code. To make the loop reliable, the harness places each click at an exact voxel in the volume and checks whether to accept the 3D prediction. To evaluate the agent, we build a diverse benchmark of 690 regions of interest (ROIs) from 35 public medical datasets across three imaging modalities. With frontier MLLMs, TriSegAgent reaches an overall Dice about 10 points above the strongest baseline, and its lead is even larger on targets below 3 cm. With flash-level MLLMs, it outperforms a recent 3D segmentation agent built on a frontier MLLM.

papers.intro:
Interactive segmentation tools, which turn a few clicks or boxes into a segmentation prediction, have been widely used for annotation across domains, from natural images [99, 54] and microscopy [9] to 3D medical volumes [75, 47, 24]. Since these tools draw most of the prediction, annotators only decide where it still needs correction [77]. Annotation thus becomes a loop of inspecting the prediction and clicking again [82]. On a 3D volume (, middle-top), guided by prior knowledge of where the target lies, an expert browses orthogonal planes of the volume, places clicks on one plane, lets the model segment, and inspects the result in different planes until the prediction is satisfactory [75, 47]. Each decision in this loop needs only a local judgment with a clear criterion: whether the prediction covers the target in the current view. This perception–decision loop maps naturally to a multimodal large language model (MLLM) agent that looks at an image, acts through tools, and judges the outcome [118, 43]. The planes displayed are the agent’s observations; the clicks are its tool calls; and the prediction overlaid on the image is the feedback for its next decision. This work therefore focuses on enabling general-purpose MLLM agents to annotate 3D volumes through such an interactive loop. Given a volume and a text goal, the agent works with an interactive segmentation model over many steps and then returns a 3D prediction ().

Running this loop on 3D volumes, however, exposes a gap between the data and the agent: the data are 3D voxel grids, whereas general-purpose MLLM agents take only 2D images as input. In 2D, one image with the prediction overlaid makes each decision fully observable at little token cost [127, 68]. Existing methods bridge this gap in three ways, none of which suits a long agent loop. The first trains a native 3D model [11, 111] at a high cost. Since 3D training data are limited, such a model transfers poorly to unseen settings. The second feeds a general-purpose MLLM the whole volume as a sequence of slices, like the frames of a video [13, 23, 37]. Each call then carries hundreds of images, although the current decision needs only a few of them. Such long inputs make the token cost explode over the many calls of the loop and lower the accuracy of each call [57, 42, 104]. The third shows only a few slices or projections at a time [106, 19], which keeps each call affordable but leaves the agent blind to error regions elsewhere. The latter two ways expose a fundamental dilemma between a limited context budget and spatial observability, and the key challenge is to design an observation that is token-compact yet informative enough to show error regions in the 3D prediction.

We address this challenge with synchronized tri-planes, three orthogonal planes that cross at one point (Fig. 2c). Inspired by how engineering drawings [46], medical image viewers [120, 31], and connectomics tools [18] display or show 3D data, we make tri-planes the observation of the agent, since they are extremely context efficient yet keep sufficient detail. To show the 3D context around the crossing point in the same detail, a slice stack needs every slice, whereas tri-planes need only three images: for a 5123512^{3} volume, Qwen2.5-VL [13] uses about 1k tokens for one set of tri-planes, two orders of magnitude fewer than the 166k of the full slice stack. Every MLLM call is therefore cheap, and the whole annotation loop remains affordable. Tri-planes also keep sufficient detail: with the pixels of only three images, they cut the volume along all three axes, so an error region that slips between sparse parallel slices is still likely to cross one of the planes. We prove that this advantage holds in the worst case, so a few sets of tri-planes are likely to show the error regions in a 3D prediction.

To make the loop reliable, we design mechanisms around two key aspects: where to click and whether to accept the prediction. First, MLLMs judge images well but are less reliable at giving exact pixel positions [91, 116, 60], so a click that the MLLM places itself can land a few pixels off, on the wrong side of the prediction boundary. We therefore let the MLLM only mark the error and pick one of a few candidate points that the harness computes in code, so every click lands on an exact voxel on the correct side of the boundary. Second, the tri-planes show only the area around their center, so a 3D prediction can look correct in the current view but still miss a distant part of the target. The agent therefore accepts a prediction only after it also passes in several other views spread across the target, and otherwise corrects the errors that these views show. We call this check multi-view verification: each correction needs only a local view, while the decision to accept considers the whole prediction. Under idealized assumptions, we prove that the chance of accepting a wrong prediction stays below a limit that falls geometrically with the number of views per check.

papers.title: One Policy, Many Bodies: Cooperative Human-Object Interaction with Heterogeneous Teams
papers.abstract: Physics-based human-object interaction (HOI) has enabled multiple characters to cooperatively transport objects, but existing cooperative controllers largely assume homogeneous embodiments and predefined interaction tasks. We ask whether a single physics-based policy can enable cooperation across diverse embodiments, team compositions, and interaction skills. We present MorphHOI, a decentralised framework built on a key insight: effective heterogeneous cooperation requires a unified representation across embodiments while accounting for differences in their physical capabilities. To realise this insight, we introduce a canonical body interface that unifies observation and action spaces, together with an embodiment-conditioned transformer that adapts cooperative decisions to the physical capabilities of each agent and its teammates. To extend cooperation to new interaction skills, we reuse the learned cooperative policy through task-specific tokens and lightweight adaptation, preserving its original capabilities. Our framework achieves success rates of up to 96.7\% on seen embodiments, 95.6\% on unseen embodiments, and 91.4\% on novel payloads. Furthermore, the learned cooperation extends to diverse interaction skills with high success rates, including box carrying, transport on stairs, and waypoint following, while preserving previously acquired cooperative capabilities.

papers.intro:
Cooperative human-object interaction (HOI) requires multiple agents to coordinate their actions towards shared goals while adapting to one another’s physical capabilities. In practice, participants often differ in body proportions, joint configurations, and strengths, making such coordination particularly challenging. For instance, carrying a large object together requires partners to agree on where to grasp, when to lift, and how to move while sharing the load. Physics-based HOI [43, 45] has progressed from individual manipulation skills [19, 59, 62, 40] to cooperative transport [16, 34]. However, existing cooperative controllers largely assume homogeneous teams, limiting their ability to coordinate agents with diverse embodiments. Moreover, extending learned cooperative behaviours to new interaction skills often requires updating the shared policy, potentially compromising previously acquired capabilities [29]. These limitations raise a central question: can a single policy enable physically plausible cooperation across heterogeneous embodiments and team compositions while remaining extensible to new interaction skills?

In practice, participants often differ in body proportions, joint configurations, and strengths, making such coordination particularly challenging. For instance, carrying a large object together requires partners to agree on where to grasp, when to lift, and how to move while sharing the load. However, existing cooperative controllers largely assume homogeneous teams, limiting their ability to coordinate agents with diverse embodiments. Moreover, extending learned cooperative behaviours to new interaction skills often requires updating the shared policy, potentially compromising previously acquired capabilities [29]. These limitations raise a central question: can a single policy enable physically plausible cooperation across heterogeneous embodiments and team compositions while remaining extensible to new interaction skills?

Answering this question poses two closely related challenges. First, cooperative control must generalise across embodiments and team compositions. Characters with different skeletons have incompatible observation and action spaces [31, 17], making it difficult to share a policy. More importantly, effective cooperation requires understanding both one’s own capabilities and those of one’s partners: characters of different heights and strengths must coordinate where to grasp, how high to lift, and how to move. This becomes harder as teams grow and diversify [5]. Second, cooperative skills should be unified and extensible across interaction tasks. Following routes, handling objects of different shapes, and traversing uneven terrain share fundamental cooperative behaviours but require different task-specific interactions. Training separate controllers limits the reuse of learned cooperation [62, 40]. A unified policy should therefore retain these shared capabilities while flexibly adapting to new interaction requirements.

A canonical body interface unifies observations through the links of a shared skeleton and maps canonical joint targets to each character’s own hinges, enabling one policy to control bodies with different skeletons and degrees of freedom (DoFs). papers.title: Neutron Spin Resonance as Probe of Triplet Pair Density Waves in CeCoIn$_5$
papers.abstract: Spin resonance modes are among the most characteristic collective excitations of unconventional superconductors, yet their microscopic origin remains unresolved. Although commonly interpreted as purely magnetic excitations, this picture does not explain the rich magnetic field evolution of these modes observed in heavy-fermion superconductors. Here we combine inelastic neutron scattering and symmetry analysis to investigate the evolution of the spin resonance modes in the heavy-fermion superconductor CeCoIn$_5$ under an in-plane magnetic field. At high fields, approaching the upper critical field of the superconductor, we discover a third resonance mode with relatively high intensity. We demonstrate that the resonance branches observed experimentally can be interpreted as collective modes of the superconducting condensate involving transitions to excited superconducting states. This framework provides a unified interpretation of the field-induced splitting of the resonance, the newly observed mode at high fields, the relative neutron scattering intensities of each mode, and provides the first direct evidence that a spin resonance mode can be associated with a singlet-triplet excitation of a superconductor.

papers.title: New applications for optimal adaptivity
papers.abstract: We introduce an explicit time-stepping scheme for ODEs, together with a residual-based a posteriori error estimator. Using this estimator, we show a new approach to proving optimality and linear reduction of adaptive algorithms for time-dependent problems that works in $H^1(0, t_{\rm end})$ and $W^{1,\infty}(0,t_{\rm end})$ norms, does not require quasi-orthogonality, and poses no restrictions on the marking parameter $\theta$. The key idea is to use the Lipschitz continuity of the semi-discretized operator to obtain a stronger form of estimator reduction. Numerical experiments illustrate the benefits of this explicit scheme coupled with adaptive refinement over uniform time stepping for classical evolution problems, regularized dynamical approximation, and neural ODEs.

papers.intro:
This work establishes a class of model problems and corresponding adaptive methods that showcase the following contributions: • Optimal adaptive convergence rates without the use of quasi-orthogonality as a theoretical tool. Even the first optimality proofs in [22, 5, 1] use orthogonality in the form of the Pythagorean identity. For increasingly involved model problems, several extensions of this orthogonality have been established under the name of quasi-orthogonality, e.g., [23, 3, 4] for non-conforming elements and [14, 13] for non-symmetric and indefinite problems. However, all versions of this quasi-orthogonality are technically involved and pose severe restrictions on the problem class, particularly in terms of nonlinearities. The use of explicit time stepping together with the Lipschitz continuity of the problem allows us to remove any form of quasi-orthogonality from the proof and thus also to remove the restrictions on the nonlinearity for p=1p=1. • Optimal convergence rates in W1,∞W^{1,\infty} with maximum marking. Except for convergence results in the L2L^{2}-norm for an H1H^{1}-problem in [7], all optimality proofs work in the natural norm of the problem. Moreover, optimality proofs for adaptive algorithms have predominantly relied on Dörfler marking [11], with exceptions including instance optimality for a modified maximum strategy [9] and the recent proof of rate optimality for standard maximum marking for the Poisson problem [19]. The simplified optimality analysis that comes with the removal of quasi-orthogonality has the added benefit that it also works in the W1,∞W^{1,\infty}-norm. It turns out that maximum marking is the natural candidate for this norm and hence many of the well-known arguments from the energy norm case transfer almost verbatim. • Provable optimality of the adaptive algorithm without restrictions on the marking parameter 0<θ<10<\theta<1. The classical proof strategy for optimal convergence requires choosing the marking parameter θ\theta in Dörfler marking sufficiently small [2]. Essentially, this means that the adaptive refinement must force aggressive local refinement to be optimal. This seems to be largely a theoretical issue of the proof as almost no practical examples are known where this behavior can be seen. The work [8] even shows that the theoretical framework in [2] is not strong enough to prove optimality without restrictions on the marking parameter. Recently, the work [10] was able to lift the restriction on the marking parameter for the Poisson problem. The key new tool in the present work is a strengthened version of estimator reduction (see [2] for an overview on this proof technique), which also removes the smallness restrictions on the marking parameter, both in the Dörfler marking and in the maximum marking. The tradeoff is the need for a fine initial mesh. • Application to neural ODEs and dynamical parametric approximation. Neural ODEs replace the classical layer structure of feed-forward neural networks with an ODE that has to be solved for training and inference of the network. The authors of the seminal paper [6] already noticed that adaptive time stepping is necessary to solve the sometimes unstable equations. Our explicit adaptive schemes are versatile enough to be applied in this setting and provide a clear advantage over standard uniform training of neural ODEs. A further application is regularized dynamical parametric approximation [15, 20], where the solution of an evolution equation is approximated by a nonlinear parametrization u⁡(t)=Φ⁡(q⁡(t))u(t)=\Phi(q(t)) with time-dependent parameters q⁡(t)q(t). For example, Φ\Phi may represent a neural network whose weights and biases evolve in time. We extend our adaptive framework to this setting and provide numerical experiments with a neural-network parametrization of a transport problem to illustrate the benefits of adaptive time stepping.

Provable optimality of the adaptive algorithm without restrictions on the marking parameter 0<θ<10<\theta<1.

Provable optimality of the adaptive algorithm without restrictions on the marking parameter 0<θ<10<\theta<1.

The classical proof strategy for optimal convergence requires choosing the marking parameter θ\theta in Dörfler marking sufficiently small [2]. Essentially, this means that the adaptive refinement must force aggressive local refinement to be optimal. This seems to be largely a theoretical issue of the proof as almost no practical examples are known where this behavior can be seen. The work [8] even shows that the theoretical framework in [2] is not strong enough to prove optimality without restrictions on the marking parameter. Recently, the work [10] was able to lift the restriction on the marking parameter for the Poisson problem. The key new tool in the present work is a strengthened version of estimator reduction (see [2] for an overview on this proof technique), which also removes the smallness restrictions on the marking parameter, both in the Dörfler marking and in the maximum marking. The tradeoff is the need for a fine initial mesh.

Application to neural ODEs and dynamical parametric approximation.

Application to neural ODEs and dynamical parametric approximation.

Neural ODEs replace the classical layer structure of feed-forward neural networks with an ODE that has to be solved for training and inference of the network. The authors of the seminal paper [6] already noticed that adaptive time stepping is necessary to solve the sometimes unstable equations. Our explicit adaptive schemes are versatile enough to be applied in this setting and provide a clear advantage over standard uniform training of neural ODEs. A further application is regularized dynamical parametric approximation [15, 20], where the solution of an evolution equation is approximated by a nonlinear parametrization u⁡(t)=Φ⁡(q⁡(t))u(t)=\Phi(q(t)) with time-dependent parameters q⁡(t)q(t). For example, Φ\Phi may represent a neural network whose weights and biases evolve in time. We extend our adaptive framework to this setting and provide numerical experiments with a neural-network parametrization of a transport problem to illustrate the benefits of adaptive time stepping.

papers.title: De Novo Generation of Odorant Molecules with Targeted Olfactory Receptor Activation Patterns
papers.abstract: Odor perception arises from a combinatorial code in which each molecule activates a specific subset of olfactory receptors (ORs), and the resulting activation pattern determines the perceived smell. We present a framework for de novo generation of molecules predicted to match target multi-receptor activation profiles. We first construct a panoramic binding matrix over 20 ORs, then cluster it to discover representative activation patterns, and finally formulate a structured selectivity loss, combining pairwise ranking, distribution matching, and complexity constraints, to steer a molecular generator via reinforcement learning. Across nine target profiles of varying complexity, our method achieves high predicted selectivity within 18000 oracle calls and provides the largest gains on profiles that are rare under the prior, especially broad-spectrum and sparse-activator targets.

A molecule that strongly activates a single target receptor may simultaneously activate unintended receptors, producing an entirely different odor percept than intended.

papers.title: BEND: Spectral Bregman Losses for Multi-Image Unlearning in Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion models memorize training images and reproduce them almost verbatim when prompted, creating copyright and privacy liabilities. Data unlearning erases the influence of specific training samples from a trained model without retraining, and is two-sided: it must forget the targets while preserving generation quality on everything else. Prior methods use the squared-L2 diffusion loss, at most with a hand-set frequency mask; however, it is known that every Bregman divergence is a mathematically valid choice and the squared-L2 is only the simplest example. BEND is the first to search this family: it fits a spectral Bregman divergence to the unlearning task through a bilevel loop, so the loss itself is shaped to forget thoroughly while protecting quality. It also redirects a memorized image to the mean of its retain images, where ReTrack, the state of the art, redirects it to a single near-copy. On Stable Diffusion, a single BEND model erases all 48 verifiably memorized benchmark images at once. It forgets at least as much as per-target, sequential, and jointly trained ReTrack (SSCD 0.084 versus 0.094-0.120), at the quality of the model before unlearning (CLIP-IQA 0.81 versus 0.64-0.69). BEND also outperforms the state of the art on CelebA-HQ in all three measures of the benchmark, and matches or exceeds it on MNIST and CIFAR-10.

papers.intro:
Diffusion models for image generation are trained by scraping enormous image datasets. They not only learn the underlying distribution, they also memorize individual training images and reproduce them almost verbatim when prompted [6, 35]. This creates a liability when such an image is copyrighted or shows a recognizable private face, since data-protection regulation increasingly grants the right to have such content removed: for example, regulators have ordered the deletion of residents’ faces from a scraped database (Clearview AI, under the GDPR [9]) and even of models trained on users’ photos (Everalbum, by the U.S. FTC [37]). Retraining from scratch to honor each removal request is prohibitively expensive. Data unlearning instead edits an already-trained model to erase the influence of specific samples with limited additional compute. The task is inherently two-sided: the model must forget the target samples while leaving its generation quality on everything else intact.

papers.title: Connected but Late: Sample Age of Commercial BLE Wearables under Wi-Fi Coexistence for Real-Time Clinical Applications
papers.abstract: Wearable sensors are increasingly being used in real-time clinical applications, such as rehabilitation robots and live therapy monitoring. As Healthcare 5.0 moves towards personalized therapies, their use will continue growing, potentially compromising communication reliability. Most wearables transmit over Bluetooth Low Energy, sharing 2.4 GHz with institutional Wi-Fi. Previous coexistence studies have focused on whether data arrive, rather than when. We measured sample age for a commercial electrocardiogram strap, from acquisition through the gateway to storage in our platform MEDWEAR, in an anechoic chamber and a hospital rehabilitation gym, and we compared it with illustrative clinical deadlines. Without load, the strap's own framing was the largest source of delay, making samples on average 280 ms and up to 550 ms old before transmission. Wi-Fi load had no measurable effect while adaptive frequency hopping could avoid the loaded channel. In a stress test, which forced the link onto the loaded channel, the link became the dominant source of delay, adding up to 11 s. The link stayed connected, but a median of 29% of samples and up to 98% (worst case) were older than 1 s on arrival at the gateway. The gym behaved mostly like the quiet chamber, but during one traffic burst, while hopping was restricted, up to 4.6% of samples were older than 1 s. These results show that a connected link can deliver late data. Therefore, sensors intended for real-time clinical applications should be profiled in situ and monitored based on sample age rather than connection status alone.
papers.intro:
Wearable health technologies are shaping healthcare by enabling continuous monitoring beyond clinical settings, and are becoming key to personalized and preventive care [1, 2, 3]. Industry 5.0 pairs humans with machines [4], and in Healthcare 5.0, these devices are not passive loggers but nodes in a wireless body area network (WBAN) that feed systems acting on what they measure [5]. Rehabilitation robotics is the clearest instance, where biosignals must reach a controller within a bounded latency for the loop to close [6].

Most commercial wearables stream over Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), which divides the 2.4 GHz band into 40 channels of 2 MHz, three for advertising and 37 for data [7, Vol. 6, Part A, Sec. 2, and Part B, Sec. 1.4.1]. Because BLE and Wi-Fi share this unlicensed band, BLE copes with interference through adaptive frequency hopping (AFH), hopping only over the data channels that the central classifies as “good” [7, Vol. 6, Part B, Sec. 4.5.8]. In hospitals, Wi-Fi concentrates on channels 1, 6, and 11 [8, 9], which leaves only 5 of the 37 data channels entirely outside their nominal 20 MHz bands, and 9 outside their 16.25 MHz occupied bands. AFH protects a link only if the central classifies channels correctly, which can fail under interference [10].

To handle this risk, U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidance calls for coexistence testing [11], for which the FDA recognizes ANSI C63.27 [12], with AAMI TIR69 [13] for risk management. papers.title: Learning the Next Best Move with Visual Diffusion Models
papers.abstract:
In this paper, we show that visual diffusion models can learn to predict the next best move (NBM) in tasks requiring sequential reasoning and lookahead, without explicitly exploring future steps or exhaustive searching at inference. Previous work demonstrated that these models can generate complete solutions to geometric and reasoning problems. Here, we show that simple fine-tuning on visual state--NBM pairs enables a pretrained model to select actions whose value depends on consequences several steps ahead. Each move is predicted directly in image space from the current state, without an explicit symbolic representation or search procedure. Repeated NBM predictions then construct a solution one decision at a time.
  We demonstrate this capability on chess puzzles and tile-based pathfinding, and show that it extends to Connect Four, Go and billiards. In chess, the model predicts legal moves and finds the best move far more often than by recalling similar training positions, including piece sacrifices whose benefit emerges only through later tactical continuations. In pathfinding, it constructs shortest paths on uniform-cost maps and cost-optimal routes across terrain tiles with different traversal costs, choosing longer routes when they are cheaper overall. These costs are learned implicitly from examples, without numerical cost supervision. These results show that direct visual move prediction can support globally informed decisions and successful sequential problem solving.

papers.intro:
“I see only one move ahead, but it is always the correct one.” — attributed to José Raúl Capablanca

“I see only one move ahead, but it is always the correct one.” — attributed to José Raúl Capablanca

Visual generative models have demonstrated a surprising ability to solve hard problems by generating their solutions as images. Beyond synthesizing realistic appearance, visual diffusion models can produce geometric configurations, complete puzzles, and construct paths that satisfy complex constraints [7, 22, 8, 5]. These findings suggest that visual generation can support forms of reasoning traditionally addressed by specialized algorithms. In this work, we investigate whether visual diffusion models can also learn to predict the next best move (NBM): choosing an action that advances a task toward its solution, without searching over future states. It’s worth mentioning that our goal is not to develop a task-specific solver (e.g., a competitive chess player), but to demonstrate and analyze an intriguing capability of visual diffusion models. We use chess, pathfinding, and other tasks as testbeds to investigate and better understand this capability.

papers.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. The framework goes beyond final accuracy in two ways. First, we evaluate exploration behavior by quantifying the extent to which agents exhibit space-filling or corner-seeking patterns in the experimental design space. Second, we decompose the reasoning process into four interpretable steps: belief update, hypothesis discrimination, discriminative experiment design, and predictive reasoning under interventions, each scored separately on reasoning traces. Across ten LLM agents, we find that stronger agents outperform both adaptive (Bayesian optimization) and non-adaptive (Latin hypercube) baselines and exhibit exploration patterns inconsistent with naive heuristics. Decomposing reasoning reveals that the stronger agents score consistently well across all four steps, whereas weaker agents often succeed at belief update and hypothesis discrimination but are less reliable at translating them into actionable designs and sharp contrastive predictions. Independent expert annotations support predictive reasoning under our stated validation criteria, while evidence for discriminative experiment design is positive but less consistent. The results suggest a gap between recognizing plausible hypotheses and translating them into contrastive predictions, with more tentative evidence for a corresponding experiment-design bottleneck. The benchmark website is available at https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/.
papers.intro:
Identifying physical and chemical systems from time-series observations is a fundamental problem in scientific discovery. This class of problems arises in multiple scientific domains where competing dynamical models must be discriminated through adaptive experimentation. Examples include kinetic mechanism identification in chemistry (Blackmond, 2005; Burés, 2016), adaptive Hamiltonian learning in quantum systems (Wang et al., 2017; Wiebe et al., 2014), gene regulatory network inference under perturbation experiments in systems biology (Gardner et al., 2003; Bonneau et al., 2006). Researchers typically refine beliefs over candidate models through a sequence of experiments designed to distinguish among them. Here, we study adaptive experiment planning in a controlled closed-world setting with fixed, known candidate mechanisms. This setting allows us to evaluate adaptive experiment planning and diagnose the reasoning processes that support it. Figure 1 summarizes the interactive benchmark and its diagnostic evaluation framework.

papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Vocabulary Expansion via Cross-Lingual Embedding Alignment
papers.abstract: Continual pretraining with vocabulary expansion is often used to make large language models (LLMs) more effective and efficient at handling new languages. However, when LLMs are extended to many languages simultaneously, the number of model parameters increases significantly. In addition, the newly added tokens do not receive the same number of training steps as the tokens in the original vocabulary, which sometimes causes vocabulary expansion to yield only limited performance improvements. We propose leveraging the semantic equivalence between words in the model's primary language and those in the extended vocabulary to transfer learned representations. In this paper, we introduce MATE, a parameter-efficient vocabulary expansion method that enables effective cross-lingual transfer with 8 times fewer additional parameters per token. MATE reduces the average tokenization compression ratio and delivers improvements on multiple benchmarks.

Prevailing solutions rely on vocabulary adaptation, such as replacing or expanding the tokenizer Li et al. (2025); Fujii et al. (2024); Cui et al. (2023). However, these methods have several drawbacks. First, they increase the number of model parameters. More importantly, standard vocabulary expansion, which initializes new target-language tokens as independent parameters, often fails to improve downstream performance Fujii et al. (2024). This may occur because the new tokens are undertrained, as they receive far fewer training steps than the original vocabulary. In addition, such practices can also lead to catastrophic forgetting Csaki et al. (2024).

To address these issues, we propose MATE (Multilingual Alignment for Token Embeddings), a parameter-efficient vocabulary expansion method grounded in cross-lingual embedding alignment. Rather than initializing the embedding of a target-language token tt independently, we identify its semantically equivalent token ee from the model’s primary language (the anchor language) that exists in the original vocabulary and align the embeddings of ee and tt by partially tying their parameters. In this way, the new token inherits rich pre-trained features while using fewer parameters, as illustrated in Figure 1. papers.title: Don't Test Where You Trained: Geographic Overlap Inflates End-to-End Driving Scores
papers.abstract: In NAVSIMv1, the standard benchmark for end-to-end driving, $89.6\%$ of the test scenes lie within 4m of a training scene. We show that this geographic overlap inflates the reported scores. We propose a geographically disjoint split of NAVSIMv1 and an evaluation that compares models trained on either split on the same scenes, which neither has seen in training. All sensor-based models we test, DiffusionDrive, Latent TransFuser, and DrivoR, lose 3.4 to 6.1 PDMS points on these scenes, mainly by leaving the road and coming close to other objects, against 1.5 points for a baseline without sensors. The loss concentrates where a training drive of the original split passed the same place. At all other places, models trained on the original split are no better than those trained on the geographic split. Models trained on the original split predict road geometry that no camera can see. The gap persists when the auxiliary map loss is removed, so the models memorize locations even without being supervised to. On nuScenes, the geographic split cuts SparseDrive's mapping accuracy by $59\%$ and also degrades its planning. Driving scores on logged scenes thus partly measure how well a model remembers the test locations. We release the split to evaluate generalization to new places.

papers.title: Magnetic Reconnection and High-Speed Jets Downstream of a Parallel Shock: Full Particle-in-cell Simulations
papers.abstract: Collisionless shocks are of fundamental interest in astrophysics and space physics as important sources of energetic particles. Downstream of quasi-parallel shocks, high-speed jets (HSJs) and magnetic reconnection have been frequently observed, while it remains unclear how their coupling shapes structured regions for particle energization. We use two-dimensional full particle-in-cell simulations to investigate HSJ generation, thin current sheet formation, and associated electron energization downstream of a parallel shock. We find that portions of foreshock ULF waves with enhanced dynamic pressure interact with a self-reforming shock front and are transmitted downstream, forming HSJs, while neighboring low pressure portions evolve into cavities. At the leading edge of the HSJs, the unique bent magnetic topology carried by the compressed ULF waves produces bow waves and locally squeezes out thin current sheets. These current sheets show reconnection signatures, including X-point topology, magnetic islands, enhanced $J\cdot E'$, and Alfvenic outflows along the local reconnecting direction. In the reconnection region associated with HSJs, the parallel electric field, betatron, and Fermi terms all contribute to adiabatic electron energization. The betatron term appears a visible signature near the X line, where the local magnetic structure is compressed by the HSJ. For the first time, we report a systematic mass-ratio dependence of HSJ morphology in full PIC simulations: lower mass ratios produce fragmented HSJs with shorter lifetimes, whereas larger mass ratios yield longer and wider HSJs with clearer bow waves as ion inertia increases.

papers.intro:
Collisionless shocks and their surrounding plasma environments contain rich wave activity, extending from the upstream all the way to the downstream (Lembège et al., 2004; Burgess et al., 2005). On localized scales, the shock front is often nonstationary, as predicted by kinetic simulations and confirmed by MMS observations, with common forms including shock front rippling (Winske and Quest, 1988; Johlander et al., 2016; Gingell et al., 2017), shock front self-reformation driven by reflected ions (Lembege and Dawson, 1987; Scholer et al., 2003; Su et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2020a), and reformation associated with the interaction of upstream ULF waves (Liu et al., 2021; Turner et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025) or whistler waves (Pantellini et al., 1992; Matsukiyo and Scholer, 2003; Matsukiyo and Matsumoto, 2024; Xu et al., 2026) with the shock surface. These nonstationary shock-front structures and their associated upstream and downstream transients can strongly modulate plasma compression, field-line distortion, and current-sheet formation near the shock.

Early observations of such structures in the terrestrial magnetosheath were reported by Němeček et al. (1998), and subsequent studies have reported HSJs in the Martian and Jovian magnetosheaths (Gunell et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024), possible analogues in the Hermean magnetosheath (Karlsson et al., 2016), and HSJs downstream of interplanetary shocks (Hietala et al., 2024). HSJs are typically characterized by dynamic pressure exceeding that of the ambient magnetosheath plasma (Archer and Horbury, 2013) and approaching upstream solar wind values (Plaschke et al., 2020), together with enhanced ion density and bulk velocity (Karlsson et al., 2018). These properties distinguish HSJs from embedded plasmoids, which show density enhancements and magnetic field variations without corresponding flow enhancement. Embedded paramagnetic plasmoids may originate from magnetic flux ropes generated by downstream magnetic reconnection (Preisser et al., 2020), whereas embedded diamagnetic plasmoids may instead have upstream solar wind origins (Karlsson et al., 2015). Extensive statistical studies have characterized the propagation, geometry, and lifetime evolution of HSJs (Karlsson et al., 2018; Raptis et al., 2020; LaMoury et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2026), as summarized in the recent review by Krämer et al. (2025). Spacecraft and ground-based observations further indicate that HSJs are geoeffective, perturbing the dayside magnetopause (Archer and Horbury, 2013; Hietala et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024), triggering ground magnetic ultra-low frequency waves (Wang et al., 2022), and producing localized ionospheric convection and auroral responses (Han et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Hietala et al., 2012).

Local hybrid (Hao et al., 2016) and global hybrid simulations have reproduced magnetosheath jets downstream of the quasi-parallel region of the terrestrial bow shock, in good agreement with observations (Chen et al., 2021; Suni et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2024a; Fatemi et al., 2024, e.g.,). In early two-dimensional hybrid simulations, compressional bow waves (BWs) are identified at the leading edge of some magnetosheath jets (Karimabadi et al., 2014). More recently, Ren et al. (2024b) simulate the fine structures of jet-driven BWs. Using THEMIS data, Liu et al. (2019) confirm HSJ-related BWs in Earth’s magnetosheath. (2023) show that HSJ generation is preferentially favored under a strictly parallel shock configuration, rather than under a general quasi-parallel geometry, especially for low plasma beta or high Alfvén Mach number. (2026) suggest that the nonlinear evolution of upstream foreshock ULF waves at a parallel shock can lead to dynamic pressure inhomogeneities along the shock surface, with high dynamic pressure regions linked to the formation of downstream HSJs.

papers.title: MQCODet: Modality Quality-Guided Collaborative Optimization for UAV-Based RGB-T Tiny Pedestrian Detection
papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based RGB-thermal (RGB-T) remote sensing provides complementary visual and thermal information for pedestrian perception under complex aerial observation conditions. However, detecting tiny pedestrians in UAV-based RGB-T imagery remains challenging due to cross-modal spatial heterogeneity, manifested as modality quality imbalance and spatial position misalignment. Existing RGB-T detectors primarily address these challenges at the feature fusion stage, without establishing an effective coupling between feature fusion and object localization, potentially resulting in suboptimal detection performance. To address this limitation, we introduce a Modality Quality-Guided Collaborative Optimization Detector (MQCODet), which extends modality quality from a fusion prior to a localization supervision cue. Specifically, we propose a Dynamic Calibration and Region-Aware Fusion (DCRF) module that progressively refines cross-modal spatial alignment and performs region-aware fusion to generate reliable multi-scale features and a scene-level modality quality prior. We further design an Efficient Contextual Interaction (ECI) encoder to enhance multi-scale feature interaction while preserving fine-grained spatial details. Moreover, we propose a Modality-Aware Adaptive (MAA) loss that incorporates the modality prior and object scale to adaptively balance spatial consistency and geometric similarity for localization supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MQCODet surpasses state-of-the-art methods on two UAV-based RGB-T tiny pedestrian detection benchmarks while achieving real-time inference on the edge platform.

papers.intro:
Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based RGB-T pedestrian detection has emerged as an important remote sensing task. UAV-based sensing systems provide flexible observation perspectives and broad spatial coverage, while RGB and thermal modalities offer complementary visual information. These advantages enable reliable pedestrian perception across diverse scenarios, including disaster rescue (Zhang et al., 2025a), traffic monitoring (Sun et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2025), and public surveillance (Du et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2018). Despite its practical value and potential for all-day perception, UAV-based RGB-T pedestrian detection remains challenging under complex imaging conditions, where modality quality exhibits substantial variation across scenes and spatial regions.

Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based RGB-T pedestrian detection has emerged as an important remote sensing task. UAV-based sensing systems provide flexible observation perspectives and broad spatial coverage, while RGB and thermal modalities offer complementary visual information. These advantages enable reliable pedestrian perception across diverse scenarios, including disaster rescue (Zhang et al., 2025a), traffic monitoring (Sun et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2025), and public surveillance (Du et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2018). Despite its practical value and potential for all-day perception, UAV-based RGB-T pedestrian detection remains challenging under complex imaging conditions, where modality quality exhibits substantial variation across scenes and spatial regions.

These variations stem from the distinct motion patterns of UAV platforms (Ma et al., 2026) and the different imaging mechanisms of RGB and thermal sensors (Hwang et al., 2015), resulting in pronounced cross-modal spatial heterogeneity that hinders reliable tiny pedestrian detection. Specifically, this heterogeneity mainly exhibits two aspects: modality quality imbalance and spatial position misalignment. Modality quality imbalance refers to the spatial heterogeneity of modality quality. For example, the visible modality degrades in low-light regions, whereas the thermal modality becomes unreliable in areas with high background radiation (see Fig. 1(a)). Such spatially varying modality quality complicates cross-modal feature fusion, as unreliable responses may impair object representations. Furthermore, inherent viewpoint differences between RGB and thermal sensors lead to spatial misalignment of the same object across the paired images, which is particularly detrimental to tiny pedestrians with limited spatial details and high sensitivity to slight spatial displacement (see Fig. 1(b)). Consequently, effectively mitigating cross-modal spatial heterogeneity is essential for UAV-based RGB-T tiny pedestrian detection under complex aerial conditions.

Existing RGB-T detection methods have explored different strategies to mitigate cross-modal spatial heterogeneity. Illumination-aware fusion methods (Zhang et al., 2023c; Hu et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025a) exploit environmental conditions to adaptively adjust the contributions of RGB and thermal modalities during fusion, improving robustness to global or local illumination changes. However, illumination cues alone cannot capture cross-modal spatial correspondence, potentially resulting in suboptimal fusion under spatial position misalignment. Alignment-aware fusion paradigms (Yuan and Wei, 2024; Guo et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2025a) establish cross-modal spatial correspondence before or during feature interaction, mitigating the adverse effects of spatial position misalignment. Nevertheless, these paradigms focus on spatial correspondence without explicitly modeling spatially varying modality reliability, potentially limiting adaptive modality fusion. Recently, some works (Zhang et al., 2023b; Zhang et al., 2025b) have explored quality-aware fusion strategies that incorporate regional modality quality to guide spatially adaptive fusion, enabling dynamic weighting of modality contributions. However, these methods primarily use modality quality to guide feature fusion, without propagating this reliability information to subsequent localization. This separation between quality-aware feature construction and quality-agnostic localization is particularly problematic for UAV-based RGB-T tiny pedestrian detection, where localization is sensitive to local modality reliability.

papers.title: Circular von Neumann-Jordan Constants in Complex Banach Spaces
papers.abstract: Replacing \(y\) by \(ty\) does not refine the classical von Neumann--Jordan constant; we instead average over unimodular phases before optimization to define upper, lower, and balanced circular constants for complex Banach spaces. The upper and lower constants are the squared norm and squared minimum modulus of a Fourier synthesis operator, linking them to optimal two-term Steinhaus type and cotype constants. We compare them with Clarkson's constant and characterize complex Hilbert spaces by the upper constant being one.Root-of-unity averages provide finite-phase approximations with explicit dimension-free errors. We compute exact one-sided values on \(L_p\)-spaces and Schatten classes, the upper constant on \(\ell_1^n\), and all three constants on \(\ell_\infty^n\), \(c_0\), \(\ell_\infty\), and \(C(K)\). We also obtain quantitative comparisons with complex convexity and smoothness moduli. Complex interpolation improves the dimension-free upper bound for finite-dimensional \(\ell_p\)-spaces, \(2<p<\infty\). A James constant estimate yields the sharp uniform-nonsquareness threshold \(1+2/\pi\) and a sufficient condition for the fixed point property of nonexpansive mappings.

papers.title: QASparse: Query-Adaptive Sparse Attention with Tailored Budgets and Tokens
papers.abstract: Long-sequence inference in large language models is constrained by the high cost of prefilling, where dense attention scales quadratically with context length. Exploiting similarity across attention heads offers a way to reduce redundant computation. Prior approaches in this direction have relied on localized query observations to determine head-level computation reuse or budget allocation. However, inter-head similarity does not imply uniform query requirements, leaving adaptation to varying budget needs and selection preferences across query regions a key challenge. We introduce QASparse, a Query-Adaptive Sparse attention mechanism with hardware-efficient execution. QASparse preserves the efficiency of shared cross-head importance estimation while adapting computational budgets and token selections to query requirements, and it executes these dynamic sparse decisions through dedicated kernels. Its query adaptivity stems from two complementary innovations: Local Budget Regression models local variations in computational demand along query positions to estimate budgets for different query regions and attention heads; Boundary Voting lets queries within each head vote over candidates near the selection cutoff using actual query/key scores, refining the retained set while preserving the initial selection size. To reduce the execution overhead of dynamic budgets, we further design length-specialized selection kernels that efficiently support query-adaptive sparse patterns across context lengths. Together, these designs efficiently combine shared estimation with local decisions while adapting both how much attention is computed and which interactions are retained. Experimental results demonstrate improved benchmark scores and faster prefill attention computation compared with existing sparse attention baselines.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) are applied to tasks such as long-document understanding and repository-level code processing, motivating efficient long-sequence inference (Liu et al., 2025; Huo et al., 2026). However, as input sequences grow longer, dense attention in the prefill stage performs QK computation for all causally visible tokens, incurring quadratic computational cost in sequence length and potentially becoming a major bottleneck in long-context prefilling (Zhao et al., 2026a; Fu, 2024). Efficient dense-attention implementations improve execution efficiency through tiling, fusion, and parallelization (Dao, 2024; You et al., 2026), while retaining QK computation that grows quadratically with input length. To reduce this cost, sparse attention performs QK computation only for tokens deemed important, omitting the remaining QK computation (Lai et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026; Jones et al., 2026; Jo et al., 2026; Song et al., 2026). Effective sparse acceleration therefore requires selecting important tokens with low overhead while largely preserving dense-attention capabilities.

To reduce the importance-estimation overhead of constructing sparse indices, a class of methods compresses queries and keys along the sequence dimension and constructs sparse indices from correlations among the compressed representations (Lai et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026b). Although this approach reduces the number of representations involved in estimation, it may obscure fine-grained correlations and distort block-importance estimates. Another line of work exploits similarities across attention heads to reduce redundant computation by sharing attention scores or sparse patterns (Wang et al., 2026b; Agarwal et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2025). ProxyAttn (Wang et al., 2026b) analyzes the similarity among different attention heads and uses pooled representative heads to provide shared importance rankings, together with online head-level budget estimation for sparse index construction. However, relying on a single shared ranking and budgets derived from local Q observations cannot accommodate the varying budget demands across query positions or the head-specific token preferences of individual queries. Consequently, queries may receive excessive or insufficient budgets and fail to select the most relevant tokens, due to the lack of query adaptivity.

To this end, we propose QASparse, a Query-Adaptive Sparse attention mechanism with hardware-efficient execution, which adaptively allocates computational budgets and selects KV tokens for different query regions and attention heads. QASparse achieves this query adaptivity through two complementary mechanisms: (1) Local Budget Regression uses attention statistics from sampled queries to model local budget variation, estimating suitable budgets across query regions and attention heads; (2) Boundary Voting uses the predicted budget to locate the selection boundary, then computes QK scores for candidates near that boundary to finalize the retained set. Together, these mechanisms enable QASparse to assign more suitable computational budgets to different query regions while maintaining low selection overhead by restricting additional decisions to a small number of boundary candidates. Furthermore, to reduce the execution overhead of dynamic token-selection decisions, we design Length-Specialized Kernels with dedicated execution paths tailored to different context lengths, thereby efficiently supporting query-adaptive sparse patterns across sequence lengths.

We evaluate QASparse on Llama3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), MegaBeam-Mistral-7B-512k (Wu & Song, 2025), GLM-4-9B-Chat-1M (Team GLM et al., 2024), and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M (Yang et al., 2025), using RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024) and InfiniteBench (Zhang et al., 2024a) to assess performance across controlled context lengths and long-range dependencies in very long contexts, respectively. papers.title: Gossamer: A Utility-Driven Architecture for Constant-Budget KV Cache Compression in Reasoning LLMs
papers.abstract:
Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to complex reasoning tasks, yet their inference efficiency is fundamentally constrained by the rapid growth of the KV cache. As reasoning contexts extend to hundreds of thousands of tokens, the key-value (KV) cache becomes the dominant contributor to both memory footprint and bandwidth demand, tightly coupling computation with memory utilization and thereby limiting scalability. Existing compression methods, such as quantization and eviction, alleviate capacity pressure but remain purely algorithmic, often introducing additional passes and compute overhead that reduce system efficiency.
  This paper presents Gossamer, a KV cache compression architecture for reasoning LLMs that bridges the algorithm--system--hardware gap. Gossamer introduces a unified utility-based action framework that dynamically selects compression operations, quantization, merging, or eviction, under a constant KV cache budget. Through cross-domain co-design, we fuse cosine-similarity estimation directly into the attention computation, exploiting idle compute cycles to perform similarity evaluation without latency or bandwidth cost. We call this mechanism Free-Lunch Utilization. This enables real-time, fine-grained KV management with near-constant memory usage and negligible overhead. Under tight memory constraints, Gossamer sustains reasoning quality comparable to uncompressed inference while improving end-to-end throughput by up to 16.7$\times$ over uncompressed baselines, 5.5$\times$ and 4.9$\times$ over the quantization-based Oaken and Ecco, and 1.8$\times$ over the eviction-based R-KV.

Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) [33, 40, 21, 1] have emerged as powerful reasoning engines, enabling complex decision-making, planning, and multi-step generation across diverse domains. As model size and reasoning context length increase, the computational and memory requirements of inference grow rapidly [42, 28, 34, 17], posing serious challenges for deploying reasoning LLMs efficiently under limited hardware resources. Modern reasoning LLMs employ a key-value (KV) cache [41, 34, 43] to accelerate autoregressive decoding. The KV cache stores attention key and value tensors from previous steps, allowing the model to reuse them for subsequent token generation instead of recomputing all past activations. While this mechanism is essential for long-form reasoning, its linearly growing size creates a substantial memory footprint and introduces severe memory bandwidth bottlenecks.

Modern reasoning LLMs employ a key-value (KV) cache [41, 34, 43] to accelerate autoregressive decoding. The KV cache stores attention key and value tensors from previous steps, allowing the model to reuse them for subsequent token generation instead of recomputing all past activations. While this mechanism is essential for long-form reasoning, its linearly growing size creates a substantial memory footprint and introduces severe memory bandwidth bottlenecks.

From the memory perspective, the KV cache expansion directly increases storage demand and bandwidth pressure. The size of the KV cache grows linearly with the reasoning context and model dimension, quickly becoming the dominant contributor to runtime memory consumption [42]. For short contexts (e.g., 512 tokens), the KV cache accounts for less than 2% of total memory usage, but at long contexts (e.g., 128K tokens), it can occupy over 84% of available capacity [18]. This growth stresses on-device memory and amplifies memory traffic, as cached data must be repeatedly accessed during each decoding step. When the KV cache exceeds available capacity, systems often resort to offloading strategies [38, 54, 31] that migrate cache data across the memory hierarchy or to external storage, introducing additional data movement and latency.

From the computation perspective, a larger KV cache directly increases the arithmetic cost of attention, since each decoding step must process more KV entries. At the same time, limited memory reduces batching opportunities [25], leading to low compute utilization and degraded throughput. This tight computation and memory coupling fundamentally limits inference efficiency for reasoning workloads. Consequently, there is a critical need for architectural techniques that reduce the KV cache footprint while maintaining reasoning quality.
