A natural response to the growth of the KV cache is compression. Existing works [2, 29, 3, 52, 18, 26, 54, 6, 27, 51, 50, 4, 12, 46, 47, 14, 45, 19] explore several directions, including quantization, pruning, and eviction-based methods. These broadly fall into two categories. The first category is local in-place compression [6, 29, 11, 18, 37]. These methods compress the KV cache by a fixed ratio, such as quantizing from FP16 to 4-bit [29] or pruning a constant fraction of tokens [11]. Such techniques delay memory exhaustion but do not fundamentally solve the problem, as the KV cache still grows linearly with context length. For efficient inference, they rely only on local information and make per-token decisions without global context awareness.

For efficient inference, they rely only on local information and make per-token decisions without global context awareness.

The second category leverages global information from previous reasoning history to guide compression. In reasoning LLMs, many cached tokens are redundant across multi-turn reasoning steps [43]. Recent global-aware methods [27, 3, 2, 43, 44, 53] compare new KV entries with the existing KV cache to decide whether to retain or evict them, effectively bounding the KV cache within a constant budget, such as 512 entries. Global-aware compression requires computing similarities such as cosine distance across the entire cache [2], which is computationally expensive. Our measurements show that a single global compression step on a 512-entry cache can take up to twelve times the latency of one attention computation. To amortize this cost, these methods commonly introduce a secondary buffer and accumulate new tokens, for example, 128 at a time, before performing global updates. While this improves amortized efficiency, it sacrifices responsiveness and does not align with real-time inference pipelines, leading to suboptimal accuracy. As a result, current KV cache compression methods remain algorithmically driven but architecturally inefficient, leaving a clear gap between compression utility and hardware efficiency.

papers.title: Reset Dependence Is Embodied: Training Protocol Changes Which Morphologies Appear Optimal
papers.abstract: Robot co-design benchmarks rank bodies after training their controllers under a fixed episode protocol, but that protocol can change the ranking itself. Consequently, two studies can select different bodies from the same corpus even when they use the same task and evaluator. We study one part of that protocol, the reset rule, which ends a training episode when the robot's torso falls below a height threshold. We train proximal policy optimization (PPO) controllers for 100 DERL-evolved UNIMAL bodies with this threshold at 20% of each body's starting torso height (Standard), at 50% (Strict), or with no threshold (Reset-free), and score every controller with the same evaluator. The threshold changes which bodies look best: the rankings after Strict and Reset-free training correlate at only 0.21, against about 0.89 if seed noise were the only difference. Removing fall resets costs some bodies far more than others. Bodies evolved on flat ground lose 45% of their per-step reward relative to Standard training, and those evolved on variable terrain only 16%. Permutation tests over bodies support this difference, and on 24 bodies, flat-ground bodies gain the most from Strict over Reset-free training under both PPO and soft actor-critic (SAC). Choosing bodies by their worst reward across the three protocols costs little: in sample, they keep at least 91% of the reward of each protocol's best bodies, and over 80% averaged across held-out seeds. Co-design benchmarks should state their reset rule, test whether their rankings depend on it, and report bodies that stay strong across protocols. Project page: https://reset-dependence.github.io.

Consequently, two studies can select different bodies from the same corpus even when they use the same task and evaluator. Co-design methods search over bodies, and recent studies also vary the task, but each commits to a single recipe for training the controllers that score the bodies (Gupta et al., 2021b; Lu et al., 2025; Ai et al., 2025). Such training and evaluation protocols are known to shape the learned controller (Henderson et al., 2018; Pardo et al., 2018; Machado et al., 2018). We ask whether they also change which body appears optimal.

papers.title: PixelOne: From Options to Pixels in a Single Forward for GUI Grounding
papers.abstract: GUI grounding requires precise clicks at low latency. Recent models such as GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift predict coordinates in one forward pass using fixed global bins with local refinement. However, screenshot downsampling removes detail needed to locate small controls, while fixed bins cover larger pixel ranges at higher resolutions. We introduce PixelOne, which transfers spatial knowledge from a search teacher to a student that predicts clicks directly from screenshots at native resolution. The teacher uses VideoJEV's text-option scorer to select rows and columns and progressively zoom into candidate regions. The student inherits the teacher's parameters and matches its distributions over explored regions through spatial distillation alongside box supervision. At inference, the same decision head selects a visual token, and a lightweight pixel head predicts the click within it, all in one forward pass. A click-aligned loss encourages pixels inside the target box to score above those outside. Across four benchmarks, PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B achieves 83.8% mean accuracy, the highest among the evaluated single-forward grounders, with a mean latency of 0.43 s per target.

Spatial readouts predict clicks directly from scores over image regions or target masks [34, 32]. By contrast, fixed-slot methods such as GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift predict distributions over global coordinate bins at predefined token positions and refine the coordinates using neighboring-bin probabilities [31, 8]. Both approaches avoid autoregressive coordinate generation and ground targets in a single forward pass. However, these models downsample high-resolution screenshots, removing details needed to locate small controls, while their global bins cover large pixel ranges at higher resolutions. These limitations motivate a direct readout that preserves image detail and predicts clicks at pixel granularity. Native decision models provide a starting point through an interface for scoring candidate options [12, 9, 47, 7, 41]. VideoJEV uses this interface to select textual answers and temporal intervals [48]. Extending it to pixel localization requires spatial candidates tied to screenshot regions and a way to resolve a click within the selected region.

We introduce PixelOne, a teacher-student framework for accurate GUI grounding from full-resolution screenshots in a single forward pass. During training, a search teacher learns to localize targets by choosing rows and columns from textual spatial options. It progressively narrows the target location across full-image and zoomed views using box supervision (Figure 2). The student inherits the teacher’s network and query/key decision head. The teacher also provides distributions over the regions explored during search, which complement the student’s box supervision. This transfer is possible because the same head scores both forms of spatial evidence (Figure 3): textual options in the teacher and visual tokens in the student. At inference, the student applies the shared decision head to visual tokens from the full-resolution screenshot and selects the token most relevant to the instruction.

papers.title: Video Generalized Category Discovery
papers.abstract: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to categorize unlabeled data from both known and unknown classes using labeled data from only the known classes. While recent GCD methods have shown promise on static images, their performance degrades in videos due to temporal dynamics, larger intra-class variation, and the lack of temporal consistency in existing approaches. We introduce VideoGCD, a framework tailored for video action recognition under the GCD setting. Our method integrates (i) a partitioned Mixture-of-Experts module that encourages specialization for known and novel categories, (ii) a novel-class balancing loss to reduce bias toward known classes, and (iii) a temporal optimal transport loss that promotes consistent routing across frames. Experiments on three video benchmarks demonstrate that VideoGCD significantly improves performance over existing GCD methods, particularly on novel categories. Our findings highlight the importance of combining temporal modeling and expert specialization for video GCD.

papers.intro:
In recent years, deep learning has achieved remarkable success in various visual recognition tasks, such as classification [21, 29], segmentation [4, 45], and object detection [14, 35], by training models on large datasets with full supervision. However, this approach assumes a closed-world setting where the categories seen during training match those encountered at test time. In many real-world applications such as autonomous driving or video surveillance, this assumption rarely holds. New classes may appear during deployment, and manual annotation is often costly or impractical. Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) [34] addresses this challenge by leveraging a small labeled dataset of known classes together with a large unlabeled dataset containing both known and unknown classes. The goal is to correctly classify the known categories while discovering and grouping the unknown ones, enabling recognition systems that can adapt without full supervision.

The goal is to correctly classify the known categories while discovering and grouping the unknown ones, enabling recognition systems that can adapt without full supervision.

The GCD problem has been explored through contrastive representation learning [34, 26, 46, 7], clustering-based discovery [24, 34], prototypical parametric classification [39, 15, 1], and prompt learning [27, 47]. While these methods have shown strong performance on static image datasets, their extension to video remains underexplored. Videos introduce unique challenges such as temporal redundancy, stronger intra-class variation, motion blur, and background clutter, all of which amplify pseudo-label noise and make novel category discovery more difficult. Moreover, existing image-based GCD methods do not enforce temporal consistency across frames, which is crucial for coherent representation learning in videos [41]. Compounding these challenges, the GCD setting introduces an additional difficulty in videos: the strong supervision available for labeled known classes often dominates the learning process, causing the model to bias its representations toward known categories while under-utilizing unlabeled samples that may belong to novel classes. In addition, video data exhibits strong temporal redundancy, where frames belonging to the same action should ideally produce consistent representations. However, frame-level features may fluctuate due to background frames, motion blur, or noisy predictions, leading to unstable similarity relationships across time. Such instability can negatively affect clustering and category discovery in video models.

VideoGCD introduces a partitioned mixture-of-experts architecture that encourages balanced capacity allocation for both known and novel categories while maintaining a shared backbone representation. To stabilize expert utilization during training, we introduce a balancing objective and a novel-class balancing loss, denoted as ℒbal\mathcal{L}_{\text{bal}} and ℒncb\mathcal{L}_{\text{ncb}}, which encourage equitable expert activation and ensure that unlabeled samples receive sufficient learning signal. To further improve stability in video representations, we introduce a temporal consistency objective based on optimal transport, denoted as ℒtot\mathcal{L}_{\text{tot}}, which aligns routing distributions across consecutive frames and encourages temporally coherent expert assignments. Combined with the standard contrastive learning objective, these components form a unified framework that promotes temporally stable representations for video-based category discovery.

papers.title: Quantum walks and conformal mappings
papers.abstract: We study the most elementary discrete model of an electron moving along a line, known as Feynman checkers, quantum walk, or the six-vertex model with special complex weights, and provide a uniform asymptotic formula for the wave function in the whole xt-plane. In addition to the well-known appearance of the Airy function that describes the transition between the oscillating and exponentially decaying regimes, we observe a second transition governed by the gamma function when the electron speed approaches the speed of light. We prove two general theorems producing uniform asymptotic formulae involving the Airy and gamma functions, using conformal mappings associated with the underlying integral representations. They are applicable in several other situations as well.

papers.intro:
One of the main open problems in mathematics is a rigorous construction of quantum field theory. For instance, the case of 44-dimensional Yang–Mills theory with a mass gap is a Millennium Prize Problem. A standard approach is constructive field theory, which often constructs a continuum theory as a limit of discrete theories [14]. This involves two limits: the continuum limit, as the discretization step tends to zero, and the infinite-volume/large-time limit, as the system size/evolution time tends to infinity. In this work, we find uniform large-time asymptotic formulae for the most elementary discrete model of an electron moving along a line, known as Feynman checkers, quantum walks, or six-vertex model with special complex weights (Figs. 1 and 2). See an elementary introduction [31] and surveys [19, 20, 38, 41].

This model is a promising direction in the development of constructive field theory because it involves real time, whereas in most other theories, time is imaginary [35, 45]. However, computations in models with real time lead to oscillatory integrals rather than exponentially damped ones. For such integrals, estimates are obstructed by the sign problem of huge cancellation during integration. Getting asymptotic formulae that are uniform in the involved parameters (and therefore most useful) is even more challenging.

Well-developed tools for such estimates are stationary-phase, saddle-point, and steepest-descent methods [18]. Their natural limitation is the collision of critical points and/or singularities as parameters vary. The latter cases can still be analyzed using the semiclassical approximation, such as Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin (Liouville–Green) method [27]. Those methods provide the main term in the asymptotic formula (and even the whole asymptotic series, which need not converge). Collision of critical points typically leads to the Airy phenomenon, i.e., the Airy function in the main term [3, 4, 30]. Collision of a critical point with a singularity can lead to other special functions, in particular the gamma function [5, 7]. The latter case can be called the gamma phenomenon. Despite numerous illuminating examples and theories [26, 29, 30, 33], we are not aware of a single general theorem providing a nontrivial uniform bound on the approximation error throughout the entire parameter domain in these collision cases (before this work). Here, a nontrivial bound means that the error term is “uniformly asymptotically smaller” than a “typical” main term.

papers.title: Bayesian sequential decision-making for adaptive early warning of bridge failure risk
papers.abstract: As a critical functionality of structural health monitoring (SHM) systems, early warning of increased bridge failure risk is essential for structural safety. However, traditional methods treat early warning merely as passive detection against a fixed safety limit and neglect evolving uncertainties and the economic consequences of decisions, leading to delayed alarms that increase the failure risk and hinder reliable and rational decision-making. This study formulates the early warning of increased structural failure risk as a sequential decision-making problem and develops a Bayesian framework for its solution. The presented framework unifies a probabilistic state transition model, an observation prediction model, cost models for early warning decisions, and a threshold-based decision strategy into a closed loop encompassing update, prediction, optimization, and decision execution. The structural state is updated iteratively via Bayes' theorem upon the arrival of new monitoring data, ensuring each decision is conditioned on the latest information. Through pre-posterior analysis over predicted future observations, the warning threshold is optimized by minimizing the expected total cost, which explicitly balances structural failure risks against warning response costs. In this way, the warning paradigm is shifted from passive detection to proactive decision-making, with the warning threshold adaptively updated as uncertainties and costs evolve. The framework was verified via two bridge case studies covering typical scenarios that lead to increased structural failure risk, including steel truss member fracture and stay cable rupture. Results demonstrate that warning decisions can be triggered in a timely and effective manner before severe consequences occur.

papers.title: EmboEagle: An Efficient Agentic Embodied Framework for Long-horizon Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation demands reliable execution across interdependent stages, yet standalone World-Action Models (WAMs) suffer from compounding physical errors, while stateless Vision-Language Model (VLM) supervision incurs prohibitive chunkwise latency and lacks 3D spatial persistence. We present EmboEagle, a closed-loop agentic framework that unifies subtask-conditioned WAM control, latent-space adaptive supervision, and memory-guided geometric recovery. First, we adapt sequential WAMs via decoupled two-stage flow matching that preserves cross-stage visual history while calibrating truncated action supervision at subtask boundaries. Second, without an auxiliary vision encoder, we distill teacher intervention decisions into a lightweight routing gate driven solely by the WAM Action Expert's pre- and post-chunk latent transitions and subtask embeddings. Third, upon invocation, the VLM decouples diagnostic status from discrete routing actions and executes parameterized recovery primitives grounded in structured memory (initial references, active grasp bindings, and tool traces), followed by mandatory post-repair verification. Across RMBench and LIBERO-Mem, EmboEagle achieves 91.3\% and 90.6\% average success, surpassing the strongest baselines by 8.0 and 9.8 percentage points, while boosting real-world success over VoLoAgent under identical executor weights. Moreover, adaptive gating cuts VLM calls by 74.2\% versus chunkwise monitoring (91.3\% vs. 93.7\% success).

papers.intro:
Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires a robot to preserve task intent across changing object configurations and grasp states, deciding when a subtask completes, retaining spatial cues needed by subsequent stages, and correcting physical errors before they compound. World-Action Models (WAMs) establish a strong foundation for this execution layer by coupling visual dynamics prediction with continuous action generation. Recent advances extend this paradigm through history-conditioned control in Long-WAM (Huang et al., 2026) and episodic visual guidance in MaP-WAM (Zhao et al., 2026a). Nevertheless, turning a capable visuomotor executor into a reliable long-horizon agent raises a complementary control question: how should a system allocate high-level supervision and translate its decisions into physical corrections during an ongoing task?

VLM-based orchestration bridges learned policies with explicit planning, monitoring, and manipulation tools (Chen et al., 2026a; Gu et al., 2026b), yet the timing of this supervision imposes a sharp efficiency–responsiveness trade-off. As contrasted in Figure 1(a–b), open-loop execution lacks error recovery, whereas querying a VLM after every action chunk repeatedly returns routine continuation commands and incurs unnecessary overhead; conversely, lengthening a fixed checking interval delays the detection of subtask completions, auxiliary tool opportunities, and failed grasps. While progress-based and event-driven triggers mitigate parts of this cost (Gu et al., 2026b), existing triggers often rely on heuristic rules or auxiliary visual processing. We instead investigate whether a lightweight predictor can use the executor’s internal representations to anticipate a teacher’s intervention decisions, including stage advancement, proactive assistance, and failure recovery.

papers.title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning
papers.abstract: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.

Faced with a spatial question in an unfamiliar environment, people move, turn, and gather the views that the question requires, then stop once the evidence is sufficient. Perception in this sense is an active process, in which what to observe is chosen in service of the task [34, 18, 32]. When the random walk is restricted to the same recent views, the strongest models outperform it by 12-26 points. Most of this lead disappears once the walk may keep everything it has seen, because evidence found earlier but no longer in view is largely lost. papers.title: Totally odd clique immersions in graphs with bounded independence number
papers.abstract:
We prove that every $n$-vertex graph with at least one edge and independence number at most an integer $a\ge2$, where $n\ge a$, contains a totally odd strong immersion of \[
  K_{\left\lceil (n+a-1)/(2a-3/2) \right\rceil}, \] with every branch path of length at most $2a-1$. We also prove that every graph $G$ with independence number at most $a$ and no totally odd strong $K_t$-immersion with branch paths of length at most $2a-1$ satisfies \[
  \chi(G)\le\left\lfloor \frac{(2a-3/2)(t-1)-a+2}{2} \right\rfloor \] where $t\ge2$. These bounds reduce the leading denominator coefficient in the general order bound from $9/4$ to $2$ and the colouring coefficient for independence number two from $3/2$ to $5/4$.

papers.title: Unresolved binaries from Gaia XP to SPHEREx
papers.abstract: Unresolved companions alter the luminosity and spectra of a star, but a colour-magnitude diagram (CMD) reveals them only when the system is over-luminous, and a Gaia photocentre orbit constrains only a combination of the mass and flux ratios. We fit the absolute Gaia BP/RP (XP) and SPHEREx spectra (XPS) of about 71,000 low-mass stars in the Gaia Catalogue of Nearby Stars with the J-CaPS XPS emulator, which predicts single-star and coeval-binary spectra on an absolute flux scale. First, more than half of known binaries lie within the main-sequence (MS) band of the CMD, because the companion is faint or lifts a metal-poor primary onto the single-star ridge. XPS recovers 86 per cent of the binaries that a CMD cut finds and 44 per cent of those it misses. Second, a small photocentre motion can come from a faint companion or a luminous one of nearly equal mass. XPS distinguishes them and recovers the mass ratios of double-lined binaries. Among substellar candidates with radial-velocity follow-up, it ranks all 11 binaries above all 16 confirmed brown-dwarf or planet hosts. The public package spbin provides this check before follow-up. Third, where XPS detects no companion light, we place an upper limit on the light of an MS companion. Among Gaia DR3 astrometric orbits with clean spectral fits, 2841 require more companion mass than XPS allows for a single MS star. Within 200 pc, their companion masses cluster at those of typical white dwarfs, and nearly circular orbits support this interpretation. Of 24 companions that joint radial-velocity and astrometric orbits show to be faint, XPS recovers 22, compared with 14 selected by the absence of a colour excess. Applied to forthcoming Gaia DR4 orbital solutions, XPS can help distinguish luminous binaries from substellar companions and identify candidate compact companions whose dynamical masses exceed the limits allowed by their light.

An unresolved companion adds light, brightening the system relative to the primary alone in the colour–magnitude diagram (CMD; Li et al. 2025a). When its temperature differs from that of the primary, it changes the shape of the spectra, which biases the labels of a single-star fit (El-Badry et al. 2018a). The Gaia Apsis pipeline accounts for such composite spectra with coeval-binary models (Creevey et al. 2023; Fouesneau et al. 2023). Gaia measures the orbit of the photocentre about the centre of mass (Halbwachs et al. 2023; Gaia Collaboration et al. 2023). Light from the companion shifts the photocentre towards it, reducing the measured orbital amplitude for a pair of main-sequence (MS) stars. Radial velocities (RVs) and excess astrometric noise (Belokurov et al. 2020; Penoyre et al. 2020) detect a companion through its orbital motion, and imaging separates the two stars when they are far enough apart.

Large samples rarely measure the light of the companion itself. A star over-luminous in the CMD is counted as a binary, a photocentre orbit is converted into a companion mass, and an orbit too large for an MS companion is taken as evidence of a white dwarf, a neutron star or a black hole. Each of these inferences assumes how much light the companion contributes. When the assumption is wrong, the companion biases the inferred properties of the system: a single-star fit to the combined light biases the luminosity, mass, age and metallicity of the primary, and an orbit interpreted without the companion light biases its mass ratio. These biases carry over to the inferred frequency and mass-ratio distribution of companions, which link star formation to the present-day stellar population (Duchêne and Kraus 2013; Moe and Di Stefano 2017; Offner et al. 2023). The solar neighbourhood, where the multiplicity census is most complete (Duquennoy and Mayor 1991; Fischer and Marcy 1992; Raghavan et al. 2010; Janson et al. 2012; Tokovinin 2014; Ward-Duong et al. 2015; Winters et al. 2019), is also where the light of companions can be measured most directly.

Cluster members share a similar age and metallicity and form a narrow single-star sequence, on which the extra light of a companion stands out. Infrared photometry increases the sensitivity to cool companions, which contribute a larger fraction of the flux at longer wavelengths, and finds companions down to low mass ratios (Malhotra et al. 2026). In the field each signature alone is degenerate. Metallicity broadens the single-star sequence, and a metal-poor primary with a luminous companion can sit on it. A near-equal-mass pair moves the photocentre little, so the orbit of a luminous companion looks like that of a low-mass companion (Halbwachs et al. 2023; Bailer-Jones and Kreidberg 2026). The same degeneracy limits the search for compact companions in Gaia orbits. An orbit that needs more mass than a single MS companion with the observed light can supply points to a white dwarf, a neutron star or a black hole (Shahaf et al. 2023; Shahaf et al. 2024; El-Badry et al. 2024), but deciding how much light the companion may add requires either a mass–luminosity relation or a measured colour. Both are misled by an unresolved pair of M dwarfs, which is fainter than a single star of the same total mass and so imitates a compact object.

Absolute spectra measure the combined light of the pair directly, without a resolved orbit or a measurable velocity separation. Their reach is set by the contrast between the two stars and by how well a composite can be told apart from the range of single-star spectra. Li et al. (2025a) showed the scale of this approach with Gaia BP/RP spectra (hereafter XP): comparing data-driven single-star and binary spectra on an absolute flux scale, they identified about 14 million binary candidates within 1 kpc, at mass ratios 0.5≤q≤10.5\leq q\leq 1. That range reflects two limits of optical data. At low mass ratios a cool companion adds little optical flux, and near equal mass the composite has the shape of a single star and stands out only by its doubled luminosity. The infrared addresses the first limit. When the companion is cooler than the primary, the flux ratio rises towards the infrared, and the molecular bands of a cool photosphere carry more information than a single infrared excess. SPHEREx provides all-sky spectra between 0.75 and 5μ​m\,\mu\mathrm{m} (Bock et al. 2026), which reach the stars of the Gaia Catalogue of Nearby Stars (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2021, GCNS;) and the cool, low-mass companions that add little light to XP.

papers.title: Dynamical calibration of a metallicity-dependent stellar mass--luminosity relation from Gaia wide binaries
papers.abstract: The mass of a main-sequence star is usually estimated from its luminosity through a mass--luminosity relation (MLR). This relation depends on metallicity, and its empirical calibration relies on few stars with measured masses. We calibrate the MLR of single main-sequence stars in the Gaia $G$ band as a function of metallicity with $10\,559$ wide binaries. The projected relative speed and separation of a wide binary constrain its total mass statistically. We describe the stellar mass as a monotone function of absolute magnitude and metallicity and fit this function to all pairs. The metallicities come from Gaia low-resolution (XP) spectra and are calibrated by requiring that both stars of a pair have the same metallicity. The likelihood includes the measurement noise, the selection of the sample and pairs with an undetected close companion. The data constrain the MLR over $3.7\lesssim M_{\mathrm{G}} \lesssim11.8$\,mag and $-0.5\lesssim\ \mathrm{[M/H]} \lesssim0.4$, with a median statistical uncertainty of $2.5\%$ in mass. Tests of the model assumptions indicate an additional systematic uncertainty of up to $5\%$. At solar metallicity the MLR agrees with the PARSEC models to within $5\%$. At the faint end, the MIST, BaSTI, Dartmouth and BHAC15 models predict masses 8 to $22\%$ below our MLR. Published masses from orbits, eclipsing binaries and asteroseismology lie within about $10\%$ of our MLR for $M_{\mathrm{G}}<10.5$ mag. For fainter stars they are about $17\%$ lower. The origin of the difference at the faint end is not yet understood. Because a shift of $0.1$ dex in metallicity changes the mass by up to $5\%$, MLRs should be compared on a common metallicity scale.

Stars less massive than the Sun dominate the stellar content of the Galaxy. M dwarfs account for about three quarters of the stars within 10 pc (Henry et al., 2018). Stars below 1​M⊙1\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot} also contain a large fraction of the stellar mass of the Galactic disc (Chabrier, 2001). The initial mass function inferred from star counts, and every quantity derived from it, such as the mass-to-light ratio of stellar populations, the contribution of dwarfs to the dynamical mass budget of the disc and the claimed variations of the initial mass function with environment and metallicity, depends directly on how masses are assigned to dwarfs. Low-mass stars are also the most common hosts of small planets (Dressing and Charbonneau, 2015), so the masses of these stars also set the inferred properties of their planets. Stellar mass is nevertheless rarely measured directly, and for most stars it is inferred from the luminosity through a mass–luminosity relation (MLR).

Wide binaries allow a calibration with far larger samples. Their orbital periods of 10410^{4} to 10610^{6} yr, at typical separations of 10310^{3} to 10410^{4} au, are too long for an orbit to be followed. A wide binary is observed at a single snapshot, which gives the projected separation ss and the projected relative speed vv of the two components. Kepler’s law nevertheless connects these two quantities to the total mass mtotm_{\rm tot}, because v​sv\sqrt{s} is proportional to mtot\sqrt{m_{\rm tot}}. For a population of pairs its distribution can be computed, so that the masses can be inferred statistically.

papers.title: Stars on the ascending helium giant branch: II. A metal-rich luminous helium sdO gone astray
papers.abstract: Hot subdwarf stars with masses above $\sim0.7~M_\odot$ expand after core helium exhaustion and ascend the helium giant branch before entering the white dwarf (WD) cooling track. In the first paper of this series, we identified the luminous helium-rich hot subdwarf HE~1518-0948 (HE~1518) as the product of a massive He-WD+He-WD merger in this evolutionary phase. Here we present a detailed analysis of a second luminous helium-rich O-type hot subdwarf (He-sdO), Gaia~DR3~5369742867090186624 (G5369). We derive an effective temperature of $55~000\pm2500$~K, a surface gravity of $\log g = 4.85\pm0.15$, and an upper limit on the hydrogen abundance of $\log (n_\mathrm{He}/n_\mathrm{H})>2.5$. The close similarity of its atmospheric parameters and its helium and carbon abundances to those of HE~1518 indicates that G5369 is also likely the product of a massive He-WD+He-WD merger. In contrast to HE~1518, G5369 is metal-rich, with an iron abundance of about twice solar. The metallicity-adjusted abundance pattern of G5369 for the elements C, N, O, and Ne is broadly consistent with the nucleosynthesis predictions of a composite He-WD merger model and is similar to the observed abundances of R~CrB stars, extreme helium stars, and the O(He) star KPD~0005+5106. The kinematics of G5369 place it near the boundary between the thick disk and halo. Its orbit, with a pericentre of $\sim$3.5 kpc, together with its high metallicity suggests that G5369 most likely originated in the inner Galaxy.

papers.intro:
Hot subdwarf stars of spectral type B (sdB) and O (sdO) populate the region below the main sequence (MS) and above the white dwarf (WD) cooling branch in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram (HRD; for reviews, see Heber (2016); Heber (2024)). Most of them are core or helium shell burning stars with no or very thin hydrogen envelopes. Most hot subdwarfs are proposed to form either through the stripping of a low-mass star (≲1.8​M⊙\lesssim 1.8\penalty\ M_{\odot}) at the tip of the red giant branch through interaction with a companion (Han et al., 2002; Han et al., 2003) or through the merger of two helium WDs (Webbink, 1984; Zhang and Jeffery, 2012a). The stripping channel produces an sdB with a canonical mass of about 0.47​M⊙0.47\penalty\ M_{\odot}, determined by the core mass required to initiate the helium flash. In contrast, He-WD+He-WD mergers produce a broader mass distribution (Dawson et al., 2026; Latour et al., 2026) and can reach ∼0.9​M⊙\sim 0.9\penalty\ M_{\odot}, the maximum mass expected from the merger of two helium WDs.

In contrast, He-WD+He-WD mergers produce a broader mass distribution (Dawson et al., 2026; Latour et al., 2026) and can reach ∼0.9​M⊙\sim 0.9\penalty\ M_{\odot}, the maximum mass expected from the merger of two helium WDs.

The stripping of intermediate-mass stars at the end of core hydrogen burning also contributes to the hot subdwarf population. Because helium ignites non-degenerately, the resulting hot subdwarf mass increases with the initial mass of the progenitor (Han et al., 2002; Arancibia-Rojas et al., 2024). Such systems can therefore produce objects that are both less and more massive than the canonical sdBs, but only a few dozen of higher-mass objects have been discovered despite being predicted in large numbers (Götberg et al., 2018). Furthermore, Dawson et al. (2026) and Latour et al. (2026) identified a population of hot subdwarfs that lies below the canonical (M=0.47M=0.47 M⊙M_{\odot}) extreme horizontal branch in the HRD, representing the low-mass end of the intermediate-mass stripping channel. Recently, Drout et al. (2023) discovered ultraviolet (UV)-bright objects below the MS in the Magellanic Clouds, and the analysis by Götberg et al. (2023) yielded parameters consistent with evolutionary tracks for masses above 1​M⊙1\penalty\ M_{\odot} for the stripped-star candidates. papers.title: Dawn of the Gaia Era: Revisiting Cold Jupiters Orbiting M Dwarfs with Astrometry+Doppler Data Joint Analysis
papers.abstract: We perform a joint analysis of ground-based radial velocities (RVs), Hipparcos Intermediate Astrometric Data, and two-epoch Gaia astrometry for known M dwarfs hosting cold Jupiters discovered through long-term spectroscopic monitoring. Among a sample of 25 planets in 19 systems, we derive robust absolute masses and orbital solutions for 13 planets in 11 systems with companion inclination uncertainties lower than 30 degrees. These include first mass measurements for five planets: GJ 328b, GJ 649b, GJ 849b and c, and GJ 9066c. We also reclassify one object, HIP 79431B, as a brown dwarf. We further compare the mass ratios of these 13 cold Jupiter systems with those of giant planets orbiting M stars characterized via transit, microlensing, and direct imaging. Without correcting for detection bias, we find that (1) there is likely a deficiency of high-mass-ratio hot Jupiters around M dwarfs compared with cold Jupiters, and (2) the local cold Jupiters orbiting M stars found by RV observations exhibit a similar mass ratio distribution as the counterparts in the Galactic bulge found by microlensing. Cold Jupiters orbiting stars with masses above $0.65~M_\odot$ tend to be more massive than those around M dwarfs. Our study establishes a sample of local cold Jupiters with precise mass determinations around M dwarfs, and reveal a tip of the iceberg in the upcoming Gaia DR4 and DR5.

papers.intro:
About two thousand giant planets have been detected to date [2, 34], yet only a small fraction of them orbit M dwarfs, even though these low-mass stars are the most abundant stellar population in the Milky Way [78, 70]. With mass ratios approaching those of brown dwarfs orbiting Sun-like stars and even some binary star systems, the formation mechanism of giant planets around M dwarfs remains under debate.

About two thousand giant planets have been detected to date [2, 34], yet only a small fraction of them orbit M dwarfs, even though these low-mass stars are the most abundant stellar population in the Milky Way [78, 70]. With mass ratios approaching those of brown dwarfs orbiting Sun-like stars and even some binary star systems, the formation mechanism of giant planets around M dwarfs remains under debate.

One of the leading planet formation theories, core accretion, postulates that the process begins with a solid core, which can then grow into a giant planet by rapidly accreting gas [129, 83, 111]. Several lines of observational evidence suggest that giant planets around M dwarfs likely form through this scenario. For example, [68] measured an occurrence rate of 0.27±0.09%0.27\pm 0.09\% for hot Jupiters orbiting early-type M dwarfs [26, 69, see also], roughly three times lower than that around Sun-like stars [125, 168, 13]. Within the core accretion framework, the lower surface density of M dwarf protoplanetary disks compared to those around Sun-like stars impedes the formation of a sufficiently massive core to initiate runaway gas accretion before the disk dissipates [94, 82, 89], which could account for the difference in occurrence rate. Moreover, formation of hot Jupiters is favored around metal-rich host stars, though the correlation seems less significant for cold Jupiters [101, 67, 110]. Stellar metallicity is thought to correlate with the amount of solid material in the protoplanetary disk for planet formation [137, 57, 142]. One would therefore naturally expect more giant planets around metal-rich stars if they formed through this bottom-up channel. Although core accretion is efficient beyond the snow line where dust is abundant [82], outer massive companions could excite the orbits of inner giant planets and drive them inward to compact orbits [114, 40]. Recent work from [66] found that the stellar multiplicity of M dwarfs hosting hot Jupiters is about six times higher than the fraction of field M dwarfs, indicating that high-eccentricity migration may play an important role in producing short-period transiting hot Jupiters around low-mass stars [65, 64, 87, 76, 88, 46, 60, e.g.,].

Nevertheless, a few Jovian-like planets orbiting very-low-mass stars with M∗≲0.2​M⊙M_{\ast}\lesssim 0.2~M_{\odot} remain challenging to explain via the core accretion route [109, 131, 27, e.g.,]. An alternative channel, gravitational instability [16, 18], is speculated to be responsible for forming such extreme-mass-ratio systems. In this scenario, a gravitationally unstable disk can condense and fragment into massive giant planets at a few AUs, a semi-major axis range to which the microlensing and RV methods are sensitive. While the majority of cold Jupiters orbiting M dwarfs have so far been discovered by microlensing [106, 72], degeneracies in orbital solutions are common, such as close/wide degeneracy [73], which causes considerable uncertainties in host-planet separations. Moreover, the microlensing technique provides projected separations of planetary systems instead of true semi-major axes in most cases [140, 139, 138, e.g.,]. As for the RV technique, a handful of wide-orbit large planets orbiting M dwarfs have also been found through blind surveys [30, 80, 131, e.g.,]. However, long-term monitoring is required to cover adequate orbital phases, making planet searches and identifications inefficient. Additionally, the sin⁡i\sin i degeneracy leaves the absolute mass of the RV-detected planets unknown, hence there is always a risk that some “planets” are sub-stellar or stellar companions [91, 163, e.g.,].

As a complement to the RV technique that traces the line-of-sight motion, the astrometric method measures the wobble of stars on the sky plane [38]. The six-dimensional kinematic information of astrometry allows full-orbit determination for the companion, enabling us to disentangle the orbital inclination and uniquely specify its true mass. With the upcoming Gaia DR4, thousands of wide-orbit giant planets orbiting low-mass M dwarfs are anticipated to be discovered [143, 124, 93], providing a golden sample for comparison with local transiting hot Jupiters as well as microlensed cold Jupiters in the Galactic Bulge to infer their formation history. Though the timeseries astrometry of Gaia DR4 is not available yet, joint analyses of RV and absolute astrometry data have already been widely applied in several works [20, 96, 51, 163, 3, 127, 132, e.g.,].

Section IV describes the details of the RV+Astrometry joint fit analysis, followed by the results for each system in Section V. We discuss our findings in Section VI before we conclude in Section VII.

papers.title: Real2Worlds2Real: Scaling Self-Improving Agentic Real2Sim2Real for Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Scaling robot manipulation learning remains challenging due to the high cost of collecting real-world interaction data. Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) offers a promising route by enabling policy learning in simulation grounded in real-world observations, yet scaling this paradigm across diverse tasks and physical interactions remains difficult. We introduce Real2Worlds2Real, a self-improving agentic framework that integrates scalable simulation-world construction with policy development. Given limited visual observations and task descriptions, its tool-orchestration harness constructs faithful digital twins and expands them into diverse, physically executable digital cousins. The agent adaptively selects tools and revisits construction decisions, using visual and execution feedback to refine geometry and physical behavior. Building on these worlds, the agent orchestrates policy development by coordinating data generation, policy learning, and refinement based on task requirements and simulation rollout feedback. Across both stages, the agent distills validated procedures into reusable skills that guide subsequent tasks. Experiments demonstrate improved world fidelity and successful real-world policy transfer, with performance gains from increasing world diversity and interaction-data volume. Skill reuse further improves world-building efficiency and long-horizon task success.

papers.intro:
Recent advances in robotic foundation models, including vision-language-action (VLA) policies [28, 3, 2] and world-action models (WAM) [4, 27, 57], have demonstrated the importance of large and diverse data for generalizable robot manipulation. Yet collecting such data on physical robots remains costly, requiring substantial human effort for teleoperation, supervision, and repeated scene setup and resets. These costs make it difficult to cover the breadth of manipulation tasks needed for generalization. Real2Sim2Real offers a promising way to overcome this bottleneck. By grounding simulation in limited real-world observations, this paradigm offers the potential to scale both the diversity of training environments and the volume of robot interaction data, supporting policies that transfer to the real world.

By grounding simulation in limited real-world observations, this paradigm offers the potential to scale both the diversity of training environments and the volume of robot interaction data, supporting policies that transfer to the real world.

Recent work has enabled the construction of visually realistic, interactive simulation environments from real observations [16, 48, 22, 20, 21], while automated scene generation and digital-cousin synthesis have expanded their diversity [11, 44, 5, 35]. However, scaling Real2Sim2Real requires more than generating additional scenes. Simulation worlds must faithfully reproduce task-relevant appearance and physical interactions while supporting diverse, physically meaningful variations that remain executable. Beyond world construction, effective robot learning also requires adapting data generation and policy refinement to different tasks, using failures observed in simulated rollouts to guide subsequent policy improvements. Together, these challenges motivate adaptive, feedback-driven approaches to both world building and policy development.

We introduce Real2Worlds2Real, a self-improving agentic Real2Sim2Real framework that transforms limited real-world observations into faithful digital twins and diverse, physically executable digital cousins for scalable robot policy development (Fig. 1). For simulation-world construction, a tool-orchestration harness enables a general-purpose agent to adaptively coordinate world building across diverse scenes and physical interactions. Guided by visual and execution feedback, the agent iteratively identifies and corrects errors in scene geometry and physical behavior. Successful correction procedures can be distilled into reusable skills, allowing experience from previous scenes to guide subsequent world building. Starting from RGB images or videos, the agent reconstructs a scene-level digital twin that faithfully captures the real-world appearance and spatial structure. It then creates a diverse family of digital cousins by introducing variations at both the object and scene levels, while ensuring that the resulting environments remain plausible and suitable for the intended manipulation tasks. Beyond rigid objects, our framework supports the generation and physics-based simulation of articulated and deformable objects, enabling realistic robot interactions across a broader range of manipulation scenarios. To further improve physical fidelity, when interaction recordings are available, the harness compares simulated rollouts with observed real-world motion, using their discrepancies to calibrate physical parameters. These capabilities enable high-fidelity simulation world building to scale across diverse scenes and physical interactions without scene-specific human intervention.

Rather than following a fixed training pipeline, the agent adaptively selects tools and learning strategies based on task requirements and available demonstrations. It can synthesize executable control programs through tool-assisted grasp and motion planning, train reinforcement learning policies with agent-designed rewards, or employ model predictive control for online planning. papers.title: Quantifying and calibrating precision gain from covariate adjustment in clinical trials with binary endpoints
papers.abstract: Covariate adjustment is widely used in randomized clinical trials to improve estimation and inference of treatment effects. For continuous endpoints, the reasoning is straightforward: prognostic baseline covariates explain outcome variability and thereby increase precision. For binary endpoints, however, the situation is more complex because conditional and marginal effects generally differ in nonlinear outcome models such as logistic regression. We develop a theoretical framework for quantifying the maximum attainable first-order precision gain from covariate adjustment when estimating marginal treatment effects for binary endpoints. We derive a closed-form identity showing that precision-gain potential is governed by an estimand- and allocation-specific combination of the treatment-specific risk functions. Building on this identity, we introduce marginal prognostic strength as a population-level measure of prognostic information and characterize when it determines precision-gain potential and when the two quantities decouple. Specifically, substantial prognostic information within both treatment arms need not translate into improved precision for the marginal treatment effect when covariates are predictive on the target effect scale. We further develop a calibration algorithm for methodological simulation studies that preserves prespecified conditional outcome structures and marginal risks while allowing data-generating mechanisms to be calibrated by marginal prognostic strength and evaluated in terms of estimand-specific precision-gain potential. Together, these results provide a theoretical and practical framework for understanding, quantifying, and calibrating potential precision gains from covariate adjustment for binary endpoints.
papers.intro:
Covariate adjustment is widely used to improve the precision of treatment-effect estimation in clinical trials. Improved precision leads to more reliable inference and may reduce the required trial size and duration, benefiting trial sponsors and society alike. Consequently, regulatory guidance explicitly encourages adjustment for prognostic baseline covariates (EMA, 2015; FDA, 2023). The underlying intuition is simple: If baseline covariates are prognostic, accounting for them should remove explainable outcome variation and thereby yield more precise estimates. Guidance from the US Food and Drug Administration, for instance, states that adjustment “will generally reduce the variability of estimation of treatment effects and thus lead to narrower confidence intervals and more powerful hypothesis testing” (FDA, 2023, p. 3). A substantial body of methodological and empirical literature supports this intuition (Benkeser et al., 2021; Kahan et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2008).

A substantial body of methodological and empirical literature supports this intuition (Benkeser et al., 2021; Kahan et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2008).

While covariate adjustment is well understood in the linear regression setting (Lin, 2013), its role is more delicate for binary endpoints. Standard models for binary data yield parameters that reflect conditional treatment effects. The treatment coefficient in a logistic regression model, for example, is a conditional log odds ratio. Although conditional effects are, in principle, most relevant from an individual-patient perspective, they depend on the specified outcome model and may be difficult to estimate consistently in a clinical trial. Marginal estimands, in contrast, quantify the population-average treatment effect and are also targeted by assumption-lean, unadjusted analyses. For these reasons, primary inference in confirmatory trials is typically directed at marginal rather than conditional effects (Van Lancker et al., 2024).

Whereas marginal and conditional estimands coincide in linear models without treatment-by-covariate interactions, this correspondence no longer holds in generalized linear models with nonlinear link functions, such as logistic regression (Daniel et al., 2021). In these approaches, regression or conditional-mean working models serve to construct estimators of marginal treatment effects. Despite the different setting, the guiding intuition remains the same as for linear models: As long as the baseline covariates are prognostic, adjusting for them should increase the efficiency of marginal treatment-effect estimators.

Related work has approached the question of precision gain from a different perspective. Li et al. (2023) considered prospective estimation of the efficiency gain from covariate adjustment in future clinical trials using external data. These authors defined efficiency parameters under a sharp null, where the treatment-arm-specific conditional outcome functions coincide, and used these to approximate efficiency under local alternatives. Our focus is complementary and particularly motivated by methodological simulation studies, where the data-generating mechanism is specified by design. This enables us to characterize first-order precision-gain potential directly under a given binary-outcome data-generating mechanism, allowing the arm-specific risk functions to differ and treatment effects to vary across covariate values. This distinction is important because arm-specific prognostic information may then combine differently across marginal estimands and need not translate directly into precision gain.

The purpose of this article is to characterize the mechanism that determines the precision gain from covariate adjustment for binary endpoints. We first derive an identity for the maximal first-order variance reduction attainable through adjustment for a given covariate set when the target estimand is a differentiable function of the treatment-specific marginal risks. This identity provides a closed-form expression for the precision-gain potential and shows how it depends jointly on the treatment-arm-specific outcome-covariate relationships, the treatment allocation ratio, and the target estimand. We then examine its relationship with marginal prognostic strength, a population-level measure of the information that baseline covariates provide about the outcome, and show why prognostic strength alone does not determine the potential precision gain. Building on these results, we develop an algorithm for methodological simulation studies that calibrates the data-generating mechanism to a specified level of marginal prognostic strength while preserving the arm-specific coefficient structure and marginal risks, and quantifies the resulting precision-gain potential for the marginal estimand and treatment allocation of interest. Finally, we illustrate the use of the algorithm in the design of a simulation study.

papers.title: Physically Informed Data-Driven Modeling of Low-Pressure Carburizing (LPC): A Self-Calibrating Boundary Condition for Carbon Flux
papers.abstract: This paper formulates an extended framework for a hybrid physically informed data-driven model of low-pressure carburizing (LPC), in which diffusive carbon transport in austenite is described by a physical equation, whereas the effective carbon flux across the gas-metal interface is treated as an unknown boundary forcing to be identified from experimental and process data. The basis for this formulation is that, in LPC, the most uncertain part of the model is not bulk diffusion but the transient surface kinetics of carbon uptake by the metal. In contrast to direct empirical relationships of the 'process regime-result' type, the proposed scheme uses machine learning as a closure operator for the boundary condition in the diffusion problem. This operator is calibrated using carbon concentration profiles, integral mass gain, surface concentration, effective case depth, and additional process measurements. Theoretically, the model is positioned as an operator-learning problem in a system constrained by a partial differential equation, physical flux constraints, inverse-problem regularization, and uncertainty quantification. The relationships between the proposed approach and physics-informed neural networks, operator learning, dynamic-system identification, boundary-operator learning, and boundary-control problems are considered. The mathematical formulation, calibration functional, identifiability conditions, preliminary tuning algorithm, and online adaptation scheme are formulated. The proposed approach is considered as a computational basis for developing interpretable digital support for LPC processes.

papers.title: Nilpotent tridiagonal matrices with entries in {-1,0,1}
papers.abstract: We determine all nilpotent tridiagonal matrices with entries in $\{-1,0,1\}$. The problem reduces to describing the set $\cN_n$ of pairs $(d,b)\in\{-1,0,1\}^n\times\{-1,1\}^{n-1}$ for which the tridiagonal matrices with diagonal $d$ and with products $b_k$ of opposite off-diagonal entries have characteristic polynomial $\lambda^n$. We show that $\cN_n$ is obtained from $\cN_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ by one of two explicit ``folding'' operations, according to the parity of $n$. As a consequence, $\cN_n$ is non-empty precisely when $n=1$ or $3\cdot2^j-1\le n\le2^{j+2}-1$ for some $j\ge0$, in which case it has $2^{\lfloor\log_2n\rfloor}$ elements. This yields a formula for the number of nilpotent $n\times n$ tridiagonal matrices with entries in $\{-1,0,1\}$, which begins $1,9,73,585,4809,39113$. The case $d=0$ is a conjecture of Corless, established in an earlier paper. The main new ingredient is a rigidity phenomenon: a pair as above, of size $n\ge2$, whose characteristic polynomial is congruent to $\lambda^n$ modulo $4$ is necessarily a fold of a smaller pair. It follows that such a pair is nilpotent as soon as its characteristic polynomial is congruent to $\lambda^n$ modulo $2^{1+\lfloor\log_2n\rfloor}$. Finally we show that the eigenvalue zero of an $m\times m$ matrix in Corless's skew-symmetric family has multiplicity at most $2^{v_2(m+1)}-1$, with equality attained. The classification, the rigidity statement, the cardinality of the sets $\cN_n$ and the criterion modulo $2^{1+\lfloor\log_2n\rfloor}$ have been formalised in Lean~4.

papers.title: Explainable Emotion and Mental Health Reasoning in Large Language Models Using Theories of Emotion
papers.abstract: Advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled a wide range of applications. However, their ability to simulate human-like behavior and reasoning remains unclear. While emotion detection is a better-established Natural Language Processing (NLP) task, existing approaches primarily focus on directly classifying text into predefined emotion classes, often overlooking the appraisal process that explains why an individual experiences a particular emotion in a given situation. In this work, we propose Psychology-based Chain-of-Thought (PsyCoT) reasoning, a theory-driven prompting strategy grounded in the Schachter-Singer and Cognitive Appraisal theories of emotion. We propose and evaluate PsyCoT for subjective NLP tasks, including emotion analysis, emotion intensity prediction, stress analysis, and depression severity identification. Our evaluation covers four levels of classification complexity: binary, multiclass, multi-label, and ordinal scaling, spanning 11 languages. We assess the performance of five state-of-the-art LLMs across these selected subjective NLP tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that PsyCoT prompt variants improve the standard chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting across the evaluated tasks. Across all evaluated tasks, PsyCoT yields F1 score gains ranging from 0.5% to 28.1%, depending on the model, task, and language configuration.

In parallel, prompt engineering techniques have become essential for maximizing LLMs’ capabilities [51, 61]. These developments position LLMs as promising tools for tackling complex NLP tasks.

In parallel, prompt engineering techniques have become essential for maximizing LLMs’ capabilities [51, 61]. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has shown strong performance gains in tasks requiring multi-step inference, particularly in mathematical, symbolic, and commonsense reasoning [63, 49]. These developments position LLMs as promising tools for tackling complex NLP tasks.

One such complex and subjective area of NLP is affective computing tasks [69]. The affective computing field has progressed beyond coarse-grained sentiment analysis (positive/negative) toward fine-grained emotion recognition [41], emotion intensity estimation [45], and mental health status assessment [54]. The current open-weight and closed-source LLM families, such as OpenAI’s GPT, Google’s Gemma and Gemini, Meta’s LLaMA, etc., have shown encouraging contextual learning (zero-shot and few-shot performance) on these subjective NLP tasks, suggesting that they internalize rich and affective knowledge during pretraining [58]. As a result, the research has increasingly explored prompt-based and instruction-tuned approaches for emotion analysis and mental health–related inferences [37].

As a result, the research has increasingly explored prompt-based and instruction-tuned approaches for emotion analysis and mental health–related inferences [37].

However, as LLMs are deployed in high-stakes affective applications, such as detecting depressive symptoms [62], psychological distress [53], or suicide risk [25], the emphasis shifts from classification accuracy alone to the explainability of the reasoning behind the decision. In this setting, it is insufficient for a model to label a text as sad, stressed, or anxious; it should also provide a rationale for these labels that is coherent, transparent, and psychologically meaningful. Reasoning that lacks grounding in human emotion processes risks being misleading, uninformative, or clinically unusable [15]. From a cognitive perspective, subjective language refers to the speaker’s or writer’s internal states, such as emotions, attitudes, beliefs, or intentions. Cognitive and psychological studies of language indicate that understanding subjectivity often requires a theory of mind (i.e., inferring the speaker’s intent or feelings) and empathy. For instance, sarcasm and irony contents are typical subjective uses of language: the literal content diverges from the intended meaning, and the listener must infer the speaker’s true attitude [58].

Cognitive and psychological studies of language indicate that understanding subjectivity often requires a theory of mind (i.e., inferring the speaker’s intent or feelings) and empathy. For instance, sarcasm and irony contents are typical subjective uses of language: the literal content diverges from the intended meaning, and the listener must infer the speaker’s true attitude [58].

To address the interpretability of subjective NLP tasks, most existing approaches rely on Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting [63], which encourages models to produce intermediate reasoning steps. While CoT is effective for mathematical and symbolic reasoning tasks governed by formal logic, it has a critical limitation when applied to psychology-oriented NLP tasks. This is because human emotion is not the result of linear logical deduction; rather, it emerges from complex interactions among situational stimuli, cognitive interpretation, and physiological mental states [55]. Consequently, the generic CoT principle of “think step-by-step” reasoning often yields explanations that are linguistically plausible but psychologically shallow. This raises a fundamental question: What does “think step-by-step” actually mean in the context of human emotion and mental health state analysis?. This is because emotion analysis is inherently subjective (varying across individuals, cultures, languages, and situations) and context-dependent [27]. Psychological research emphasizes that emotions are processes (not labels) shaped by appraisal, arousal, and interpretation [65]. The standard CoT prompting largely ignores this psychological grounding, treating affective inference as a generic reasoning problem. As a result, LLMs may simulate emotional outcomes without modeling the mechanisms that generate them.

Human cognitive processes have been studied in numerous psychological theories of emotion. Schachter–Singer Two-Factor Theory (2FT)[52] and Cognitive Appraisal Theory (CAT) are among the most common and well-known emotion theories [30]. The 2FT theory posits that emotion arises from the interaction between physiological arousal and cognitive labeling of that arousal. Conversely, CAT argues that emotions are elicited by an individual’s evaluation of events in relation to personal goals, beliefs, and well-being [30].

Schachter–Singer Two-Factor Theory (2FT)[52] and Cognitive Appraisal Theory (CAT) are among the most common and well-known emotion theories [30]. The 2FT theory posits that emotion arises from the interaction between physiological arousal and cognitive labeling of that arousal. Conversely, CAT argues that emotions are elicited by an individual’s evaluation of events in relation to personal goals, beliefs, and well-being [30].

Achieving meaningful explainability in affective computing requires that LLM reasoning be grounded in psychological theory rather than generic logical decomposition [18]. This shift moves from prompting LLMs to “think like logicians” toward prompting them to “process emotions like humans.” To this end, we propose a theory-driven prompting framework that operationalizes two established psychological theories of emotion into structured prompting schemas for affective computing NLP tasks: the Schachter–Singer Two-Factor Theory (2FT), which characterizes emotion as a combination of physiological arousal and cognitive labeling [52], and the Cognitive Appraisal Theory (CAT), which posits that emotions arise from individuals’ evaluations of events in relation to their goals and well-being [30].

This shift moves from prompting LLMs to “think like logicians” toward prompting them to “process emotions like humans.” To this end, we propose a theory-driven prompting framework that operationalizes two established psychological theories of emotion into structured prompting schemas for affective computing NLP tasks: the Schachter–Singer Two-Factor Theory (2FT), which characterizes emotion as a combination of physiological arousal and cognitive labeling [52], and the Cognitive Appraisal Theory (CAT), which posits that emotions arise from individuals’ evaluations of events in relation to their goals and well-being [30].

These theories suggest that understanding why an emotion occurs requires analyzing antecedent events, appraisal dimensions, and arousal-related components—elements that are not explicitly represented in standard CoT prompting. The proposed theory-based prompts guide LLMs to (1) identify situational antecedents, (2) perform cognitive appraisals, (3) infer physiological or arousal-related indicators, and (4) integrate these components into coherent inferences about emotion category, emotional intensity, and mental health status (e.g., stress and depression severity). This work tends to answer the following Research questions (RQs): • RQ1: Can LLMs mimic human psychological reasoning in assessing and explaining emotional and mental health states? • RQ2: How does psychologically grounded reasoning improve LLMs’ emotion understanding compared to chain-of-thought (COT) reasoning? • RQ3: How does the emotional intelligence of LLMs vary across different prompt variants, model architectures, parameter sizes, languages, and affective computing NLP tasks?

papers.title: Sharp integral Ricci pinching on manifolds with positive total scalar curvature
papers.abstract: Let $(M,g)$ be a closed connected Riemannian three-manifold with $\int_M R \mathrm{d}v>0$, and assume that $M$ is not diffeomorphic to a spherical space form. We prove the sharp integral Ricci pinching inequality $$\mathrm{vol}(g)\int_M |\mathrm{Ric}^{\circ}|^2 \mathrm{d}v \geq \frac{1}{6}\left(\int_M R \mathrm{d}v\right)^2.$$ Moreover, equality holds if and only if $(M,g)$ is locally isometric to $\mathbb{S}^2(a)\times\mathbb{R}$ for some $a>0$. By the same method, we prove $\mathrm{vol}(g)\int_M |\mathrm{Ric}^{\circ}|^2 \mathrm{d}v \geq \frac{1}{12}\left(\int_M R \mathrm{d}v\right)^2$ on closed four-manifolds with $\int_M R \mathrm{d}v>0$ that have a finite cover with positive first Betti number, and we provide a new proof of Gursky's inequality. We also show that the corresponding inequality fails in every dimension $n\geq 5$, and we give a metric on $\mathbb{S}^2\times\mathbb{S}^1$ that disproves a conjecture of Ge, Li and Lian.

papers.title: SYCLDB: A Cross-Vendor Heterogeneous Analytical DBMS
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of AI and analytical workloads has increased the need for fast, interactive analytical data processing. This, in turn, has led to a surge of interest in designing accelerated analytical database engines that can exploit modern GPUs to scale computation. While GPUs provide the massive data-parallelism required by modern analytics, the software landscape remains dominated by closed-source, vendor-locked programming models, like CUDA, limiting portability across multi-vendor GPUs. In this work, we present SYCLDB, an end-to-end analytical database engine built upon the SYCL open standard, designed to enable efficient, hardware-agnostic execution across a wide range of accelerators using a single codebase. By implementing core relational operators as modular SYCL kernels, integrating them with a SQL frontend based on Apache Calcite and Apache Thrift, and supporting Apache Arrow for efficient columnar ingestion, SYCLDB reduces dependence on vendor-specific GPU programming stacks by enabling a single SYCL codebase to execute analytical query pipelines across Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA GPUs.
papers.intro:
The growing popularity of AI and analytics in virtually all application domains has led to a rapid increase in the amount of data gathered by enterprises and scientific institutions alike, with the global datasphere being projected to reach 250ZB by the year 2025. Modern analytics and AI workloads are incredibly diverse and consist of a range of scalar, vector, and matrix computations. Thus, the traditional workhorse of the computing industry, the general-purpose CPU, cannot be optimized to meet the diverse requirements of such heterogeneous workloads. papers.title: X-BQSR: Holistic Acceleration of Base Quality Recalibration for Scalable Genomic Analysis
papers.abstract:
With the continued decline in sequencing costs, genomics-based precision medicine is gaining increasing importance. The Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) is the standard framework for converting raw genomic data into actionable variants, but one of its most expensive steps is base quality score recalibration (BQSR), which corrects systematic sequencing errors. Despite significant work on accelerating other parts of the variant calling pipeline, BQSR has not been systematically explored on GPUs.
  In this work, we analyze BQSR to identify computational and I/O bottlenecks and show that simply offloading key stages to an accelerator is insufficient to achieve overall gains. We then present X-BQSR, a holistic redesign of the entire BQSR pipeline, including I/O, compression, and kernel execution, to better leverage GPU parallelism. We implement X-BQSR using portable SYCL kernels for NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs, along with native CUDA and HIP backends for comparison, and we evaluate its performance against previous FPGA work. Our evaluation shows up to 141.7x acceleration compared to standard GATK and 8.7x acceleration compared to a proprietary GPU-accelerated solution.

As we move into the era of $100 sequencing, genomics-driven precision medicine efforts have become widespread in both research and clinical practice. Germline genomic analysis, or the task of studying mutations that are inherited and present in every cell, is of vital importance as it has several applications, from clinical diagnosis of rare diseases in humans, to population-genomics studies that map genetic diversity in other organisms. The gold standard computational pipeline used for germline genomic analysis is the GATK [13, 5, 1] germline variant calling pipeline shown in Figure 1.

It is well known that the GATK pipeline is computationally intensive. For instance, an evaluation by Intel [17] showed that the pipeline took 1.5 days to run the pipeline for a whole-genome sequencing dataset at 30×\times coverage on a 36-core CPU. This naturally makes the pipeline a key bottleneck in any genomic analysis that processes multiple such sequences, and hence, a key optimization target for hardware-accelerated solutions from both industry and academia. On the research front, several solutions have been proposed to accelerate the sequence alignment and variant discovery stages of the GATK pipeline shown in Figure 1 using CPU with highly optimized parallel processing and analysis tools [4], GPUs [16, 9, 12, 7, 10], FPGAs [11, 3], and other custom accelerators [2].

While the NVIDIA Parabricks library provides a high-performance commercial solution for BQSR acceleration [15], it is a closed-source binary. This opacity prevents the research community from inspecting its underlying strategies, and its CUDA-based nature lacks portability to multi-vendor accelerators, such as Intel Flex or AMD Instinct GPUs.

In this work, we bridge this gap by making several contributions. First, we present an in-depth analysis of BQSR to identify various computational and I/O bottlenecks in the CPU-based implementation and to identify GPU-offload targets for an accelerated redesign. Second, we present X-BQSR, a redesign of the core BQSR algorithms to unlock the massive SIMT parallelism of GPUs. In doing so, we not only develop optimized GPU kernels for performing the core computation but also perform a holistic redesign of all other aspects of BQSR including I/O, compression, memory management, and data transfers, to ensure that the improvement unlocked by GPU acceleration is not overshadowed by other hidden overheads. Third, we implement three variants of X-BQSR using CUDA, HIP, and SYCL. Our SYCL X-BQSR implementation is the first, portable, vendor-neutral, open-source implementation of BQSR that can run on multicore CPUs, integrated GPUs, and multi-vendor discrete GPUs using a single code base. Finally, we present a rigorous evaluation comparing X-BQSR with the original single-threaded GATK BQSR, Spark-enabled multi-threaded GATK BQSR, FPGA BQSR from Lo et al., and NVIDIA Parabricks BQSR. We plan to make our code fully open source together with the camera-ready version of our manuscript.
