papers.title: High-Resolution 3D Micro-CT Database of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) Coils for More Accurate Modelling, Technology Benchmarking, and Progress in Coil Design
papers.abstract: Accurate modelling of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) coils requires coil-specific geometric and electrical parameters. Yet detailed manufacturer models are rarely available, and internals may be widely available to companies in the field but not to researchers. The development of new coils should ideally build on all existing prior art. This work presents a technology benchmark and modelling-ready dataset for seventeen widely used commercial TMS coils across multiple manufacturers and geometries. High-resolution micro-CT (0.0495 mm resolution, material and density contrast) serves to reconstruct winding and casing structures and to extract parameters directly usable in numerical models, including loop dimensions, conductor cross-section, turn count, winding height, and winding-to-surface (casing) thickness. Complementary electrical measurements provide spectral impedance (series resistance and inductance) scans from 20 Hz to 200 kHz, together with dc resistance. In addition to baseline geometry and impedance, the study documents practical construction features relevant to safety and usability with detailed insights into their internal construction (e.g., cooling architectures and embedded sensing). The resulting benchmark dataset supports coil-specific electric-field simulations, reduces modelling uncertainty associated with generic assumptions (e.g., fixed coil-scalp spacing), and provides a quantitative reference for designing and evaluating new coil technologies against established commercial solutions. As a simulation-readiness example, we generated a calibrated CT-derived MCB70 line-current model for SimNIBS and evaluated its effect on predicted electric-field metrics. Compared with the SimNIBS MCB70 model, the CT-derived model produced measurable differences under identical placement conditions. We provide the dataset online.
papers.intro:
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a non-invasive method to probe and modulate brain circuits [1]. TMS uses strong, brief current pulses to induce a spatial electric field profile through a stimulation coil to write signals into neural circuits or to modify endogenous neuronal activity [2]. The locus of activation in the brain is approximately in the area where the induced electric field is maximal [3]. The design of the TMS coil significantly affects this location and efficacy of stimulation delivery in the brain [4, 5]. In order to provide a map of direct neural activation by TMS, the induced electric field distributions generated by different coil types have been characterised by theoretical calculations [6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14], numerical simulation models [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22], and measurements of the electric currents induced in phantoms [23, 24] or in vivo [25, 26]. However, only a few commercial coils have been modelled in more detailed computational studies, and analytical studies typically employ highly idealised circular and/or figure-of-eight coil geometries [22, 5, 27, 28].

The geometry and structure of the TMS coil determine the strength and spatial distribution of the induced electric field, which determines the focality of stimulation and the depth at which neurons can be stimulated [29, 30]. However, despite the wide range of coil designs available, detailed information on key characteristics remains insufficiently documented in the literature [31]. Knowledge of the characterisation of specific coils and how they compare to other coils is valuable for selecting the optimal coil for a given application or to accurately model and predict stimulation outcomes, as well as the development of novel coils. For most older coils, although once widely used, their winding pattern and the technology are poorly characterised and models are missing as manufacturers closed the business or stopped manufacturing for other reasons. As they have been neither characterised nor modelled, available results cannot be fully interpreted, and valuable coil technology is forgotten.

Different manufacturers have created a variety of TMS coil designs, each incorporating unique technological features to influence the stimulation properties [4]. Different coil geometries, which include parameters such as coil size, shape, and number of turns, provide distinct advantages to target particular regions of the brain. The initial TMS system used a circular coil, which induces a non-focal ring-shaped electric field under the coil perimeter [32, 33, 34]. The desire to overcome the limitations of circular coils in terms of focality has led to the development of the figure-of-eight coil, also known as the butterfly coil, which consists of two adjacent loops and produces a more concentrated electric field at their intersection [35, 36]. The figure-of-eight coil enables much more focal brain stimulation, and it can generate a higher electric field at the targeted centre point compared to areas just a few centimetres away. Thus, it rapidly became the standard for cortical mapping and targeted stimulation in both research and clinical settings [29].

Practically all coils for focal brain stimulation to date use some form of figure-of-eight design. In these coils, the two circles are arranged side by side or overlap. Most coils are furthermore flat. Angled or curved figure-of-eight coils in contrast to flat ones can improve the efficiency [37, 38, 5]. The curved or angled surface can reduce the required pulse energy and improve efficiency but typically complicates handling for many operators and perfectly tangential alignment on the round head [39]. Non-concentric figure-of-eight windings in contrast to previous (and still dominant) concentric loops spread out the outer parts of the loops and concentrate the windings as well as the induced electric field in the centre. Other coil configurations have been developed to achieve specific stimulation goals. Racetrack coils feature an elongated winding shape that covers a broader area than a standard circular coil, typically for neuromuscular and other peripheral stimulation [41, 42, 43, 44]. In contrast, the cone coil tilts the winding to conform to scalp curvature, to increase the depth of penetration [27]. So-called H coils distribute the winding across the entire frontal part of the head [49, 50, 51, 52]. The design includes a base portion that runs largely tangential to the scalp, whereas the return portions typically remain farther from the head, where they produce greater stray flux associated with energy need and loss [53]. In contrast to focal stimulation with figure-of-eight designs, H coils offer more widespread stimulation. The smaller dependence on highly precise and accurate placement may explain their high efficacy in clinical applications [54, 55, 56, 57, 58]. H coils are currently only offered by one supplier so that their availability remains limited despite their apparently high performance. Limited knowledge about the internals also seems to hamper further development, both commercially and academically. First analyses indicate considerable potential for energy and complexity improvements [53].

papers.title: Ask Again: Answer-List Instability in Generative Engines
papers.abstract: Visibility in generative search engines is measured by which entities appear in responses, and in what order. Ask an engine the same question twice and the answer list can change: a different ordering, or different items altogether. Across 60,000 responses, we find that answers to the same prompt name a different first item 32% of the time, and even two answers with the same items disagree on which comes first. The first position is a measurement target of its own. A "clear leader" emerges after seven or eight runs, which are the budgets recommended for brand and source monitoring, but a "close leader" only about half the time. After 25 runs, a close leader is identified only 60% of the time. Variability between engines is larger than within the same engine. For open-ended prompts, the gap is more than double that for determinate ones. Search queries and cited sites observed leave most of the disagreement unexplained. Visibility measurement should report, for each engine, which items appear and how often each comes first, each with its own quantification of uncertainty.

papers.intro:
Generative engines answer information needs with composed responses informed by web retrieval. These answers contain rankings: the first product, institution, treatment, warning sign, or recommendation is usually more salient than those that follow. In generative engine optimization (GEO), creators, brands, and researchers measure whether an entity appears and in what order (Aggarwal et al., 2024; Puerto et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026; Bagga et al., 2025). Such a measurement is meaningful only if run-to-run variation is known. That variation is documented for cited domains and brand mentions (Sielinski, 2026b; Schulte et al., 2026), but not for what a user actually sees: an answer that lists particular items in a particular order. Replication can fail there in two ways. An engine can keep returning nearly the same list while rotating the first item, or it can resample most of the list with each request.

papers.title: Robust Trajectory Prediction Under Sensing and V2X Noise: Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies
papers.abstract: Anticipating the future behavior of surrounding objects is key for the safe and efficient navigation of autonomous vehicles. State-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models are typically trained and evaluated on large-scale, highly curated datasets obtained by filtering any object detection and tracking noise through extensive offline post-processing. However, in real-world deployments, the detected objects' state (position, heading, and speed) estimates are inherently affected by sensing and localization uncertainties. These uncertainties can be even higher for connected and automated vehicles receiving information from other road users through Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications. In this paper, we first investigate the sensitivity of five state-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models to realistic noisy object state estimates. Numerical results show that prediction accuracy degrades by up to a 6x factor as the noise level increases, highlighting the models' sensitivity to the mismatch between the noise conditions encountered during training and those experienced at deployment. We then show that retraining models on a more realistic noise-augmented dataset is a more effective strategy to mitigate the impact of noisy object state estimates on trajectory prediction accuracy than using denoising modules at the input. Retrained models limit the prediction accuracy degradation below a 1.5x factor. The noise-augmented dataset is openly released to support further research.

papers.title: JEPA-Shield: Safe Diffusion Planning with Latent World Models via Conformal Shielding
papers.abstract: Latent world models enable planning from images, but their predictions do not directly establish whether a robot will satisfy physical constraints. We present JEPA-Shield, which connects a frozen action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world model to task-space safety enforcement. Two downstream models predict relative motion from imagined latent rollouts and decode unsafe geometry from the current image. Split conformal prediction turns end-to-end motion-prediction errors into multi-horizon uncertainty tubes. A backup-based shield checks these tubes against physical constraints and screens both candidate trajectories and final proposals in diffusion-inspired sampling-based model predictive control. Under the stated exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, we establish probabilistic constraint satisfaction at action-block boundaries for a returned plan executed without replanning. We also introduce VParkBench, with geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks and a editable photorealistic Gaussian-splatting environment. In closed-loop evaluation, JEPA-Shield achieves success rates of 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, respectively, with no observed constraint violations. Ablations show complementary benefits from shielding and uncertainty calibration. The results demonstrate the importance of grounding latent world-model predictions in task-space quantities and explicitly accounting for prediction uncertainty in safety-critical planning.

Planning from images requires more than predicting what a robot will see next. A candidate maneuver must avoid obstacles, remain within the workspace, and, for articulated vehicles, avoid jackknifing. These requirements concern physical motion and geometry, not similarity to a goal image. Optimization-based planning can enforce explicitly modeled constraints, but errors in perception and scene reconstruction can make their evaluation unreliable [1].

papers.title: Complexity of the Infinity and the Modulo-Counting Quantifiers in Automatic Structures
papers.abstract: Automatic structures allow us to decide their first-order theory using automata-theoretic techniques. The complexity of this decision problem for formulas in prenex normal form depends on the quantifier alternation depth, e.g., it is PSPACE-complete for formulas with quantifier-prefix $\exists\exists\cdots\exists$. Blumensath observed that the decidability also holds if one extends first-order logic with the infinity quantifier. His decision procedure introduces many more quantifier alternations such that, even for formulas with quantifier prefix $\exists^\infty\exists^\infty\cdots\exists^\infty$ of length $n$, his decision procedure runs in $(2n-1)$-fold exponential space. We show that this is not necessary. To be more precise, we prove that handling the infinity quantifier is not more costly than handling the existential quantifier. On the other hand, we also show that addition of the modulo-counting quantifier to first-order logic results in a much higher complexity.

papers.intro:
The use of finite automata for the investigation of logical theories has been pioneered by Büchi, Rabin et al. in the sixties. Automatic structures form a systematic formulation of this approach; for the first time (according to the knowledge of the authors), they appeared in the work of Hogdson [9]. Khoussainov and Nerode [12] took up the idea and work by Blumensath and Grädel [4, 2, 3] popularized it. For surveys on this topic see [8, 19] and for more recent results see [5, 7, 17].

Automatic structures form a systematic formulation of this approach; for the first time (according to the knowledge of the authors), they appeared in the work of Hogdson [9]. Khoussainov and Nerode [12] took up the idea and work by Blumensath and Grädel [4, 2, 3] popularized it. For surveys on this topic see [8, 19] and for more recent results see [5, 7, 17].

Automatic structures, e.g., infinite directed graphs, are given by a finite automaton for the universe (e.g., set of nodes) and a synchronous multi-tape automaton for the relations (e.g., a synchronous 2-tape automaton for the edge relation). This allows the use of automata theoretic techniques in the investigation of the logical theory of the represented structure. The first result in this direction produces, from automata for the structure and a first-order formula, a synchronous multi-head automaton accepting the set of tuples that satisfy the formula. Soon, this was extended to stronger logics that contain, in addition to the usual existential quantification ∃\exists, the infinity quantifier ∃∞\exists^{\infty} [4, 2, 3], modulo-counting quantifiers ∃(p,q)\exists^{(p,q)} [13], Ramsey’s quantifier ∃ram\exists^{\mathrm{ram}} [18] and an extension thereof [15], and the boundedness quantifier [16]. Since the emptiness of a regular language is decidable, these insights give rise to a uniform algorithm that takes an automatic structure and a logical sentence (that can contain all the above quantifiers) and decides whether the formula holds in the structure.

papers.title: Gaze Graphs: A Scene-Level Representation of Visual Attention in the Operating Room
papers.abstract: Purpose: Analyzing clinicians' visual attention from exocentric camera views can support surgical scene understanding without requiring wearable eye trackers. However, existing gaze-following research in the operating room (OR) estimates only 2D gaze locations without identifying attended scene entities or localizing gaze targets in 3D space. In this work, we investigate gaze graphs as a scene-level representation of visual attention that connects clinicians to attended scene entities, and evaluate their utility for fine-grained surgical action recognition and semantic scene graph (SSG) generation. Methods: We extend the public EgoExOR dataset with gaze annotations to create EgoExOR-Gaze, the first benchmark for multi-view gaze graph generation in the OR. We propose a novel architecture that jointly estimates 3D gaze targets and predicts attended entities using only exocentric camera views. Specifically, our approach exploits 3D gaze geometry to sample local visual features across multiple views for attended entity prediction. We further utilize predicted gaze graphs for fine-grained surgical action recognition and SSG generation. Results: For gaze graph generation, our model outperforms both exocentric-only and combined exocentric-egocentric baselines. For surgical action recognition, our model incorporating predicted gaze graphs outperforms both exocentric and egocentric baselines across all evaluated metrics, with particularly strong gains in temporal metrics. For SSG generation, incorporating gaze graphs improves macro-F1 from 0.42 to 0.52 compared to exocentric inputs alone, although performance remains below that achieved with egocentric inputs. Conclusion: Our results demonstrate the value of gaze graphs for surgical action recognition and SSG generation, highlighting the importance of explicitly modeling scene-level visual attention even when egocentric views are unavailable.

papers.intro:
The operating room (OR) is a highly dynamic, collaborative environment where multiple clinicians interact with patients, surgical instruments, medical equipment, and one another throughout surgical procedures. Understanding the relationships among these scene entities is fundamental to interpreting surgical activities and workflows, ultimately supporting the development of context-aware assistance systems [11]. Existing approaches commonly characterize these relationships through observable actions and spatial configurations, such as holding surgical instruments, operating on patients, or standing near the operating table [10]. However, these relations do not explicitly represent clinicians’ visual attention, which plays an important role in situation awareness in the OR [17, 5]. For instance, clinicians may observe their colleagues’ actions without participating, monitor medical equipment without physical interaction, or share a common visual focus while performing different tasks. These examples motivate scene-level gaze analysis, which captures attentional relationships and provides complementary information for understanding surgical scenes.

For instance, clinicians may observe their colleagues’ actions without participating, monitor medical equipment without physical interaction, or share a common visual focus while performing different tasks. These examples motivate scene-level gaze analysis, which captures attentional relationships and provides complementary information for understanding surgical scenes.

Over the past decades, researchers have investigated clinicians’ visual attention using wearable or head-mounted eye-tracking systems [14, 1, 4, 9]. However, collecting synchronized egocentric gaze data from the OR team requires configuring and coordinating multiple eye trackers, making large-scale deployment technically challenging. Moreover, wearing these devices during surgical procedures may disrupt clinical workflows and pose challenges to maintaining sterile conditions. To avoid eye trackers, researchers have introduced gaze-following in the surgical domain to predict where clinicians are looking using exocentric camera views [2]. These gaze predictions have demonstrated their value in downstream tasks, including clinical role prediction, surgical phase recognition, and team communication detection. Nevertheless, this work estimates gaze targets only as 2D locations in individual camera views, without explicitly identifying the attended scene entities or recovering their 3D positions. These limitations make it difficult to represent clinicians’ visual attention toward scene entities consistently across multiple camera views.

Beyond predicting 2D gaze points, gaze object detection has been explored in general computer vision and aims to identify the objects individuals are looking at [19]. However, these approaches primarily focus on individual gaze targets rather than modeling attentional relations at the scene level. For scene-level understanding, researchers have explored gaze-based graph representations for social interaction recognition [7], and introduced semantic scene graphs (SSGs) into the OR to represent scene entities and their relations [10, 9]. Inspired by these works, we investigate gaze graphs as a specialized form of SSG that focuses exclusively on “looking” relations between clinicians and scene entities, rather than the broader range of relations modeled by existing surgical SSGs. We hypothesize that gaze graphs can serve not only as an effective representation of scene-level visual attention for downstream surgical workflow analysis, but also as an intermediate representation for generating more comprehensive SSGs.

We hypothesize that gaze graphs can serve not only as an effective representation of scene-level visual attention for downstream surgical workflow analysis, but also as an intermediate representation for generating more comprehensive SSGs.

To investigate these hypotheses, we build upon the EgoExOR dataset [9] by extending its annotations with complete “looking” relations, head bounding boxes, and 3D gaze target points. We then propose a novel multi-view architecture for gaze graph generation using only exocentric views. Our approach outperforms existing SSG generation baselines in predicting “looking” relations. We further evaluate the generated gaze graphs on two downstream tasks. First, we incorporate gaze graphs as additional inputs to a transformer-based model for fine-grained surgical action recognition on the OR-Action benchmark [18]. Second, we explore the use of gaze graphs as a practical alternative to egocentric views for SSG generation. Experimental results show that generated gaze graphs substantially improve fine-grained surgical action recognition. For SSG generation, incorporating gaze graphs improves performance over using exocentric views alone, but does not fully match the performance achieved with egocentric views, particularly for relations requiring fine-grained first-person visual information.

papers.title: The Role of Mathematicians in Mathematics
papers.abstract: Some reflections on the role of mathematicians in an age of proofs found and verified by machines.

papers.title: On simultaneous left- and right-homometric sets on the positive affine line group
papers.abstract: On a non-abelian group $G$, the homometry problem comes in two flavors, depending on whether differences are computed on the left or on the right. A natural question is to determine whether simultaneously left- and right-homometric subsets of $G$ exist. This question has been answered positively in the case of dihedral groups by Genuys and Popoff. We here prove that no such subsets exist on the positive affine line group, if we impose that the subgroups generated by their left- and right-differences be non-abelian.

papers.title: The generalized Franchetta conjecture for some hyper-K\"ahler varieties, III
papers.abstract:
The generalized Franchetta conjecture states that for a locally complete family of polarized hyper-K\"ahler varieties, the generically defined cycles on any fiber of the universal family over the moduli stack inject into cohomology via the cycle class map. We prove the generalized Franchetta conjecture for the family of double EPW sextics discovered by O'Grady and for the family of double EPW cubes discovered by Iliev-Kapustka-Kapustka-Ranestad. We also prove a Franchetta-type result for the relative square of the universal family of double EPW sextics, which allows to relate double EPW sextics and Gushel-Mukai fourfolds on the level of motives.
  The proof involves the geometry of Gushel-Mukai fourfolds, whose Kuznetsov component allows to realize double EPW sextics and cubes as moduli spaces of Bridgeland-stable objects, relatively over the parameter space of Gushel-Mukai fourfolds. A key step is that the canonical Chow-K\"unneth decomposition of special Gushel-Mukai fourfolds is multiplicative; we use this to show that generically defined cycles on the third power of a special Gushel-Mukai fourfold inject into cohomology via the cycle class map. Along the way, we also show that the canonical Chow-K\"unneth decomposition of any Gushel-Mukai sixfold is multiplicative.

papers.title: Towards Automatic Ion Identification in Storage Rings
papers.abstract: Resonant Schottky detectors provide non-destructive, single-ion-sensitive measurements of revolution frequencies and intensities of ion species stored in a heavy-ion storage ring. These high-\(Q\) cavities allow analysis of high-order harmonics of the revolution frequencies to magnify absolute frequency separations. Adjacent harmonic ranges can, however, overlap within the detector band, making frequency alone insufficient for determining the ion's mass-to-charge ratio $(m/q)$. We present a proof-of-concept for an automated harmonic de-overlapping method using spectral shapes in combined Schottky and Isochronous Mass Spectrometry. The empirical ansatz is that, for a fixed ion-optical setting, each peak, corresponding to a specific ion species with given $m/q$ ratio, has a characteristic profile that evolves smoothly with changing $m/q$. Occurrences of the same local structure at different harmonics should therefore retain almost identical shapes after frequency rescaling. Applied to a 245\,MHz spectrum accumulated from 11\,452 injections at the Experimental Storage Ring at GSI, the method organizes 16 of 32 detected structures into five candidate families and reconstructs their fundamental-frequency representation. Reducing the complex mixed-harmonic spectrum to this smaller candidate set solves the challenging task of finding initial anchors for the ion identification.

papers.title: Degenerate symmetric formulation and principal subsystems for chemically reacting multi-temperature fluid mixtures
papers.abstract: We construct a degenerate symmetric first-order formulation and principal subsystems for chemically reacting multi-temperature fluid mixtures with independent constituent velocities and temperatures, viscosity, and heat conduction. Starting from the entropy-admissible Class-III theory of arXiv:2610.37637, we characterize when its prescribed constituent Euler fluxes are generated by scalar potentials in the conservative entropy variables. Under the stated hypotheses the necessary and sufficient condition is that the separate Gibbs--Duhem one-forms $\omega_i$ vanish. This implies locally additive entropy, but it is not required by the general parent theory. In this subclass, the complete main field contains multipliers for both conservative balances and zero-storage constitutive equations. The spatial Hessians are symmetric, and the temporal Hessian is positive semidefinite and singular. For separated transport laws, eliminating auxiliary variables factorizes the positive-semidefinite dissipative principal symbol. We extend the algebraic Boillat--Ruggeri principal-subsystem construction to degenerate systems. Commuting restrictions yield a dissipative common-temperature system and a nested hierarchy of grouped-temperature Euler subsystems. Classical characteristic interlacing applies within the nested Euler hierarchy, whose temporal Hessians are positive definite. Separately, constrained entropy maximization defines an energy-equivalent common temperature and provides a thermodynamic Class-III-to-Class-II reduction for additive and nonadditive parent entropies. For a thermally reconstructed reference state, the full relative entropy splits exactly into the thermal projection deficit and the relative entropy of the retained variables. We derive the Class-II entropy-production identity and distinguish the thermodynamic projection from principal restrictions and dynamical relaxation limits.

papers.intro:
Chemically reacting fluid mixtures can be described at different levels of resolution. Classical diffusion theories employ a single barycentric velocity and a common temperature, with diffusive fluxes prescribed by constitutive relations such as Fick’s law or the Maxwell–Stefan equations. More detailed models allow different constituent velocities, while the most resolved descriptions also assign independent temperatures to the constituents. These levels are commonly called Classes I, II, and III, respectively [9, Section 7.1] and [3]. In [4] we developed an entropy-consistent Class-III theory including chemical reactions, interconstituent exchanges, viscosity, and heat conduction, allowing nonadditive entropy.

Chemically reacting fluid mixtures can be described at different levels of resolution. Classical diffusion theories employ a single barycentric velocity and a common temperature, with diffusive fluxes prescribed by constitutive relations such as Fick’s law or the Maxwell–Stefan equations. More detailed models allow different constituent velocities, while the most resolved descriptions also assign independent temperatures to the constituents. These levels are commonly called Classes I, II, and III, respectively [9, Section 7.1] and [3]. In [4] we developed an entropy-consistent Class-III theory including chemical reactions, interconstituent exchanges, viscosity, and heat conduction, allowing nonadditive entropy.

An early general covariant construction of the main field and the associated symmetric conservative formulation was given by Ruggeri and Strumia [20]. The treatment of fluid mixtures within Rational Extended Thermodynamics was developed systematically by Müller and Ruggeri [14, Chapters 5 and 7]. For nonreacting Euler mixtures with constituentwise thermodynamics, Ruggeri and Simić [17] constructed the symmetric hyperbolic multi-temperature formulation, identified its single-temperature principal subsystem, and studied the subcharacteristic inequalities, the Shizuta–Kawashima condition and a binary example. Subsequent work clarified the energy-equivalent average temperature, dynamical pressure, and Maxwellian iteration for nonreacting multi-temperature mixtures [7, 18]. See also the systematic account in [21, Chapters 28, 29 and 31]. Related symmetric formulations for single-fluid equations and hyperbolic–parabolic normal forms appear in [8, 10]. For multicomponent reactive flows in a different, common-velocity, common-temperature setting, Giovangigli and Massot [6] obtained a symmetric form and a hyperbolic–parabolic normal form. Their model is distinct from the present Class-III system with independent constituent velocities and temperatures and zero-storage constitutive equations.

papers.title: Blind to What They Can Fix: A Detection Gap in Self-Improving Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents can write programs that carry out a task without calling a model at every step, so the task runs fast and its logic stays open to inspection. Agents improve these programs by running them, studying their failures, and revising the code, a form of recursive self-improvement (RSI). We ask whether this process also yields runtime checks that can be trusted. In five task domains, with up to seven author models, agents bring their programs to high scores. Yet when the environment changes, the checks they were told to write stay silent on half or more of the resulting failures in four domains. These failures can be detected and repaired: a monitor built from records of normal runs catches most of them in three domains, and the same agents usually repair them once called. The checks do not examine the recorded relations that reveal the failures, and the strongest agent writes checks that catch most of them once told that its checks are the only thing that calls it back. An unreported failure stays unrepaired, which limits what self-improvement is worth in autonomous operation. Evaluations of self-improvement should measure not only scores but also whether a system notices its own failures.

Programs written by AI agents run tasks efficiently and keep their decision logic in plain view. Such a program makes recurring decisions without calling a large language model before each action. Its logic is written as explicit conditions, rules, and actions that people can read, test, reuse, and change (Zhang et al., 2026).

A high task score does not tell us whether a system can notice new failures. During development the agent tests the program and sees every failure. During deployment nobody is watching, so the system itself must decide when something needs attention, and a change in the environment can make a good program fail while every action it takes remains valid. We therefore change regularities of the environment that programs may rely on, confirm that the task can still be done, and measure three things on the same pairs of program and change: task performance, failure detection, and repair when the agent is called.

papers.title: Innata-0: A Native Embodied World System with Model-Agent Co-Design
papers.abstract: The physical world is open-ended, dynamic, and partially observable. While foundation models have advanced embodied intelligence, standalone models struggle with long-horizon execution, and simply integrating models with agents may lead to inconsistencies between planning and physical control. To support reliable and adaptive behaviors in the physical world, we introduce Innata-0, a native embodied world system. Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery. A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement. Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation. Innata-0 represents our first step toward physical intelligence, and we see it as the beginning of a much longer journey.

papers.title: Non-Equilibrium Steady States in Nucleosynthesis
papers.abstract: Steady-state behavior underlies many nucleosynthesis processes in which the population number of nuclei can remain nearly constant despite the rapid nuclear reactions. While existing theoretical descriptions largely focus on established chemical equilibrium, as in nuclear statistical equilibrium (NSE) and quasi equilibrium (QSE), non-equilibrium steady states (NESSs) can form in process-specific approximations such as classical $\beta$-flow $r$-process. We develop a general framework for describing NESSs in nuclear reaction networks by formulating the steady-state condition as a balance of reaction flows within a reduced linear description of the relevant network subset. We apply the framework to four representative nucleosynthesis scenarios spanning different steady-state regimes: disequilibrium between nucleons and $\alpha$ particles during $\alpha$-rich freeze-out, the classical $\beta$-flow steady state, the neutrino-assisted $\nu r$-process, and the fission-cycling phase of the $r$-process. In particular, the fission-cycling scenario is described by a quasi-steady-state (QSS) approximation maintaining the population ratios between two nuclei while not conserving the total number of nuclei. The framework reproduces the characteristic abundance pattern for each case while providing a unified interpretation of the underlying steady-state behavior. The eigenvalue spectrum reveals network structure and characterizes the relaxation timescales of abundance distributions. These results establish a general approach for analyzing nucleosynthesis beyond the condition of chemical equilibrium and provide a foundation for extending graph-based methods to complicated nuclear reaction networks.

papers.title: Cyclic changes of frame for designing non-retracing verification cases for numerical interface tracking
papers.abstract: A forward-backward deformation test supplies an exact final interface, but retracing can allow errors from the two halves to cancel. We construct alternative tests by superposing a cyclic change of frame on the same base deformation. The frame returns to its starting pose, preserving the exact final phase and the deformation history up to rigid placement. A small returning translation can keep trajectories close to the retraced ones. A full rotation about a fixed centre or axis gives closed paths with nonzero winding for material labels that stay off that centre or axis. For incompressible base fields the transformed velocity is divergence-free. We construct discretely solenoidal face fluxes for geometric volume-of-fluid advection by circulating the transformed potential. In three TwoPhaseFlow benchmarks, with a shared time grid for each pair, a full-turn frame increased the final cell-average shape discrepancy in all 30 comparisons, with a median factor of 1.50. The fitted convergence exponent decreased in each of the six benchmark-reconstruction comparisons over the tested grids.

papers.title: PRIMEAPE: A Multilingual Benchmark for Fine-Grained Meta-Evaluation of Judge Models
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly serve as judges of other models, shaping benchmark rankings and model development. Yet, a judge whose rationale consistently supports its verdict may still disagree with human preferences. To study this, we introduce PRIMEAPE, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating judge verdicts and rationales. PRIMEAPE provides 2,205 response pairs covering 243 instructions in English, French, Spanish, Urdu, Hindi, Norwegian Bokm{\aa}l, and Yoruba, with 11k human annotations of preferences and rationales across relevance, naturalness, truthfulness, safety, and overall quality. Our evaluation of twelve open- and closed-weight judges reveals that aggregate performance conceals differences across languages and criteria, while requesting rationales does not consistently improve agreement with human preferences. Judges also favor the first position, longer responses, and responses from related models, with effects that vary across criteria and languages. Crucially, judges can justify verdicts that disagree with human preferences while maintaining consistency between their verdicts and rationales. These findings show that consistency with a judge's own verdict does not establish alignment with human judgment. PRIMEAPE enables assessment of both, providing a foundation for more reliable multilingual judges. We release our benchmark and all annotation materials under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license at github.com/Toloka/primeape.

papers.title: The norm axiom and factor hyperfields
papers.abstract: Touchard and the author asked whether every valued hyperfield, in Krasner's sense with the norm axiom, is of the form $\mathcal{H}_\rho(K)$: a valued field $K$ read up to relative error $\rho$. The question turns on the norm axiom. If a valued hyperfield is a quotient $K^\times/T\cup\{0\}$ of a field, the norm axiom forces $T=1+\mathfrak{m}_\rho$ for a valuation on $K$. This completes the proof of a published proposition, and it makes the question equivalent to asking whether every Krasner valued hyperfield is such a quotient. For value group $\mathbb{Z}$ we prove directly that it is. Without the norm axiom the answer is negative. Layering a hyperfield over a non-trivial ordered abelian group gives a factor hyperfield exactly when the hyperfield itself is one, so Massouros's hyperfields yield hyperfields with a non-trivial valuation, satisfying all the other axioms, that are not factor hyperfields. The general question remains open.

papers.title: Luminosity function of millisecond pulsars in globular clusters from their gamma-ray emission
papers.abstract: Millisecond pulsars (MSPs) are widely believed to be responsible for the gamma-ray emission of globular clusters (GCs), yet the underlying MSP gamma-ray luminosity function remains uncertain. Existing GC-based determinations of the latter often rely on external prescriptions for the number of MSPs in each cluster. In this work, we constrain the MSP gamma-ray luminosity function in Milky-Way GCs directly from gamma-ray spectral energy distributions (SEDs), establishing an inference strategy that remains computationally viable for joint analyses of large GC samples. We construct a forward model in which each GC hosts a population of MSPs whose luminosities are drawn from a universal log-normal luminosity function. Synthetic GC SEDs are generated by summing individual MSP spectra, and we infer posterior distributions using first a likelihood-based nested sampling method and then a simulation-based inference (SBI) approach. We show how the likelihood-based method becomes rapidly impractical as the number of jointly modelled clusters (and cluster-specific latent parameters) increases, whereas the SBI approach scales mildly with sample size and reproduces the likelihood-based posteriors in regimes where direct sampling is feasible. We then apply the SBI pipeline to Fermi-LAT SEDs from the 4FGL-DR4 catalog for a sample of 36 GC-associated sources, augmented by dedicated phase-resolved ON/OFF SEDs for two clusters hosting individually detected MSPs. For the real data sample, we obtain informative constraints on the luminosity-function parameters consistent with previous analyses that constrain the cluster-specific MSP counts via complementary multi-wavelength information.

papers.title: Generalized Caffarelli--Kohn--Nirenberg and related inequalities for Grushin-type gradients
papers.abstract:
In this paper, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for a generalized Caffarelli--Kohn--Nirenberg inequality involving the Grushin-type gradient $
abla_G=(
abla_x,|x|^\alpha
abla_y)$, where $\alpha\geq0$, in arbitrary dimensions. When $\alpha=0$, our results recover the classical Caffarelli--Kohn--Nirenberg inequalities and extend the mixed radial and cylindrical weight inequalities of Li and Yan \cite{LY23} to arbitrary dimensions of the $y$ variables. Our approach combines a change of variables with approximation arguments to reduce the Grushin inequalities to Euclidean inequalities with mixed weights. We also characterize the admissible parameters in Hardy--Sobolev inequalities, including the endpoint cases $p=1$ and $q=p$, and derive multiplicative Sobolev and Gagliardo--Nirenberg inequalities. Finally, we establish a weighted Moser--Trudinger inequality on bounded domains and deduce exponential integrability for subcritical growth with arbitrary locally integrable cylindrical power weights. By letting $\alpha=0$, our results also yield the corresponding inequalities for the Euclidean gradient.

papers.title: The FRB Population Revisited: Rate, Energy, Evolution, and Host-DM Constraints from the Second CHIME/FRB Catalog
papers.abstract: We present a study that simultaneously fits for key fast radio burst (FRB) population properties using the Second CHIME/FRB Catalog while calibrating for instrumental selection effects. Our inferred volumetric rate at $z=0$ is $1.1^{+0.4}_{-0.3}\times 10^{5}\,{\rm Gpc}^{-3}\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ above an isotropic-equivalent energy of $10^{39}$ erg and below a scattering timescale of 30 ms at 600 MHz. The evolution of the FRB rate relative to the cosmic star formation rate remains statistically unconstrained. Assuming a Schechter function for the energy distribution, isotropic emission, and 1-GHz emission bandwidth, we find a characteristic maximum energy of $2.0^{+2.6}_{-1.0} \times 10^{41}$ erg and a differential power-law index of $-1.41\,^{+0.27}_{-0.21}({\rm stat.})\,\pm\,0.35({\rm sys.})$. The host galaxy contribution to the observed dispersion measure (DM) is modeled as a log-normal distribution; assuming a total Galactic contribution of 80 $\text{pc cm}^{-3}$, we find a median host-galaxy DM contribution of $199^{+34}_{-36}\;\text{pc cm}^{-3}$ in the rest-frame. Finally, we find that the average FRB spectrum, described by a spectral index of $\alpha=-1.0^{+0.5}_{-0.6}$, is inconsistent with being flat at the $\sim2\sigma$ level. We note an excess of high-S/N bursts at low DMs in the observed sample that is not predicted by the best-fit model. Testing alternative models does not alleviate this tension; future population studies may mitigate this limitation by incorporating robust fluence and redshift measurements.

papers.title: Look Back: Reinforcement Learning with Counterfactual World Models
papers.abstract: Agents in complex, stochastic environments must contend with dynamics that can exceed their world models' predictive capacity and randomness that obscure the consequences of their actions. We hypothesize that, compared to imagining entirely new trajectories in such complex environments, it can be easier to transform observed trajectories with alternative actions. Counterfactual world models condition on observations to predict alternative outcomes under the same underlying environmental randomness, using experience as a reference for predicting action-dependent changes. We present a policy gradient estimator, REINFORCE Look Back (RLB), that uses counterfactual returns as baselines to distinguish action effects from environmental luck, and prove conditions for unbiasedness and variance reduction. In settings where environmental evolution is harder to predict than action-induced changes, we show that counterfactual world models are easier to learn and support better policy learning than ordinary world models. Our findings suggest that counterfactual thinking can help agents learn effective behavior without independently reproducing the full complexity of their worlds.

papers.title: MagPot: A magnetoelastic potential generator for molecular dynamics simulations
papers.abstract: Magnetoelastic phenomena originate from the coupling between atomic displacements and magnetic degrees of freedom, and their atomistic simulation requires interatomic models in which magnetic interactions depend explicitly on interatomic distance. This paper presents MagPot, a Python program that generates Bethe-Slater parameter sets for spin-lattice molecular dynamics simulations using the SPIN package of the Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS). From a compact set of material properties, the program determines the radial functions describing Heisenberg exchange and the dipole and quadrupole contributions of the two-ion N\'eel interaction. Version 1.0 supports simple-cubic, body-centred-cubic and face-centred-cubic lattices with ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic configurations. A central feature of MagPot is its modular architecture, which allows the magnetic contribution it generates to be combined additively with a broad range of compatible non-magnetic interatomic potentials. The parameterisation workflow is assessed through equation-of-state, Curie-temperature, volume-magnetostriction, pressure-dependent magnetocrystalline-anisotropy and anisotropic-magnetoelastic tests. By automating the construction of the magnetic contribution to the interatomic model, MagPot offers a straightforward and reproducible route from material properties to LAMMPS-ready magnetic interactions, facilitating large-scale atomistic simulations of magnetoelasticity and magnetostriction, as well as physical phenomena associated with magnon-phonon coupling.

papers.title: When Simpler Beats Learned: Dual-Weighted Sampling vs. Machine Learning for the Pricing Subproblem in Graph Coloring
papers.abstract: The graph coloring problem can be solved to optimality by branch-and-price (B&P), but its performance hinges on the column generation (CG) step, where each iteration requires solving a maximum weight independent set (MWIS) pricing problem. The state-of-the-art machine-learning (ML) pricing heuristic follows a prediction-sampling paradigm: a learned model scores each vertex of a graph, and independent sets are sampled from the induced distribution. We observe, however, that the scoring procedure does not need to be learned, and critically assess the role of ML by replacing the learned scores with the dual solution of the restricted master problem, resulting in Dual-Weighted Sampling, a proposed lightweight alternative that requires no feature engineering or training. Within a unified CG and B&P framework that varies only the pricing oracle, Dual-Weighted Sampling outperforms MLPH, hand-crafted heuristics, and exact solvers on the established graph coloring benchmark in both runtime and solution quality. In particular, it remains competitive on the DIMACS random family, where MLPH was shown strongest in the original evaluation, while achieving more than a two-fold speedup in CG runtime on recursive-sparse and real-world graph families.

papers.title: Essentially Order-Preserving Fourth-Order Exponential Runge--Kutta Methods for Non-Commuting Operators
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the convergence of explicit exponential Runge--Kutta methods for the linear evolution equation \(u'(t)+Au(t)=Bu(t)\), where \(-A\) generates an analytic semigroup, \(B\) is unbounded and relatively bounded with respect to \(A\), and \(A\) and \(B\) do not commute. It is known from our previous work on order reduction of exponential Runge--Kutta methods for non-commuting operators that this non-commutativity can cause order reduction even for linear problems. In a further work on third-order methods, we showed that this reduction can be avoided by adding a stage and imposing higher regularity on the initial data. Here we treat the fourth-order case. We identify conditions on the coefficients of explicit fourth-order exponential Runge--Kutta methods under which the full order four is retained for this class of problems, and we state the convergence rate as a function of the regularity of \(u_0\). The analysis shows precisely which defect terms, caused by the non-commutativity of \(A\) and \(B\), are eliminated by these conditions. The classical methods of Krogstad and of Strehmel--Weiner do not satisfy them and converge only with order \(11/4\) under the corresponding regularity assumptions, whereas the six-stage method expRK4s6, constructed by Luan (2021), satisfies them and attains order four. Numerical experiments for an advection--diffusion problem involving non-commuting operators confirm the theoretical convergence rates.

papers.title: Parking Functions inspired by board games
papers.abstract: We introduce two new parking schemes inspired by the classic board games Monopoly and backgammon. We consider a one-way street with $n$ parking spots and a queue of $n$ cars waiting to park. Each car has a preferred parking spot and enters in sequence to park. Under the Monopoly parking scheme, if a car finds its preferred spot occupied, it returns to the start of the street and parks in the first available spot it encounters. Under the backgammon parking scheme, if a car finds its preferred spot occupied, it bumps the already parked car out of that spot and takes its place. The bumped car then returns to the start of the street and parks in the first available spot it encounters. A preference list is a parking function for a given parking scheme if all cars successfully park under that scheme. We prove that all preference lists are parking functions under both the Monopoly and backgammon parking schemes. However, the final parking order differs significantly between the two schemes. For a fixed permutation $\pi$, we provide a product formula for the number of Monopoly parking functions resulting in the outcome $\pi$. Analogously, we show that the number of backgammon parking functions with outcome $\pi$ is bounded below by $2^{n-1}$ and bounded above by the $n$-th Catalan number. We also obtain exact formulas involving Motzkin numbers for several families of outcomes. We define the displacement of a car as the absolute difference between the spot where a car ultimately parks and its preferred spot. Displacement multisets encode the displacements for cars with nonzero displacement. We provide formulas for the number of backgammon parking functions with a fixed displacement multiset of cardinality at most $2$, as well as for the number of Monopoly parking functions whose displacement multiset is a given singleton set. We conclude with some directions for further research.

papers.title: Backward Error and Scaling in Level-Based ILU(k) and IC(k) Preconditioners
papers.abstract: We analyse the effect of rounding errors and diagonal scaling on level-based ILU($k$) and IC($k$) preconditioners. Because the sparsity pattern is fixed in advance, the computed factors are those that the incomplete factorization produces, in exact arithmetic, for a nearby matrix, and the deviation of the preconditioned matrix from the identity is bounded by an incompleteness term plus a rounding term. When no shift or pivot modification is needed, scaling leaves the iterates unchanged in exact arithmetic but can change the quantities in this bound by orders of magnitude. For IC($k$), we bound the change in the preconditioned eigenvalues caused by rounding by a multiple of the Skeel condition number of the incomplete factor, which does not depend on the scaling, and we show that after Jacobi scaling the entries of the factor are bounded, so that in half precision a breakdown can be detected before any overflow. Experiments in double, single and half precision illustrate the theory.

papers.title: Equivalence and origin of discrepancies between transfer matrix method and multiple reflection model of surface induced second harmonic generation
papers.abstract: Second harmonic generation (SHG) spectroscopy is a sensitive tool to study surfaces and interfaces in thin films. To understand the layer boundaries and interpret the measured data, it is essential to use a theoretical model describing the SHG generation in the thin film. The transfer matrix method and multiple reflection model are two numerical techniques which have been commonly utilized in the calculation of surface-induced SHG. Here, we demonstrate that, despite the expected equivalence of the approaches, the two methods can lead to controversial results for the same input properties and second-order susceptibility tensors. The discrepancies resulting in different SHG intensity from both methods are caused by inconsistent numerical implementation of the interface SHG. We describe the conditions for the implementation to achieve the equivalence between the two models. Moreover, we identify the physical constraint that has to be imposed in numerical implementation to get identical results from both methods.

papers.title: Interactions between the magnetised jets in the twin radio galaxy J104455+354055
papers.abstract: Pairs of galaxies in which both objects host kiloparsec-scale radio jets are extremely rare. Such systems provide unique opportunity to study the formation of relativistic jets and their resistance to side-way collisions with each other prior to their eventual merger. We analyse the radio data for the twin radio galaxy J104455+354055 associated with a pair of distant elliptical galaxies (z=0.163). The radio jets of both sources avoid disruption/merging for the initial tens of kiloparsecs. We investigate the role of the magnetic fields in the propagation of these radio jets. We used VLA radio data at high frequencies in both compact and extended array configurations to obtain sensitive high-resolution polarimetric data and study the properties of the magnetic fields in all jets. Polarisation data suggest shearing of the magnetic fields at points where the jets bend. The orientation of the magnetic field parallel to jet axis helps confine the jet. Such field configuration in two adjacent jets seems to prevent them from merging. The strength of the magnetic field slightly increases in jet bends and the associated shearing enhances the ordered component of the magnetic field. The more diffuse radio plumes at the end of each jet have comparable strengths and energies of the magnetic field. The twin radio galaxy J104455+354055 provides a unique possibility to study the interplay of radio jets of two radio galaxies. The analysis of the properties of the magnetic fields observed along the radio jets suggests that the wiggles and bends of these jets, caused by the likely interactions of the host galaxies, could be also governed by the magnetic fields that may prevent them from merging. The derived strengths and energies of the magnetic field in different parts of the jets should allow us to improve the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of radio galaxies.

papers.title: An Alphabet-Size Bound for the Information Bottleneck Function
papers.abstract: The information bottleneck function gives a measure of optimal preservation of correlation between some random variable $X$ and some side information $Y$ while compressing $X$ into a new random variable $W$ with bounded remaining correlation to $X$. As such, the information bottleneck has found many natural applications in machine learning, coding and video compression. The main objective in order to calculate the information bottleneck is to find the optimal representation on $W$. This could in principle be arbitrarily complicated, but fortunately it is known that the cardinality of $W$ can be restricted as $|{\cal W}|\leq|{\cal X}|+1$ which makes the calculation possible for finite $|{\cal X}|$. Now, for many practical applications, e.g. in machine learning, $X$ represents a potentially very large data space, while $Y$ is from a comparably small set of labels. This raises the question whether the known cardinality bound can be improved in such situations. We show that the information bottleneck function can always be approximated up to an error $\delta(\epsilon,|{\cal Y}|)$ with a cardinality $|{\cal W}| \leq f(\epsilon,|{\cal Y}|)$, for explicitly given functions $\delta$ and $f$ of an approximation parameter $\epsilon>0$ and the cardinality of ${\cal Y}$. Finally, we generalize the known cardinality bounds to the case were some of the random variables represent quantum information.

papers.title: On the number theory of the Greeks. I. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
papers.abstract: In this article we present Euclid's fundamental theorem of number theory and give evidence for the claim that this theorem, which is largely unknown today, was as familiar to number theorists before Gauss as the Gaussian version of the fundamental theorem is to us.

papers.title: On the Number Theory of the Greeks. II. Gauss's Lemmas and Riesz Domains
papers.abstract: In the second part of our article on Euclid's four number theorem we start from the notion of incommensurability and take a closer look at irrationality proofs for algebraic numbers. Along the way we encounter Gauss's Lemma, integral closure and Dedekind's Prague theorem, and finally we arrive back at the four number theorem.

papers.title: The JWST Resolved Stellar Populations Early Release Science Program. X. Cross-Observatory Proper Motion Measurements with HST and JWST
papers.abstract: We present the first absolute systemic proper motion (PM) of a galaxy measured by combining Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and JWST imaging. The PM of WLM, an isolated dwarf galaxy at $\sim$1 Mpc, is measured against background galaxies with Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) F814W imaging from 2015 and 2024 and NIRCam imaging from 2022 and 2024. The two ACS epochs give a systemic PM of $(\mu_{\alpha}^*, \mu_{\delta}) = (+0.087 \pm 0.019, -0.079 \pm 0.017)$ mas yr$^{-1}$ from 145 galaxies over 8.93 years, which agrees with previous Gaia-based PMs to within 0.4$\sigma$ and is the most precise PM of WLM. For the HST-to-JWST PMs, we fit each NIRCam detector separately, match the point-spread functions with empirically derived convolution kernels, and correct biases with injected galaxies. With an F090W second epoch, the PM is $(+0.081 \pm 0.045, -0.113 \pm 0.046)$ mas yr$^{-1}$ from 43 galaxies over 7.02 years, which, like the F150W PM, agrees with HST-to-HST over the same area to within 1$\sigma$, while F200W differs by $\sim$2$\sigma$. The long-wavelength F250M and F430M PMs are consistent to within 1$\sigma$, though less precise. Fewer galaxies can be used at wavelengths farther from F814W. A cross-observatory systematic of $\sim$0.05 mas yr$^{-1}$ cannot be ruled out over 7 years. At equal baselines, an F090W second epoch is at least as precise as our second ACS epoch over the same area. We recommend the NIRCam filter closest in wavelength to the first-epoch filter, though the long-wavelength filters show promise for closer targets or longer baselines.

papers.title: X-ray polarimetry of a magnetar in the aftermath of an anti-glitch: Revisiting 1E 2259+586 with IXPE
papers.abstract: Magnetars display timing anomalies such as glitches and anti-glitches. 1E 2259+586, whose properties in the X-ray band were recently investigated through a joint XMM/IXPE observation campaign, has been observed to have multiple glitches and three anti-glitches, the most recent occurring in May 2025. Although the X-ray emission is currently decaying, the flux, which roughly doubled at the onset of the anti-glitch, had not yet returned to its original level at the time of the IXPE observation, and the pulse profile has also shown significant evolution. We present an analysis of the recent IXPE observation of 1E 2259+586 from late April to early May 2026. We compare the post-anti-glitch polarisation results with those obtained from the previous IXPE observation in 2023. This provides an unprecedented opportunity to monitor the spectro-polarimetric evolution of a magnetar in the wake of a hallmark event such as an anti-glitch. A dedicated 400ks IXPE DDT observation was approved to track possible changes in the polarisation with respect to the pre-anti-glitch campaign. Spectral and polarimetric properties were jointly modelled within the xspec and ixpeobssim suites, and the analysis was further expanded using a maximum-likelihood technique. No significant detection was found in the phase-averaged and energy-integrated spectrum of this observation. However, despite the significantly shorter exposure, polarisation was clearly detected in the phase-resolved spectrum and the degree of polarisation was found to have a higher best-fitting value, though still statistically consistent, than the previous measurement from 2023, reaching a level >30% in correspondence to the pulse profile minimum. In spite of some slight differences between the two observations, the polarisation trends remain largely consistent and indicate that the source has mostly returned to its pre-event state.

papers.title: BiSAT: Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization for Speech Language Models
papers.abstract: Speech language models (LMs) generate speech as sequences of discrete tokens. Their tokenizer must therefore preserve both acoustic detail and linguistic content at a low bitrate. Semantic-enhanced tokenizers may lose acoustic detail, whereas acoustic-oriented tokenizers retain acoustic variation that makes language modeling harder. Unified tokenizers combine both, but representing acoustic detail and linguistic content within a single feature space can cause interference between the two objectives, and existing approaches typically align acoustic representations to fixed semantic targets from a frozen teacher. We propose Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization (BiSAT), a unified tokenization framework with separate acoustic and semantic branches aligned by a shared-index mechanism. This design learns acoustic and semantic representations in separate continuous spaces while producing a single discrete code sequence, and it jointly optimizes both encoders without relying on fixed semantic teacher targets. Based on BiSAT, we develop BiSAT-TTS, a zero-shot text-to-speech system comprising an autoregressive text-speech LM and a conditional flow-matching acoustic decoder. Reconstruction, downstream understanding, and diagnostic analyses show that BiSAT effectively preserves semantic and acoustic information in the code stream, performs well on in-the-wild and out-of-domain speech, and learns complementary codebook representations. The frozen-code understanding results also support its feasibility and potential for code-based reward modeling in reinforcement learning post-training. BiSAT-TTS performs comparably to state-of-the-art speech LM-based TTS baselines with less training data, further supporting BiSAT's effectiveness for speech language modeling. The audio demos are available at https://seekmind-lab.github.io/bisat-demo.

papers.title: Interpretable morphology-based marked statistics
papers.abstract: The shapes and environments of cosmic structures carry cosmological information beyond the matter power spectrum. Recovering this information while retaining a physical understanding is a central challenge for cosmological inference. We construct an interpretable, rotation-equivariant neural marking scheme that reweights the matter field, combining learned density responses with explicit measures of local morphology. This approach enables direct inspection of the learned transformations, while retaining the advantages of a two-point function analysis. We employ a contrastive learning framework to align the marked summaries with the respective cosmological parameters. In real-space matter simulations, the learned marked spectra recover information beyond the ordinary power spectrum, tightening marginalized Fisher constraints on $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_m$ by factors of $1.7\times$ and $1.5\times$ relative to the power spectrum plus bispectrum at $k_{\mathrm{max}}=0.3\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$. Without retraining, our mark also improves a neutrino-mass forecast by a factor of $1.5\times$ relative to the power spectrum at the same scale cut. Across the cosmological prior, our marking scheme also improve the prediction errors in both parameters by $1.3\times$ over the best tested classical mark at $k_{\mathrm{max}}=0.2\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$. A qualitative comparison with neural forecasts motivates the possibility that these different compressions approach a common information level. Neural marked statistics thus offer a route to extracting non-Gaussian information from cosmological surveys, combining interpretable, physically motivated transformations with the practical advantages of two-point estimators.

papers.title: LoKiTO: Local Kinodynamic Trajectory Optimization for UAVs based on Memory-Efficient Neural Distance Fields
papers.abstract: This paper introduces LoKiTO, a 3D local kinodynamic trajectory optimizer that combines a Chebyshev polynomial parameterization with an online neural Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF) representation for aerial robotics. While current gradient-based planners often struggle with the high memory requirements of explicit volumetric maps or fail to strictly enforce dynamic limits, LoKiTO embeds kinodynamic constraints directly into a modular cost function and exploits the numerical conditioning properties of the Chebyshev basis. Collision awareness is provided by a continuous, memory-efficient neural ESDF updated online from LiDAR measurements, which drastically reduces map memory consumption to approximately 1.0 MB. Benchmarking in highly cluttered simulated environments against state-of-the-art baselines (Fast-Planner and EGO-Planner) demonstrates the superiority of our approach. Experimental results show that LoKiTO achieves over 99.4% dynamic feasibility compliance, significantly outperforming the baselines, and maintaining higher median clearance from obstacles. By coupling a well-conditioned continuous parameterization with explicit kinodynamic reasoning, LoKiTO provides a practical and extensible basis for local replanning in aerial robotics.

papers.title: World Models for Ocean Engineering: A Critical Review of Maritime Autonomy, Adaptive Latent Prediction, Digital Twins, and Biodiversity Monitoring
papers.abstract: Marine robots face partial observability, non-stationary dynamics, and sparse communication, motivating WMs that learn compact predictive states for planning. This review develops a functional taxonomy of WMs for ocean engineering, focusing on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) and AdaJEPA's test-time adaptation within model predictive control, mapping them to navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring, and separating demonstrated evidence from prospective applications. The synthesis identifies key Gaps: benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, safe adaptation and proposes a research agenda for physics-informed, deployment-adaptive marine WMs validated through simulation and field missions.

papers.title: What the annual energy balance hides: the coordination value of digital platforms for positive energy districts
papers.abstract: Positive energy districts (PEDs) are usually assessed by annual net energy, whereas distribution networks operate hour by hour. An annually positive district still imports on low-generation hours and exports or curtails on high-generation hours. How large this hourly imbalance is behind an annual balance, and how much of it coordination among prosumers can close without new physical capacity, is not established. This paper models a multi-carrier prosumer community coupling electricity and heat behind a shared grid connection with a net-export hosting limit. The model is solved as a centralized community problem and as a price-taking peer-to-peer (P2P) market. Under convexity, the equilibrium implements the regularized community optimum and the P2P and congestion prices are the duals of the pool-clearing and hosting constraints. The model is calibrated to six European district archetypes with constructed hourly profiles. Hourly self-sufficiency is only 48-50% in the four deeply studied districts and ranges from 48-55% across all six, leaving a no-platform coordination gap of 2.8-5.9% of no-platform economic cost. The shared-forecast step recovers only 6-18% of the gap, while grid-aware pricing reduces curtailment by 45% in the primary district. Coordination mainly reduces surplus-side inefficiency, whereas closing the deficit side requires storage. The results are scenario-based projections for calibrated archetypes, and the operating benefit is small and contingent on binding hosting limits and high feed-in remuneration. For regulators and distribution system operators this supports hourly, bidirectional indicators alongside the annual positive-energy target, and a congestion charge active only in binding hours with a predetermined refund, while the business case for a platform at district scale rests on grid-side value and aggregation across districts.

papers.title: Asymptotic insolubility of alternating groups
papers.abstract: Let $a,b\in\mathrm{Aut}(A_n)$ with $a\neq 1$, and let $s$ be chosen uniformly in $A_n$. We show that the probability that $\langle a, bs\rangle$ is insoluble tends to $1$ as $n\to\infty$, uniformly in $a$ and $b$. More precisely, this probability is at least $1-O(n^{-1/24})$. The proof combines a bound in terms of the support of $a$ with estimates on permutations lying in transitive subgroups of the symmetric group.

papers.title: Stability and bifurcation of shrinking spheres for the fractional mean curvature flow
papers.abstract: We study the fractional mean curvature flow near shrinking spheres. The first shape eigenvalue changes sign at \(s_*(n)=(\sqrt{n^2+6n+1}-n-1)/2\). Above this threshold, sufficiently small perturbations of a sphere become extinct at one point, and their extinction rescalings converge exponentially to the round shrinker. Below the threshold, the sphere is nonlinearly unstable modulo translations and dilations. We also construct smooth, strictly convex, nonspherical homothetic shrinkers bifurcating from the spherical family near the threshold. In the plane, the noncircular branch bifurcates on the side \(s>s_*(2)\).

papers.title: Endpoint-Conditioned Process Value: What an Endpoint-Blind Process Score Adds Once Terminal Status and Cost Are Known
papers.abstract: Trajectory metrics promise information beyond final-answer accuracy, but no one has measured what a process score adds once an evaluation knows the outcome and the cost. We build that comparison: a sealed consequence needing an artifact neither agent nor judge ever sees, an operational baseline of terminal status and cost, and judge scale and evidence access as experimental factors. On 1,255 trajectories over 158 test-generation tasks in 7 Python repositories, the answer is gated on the judge. Four judges from 4B to 14B, one reasoning before scoring, add nothing an interval separates from zero; a Qwen3 32B judge on identical trajectories adds +0.050 AUC (95% CI [+0.020, +0.081]) and survives a refitting bootstrap ([+0.013, +0.095]). Most of what it adds is recoverable from eight behavioural counters, so a harness should log them (the judge adds +0.020 beyond them). What the judge is shown moves it further: disclosing the terminal verdict inflates its standalone discrimination by +0.103, while reference disclosure and tool-output redaction move it by nothing an interval separates from zero. A process metric reported without the judge's scale and evidence access does not identify a quantity. We release the protocol, the sealed-endpoint harness, and all trajectories.

papers.title: VistaTree: Question Answering over Long Multimodal Documents with Image-Derived Summary Trees
papers.abstract: Answering questions over long multimodal documents requires locating relevant evidence across pages containing text, tables, and figures. When the document exceeds the model's context window, selective retrieval becomes necessary. We introduce VistaTree, a document question-answering agent that builds a summary tree directly from rendered page images. VistaTree segments documents into contiguous page spans, recursively groups them into a topic hierarchy, and refines sibling summaries to distinguish neighboring sections. At query time, the agent uses node summaries to select relevant nodes and reads the corresponding pages, using hierarchical navigation when the full outline exceeds the context budget. Experiments on MMLongBench-Doc and LongDocURL evaluate answer quality and retrieval cost using a locally hosted vision-language model, and quantify the performance gap between global and hierarchical access to the index.

authors.name: Xiaochen Zheng
authors.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Pyroelectric Harvesting from Steady Heat Sources via Active Piezoelectric Thermal Switching
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates pyroelectric energy harvesting from a steady heat source using active piezoelectric thermal switching in a PZT/Si bimorph cantilever. The same PZT layer serves as both the mechanical actuator and the pyroelectric energy-conversion element. Dual output electrodes enable separation of the pyroelectric and piezoelectric signals. Pyroelectric energy harvesting is experimentally demonstrated at frequencies up to 110 Hz and temperature differences as small as 5 K. Comparison with the response predicted from the independently measured pyroelectric coefficient, together with transient thermal simulations, identifies dynamic interfacial heat transfer as a key limitation to high-frequency operation. This work demonstrates a compact MEMS approach for higher-frequency pyroelectric energy harvesting from low-grade steady heat sources.
