papers.title: Digital Models of Widely-Used Powder Characterisation Tools and their Application in DEM Calibration Part III: Packing and Flow Testers
papers.abstract: Accurate calibration remains a critical challenge in the field of discrete element method (DEM) simulations. To work towards more standardised and rigorous methods, this research contributes to a growing open-source library of digital models that faithfully replicate powder characterisation instruments. This paper expands that library by developing and validating digital models for two widely used instruments: the GranuFlow flow through an orifice tester and the GranuPack tapped density analyser. These models are designed to replicate the experimental instruments while incorporating computational optimisations to improve efficiency without compromising on accuracy. An example application of the digital models is shown through a calibration case study for two example materials: micro-crystalline cellulose (MCC) and ion exchange resin. The calibrated models show strong agreement with experimental data through cross-validation, yielding a relative percentage error of 0.57\% for the Hausner ratio (the ion exchange resin) and 4.17\% for a Beverloo fitting parameter (MCC). The addition of these validated, open-source models provides the DEM community with further models for more robust, multi-instrument calibration, and potential for more insight into bulk behaviours under different conditions.

authors.name: A. Neveu
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Wavelet determinantal samplers: Optimal approximation rates adapting to regularity
papers.abstract: We construct wavelet-based determinantal samplers on manifolds and geometric graphs whose approximation rates adapt to the regularity of the observable. On a Riemannian manifold of dimension $m$, our wavelet DPPs satisfy variance reduction of order $n^{1-2s/m}$ for linear statistics of both $s$-H\"older and $H^s$ observables, where $0<s\le1$. Using these samplers, we further construct unbiased quadrature rules with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$ using at most $3n/2$ function evaluations, matching the classical optimal randomized integration exponent. For point clouds sampled from an $m$-dimensional manifold, we develop corresponding determinantal samplers on two standard classes of geometric random graphs: $\varepsilon$-graphs and symmetric $k$-nearest-neighbour graphs. These samplers satisfy the same variance reduction for linear statistics of $s$-H\"older observables and yield conditionally unbiased estimators of empirical averages with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$, using at most $2n$ function evaluations. In both settings, the rates are governed by the intrinsic dimension $m$ and the regularity $s$ of the observable.

papers.title: COSIMA Cookbook: a community-driven resource for ocean and sea-ice modelling science
papers.abstract: The COSIMA Cookbook is an open educational resource for analysing ocean and sea-ice model output in Jupyter notebooks. It has been developed by the Consortium for Ocean--Sea Ice Modelling in Australia (COSIMA) as a community resource for researchers, students, and practitioners working with large gridded datasets, especially output from the ACCESS ocean--sea ice model configurations. The Cookbook is organised around a gastronomy theme: ``Cooking Tutorials'' teach generic, transferable techniques for handling model output, while "Easy Recipes", "Advanced Recipes" and "Regional Specialties" are self-contained notebooks that show how to perform concrete diagnostics and analyses. Along the way, the notebooks demonstrate open-source tools for the scientific analysis of large data, including Intake catalogues, Xarray, Dask, xgcm, xESMF, eofs, Parcels, matplotlib and Cartopy. The Cookbook addresses the steep entry cost of analysing climate model output: it packages expert, often tacit, knowledge into complete, well-documented and reusable workflows, in the same medium in which researchers actually work. It is developed openly on GitHub, is published as a documentation website, and is continuously reviewed and extended by its community through pull requests and regular hackathons. The easy access to data and analysis it provides has contributed to the international adoption of ACCESS ocean and sea-ice model configurations, and has facilitated well over 100 peer-reviewed papers and more than 20 PhD projects.

authors.name: Matthis Auger
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

authors.name: Jan Jaap Meijer
authors.institution: ARC Centre of Excellence for Climate Extremes

papers.title: Organ-scale pulsatile blood flow reconstruction in the avian yolk sac embryo
papers.abstract: The hemodynamic forces on endothelial cells in developing vascular networks vary over the cardiac cycle. Resolving these variations throughout the yolk sac requires imaging individual regions of the vasculature at different times. We reconstructed mean and pulsatile blood flow in a 21-somite quail embryo from 53 overlapping high-speed microscopy recordings acquired over 3.7 h. We reconciled mean-flow measurements using conservation of flux at vascular junctions and synchronized cardiac phases using vessels shared between recordings. Of the 7,009 vessels with flow measurements in the computational domain, we reconstructed pulsatile flow in 5,214. Relative pulsatility decreased along an arterial-side path but increased along a venous-return path, where downstream flow oscillations preceded those upstream. Across the plexus, phase lags relative to the vitelline veins increased toward the vascular margin. A distributed resistance--compliance model with uniform vessel distensibility reproduced many of these spatial variations. Our results suggest that vascular geometry and compliance, together with pulsatile forcing from both arterial and venous boundaries, determine the local flow waveforms within the developing plexus.

papers.title: Initial Field Test of a Quadrupedal Robot at SLAC Beam Dump East (BDE): A Sandbox for Robotics in Accelerator Operations
papers.abstract: Deploying field robotics in large scale particle accelerator facilities offers significant potential to enhance operational efficiency, promote facility sustainability, and reduce personnel exposure to radiation and other hazards. As key underlying technologies mature, field robotics are seeing broader deployment across various industrial sectors. However, accelerator facilities have remained cautious in adopting these systems, primarily due to concerns regarding cost versus return on investment and the risk of equipment collisions. In addition, operational experience with SLAC's Remotely Operated Accelerator Monitoring platform, ROAM highlighted critical technical challenges, including radiation tolerance and poor network connectivity in enclosed accelerator areas. This paper presents the findings from a recent test drive of a Boston Dynamics SPOT quadrupedal robot equipped with a SPOT Arm payload conducted at SLAC's Beam Dump East facility. We evaluate the technical feasibility and operational considerations of deploying quadrupedal field robotics within accelerator environments. Furthermore, we report key practical challenges, such as protective suits that impede navigation sensors and low light infrared navigation in unlit spaces. Finally, we outline potential development pathways toward adaptive learning and autonomous execution for future routine field robotics operations in accelerator facilities.

authors.name: A. Saad
authors.institution: King Faisal Specialist Hospital & Research Centre

papers.title: Geometry of ground states in the long-range Ising model
papers.abstract:
We study the ground states of the ferromagnetic Ising model on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with long-range interactions and prescribed exterior data. We first show that the half-space configuration is a ground state, by means of a discrete calibration (which is the lattice counterpart of the calibrations of Cabr\'e and Pagliari for nonlocal minimal surfaces). In dimension $d\ge2$ and for positive kernels, the half-space configuration is the unique minimizer in every finite domain, and it is "stable" with respect to perturbations of the exterior datum whose energy is below half of a positive excitation gap. This rigidity has no counterpart in the continuum.
  For general exterior data and positive kernels, we show that along a monotone family the minimizer is unique except for finitely many data. This can be considered a "generic uniqueness result" that provides the discrete counterpart of a recent work of Dipierro, Fern\'andez-Real and Valdinoci in the continuum.
  We then introduce a pointwise notion, called perception, which is the lattice counterpart of the instability and stickiness phenomena for nonlocal minimal surfaces discovered by Dipierro, Savin and Valdinoci. We give a local criterion for the half-space configuration to be perceptive at a given site.
  Finally, we consider a box with exterior datum $+1$ above and below a slab and $-1$ on its sides. For fractional kernels with small exponent, the minimizer is $+1$ in the whole box, and its positive phase is connected. For short-range kernels, instead, the negative phase may enter the box, and the positive phase may be disconnected. Moreover, if the datum is $-1$ around the box and $+1$ only at distance two from it, the configuration identically $-1$ is perceptive at every boundary site of the box for fractional kernels with small exponent.

papers.title: MSBench: Benchmarking Script-Controlled Multi-Shot Text-to-Video Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) models can now generate visually plausible short clips, but multi-shot generation requires a different set of skills: composing multiple shots with intended cut timing, transition style, camera language, and cross-shot continuity. How far this multi-shot output can be controlled from text remains unmeasured: existing benchmarks either evaluate single shots or, when they provide shot-level scripts, typically check whether the requested shots appear but not when they change or how they are joined. We introduce MSBench, a benchmark for controllable text-driven multi-shot video generation built around structured Scene-Entity-Shot mini-scripts that specify each shot's time span, camera state, content, and outgoing transition. MSBench defines a four-dimensional hybrid evaluation framework spanning Visual Quality, Dynamic Quality, Semantic Alignment, and Cross-Shot Consistency with 11 sub-metrics. Experiments on 14 commercial and open-source systems show that visual quality does little to separate the systems, whereas multi-shot control does: many models cut mainly on scene changes and render requested gradual transitions as hard cuts. Human evaluations further validate MSBench, with its system ranking reaching a Spearman correlation of 0.87 with human preferences. The project page is available at https://totalhuang.github.io/MSBench-page/.

authors.name: Tao Huang
authors.institution: Henan University of Science and Technology

authors.name: ZiHao Liang
authors.institution: Vaughn College of Aeronautics and Technology

papers.title: Domain advantage in two-dimensional quantum-device design with multi-modal agentic harness
papers.abstract: High-quality two-dimensional quantum devices are commonly fabricated from mechanically exfoliated crystals, whose irregular shapes and placement require a lithographic layout tailored to each specimen. Drawing these layouts remains largely manual. We introduce qlaybench, a benchmark that tests whether language-model agents can turn microscope images and experimental requirements into device layouts that fit the specimen. Agents with conventional tools often construct devices when material outlines are supplied, but struggle to identify those outlines from images. Modelled on the human workflow, qlaybot, a multimodal agentic harness, connects image interpretation to the tools used to align images, draw device features and inspect the resulting layout. We evaluate each layout with checks drawn from practical design experience, asking whether it fits the specimen and connects its intended components. With greater computational effort, an agent using qlaybot passes 81.5% of the benchmark tasks, compared with 24.1% when it uses conventional tools. This domain advantage highlights the importance of connecting scientific interpretation of a specimen to geometric design and provides a route towards reducing manual effort in two-dimensional quantum-device fabrication.

authors.name: Shenhao Miao
authors.institution: Collaborative Innovation Center of Advanced Microstructures

papers.title: Metastable states are precursors of Turing patterns in Adaptive Networks
papers.abstract: In networked reaction-diffusion systems, emergence of patterns from a homogeneous equilibrium can be described by Turing instability. Recently, Turing theory has been developed to include adaptive networks where, i.e., link weights change as a function of the states of the nodes. In this work we show that metastable states, defined as long living transient epochs with unique dynamical properties, could be observed in a range of parameters between Turing patterns and absence of any spatial pattern. Stated differently in the metastable regime the system ''switches'' between the homogeneous solution and the Turing pattern, never settling in any of those states, i.e., alternating silent and spiking regimes. By using phase diagrams and recurrence plots, we have numerically shown the existence of metastable states for the Brusselator model. Moreover, the dependence of the emergence of the metastable states on the adaptive control parameter has been characterized. The applicability of methods and ideas proposed in this work go beyond the considered case, they can help us in understanding conditions under which metastable states arise and could thus be informative to predict and control the latter.

papers.title: BitShare: Sensitivity-Aware Binning and Bit Sharing for Compacting LLM Weight Storage
papers.abstract: Decoding with large language models at small batch sizes is limited by memory bandwidth, so the bits stored per weight largely set its cost. Group-wise integer quantization stores every weight of a group at the same precision, although the input channels of a group differ in sensitivity. We present BITSHARE, a codebook-free weight format that keeps the integer grid and the dequantizer of group-wise quantization but varies precision within each group. Sensitivity-aware binning places the channels of each group into three bins at fixed positions, and static bit sharing with optimal bit-value allocation lets the less sensitive weights share their lower bits, each stored once per group or once per pair of weights. A sharing-aware version of GPTQ chooses every stored value, with no fine-tuning and no codebook. BITSHARE has two modes. BITSHARE-U gives every group the same layout, so its decoder routes bits by fixed wiring, while BITSHARE-N chooses a layout per group within the same bit budget. With calibration on the Pile and at the same storage, both modes have lower perplexity than GPTQ at 3 and 2 bits on WikiText-2 and C4. At 2 bits across Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, BITSHARE-N lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by up to 70% against SliM-LLM and up to 35% against GPTAQ. At the 2-bit perplexity of SliM-LLM, BITSHARE-U stores 13.6-19.4% fewer bits per weight, cutting DRAM weight traffic by the same fraction. A verified hardware decoder implementation synthesized in SkyWater 130 nm reconstructs BITSHARE weights at the throughput of INT-n and SliM-LLM decoders.

papers.title: For whom the Bell tolls: joint measurements and state updates in quantum field theory
papers.abstract: State update rules and their behaviour in Bell tests play an important role in the study of measurement schemes and quantum information. We consider the state updates of the Fewster-Verch measurement framework for quantum field theory using their connection to the probability distribution of measurement outcomes. We focus on a set of observables of the form $A(f_i)^*A(f_i)$, where $A(f)$ is the (complex) smeared field operator for any theory induced by a formally hermitian, Green hyperbolic differential operator, and where the $(A(f_i))_{i=1, \dots, m}$ are assumed to be normal and mutually commuting. Under the assumption that these operators have a sufficiently nice representation on a bosonic Fock space, we derive the joint moment generating functional and the unique joint probability distribution for the observables $(A(f_i)^*A(f_i))_{i=1,\dots,m}$. As an application of these results, we construct a model of a Bell inequality test within quantum field theory using a recently developed coupled Proca-scalar model for polarization measurements. We show that our Bell test model can violate the CHSH inequality, approaching Tsirelson's bound for maximally entangled states in the limit where vacuum effects are perfectly rejected. These results show that the state update rules derived in the Fewster-Verch framework are compatible with strongly quantum correlations. They also support a viewpoint in which state updates should be understood in relation to available information.

papers.title: Strain-transfer at the Cu nanoparticle-Si(111) interface: static atomistic modelling and simulated Bragg CDI
papers.abstract: Substrate strain offers a route to control deformation in supported metallic nanoparticles, provided that interfacial coupling transmits the imposed loading into the particle. We assess this feasibility using five static Cu/Si(111) configurations spanning 0-2% biaxial tensile substrate strain. A 211,288-atom Cu particle is supported by a nominally 50 x 50 x 20 nm Si slab with its bottom 1 nm fixed, using the Jelinek modified embeddedatom potential. Relative to the relaxed supported 0% state, Cu-only local fits reveal heterogeneous, anisotropic deformation: particle-wide mean hydrostatic strain is negative at every nonzero loading, from -3.12 x 10-6 to -8.84 x 10-6, while the upper-particle mean varies nonmonotonically. Simulated Bragg CDI of Cu(111), obtained by inversion of known complex atomic scattering amplitudes, maps loading-dependent projected displacement and strain. The combined atomistic and Bragg CDI representations provide strong preliminary support for the feasibility of substrate-mediated strain transfer in this idealized system and identify spatial signatures for experimental investigation. Experiments remain indispensable to confirm transfer in real Cu/Si(111) nanoparticles and determine its magnitude.

papers.title: Origins of City Reputation: Measuring Trust and Bias in Online Reviews Using Agentic AI and NLP
papers.abstract: Online reviews aggregate millions of individual judgments into signals that shape where people eat, stay and travel to, and increasingly read them as evidence of the reputation of places. Nevertheless, whether such reputations really reflect the places or more the instruments used to measure them is unclear. Here we compare two instruments for measuring trust and bias in 100,000 Yelp reviews from ten US cities: a large language model based agentic system including an evaluator critic loop, and a corpus-based tool built on pretrained classifiers, lexicons and rule-based features. Our results show that the two instruments agree on credibility, but not at all on plausibility. They also respond to different use of words and phrases. The corpus-based better flagged complaints and generalizations, whereas the agent better quoted references to social groups. We also found that with five examples, the agent treats ordinary superlatives as bias far more often than with none or one. Aggregated to cities, both instruments find little variation as less than half a percent of the variance of review level reputation lies between cities. This small differences between cities mostly arise from different levels of trust (in case of the agentic tool) and from bias (in case of the corpus-based tool), and the two instruments rank the cities differently. Reputation derived from platform reviews therefore depends on how the reviews are processed and analyzed. As platforms delegate this to language models, the definitions and examples built into these models become part of how places are valued.

papers.title: FGSCalib: Targetless Camera-LiDAR Extrinsic Calibration from Foreground Segmentation
papers.abstract: Camera-LiDAR pairs installed as fixed infrastructure need periodic recalibration, but a calibration target takes the installation out of service. We present FGSCalib, a targetless method that calibrates a stationary camera-LiDAR pair from the objects moving in its view. We only assume that arbitrary moving objects are present in the scene: each sensor separates the moving foreground from the static background, without relying on object classes. With the correct extrinsic, the LiDAR foreground points project onto the camera foreground. FGSCalib turns the camera mask into a boundary-proximity field and finds the extrinsic by two-stage simulated annealing over selected frame pairs. It needs no measured initial extrinsic (random starts give similar results) and works with both rotating and non-repetitive LiDARs. We evaluate it on 21 simulated scenarios with exact ground truth and on 72 real ones (nine camera-LiDAR pairs in eight scenes), with a reference averaged from 43 manual calibrations. In simulation the median error is 5.3 cm and 0.19{\deg}. On real data we use a tolerance of 18 cm and 1.8{\deg}, met by 93% of single manual calibrations. Keeping the lowest-cost of five runs, FGSCalib meets it in 51 of the 72 scenarios: in 20 of 24 with the Livox, where the strongest of five baselines reaches 11, and in 31 of 48 with the two rotating LiDARs, where only one baseline estimate does. Its median error is 9.5 cm and 0.9{\deg}, against 7.3 cm and 0.7{\deg} for a single manual calibration. The code and the dataset are available online.

authors.name: Csaba Benedek
authors.institution: HUN-REN Institute for Computer Science and Control

papers.title: Finsler--Sobolev inequalities: optimality & rigidity
papers.abstract: We establish optimal Sobolev and logarithmic-Sobolev inequalities on non-compact, possibly non-reversible Finsler manifolds with non-negative weighted Ricci curvature. The optimal constants exhibit no dependence on reversibility -- confirming Ohta's conjectural principle -- being governed solely by the forward and backward asymptotic volume ratios. We then apply the logarithmic-Sobolev inequality to establish the optimal hypercontractivity estimate for the heat flow in the same geometric setting. The equality cases of the above optimal inequalities imply strong rigidity in the underlying manifold, characterized by fine properties of the flag and $S$-curvatures as well as the precise profiles of the corresponding extremizers. We illustrate our results by examples including Randers metrics obtained by Zermelo navigation with Killing vector fields, and weighted convex cones in $\mathbb{R}^n$ endowed with arbitrary Minkowski norms, the latter showing that the forward and backward asymptotic volume ratios may differ.

papers.title: Note on polychromatic coloring of hereditary hypergraph families III
papers.abstract: For every integer $h\ge4$ we construct a hereditary family of hypergraphs with $m_2=h$ and \[ m_3\ge 2(h-1)+2\left\lfloor\frac{h-1}{3}\right\rfloor+1 \approx \frac{8}{3}m_2. \] This improves the lower bound $m_3\ge 2m_2$ from the preceding notes for every $m_2\ge4$. We also show that the worst-case integrality gap of the weighted transversal problem over hereditary families with $m_2\le h$ is between $h-1$ and $5000h$. As a consequence, every such family admits strong $\varepsilon$-nets of size at most $5000h/\varepsilon$.

papers.title: ActWithin: Bounding Wrong-Payment Risk in Delegated Payment Batches
papers.abstract: A delegated payment agent can hold valid rights for incompatible revisions of a batch. We study the window in which the selected revision cannot be verified by the execution deadline. For batches that permit every subset of up to q revisions, ActWithin compiles the limit into a shared quota of q successful replacement payments. If approved plans are mutually replayable with the same observable inputs, deadlines, and resources, this quota preserves normal completion without additional approvals and minimizes worst-case wrong-payment principal for arbitrary positive amounts. A dynamic program computes its exact risk and witness. For amount-preserving recipient changes, we derive the exact risk of the tightest single amount cap on the same replacement group, provided mixed payment subsets can settle within the window. A two-phase result isolates the risk to payments due before trusted verification. Against the amount cap, an exploratory setting with 16-64 payments and one quarter of positions revisable yields aggregate reductions of 16.23-16.88% on adapted IBM AMLSim amounts and 10.12-12.52% on an adapted controlled catalog. The 760 funded original controlled paths with constructed single-position revisions yield 2.69%. In one local MetaMask fixture, both policies complete all 37 normal plans and the worst wrong debit falls from 93,962 to 81,056 test wei.

papers.title: Towards a faster parameterized algorithm for Chordal Vertex Deletion
papers.abstract: The \textsc{Chordal Vertex Deletion} (\chvd{}) problem asks whether an input graph $G$ can be made chordal by removing at most $k$ vertices. When $k$ is taken as parameter, this problem is known to be fixed-parameter tractable \cite{M10,CM16}. However, it is still open whether \chvd{} admits a single-exponential FPT algorithm, i.e. an algorithm with running time $O(\alpha^k |V(G)|^c)$ for some constant $\alpha$ independent of $k$. Towards this goal, we describe an FPT algorithm for the compression version of \chvd{} with the following specification. Given an instance $I = (G,k,X)$ of the disjoint \chvd{} compression problem such that $|X| = k+1$, $G - X$ is chordal and its longest chordless path has length $L$, we solve $I$ in time $O((L+1)^{3k} k^2 |V(G)|^4)$.

papers.title: Construction of Universal Safe Stabilizing Formulas with Weighted Centroid Methodology
papers.abstract: Control Lyapunov and control barrier functions ensure stability and safety, respectively, by imposing state-dependent affine constraints on the control input. Controller design can therefore be viewed as the problem of selecting an admissible input from the set defined by these constraints. This paper adopts this perspective and develops a weighted-centroid methodology for constructing explicit feedback formulas that are provably smooth. The selection method relies on the fact that weighted centroids of a convex set lie within the set. We establish conditions on the weight functions that guarantee smoothness and continuity for several classes of constraints, including single constraints, mirrored constraints, linearly independent multiple constraints, and two-constraint Gaussian constructions. The framework recovers Sontag's universal formula and generates other new explicit formulas. When specialized to control-theoretic settings, the resulting formulas yield smooth safety filters, stabilizing controllers, and safe-stabilizing controllers. Simulation and hardware experiments on a small quadrotor illustrate the practical benefits of the proposed construction.

authors.name: Aaron D. Ames
authors.institution: Budapest University of Technology and Economics

papers.title: Explicit exponent bounds for sums of consecutive powers
papers.abstract: Let $x^k+(x+1)^k=y^n$, where $x,y,k,n$ are positive integers with $k\ge2$ and $n\ge3$. We prove that $n<52k^2\log(2k)\log^2(50k)$ for odd $k$ and $n<216k\log^2(2500k)$ for even $k$. For odd $k$, an exact valuation formula reduces the problem to a linear form in two real logarithms. For even $k$, we use factorization in $\mathbb Z[i]$ and a bound of Yamada. When $k=5$, we prove that the original exponent $n$ is one of the 34 primes between $23$ and $181$, inclusive. Every solution satisfies $2x+1=u^n$ with $u>10^{1000}$. A gap between successive rational approximations to $2^{-4/n}$, together with the Thue--Siegel principle, gives at most four solutions for each of $n=23,29$ and at most three for each larger prime in this range. Thus there are at most 104 positive integer triples $(x,y,n)$ in the quintic case. All bounds are unconditional.

authors.name: Akos Pinter
authors.institution: Budapest University of Technology and Economics

papers.title: Modeling the chemical impacts of luminosity outbursts in protostellar envelopes
papers.abstract: Some protostars undergo episodic accretion, resulting in luminosity outbursts that heat their envelopes. The increase in temperature alters the position of the snowlines, which return to their original locations on different timescales depending on the species. However, the chemical effects of luminosity outbursts in protostellar envelopes, including their long-term consequences, remain poorly explored. We investigate the chemical impact of luminosity outbursts on the envelope of a solar-type protostar, accounting for its dynamics, and identify trends in the molecular response relative to both ongoing and past outburst activity. We combined the dynamic semi-analytic code APE with the three-phase chemical model NAUTILUS to predict the time evolution of 83 molecular abundances between 10 and 10,000 au in the collapsing envelope. The outburst was parameterized by increasing the protostellar luminosity by a factor of 100 for 100 years. The outburst shifts molecular snowlines outward by up to a factor of ten, thus enriching the gas phase through thermal desorption. Most species return to their pre-outburst state within a few thousand years at most for r$\leq$1000 au and remain in that state thereafter. However, eight molecules (HOCH2CHO, CH3COCH2OH, C2H5CHO, OCS, SO2, C2S, C3S, and HC3N) show abundance deviations 10$-$50 kyr after the outburst in the warm inner regions (T$\geq$100 K), due to the inward transport of chemically altered material. Eight other species (CH3O, C2O, NH2, HCCO, HCNO, HNO, NO, and NCO) show enhanced gas-phase abundances at intermediate radii ($\sim$300$-$1500 au). Overall, most molecules are impacted by outward snowline shifts. With the exception of HOCH2CHO, CH3COCH2OH, and C2H5CHO, all complex organic molecules (COMs) are expected to exhibit similar abundances in the warm inner regions of protostars (hot corino), regardless of whether they undergo outbursts.

authors.name: Antoine Espagnet

papers.title: General bounds for metric dimension of diameter-two graphs with applications
papers.abstract: We study the metric dimension of several classes of graphs with diameter two. First, we establish a general lower bound for the metric dimension of graphs with diameter two in terms of their order and maximum degree. We then apply our results to Grassmann graphs, Moore graphs, and bilinear forms graphs. For Kneser graphs, we obtain new upper bounds, while for $G_q(n,2)$ Grassmann graphs we establish new upper bounds provided by constructions of resolving sets. For Moore graphs of diameter two, we derive improved lower bounds, and for $H_q(n,2)$ bilinear forms graphs, we obtain new upper and lower bounds on their metric dimension.

papers.title: Identax: A Toolbox for Efficient Learning of Linear, Parameter-Varying, and Nonlinear Systems in JAX
papers.abstract: Accurate data-driven modelling of dynamical systems is increasingly important across engineering disciplines, yet state-of-the-art identification methods are often computationally demanding, opaque, or poorly scalable. We present Identax, a JAX toolbox for identifying linear, Linear Parameter-Varying (LPV) and nonlinear systems, designed as an extensible foundation for system identification research. Its modular design allows model structures, identification criteria and optimization methods to be extended independently. The first release provides state-space and Linear Fractional Representation (LFR) models, multiple-shooting criteria for parallel training, and a transparent optimization pipeline. On the Silverbox benchmark, an LPV-LFR model outperforms all previous black-box results while training in under three minutes on a CPU. On a control moment gyroscope, Identax matches state-of-the-art accuracy.

papers.title: On convergence rate bounds for Markovian push-sum algorithms
papers.abstract: In this work we establish an upper bound on the almost sure convergence rate of a broad class of push-sum algorithms, more precisely for those where message passing events follow a Markovian dynamics, or a Hidden Markov Model. In this context, having a computationally accessible quantity at hand is of top priority; we thus formulate tools to cut down the complexity of obtaining the stated bound. Furthermore, we introduce a transformation to adjust a given push-sum scheme in a way that the bound on the rate provably improves -- and often so does the true convergence rate. Theoretical understanding is complemented by numerical results, where the quality of all three directions is demonstrated: for the bound on the rate, for the computational complexity and for the improvement strategy.

authors.name: Miklos Kornyik
authors.institution: HUN-REN Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics

papers.title: A quasi-tree expansion for the two variable Bollob\'as--Riordan polynomial using a single basepoint
papers.abstract: We give a quasi-tree expansion formula for the two variable Bollob\'as--Riordan polynomial of ribbon graphs that uses a single basepoint (a point on the boundary of the ribbon graph) as auxiliary datum.

papers.title: Separating Module Gain From Transport Plan Contribution in Audio-Visual Dynamic Facial Expression Recognition
papers.abstract: A cross-modal routing module can improve over its backbone while its transport plan accounts for no demonstrable part of that improvement. In ABVnet with DFEW, Sinkhorn cross-modal routing (SCR) exceeds the retrained baseline by 0.87 unweighted average recall (UAR) points, a resolved difference, yet sits 0.17 points above an individually trained, parameter-matched pooled variant, an unresolved difference that establishes no equivalence; under the development protocol the comparison with the baseline reverses. Separating the two needs comparisons a module-against-backbone test cannot supply: parameter-matched variants changing only the plan rule, and interventions replacing the plan without retraining. The evaluation covers MMA-DFER and ABVnet on DFEW and MAFW, and MMA-DFER on CREMA-D, with a single training run per configuration and paired fold intervals. ABVnet with DFEW motivated the follow-up after the broader results were available. Replacing the plan everywhere with a uniform one reduces UAR by 0.72, whereas permuting its rows gives an unresolved difference of -0.20 UAR points; permutation is less damaging by 0.51 UAR points, a resolved contrast. Replacing the plan with the product of its own marginals, preserving both marginals and removing only frame-specific mixtures, reduces UAR by 0.70. These reductions concern reliance at inference; attribution of the module gain to the transport plan remains unestablished. Under the 1.5 fold-dependence widening, the baseline gain remains resolved, whereas the replacement reductions and the paired contrast are unresolved.

authors.institution: National Institute Of Hygiene And Epidemiology

papers.title: Reconstruction and geometry of $4\times4$ quantum Sudoku
papers.abstract: We study the reconstruction and geometry of $4 \times 4$ quantum Sudoku, viewed as arrays of rank-one projections whose rows, columns and blocks decompose the identity. We give necessary and sufficient conditions for two prescribed opposite blocks to admit a completion, prove its uniqueness, and obtain explicit reconstruction formulas, also expressed in the language of quantum logic. The sixteen overlaps between these blocks determine the unitary equivalence class of the grid, while the number of nonzero overlaps equals its cardinality. Using a matrix representation, we parametrise the equivalence classes by five closed squares, with the sides of one square identified with the diagonals of the other four. The quotient by classical cell symmetries is a closed disc containing exactly two classical classes. Finally, measurement in the basis of the first block gives a fractional Sudoku that retains the full unitary class and is a convex combination of at most four classical grids. This measurement map embeds the five-square model into a seven-dimensional polytope whose vertices are the twelve classical Sudoku.

authors.name: Karol Zyczkowski
authors.institution: Institute of Theoretical and Applied Informatics

papers.title: Confidence-Aware Discriminative Readout of Neutral-Atom Arrays
papers.abstract: Fast and reliable detection is a central requirement for neutral atom quantum computers, yet fluorescence imaging remains a limiting step for rapid experimental cycling, large-scale array operation, and quantum-error-correction protocols. In this work, we demonstrate confidence-aware readout of $^{171}\mathrm{Yb}$ atoms in optical tweezers using a discriminative classifier. Rather than forcing each atom-site image directly into a hard binary outcome, the proposed readout produces a measurement reliability score. This score is produced by a logistic-regression classifier trained on features derived from both the total photon count and the spatial pattern of fluorescence at each site. The resulting classifier achieves the same readout fidelity with approximately half the imaging time. At an exposure of 10 ms, it achieves $99.83\%$ readout fidelity, comparable to the $99.82\%$ achieved by conventional photon-count thresholding at 20 ms. Importantly, the classifier score enables low-confidence outcomes to be converted into measurement-level erasures, leaving fewer residual unflagged errors at a fixed erasure budget. This improvement is further accompanied by strong false-positive suppression, which is important for downstream operations such as atom rearrangement where false positives can create target defects. Monte Carlo rearrangement simulations show that the reduced false-positive rate and confidence-based erasure conversion improve predicted defect-free assembly performance. This work establishes confidence-aware readout using a discriminative classifier as a practical paradigm for fast and scalable neutral-atom quantum computing.

papers.title: A Closed-Form Temporal Readout for Surgical Triplet Recognition
papers.abstract: Surgical triplet recognition requires identifying which instrument performs which action on which anatomical target, and following these interactions as they unfold over time. The task is challenging because several triplets can occur at once, their components span very different durations, and the evidence for an interaction is rarely complete in a single frame. We introduce STRIDE, a post-hoc temporal readout that adds temporal context to any trained recogniser. It averages the recogniser's features and logits over a few fixed temporal windows and combines them with the current frame through ridge regression, solved in closed form on a CPU. Applied as a plug-and-play readout to nine existing methods, STRIDE improves $AP_{IVT}$ in 24 of 27 method-dataset pairs, by up to 7.4 points. Moreover, we propose a simple pipeline consisting of an adapted foundation vision encoder with a linear classifier and STRIDE. Across thirteen encoders, STRIDE improves 37 of 39 encoder-dataset pairs by up to 7.2 points. STRIDE reduces false alarms by 41%, at the cost of a slower response at interaction boundaries. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

authors.institution: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Bernard Ghanem

papers.title: Observation of collective flatbands in hybrid Mie-grating THz metasurfaces
papers.abstract: We propose a novel type of functional metasurfaces created by a hybridization of Mie resonators with high-index optical gratings. We demonstrate that such hybrid metasurfaces possess flatbands characterized by zero group velocity and strong energy localization. We experimentally observe the flatbands in free-standing terahertz (THz) metasurfaces, where dielectric interconnections between Mie resonators, forming the grating, mediate multipolar hybridization and provide a geometric control over collective resonances. Our THz near-field measurements with a dipole excitation uncover long-lived coherent oscillations associated with the quasi-flat magnetic-dipolar resonant modes, while a spatial mapping resolves the resonant electromagnetic response across the dielectric interconnections. We vary the grating width continuously to tune the hybrid magnetic-dipolar resonances and substantially enhance the quality factor (Q factor), while preserving the quasi-!atband dispersion. Complementary Bloch-resolved Purcell calculations reveal the substantial Purcell enhancement with increasing Q factor, followed by a trend towards saturation and highlighting the interplay between radiative confinement and local emitter-mode coupling. We believe our findings establish the engineering of dielectric interconnections in periodic lattices as a novel strategy for spectrally tuning high-Q flatbands in these metastructures, tailoring localized electromagnetic interactions in functional optical metasurfaces.

papers.title: Unpacking the Evaluators: How Configuration Shapes the Evaluation of Alignment in Explainable AI
papers.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) evaluation fundamentally requires human-centered evaluation, assessing whether explanations align with human reasoning and expert knowledge. However, such evaluations often require expert-driven manual validation and are difficult to scale, leading to the widespread use of alignment-based metrics, where attribution maps are compared against predefined ground-truth (GT) representations. Despite their popularity, alignment evaluations are implicitly bias towards multiple design choices made during the evaluation process, for example GT representations, metric families, metric formulations (soft vs. hard), and thresholding strategies. In this paper, we formalize alignment evaluation as a structured evaluation configuration space through which the influence of these design choices can be systematically analyzed. We further introduce a structured alignment evaluation framework that models interactions between XAI methods, GT representations, metric families, metric formulations, and thresholding strategies across 2D and 3D synthetic and real-world datasets. In addition, we propose a novel taxonomy of XAI output behavior based on local entropy and boundary mass ratio, enabling structured characterization of attribution patterns for alignment evaluation. Our experiments reveal systematic flows (triples of XAI-GT-metric configurations), showing that alignment outcomes provide distinct behavior patterns under certain configurations, such as soft/hard metric implementations. We further observe varying levels of threshold sensitivity across metric families and attribution structures. These findings demonstrate that alignment evaluation cannot be treated as a fixed or invariant measure of explanation quality, and provide practical guidance for designing more reliable and behavior-aware XAI evaluation protocols.

papers.title: Label-free self-calibration of a segmented HPGe $\gamma$-ray tracking array from the Compton scattering constraint
papers.abstract: Pulse-shape analysis in segmented HPGe $\gamma$-ray tracking arrays such as AGATA relies on reference signals for known interaction positions, which are costly to measure and only approximate when calculated. In a simulation of 51 AGATA crystals, we show that the interaction positions can be learned from the pulses without position labels. For a \Co\ photon that is Compton scattered in one segment and absorbed in another, the scattering angle follows both from the deposited energies and from the positions of the source and of the two interactions. A neural network shared by all crystals predicts one position per fired segment and is trained only to make these two angles agree; the unmeasured order of the two interactions and the selection of the pairs are revised during training. The pulses, synthesised from AGATAGeFEM bases for $2.79\times10^{6}$ pairs of fired segments whose energies add up to a \Co\ line, selected from $4\times10^{7}$ simulated decays, include noise, cross-talk, trigger-time jitter and differences between crystals. For the hits of held-out pairs, the mean three-dimensional position error falls from 10.4~mm with the segment centres to 1.65~mm, with a FWHM of 1.0--1.3~mm in each coordinate, compared with 1.07~mm for the same network trained on the simulated positions. The constraint determines the positions along the crystal axes only weakly, and at small scattering angles it pulls low-energy first interactions towards the source, which is why deposits below 200~keV are excluded. Even with the simulated positions, the two angles differ, mainly because a segment with several interactions is described by a single position and energy rather than because of Doppler broadening.

papers.title: Enumerative Chromatic Choosability of Complete Multipartite Graphs with Small Partite Sets
papers.abstract: Chromatic choosability is a notion of fundamental importance in list coloring. A graph is chromatic-choosable when its chromatic number is equal to its list chromatic number. In their 1979 paper on list coloring, Erd\H{o}s, Rubin, and Taylor showed that complete $m$-partite graphs with every partite set of size 2, denoted by $K_{2*m}$, are chromatic-choosable. In 1990, Kostochka and Sidorenko introduced the list color function of a graph $G$, denoted by $P_{\ell}(G,m)$, which is the list analogue of the chromatic polynomial of $G$, $P(G,m)$. A graph $G$ is enumeratively chromatic-choosable when $P_{\ell}(G,m) = P(G,m)$ whenever $m \in \mathbb{N}$. In this paper, we explore the question as to whether $K_{2*m}$ satisfies this stronger property. We establish a recursive lower bound on $P_{\ell}(K_{2*m},m)$ and prove that $K_{2*3}$ and $K_{2*4}$ are weakly enumeratively chromatic-choosable, meaning that equality holds at the chromatic number. We also develop a general lower bound for the list color function of certain joins with complete graphs and use it to prove that $K_p\vee K_{2*5}$ is weakly enumeratively chromatic-choosable whenever $p\geq 15$, and that $K_p\vee K_{2,2,3}$ is weakly enumeratively chromatic-choosable whenever $p\geq 3$. These results provide progress toward a weaker form of a conjecture of Allred and Mudrock concerning the enumerative chromatic choosability of complete graph joins.

authors.name: Sarah Allred
authors.institution: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey

papers.title: ARC: Adaptive Rollout Control for Efficient Synchronous LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Synchronous reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models proceeds through a repeated rollout--barrier--update loop. Each update must wait for a fixed number of complete, group-relative training samples, yet individual response lengths and reward outcomes vary widely and only emerge as generation progresses. Static admission and unconditional completion therefore leave accelerators idle in some steps, and waste computation generating samples that will never contribute to the current update. We present ARC, a closed-loop rollout architecture that governs synchronous RL rollout at group granularity. ARC uses \textit{Calibrated Streaming Backfill} to judge from partial observations whether a group is still worth completing, backfilling a fresh candidate immediately when it is not; \textit{Deferred Group Completion} to park an uncertain early stop and resume it later instead of discarding it outright, bounded by a resume-cycle limit that guarantees termination; and \textit{Adaptive Admission} and \textit{Pipelining} to order admitted samples by early-measured duration and to admit further candidates only while expected supply still falls short of the target number of accepted groups. Under online evaluation, ARC reduces rollout time by $37.4\%$, a $1.60\times$ speedup, and improves effective GRPO throughput by $50.1\%$ over existing baselines, while directly recovering 98.9\% of the training groups that would ultimately have been kept.

authors.name: Xiao Zhou
authors.institution: Henan University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Huitian Xue
authors.institution: Hunan University of Traditional Chinese Medicine

papers.title: SF-Flow: Spectral Flow Matching with High Structural Fidelity for Hallucination-Suppressed Scientific Image Generation
papers.abstract: Scientific image generation focuses on reproducing experimental appearance while following a prescribed spatial layout. A key challenge is acute data sparsity, which requires operating with unpaired collections of materials (real images and prescribed layouts), where no direct supervision is feasible. Work on unpaired translation has shown that it is possible to reproduce the texture and intensity variations of real images, but it is extremely hard to retain the intended phase boundaries in the prescribed locations. This paper tackles this challenge and introduces SF-Flow, a flow-matching model trained only on real material images that imposes spectral constraints during generation, producing images that are high-fidelity and consistent with the prescribed layouts. Because layouts enter only at generation time, the approach extends to layout maps outside the distribution of any available training layouts. We evaluate the method on synchrotron tomography of concrete, lens-coupled laboratory microCT of powders, and industrial XCT of additively manufactured metal. Without instrument-specific modeling, we show that SF-Flow achieves substantially higher template agreement and joint fidelity--structure score than previous methods, including contrastive unpaired translation.

authors.name: Patxi Fernandez-Zelaia
authors.institution: Government of the United States of America

papers.title: Same Executions, Different Gaps: Judgment Rules in Web-Agent Evaluation
papers.abstract: Success-rate gains guide the development of web agents. Yet knowing which agent ranks first does not tell us how much confidence to place in its reported advantage. We study the comparison itself: how success is defined, what evidence supports the judgments, and how the difference between agents is estimated. On fixed web-agent executions, changing a judge from predicting likely completion to requiring recorded support can remove most of a reported lead without changing the ranking. This effect persists when unresolved completion is distinguished from supported failure. Controlled source additions explain how missing relations between task requirements, objects and observations can conceal a difference or create an apparent advantage. We also find that making both agents' score estimates more accurate can make their difference less accurate, because their original errors partly canceled. To estimate a chosen outcome difference, we combine judge predictions with reference labels for sampled task pairs. Across four released execution systems, regression fitted on the same 50 labeled pairs reduces estimation error relative to direct paired sampling. The results give agent researchers a practical basis for assessing claimed improvements: make the comparison target explicit, retain the evidence needed to check it, and use paired labels to estimate the difference directly.

papers.title: Closure of averaged Einstein equations by DESI data
papers.abstract: We benchmark the hypothesis that the redshift dependence of postulated dark energy in the standard model, measured by the DESI collaboration, is a natural outcome of dark energy-free models of structure formation in general relativity. We recall fundamental results and the properties of averaged dust cosmologies that suggest to replace the dark energy equation of state through the nonperturbative impact of the inhomogeneous geometry. The relevant mechanism can be phrased in terms of an effective mean field description of inhomogeneities using the fluid analogy of a scalar field (the `morphon'). Without violating energy conditions this effective field exhibits a cross-over to phantom behaviour, compatible with observations. The exact dark energy-free framework needs a single closure condition that we implement in terms of parametrizations of the 3-years data of the DESI team. The resulting redshift dependence of effective cosmological characteristics is then illustrated and subject to physical interpretation. The aim of this paper is to set a benchmark that has to be met by any structure formation model or simulation investigated within general relativity in a flow-orthogonal foliation of spacetime, given the hypothesis.

papers.title: Computing $ab+cd$ and other expressions with correct rounding in binary floating-point arithmetic
papers.abstract: We introduce two ``high-level'' algorithms that make it possible to evaluate the sum $(x\_h+x\_\ell) + (y\_h+y\_\ell)$ of two double-word numbers with correct rounding in binary floating-point arithmetic. These algorithms allow one to evaluate expressions of the form $ab+cd$, $a+b+cd$, $a+b+c+d$, and $abc$ with correct rounding, where $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$ are floating-point numbers.

authors.name: Stef Graillat
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Exact solution of the long-range voter model in arbitrary dimensions: correlations and effective-dimensional scaling
papers.abstract: Long-range interactions can profoundly alter collective ordering and critical behavior, yet exact ana- lytical results for non-equilibrium systems with such interactions remain scarce. We obtain an exact analytical solution for the spatial correlation function of the voter model with long-range interac- tions in arbitrary spatial dimension. Starting from the evolution equation for the Fourier modes, we identify the long-wavelength dispersion generated by the interaction kernel and derive the resulting coarsening and stationary scaling regimes. The solution yields the critical condition separating these regimes, the characteristic coarsening length, and the asymptotic decay of stationary correlations. These results establish an exact effective-dimensional correspondence: the long-range model in dimen- sion d, with interaction exponent \b{eta}, exhibits the same scaling exponents as a short-range voter model in the effective dimension deff = 2d/\b{eta}. The correspondence holds across the coarsening, marginal, and stationary regimes, while the associated scaling functions need not coincide

papers.title: Probabilistic well-posedness of dispersive PDEs beyond variance blowup II: quadratic nonlinear wave equation
papers.abstract: We study the quadratic nonlinear wave equation (NLW), posed on the two-dimensional torus, with rough Gaussian random initial data beyond the variance blowup threshold observed by Okamoto and the fourth author (2021). By introducing a suitable vanishing multiplicative renormalization constant on the frequency-truncated Gaussian random initial data, we prove that the corresponding solutions converge in law to a solution to the stochastic NLW with zero initial data, driven by a Gaussian space-time noise whose temporal covariance at each spatial Fourier mode is given by the Bessel function of order $0$. We also show that the solution to the limiting equation almost surely blows up in a finite time, and that the convergence above holds on every compact time interval before the maximal existence time. %on the maximal time of existence. A main new ingredient is the analysis of the oscillatory covariance of the second Picard iterates. We identify the limiting covariance by averaging the leading oscillatory phase over the angular variable. In contrast to our previous work on the Benjamin-Bona-Mahony equation (2025), multilinear dispersive smoothing plays an essential role both in proving tightness of the second Picard iterates and in controlling the rough nonlinear interactions via paracontrolled analysis. The resulting gain of a quarter of a derivative persists in the limit, where it is reflected in the decay of the Bessel covariance.

authors.name: Guopeng Li
authors.institution: North China University of Science and Technology

papers.title: LayerCake v1.0: a framework for low- to intermediate-order automated models development
papers.abstract: A new model development framework called LayerCake is presented. It is written in the Python language and relies on the Sympy symbolic computation package to compute the Galerkin projection of two-dimensional spatially extended geophysical models. These projections provide their time evolution operator in the spectral space on a restricted set of modes. The resulting tendencies of the models can be evaluated either numerically (for time integration) or symbolically (for parameters sensitivity analysis and bifurcation analysis). We provide several simple examples of geophysical models to showcase the capabilities of the framework, and we hint at how more complex systems can be designed.

papers.title: Beyond PINNs: Boundary-Enriched Holomorphic Networks for Laplace Problems
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) solve partial differential equations by penalizing their residual, but this formulation can be difficult to optimize for solutions with singular behaviour. We focus specifically on the two-dimensional Laplace equation, whose strong analytical structure allows the governing equation to be enforced directly in the neural representation. We compare a hybrid harmonic-neural model with a holomorphic neural network whose output is harmonic by construction and therefore requires only boundary training. We further enrich the holomorphic model with singular functions chosen according to the interior angle and boundary conditions at each junction of boundary segments. On six singular benchmarks, the enriched model is the most accurate of the neural models we compare. On the four with a closed-form solution, however, that solution lies in the span of the enrichment terms, and a least-squares fit of these terms alone is exact to rounding error. On Motz's problem and the cracked beam, the neural core reduces the relative error of the recovered leading singular coefficient from about $10^{-2}$, for a least-squares fit with the same four terms, to about $10^{-6}$, and on four variants whose solution has a smooth part outside the span, the network is $4\times10^{4}$ to $2\times10^{7}$ times more accurate than a fit of its singular terms alone; classical least-squares fits with more singular terms, or with harmonic polynomials and rational poles, are more accurate still. Our results demonstrate how exploiting problem-specific analytical structure can provide an alternative to base and residual PINNs for challenging scientific computing problems.

papers.title: Rethinking Visual Token Retention in Multimodal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Autoregressive Large Vision-Language Models solve multimodal reasoning tasks by retaining hundreds or thousands of visual tokens, allowing every generated token to attend to the visual tokens at any time during the generation process. However, whether continuous access to these visual tokens is necessary remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate how visual token influence evolves along two dimensions: generation time and transformer depth. Using long-form visual reasoning benchmarks and multiple model scales, we first analyze the attention dynamics across generation time and transformer depth. We identify a temporal and depth-wise structure in the use of visual information. Visual attention peaks during the initial generation steps and then rapidly declines as attention shifts toward previously generated reasoning tokens. Across depth, visual influence is concentrated in intermediate layers and becomes very weak in the final layers. We further verify these observations with causal intervention that removes all visual tokens across generation time and model depth. These interventions confirm that visual-token dependence in multimodal reasoning is neither temporally persistent nor uniformly distributed across transformer depth. Thus, retaining the complete visual context at every layer and decoding step may be unnecessary. Our experiments demonstrate that we can remove up to 59\% of tokens from the full input prompt across generation time and 11\% across all transformer layers, while incurring only a very small performance drop. On video benchmarks, up to 65\% of the input prompt tokens can be removed during generation without affecting performance.

papers.title: Evaluating VLT SPHERE for Probing Diffuse Circumstellar Regions of Evolved Stars
papers.abstract: Red and Yellow Supergiant stars, generally found in late evolutionary stages with high mass loss, provide test cases for evaluating high-contrast imaging performance. Determining how well adaptive optics combined with coronagraphy isolates faint circumstellar emission allows us to define its true sensitivity limits for evolved stars and refine future high-contrast observing strategies. We conducted a pilot study of seven nearby (within 0.8 kpc), bright (V-band magnitude of 10 or less) evolved red and yellow supergiants. We selected these targets to evaluate the ability of the VLT's SPHERE/IRDIS high-contrast imaging instrument to detect faint, diffuse circumstellar emission in four infrared filters (J1, J2, K1, and K2). We processed the data using RDI to remove the stellar PSF, AO speckles, and diffraction patterns. We extracted radial profiles and performed Radon transform analysis to search for faint extended emission around each target. We detect no extended circumstellar emission in our high-contrast images or clear infrared excess in the SEDs of our seven targets. Injection-recovery tests demonstrate sensitivity to diffuse emission at contrasts of approximately 3.5 mag in the J1 and approximately 2.0 mag in K1 relative to the residual coronagraphic PSF halo. This study provides the first results that elucidate the observational conditions under which SPHERE/IRDIS fails to recover low surface brightness emission and highlights the observational factors that most strongly control detectability, including filter choice, sky calibration, and reference-star matching. Our results motivate future studies to prioritize targets with infrared excess and optimize observing strategies to improve sensitivity to faint circumstellar emission around evolved massive stars.

authors.name: Saida M. Caballero-Nieves
authors.institution: Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University Daytona Beach Florida Campus

authors.name: Keefe J. Kamp
authors.institution: Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University Daytona Beach Florida Campus

papers.title: LITMUS - Literature Informed Testbed for Mapping Usecases and Synthesizing Risk-Cards
papers.abstract: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in real-world applications has heightened the need for systematic, safety-oriented deployment frameworks. Existing approaches typically prioritize the construction of datasets and risk cards around the LLM and AI architecture itself, yet they provide scant consideration for the specific use-case that drives model selection. This omission is problematic because any practical AI deployment begins with a detailed use-case description that informs the assessment of contextual hazards. In this paper, we introduce a structured pipeline that, given a use-case, automatically produces a tailored dataset and an accompanying risk card. The process ensures that identified risks are tightly coupled to the use-case, and it offers traceable evidence from peer-reviewed literature to substantiate each risk to use-case relationship. Prior claim-verification methods (FActScore, FactReasoner) have been validated for factual claims. Risk-relevance is a hypothetical claim about possible harm, and whether evidence retrieval can meaningfully assess such claims remains untested. Literature-Informed Testbed for Mapping Use-cases and Synthesizing (LITMUS) risk cards are the first systematic attempt to characterize this adaptation. We evaluated the pipeline using the MIT Risk Taxonomy and achieved a 0.91 F1-score with a list of 320 samples from the benchmark risk dataset that was considered. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in generating robust, evidence-based risk assessments for LLM deployments.

papers.title: Scaled Relative Graph Separation for Unbounded Nonlinear Systems
papers.abstract: We investigate stability analysis of one-channel nonlinear feedback systems based on the recent notion of scaled relative graph (SRG). Our focus is on the SRG separation in the complex plane for feedback stability analysis that involves possibly unbounded open-loop nonlinear systems. Subject to a technical assumption, a homotopy-based SRG separation theorem is developed as the main result, where the incremental directed gap is utilized as a key instrument to quantify robust feedback stability along the homotopy path. Doing so enables us to incorporate commonly used integrators as unbounded systems in the SRG-based framework. Specializations of the main result to linear systems, along with illustrative examples, are also provided to demonstrate its effectiveness.

authors.name: Sei Zhen Khong
authors.institution: Université de Pau et des Pays de l'Adour

papers.title: Stellar Temporal Intensity Interferometry with Adaptive Optics at the Palomar Observatory
papers.abstract: Spatial intensity interferometry has seen a major resurgence in astronomy due to its immunity to atmospheric phase turbulence, but its temporal counterpart - a cornerstone of quantum optics - has remained largely unexplored for astronomical sources. Here, we demonstrate that high-visibility temporal photon bunching signatures from stellar sources are now accessible by combining ultra-narrowband spectral filtering with high-speed single-photon counting detectors. Leveraging the adaptive optics architecture at the Palomar Observatory, we report the first observation of resolved stellar temporal photon bunching, with a peak of $g^{(2)}(\tau=0) = 1.3 \pm 0.1$, from the red supergiant $\alpha$ Her. This advance establishes stellar temporal intensity interferometry as a viable observational modality, bridging quantum optics with high-resolution stellar astrophysics.

papers.title: Analytic nuclear gradients for electronic resonances with the equation-of-motion coupled-cluster method and complex basis functions
papers.abstract: We present the general theory for and an efficient implementation of the analytic nuclear gradient for states which are metastable with respect to electronic decay within the equation-of-motion coupled-cluster singles-and-doubles family of methods using complex-scaled basis functions. We highlight the differences of our approach with the complex-absorbing potential method and outline a computational protocol for geometry optimisations and we use the method to compute equilibrium structures and harmonic vibrational frequencies of a number of temporary anion shape resonances and core-ionised Feshbach resonances.

papers.title: The monodromy conjecture for remarkable poles
papers.abstract: We prove the strong monodromy conjecture for the remarkable numbers of a regular function f on a smooth complex variety. We show more generally that the log canonical modification of f computes the remarkable numbers and gives roots of the Bernstein-Sato polynomial of f.

papers.title: SONATI: Spatio-temporal ocean neighbourhood asymmetric transformer for imputation of sparse, tabular data with uncertainty
papers.abstract: Missing value imputation is often a prerequisite for downstream analyses. In oceanography, observational data are frequently structured in a tabular manner, highly sparse and exhibit spatio-temporal structures that classical imputers such as k-nearest neighbours or MissForest are not suited to exploit. We present the Spatio-temporal Ocean Neighbourhood Asymmetric Transformer for Imputation (SONATI), a masked, factorised time-space transformer operating on pre-computed, local time and space neighbourhoods, which reduces computational complexity compared to global attention. SONATI is designed to work with tabular data and is thus in principle able to work on both gridded and unstructured data, though evaluation here was performed on gridded North Atlantic data only. It provides aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties through a negative log-likelihood loss and multiple forward passes with Monte Carlo dropout. Systematic ablations on attention type and masking strategies guided the final architecture design. The results showed that SONATI outperformed classical and transformer-based methods by at least 12.5% in terms of root mean squared error (RMSE) on a large observational oceanographic dataset with key biogeochemical and physical parameters in the North Atlantic (potential temperature, salinity, oxygen, nitrate, silicate and phosphate). Attention type and masking strategy strongly affected imputation accuracy and smoothness of the produced oceanographic fields. Best results were achieved by factorised time-space attention and combined geographic and per-sample masking. The combined masking strategy reduced the imputation error by 14.3% compared to per-sample masking only. Uncertainties were moderately well calibrated (miscalibration area at observed locations $0.074\pm0.012$) and moderately correlated with the imputation error.

papers.title: SayDo: Benchmarking the Safety of Frontier Models from Chat to Closed-Loop Robot Control
papers.abstract: Frontier vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as high-level robot controllers, yet their safety is evaluated almost entirely in text. We introduce SayDo, a benchmark that assesses the propensity of frontier models to cause harm in embodied contexts. SayDo comprises eleven laboratory and household tasks that pair a benign instruction with a hazard latent in the scene. Tasks are implemented in six settings along an embodiment gradient, from chat questions about an imagined robot to closed-loop control of a simulated robot arm. Benign controls, safe-alternative variants and scripted operator pushback complement each task. Across six open- and closed-weight VLMs and 11,480 episodes, hazardous-action rates rise from 14% in chat to 47% in the simulator, and from 2% to 80% for the most affected model. The increase is largely driven by open-weight models. We find that models flag hazards before acting in 73% of unsafe episodes and give way to pushback about twice as often when controlling robots as in chat. The safest models also show signs of overcaution on benign controls. Safety evaluations run in text therefore do not predict the safety behavior of the same models when used as robot controllers.

papers.title: Learning a Food World Model That Predicts the Next State from Production Data
papers.abstract: Food assembly robots pick ingredients from a pan, and every pick must deliver a target weight. We learn a world model of food picking from 61,773 production picks, labeled automatically by a camera and a scale (self-supervised learning). From the pre-pick heightmap of the pan on a 2.5 mm grid, the commanded pick action, the food and the utensil, the model predicts the post-pick heightmap and the picked mass with uncertainty. We evaluate the mass prediction on 12,294 held-out picks of nine foods. The production controller keeps each pick near its commanded target. The model's root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 10.93 g is 9% lower than that of the commanded target or of a per-food mean. This RMSE is 24% lower than that of the controller's internal mass estimate. Gradient-boosted trees on 20 hand-crafted features have a 0.2 g lower RMSE, but they predict only the mass, not the next state that planning and policy learning need. Using the predicted uncertainty, we decline the most uncertain picks and answer 89.4% of picks with an RMSE of 10.28 g. The prediction barely responds to the commanded volume and depth, because they vary little in closed-loop production. The model also fails without warning at target weights not seen in training. Future directions include action-primitive conditioning and a more general model across foods and utensils. We give recommendations for learning world models from production data.

papers.title: Eight limit cycles in a three-dimensional competitive Lotka-Volterra system
papers.abstract: Gyllenberg and Yan conjectured that a three-dimensional competitive Lotka-Volterra system can have at least five limit cycles. We prove the conjecture by constructing a strictly competitive system in which eight distinct limit cycles coexist near a single positive equilibrium. For each $m=5,6,7,8$, we construct a weak focus of order $m$ and identify parameter directions on the Hopf hypersurface that allow us to vary the first $m-1$ focus quantities independently. We choose these quantities so that the drift of a scalar amplitude function alternates in sign on $m$ nested level curves, forcing a limit cycle between each consecutive pair. A perturbation transverse to the Hopf hypersurface creates one additional cycle inside the others. The one-turn displacement map shows that both local counts are sharp. For each $m$, we give a rigorous computer-assisted proof that an explicit rational interaction matrix yields at least $m$ distinct hyperbolic limit cycles. We thank GPT-6 Astra for helping us compare earlier constructions, identify the main obstacle to extending them, and develop the present approach.

papers.title: Zariski-constructible functions of class $\mathcal{C}^k$
papers.abstract:
Let $R$ be a real closed field. A Zariski-constructible subset of $R^n$, $\mathcal{ZC}$-set for short, is a Boolean combination of algebraic subsets of $R^n$. Euclidean closed Zariski-constructible subsets of $R^n$ are the closed subsets of a Noetherian topology finer than the Zariski topology of $R^n$.
  Let $k\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$. Let $U\subset R^n$ be a $\mathcal{ZC}$-open set. We say that a function $f:U\to R$ of class $\mathcal{C}^k$ is a Zariski-constructible function, $\mathcal{ZC}^k$-function for short, if its graph is a $\mathcal{ZC}$-set. For instance, regular and $k$-regulous functions on $R^n$ are $\mathcal{ZC}^k$-functions. We show that the ring $\mathcal{ZC}^k(U)$ of $\mathcal{ZC}^k$-functions on a $\mathcal{ZC}$-open set is way richer, even for $k=\infty$, although $\infty$-regulous functions are just regular. Then, we extend the notion of $\mathcal{ZC}^k$-function over any $\mathcal{ZC}$-locally closed subset $X$ of $R^n$.
  This paper is mainly devoted to the study of the geometric and algebraic properties of the ring $\mathcal{ZC}^k(X)$ of $\mathcal{ZC}^k$-functions on a $\mathcal{ZC}$-locally closed subset $X$ of $R^n$. From now on, assume that $k\in\mathbb N$. We show that $\mathcal{ZC}$-closed subsets $X$ of $R^n$ are exactly the zero loci of $\mathcal{ZC}^k$-functions on $R^n$. We show that the Nullstellensatz holds in the ring $\mathcal{ZC}^k(U)$, where $U$ is a $\mathcal{ZC}$-open subset of $R^n$, and that this ring is radically principal. As a consequence of the Nullstellensatz, we prove that any $\mathcal{ZC}^k$-function on a $\mathcal{ZC}$-locally closed subset $X$ of $R^n$ extends to a $\mathcal{ZC}$-open neighborhood $U$ of $X$. Then, we translate our results into the language of sheaves of $\mathcal{ZC}^k$-functions on $\mathcal{ZC}$-locally closed sets, from which we deduce a $\mathcal{ZC}^k$-version of Cartan's theorems A and B.

papers.title: Fishburn Numbers Count Homogeneous Games
papers.abstract: We prove a new combinatorial interpretation for Fishburn numbers, in that they count the number of homogeneous games; specifically homogeneous games without dummy players, which we show extends to homogeneous games via the partial sums of Fishburn numbers. In doing so, we settle two conjectures commented in the OEIS A189359 entry, and finish off by providing some immediate consequences on homogeneous game counts; including an asymptotic formula and congruences.

papers.title: Project financing in vanishing forests: Do investors care about nature protection?
papers.abstract: Biodiversity risks are increasingly recognized by financial market participants, yet their measurement at the corporate-entity level obscures the locations and assets through which they arise. Project finance links identifiable physical assets to dedicated financing contracts, allowing us to examine this transmission more directly. By linking 9,037 project-loan pairs in 115 countries, we relate bank loan spreads to projects' proximity to protected areas, surrounding forest loss and lenders' nature policies. We find that lenders price proximity to protected areas only when they also have explicit nature risk policies and particularly within 1.5 km buffers from the project location. Realised forest loss around a project is priced more consistently than forest loss after the loan is signed, and risk pricing near protected areas strengthens after the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. Listed company sponsors also experience negative, but short-lived, abnormal returns around loan signings for projects within 30 km of protected areas or in high-forest-loss landscapes. Our results suggest that while nature risk is partially priced in project finance, this is not a strong incentive to deter significant harm to nature.

papers.title: Asteroseismic investigation of intermediate age open star cluster NGC 2126
papers.abstract: We present a preliminary asteroseismic investigation of the pulsating stars in the intermediate-age open cluster NGC 2126. The TESS Full Frame Images and ground-based photometry from the previous study, Dileep et al. (2025), were used to identify the pulsation modes of {\delta} Scuti member stars using period-luminosity relations and pulsation modelling. Our analysis resulted in a tentative identification up to the first radial overtone in stars N1, N2 and ZV1. Additionally, the second radial overtone was secured in N1. The disentangled pulsation and eclipse light curves of the binary star V551 Aur (V6) from our previous research were employed to study pulsation amplitude and phase modulations across the orbital period. The primary component of V6 exhibits pulsations showing amplitude and phase modulations, indicating tidal influence on the oscillations. Modelling the pulsation as the fundamental radial mode reveals that in order for the mode to be radial, the star must be significantly brighter than observed. Hence, the mode is not the fundamental radial mode or the overtones. Low-resolution spectroscopy was used to search for chemical peculiarities in the pulsating members, and we found that star ID 143 has features similar to an Am star.
