papers.abstract: Next-generation wireless networks increasingly rely on low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites for broad coverage and low latency, making efficient handover management essential. We formulate satellite handover as a combinatorial optimization problem, assigning each ground user to exactly one capacity-limited, visible satellite while minimizing network handover costs. We propose a reinforcement learning (RL)-based branch-and-price (B&P) framework with learned multiple-column selection (MCS) to accelerate column generation while retaining exact dynamic programming pricing. We also develop two lightweight heuristic policies: handover-aware visibility duration (HAVD) for online decisions and congestion-aware predictive (CAP) for offline planning. Additionally, a local-search repair algorithm adapts precomputed B&P or MCS-B&P solutions to demand perturbations through single-flip and per-user trajectory re-optimization, avoiding complete re-optimization. Simulations using realistic large scale constellations, including Starlink Gen-1, demonstrate that MCS-B&P achieves solution quality comparable to exact B&P with fewer column-generation iterations, fewer branch-and-bound nodes, and reduced computation time. HAVD and CAP offer effective online and offline cost-latency trade-offs, while local-search repair recovers most performance losses due to demand perturbations at a fraction of the computational cost of full re-optimization.

papers.title: CrysLDM: Latent Diffusion Model for Crystal Material Generation
papers.abstract: Generating new crystal materials with desirable chemical properties has long been a challenging task. Existing diffusion models operate in feature space, requiring complex diffusion architectures to model the joint distribution of atom types, coordinates, and lattice structures. This complexity increases the number of diffusion steps, leading to higher training and sampling costs. In this work, we aim to generate novel crystal materials within a time- and resource-constrained setup, where existing models are not well-suited. To address this, we propose CrysLDM, a novel latent diffusion model for 3D crystal materials, which integrates a variational autoencoder and a diffusion model. The VAE encoder maps 3D crystal structures into a latent space, where the diffusion model operates. Since CrysLDM leverages a smooth, lower-dimensional latent space, it simplifies the generative process and accelerates both training and inference. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets and tasks, we show that CrysLDM generates stable and valid materials with quality comparable to state-of-the-art methods, while being significantly more efficient in terms of computational resources and time.

papers.title: LeJEPA Features Are Not Isotropic, and Should Not Be
papers.abstract: The SIGReg term in LeJEPA regularizes features to have an isotropic Gaussian distribution. Our first result is to show that this regularizer, in practice, cannot achieve its goal. We design a modified regularizer to enforce the objective better. This leads to slightly improved performance. For example, on ImageNet-100, our modified regularizer reaches the final accuracy of SIGReg in 1.3$\times$ fewer epochs. Our second result argues that self-supervised encoders should not have isotropic Gaussian features. We show that the alignment term in LeJEPA conflicts with SIGReg, because it couples the magnitude of the features with their directions. In contrast, isotropic Gaussian features would entail independent magnitude and directions. Features obtained with LeJEPA are, in fact, not isotropic. So LeJEPA has two issues. Its regularizer is weak, and the isotropic Gaussian target is too strict. Our third result is about reformulating the isotropic Gaussian regularizer to enforce only the marginal distributions of the magnitude and direction, without enforcing independence. This leads to a simple regularization term, PolarReg, that can be optimized reliably across many different datasets, batch sizes and embedding dimensions without any hyper-parameter changes. On ImageNet-1k, our technique matches the accuracy of LeJEPA and its variants in 4.7$\times$ fewer epochs. It improves the final accuracy by 1.8 points.

papers.title: PFN-Syn: Generating Synthetic Tabular Data with Prior-Data Fitted Networks
papers.abstract: Synthetic tabular data can help enable data sharing and model development in privacy-sensitive domains, but existing generators often require dataset-specific training and substantial computation. We introduce PFN-Syn, a training-free framework for synthetic tabular data generation based on prior-data fitted networks. We evaluate PFN-Syn against training-based generators on eight binary classification datasets. PFN-Syn achieves the highest average downstream utility among evaluated synthetic generators, with higher generation throughput than training-based baselines, while maintaining competitive distributional similarity and distance-to-closest-record privacy behavior. Our results suggest that tabular foundation models can serve as useful building blocks for practical synthetic tabular data generation.

papers.title: Moore spaces, polyhedral products, and positive scalar curvature
papers.abstract: Gromov conjectured that the macroscopic dimension of the universal cover of a closed $n$-manifold of positive scalar curvature is at most $n-2$. Gromov's conjecture holds for a closed spin manifold of dimension $n\geq 5$, provided that its fundamental group has property $(*)_m$, i.e., its classifying space is stably homotopy equivalent to a wedge of Moore spaces. We prove property $(*)_m$ for a large class of groups, including for instance the fundamental groups of closed hyperbolic $3$-manifolds, the commutator subgroups of right-angled Coxeter groups with low-dimensional nerves, pure braid groups, and many graph products thereof. As an additional application of independent interest, we show that there are finite-index subgroups of right-angled Artin groups that do not have property $(*)_m$ and can have arbitrary torsion in their (co)homology in any degree.

papers.title: JEPA-Tuner: From Predictive Fine-Tuning to Asynchronous Execution of Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate sequences of actions from visual observations, proprioceptive states, and language instructions. In embodied interaction, executing these actions influences subsequent observations and robot states, providing a natural predictive signal for policy learning. However, standard action-supervised fine-tuning does not explicitly capture these action-conditioned temporal dependencies in the guidance consumed by the action predictor. We introduce JEPA-Tuner, a predictive fine-tuning framework that regularizes the VLA's native policy guidance through action-conditioned future prediction. During fine-tuning, a predictor in JEPA-Tuner learns to match guidance encoded from a future observation given the current guidance and committed actions. This objective encourages a cross-modal guidance adapter to capture how the scene and robot state evolve under those actions, while jointly training the action expert on both observed and predicted guidance keeps the representation informative for control. In addition, when deploying the VLA model with asynchronous action-chunk inference, the pre-trained predictor will anticipate the guidance needed at the next chunk boundary. The policy can thus generate the next chunk in advance and execute it from its first action without overlap correction or additional predictor training, enabling efficient and high-quality asynchronous execution. Experiments on LIBERO and Meta-World show that JEPA-Tuner improves task success under synchronous inference with better multi-modal guidance embeddings. For asynchronous control, JEPA-Tuner improves performance and smoothness across different latency settings on both LIBERO simulator and multi-size real robot demonstrations. The project website with video demos is at https://qujx.github.io/JEPA-Tuner-Website.

authors.name: Yi Liu
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology Liaoning

papers.title: Principal subspaces of affine vertex algebras at admissible levels
papers.abstract: We classify generic principal subspaces of admissible affine vertex algebras for all simple Lie algebras. The nongeneric cases occur precisely at denominator two in types $B,C,F_4$ and at denominator three in type $G_2$. The proof uses geometry of nilpotent orbits combined with positive root null vectors. Surprisingly, null vectors needed for our classification are explicitly known and already studied in the literature. We then study the exceptional principal subspaces at the level of their $C_2$-algebras and arc algebras. For $\mathfrak{sp}_4$ at level $-\frac12$ and $G_2$ at level $-\frac53$, we prove classical freeness and obtain product character formulas. In type $C_n$ at level $-\frac12$, classical freeness fails for $n\ge4$. For $n=3$, we combine the functional model method of Feigin and Stoyanovsky, and a flat degeneration of the explicit realization of $L_{-3/2}(\mathfrak{sl}_3)$ to prove a product character formula, while classical freeness in this case remains conjectural. The principal subspace of $L_{-5/2}(F_4)$ is also conjecturally classically free.

papers.title: Probability-Feasible Historical Transport: Sharp Bounds and Falsification Tests for Distributional Pre-Trend Designs
papers.abstract: Distributional difference-in-differences studies often assume that the post-policy gap between treated and comparison groups is a mixture of pre-policy gaps. This historical-transport assumption can fail in ways that one-statistic checks miss. When policy events are pooled, the average counterfactual can be a valid distribution although no event's counterfactual is, and pooled bounds can exclude the true average effect. Mixtures of past gaps can assign negative probability to outcomes, and cutoff-by-cutoff bounds can be incompatible. We characterize sharp bounds and give breakdown radii, a grid-free confidence region, and tests with and without an experiment. The tests reject transport in the National Supported Work data and expose impossible state counterfactuals behind a pooled minimum-wage bound. For the 1993 Earned Income Tax Credit expansion they pass through 1995, when bounds put single mothers' employment gain relative to childless women at 5 to 7 points; the gain stays positive after dropping early welfare-waiver states.

authors.name: Ulrich Hounyo
authors.institution: University at Albany, State University of New York

papers.title: Nonequilibrium fluctuations could explain the hot mitochondria paradox
papers.abstract: Several different experiments have found apparent temperature differences of up to 10 K between the interior of mitochondria and the rest of the cellular environment. The physics of heat conduction, however, precludes the steady-state existence of a temperature difference greater than the microkelvin scale within the cell, absent a far greater energy budget. Nearly a decade after the first reported measurement, this apparent paradox remains unexplained. Here, we propose an explanation which allows the elevated temperature measurements to coexist with the theoretical impossibility of a true 10 K steady-state temperature difference. We suggest that nonequilibrium fluctuations within the cellular environment, combined with molecular temperature probes sensitive to specific ranges of frequencies, can lead to apparent 10 K temperature differences with a biologically attainable power budget.

papers.title: Bound to be Complete: Efficient Verification for SQL Equivalence via U-Expressions
papers.abstract:
Automated verification of SQL query equivalence is a fundamental problem in database area. Recent works developed verifiers with guaranteed completeness, which can generate counterexamples to disprove non-equivalent queries and are useful in various scenarios. However, they have to solve complex formulas and can fail to produce counterexamples within a reasonable time budget.
  This paper presents a new complete verifier called SQLution, which not only greatly reduces the verification time, but also supports more SQL features. The key insight is to represent SQL semantics using U-expression, a functional algebra that can model SQL with significantly simpler formulas than prior works, thereby leading to more efficient SMT solving. To turn this insight into a practical verifier, SQLution further tackles two technical challenges associated with modeling SQL using U-expression, namely, the lack of tuple ordering and the presence of unbounded summations. In particular, to support tuple ordering, SQLution proposes order semantics encoding which combines U-expressions with first-order logic. To handle unbounded summation, SQLution introduces unbounded summation expansion to transform them into bounded summations, which can be directly encoded into FOL formulas. Evaluation shows that compared with state-of-the-art verifiers, SQLution can support all 271 non-equivalent query pairs derived from the Spider dataset and reduces verification time by up to 98.6%.

authors.name: Haoran Ding
authors.institution: State Grid Liaoning Electric Power Company (China)

authors.name: Jinyang Li
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Praxis: Practical Witness Encryption for NP
papers.abstract:
Witness encryption encrypts a message to an NP statement so that whoever holds a witness can decrypt. Over a decade after its introduction, known constructions for general NP statements are far from practical or rest on heuristic or broken assumptions. We propose Praxis, a practical scheme for NP, and prove it extractable in the bilinear generic group and random oracle models under Module-SIS. Our instantiation encrypts to a Groth16 verifier on BN254, set up honestly, which serves every NP relation at the same cost: at $100$-bit security, its ciphertext is $7.88$ GiB, encryption takes $2^{34.2}$ base-field multiplications, and decryption with a Groth16 proof $2^{33.0}$ on average. We give Lean 4 proofs of correctness and extraction at this instantiation's parameters.
  Praxis starts from the rank-gap template of the recent feasibility result [Hair and Sahai, arXiv 2026]. Where they raise the gap to keep decryption polynomial, we fix it, so decryption ends with a search that is exponential but concretely fast: $O(2^{\lambda/4} N^{1/4})$ expected operations for a statement in $N$ Boolean unknowns at $\lambda$-bit security. A quadratic arithmetic program makes our hidden matrix low rank, so where their ciphertext encodes a basis of a matrix space, ours holds factors of width two, which a pairing multiplies. Weights and identities from an extension field tie copies of this matrix, so an adversary telling encryptions apart yields a witness or a Module-SIS solution. For the same Groth16 statement and $100$-bit security level, Praxis reduces the ciphertext size and the cost of encryption of either of their constructions by over ten orders of magnitude, and that of decryption by over six.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating the Fragility of Self-Rewarding Optimization
papers.abstract: Self-rewarding optimization (SRO) promises to improve language models by enabling them to generate their own reward signals. Yet when and how SRO succeeds or fails remains poorly understood. We reveal that SRO is fundamentally fragile: even seemingly benign perturbations to training prompts can corrupt the self-generated preference signal and trigger iterative collapse. We demonstrate this through two prompt-level attacks that serve as controlled stress tests: a Re-Ranking attack that concentrates training on prompts where self-reward diverges from an oracle, and a Preamble attack that learns short prefixes inflating self-reward without any gain in oracle quality. To explain why these attacks succeed, we introduce self-reward fidelity (SRF), a metric quantifying on-policy agreement between self-evaluated and oracle rewards. We show that SRF can serve as a diagnostic signal of self-supervision reliability, and that controlled SRF perturbations induce a phase-transition region: SRO improves when SRF remains sufficiently high, but collapses once SRF drops below a model- and task-dependent threshold. This analysis motivates Projection Decoupling Defense, which suppresses SRO update components along directions to which the reward generator is locally sensitive, improving SRO robustness under adversarial conditions. This work sheds light on the fragility of SRO and charts promising directions toward making it more robust.

papers.title: Demystifying Classifier-Free Guidance for Auto-Regressive Image Generation
papers.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) has been widely adopted in autoregressive (AR) models for high-quality image generation. Despite its strong empirical performance, its mechanism in AR models remains unclear. This paper demystifies the mechanism of CFG through both empirical and theoretical studies. By examining the top-ranked semantics of different components in CFG, we show that texture information is primarily encoded in the difference between the conditional and unconditional logits, whereas both logits share previous-token repetition as their leading semantics. This strong repetition semantics obscures the desired texture information, causing greedy decoding from the conditional logits alone to produce nearly pure-color images. Through a training-dynamics analysis of shallow transformers, we prove that this shared repetition semantics does not arise from limitations or failures of pretraining, but instead originates from the texture sparsity of images. We further show that CFG improves generation quality by rectifying this repetition bias during inference. Motivated by the shared semantics between conditional and unconditional logits, we propose Attention Weight Reuse (AttnReuse), which reuses intermediate attention computations from the conditional-logit forward pass to accelerate the unconditional-logit computation. AttnReuse reduces about $25\%$ of attention computation with little performance degradation across different models.

authors.name: Jiachun Pan
authors.institution: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College

papers.title: Grounding Collaborative Agents in Group Cognition
papers.abstract: Collaborative agents joining an ongoing team rely on shared context to connect multi-party interaction histories with downstream coordination decisions. Existing work typically focuses either on retrieving historical facts from conversation logs, which surfaces isolated evidence without capturing who knows or owns what, or on evaluating end-to-end interactions, which conflates preparation with execution and lacks direct supervision because a team's history has no single ground-truth summary. To bridge this gap, we formulate group briefing, the task of reconstructing task-relevant group cognition across participants' expressed beliefs, group dynamics, and grounding gaps, and introduce a four-domain benchmark of 1,351 requests and 9,975 verified reference points paired with a two-stage evaluation pipeline combining reference-point coverage and downstream collaboration simulation. Using this pipeline, we show that GroupBrief, a simple task-guided approach that iteratively probes the message history and synthesizes a structured brief without offline memory indexing or graph construction, outperforms ten retrieval and agent-memory baselines in overall coverage with gpt-5.4-mini, while benchmarking nine language models reveals that prospective friction remains harder to recover than past state across model scales. We further use reference-point coverage as a feedback signal for harness optimization, refining GroupBrief's retrieval and synthesis instructions while keeping model weights frozen. On held-out Test projects, GroupBrief (optimized) improves coverage by 2.54 percentage points for gpt-5.4-mini and 12.88 for gpt-5.6-luna, achieving 64.46% and 68.42% preference over no brief in downstream simulations. These results establish our benchmark and evaluation pipeline as a foundation for measuring and optimizing how collaborative agents ground in group cognition.

papers.title: The broken-sample problem revisited II: Detecting hidden linear dependencies
papers.abstract:
We study the detection problem for shuffled linear regression, in which the covariates and the responses are either independent or linearly related through a latent correspondence. Consider independent standard Gaussian covariates \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\in\mathbb R^d\) and scalar responses \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\). In a shuffled linear model, \(Y_i=\langle X_{\pi_*(i)},\beta_*\rangle+\sigma Z_i\), where both the permutation \(\pi_*\) and the regression coefficient $\beta_*$ are latent and $Z_i$'s are white Gaussian noise. The goal is to distinguish this model from one in which the covariates and responses are independent with the same marginal distribution.
  In the low-dimensional regime of $d \ll \frac{\log n}{\log\log n}$, we show that the detection threshold is given by $\sigma=o(1)$ for fixed $d$ and $\sigma^2 = \Theta(\frac{1}{d\log d})$ for growing $d$; both thresholds are achieved in nearly linear time using moment-based test statistics inspired by matched filters in signal processing. For higher dimensions, tests based on sliced Wasserstein distance succeed when $\sigma^2 = o(\frac{1}{(d\log d)^2})$, while the optimal threshold remains open.
  As a by-product, we show that the shuffled linear model exhibits an ``all-or-nothing'' phase transition for estimating $\beta_*$ at $\sigma^2\asymp \frac{1}{d\log d}$ in low dimensions. In particular, $\beta_*$ can be consistently estimated in nearly linear time, even when it is information-theoretically impossible to recover any positive fraction of the latent matching $\pi^*$.

papers.title: Neural Agent Compiler: Learning to Schedule Soft Dependencies
papers.abstract: Large language model agents accomplish complex tasks by coordinating multiple reasoning steps and tool operations, which form dependencies among their operations. Existing orchestration methods primarily consider hard dependencies that determine when an operation can legally begin, but overlook soft dependencies, i.e., information that is not required for execution but may improve an already executable operation. We identify soft-dependency scheduling as an important problem in agent execution. To this end, we introduce Neural Agent Compiler (NAC), a learned scheduler that predicts the task-quality and resource consequences of three execution modes and selects the highest-utility legal mode at a scheduling boundary. NAC represents the executable continuation, pending information event, and resource state in a shared memory, and uses a utility function to adapt the consequence predictions to different resource preferences. Across AppWorld, WebShop, and $\tau^2$-bench, NAC achieves 276/417 AppWorld task completions, a 74.69 WebShop Task Score, and 59/100 $\tau^2$-bench successes. Additional studies show that the learned scheduler reduces execution work, establishing soft-dependency scheduling as a promising solution for orchestrating tool-using agents.

authors.name: Bo Sun
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Probe Before You Learn: Allocating Prompts from Initial Gradients under Label Noise
papers.abstract: Prompt learning provides a parameter-efficient way to adapt pretrained vision--language models through text and visual prompts, but noisy labels prevalent in real-world data inevitably bias prompt updates and thereby undermine adaptation effectiveness. Prior work on robust prompt learning focuses on suppressing unreliable updates under noisy supervision. We uncover a pivotal yet overlooked aspect--prompt allocation: shifting the parameter budget between text and visual prompts can substantially enhance robustness while keeping the training objective and total budget fixed. However, suitable prompt allocations vary across tasks and are unknown a priori, rendering brute-force candidate training computationally prohibitive. We propose GPrompt, a training-free method that derives allocation between text and visual prompts using only loss gradients at initialization before prompt optimization. Using a small sample of images and generated pseudo-labels as shared supervision, GPrompt performs an initialization probe to extract paired text and visual loss gradients, and characterizes the geometry of their trace-normalized Gram matrices through both concentration within each modality and overlap between modalities. GPrompt then derives a closed-form allocation, and projects it onto feasible prompt counts under the exact parameter budget, enabling task-specific selection without training candidate configurations. Experiments across eleven datasets show that GPrompt outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 7.75% while selecting configurations close to the best allocation identified through exhaustive training. The average runtime of gradient probe across datasets is 99.9% lower than that of exhaustive candidate training.

authors.name: Sheng Sun
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: FL-CsLoc-DH: A Federated Learning-Based Crowdsensing Localization under Dual Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Mobile Crowdsensing (MCS) provides a scalable way to collect indoor fingerprints and reduce professional calibration effort. To protect the location privacy of participating clients, Federated Learning (FL) is used so that raw fingerprints and measurement trajectories remain local. However, owing to the open and uncontrollable nature of MCS, participating clients collect fingerprints in different propagation environments and possess unequal labeling availability. These conditions jointly cause data and annotation heterogeneity, which degrades FL-based crowdsensing localization. In this work, we propose FL-CsLoc-DH, a federated semi-supervised learning framework for crowdsensing localization under dual heterogeneity. FL-CsLoc-DH coordinates Two-Stage Noisy Gradient Rejection (TS-NGR), Soft Fisher Confidence Alignment (S-FCA), and Trajectory-Smoothed Model Averaging (T-SMA) throughout localization model learning. TS-NGR suppresses unreliable client updates caused jointly by environment dependent data shifts and noisy pseudo labels. S-FCA limits parameter increments dominated by unlabeled data, thereby alleviating annotation heterogeneity during local training. T-SMA smooths the aggregated global localization model trajectory to reduce drift induced by data heterogeneity. Experiment results show that the three mechanisms provide complementary improvements in localization accuracy under the MCS environment while retaining raw client data locally.

authors.name: Zixuan Ai
authors.institution: State Key Laboratory of Food Science and Technology

authors.name: Feng Shu
authors.institution: Nanjing University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Can Cities Have Personalities? Introducing the SCD City Personality Assessment
papers.abstract: Descriptions of cities are shaped by human experience and institutional narratives. We introduce the SCD City Personality Assessment (SCD-CPA), a method that instantiates document-grounded ChatGPT city personas and interrogates each with an identical 24-statement instrument inspired by the four-pair structure of the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator. Rather than asking a general-purpose model to characterize cities freely, we configure a separate document-grounded conversational agent for each city and use alternative evidence portraits to compare documentary inputs. The resulting four bipolar dimensions and four-letter summaries use independently defined urban concepts and scoring rules. Tokyo, New York, and Paris form the methodological evaluation (33 assessments across repeated sessions, three GPT-6 effort settings, and alternative portraits): Tokyo's original portrait yielded 85.4% exact within-setting item agreement, while evidence substitutions shifted some dimension strengths. A five-city application to Shanghai, Dubai, Mumbai, Lagos, and Sao Paulo (15 assessments) yielded 77.8% exact and 99.4% within-one-point cross-setting agreement, indicating consistency under the tested configurations. By treating each city conversational agent as a reproducible, evidence-conditioned experimental configuration, SCD-CPA makes documented city-character perceptions comparable and exposes their sensitivity to source selection. Although the documentary evidence is explicitly controlled, the model's internal interpretation of that evidence cannot be fully observed. We also examine the robustness of SCD-CPA across three AI reasoning-effort settings. The observed consistency suggests that the methodology is relatively insensitive to the tested configuration differences and provides a framework for evaluating its stability as future generations of AI models become available.

papers.title: Attention Latent Feedback
papers.abstract: During autoregressive decoding, the deeper representations of the previous token have already been computed, yet shallow layers at the current token cannot read them directly because standard self-attention connects positions only at the same depth. We introduce Attention Latent Feedback (ALF), an architecture that allows every sublayer to attend to the outputs of the deeper layers at the previous position. Training unrolls this cross-position recurrence into two parallel passes, whereas decoding remains single-pass using cached previous-token states. Across mixture-of-experts models with up to 4.0B parameters, ALF lowers held-out loss by 0.022-0.024 nats over the standard residual with about 1.1% decoding FLOP overhead, and consistently outperforms prior final-state feedback across all three scales on both standard and attention residual backbones. On MoE-1.6B, ALF matches a $1.38\times$ larger baseline token budget, and on MoE-4.0B it lifts average accuracy across seventeen downstream benchmarks from 45.1% to 47.0%. Analysis further reveals that intermediate and nearby deeper layers drive most of this benefit, allowing a fixed nearest-window variant to retain 89%-94% of the gain at linear read cost while learned attention widens its margin with scale.

papers.title: Pruning Autonomous Driving VLAs: What to Preserve for Reasoning and Action
papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures. In the action expert, MLP channels exhibit more stable importance rankings across denoising steps than query heads, and a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the measured importance. Based on these findings, we propose MoOP, which combines importance ranks from both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select a fixed subset of expert MLP channels. At 24.0% total parameter reduction, VLM-only pruning with MoOP performs comparably to or slightly better than the strongest baselines in driving, while retaining 94.0% of the dense model's LingoQA score, far above all other methods. At a higher reduction of 30.0%, MoOP degrades much less than every other method, as it is the only one whose reasoning does not collapse. Removing 93.75% of expert MLP channels increases total parameter reduction to 39.4%, with nearly unchanged open-loop errors relative to VLM-only pruning and competitive closed-loop performance. The resulting model achieves a 1.37x end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6% lower peak memory than the dense model, without post-pruning fine-tuning.

papers.title: Intertwined Magneto-Structural Criticality Driving Heterogeneous Collective-Pseudospin Dynamics in Sr2IrO4
papers.abstract: Correlated quantum phenomena arising from spin-orbit-coupled degrees of freedom provide foundational paradigms in emerging quantum technologies and spin-based functionalities. Elucidating the cooperative behaviors of these systems requires a precise probing of their intertwined magnetic and structural configurations. Using complementary resonant X-ray diffraction and high-energy total scattering measurements on single crystals of Sr2IrO4, we observe that spontaneous structural distortions scale quadratically with the magnetic order parameter. Importantly, the lattice distortion inherits the characteristic 2D XY -like critical behavior of the underlying antiferromagnetic order. X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) reveals multiscale, temperature- and wave-vector-dependent magnetic dynamics characterized by compressed-exponential relaxation and signatures of critical slowing down near the magnetic transition. These findings suggest the role of spin-orbit coupling and local structural distortions as the possible mechanism orchestrating such unconventional dynamics.

papers.title: A Fiber-Optic Platform for Cryogenic Laser-Pump Neutron-Probe Magneto-Optical Measurements
papers.abstract: We report a fiber-optic laser-pump neutron-probe method for momentum- and frequency-resolved magneto-optical measurements. The technique uses inelastic neutron scattering to measure time-dependent two-point magnetization correlations, S(Q,$\omega$), after resonant photoexcitation at cryogenic temperatures. We demonstrate it by measuring nonequilibrium thermalization dynamics in Yb-based quantum magnets.

papers.title: Benchmarking VLM Medical Hallucination across 5 Modalities
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) within the medical domain remain a difficult and not well-understood problem, and it is still unclear where these models break down. Although several benchmarks targeting medical hallucination have been introduced, they often lack broad coverage across different medical imaging modalities. We introduce Multi-Med, a medical hallucination benchmark containing 1,000 image-question pairs spanning five distinct modalities. Using this benchmark, we perform an in-depth experimental study of 10 widely used VLMs across five modalities and four question categories. Our findings indicate that model performance differs substantially depending on the imaging modality and question type, and that the differences among the best-performing models are not statistically significant.

papers.title: PINE: Point, Instance and Normal Estimation in One-Step Diffusion Model
papers.abstract: Understanding a scene requires both geometry and semantics: geometry recovers its spatial structure, and semantics separates it into objects. Current models obtain the two from separate networks or separate passes. We present PINE, a one-step Omni Diffusion Transformer that predicts the point map, the surface normals, and the instance map of an image in one forward pass. PINE treats each map as a token stream, and a stream mask decides which streams interact. A camera-aware ray encoding positions every token by its camera ray rather than its pixel. Grounding attention adds the affinity of pretrained DINOv3 features to the attention logits. Trained on only 139K synthetic images for geometry, PINE achieves state-of-the-art point maps whether or not intrinsics are given and the best average rank on surface normals. It also exceeds SAM on large objects with less than 1 percent of its training images, and it predicts all three maps 5.7x faster than MoGe-3 with SAM.

authors.name: Jie Ni
authors.institution: Second Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University

authors.name: Yongtai Liu
authors.institution: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College

papers.title: PhyMind: Physics-Informed Masked Autoencoding for EEG Foundation Models
papers.abstract: EEG foundation models are pre-trained almost exclusively with masked reconstruction through a free-form decoder, sometimes with hand-crafted spectral targets added, as in MANAS-2. We study what happens when that decoder is replaced by a generative forward model of EEG. PhyMind keeps a standard masked transformer encoder, but its decoder must explain the masked signal through 68 cortical regions, each driven by damped stochastic oscillators and an aperiodic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, projected to the recording's own montage by a fixed boundary-element lead field evaluated per derivation. Training combines masked reconstruction with a Whittle spectral likelihood, an oscillator-dynamics residual, a minimum-norm source prior and a penalised neural residual. In a controlled comparison (same encoder, data, steps and seed), the physics decoder produces encoder tokens whose spectral content is far more linearly decodable than with a masked-autoencoder decoder or with the MANAS-2 objective: mean R^2 on a token-level spectral probe with amplitude-normalised targets is 0.67/0.77/0.77 on three datasets, against 0.24/0.50/0.50 (MAE) and 0.48/0.67/0.66 (MANAS-2 objective), approaching the released 92.8M-parameter MANAS-2 (0.71/0.81/0.80). Downstream gains in the controlled setting are small (four-task mean balanced accuracy 56.6 vs. 53.8 for MAE frozen, 63.8 vs. 62.7 fine-tuned). Region-level features from the physics decoder raise frozen four-class motor-imagery accuracy by 7-14 points, so a 7.2M-parameter model pre-trained on 3k hours of open EEG is comparable to the released MANAS-2 with frozen features (63.0 vs. 61.6). After full fine-tuning, MANAS-2 remains better (66.8 vs. 65.4 for our best model). The inferred sources do not reproduce the lateralisation that a classical inverse solution finds in motor imagery, so we do not claim anatomical interpretability. Code and weights are released.

authors.name: A Adith
authors.institution: Dr D Y Patil Dental College & Hospital

papers.title: What Counts as Attack Success? Evaluating Harmfulness in Red Teaming LLMs
papers.abstract: Judging whether a model response is harmful requires contextual and normative choices, yet red-teaming studies often delegate this judgment to automated evaluators. We examine how harmfulness criteria are specified in red-teaming research and how they carry through to reported results. Reviewing 76 papers, we find that many adopt their criteria from prior datasets, classifiers, or judge prompts rather than defining harmfulness themselves. Applying evaluators from these papers to identical outputs, we find that they can reach different judgments on the same response, which can change conclusions when comparing models. These differences arise partly because evaluators draw the boundary of harm in different places: some count any response that does not refuse, while others count only output that could plausibly cause harm. We argue that red-teaming studies should state their harmfulness criteria and report how they chose and validated their evaluators to support more reliable measurement and interpretation.

authors.name: Adriana Alvarado Garcia
authors.institution: IBM Research - Thomas J. Watson Research Center

papers.title: Mitigating Backdoors in Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models because they can predict multiple tokens in parallel rather than generating tokens sequentially. However, recent studies have shown that MDLMs are vulnerable to backdoor attacks: when an input contains an attacker-chosen trigger, a backdoored model generates a targeted output, such as malicious code, while otherwise behaving normally. Despite this threat, backdoor defenses for MDLMs remain largely underexplored. We present UNMASK, the first defense framework for MDLMs that detects trigger-containing inputs, localizes the trigger tokens, and removes the backdoor from the compromised model. UNMASK exploits two fundamental properties of backdoor triggers, specificity and dominance, to assign a suspiciousness score to each input token. By leveraging two distinctive capabilities of MDLMs, parallel token prediction and token reconstruction at arbitrary positions, UNMASK computes these scores both effectively and efficiently. We further provide a theoretical analysis supporting the design of UNMASK. Evaluations across 40 settings spanning two attacks and four models show that UNMASK detects 99.3% of trigger-containing inputs at a 5% false-positive rate, substantially outperforming the strongest adapted baseline, which achieves 54.8%. UNMASK also achieves over 99% trigger-localization accuracy and reduces the average attack success rate from 95% to 1%, while largely preserving the model's utility on clean inputs.

authors.name: Jiaheng Zhang
authors.institution: Hunan University of Traditional Chinese Medicine

authors.name: Pin-Yu Chen
authors.institution: IBM Research - Thomas J. Watson Research Center

papers.title: Policy Invariance Is Not Learning Invariance: Potential-Based Reward Shaping for Navigation with a Limited View
papers.abstract: Potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) does not change the optimal policy, but how much it speeds up learning depends on the potential and on effects outside this guarantee. We analyse how PBRS changes the one-step reward while it preserves the discounted return: a per-step $(\gamma-1)\Phi$ term, the terminal-state rule, a constant shift of the potential, and positive cycles in a bonus that is not potential-based. We then measure these consequences in pre-registered experiments with a PPO agent. The agent has a limited egocentric view and is tested on two MiniGrid navigation tasks (160 runs, 10 seeds per condition). On LavaCrossing, a geodesic (BFS) potential learned faster than both the sparse baseline and a Euclidean potential with a 7x7 and a 5x5 view (AUC difference +0.27 to +0.39, Holm p between 0.007 and 0.0499). The Euclidean potential did not differ from the baseline. In 20 runs with a non-potential bonus, none of the agents learned the task. The Euclidean potential caused more than twice as many deaths in lava during early training. View size did not detectably change the benefit of shaping. With a 5x5 view on SimpleCrossing, some BFS runs got stuck in loops and never learned; shifting the potential did not remove this, so the per-step term alone does not explain it.

papers.title: On extracting Science information from a large data set of RXTE X-ray binary spectra using KDE technique
papers.abstract: Machine Learning/Neural Networks have been successively and extensively used in Astronomy (and other subjects) for class identification of objects based on large data sets. However, it remains difficult to extract other science information, such as what the characteristics of the class are that allow for definite identification, and whether there are objects in the sample that are unique and hence of possible science interest. An alternate approach based on rank ordering of variables and Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) may be used for class identification and to infer such science information. We test the method on a previously analyzed data set of RXTE spectra of low-mass X-ray binaries and find that black hole and neutron star systems can be distinguished at an accuracy level of ~93%, which is comparable to deep learning techniques. The soft state spectra of black hole systems are distinct from neutron star ones. For the whole sample, observations of the pulsar 4U 1907+097 (which was inadvertently introduced into the data set) were clearly found to be unique. The previously reported hyper-soft states of GRO J1655-40 and XTE J1550-564 are found to be unique among black hole spectra. For the rest of the neutron stars, the method identifies some unreported spectra of EXO 1745-248 as unique because they seem to be relativistic reflection-dominated spectra. We discuss the potential and scalability of this method.

authors.name: Ranjeev Misra
authors.institution: Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics

authors.name: Ajit Kembhavi
authors.institution: Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics

papers.title: ArrythML-II: An Optimized TinyML Framework for ECG Arrhythmia Detection and Multi-Class Beat Classification on Wearable Devices
papers.abstract: This paper presents ArrythML-II, an optimized TinyML framework for on-device ECG arrhythmia detection and multi-class beat classification on wearable platforms. A systematic hyperparameter optimization framework is developed to identify compact autoencoder architectures for binary ECG arrhythmia detection. A custom scoring mechanism jointly considers detection performance, reconstruction-error thresholds, and model size to guide architecture selection. The framework is further extended to six-class ECG beat classification using a lightweight classifier derived from the optimized autoencoder architecture. Both models are INT8 quantized and deployed using TensorFlow Lite Micro on a custom-developed, battery-operated, single-lead ECG device based on the PSoC~6 microcontroller. The deployed autoencoder and classifier have model sizes of approximately 44~KB and 22~KB, respectively, with end-to-end processing times of 5.1~ms and 4.7~ms per ECG segment. Model inference accounts for 3.95~ms and 1.38~ms of these processing times, respectively. In the refined arrhythmia detection evaluation using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, the autoencoder achieved an accuracy of 84.76\%, precision of 82.68\%, and recall of 77.99\%. The multi-class classifier achieved 82.29\% accuracy, weighted precision of 90.18\%, and weighted recall of 82.29\%. Beyond offline model evaluation, the wearable platform is validated using preloaded ECG segments, live ECG signals, and an ESP32-S3-based ECG emulator that replays annotated MIT-BIH recordings as analog waveforms. The results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating optimized TinyML models into wearable platforms for real-time ECG analysis.

papers.title: Mirror Descent at the Edge of Stability
papers.abstract: In many deep learning settings, gradient descent has been shown to operate at the edge of stability -- a regime where the largest eigenvalue of the loss Hessian hovers around $2/\eta$. We study this phenomenon in mirror descent, a generalization of gradient descent. As mirror descent is non-Euclidean, existing explanations of the edge of stability phase do not extend to this setting. We generalize the existing notion of sharpness to introduce mirror sharpness, which measures the curvature of the loss with respect to the mirror potential. Empirically, we observe that the mirror sharpness hovers slightly above the $2/\eta$ threshold. Furthermore, we derive a dual central flow ODE for mirror descent that models iterates in continuous time at the onset of edge of stability. Our ODE provides insights into the difficulties of extending existing arguments for why sharpness stabilizes at $2/\eta$ from gradient descent to mirror descent in full generality.

papers.title: What Information Survives Authenticated Byzantine Communication?
papers.abstract: Two principals independently approve actions for a delegate that can choose a route to a goal and carry it out under current policy. A stable work-order receipt records the routes authorized at issuance. For intersection policies, we characterize the leading number of reachable joint configurations under overlapping updates. The lower bound uses the first writer's ability to finish before its peer invokes an update. The matching protocol checks an older route against the changed principal's policy because the unchanged principal already approved each of its steps. When each route has a command unique to it, the count has a closed form in terms of unions of route supports. Two three-command workflows with four possible receipts each have leading counts of $360$ and $328$ under encoded overwrite, and both have append count $1024$. Exact policy read-back forces at least six bits per block in both cases. Route overlap affects the count even when route lengths are fixed. The construction preserves authorization, withdrawal, stable recovery, and progress after stabilization with one coordinator crash.

authors.name: Arnab Mallick
authors.institution: Centre for Development of Advanced Computing

authors.name: Indraveni Chebolu
authors.institution: Centre for Development of Advanced Computing

papers.title: Roman-Type Domination on Bisplit Graphs: Hardness and Inapproximability
papers.abstract: Inspired by the structure and name of split graphs, bisplit graphs have three independent sets $I,A,B$, where every vertex of $A$ is adjacent to every vertex of $B$, and vertices of $I$ may have arbitrary neighborhoods in the core $A\cup B$. Thus they have a complete bipartite core together with the remaining vertices, making them a structured setting in which to study how core size affects complexity. Mann and Fernau's construction already implies NP-completeness of perfect Roman domination on bisplit graphs with a singleton core side \citep[Theorem~20]{mann-fernau-pr}. Motivated by this result, we study all four Roman-type domination problems across further core-size regimes: we prove NP-completeness when one core side has size one or two, and when both sides have size at least three. For perfect Italian domination, even deciding whether prescribed core labels of total weight two can be extended is NP-complete on bipartite bisplit graphs. Approximation is also addressed: for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$, unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, no $n^{1-\varepsilon}$-approximation exists for perfect Roman domination when one core side has fixed size $1$, $2$, or $3$, or for perfect Italian domination on bipartite bisplit graphs whose two core sides grow with the input. All four problems are fixed-parameter tractable for both parameters. Given supplied modulators of size $k$, the running-time bases, in the order Roman, perfect Roman, Italian, and perfect Italian, are $4,11,11,18$ for cluster vertex deletion and $6,11,11,18$ for biclique-cluster vertex deletion, up to polynomial factors. The $4^k$ Roman cluster-deletion bound is known; the other bounds follow from our dynamic programs. To our knowledge, the latter parameter has not previously been studied explicitly for domination variants.

papers.title: RoFE: Rotated Frozen Embeddings for Low-Data Multimodal Tabular Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal tabular learning combines tabular data with images and text, often in settings where labeled data are scarce. Tabular foundation models such as prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) offer a promising solution via in-context learning without task-specific training. However, modern image and text encoders produce embeddings with hundreds or thousands of dimensions, far exceeding the number of features encountered during PFN pretraining. Existing approaches bridge this gap using principal component analysis (PCA) to compress frozen embeddings. Surprisingly, we find that this PCA interface can underperform simple linear classifiers when labeled examples are scarce, even though PFNs are designed for small datasets. We identify the underlying failure mechanism: the PFN's per-column standardization removes the variances of the PCA scores. When the PCA keeps every direction of the labeled examples, the examples collapse into a regular simplex in which all pairwise distances are equal. To address this problem, we propose Rotated Frozen Embeddings (RoFE), a training-free method that rotates PCA scores before PFN inference. We theoretically show that rotation makes the column variances nearly equal, so that standardization approximately preserves the embedding geometry. Across image and text classification tasks, encoders, and tabular foundation models, RoFE improves low-data performance over the PCA interface and outperforms baselines that require task-specific training. The improvements also extend to regression.

authors.name: Aarti Darji
authors.institution: The University of Texas at Arlington

papers.title: Selective Verification in Multi-Agent Orchestration with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Agents can agree because they relied on the same flawed evidence. We use an exact model of nine binary votes to examine when a verifier should intervene. In the main comparison, workers err 20 percent of the time under ordinary conditions, shared failures occur in 10 percent of cases, and the verifier errs 2 percent of the time in either state. When worker error during a shared failure is 80 percent, checking close votes yields 7.93 percent verdict error, compared with 9.06 percent for random checks at the same expected check rate. The ordering reverses at 90 percent worker error during failure. At the matched check rate for that regime, checking close votes yields 9.98 percent error, random checks yield 9.41 percent, and ranking checks by their expected error reduction yields 6.73 percent. The model also shows that passing branch vote counts preserves the flat majority and reduces the number of messages the root receives. A design guide and a documentation audit of four Python frameworks translate these findings into implementation choices.

papers.title: SAMA: Training-Free Consensus Ridge Tracking for Camera-Based Heart Rate on Five Public Datasets
papers.abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) is usually benchmarked by one heart rate per video, a figure that hides the short windows in which a tele-consultation would actually read the pulse. We present SAMA, a training-free estimator that (i) forms a quality-weighted consensus of POS and CHROM chrominance spectra, (ii) discounts frequencies occupied by pulse-free references derived from the same frames (frame motion, skin-mask geometry and background brightness), (iii) follows the heart rate through time with a Viterbi ridge under a random-walk prior, and (iv) returns a track-filtered, amplitude-normalised waveform with a per-window confidence. No parameter is learned and no dataset-specific tuning is used. On 218 recordings from 111 participants in five public datasets (UBFC-rPPG, PURE, SUMS, M3PD and a two-participant subset of MMPD), all processed with the same fixed face box and scored with a re-implementation of the rPPG-Toolbox protocol, SAMA has the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) averaged over datasets at every protocol level: 4.40 against 5.13,bpm for POS per video, 4.80 against 5.43 on 30,s windows and 5.05 against 6.59 on 10,s windows. Pooled over participants, the bootstrap interval of its paired difference from POS excludes zero on 30,s and 10,s windows (Wilcoxon p=0.11 and 0.004) but not per video, and it does not beat POS on SUMS per video or on the MMPD subset. Withholding the 20\% least confident windows lowers the pooled 10,s error from 4.06 to 2.33,bpm. We also show that the per-video protocol has a floor of 1.2--1.6,bpm on datasets where heart rate drifts, and that skin tone cannot be recovered from uncalibrated video, which motivates the instrumented, skin-tone-stratified collection we propose for the Indian population. The method does not surpass the best published neural networks on UBFC-rPPG; we report where it stands against them without re-running them.

papers.title: Generating Safety-Critical Driving Scenarios from Role-Typed Signal Temporal Logic Specifications Drafted by Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety-critical scenarios are rare in recorded driving and must be generated to test and train motion planners of automated vehicles. In guided diffusion models, each scenario type needs its own weighted objective, separate from the validity check. Optimized together with the attacker, the vehicle under test can cancel the attack or draw it toward itself. We state each scenario as a signal temporal logic specification with clauses typed by role. Every clause names the agent it may change and the agents it may read, and the vehicle under test reads the attacker only from the attack onset. A large language model drafts the specification from a description, and a type checker accepts it. A compiler derives the optimization: it edits a diffusion model's samples by the smallest change that satisfies the specification, each clause moves only its owner, the attacker is solved against the unreacted vehicle under test before its response, and the monitor of the same specification decides acceptance. On nuScenes and CommonRoad, judged independently of the specification, one parameter set produced valid scenarios at a rate 0.14 above a weighted objective tuned per scenario type, and descriptions yielded at least one valid scenario for 11 of the 16 pre-crash types expressible in the public data. Learned planners fail more often on the generated scenarios than on their seeds. Fine-tuning on them lowers a planner's failure rate on critical scenarios, and the time headway one clause of the label requires, not the generator, sets the size of the gain.

papers.title: ReDiffDet: Rotation-equivariant Diffusion Model for Oriented Object Detection
papers.abstract: The diffusion model has been successfully applied to various detection tasks. However, it still faces several challenges when used for oriented object detection: objects that are arbitrarily rotated require the diffusion model to encode their orientation information; uncontrollable random boxes inaccurately locate objects with dense arrangements and extreme aspect ratios; oriented boxes result in the misalignment between them and image features. To overcome these limitations, we propose ReDiffDet, a framework that formulates oriented object detection as a rotation-equivariant denoising diffusion process. First, we represent an oriented box as a 2D Gaussian distribution, forming the basis of the denoising paradigm. The reverse process can be proven to be rotation-equivariant within this representation and model framework. Second, we design a conditional encoder with conditional boxes to prevent boxes from being randomly placed across the entire image. Third, we propose an aligned decoder for alignment between oriented boxes and image features. The extensive experiments demonstrate ReDiffDet achieves promising performance and significantly outperforms the diffusion model baseline.

papers.title: GSDet: Gaussian Splatting for Oriented Object Detection
papers.abstract: Oriented object detection has advanced with the development of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformers. However, modern detectors still rely on predefined object candidates, such as anchors in CNN-based methods or queries in transformer-based methods, which struggle to capture spatial information effectively. To address the limitations, we propose GSDet, a novel framework that formulates oriented object detection as Gaussian splatting. Specifically, our approach performs detection within a 3D feature space constructed from image features, where 3D Gaussians are employed to represent oriented objects. These 3D Gaussians are projected onto the image plane to form 2D Gaussians, which are then transformed into oriented boxes. Furthermore, we optimize the mean, anisotropic covariance, and confidence scores of these randomly initialized 3D Gaussians, using a decoder that incorporates 3D Gaussian sampling. Moreover, our method exhibits flexibility, enabling adaptive control and a dynamic number of Gaussians during inference. Experiments on 3 datasets indicate that GSDet achieves AP$_{50}$ gains of 0.7\% on DIOR-R, 0.3\% on DOTA-v1.0, and 0.55\% on DOTA-v1.5 when evaluated with adaptive control and outperforms mainstream detectors.

papers.title: A Nepali-Accented English Evaluation Dataset for Automatic Speech Recognition
papers.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems perform strongly on native-English benchmarks, yet their accuracy degrades sharply when the input speech comes from under represented non-native accents. Nepali-accented English is particularly under-served: existing resources either focus on native Nepali speech, cover broader multi-accent settings without dedicated Nepali evaluation, or provide only limited Nepali-accent coverage. This paper presents a Nepali-accented English evaluation dataset designed to support robust ASR benchmarking under accent mismatch. The corpus was collected through a web-based platform that did not collect directly identifying metadata and contains recordings from 57 speakers. Each session follows a fixed 22-prompt protocol consisting of 11 phonetic prompts, 10 domain prompts, and 1 spontaneous prompt, providing complementary coverage of pronunciation, topical vocabulary, and natural speaking style. In addition to transcribed speech, the dataset includes participant metadata for coarse exploratory subgroup analysis and speaker-level manual recording-quality labels. Manual quality assessment shows that 50.9% of sessions are clean and 42.1% contain only mild noise. As a descriptive reference, open-source ASR baselines are substantially worse on this corpus than the corresponding LibriSpeech test-clean values reported in official model cards, reaching 38.15-55.00% WER on the collected set versus reported 2-4% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean. These baseline results position the corpus as a practical held-out resource for evaluating accent robustness and out-of-distribution generalization on Nepali-accented English.

papers.title: PhysPPF: Learning Robotic Manipulation with Past, Present, and Future Physical Representations
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced robotic manipulation, yet complex tasks requiring both precise 3D contact and long-horizon coordination remain challenging. Most existing studies enhance spatial perception or temporal reasoning in VLAs separately. Spatial methods primarily inject geometric or affordance priors into current-frame perception without tracking multi-step transitions, while history-aware and world-model VLAs typically capture past context or future dynamics in 2D feature or pixel spaces, either lacking explicit 3D contact cues or incurring high generation overhead. To address this, we propose PhysPPF, a VLA framework that performs unified spatiotemporal modeling in a compact physical token space. Spatially, WWH (What-Where-How) distills pretrained perception teachers exclusively during training into compact token groups capturing what 3D structures occupy the scene, where to interact, and how the gripper should approach, without test-time 3D encoders. Temporally, operating directly in this WWH space without pixel reconstruction, PPF (Past-Present-Future) consolidates executed states into a bounded past physical memory and jointly infers present and future physical tokens via an asymmetric world model. Parallel gated branches then inject these past, present, and future representations into a flow-matching action expert to guide manipulation without cross-temporal interference. Extensive experiments on SimplerEnv, CALVIN, and LIBERO show that PhysPPF consistently outperforms existing spatial, history-aware, and world-model VLAs with modest latency and parameter overhead, improving over the StarVLA baseline by +17.2 points on SimplerEnv, +29.3 points on CALVIN, and +3.5 points on LIBERO.

papers.title: Look Before You Leap: Re-Architecting Disk-Resident Vector Search with TriVS
papers.abstract:
Disk-resident approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) scales vector search beyond DRAM, yet state-of-the-art systems remain I/O-bound, even with fast SSDs and sophisticated I/O execution. To understand this bottleneck, we conduct an I/O-centric analysis that breaks each query down into an approach phase that locates a query-near region and a converge phase that resolves the final top-k. This analysis reveals complementary I/O tradeoffs: cluster-based search circumvents approach-phase I/O through in-memory routing but reads coarse-grained, full clusters during convergence, whereas graph-based search employs fine-grained, vector-level I/O throughout, enabling efficient convergence at the cost of inevitable I/O during the approach phase.
  To combine the complementary I/O benefits of the two granularities, we present TriVS, a new paradigm that re-architects disk-resident vector search as a trilogy: approach coarsely, distill progressively, and converge exactly. Its key innovations come in two parts. First, it decouples the approach and converge phases from a single search granularity, employing cluster-based search to avoid approach-phase I/O and leveraging vector-level I/O for efficient convergence. Second, to bridge the two granularities, it introduces a new in-memory distill phase between the original two, progressively reducing routed clusters to a vector-level shortlist using compact quantized vectors before disk access. Moreover, coarser clustering shrinks the centroid-routing index, allowing TriVS to reallocate existing memory to distillation rather than expand its memory budget. Our evaluation on five datasets spanning diverse vector types and scales shows that, at Recall@10=0.9, TriVS achieves on average 3.42X PipeANN's throughput, 51.2% lower latency, and 63.7% less disk I/O, while using less memory and storage than PipeANN.
