Its factor branch encodes all stocks' values for one factor as a token, applies self-attention across factors, and maps the result back to one return forecast per stock. A second branch applies attention across stocks in the same panel. A gate combines their forecasts using trailing factor covariance and market volatility. We evaluate both branches on NASDAQ, NYSE, and S&P 500 with the benchmarks' five price features and with 158 factors computed from the same data. On the 158-factor NASDAQ panel, averaging the two forecasts yields an information coefficient (IC) of 0.0421, compared with 0.0392 for the strongest external baseline. The gate raises IC to 0.0443 and gives the highest annualized excess return after costs. The equal-weight ensemble has the higher portfolio information ratio. Both combinations also improve on the strongest external baseline in mean IC on the other two 158-factor panels. On the five-feature NYSE panel, the differences are within the variation across seeds. ```

papers.title: ReVAgent: Multi-Agent Reasoning-Intensive Video Generation
papers.abstract: A central challenge in generating instructional videos for reasoning-intensive topics is to show how and why the state changes at each step. Even when an animation renders successfully, the depicted object relationships and state transitions can conflict with the explanation, making the reasoning difficult to follow. We present ReVAgent, a multi-agent framework that solves a problem, generates keyframes for its explanation, and synthesizes an instructional video. The agents share the execution record of a solution program, reuse intermediate results and constructions in the scenes, and check rendered keyframes to guide revisions to the solution or the scenes. We also introduce a multidimensional rubric for assessing whether generated videos present the problem clearly, organize the steps coherently, and use visuals to explain the reasoning. We calibrate a multimodal judge using human ratings and apply it to instructional videos for mathematics and algorithms. In the evaluated samples, ReVAgent presents multi-step reasoning coherently and uses diagrams to show how key operations lead to subsequent states.

authors.name: Yehui Yang
authors.institution: Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics

papers.title: Accurate Products, Inaccurate Inverse: Emulated FP64 BLAS in Blocked Triangular Inversion
papers.abstract: FP64 emulation on integer tensor units now ships in cuBLAS and GEMMul8, and each emulated matrix product can be checked against an accuracy grade. We ask if a routine built from such products inherits their accuracy, and show that blocked triangular inversion, the core of LAPACK's inverse of a symmetric positive definite matrix, does not. Under fixed-precision emulation every product passes the grade-B error bound of Demmel et al., yet the inverse errs at 7.1e-2, against 2.0e-15 natively. The matrices are well conditioned after diagonal scaling, but the scaling spans 64 binades. The cause is one product, T = X22 L21, whose summed index carries both the diagonal scaling and its inverse, which a grade-B bound does not absorb. Computing those products natively restores native accuracy; leaving any one of them emulated does not. The pattern holds on four GPUs, and on real covariance matrices the fixed-precision routes lose up to about four orders of accuracy. Equilibration, a solve-based association and cuBLAS's automatic dynamic precision avoid the loss, and an exact error recurrence audits a completed run. On an RTX 4090 the fastest accurate emulated inversion takes 0.40 of cuSOLVER's time. Where each product's scaling falls decides if per-product accuracy carries over to a composite routine, and that is what builders of emulated libraries need to check.

papers.title: Attention Temperature Confounds Zero-Shot Context Extension
papers.abstract: A training-time attention change is usually judged for zero-shot context extension against a dense baseline beyond the training length at the default temperature, $\tau = 1$. The outcome depends on how miscalibrated the baseline is there: the share of perplexity it recovers when its logits are sharpened by one scalar. Under the standard recipe (fp32 master weights), an 8k-trained baseline is 8-15% miscalibrated at 30k in three seed-paired 365M twins; in one of them this makes the block-sparse-trained twin look 7% better, which calibration removes. In pure-bf16 training without master weights the miscalibration is several times larger: an AdamW step ($\beta_2 = 0.95$) on a gain initialised at 1.0 is below half the bf16 spacing at peak learning rates under $1.7\times10^{-3}$, so gains never move (22 checkpoints), the baseline is 37-58% miscalibrated, and block-sparse pretraining, attention dropout and ALiBi look 6-35% better. Calibrating one temperature per model and length removes all three advantages, leaves ALiBi 5% behind RoPE and keeps part of the gain of a positive control, NTK-aware scaling. Unfreezing the gains reverses the block-sparse advantage at 365M and removes 71-89% of it at 1.2B. We recommend reporting extension results at calibrated temperatures and checking that normalisation gains moved.

papers.title: Euler Characteristics of Perverse Sheaves on Complex Ball Quotients
papers.abstract:
Let $X=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{B}^n$ be a finite-volume complex ball quotient with neat lattice. We prove that every nonzero algebraically constructible perverse sheaf on $X$ has positive Euler characteristic. More generally, we establish a criterion for strict positivity on smooth quasi-projective varieties whose logarithmic cotangent bundle is nef and admits an ample negative rational twist of the boundary divisor.
  For perverse sheaves with positive-dimensional support, we give a lower bound in terms of the intrinsic geometry of $X$ for both proper and nonproper quotients. The bound depends on the systole of $X$ and tends to infinity with it. In particular, the minimum Euler characteristic among perverse sheaves with positive-dimensional support tends to infinity as one passes to higher levels of any cofinal normal tower of finite covers. We also deduce lower bounds for the middle intersection Betti numbers of projective subvarieties and boundedness of supports with bounded middle intersection cohomology.

papers.title: Four consistent estimates of $H_0$ from a $\Lambda$CDM inference network given CMB data
papers.abstract: We organize inferences from cosmic microwave background (CMB) data, of the current rate of expansion, $H_0$, into a network whose structure is informed by a scaling symmetry of the Einstein-Boltzmann evolution equations. There are four distinct routes through this network from a calibrating anchor to $H_0$. Given key assumptions of the $\Lambda$CDM model, they are mutually consistent. This consistency is a significant feature of the $\Lambda$CDM model's compatibility with CMB data. The redundancy in $H_0$ determinations illuminates a hurdle to resolving the $H_0$ tension with alternative cosmological models.

papers.title: Regularizing Hard Examples Improves Adversarial Robustness
papers.abstract: Recent studies have validated that pruning hard-to-learn examples from training improves the generalization performance of neural networks (NNs). In this study, we investigate this intriguing phenomenon -- the negative effect of hard examples on generalization -- in adversarial training. Particularly, we theoretically demonstrate that the increase in the difficulty of hard examples in adversarial training is significantly greater than the increase in the difficulty of easy examples. Furthermore, we verify that hard examples are only fitted through memorization of the label in adversarial training. We conduct both theoretical and empirical analyses of this memorization phenomenon, showing that pruning hard examples in adversarial training can enhance the model's robustness. However, the challenge remains in finding the optimal threshold for removing hard examples that degrade robustness performance. Based upon these observations, we propose a new approach, difficulty proportional label smoothing (DPLS), to adaptively mitigate the negative effect of hard examples, thereby improving the adversarial robustness of NNs. Notably, our experimental result indicates that our method can successfully leverage hard examples while circumventing the negative effect.

papers.title: Tabular Foundation Models Are Surprisingly Effective In-Context Robot Learners
papers.abstract: Can foundation models pretrained for generic numerical prediction serve as in-context robot learners? We investigate this question through tabular foundation models (TFMs), which are pretrained to infer input-output relationships from labeled examples in context. We introduce TabAct, which casts visual imitation as numerical prediction: frozen visual features and robot proprioception form the inputs, future action chunks form the targets, and each demonstration time step provides one labeled example that conditions a frozen TFM for closed-loop control. The predictor receives no robot-specific training or target-task fine-tuning. With one target-task demonstration available to each method, TabAct with TabICLv2 achieves the highest average success among all evaluated methods on both LIBERO and Meta-World, exceeding the strongest baseline by 20.9 and 5.8 percentage points, respectively. Additional demonstrations improve control without updating model weights: with five demonstrations, success reaches 94.2% on LIBERO-Object. These results demonstrate that generic numerical pretraining can provide an effective foundation for in-context robot learning.

authors.name: Heng-Zhuang Li
authors.institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

papers.title: GlanceNav: Efficient Vision-and-Language Navigation with Streaming Memory and Counterfactual Rewind
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become strong policies for vision-and-language navigation (VLN). However, most of them encode a sample of past frames again at every decision and are trained on isolated decisions, so computation is redundant and the usable history is short. They also learn from their own mistakes through outcome rewards that give one scalar to a whole episode. We ask whether a navigator can encode each frame only once, at a constant cost per step, and still remember what matters and learn efficiently from its mistakes. We present GlanceNav, a streaming navigator built on a hybrid MLLM. Its Gated DeltaNet layers carry a recurrent state through the whole episode, while its attention layers keep a short window of recent observations and a small bank of keyframes, selected by how much each frame changes the recurrent state. This constant-size memory keeps the cost per step fixed and allows training on whole episodes with the same memory as at inference. Because the entire memory can also be copied in constant time, we further propose Counterfactual Rewind (CoRe), a reinforcement learning stage that rewinds a drifting rollout to its closest approach to the goal, lets an expert correct a few actions, and credits decisions by the resulting change in outcome. Trained only on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE training splits, with 1,000 instructions for reinforcement learning, a 4B GlanceNav reaches success rates of 71.9% and 73.6% on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen. On R2R-CE, it outperforms the strongest previous single-RGB method trained without external data by 9.1 points, while running at 104 ms per step.

papers.title: CHICO: Bridging Sparse Metadata and Multimodal Evidence in Cultural Heritage Collections
papers.abstract: Cultural heritage aggregators provide access to millions of digitized items. Yet their catalog records often contain sparse, heterogeneous metadata, with associated media links that may not lead to accessible images. Structuring and validating these resources for multimodal AI research can support reproducible experimentation. To this end, we present CHICO (Cultural Heritage Images and Catalog Objects), a multimodal dataset derived from Europeana that brings together curated catalog fields, images, and contextual information to support evidence-grounded description generation while retaining the original Europeana records. It comprises more than 60,000 cultural heritage records with associated images. Although originally developed for that purpose, it can also support multimodal information retrieval, metadata enrichment, and evidence-based evaluation.

papers.title: EEG Decoding in Context: A Framework for Tuning-Free EEG Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) decoding is a central route toward brain-computer interfaces for communication, rehabilitation, cognitive assessment, and neurological monitoring. Recent EEG foundation models have substantially advanced reusable signal representations, but their downstream use still typically requires a task-specific decoder, gradient-based adaptation, and validation-driven model selection. We investigate a complementary foundation-model paradigm based on in-context learning: labeled EEG recordings define the decoding task as context, and new recordings are predicted without updating model parameters. We first pair raw EEG features with a pretrained general-purpose in-context predictor. This direct formulation provides a promising starting point, but its performance remains limited and unstable and does not generalize reliably across EEG paradigms. We find that suitable context construction can address these limitations by improving the effective signal-to-noise ratio and exposing temporal and spatial structure. Building on this insight, we introduce a general framework that combines EEG-specific context construction with a frozen in-context predictor and a metric-based context adaptation mechanism, which matches each downstream task to an appropriate context representation without relying on validation data. Across ten datasets spanning seven EEG decoding paradigms, our method achieves the highest mean BAcc among eleven specialized and fine-tuned EEG baselines, without task-specific parameter updates or validation-based model selection. This framework provides a practical path toward tuning-free EEG foundation models in which adaptation is expressed through context rather than parameter updates.

papers.title: STEdgeFormer: MCU and NPU Deployable Transformer Architecture
papers.abstract: Transformer-based sequence models have achieved strong performance in language and time-series modeling, but self-attention remains computationally and memory intensive for deployment on resource-constrained edge accelerators. We propose STEdgeFormer, a lightweight, hardware-aware sequence architecture designed for efficient execution on embedded neural accelerators. STEdgeFormer combines polynomial mixture layers and DyT normalization with an accelerator-aware causal memory block, replacing pairwise self-attention with compact causal aggregation. On TinyStories, the fully NPU-supported STEdgeFormer (MW) achieves a perplexity of 7.39 with 4.12M parameters and 6.51 MB RAM, with an end-to-end latency of 40 ms. In comparison, the standard 4.12M-parameter configuration achieves a lower perplexity of 6.79 but requires CPU fallback for unsupported operators, resulting in 1450 ms latency. Vanilla Transformer, on the other hand, achieves a perplexity score of 5.71 using a 4.40M-parameter model, but it cannot be deployed on the hardware. On downstream tasks, STEdgeFormer achieves 94% accuracy on ECG5000 and 93% accuracy on Speech Commands with 1.39M parameters. These results demonstrate that hardware-aware architectural choices and operator compatibility can have a substantial impact on practical inference latency, beyond model size and task accuracy alone. Rather than targeting state-of-the-art accuracy on individual benchmarks, STEdgeFormer is designed to provide a deployable sequence modeling architecture under the memory, computational, and operator constraints of embedded neural accelerators.

papers.title: Real-Time 250-kHz Spectral-Domain Optical Coherence Tomography Using a Jetson AGX Orin
papers.abstract: High-performance optical coherence tomography (OCT) relies on desktop workstations for data acquisition, reconstruction, and visualization, limiting integration into compact imaging systems. We evaluated whether an embedded GPU platform could sustain real-time operation of a 250-kHz spectral-domain OCT instrument without a desktop computer. A custom C++/CUDA OCT engine running on a NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB was developed and integrated with a 2048-pixel spectrometer, Camera Link frame grabber, and galvanometer scanner, and compared against an RTX A4500 workstation under the same scan protocols. Both systems maintained mean B-scan processing latency well below the corresponding B-scan acquisition intervals. Although the RTX A4500 workstation achieved lower reconstruction latency, Jetson eliminated explicit host-to-device transfer and exhibited more consistent processing latency. Furthermore, the measured active wall power was 67 W for the Jetson and 155 W for the workstation, corresponding to approximately 2.3 times greater wall-energy efficiency for the Jetson. In a separate 62.6-min GUI-enabled measurement, the Jetson processed 800,000 B-scans without frame loss while maintaining real-time reconstruction and visualization. These results demonstrate that embedded computing can support high-speed OCT acquisition, processing, and control while reducing wall-power demand and computing-platform size.

authors.name: Jungeun Won
authors.institution: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

papers.title: S$^2$LMR: Supervised Sequential Long-Context Multi-Step Retriever
papers.abstract: Multi-step retrieval over long contexts is a key capability for retrieval-augmented generation, but strong existing approaches are costly and complex to train. Supervised retrievers are far simpler and cheaper, yet they fall well behind in this setting. We show that this gap stems not from supervised training itself, but from three misalignments between training and inference: easy training negatives, noisy retrieval prefixes, and position-agnostic scoring. Guided by this analysis, we introduce S$^2$LMR, a simple yet effective supervised sequential retriever that models multi-step retrieval as the evolution of an explicit textual state encoded by a single shared Transformer. On long-context reasoning, multi-hop QA, and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks with context lengths ranging from 4K to 10M tokens, S$^2$LMR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, substantially outperforming prior supervised retrievers. Notably, it requires only $\sim$2 hours of training on a single A6000 for contexts of up to 10M tokens, while remaining robust across a wide range of hyperparameter settings.

authors.name: Kaiyi Ji
authors.institution: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

papers.title: AgriManager: A Framework and Benchmark for LLM-RL Generalization in Agricultural Management
papers.abstract: Agricultural management is heterogeneous along two axes. The first is distributional shift within a fixed task interface: weather, crops, and prices vary across years and locations while sensors, actions, and objective stay fixed. The second is structural shift across interfaces: different farms expose different observed variables, available actions, and management objectives. We formalize the second axis as schema shift: variation in the policy-facing schema $\Sigma = (\Sigma_O, \Sigma_A, \Sigma_R)$ between training and deployment. We test whether LLM-RL generalizes across both axes with AgriManager, to our knowledge the first framework that trains LLM policies with RL across multiple process-based crop simulators, unifying DSSAT, WOFOST, and Cycles. We design a three-tier generalization ladder: Tier 1 within-schema distributional shift, Tier 2 single-axis schema shift along $\Sigma_O / \Sigma_A / \Sigma_R$, Tier 3 compositional schema shift across simulators, all scored on a frozen held-out test suite with three training seeds per method. Within fixed schemas, Qwen3-4B trained by RL with explicit reasoning exceeds neural-network PPO trained with the same interaction budget; without reasoning, training stalls near no-action where the reward penalizes input use. Under single-axis schema shift, $\Sigma_O$ transfer needs decision-critical state, $\Sigma_A$ results are consistent with joint action-menu coverage, and with reasoning a policy trained on yield alone transfers to unseen objectives. Under compositional schema shift, single-source training mostly hurts zero-shot transfer across simulators, and a unified policy trained only on other combinations of the same components recovers about 86% of the gain of a specialist trained on the target combination on DSSAT and stays below the specialists on the WOFOST and Cycles profit targets. Project page: https://agrimanager-framework.github.io

papers.title: AlpaSafe: Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection for Vision-Language-Action Models in Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Reasoning-based driving vision-language-action (VLA) models propose multiple candidate trajectories at each decision, yet only one is executed. Standard evaluation scores the best candidate, assuming an oracle selector that deployment lacks, and leaves the risk of the executed candidate unexamined. Existing online evaluators typically close this gap with a purpose-trained scene or world model, often rolling out each candidate through it at inference time. We introduce AlpaSafe, a risk-aware trajectory selector that reuses the scene representation a frozen driving VLA computes while proposing its candidates. AlpaSafe reads the last hidden token of the VLA's prompt prefill. A lightweight head, trained on the closed-loop simulation outcomes of the candidates, fuses this token with each candidate trajectory and predicts a relative score and collision/offroad logits. A fixed rule removes candidates dominated on the two risk logits and selects the highest-scoring candidate among those remaining, adding neither rollouts nor VLA training. Experiments on 525 AlpaSim scenes show that AlpaSafe outperforms Alpamayo's default first-sample rule and uniform random selection in selected regret and top-1 agreement, and reduces the collision-at-fault or offroad rate from 6.41% and 6.10% to 4.93%. The selector has 1.7M parameters and takes 0.75 ms per decision.

authors.name: Mingyu Guo
authors.institution: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

papers.title: VeriLadder: A Multi-Agent Specification Refinement System for Tool-Verified Verilog Datasets
papers.abstract: Training data is a bottleneck in AI, especially for large language models (LLMs) that write Verilog, because register-transfer-level (RTL) code is rarely published and existing datasets mostly check code for syntax, not instruction correctness. This paper presents VeriLadder, a five-level Verilog dataset, and the multi-agent framework that builds it, in which LLM agents write and revise specifications, and EDA tools (a synthesizer and a formal equivalence checker) decide what is accepted. Its levels follow an engineer's checks. Level 1 labels designs from two large Verilog corpora, namely RTLCoder and PyraNet, with synthesis results, failure causes, critical warnings and post-synthesis metrics. 28% of RTLCoder designs fail synthesis and are kept as negatives. Level 2 grades each instruction on four specification qualities, and low grades predict failed rebuilds. Level 3 rewrites each instruction into a refined specification and accepts it only if an LLM from another model family, reading only that specification, writes a circuit formally equivalent to the original. This raises the share of rebuildable designs from 26.1% to 78.2%, keeping every failed specification with its counterexample. Levels 4 and 5 add verified paraphrases and one-fact variants, hard negatives that differ only in one behavior from the verified design. VeriLadder labels the synthesizability of 716,627 designs and, from RTLCoder, provides 11,247 refined specifications, 32,393 paraphrases and 8,397 one-fact variants. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on VeriLadder raises functional pass@1 from 31.7% to 50.0% on VerilogEval v2 and from 35.0% to 45.2% on RTLLM v2. The dataset and fine-tuned models are publicly available.

papers.title: Who Gets to Do Computing Research? Rethinking Access, Funding, and the Cost of Research -- How do we ensure that everyone with the ideas, ability, and desire to contribute to computing research can do so?
papers.abstract:
The future of computing research will be shaped not just by the questions we ask, but also by who has the opportunity to pursue them. Major investments in advanced computing, including artificial/super intelligence (AI) and quantum computing (QC), are expanding opportunities for discovery and innovation. Pursuing these opportunities requires more than a promising idea: researchers also need time, infrastructure, technical expertise, and support to compete for and administer funding.
  Access to these resources varies across institutions and may shape who can participate and which research directions they can pursue. A healthy computing research ecosystem depends on research taking place at institutions with different missions and resources, not only at the best-resourced ones.
  Computing research spans a broad spectrum of resource requirements, from theoretical work and software developed by small teams to experiments requiring specialized hardware, large datasets, and substantial technical support. Preserving opportunities across this range requires understanding not only the resources needed to conduct research, but also the costs of securing them.
  What does it cost an institution -- and an individual researcher -- to participate in computing research? This article invites computing researchers, university leaders, funding agencies, and industry partners to examine how funding structures, access to infrastructure, administrative responsibilities, and institutional expectations affect research opportunities, and how meaningful pathways can be preserved across institutions with different missions and resources.

papers.title: Cross-Site Transformers Are Robust Heart Rate Estimators
papers.abstract: Single-site heart-rate estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) degrades sharply under real-world motion. Multi-site PPG provides a natural solution, but existing models fuse sites as generic sensor channels rather than exploiting their hemodynamic structure: each heartbeat propagates along the arterial tree, appearing across body sites as delayed and transformed copies of the same cardiac event. We propose the Cross-Site Transformer, which introduces a hemodynamically informed inductive bias by restricting multi-sensor fusion to cross-attention between PPG sites. On WildPPG, the largest in-the-wild benchmark available, our model establishes a new single-model state of the art, reducing error by 21% over the previous best and 35% over the best prior transformer. The same cross-site restriction makes the trained network directly auditable. Because each cross-attention head lies on one directed pathway between sites, causal resample ablation can isolate and test each direction of information flow. Ablating the chest-to-wrist pathway doubles error, whereas the reverse costs far less. Encoding hemodynamic structure into attention routing thus improves real-world sensing robustness and enables rigorous auditing of multi-sensor fusion.

papers.title: Taking the PULSE of Enterprise Workflows: Evaluating Persistent Project-State Understanding
papers.abstract: Enterprise agents must maintain an up-to-date understanding of work distributed across heterogeneous artifacts, evolving over time, and unevenly visible to different collaborators. We formulate this challenge as persistent project-state understanding (PPSU) and introduce PULSE, a benchmark of 1,573 questions over 30 enterprise project histories. PULSE constructs deterministic, time-indexed project state and documented collaborator views from source-linked records, and evaluates three families of questions: open loops, project evolution, and view gaps. Across retrieval agents, graph- and memory-augmented retrieval, long-context, and oracle conditions, we find substantial headroom for current systems. Retrieval and extraction account for the largest share of the gap, but providing explicit project state on top of gold evidence yields further substantial gains, showing that PPSU cannot be reduced to retrieval alone. Further analysis shows that questions requiring information to be reconciled across multiple parts of the project history remain difficult even when the relevant evidence is provided, while project-state synthesis and perspective conditioning remain persistent challenges. These results motivate enterprise agents that explicitly maintain and reconcile temporally grounded state across sources, actors, and time.

papers.title: A discontinuous Galerkin method for the evolutionary Navier-Stokes-Darcy model
papers.abstract: In this paper, we have analysed a discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method for the coupled surface-subsurface flow, which is modelled by the evolutionary Navier-Stokes-Darcy (NSD) equations. While the DG method has been applied for the spatial discretization of both Navier-Stokes and Darcy equations, for time, we have employed the first-order backward Euler scheme. The fully discrete error analysis has been carried out for both velocity and pressure of the Navier-Stokes equations, and for the piezometric head of the Darcy equation, and optimal estimates have been derived. Our analysis relies on appropriate treatments of the nonlinear convective term from the Navier-Stokes equations, along with the interface conditions that couple the system. We have employed a modified Oseen operator on an appropriate DG setup along with the standard duality argument to derive optimal error estimates in the L2-norm for the unknowns, which are novel for the NSD equations within the DG framework and are supported by numerical simulations demonstrating the scheme's efficiency.

papers.title: A locally conservative LDG method for the evolutionary Navier-Stokes-Darcy coupled problem
papers.abstract: This paper proposes and investigates a local discontinuous Galerkin (LDG) method for the evolutionary Navier-Stokes-Darcy coupled problem representing the interaction between incompressible flows and porous media flows through the Beavers-Joseph-Saffman interface conditions. A fully discrete numerical scheme has been proposed and analyzed employing backward Euler temporal discretization and a locally conservative LDG scheme for the space discretization. The well-posedness of the numerical scheme has been obtained under a small data condition. Optimal a priori error estimates have been proven in the energy norm, as well as the L2-norm for t>0. Numerical experiments ensure the efficiency of the theoretical results

papers.title: Learning a Rule Bank to Revise 3D CT Reports with Independent Evidence
papers.abstract: Vision--language models can generate fluent radiology reports from 3D chest CT scans, yet they may still omit abnormalities or misstate findings. Independent image analysis using models separate from the report model provides additional observations, but acting on uncertain evidence may introduce new errors. We propose an agent system that learns a revision policy represented as an executable rule bank for each report model. Inspired by experience banks, the agent proposes and refines rules using revision outcomes across development cases. During inference, the retained rules guide local edits using independent classifier predictions and quantitative image measurements without retraining the report model. Unedited sentences are preserved, and each change is linked to the rule that triggered it. On CT-RATE, revision increases CE-F1 by 11.5 points for SelfCue-KD and 0.9 points for NV-Reason-CT, with gains across five draft-sampling seeds. SelfCue-KD's CT-FineBench score also increases by 15.2 points. Draft-only rule learning yields limited gains, while the two image-evidence sources provide complementary benefits for abnormality detection. Measurements also supply numerical details missing from the drafts. These results support learning model-specific rules to control how independent image evidence informs report revision. Code is available at https://github.com/renjie-liang/CT-RuleBank.

papers.title: The marginal sine-Gordon field theory
papers.abstract: At $\beta_*^2=8\pi$ we construct the two-dimensional sine--Gordon vacuum from a noncompact real lattice field with nearest-neighbor kinetic energy, positive cosine activity and zero Dirichlet data. Its mass $M$ is the lower edge of the energy spectrum above the vacuum. In units of the length $a_{\rm exit}$ at which the flow leaves weak coupling it obeys $0<c_-\le M a_{\rm exit}\le c_+<\infty$ on compact positive endpoint intervals, with uniform constants. A prescribed response to a smooth background in a fixed square determines the nonlinear asymptotically free bare parameters at each sufficiently fine cutoff. In the local relativistic continuum theory the vacuum is unique, physical dilation realizes every positive mass, and literal derivatives generate the reflected Hilbert space even for finite composite and contact families. Variance and exponential moments of a derivative smear rule out a Gaussian law. A connected correlation of some finite even order above two is nonzero on separated supports. The construction gives universality for the specified finite nonnegative higher harmonics, the field equation, topological current and geometric stress tensor with their Ward, trace and contact identities, and a normalized source-transfer theorem with explicit finite-scale hypotheses.

papers.title: VADE: A Verifiable Agent Data Engine from Professional Sources
papers.abstract: Language agents have shown their practical value, particularly in software engineering, where abundant public code and executable tests support training and evaluation at scale. Extending this success to other professional domains, such as law and finance, is not straightforward: many agent tasks involve open-ended analysis, making outcomes hard to verify and, in turn, hard to use as scalable supervision. As a result, high-quality tasks in these domains are still largely expert-authored, making them expensive to scale and limiting their use for training. To address this bottleneck, we introduce VADE, a data engine that automatically constructs verifiable analysis tasks from public sources used in professional practice. VADE exploits a simple asymmetry: professional analyses are difficult to solve because the relevant evidence must first be found and interpreted, but much easier to verify once that evidence is fixed. During task synthesis, the engine constructs a reference analysis from source evidence and asks an independent agent to reproduce its conclusions from the same evidence without seeing it. Only after the analysis is verified is it compiled into an open-ended task with an item-level scoring contract, allowing the same task to support both evaluation and training. We apply VADE across four professional domains; in an independent expert review of 186 finance tasks, 93.5% meet a high bar for source fidelity, answer correctness, and evaluation fairness. In finance, these tasks expose substantial remaining model errors, particularly unsupported facts and inferences, while training on verified solver trajectories improves held-out performance and yields gains that transfer to public finance benchmarks such as Finance Agent Benchmark v2. Together, these results suggest a practical path toward scalable, verifiable supervision for open-ended professional tasks.

papers.title: A general triangle generation of the $d$-dimensional Genocchi numbers
papers.abstract: We establish a uniform recurrence relation for the rook numbers of generalized Genocchi boards of dimension $d\geq 3$. The recurrence for each row of the rook-number triangle is expressed in terms of the preceding row, with coefficients given by products of consecutive powers and finite sums involving Stirling numbers of the second kind. The proof decomposes the boundary of the board into blocks that correspond to the coordinates equal to 1. A coordinatewise counting argument then shows that the number of extensions of a fixed interior placement depends on a boundary partition only through the number of its blocks and the size of their union. We also express the coefficients as finite differences, recovering the previously established recurrences in dimensions three through five, and give the six-dimensional specialization. As a complementary result, we formulate an injection model that provides a direct bijective proof of a formerly established identification of the diagonal rook numbers with generalized Genocchi numbers.

papers.title: Information Access and Gain-Loss Framing in Six Large Language Models and Human Decision Makers
papers.abstract: A risky choice can be described by what will be saved or what will be lost, and people often choose differently depending on that wording. We test whether six large language models (LLMs) show this gain-loss framing effect, and whether it shrinks when they can first read more about the options. GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen3 235B and Llama 4 Maverick made 11,519 choices across four risk scenarios, each in its original wording, two paraphrases and a mirrored version in the opposite wording. Before choosing, a model could open up to 0, 2, 3 or 4 of seven information cards. With no cards, all six models showed large framing effects: the share choosing the safe option was 27 to 79 percentage points lower under loss than under gain wording. The gap was smaller at 2 cards than with no cards in every model. Against a 10-point threshold set in our analysis plan, GPT-4.1 fell within it at 4 cards and Qwen3 only at 2 cards; in the plan's pooled comparison over all versions, GPT-4.1 was within it from 2 cards and GPT-4o from 3. GPT-4o-mini and Llama 4 Maverick kept gaps of 28 to 66 points with cards, and for GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3 the gap grew again from 2 to 4 cards. Part of the drop from 0 to 2 cards may reflect a change in prompt format, and most card content counted against the risky option, which may favor the safe choice. In an exploratory comparison with 198 students who saw the same scenarios and cards but opened cards one at a time and chose how many, decisions made after opening 0 or 1 cards showed a 19-point difference between the gain scenarios, asked first, and the loss scenarios, asked later, and no clear difference appeared in decisions made after opening more, though this design cannot show that cards reduced framing in people. With these cards, in the balanced comparison 17 of 18 card gaps were below the model's no-card gap, but few were within the threshold.

papers.title: Numerical Study of Flow and Cavitation in Single-Liquid Injectors with Sharp-Edged and Chamfered Orifice Inlets
papers.abstract: In the current work, the investigators used Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to investigate water flow and cavitation in single-liquid injectors with sharp-edged and chamfered orifice inlets. The k-{\omega} Shear Stress Transport (SST) turbulence model was used along with the Zwart-Gerber-Belamri (ZGB) cavitation model and the Volume of Fluid (VOF) method. The CFD predictions for the volumetric flow rate were validated against existing experimental data for the sharp-edged and chamfered orifice inlets. Pressure drops ranging between 0.07 MPa and 0.59 MPa were considered along with orifice length-to-diameter ratios of 2, 5, and 10. Strong cavitation was observed for the sharp-edged orifice inlet cases with a length-to-diameter ratio of 5 and a pressure drop larger than 0.2 MPa. A hydraulic flip was observed for the sharp-edged orifice inlet with a length-to-diameter ratio of 5 and a pressure drop of 0.59 MPa, which was consistent with the findings from the previous experimental study. Cavitation inception was observed for the chamfered orifice inlet cases with a length-to-diameter ratio of 5 and pressure drops larger than 0.2 MPa. For the sharp-edged orifice inlet with orifice length-to-diameter ratios of 2 and 10, a strong cavitation was observed inside the orifice.

papers.title: Contrastive Gradient Guidance for Test-Time Multi-Preference Alignment of Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Aligning pre-trained diffusion models with multiple context-dependent preferences requires adapting generation at test time rather than relying on offline fine-tuning, which requires hyperparameter tuning and a new training run for each preference trade-off. Existing approaches compress diverse preferences into a single scalar reward objective for fine-tuning or test-time guidance rather than directly reusing existing generative experts released for different purposes and obtained through different fine-tuning methods. In this work, we propose Contrastive Gradient Guidance (CGG), a test-time compositional generative framework that reformulates multi-preference alignment as a composition of distributions. CGG represents each preference as a contrastive preference pair of favored experts and unfavored anti-experts, whose score difference forms a contrastive gradient guidance signal that combines denoising directions (gradients) from off-the-shelf diffusion models during sampling. Experiments show that CGG reuses pre-trained and fine-tuned models as favored experts or anti-experts to control output style and safety, and that it can be combined with existing sampling-based reward guidance. With a single fixed scale per pair, CGG composes five preferences at once and gives a more balanced trade-off across text-image preference, concept control, photographic fidelity, and safety than offline fine-tuning, weight-space merging, and reward steering.

papers.title: A colour-marker tracker for pose estimation of slender surgical instruments: vision-language-model-guided adaptive colour calibration
papers.abstract: Slender surgical instruments need small, narrow markers for camera-based pose estimation. A colour-stripe marker fits this requirement, but its colours in the image drift from the design values with lighting, printing and camera settings. Because the colours can only be corrected after the marker has been found, methods that rely on the design colours face a circular problem. We propose vision-language-model (VLM)-based adaptive colour calibration and compare it with two rule-based methods, which re-measure the colours from detections made with the design colours: Initial colour update does so once after tracking starts, and Colour adaptation continuously during tracking. VLM guidance uses a fine-tuned VLM to find the markers without relying on the design colours and builds the colour profile from their pixels. Recall/F1 (%) for Initial colour update, Colour adaptation and VLM guidance were 92.0/95.7, 87.8/93.3 and 98.2/99.1 on 672 synthetic image pairs; 51.3/67.2, 48.8/65.0 and 83.8/87.0 on eight degraded laboratory videos; and 38.9/55.2, 19.7/29.7 and 100/100 on a surgical-robot (da Vinci) video with strongly shifted colours. In that video the rule-based methods never found the purple/cyan marker, whereas VLM guidance found all 234 markers with no false positives. In a simulation, the hue boundary between the two stripes moved by less than 0.1 pixel for exposure gains of 0.5-2.0, compared with 2.9-4.0 pixels for a boundary found with a fixed brightness threshold. When the degradation is mild, the rule-based methods, which need no training and no GPU, are sufficient. When the colours change greatly, the gain comes from a VLM-guided candidate search that does not rely on the design colours. Combining colour-stripe markers with adaptive colour calibration enables tracking of slender surgical instruments with small markers.

authors.name: Jaesung Hong
authors.institution: Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: Managing Uncertainty in Teacher Vibe Coding: A Comparison of Teacher and Expert Workflows
papers.abstract: Vibe coding, or natural language software development, enables teachers to become creators of digital teaching artifacts. However, novice educators oftentimes face different barriers. This qualitative study examined the workflows of pre-service teachers, in-service teachers, and expert developers through think-aloud protocols. Findings reveal vibe coding operates through a loop of problem framing, development, and verification governed by uncertainty management. Teachers reduced uncertainty by grounding designs in authentic needs: pre-service teachers drew on pedagogical principles, whereas in-service teachers relied on everyday teaching challenges. Conversely, Experts reduced ambiguity by constraining requirements, decomposing artifacts into testable modules, and automating tests. These differences reveal complementary forms of pedagogical, contextual, and technical expertise. Future work may be about supporting nontechnical teachers in developing reliable and educational applications.

papers.title: Reasoning Beyond Imitation: Observation Conditioned Distillation for Video LLMs
papers.abstract: Reasoning distillation offers a promising approach to transfer temporal reasoning capabilities of powerful Video-LLMs to open-source student models. However, teacher and student Video-LLMs may construct different temporal observations from the same video due to the adoption of distinct video sampling pipelines. A reasoning trajectory valid under the teacher's observations may rely on evidence inaccessible to the student and thus cannot be directly executed based on the student's observations. We formalize this as a conditional target mismatch, thereby revealing the Reasoning Acquisition-Execution Gap. To bridge this gap, we propose an acquisition-to-execution framework that first distills teacher trajectories into a student reasoning prior and then further optimizes the execution capability of this prior across multiple observations. We further introduce Execution-Aware Reference Regularization, which retains the existing prior when it is executable under current observations, while allowing a greater degree of adaptive adjustment when it is not. Experiments across multiple Video-LLM backbones and six video reasoning benchmarks show that explicitly optimizing observation-conditioned execution consistently outperforms supervised distillation and standard RL-based optimization, with gains extending to held-out out-of-domain benchmarks.

papers.title: Constrained Diffusion from Binary Evaluations via Learned Doob h-Functions
papers.abstract: Conditional generation under constraints that can only be checked on a finished sample, such as a molecular property filter, remains challenging for diffusion models: most guidance methods require differentiable measurement operators, paired conditional data, or rollouts of the base model at every step. We present a framework grounded in the Doob $h$-transform that reduces conditional generation to learning a single function, the probability that a noisy sample denoises into the constraint set. We learn this function from binary clean-sample evaluations alone, by squared-error regression on forward-noised labels; the base model is frozen, one lightweight head is trained per constraint, and noisy-state classifier guidance arises as a special case. The exact guidance step fades where the constraint signal provably vanishes and carries a factor of the inverse probability across samples, which normalized guidance discards: with the schedule and mean step size held fixed, equalizing the step costs 17.0 to 18.5 points of constraint satisfaction on CIFAR-10 at comparable FID, across independently trained estimators. Guidance is more than 50$\times$ cheaper per satisfying sample than rejection sampling at a 1.7% base rate, raises a Lipinski-type property filter on QM9 from 54.3% to 96.8%, and lifts satisfaction on Stable Diffusion 1.5 from 7.2% to 60.0% at one sixteenth of the cost of derivative-free selection, which reaches 9.0%. These results demonstrate that binary evaluations of clean samples are sufficient supervision for constrained generation across pixel, latent, and molecular diffusion.

papers.title: Cumulants, Partitions, and Generalizations of P\'olya's Characterization of the Normal Distribution

P'olya (1923) proved the celebrated result that if $\sqrt{2}X_1 =^L X_1+X_2$ then $X_1$ is normally distributed. P'olya's theorem has been extended in many ways, e.g., to the case of random coefficients $R_1,R_2$ such that, under certain regularity conditions, if $(R_1^2+R_2^2)^{1/2}X_1 =^L R_1X_1+R_2X_2$, then $X_1$ is normally distributed.
  In this article, P'olya's theorem is generalized {\it via} the combinatorics of $\Pi_n$, the set-partitions of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Let $X_j,R_j$, $j=1,\ldots,n$, be mutually independent random variables, where $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are identically distributed. For each $

papers.title: Pseudo-Altermagnetism in Non-Hermitian Systems
papers.abstract: Altermagnetism has attracted growing attention, and its analogs have been actively explored across classical platforms. Here, we introduce pseudo-altermagnetism in non-Hermitian systems, where balanced gain and loss plays the role of the altermagnetic spin, and the opposite gain and loss sublattices are related by an antiunitary symmetry $O$ with $O\bm k\neq \bm k$ for generic momentum $\bm k$. Using a two-dimensional non-Hermitian system with $O=C_{4z}\mathcal{T}$ symmetry as a representative example, we find that pseudo-altermagnetism not only leads to a momentum-dependent gain and loss distribution analogous to the momentum-dependent spin splitting of altermagnets, but also exhibits intrinsic non-Hermitian properties. The bands of $C_{4z}\mathcal{T}$-invariant non-Hermitian systems are either isolated or paired by $C_{4z}\mathcal{T}$, and both cases are guaranteed to host movable but unremovable nodal structures, characterized by the zeros of two distinct quantities. An isolated band exhibits two movable but unremovable Hermitian spectral lines, whose generic points are not invariant under $C_{4z}\mathcal{T}$, in sharp contrast to the conventional Hermitian spectra enforced only at the fixed points of an antiunitary symmetry. The paired bands, in turn, feature a movable but unremovable nodal network formed by the union of real-part and imaginary-part degeneracy lines, whose intersections are generally exceptional points. We further demonstrate these findings in a non-Hermitian photonic crystal. Our results establish a symmetry-based bridge between non-Hermitian physics and altermagnetism, and provide novel mechanisms of Hermitian spectra beyond $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry.

papers.title: ANOR: Scaling Sparse Attention with a GPU-PNM Computing Hierarchy
papers.abstract: Serving large language models with long contexts requires keeping the key-value (KV) cache of every request, which can exceed GPU memory capacity. Sparse attention reads only a small, query-dependent subset of this cache at each decoding step, yet must retain the full cache because later steps may select other entries. Processing-near-memory (PNM) devices attached through Compute Express Link (CXL) can hold the full cache and compute attention where it resides. Prior GPU-PNM systems for sparse attention are PNM-centric, processing most of the attention on the PNM. As existing CXL-PNM devices provide far less memory bandwidth than GPU HBM, this PNM-centric execution makes the PNM the bottleneck and leaves the GPU idle waiting for attention results. We present ANOR, a GPU-PNM joint acceleration system that exploits the selection locality of sparse attention by computing most of the attention on the GPU from a cache of recently selected entries and processing only the misses on the PNM. As the PNM processes cache misses directly, GPU cache updates can be decoupled from current-step execution. We develop a bounded cache-update policy that limits updates to the point where the hit ratio of later steps saturates, reducing GPU-facing link traffic. We add a small on-chip Early Streaming Buffer (ESB) that captures KV data during PNM attention and streams it to the GPU, avoiding most redundant DRAM reads despite the bandwidth mismatch between PNM memory and the GPU-facing link. We also propose an adaptive cache-factor mechanism that adjusts GPU cache size to the serving load, balancing hit ratio and batch size. Across two models and three long-context agentic workloads, ANOR improves decode throughput by 2.3x over HiSparse and 2.0x over a PNM baseline on average. These results show that PNM is most effective not as the primary attention engine but as a computing tier of the GPU memory hierarchy.

papers.title: On the distribution function for cross-correlation estimators in cosmology and beyond
papers.abstract: The ubiquitous Gaussian distribution, $e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$, has mean of zero and variance of 1. It is well known that the estimator $\widehat{x^2} = N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N x_i^2$ for the variance obtained from $N$ samples $x_i$ is drawn from a $\chi_n^2$ distribution, a result used often to assess the implications of data for a model. One often also needs to measure the covariance, or cross-correlation, of two different variables $x$ and $y$. If the distributions for $x$ and $y$ are both gaussian but independent of each other, the estimator $N^{-1}\sum_i x_i y_i$ for the cross-correlation is distributed about its expectation value (zero) with variance unity. The distribution function for this estimator may also be required to interpret data, for example in the measurement of cosmological cross-correlations. This distribution---the cross-correlation analog of the $\chi_n^2$ distribution---appears in the literature, but it has not been widely internalized by many in the field. We therefore here present two pedagogical derivations of this distribution and discuss some of its properties. We discuss in particular the connection to cosmological observables, but note several other areas of physics where these results may apply.

papers.title: When Video Verifier Scores Mislead: Capability Assessment and Verifier Selection
papers.abstract: Video verifiers judge whether a candidate answer or trajectory agrees with a video, and are themselves chosen by a score. We show that this score depends on two choices in the test, the type of negative and the judgment interface, strongly enough to reverse conclusions about what a model can do and which verifier to deploy. We separate the two with controlled constructions that have exact truth conditions: endpoint-matched negatives, wrong only in their internal states, and a truth-switch test, in which the same two candidates swap correctness between two videos. Under direct judgment, where the verdict is read from answer scores, models that reject a visibly wrong start fall to near chance against endpoint-matched negatives. When the frames disclose each event, writing out reasoning before the answer lifts three of four models from under 10% to 70-100% on the truth-switch test, and staged inputs trace the direct failure to one step, composing events into states. But when the event must first be found, on human-validated natural video, the same change brings no significant gain under a protocol common to all models and can lower accuracy if one candidate denies that the event occurs. The negative type also changes which verifier is selected: one chosen on event-denial negatives is 8.9 points less accurate against negatives that keep the event and change a detail, the errors a generator mostly makes, and recovers about half as much accuracy when it reranks that generator's answers. A verifier should be evaluated on the errors it will face, and neither a low direct score nor a gain from reasoning should be read as a property of the model alone.

papers.title: From atomic events to material degradation across metre and year scales
papers.abstract: Material degradation emerges from microscopic events whose consequences accumulate over years, yet mechanism-resolved simulations remain confined below engineering timescales. The challenge is not just the sheer number of events: atomistic evolution is dominated by recurrent local motion, with only a tiny fraction driving lasting structural change. This distinction is not encoded in an instantaneous atomic configuration. Locally indistinguishable states can exhibit different event competition, escape times, and long-horizon outcomes, revealing missing kinetic context as a critical information bottleneck. This context spans space and time: the future consequence of a local transition depends on its surrounding defect environment and the kinetic history leading to its current state. To solve this, AtomWorld reconstructs a predictive kinetic state from multiscale structural observations and trajectory history, distinguishing transient fluctuations from microscopic pathways that drive persistent structural evolution. Learning operates only over transitions admitted by the underlying kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) process, preserving event legality, state evolution, and physical time. Across BCC Fe-Cu precipitation, FCC Ni-Cr-Al ordering, and HCP Zr-H interstitial transport, restoring kinetic context consistently advances persistent evolution while maintaining physical fidelity and transferring to unseen conditions. In irradiated reactor-pressure-vessel steel, this approach achieves up to 420-fold greater persistent evolution under matched event budgets. Combined with scalable execution, it successfully extends mechanism-resolved trajectories to service-year timescales across metre-scale heterogeneous domains.

papers.title: Selective ROM Weight Storage for Responsive LLM Control on Edge Robots
papers.abstract: Edge robots increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for complex tasks, demanding efficient inference alongside timely control. Limited memory capacity constrains model deployment, while repeated weight transfers during decoding compete with activations and KV cache for external bandwidth. Sequential generation of robot actions further delays decisions and periodic control on shared hardware. We present a hybrid memory architecture with heterogeneous scheduling to address these bottlenecks jointly. Banked ROM stores selected fixed weights and supplies a standard compute array through a dedicated datapath. LPDDR retains the remaining weights and mutable state, preserving model flexibility. Coordinated operand delivery and preemption at output slice boundaries accelerate inference while limiting interference with periodic control. A structured decision interface scores candidate phases in a single forward pass, avoiding sequential token generation for routine choices. Together, these mechanisms improve memory service, compute access, and decision execution for edge robotic workloads. Experiments with Qwen3-8B achieve a peak decode speedup of 1.56$\times$ and reduce P99 task response time by a factor of approximately 227.27$\times$, while completing 100.00\% of the tested grasping and transport tasks.

papers.title: ReCoRain: Reliability-Coupled Content and Noise Conditioning for Event-Guided Video Deraining
papers.abstract: Event-guided video deraining depends on reliable cross-frame correspondences, yet events generated by scene motion, rain, and sensor noise can provide ambiguous matching evidence. In diffusion-based restoration, an incorrect match can transfer unrelated content and correlate initial noise between unrelated scene locations. We propose ReCoRain, an event-guided residual video diffusion framework that couples temporal content transfer and noise correlation through a common assessment of correspondence reliability. This assessment combines RGB appearance, interval-event evidence, and forward-backward motion consistency. The content path aggregates neighboring features according to alignment reliability, while the noise path uses composed backward motion fields and their associated reliability estimates to regulate initial-noise sharing across the latent sequence. We use the same conditional noise construction during residual flow-matching training and inference, incorporating temporal noise coordination into the learned restoration process. Temporal supervision matches motion-compensated inter-frame differences in restored and clean videos under the same teacher-estimated flow and visibility mask, accommodating legitimate appearance changes. ReCoRain achieves 32.09 dB PSNR on NTURain-Syn and 28.73 dB on RainSynLight25. Enabling reliability gates in both paths reduces warping error by 33.0% relative to disabling both gates.

papers.title: Validating Gaia DR3 Astrometric Accelerations with Close Visual Binaries
papers.abstract: We validate a subset of the astrometric accelerations reported in Gaia DR3 non-single-star solutions by their consistency with the gravitational pull of known, resolved companions. Cross-matching 338,215 DR3 acceleration solutions against the Washington Double Star (WDS) catalog of visual binaries yields 2,466 unique pairs within 2". For each pair we compare the measured acceleration with alpha_max, the Newtonian bound on the acceleration the companion can impart on the Gaia-tracked photocenter. For 98.1% of the pairs the measured acceleration exceeds this bound by more than a factor of 10, so the cataloged companion cannot be responsible and the perturber must be a closer, unresolved one. The remaining 45 plausible wide binaries are close pairs at the WDS resolution limit. We fit orbits with an updated orvara, extended to accept the DR3 acceleration and jerk coefficients as direct constraints and released with htof as part of this work. The fits converge for 16 of the 45 and one boundary case, the rest having too few resolved measures or a perturber other than the cataloged pair, and 13 of the 17 carry enough data to test the coefficients. Eleven of the 13 statistically accommodate the reported accelerations, for seven- and nine-parameter solutions alike, and the dynamical companion masses agree with the photometric estimates where the photocenter conversion is well determined. Independently of the fits, 33 of the 43 plausible systems with a usable position angle (77%) have the acceleration directed within 45 degrees of the primary-companion axis, against 50% for a control sample: DR3's measured accelerations point in the directions of the cataloged companions.

papers.title: Counting Eulerian Orientations in Regular Graphs
papers.abstract: Let $G$ be a pseudograph, and let $\varepsilon(G)$ denote the number of Eulerian orientations of $G$. Lieb and Wu, and later Schrijver, showed that if $G$ has degree sequence $(d_1,d_2,\dots,d_n)$, where each $d_i$ is a positive even integer, then \[ \varepsilon(G) \geq \prod_{i = 1}^n 2^{-d_i/2} \binom{d_i}{d_i/2}.\] Schrijver conjectured that for simple $d$-regular graphs, $\varepsilon(G)\leq\varepsilon(K_{d+1})^{n/(d+1)}$, with equality attained by disjoint unions of cliques of order $d+1$. In this paper, we prove a multigraph bound that implies the known case $d=4$, and we also improve Schrijver's lower bound for $d$-regular graphs, using an inductive relation between $\varepsilon(G)$ and the number $\ell_i(G)$ of cycles of each possible length $i \geq 1$ in $G$. We define \[ \ell(G) = \sum_{i = 1}^n \frac{\ell_i(G)}{(d - 1)^i}\] and we prove with $\lambda = (d - 1)\log(1 + 1/(d - 1))$ that for all $d \geq 2$, \[ \varepsilon(G) \geq \exp(\lambda \ell(G)) \cdot S_d(n),\] where $S_d(n)$ denotes $2^{-dn/2}\binom{d}{d/2}^n$. The bound sharply improves the lower bound of Lieb, Wu and Schrijver, and gives good estimates for $\varepsilon(G)$ for various graphs, such as integer lattices. The bound is almost tight for random regular graphs, and we conjecture for each even $d \geq 4$ that there exists a constant $c_d > 0$ such that $\varepsilon(G) \leq \exp(c_d\lambda \ell(G)) \cdot S_d(n)$ for every $n$-vertex $d$-regular pseudograph.

papers.title: Information-Theoretic Analysis of Multi-Objective Bandits: Pareto Violations & Gap-Based Regret
papers.abstract: We study Bayesian multi-objective bandits and ask an information-theoretic question: what aspects of an unknown environment must be resolved to achieve low regret? We show that the answer depends on the regret criterion and the information needed to represent its loss. For Pareto-violation regret, which incurs unit loss whenever a dominated action is selected, the Pareto-optimal set is a natural information target. We introduce a predictive separation measure for competing candidate Pareto sets, connect it to information gain about the unknown set, and use this connection to analyze Thompson Sampling and develop an Information-Directed Sampling strategy. We establish sublinear Bayesian regret under uniform and polynomially decaying separation and prove a lower bound showing that weak separation can impose an unavoidable statistical cost. We then study gap-based Pareto regret, which quantifies the magnitude of Pareto suboptimality. Here, Pareto-set information is generally too coarse: distinct environments can share the same Pareto set while inducing different reward geometries and Pareto gaps, and averaging environments consistent with one Pareto set need not preserve Pareto dominance. This motivates retaining finer information about the environment. We develop parameter-level information-theoretic analyses of Thompson Sampling and Information-Directed Sampling to derive gap-based regret guarantees. Under sublinear information budgets, Pareto Thompson Sampling also achieves sublinear gap regret while recovering the full Pareto set on the same run, with a related guarantee for a fixed mixture with gap-based IDS. Together, our results reveal a hierarchy of information requirements: binary Pareto membership can be controlled through set-level information, whereas quantitative Pareto-gap suboptimality can require finer knowledge of reward geometry.

papers.title: When Source-Domain Validation Fails to Transfer: A Staged Study of Hyperparameter Selection
papers.abstract: Hyperparameters for an unseen domain are often selected using held-out examples from the available source domains. Withholding entire source domains during validation seems to better reflect deployment shift, but does this produce better selections on independent targets? We investigate this question through two complementary studies. A preliminary factorial experiment crosses particle swarm optimization and random search with pooled source validation and a leave-one-source-domain-out mean-minimum fitness on PACS and Multi-Domain Sentiment. The domain-aware fitness does not provide a consistent target advantage. We then separate selector development from confirmation using a shared pool of 64 configurations per task across four image benchmarks. Complete target-performance landscapes on VLCS and Office-Home inform one rule: retain the top 16 configurations by pooled source validation, then select the largest leave-one-source-domain-out mean-minus-standard-deviation score. The rule is frozen before evaluation on TerraIncognita and SVIRO. Across their 14 target domains, its equal-dataset-weighted balanced-accuracy difference from pooled validation is +0.097 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [-0.685, +0.960]), with five wins and nine losses. Exploratory analyses reveal substantial variation across datasets, target domains, and training seeds. These results do not establish equivalence or a general failure of domain-aware validation. They show that the evaluated source-domain criteria did not establish reliable target gains under the tested protocols, and motivate assessing selection rules on datasets independent of those used to develop them.

papers.title: Compatible expansions and rigidity in subtraction games with a single pass
papers.abstract: We study normal-play subtraction games with one globally shared pass. An expansion of the subtraction set is pass-equivalent if it leaves the pass-available Sprague--Grundy sequence unchanged. We show that pure periodicity of the ordinary sequence, together with an eventual translation identity for the pass-available sequence, forces every pass-equivalent expansion to preserve the ordinary sequence. For two-element sets $\{x,y\}$, we classify the compatible additional moves: they are exactly $x+1,\ldots,y-1$ when $y\leq 2x$, and there are none when $y>2x$. We extend this result to sets in short intervals. An exact recurrence certificate also exhibits a three-element set for which pass-state rigidity fails.

papers.title: NoveltyGate: Novelty, Not Error, Decides Which VLA Prefix Tokens to Compute Exactly
papers.abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $\pi_{0.5}$ re-encode the camera images and the instruction with a 2B-parameter backbone at every control step, and the feed-forward layers of this prefix account for most of its compute. A natural way to save this compute is to send most tokens through a low-rank MLP and compute exactly only the tokens whose approximation error is large. We find that this intuition is wrong. Even a verifier that knows every token's exact error picks the wrong tokens, producing 1.3--1.7$\times$ larger action deviation than a simple test of whether a token's input is novel, that is, whether it falls outside the subspace seen during calibration. Large errors concentrate in tokens the policy relies on little, such as the third-person camera, while the novelty test favors the wrist camera, a view the action depends on heavily. We call this the error--reliance gap. Building on it, we propose NoveltyGate, a training-free method that routes each prefix token, once per layer and before any multiplication, to either a low-rank or the original MLP. Deciding once per layer instead of once per matrix product avoids moving wide intermediate tensors and keeps every shape static, so the whole prefix runs as a single CUDA graph. On LIBERO, NoveltyGate accelerates the $\pi_{0.5}$ prefix by up to 1.61$\times$, stays 2.7--2.9$\times$ closer to the original policy than channel pruning and low-rank compression at equal compute, and preserves closed-loop task success.

papers.title: Precision-Aware Learning Rate Transfer Across Block Count in LLM Post-Training
papers.abstract: The post-training of pretrained large language models, including supervised finetuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), is very sensitive to the learning rate, and tuning it through grid search is costly in both computation and memory. In this work, we propose \textbf{TipSweep}, a method to transfer the learning rate across the number of trainable transformer blocks. To do so efficiently, we search for the best learning rate by training only the last $k_0$ blocks (in our experiments, typically $k_0=1$), and provide scaling rules that predict the optimal learning rate when training any set of $k$ blocks, including when $k=L$ (the full transformer). Across experiments with models ranging from 1 to 7 billion parameters, we observe that the optimal learning rate follows precision-dependent scaling rules: the optimal rate scales approximately as $k^{-1}$ with float32 (FP32) master weights, but as $k^{-1/2}$ when updates are applied directly to bfloat16 (BF16) weights without a master copy. We explain both rules using an analytical model that accounts for update rounding, under assumptions supported by profiling experiments. Finally, we develop two prototypes of the learning rate search for a 6.7-billion-parameter model. The first fits the search on a single consumer GPU with 16 GiB of memory. The second speeds up the search on a high-end GPU by evaluating all candidate learning rates in a single pass over the data, so that a five-candidate search takes about half the GPU hours of one full-depth ($k=L$) run.

papers.title: The mean orders of even and odd permutations
papers.abstract: We compare the sums of the orders of the even and odd permutations of a given degree. For all large degrees the odd permutations have the larger sum. The excess equals the sum of orders of the permutations of odd order up to a relative error decaying faster than any power of the degree. Following Goh and Schmutz, we determine the logarithm of this sum over the group order asymptotically, with an explicit constant. Hence the ratio of the sums of element orders of the symmetric and alternating groups tends to two from above. The proof rests on an exact identity for generating functions. It isolates cycles of length a large prime times a small factor. Inclusion and exclusion over small odd primes enlarges this family. Each Euler factor is bounded by its maximum modulus. All constants are certified in ball arithmetic. Exact values up to degree 150 suggest that the odd permutations have the larger sum from degree four on.

papers.title: Model-Averaged Shrinkage Estimation of the Spectral Density Using Welch's Method
papers.abstract: We propose a shrinkage estimator of the spectral density based on a three-level hierarchical model. At the first level, we smooth Welch's spectral density estimator and model it as arriving from a Gaussian distribution centered at the true spectral density. In the second level, we place a normal prior on the true spectral density. We center this prior at a spectral density estimated assuming the data from an ARMA($p$,$q$) process. From these two levels, we create a conditionally specified shrinkage estimator. The conditional specification, of course, is the order of the ARMA process, i.e., the values of $p$ and $q$. We avoid selecting a particular order by creating a third level in which priors are placed on $p$ and $q$. Our final estimator is then a weighted average of shrinkage estimators. The average is taken over a set of ARMA($p$, $q$) models, and the weights are governed by the posteriors of $p$ and $q$. The methods introduced in this paper are similar to those presented in Botts and Daniels, but distinct from them in one critical way: the first level of the hierarchy. In the first level of our model, we borrow from recently developed theoretical results of Welch's spectral density estimator. Our estimator is consistent, computationally simple, and has performance comparable (and often superior) to other estimators.

authors.name: Carsten Botts
authors.institution: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory

papers.title: FAS-Assisted Self-Interference Mitigation for In-Band Full-Duplex Communications
papers.abstract: In-band full-duplex (IBFD) communication relies on effective self-interference cancellation (SIC) to overcome the strong loopback self-interference (SI). While fluid antenna system (FAS)-assisted SIC offers superior SI suppression by dynamically selecting the FAS port to minimize the residual SI power, it incurs high pilot overhead to acquire channel state information (CSI) for both forward and loopback channels. This raises the question of whether forward channel CSI is necessary for effective SI mitigation. To address this challenge, we propose a pilot-efficient FAS-assisted SI mitigation (FAS-SIM) approach that selects the FAS port solely based on the loopback SI channel. Theoretical performance analysis of the forward signal is provided. Numerical results then reveal that FAS-SIM achieves SI suppression and a forward-link rate comparable to the conventional method, while reducing port-selection training overhead by 50%, offering a low-overhead solution for IBFD communications.

papers.title: Which Failure Does an Intervention Repair? When Agent Interventions Help, and Where Self-Evolving Skills Stall
papers.abstract: An intervention that improves one agent can break another, and adding a stronger harness on top need not repair the damage. Agent interventions such as skills, harnesses, and extra inference budget are nonetheless usually credited with one average gain, measured under one setup. We ask instead when each intervention helps and which failure it repairs. A matched factorial study over nine benchmarks, four models, four skill conditions, four harness levels, and three budgets, with nearly 0.9 million trajectories, changes one axis at a time. No configuration is best everywhere, interventions interact rather than add, and a harness can absorb a skill's gain, rescue a failure the skill causes, or leave the gain intact. The failure left by the current system points to the fix: missing knowledge to a stronger model, execution errors to a richer harness. Yet feedback is not recovery: a matched recovery repairs mainly failures that leave a visible error signal. Skills that evolve from the agent's own experience hit a bottleneck: they rarely beat a short human-written skill, can learn dataset shortcuts, break when moved to another model, and cannot supply missing facts, which outside information does. A benchmark-level switch to the model favored by a 20-task labeled pilot achieves both higher performance and lower cost than always using the stronger model. Agent interventions should be judged by which failure they repair and under which configuration.

papers.title: EmoRouter: Adaptive Modality Cascading for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) involves detecting the underlying emotion behind each utterance within a conversation, which is essential for emotionally aware human-computer interaction. While omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) demonstrate strong capability for MER by jointly processing modalities including text, audio, and vision, different modality combinations yield different prediction outcomes across utterances: acoustic and visual inputs can help recover annotated labels missed by text-only inference, but can also turn correct predictions into errors. Processing all modalities for every utterance is also computationally expensive. To this end, we introduce EmoRouter, a training-free, model-agnostic framework for adaptive modality cascading that selects an exit tier for each utterance along a predefined modality order. The routing is guided by prediction-uncertainty estimates derived from Conformal Prediction. EmoRouter routes each utterance through a sequence of increasing-cost modality levels and exits at the first level when the model is confident in the emotion. To determine when to exit, we propose Conformal Set Contraction, a structural calibration criterion that calibrates the per-tier CP error budgets used for these exit decisions. Comprehensive evaluations on 4 MER benchmarks and 3 Omni-LLMs reveal that EmoRouter matches or outperforms the full modalities while reducing inference latency by 67.9--94.5%. Furthermore, EmoRouter demonstrates high transferability across different models, validating its robustness. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyi-lab/EmoRouter.

papers.title: Wrist-Camera Video Diffusion as Generalizable Robot Policies
papers.abstract: A generalist manipulation policy should perform new tasks, operate in unfamiliar scenes, and transfer skills across robot embodiments.
