papers.title: Persuasion from Within: Model-Based Insider Attacks in Multi-Agent LLM Debate and Consensus
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems for collective decision-making, such as multi-agent debate and consensus games, in which agents exchange messages and update their answers over multiple rounds and a resolution mechanism aggregates them into a final outcome. Most multi-agent LLM frameworks assume that every participant shares the system objective. In practice, however, a malicious agent can join as a legitimate member of the group and persuade the other agents toward a hidden adversarial goal. We formalize such attacks as a sequential decision-making problem in which the insider seeks to degrade the utility of the collective outcome. We propose a model-based insider attack that learns to persuade a group of agents: the insider first learns a world model of the benign agents from offline trajectories and then uses it both to train a persuasion policy and to plan its messages. In two case studies involving a numerical consensus game and a multi-agent debate, the learned insider is the most effective and the stealthiest attack we evaluate, outperforming both prompt-based and trained LLM persuaders from prior work. The attack also transfers to other target models, larger groups, and unseen datasets, and remains effective under existing Byzantine-resilience defenses. The learned insider also enables a new defense: adversarially training benign agents on the attack data largely removes both our attack and the strongest prior persuasion attack. These results show that combining world models with reinforcement learning and planning is an effective route to both attacking and hardening language-based multi-agent systems.

papers.title: Deneb-Vritra: Descriptions, Edges and Names Examined by Blocking Via Restoring Token Representations and Attention
papers.abstract: Laya is a 421M-parameter encoder that answers a question about a text in one pass: each answer option, written as a name plus a description, gets a marker token, and one score is read from the network at each marker. We first confirm that such models can follow an option's name when it contradicts the description; the question is where in the network this happens. We locate it. On 951 synthetic questions we move each name onto another option's description and count how often the model picks the option with the right name (the name shortcut): 53% for the released checkpoint, 59% for our fine-tune v1, 11% for a fine-tune with name randomisation. On a 320-item sample, blocking attention from each marker to its own name tokens in layers 14 to 17 of 28 cuts v1's shortcut from 67% to 16% (19% on two schemas held out from component selection) while accuracy with the original names stays at 90%; blocking marker edges to the question, other options or text has no effect. No single head matters (largest effect 9 points), and restoring clean marker states undoes the swap from layer 16. Attention mass tracks the window by layer but not by head. Repeated on 5 checkpoints (released, fine-tuned, name-randomised, and a pair trained without two schemas), the knockout finds similar layers; in the name-randomised ones, blocking the description edges instead brings the shortcut back to 56-58%, so the read persists and is outvoted. Marker states decode the name from layer 0; a one-direction probe erasure changed nothing but was weaker than a random edit. Copying layers 0-13 or 14-27 of a name-randomised sibling into a fine-tune recovers 66% and 65% (v1); 21% and 45% (pair A) of its shortcut reduction. 9 of the 12 predictions we could score, written before running, failed. Head sweeps cover 5 of 5 checkpoints; data are synthetic and LLM-labelled; one architecture.

papers.title: How many mistakes does it take to learn an interval? Exact Littlestone dimensions of intervals and their unions
papers.abstract: The Littlestone dimension of a hypothesis class equals the smallest number of mistakes an online learner can guarantee against an adaptive adversary. For discrete intervals and unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points, only its order of growth was known. We determine it exactly. For every switch budget $k$ (with both end labels fixed when $k$ is odd), the smallest size on which $d$ mistakes can be forced follows a three-regime law: $d+1$ while $d\le k$, then $2d-k+1$, and beyond $d=\lceil 3k/2\rceil+k-1$ doubling the size adds exactly $k$ mistakes. Unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points correspond to $k=2j$ and size $m+1$, and a single interval gives the thresholds $1,2,3,5,7,10,14,20,\dots$. The natural learner that waits for a positive example and binary-searches both endpoints is not optimal: it can be forced into one extra mistake for 50,847 of the domain sizes below $10^5$. Upper bounds come from a gap potential and a block-pairing learner, and lower bounds from adversary strategies and a refinement step. These tools give an explicit optimal learner with $O(\log m)$ time per round, which on random streams makes more mistakes on average than the natural learner. For randomised learners, we compute the randomised Littlestone dimension of thresholds exactly and prove that a greedy adversary forces an explicit closed-form number of expected mistakes on intervals; this bound is within $0.64$ of optimal and, we conjecture, exact (confirmed for $m\le70$). Exact computation tests every result, and the formulas for every switch budget are machine-checked in Lean 4.

papers.title: Advancements in Diabetic Retinopathy Classification Using Novel Multi-Stacked U-Net Architectures
papers.abstract: Diabetes leads to several health complications throughout the body, with the complication in the eyes being Diabetic Retinopathy. It leads to damaging or abnormal changes in the blood vessels' structure, causing vision loss. The need for massive screening of a large population of diabetic patients has created a necessity for computer-aided, fully automatic diagnosis of DR. CNNs have shown great promise in the classification of DR based on the Fundus images. Building a reliable model faces considerable challenges due to the limited availability of high-quality annotated datasets and issues with varying image quality and class imbalances. This paper aims to demonstrate the UNET, and its Stacked Architecture variant and their performance across several datasets. This paper has compared and studied the UNET architecture's performance across multiple stacks and has come to a soft conclusion that the architecture performs its best at three stacks, and any more leads to deterioration of its performance. The model aims at classifying the images into five categories, 0 to 4, where 0 is no DR, and 4 is proliferative DR.

papers.title: From local competition to bump attractors:how excitation width sets capacity, interference and updating in recurrent models of visual working memory
papers.abstract: On-centre off-surround (OCOS) networks and bump attractors, the two main recurrent models of visual working memory, differ chiefly in how far recurrent excitation spreads. We place them in one family parameterised by excitation width at fixed total excitation, and ask how stable each stored item is and what it costs the circuit to hold and change it. The answer is that excitation width sets the price of continuity. In the OCOS limit, which we solve exactly by completing the energy-function formalism of \citet{Sengupta2024}, an item occupies a single unit, relaxes quickly and never drifts, and capacity follows in closed form, exact over all stable states. As excitation widens towards a bump-like regime, items become continuous but costly: per item, the circuit uses 15--29 units instead of one and 6.5--11 times the activity, relaxes 35--60 times more slowly after a perturbation, needs a 35--230 times stronger cue to accept a second item, and holds 7--10 items instead of at least 40. Under noise, with background false alarms approximately matched, about a third of wide items drift, whereas narrow items never move. Yet even as an item's translation mode softens towards zero, items remain locked to the lattice. Locking is poorly predicted by energy differences between item positions, but strongly predicted by how far the unit just beyond an item's edge sits below threshold (rank correlation 0.91 across 40 parameter settings). Where that margin vanishes, a new input captures the stored item instead of being added to memory.

papers.title: Quadratic periods and preperiods in subtraction games with one varying move
papers.abstract: We give two infinite families of counterexamples to Zhang's conjectures on the period and preperiod of the Sprague-Grundy sequence when a single move c is adjoined to a fixed subtraction set S. For S = {4,5,10} and c = 15t+13 with t >= 2, the least period is c+19 and the least preperiod is (c^2+21c+8)/15. For S = {3,7,10} and c = 90t+9 with t >= 1, the least period is (c^2+26c+615)/30 and the least preperiod is 19 less than the period. The latter quadratic period also occurs in the outcome sequence, which is periodic from its first term. The proofs construct the sequences from fixed words and reduce the mex recurrence to a finite table of local identities.

papers.title: AdapToC: A Unified Framework for Multi-Task Visual Token Communication
papers.abstract: Pretrained discrete visual tokenizers supply compact latents for synthesis, recognition, and embodied perception, yet wireless token streaming remains fragile. Under fading and noisy pilots, hard cyclic redundancy check (CRC) erasures turn corrupted blocks into missing tokens while frozen decoders amplify edge errors, which can collapse unequal error protection (UEP) into a binary choice between strong coding and omission under severe fading. Soft bit posteriors break this collapse. We present AdapToC, a single-pass transceiver that restores multi-tier rate-distortion tradeoffs without altering tokenizer weights or differentiating through pixel decoders. We align codebook geometry to the channel via offline frequency-weighted Pseudo-Gray relabeling and Halton dispersion to contract bit and burst errors with zero overhead. Because soft recovery pulls intermediate rates onto the three-tier convex hull, our unit-gated AdaLN sender schedules protection tiers across channel budgets, while our pilot-calibrated receiver feeds factorized codebook posteriors into a ConvNeXt-attention restorer with CRC bypass. We co-train AdapToC solely in latent space via counterfactual utility estimation and codebook cross-entropy regularization. On identical VQGAN-f16 tokens, AdapToC outperforms TONIC and adaptive TokenCom+AMC, cuts multi-SNR Rayleigh LPIPS from 0.6551 to 0.3312 within the frozen-tokenizer PSNR ceiling, and saves 43.8% Rician-K6 symbols at matched quality. Our single-pass restorer runs 8.3x faster than iterative resampling, raises accuracy while accelerating decoder-free recognition 20.6x, and improves fidelity plug-and-play across TiTok, VAR, and zero-shot NuPlan.

papers.title: How long must an honest confidence interval be after causal discovery? Benign and malignant weak edges
papers.abstract: After causal discovery, a confidence interval for a total effect valid uniformly over the model class must pay for structural uncertainty. We measure this price by the worst-case ratio of expected length to that of the efficient interval knowing the graph, for linear Gaussian models with a known superset of the adjacencies and k-triangle faithfulness. The global price is of order sqrt(n) once one edge can be malignant, so we study it locally, near a generic distribution with one edge absent. Our main result classifies this weak edge by Meek closures. It is benign if deleting it leaves the effect identifiable in the resulting MPDAG and Markov equivalent explanations agree; the local price is then bounded, and otherwise, for small k, of order sqrt(n). At benign edges the price is of order R+K, with R a ratio of efficient lengths and K a cross-model constant. It equals one, so that honesty is free, exactly when K = 0, generically decided by a d-separation. For two Markov classes it is determined within a factor 3.40, and its upper bound is approached without knowing the base point or the weak edge. A further graphical condition gives the rate uniformly in a second edge's margin.

papers.title: JaxNaviSim: A GPU-Accelerated, Data-Driven Simulator and Learning Benchmark for Maritime Navigation
papers.abstract: Coordinating vessels through the shared waterways of busy ports grows more challenging as vessel traffic increases. Port authorities need realistic simulations to assess how arrival schedules, anchorage assignments, and routes affect vessel throughput and navigation safety. Existing AIS-based trajectory models predict a vessel's track from its past trajectory in an open-loop fashion. They do not simulate step-by-step responses to other ships or test whether a vessel collides or reaches its goal. To address this problem, we introduce JaxNaviSim, a data-driven simulator and learning benchmark coupling Automatic Identification System (AIS) data with fast, controllable traffic simulation, in which learned models steer vessels through recorded traffic. First, we release a dataset of ~141 million AIS records from over 30K vessels across eight high-density regions of the Singapore Strait, among the world's busiest waterways, with ~6.7 million vessel-hours. Unlike several existing AIS datasets which mostly cover open seas, ours captures close-quarters vessel traffic in the narrow strait. Second, we define a navigation task for each recorded vessel trajectory. A model steers that vessel every 10 s from its recorded state to its anchoring point or region exit, while surrounding ships follow their recorded tracks or are steered by the model. We implement a JAX simulator that runs these tasks in large batches on a GPU. We also incorporate multiple vessel dynamics models and sea surface currents. Finally, we benchmark imitation learning (IL), offline and online RL, and include Predictive Action Refinement (PAR) as a safety baseline that cuts collision rates to 1-3%. The comparison shows that low tracking error does not ensure arrival, and learned policies can reach most destinations yet collide in 20-45% of episodes.

papers.title: Anisoplanatic Blind Deconvolution using Phase Diversity
papers.abstract: Atmospheric turbulence distorts the wavefront of light from a distant scene and blurs its image. Over a field of view wider than the isoplanatic angle, the distortion varies with direction and evolves in time, so no single wavefront describes the blur. Multiframe blind deconvolution (MFBD) can recover the scene from measurements spread over a long acquisition, but falls short during fast imaging because of limited diversity across measurements. We present coded anisoplanatic blind deconvolution (CA-BD), in which a pupil-plane spatial light modulator (SLM) applies a different known phase code to every measurement, with no wavefront sensor or deformable mirror, so that the measurements carry diversity even within a short acquisition. A per-pixel single-layer estimator recovers the object and spatially varying phases from the coded measurements. In simulation, a Cram\'er-Rao bound analysis shows that under anisoplanatism direct imaging needs about 41 times the photons of coded imaging for equal phase precision in strong turbulence. At the stronger of two turbulence strengths, CA-BD outperforms tuned MFBD on average at every burst length. It reduces the phase mean squared error 3.5x for stationary turbulence and 2-3x for time-varying turbulence. Measurements taken within a few coherence times benefit most from the known coded SLM patterns, making faster SLMs the key to its full advantage in time-varying turbulence.

papers.title: The Complexity of Oracle-Efficient Realizable Transductive Learning
papers.abstract: In realizable transductive online learning, the learner knows the entire sequence of $T$ instances in advance, and the labels are consistent with one of $N$ hypotheses. With explicit access to the hypothesis class, the halving algorithm makes at most $\log_2 N$ mistakes. Can a comparable guarantee be achieved using only polynomially many empirical risk minimization (ERM) queries? We answer this question negatively, even for a weighted-ERM oracle that optimizes arbitrary real-valued linear objectives and returns a complete maximizing hypothesis. For every fixed $\beta\in(0,1)$ and every randomized learner making polynomially many oracle queries, there exists a fixed realizable instance with exactly $N=2^{\lfloor T^\beta\rfloor}$ hypotheses on which the learner makes $\Omega_\beta(\sqrt{T\log N})$ mistakes in expectation. This matches the agnostic-rate upper bound achieved by random playout using $O(T)$ oracle calls. The separation persists for much smaller classes as well: along a sequence with $\log N=\Theta((\log T)^2)$, we establish a mistake lower bound of $\exp(\Omega(\log T/\log\log T))$. Our main technical contribution is a composition lemma that combines two realizable prediction problems such that their mistake lower bounds add, up to a small loss, while their hypothesis class sizes grow only additively. Iterating this lemma yields a family of hard instances spanning the desired parameter regimes, establishing a sharp separation between information-theoretic and oracle-efficient mistake guarantees.

papers.title: Spatially Grounded Latent Lookahead for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from strong semantic representations that support object recognition and instruction understanding. However, precise manipulation also depends on resolving object locations and workspace relations, and on selecting actions with an estimate of how the scene will evolve. Existing geometry-aware methods make the current scene more explicit, while predictive methods model future observations or representations. Yet future information is often neither grounded in a control-relevant spatial state nor directly used to guide action generation. We introduce Spatially Grounded Latent Lookahead (SG-LL), which uses the grounded present as the reference for predicting an actionable near-future representation. A frozen spatial teacher first distills geometric priors into policy-connected spatial tokens. A current-conditioned bottleneck then learns a compact latent that captures future information relative to the present scene. This latent is predicted from the current policy context and initial Action Expert features, without access to future observations or the spatial teacher. Finally, zero-initialized residual fusion incorporates the predicted latent into the Action Expert to refine action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and three real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improvements over
  in both simulation and real-robot settings.

authors.name: Qihang Chen
authors.institution: Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications

papers.title: LIBERO-MOR: A Multimodal Robustness Benchmark Across the Vision-Language-Action Pipeline
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on robot manipulation benchmarks. Translating this progress into reliable deployment calls for systematic evaluation of how policies respond to variations throughout the robot interaction loop. We introduce LIBERO-MOR, a multimodal robustness benchmark across the vision-language-action pipeline. Built on standard LIBERO, it covers five deployment-facing domains: vision, language, proprioception, action execution, and environment. The benchmark comprises 22 deployment-inspired perturbations, each evaluated at three severity levels across 40 tasks under a paired clean-perturbed protocol, enabling controlled and reproducible comparisons. We evaluate seven representative VLA models spanning diverse action-generation mechanisms. Our experiments reveal substantial robustness gaps behind high clean-task success, together with shared vulnerabilities and distinct model-specific failure patterns across domains. Severity analysis further distinguishes progressive degradation, collapse at stronger interventions, and failures triggered at the mildest tested level. By connecting aggregate performance to pipeline domains, individual perturbations, and intervention strength, LIBERO-MOR provides a systematic framework for diagnosing VLA robustness and guiding the development of more reliable robot policies.

authors.name: Qihang Chen
authors.institution: Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications

papers.title: Mirrored Min-of-K Training
papers.abstract: Min-of-K (MoK) training is widely used to train models that produce diverse outputs from random noise. For each target, it draws K outputs from the model and backpropagates only through the one closest to the target. However, MoK generally does not make the generated distribution match the data distribution. In this paper, we analyze the MoK bias across all values of K and show that tuning K shifts between failure modes, from mode dropping at small K to distribution flattening at large K. We further prove that every nontrivial loss based only on target-candidate distances fails to recover some data distribution, since these distances do not reveal how the candidates are placed relative to each other. Based on these analyses, we propose mirrored MoK (MMoK), a drop-in modification of MoK training that draws one extra sample from the model, applies the closest-candidate selection rule against it, and subtracts the resulting distance. Since this distance is measured between samples of the model, it provides additional information about how the candidates are placed relative to each other. We prove that MMoK can in principle recover data distributions that MoK cannot. We empirically validate MMoK on five scenarios, namely synthetic mixtures, pedestrian and vehicle trajectory prediction, tropical cyclone forecasting, robotic policy learning, and ambiguous medical image segmentation. The results confirm the effectiveness and generality of MMoK in both distribution learning and task performance.

papers.title: JKO-GRPO: Augmenting GRPO with Wasserstein Proximal Steps for Flow-Matching VLAs
papers.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $\pi_0,\pi_{0.5}$ generate continuous action chunks by flow matching, and online reinforcement learning (RL) can improve them beyond supervised fine-tuning. Existing methods, such as Flow-GRPO and $\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}$, optimize likelihood ratios of stochastic denoising transitions, which reweight the sampled actions by their advantages but do not use the distances between them. We propose JKO-GRPO, which augments Flow-GRPO with Wasserstein proximal steps, with two contributions: (1) At each state, we treat the group of sampled actions as an empirical distribution and formulate policy improvement as a Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) step. We use a soft discrete $c$-transform to construct transport targets from group-relative advantages and combine shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler onto these targets and combined with the clipped Flow-GRPO objective without Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. (2) We extend this approach to sequential VLA control through random-time branching: we select one or multiple action-chunk indices along old-policy trajectories and independently apply group-level JKO updates using candidate continuations from the corresponding states.

papers.title: CarlHOI: Counterfactual Predictive Imagination for Generalizable Multi-Humanoid Object Interaction under Constrained Environments
papers.abstract: Recent advances in physics-based humanoid control enable teams of varying sizes to coordinate their movements and cooperatively transport shared objects. However, adapting learned cooperative behaviors to unseen environmental constraints remains challenging, particularly when obstacles require coordinated detours and changes in team configuration. We propose CarlHOI, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built upon a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model (CarlWM) for human-object interaction (HOI), enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt to unseen environmental constraints without retraining their underlying cooperative control policies. CarlHOI explicitly represents the shared object, individual humanoids, and environmental obstacles as interacting entities. Trained offline using counterfactual simulator rollouts, the model imagines alternative collective futures under different shared waypoint commands, predicting how the coupled humanoid team and object would respond. By evaluating these imagined outcomes through predicted progress, failure, and contact risks, and long-horizon value estimates, CarlHOI selects adaptive guidance commands while preserving the pretrained cooperative controller. We introduce a benchmark comprising three challenging obstacle-constrained transport tasks to evaluate adaptation and generalization. Despite being trained exclusively with four humanoids, our model generalizes without retraining to teams of two to ten humanoids, unseen obstacle geometries and placements, unseen objects, and novel combinations of environmental constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved cooperative transport success over evaluated baselines across diverse configurations. Results highlight the potential of counterfactual predictive imagination to extend pretrained multi-humanoid cooperative skills beyond their original training conditions.

papers.title: Confidently Lost: Silent Failure and Edge Deployment of Dense Visual SLAM under Photon Starvation
papers.abstract: Dense visual SLAM built on learned two-view geometry is evaluated in good light; in low light it fails silently. Two frames of 9-level quantized noise, no scene at all, give MASt3R-SLAM's network a cross-view geometric self-consistency of 0.936; a real dark frame pair gives 0.935. Starved of structure, the network invents the same geometry for both views and the system trusts the agreement: on a dark sequence it consumes 1,605 frames, emits 7 keyframes, rejects no factor-graph edges and reports full frame rate, while over 95% of the correspondences it accepts violate the ground-truth epipolar geometry. One inflated statistic is read by two subsystems against thresholds in opposite directions, so keyframing starves while relocalization accepts almost every candidate. The same statistic, read at keyframe-pair baselines, separates the confident collapse from working runs on the ETH3D dark sequences without ground truth or extra computation (in-sample). Low-light-adapted weights take tracked trajectories from 1/6 to 5/6, as does retuning two thresholds; neither yields accurate ones, because the adaptation withdraws confidence from wrong geometry rather than finding right geometry. Replayed on a Jetson AGX Orin carried by a legged robot, the mechanism's signature reproduces on the two darkest of four routes, and which of its faces appears varies with route geometry and sensor encoding. The network does not lose confidence in the dark; it manufactures it.

papers.title: MASTO: Missed-thrust Aware Stochastic Trajectory Optimization
papers.abstract: Missed Thrust Events (MTEs) are a major roadblock towards widespread adoption of low-thrust propulsion for deep space missions. Unplanned thruster outages have previously been difficult to directly incorporate in the preliminary mission design process, and current approaches mostly introduce robustness by conservative heuristics such as mandatory coasting arcs, which do not possess any safety guarantees, and usually only consider one missed-thrust event. Therefore, in this work, we utilize a stochastic hybrid system framework to model a spacecraft as a Markov jump system that can switch between nominal and failure mode. We formulate the Missed-thrust resilient trajectory optimization problem as a Markov jump covariance steering problem, and propose a sequential convex programming-based approach, which can also respect chance constraints. We demonstrate our framework on two complex three-dimensional transfers in the Earth-Moon circular restricted three body problem, showcasing robustness against a range of MTEs, while respecting chance constraints. We further analyze controller performance across a range of MTE-probability distributions, offering valuable insights into the MTE-resilient trajectory design trade space.

papers.title: Optimistic Online Learning for Coding Agents with Aggregate Feedback
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents operating on Web development platforms can interact with repositories, issue trackers, and continuous integration services to carry out long-horizon software engineering tasks. However, behavioral drift remains a major bottleneck in such multi-turn reasoning and action trajectories. To mitigate this, activation steering has emerged as a promising approach for regularizing agent behaviors by intervening on the LLM's transformer residual streams. Nonetheless, existing methods typically apply a static steering policy across all tasks, overlooking the fact that a single policy is rarely effective across heterogeneous tasks and varying execution turns. This limitation motivates dynamic online selection among candidate steering policies. Yet, doing so in long-horizon agentic settings is challenging: verifiable task-level feedback is only revealed upon task completion, leaving the contributions of individual steering turns unobserved. To address this challenge, we formulate online steering-policy selection as a multi-armed bandit problem with delayed task-level feedback and turn-level predictive hints derived from residual-stream activations. Within this formulation, we introduce Online Optimistic Activation Steering, a meta-framework that uses hints to guide within-task steering policy selection and leverages terminal task-level feedback to correct cumulative reward estimates. Theoretically, against the best fixed policy in hindsight, we prove regret bounds that tighten with increasing hint accuracy and establish a matching lower bound with respect to prediction error and candidate policy count. Empirical evaluations on realistic coding benchmarks demonstrate that our framework outperforms both static steering policies and naive online adaptive baselines.

authors.name: See-Kiong Ng
authors.institution: Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China

papers.title: AnchorCredit: Output-Anchored Credit Assignment for Structured Generation with Multiple Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: In Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and related methods typically compute group-relative advantages from response rewards and broadcast the same advantage to every generated token in a response to guide policy updates. However, we identify a systematic problem of cross-component credit misassignment in tasks with multiple verifiable results, such as joint multi-attribute prediction: low rewards for some components can penalize a well-performing component and its associated reasoning. To address this problem, we propose AnchorCredit. The method uses the policy model's attention from output anchors to preceding reasoning sentences to estimate sentence-component associations and assign component-specific advantages to the relevant reasoning, without additional relevance annotations or a separate relevance discriminator. To support the study of credit assignment with multiple verifiable rewards, we construct ProductAttr, a benchmark of 7,200 real product image-text samples. Experiments show that AnchorCredit outperforms existing baselines on this benchmark. Experiments on the public Nutrition5k dataset further support the method's effectiveness in this setting.

papers.title: Tropical Geometry-based ReLU Lyapunov Function and Controller Synthesis
papers.abstract: We investigate the joint synthesis of neural network Lyapunov functions and stabilizing controllers for systems modeled as neural ordinary differential equations (neural ODEs) with ReLU activations. Our approach leverages tools from tropical geometry, an emerging analytical framework for characterizing properties of ReLU neural networks. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to introduce tropical geometry-based methods into control theory. We represent candidate Lyapunov functions as tropical quotients of tropical signomials, which allows us to enforce the equilibrium condition at the origin and formulate constraints ensuring positive definiteness over a prescribed region of interest. We construct a total Lie surface representing the Lie derivative of the candidate Lyapunov function along the neural ODE dynamics and formulate an optimization problem to find Lyapunov parameters that ensure its negativity throughout the region of interest. This enables the systematic search for Lyapunov functions satisfying the desired stability conditions. Finally, we extend this framework to jointly synthesize a ReLU neural network stabilizing controller and a neural Lyapunov function, providing a unified approach to stability analysis and controller synthesis. We validate our proposed method on several nonlinear systems approximated as neural ODEs, demonstrating applications to Lyapunov function synthesis as well as joint Lyapunov function and controller synthesis.

papers.title: Scheduling of Variable-Speed Pumped Storage via Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Variable-speed pumped storage hydropower (VSPSH) plants modulate power continuously in both generation and pumping, a match for the net-load ramps of rising wind and solar. Their flexibility is bounded by hydraulics rather than by a power rating, so the deliverable power range shifts with net head and excludes small outputs entirely. This paper addresses bidding and dispatch for such a plant across a two-settlement market with a hierarchical reinforcement-learning formulation. Its two layers are circularly dependent: a real-time (RT) bid is defined only against a cleared day-ahead (DA) commitment, and the DA reward only against an RT dispatch policy. Our proposed feasibility-constrained domain randomization breaks the cycle by training the RT layer on generated deliverable DA schedules before any bidding policy exists; the DA layer then optimizes against that frozen RT behavior, and the two alternate. Learning a policy at once profitable and deliverable is obstructed by the nonconvex operating region: penalizing infeasibility competes against the revenue the offer earns, discouraging an undeliverable offer without preventing one. We therefore pursue safety through action-space modification rather than through the reward, combining action masking of the bid space, projection of each commitment before settlement, and replacement by a fail-safe controller. Over 48 out-of-sample days it earns $3,313/day more than an equivalent penalty formulation while holding undeliverable commitment at a median of zero, which the penalty formulation does not, and no ablation improves on it without giving up deliverability or the storage target.

papers.title: ActField: Learning Action Effects as Continuous-Time Latent Dynamics
papers.abstract: Learning how actions change visual states is essential for prediction and decision-making in embodied tasks. Existing action-conditioned JEPA world models typically predict future representations at discrete observation intervals, leaving the temporal evolution of action effects implicit. We introduce ActField, a continuous-time JEPA world model that explicitly models latent state evolution through an action-conditioned vector field integrated over physical time. ActField separates action-independent evolution from action-induced changes, with the latter modulated by the latent context. A reference-conditioned representation and multi-step dynamics loss further support accurate long-horizon prediction. Together, these components provide a structured and temporally continuous formulation for predicting action-conditioned visual dynamics. Experiments across LIBERO, DROID, and BEHAVIOR demonstrate improved visual prediction fidelity and more accurate action-induced motion prediction over existing world models. Further evaluations on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate the utility of ActField in improving downstream policy planning through VLM-guided action selection.

papers.title: EvoViM: Recursively Self-Evolving Visual Agents for Exploration with Deferred Queries
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. The program retains images and computes directly on pixels, and its operations decide how this evidence is used in each task. During memory evolution, the same model traces failures in its visual trajectories to the operations that lost or misused evidence and revises them. It also rewrites the notes and analysis tools that guide later revisions, which then build on earlier findings and skip changes that have already failed. We evaluate EvoViM with three multimodal models on six tasks covering visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three tasks with deferred queries. Across the six tasks, EvoViM improves the average score over AutoMem, the strongest baseline in the main comparison, by 31.3-47.6 points on held-out episodes. Programs written once from the initial environment instructions perform substantially worse, highlighting the value of interaction experience in shaping how visual evidence is retained and used. Code and dataset are available at https://evovim.github.io/.

papers.title: BridgeMVS: Bridging Multi-View Stereo and Monodepth via Bidirectional Dynamic Fusion
papers.abstract: Multi-View Stereo (MVS) and Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) provide complementary cues for dense 3D reconstruction. While MVS leverages explicit geometry for metric depth, it struggles in challenging regions where feature matching is unreliable. Conversely, MDE provides robust structural priors but typically yields scale-ambiguous results. Existing hybrid methods mainly exploit monocular cues in a unidirectional manner, leaving the mutual enhancement between MDE and MVS insufficiently explored. To address this limitation, we propose BridgeMVS, a unified cascaded multi-stage MVS framework that bridges monocular depth features and multi-view cost volume representations through Bidirectional Dynamic Fusion (BDF). At each stage, BDF performs dynamic mono-to-cost and cost-to-mono updates, where monocular structural features guide cost volume refinement for more robust MVS depth estimation, while multi-view geometric evidence recalibrates monocular representations to improve their metric-scale consistency. Furthermore, the fused monocular and multi-view representations are progressively propagated from coarse to fine stages and constrained by stage-wise relative-scale MDE supervision and metric-scale MVS supervision, enabling cross-branch interactions to benefit subsequent high-resolution depth estimation. In addition, BDF is designed as a plug-and-play module that can be conveniently integrated into existing cascaded MVS frameworks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BridgeMVS achieves state-of-the-art performance on the DTU, Tanks-and-Temples, and ETH3D benchmarks, while simultaneously boosting the accuracy of monocular depth estimation. Notably, BridgeMVS ranks first on both the Tanks-and-Temples Intermediate and Advanced benchmarks. The source code is available at \href{https://github.com/JianfeiJ/BridgeMVS}{https://github.com/JianfeiJ/BridgeMVS}.

authors.name: Jiansheng Chen

papers.title: Extremal adjacency and distance spectral radii of graph powers
papers.abstract: Let $G$ be a connected graph of order $n$, and let $G^k$ denote its $k$-th power. We prove that, for every integer $k\geq1$, \[ \rho(G^k)\geq \rho(P_n^k) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \rho_D(G^k)\leq \rho_D(P_n^k), \] where $P_n$ is the path of order $n$, and $\rho$ and $\rho_D$ are the adjacency and distance spectral radii, respectively. If $n\geq k+2$, equality in either inequality holds precisely when $G\cong P_n$. If $n\leq k+1$, every connected graph of order $n$ has complete $k$-th power, and both inequalities are equalities. The adjacency bound is proved by transferring a terminal vertex between pendant paths and applying a reflection rearrangement to a Rayleigh quotient. For the distance bound, a transfer of an entire pendant path is required; a Schur-complement comparison and estimates for the antisymmetric subspace of a path-power distance matrix yield the result. We also give examples showing why the two adjacency arguments do not extend directly to the distance spectral radius.

papers.title: Strain-driven terahertz phase modulation in piezoelectric and nonlinear optical crystals: mechanisms, material developments, and modulation strategies
papers.abstract: Terahertz (THz) technology has witnessed notable developments in sensing, spectroscopy, imaging, and wireless communication which have increased the demand for high-performance THz modulators. Among the various approaches for controlling the THz waves, the application of external stimuli such as optical pumping and thermal or electric fields is widely employed as a promising strategy for modulation. This review focuses on recent advances in THz modulation based on different materials including 2D semiconductors and metamaterials with attention to their response under external stimuli. In addition, strain-driven THz modulation in non-centrosymmetric piezoelectric materials including organic and semi-organic crystals is examined with an emphasis on their ability to establish strong coupling between propagating THz waves and lattice vibrations under piezoelectric resonance conditions. We further highlight earlier reports on strain-driven THz modulation in lithium niobate (LiNbO3) and critically assess the potential of several other nonlinear optical crystals exhibiting piezoelectric resonance peaks suitable for strain-driven THz modulation. An overview of THz modulators integrated with tunable materials is presented highlighting their operating principles and key performance metrics comprising modulation speed, bandwidth, modulation depth and insertion loss.

authors.name: Aarifa Muhammed Ashraf
authors.institution: SRM Institute of Science and Technology

authors.name: Rajaboopathi Mani
authors.institution: SRM Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: Unified Schur multiple zeta functions
papers.abstract: We define symmetric multiple zeta values, unified zeta functions, and finite zeta values in the Schur setting. We establish a Jacobi--Trudi formula and a Giambelli formula for unified Schur multiple zeta functions, and we show that there is a one-to-one correspondence between finite and symmetric Schur multiple zeta values under the Kaneko--Zagier conjecture. We also show a vanishing property for a symmetric sum of finite Schur multiple zeta values, generalizing a result obtained by Hoffman for finite multiple zeta values.

papers.title: History-bearing thalamocortical signals reconstruct and redirect later decisions in a circuit model
papers.abstract: Experience can guide an ambiguous choice or bias a choice despite strong current evidence. We asked how a thalamocortical circuit carries historical content forward and regulates its influence across successive decisions. In published data from adult male mice, suppressing posterior parietal cortex (PPC) or pulvinar (PUL) improved current judgments most when sensory history conflicted with the stimulus, reflecting reduced historical weighting. In trained thalamocortical circuit models, replaying recorded PUL input to PPC reconstructed a historical trace after equalizing complete recipient states across histories. Replaying the opposite history redirected the later choice, even after the circuit correctly judged an intervening strong stimulus. This historical message occupied a low-dimensional direction in thalamic output that remained broadly reachable under firing-rate bounds; redistributing the arriving current at matched energy showed that fine spatial organization, beyond total input strength, selectively shapes later history use without disrupting current choices. Strong sensory evidence suppressed historical output while preserving internal state differences, whereas ambiguity recruited neuronal rectification thresholds and readout alignment to express history. Small shifts in the cortical operating point modulated later historical influence, and partial attenuation of recurrent drive reduced it across all circuits while preserving current commitments; correspondingly, recurrent dynamics were essential for predicting post-stimulus trajectories in held-out histories. Together, these findings distinguish three operations in history-guided choice: returning thalamocortical input determines which past is reconstructed, recurrent dynamics carry its influence forward across intervening demands, and current sensory evidence gates how strongly it enters the decision.

papers.title: Singularities of Mean Curvature Flow with Bounded Total Curvature II: Multiplicity One
papers.abstract: Let \(M_t^n\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\) be a smooth mean curvature flow of closed embedded hypersurfaces, with \(n\ge3\), and let \(T\) be its first singular time. If the integral of \(|A|^n\) is uniformly bounded for \(t<T\), every nonzero tangent flow at time \(T\) has multiplicity one. At each singular point the tangent flow is unique, and the rescaled flow converges locally smoothly to a closed self-shrinker.

authors.name: Yongheng Han
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology of China

papers.title: A2I-VLA: A Two-Stage Vision-Language-Action model with Semantic-Physical Alignment and Integration
papers.abstract: Force and tactile feedback provide essential information about physical interactions in contact-rich manipulation that visual observations alone cannot reliably capture.However, integrating these signals into vision-language-action (VLA) models remains challenging owing to the representational gap between visual-language semantics and physical measurements.To address this challenge, we propose A2I-VLA, a two-stage VLA framework that first learns semantically Aligned force-tactile representations and then Integrates them into a VLA model.In Stage I, a cross-modal alignment loss is introduced to promote correspondence between semantic and physical representations. The tactile and force feature streams are then integrated through a hierarchical multimodal fusion network, and the resulting representations are jointly supervised by future wrench and action prediction losses. The former encourages the model to anticipate physical responses, while the latter associates force-tactile observations with task-relevant manipulation behaviors.In Stage II, a gated cross-attention bridge module adaptively integrates the hierarchical physical features learned in Stage I into the VLA model to guide action generation.Real-world experiments demonstrate that the proposed A2I-VLA significantly outperforms the baseline PI05 across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, improving the success rate from 70% to 95%.

papers.title: Optimal first eigenvalue estimates for positive holomorphic sectional curvature
papers.abstract: Let $(M,\omega_g)$ be a compact K\"ahler manifold with holomorphic sectional curvature $\geq 2$. We prove that the first positive eigenvalue of the Laplacian $\Delta_d$ satisfies $$\lambda_1\geq 4, $$ and $\lambda_1=4$ if and only if $(M,\omega_g)$ is holomorphically isometric to $(\mathbb{P}^1,\omega_{\mathrm{FS}})$.

authors.name: Mingwei Wang
authors.institution: Xi'an University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Machine Learning Electronic Hamiltonian with Long-Range Effects and External Fields
papers.abstract: Conventional machine-learning electronic Hamiltonian (MLEH) models rely on a local-environment approximation and can miss the effects of long-range (LR) interactions and external fields. Here, we introduce MLEH-LR, a framework that incorporates these effects into Hamiltonian prediction. Benchmarks across materials with different polarizations and dimensionalities demonstrate substantial improvements in the accuracy of the predicted Hamiltonians and resulting electronic structures. MLEH-LR enables accurate, large-scale, high-throughput electronic-structure calculations, as demonstrated for zigzag boron nitride ribbons under transverse electric fields. These calculations allow us to formulate a quantitative relation describing the joint width and field dependence of the band gap and to reveal the electronic mechanisms underlying its field response. Our work provides an efficient method and tool for studying electronic structure in materials where long-range electrostatics and external fields play an important role.

papers.title: Controlled One-Click Benchmarking and Post-Fusion Recalibration for Support-Conditioned Medical Segmentation
papers.abstract: Sparse-prompt medical segmentation is hard to compare when prompts, supports, thresholds, and splits differ. This paper uses a controlled one-click protocol: each test image receives one positive foreground click, training-only support, validation-only checkpoint selection, and no test-time threshold tuning. We propose {Support-Aware Recalibration (SAR)}, a late post-fusion recalibration block for MultiverSeg that combines large-kernel spatial gating with squeeze-and-excitation channel recalibration after support--query fusion. BUSI, NerveUS-BP-present, and Kvasir-SEG are evaluated with matched 697 foreground-present sample budgets, shared splits/clicks, and threshold-free Dice-AUC/IoU-AUC. Compared with a protocol-matched raw-support MultiverSeg baseline, the main SAR configuration shows favorable mean Dice-AUC/IoU-AUC performance on BUSI, NerveUS-BP-present, and Kvasir-SEG, while reducing logged training time in this implementation. These controlled results indicate that late post-fusion recalibration is useful under a leakage-controlled one-click protocol.
