We show that three structural properties of modern hybrid NoPE architectures -- bounded sliding windows, a 1,024-token banded relative bias whose tail is identically zero, and unit-RMS value normalization -- combine with an orthonormal Subsampled Randomized Fourier Transform (SRFT) to enable calibration-free, scale-free 2.000-bit Value and 2.125-bit Key Lloyd-Max compression (2.0625 effective bits/coordinate, $7.76\times$ smaller than bf16) on the 8 global visits' far prefix $[0, N-1024)$, merged with the exact bf16 local window and learned sink via online log-sum-exp. A custom GQA-packed Metal decode kernel with a 256-entry half4 LUT and Block-8 lazy exp2 rescaling reaches 73.4 GB/s and runs Inkling-2-Mini at 17.09 tok/s at 256K ($3.36\times$ faster than bf16), 13.81 tok/s at 512K, and 9.52 tok/s at 1,048,576 tokens in 19.49 GiB peak memory (4.37 GiB KV). Across $4\times 4096$ WikiText-2 windows, 3.06-bit SRFT is lossless ($\Delta$PPL $= -0.007$), 2.56-bit K3/V2 adds $+0.024$, and 2.06-bit adds $+0.130$ while achieving 100% (3/3) exact 7-digit passkey retrieval at 8K, 16K, and 32K.

papers.title: Preflight: Agentic Last-Mile Verification for AI Software Supply Chains
papers.abstract: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.

papers.title: Large Deviations and Critical Scaling in the Finite-Population Granovetter Threshold Model
papers.abstract: We develop a systematic asymptotic analysis of the exact finite-population solution of Granovetter's threshold model, in which a single initial instigator triggers a cascade among agents with independently distributed adoption thresholds. By expressing the propagation probability as an order-statistic boundary-crossing event, we formulate its macroscopic large-deviation rate as a constrained relative-entropy minimization problem. For Beta-distributed thresholds, we obtain explicit solutions for all shape parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$, identifying four possible optimal empirical threshold profiles: fully free, fully pinned, pinned--free, and free--pinned. These profiles determine both the exponential probability of macroscopic cascades and the threshold configurations responsible for their occurrence. Importance-sampling estimates confirm the analytical rate functions, while sequential Monte Carlo simulations independently reproduce the predicted optimal profiles. We also revisit the critical scaling near $\alpha_c=1$ and confirm the principal finite-size scaling laws: the mean active fraction decays as $N^{-1/2}$ for uniform thresholds and as $N^{-1}$ for $\alpha=1$ and $0<\beta<1$. In the latter regime, we further derive an explicit scaling function for the logarithmic critical window from the microscopic branching-process limit. Our results provide a general framework for determining the probabilities and characteristic configurations of rare collective events in threshold-driven cascade processes

papers.title: Gray II, K\"ahler Nullity and Ricci Flow on Generalized Flag Manifolds with Two Isotropy Summands
papers.abstract: We investigate Gray's second curvature identity, K\"ahler nullity, and homogeneous Ricci flow on generalized flag manifolds with two isotropy summands. We prove that every invariant metric satisfies Gray's second identity for both invariant almost complex structures. For the non-integrable structure, the K\"ahler nullity is trivial except at a distinguished metric ratio, where it coincides with the vertical distribution of a homogeneous fibration. This distribution is integrable and has totally geodesic leaves. For the integrable structure, the K\"ahler nullity exhibits a different behavior and need not be integrable away from the K\"ahler locus. Finally, we reduce the normalized homogeneous Ricci flow to an autonomous equation for the ratio of the metric parameters. The resulting dynamics identify two invariant Einstein directions and show that the K\"ahler--Einstein direction is attracting, while the other is repelling.

papers.title: A Keller--Segel Chemotaxis Model on One-Dimensional Moving Domains
papers.abstract: We study a one-dimensional Keller--Segel system on an interval whose boundary moves according to a prescribed contracting law. The boundary motion makes the problem genuinely nonautonomous and destroys the mass conservation available on fixed domains. A time-dependent change of variables, combined with a time reparametrization, reduces the problem to a semilinear system on a fixed interval with time-independent principal part and nonautonomous transport terms. We prove global well-posedness and regularity of weak solutions, and we show that the contraction of the domain yields a uniform bound on the total mass. For the long-time dynamics, our main tool is a singular Gronwall type inequality with an exponentially damped kernel, for which we provide a self-contained version with explicit decay rate and constants, tailored to our setting; under a small gain condition on the boundary velocities, it yields dissipativity with an explicit exponential decay rate, which cannot be obtained from the classical inequality of Henry. With it we prove the existence of the minimal pullback attractor in the universe of families of bounded sets, on the moving domain and then on the fixed rescaled reference domains. Finally, numerical simulations on contracting domains illustrate the effect of the boundary motion on cell aggregation.

papers.title: The Z[tau]-foam: Goodman-Strauss's Dodecafoam as arithmetic in the icosahedral module
papers.abstract: Goodman-Strauss's Dodecafoam is a substitution that fills the regular dodecahedron with dodecahedral bubbles of sizes tau^{-k}, tau=(1+sqrt(5))/2, using the seven kinds of cells into which the twelve planes of its stellation cut it. We rewrite it as exact arithmetic in one Z[tau]-module of rank three, the span M of the six five-fold axes, on which the icosahedral group acts by 120 matrices in GL(3,Z[tau]). A placed inflated copy of a cell is a union of cells iff its facet levels lie in {+-1,+-tau^3} and it lies in the dodecahedron. Solving this finite linear system for all scales at once gives exactly the 22 rules known from a geometric search; no rule exists at any scale other than 1,tau,tau^2,tau^3. The substitution becomes integer arithmetic on six-tuples and reproduces the bubbles of the geometric foam exactly. Whether a point of M is the centre of a bubble of size tau^{-k} is decided by at most k+3 exact sign vectors (its address), without building the foam, and all bubbles of one size are obtained by sieving the points of M whose Galois conjugate satisfies |x^*|<=2 tau^k, a bound we prove with computer assistance. The number of bubbles of size tau^{-k} is A beta^k+O(|beta'|^k) with beta=(1+sqrt(29))/2. Hence the closure of the rescaled conjugates of the bubble centres has box dimension at most log_tau(beta)=2.4123<3, and the bubbles are not selected by any cut-and-project window with interior. The other foams of the 1999 article are sub-foams of this one. The 50400 substitutions allowed by the rule list give 18899 bubble sets, and the Dodecafoam is a product set of 13440 of them, to the depth tested. In four dimensions the same linear system, for the star cut of the 120-cell, reproduces the 718 clusters of a geometric search and adds the scale sqrt(5) tau^2.

papers.title: Threshold Generalized Autoregressive Moving Average Models
papers.abstract: Non-Gaussian time series often exhibit nonlinear dynamics and changes in dependence structures that may not be adequately captured by conventional single-regime models. To address this limitation, we introduce a class of threshold generalized autoregressive moving-average (TGARMA) models that combines observation-driven GARMA dynamics with threshold-based regime switching. The proposed framework accommodates multiple regimes, determined by a lagged endogenous or exogenous threshold variable, and allows regression coefficients, autoregressive and moving-average orders and coefficients, and, where applicable, dispersion parameters to vary across regimes. Parameters are estimated by maximum partial likelihood, while model selection is conducted using information criteria. We examine model admissibility and stability, assess model adequacy through residual diagnostics, and conduct a Monte Carlo simulation study to investigate the finite-sample performance of the estimators. The proposed methodology is illustrated using monthly counts of hospitalizations due to respiratory diseases among older adults in S\~ao Paulo, Brazil. In this application, the TGARMA model outperforms its single-regime GARMA counterpart in terms of in-sample mean squared error, highlighting the potential benefits of incorporating regime-dependent dynamics into the analysis of non-Gaussian time series.

papers.title: Escriba-OCR: A 1B Vision-Language Model for Error-Preserving Transcription of Handwritten Portuguese Essays
papers.abstract: Feedback tools and research on learner writing need transcriptions of handwritten essays that keep exactly what the student wrote: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions. Vision-language models (VLMs) read handwriting well, but they also tend to rewrite it into correct language. We measure this on BRESSAY, 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays, with a benchmark that adds error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure to the character error rate (CER) and uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We restrict the study to open-weight models that schools can run on their own hardware. Of 22 open baselines, the best, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B, reaches 5.6% CER on the 199 test pages; none reproduces the edit markup reliably, and every VLM replaces 39-78% of the words absent from a Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B on the 647 training pages in 85 minutes on one GPU. The resulting Escriba-OCR-1B reaches 2.06% CER, 3.5 points below the best baseline (95% CI [-4.2, -2.9]); under the ICDAR 2024 competition metric it reaches 2.1% CER, below the best published page-level results (2.2-2.4%). It recovers 67% of insertions and 77% of illegible deletions, and reproduces the line structure of 97% of the pages, but still normalises 60% of likely misspellings. Three seeds agree within 0.04 CER points, and quantised to 4 bits the model runs on an ordinary CPU at about one minute per page. On 40 letters of another corpus it matches its base model (without that model's appended comments) but misreads unseen words more often; weight interpolation recovers half the gap. A teacher's review finds that 45% of the judgeable apparent corrections are errors in the BRESSAY ground truth, so dictionary-based scores likely understate preservation. We release the model, the benchmark code and the review data.

papers.title: A Matrix-Valued Quotient and a Compatible Bilinear Product on Euclidean Vector Spaces
papers.abstract: We introduce a matrix-valued quotient and a compatible bilinear product on finite-dimensional Euclidean vector spaces. The quotient is constructed from a bilinear matrix-valued map satisfying a prescribed vector transport identity. We investigate its algebraic structure and establish uniqueness results under orthogonal equivariance and additional structural conditions. We also derive a variational characterization based on the Frobenius norm and examine the spectral properties of the associated matrices, including their determinants and invertibility conditions. The two-dimensional construction is related to complex arithmetic, while the three-dimensional formulation admits a representation using skew-symmetric matrices. The results clarify the relationship between vector transport, matrix algebra, and Euclidean geometry, and extend the framework introduced in our earlier work on vector division and multiplication.

papers.title: Spectral radii of connected graphs with prescribed maximum degree
papers.abstract:
For a real number $\alpha>0$ and a positive integer $r$, we give recursive characterizations of the existence of finite simple connected graphs $G$ with adjacency spectral radius $\rho(G)=\alpha$ and maximum degree $\Delta(G)\le r$ (or $=r$). Adding one vertex to a graph $F$ at a time to update the Schur-complement $q=\alpha-{\mathbf b}^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}{\mathbf b}$, where $B=\alpha I-A(F)$ is positive definite and ${\mathbf b}$ is a nonzero $0$--$1$ that specifies the neighbours of $z$ in $F$. Realizability is characterized by admissible constructions with positive intermediate outputs $q$ and a final zero output. We also establish a reduction for a graph $G$ obtained by attaching pairwise disjoint rooted trees, each by a single edge, to a nonempty connected graph $H$. Assume that $\alpha I-A(T)\succ0$ for every attached tree $T$. For each $z\in V(H)$, let $q_{z,1},\ldots,q_{z,s_z}$ be the positive root pivots obtained by the scalar tree recursion for the trees attached to $z$, and set
  \[
  a_z=\alpha-\sum_{j=1}^{s_z}q_{z,j}^{-1},
  \qquad
  M_H(\mathbf a)=\operatorname{diag}(a_z:z\in V(H))-A(H),
  \] where an empty sum is zero. Then $\rho(G)=\alpha$ if and only if $M_H(\mathbf a)\succeq0$ and $\det M_H(\mathbf a)=0$. Taking $H=K_1$ recovers the tree criteria, while $\delta(H)\geq2$ gives criteria for graphs with prescribed 2-core $H$. In particular, for unicyclic graphs of prescribed cycle length, path continuants reduce the spectral condition to positivity inequalities and one scalar equation.

papers.title: Measuring Human-AI and AI-AI Teams in Multi-turn Layout Creation
papers.abstract: Co-creating layouts such as websites and slides is a useful testbed for evaluating multi-turn instruction following of LLM systems. Since an intended layout's appearance cannot be well expressed in a single turn, the user must wait for the LLM to generate a layout then iteratively refine it with the LLM over multiple turns. We present a small-scale, exploratory (n=6) study of this multi-turn process to compare the differences of human-AI and AI-AI teams on the same layout-generation task. Given a reference wire-frame layout, a participant or a language model 'speaker' issues natural-language instructions to a fixed 'listener' LLM over multiple turns until the speaker is satisfied. Rather than an LLM as the judge, we fit a scoring function over geometric layout features using curated human preference data (n=19). We find that LLMs tend to encode the entire layout in the first turn, while humans iterate over many turns on average, writing much shorter instructions. We also find that human-AI teams consistently scored lower than AI-AI teams. This gap is driven by a limiter of human participants in specifying precise sizes and positions (e.g. 42 pixels to the right). Humans perform almost at par with language models on other features like ordering the elements into nested structures. We then perform interventions on the speaker LLMs to make them more human-like, and find it difficult. This raises the challenge of using LLMs as user models to evaluate multi-turn co-creation tasks.

papers.title: Fixed or Deleted? External Feedback Lets Cheaper AI Coding Agents Repair Rule Violations
papers.abstract: Many defects violate project rules that the code itself does not reveal, such as layering constraints or required tests. We study whether LLM coding agents repair such violations better when an external checker reports them, with their location and a repair goal. Three models, a small, medium and large model, driven by an AI agent, worked on 25 pull requests with 31 planted defects in ten open-source projects, plus 5 correct controls, five times alone and five times with findings from CodeAssure (CA), a commercial checker. We also compare with GitHub Copilot code review, and compare CodeAssure's detection with nine free static-analysis tools run out of the box, including Semgrep and SonarQube Community. Counting a run as repaired only when the repaired code also compiles and keeps its feature, CA findings raised the repair rate from 26% to 69% for the smallest model, from 46% to 90% for the medium model and from 45% to 93% for the largest model (pull-request-level p < 0.001), and from 39% to 84% over all runs. Every Java, TypeScript and Python repair compiled. We found that agents often cleared a defect by deleting a newly added file. Metrics based on whether the defect is gone count feature deletion as a success. The largest model alone did so in 44 of 125 runs. CA includes a check for deleted files that largely prevents this. In an ablation with the check turned off, removals rose from 9 to 65 out of 375 runs and the repair rate fell to 54% (small), 70% (medium) and 85% (large model). The CA workflow also outperformed Copilot code review (p < 0.001). Together, the free tools detected 8 of the 31 defects, and CA detected all 31. With CA, the medium model repaired 90% of runs, against 45% for the largest model alone, at about one fifth of the mean cost per run ($0.17 against $0.91).

papers.title: On derived Galois deformation rings in characteristic 0 and a conjecture of Venkatesh
papers.abstract: Let $\Pi$ be a regular algebraic cuspidal automorphic representation of $\operatorname{GL}_n$ over a CM field $F$, and $\rho$ its associated Galois representation in characteristic 0. With mild assumptions, we use the Taylor--Wiles method to define a free action of the potentially semistable derived deformation ring of $\rho$ on the $\Pi$-part of the $p$-adic cohomology of $\operatorname{GL}_n/F$, confirming a prediction of Venkatesh. As a key step, we establish an equivalence between the derived deformation ring of $\rho$ with the completion at the point corresponding to $\rho$ of the derived deformation ring of the mod $p$ reduction $\bar{\rho}$, generalising well-known results by Kisin.

papers.title: Donnan Grand Canonical Monte Carlo Simulations with Fast Ewald Summation for Calculating Individual Ionic Chemical Potentials
papers.abstract: We present a Donnan Grand Canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulation method using fast Ewald summation to accurately and efficiently calculate the individual ionic excess chemical potentials of $\alpha_+:\alpha_-$ electrolyte solutions. By introducing a dynamic inner electrostatic potential that acts to penalize net charge fluctuations and maintain average charge neutrality ($\langle Q_t \rangle = 0$), the method enables single-ion GCMC trial moves without sacrificing convergence speed or breaking thermodynamic consistency. Unlike the Widom particle insertion method---which suffers from severe phase-space sampling bottlenecks and requires separate virtual insertions for each ionic species---the Donnan GCMC protocol simultaneously yields the individual excess chemical potentials $\mu_+^{\text{ex}}$ and $\mu_-^{\text{ex}}$ corresponding to a resulting bulk concentration $c_b$ with rapid numerical convergence. Varying the reference activity parameter $c_r$ allows us to efficiently construct the complete $\mu_\pm^{\text{ex}}(c_b)$ curves. Comparison with the Mean Spherical Approximation (MSA) demonstrates excellent agreement for size-symmetric electrolytes, while highlighting the failure of linear-response theories for size-asymmetric ions where electrostatic correlations and cavity effects become strongly coupled.

papers.title: Detectable Epistemic Attack Layers: A Coverage Theorem and Standardized Harness for Conversation-History Integrity
papers.abstract: Conversation history is infrastructure: deployed language models rely on application layers to store and reinject prior turns, and that stored state is writable. We formalize session-level contamination by attack layer, state a coverage theorem, and measure its scope: each deployment-layer verification tier covers exactly its layer and is sound with respect to the others; instruction overrides are not detectable without false positives; and composite vectors evade per-fragment verification. A standardized harness applied to eight mechanism families across 3,249 sessions and three model families makes these claims checkable. First, pattern-based detection pays a measured false-positive price: the classic defenses flag 35 to 50 percent of benign sessions, and the naive refusal floor reaches only 2.4 percent attack-cell adoption while destroying 33 to 100 percent of benign turns, whereas provenance-gated channel separation achieves adoption at or below 1.2 percent with zero false positives and zero utility loss. Second, in the exploratory instruction-override extension, the gates' boundary is a cliff: directives rephrased without shape markers bypass them at control-equivalent rates, 47.7 to 49.5 percent against 0.0 percent for the shaped class, placing that class in the model-internal lane. Third, the deterministic core is storage-layer detection at 126 of 126 per model with zero false positives. External anchors reproduce published attack pressure, with PoisonedRAG falling from 70 to 0 percent under the full stack. For practitioners: authenticate stored history and content provenance with deterministic tiers, scope instruction-layer mitigation to provenance-gated designs whose measured benign cost is zero, and monitor composition at the trajectory level rather than per fragment. All protocols and acceptance criteria are pre-registered; the stack and harness are released.

papers.title: Engineering strategies for high-performance self-powered zinc oxide (ZnO) ultraviolet photodetectors: a design-oriented review
papers.abstract: Self-powered ultraviolet (UV) photodetectors generate a signal at zero applied bias, removing standby power and suppressing dark current, suiting battery-free Internet-of-Things sensing. Zinc oxide (ZnO) is the archetypal absorber for this task: UV-selective, earth-abundant, non-toxic, and processable at low temperature from solution. Operating it without bias, however, requires a built-in asymmetry that pristine ZnO rarely provides. Because the literature is organized by material or mechanism, the design logic remains obscured. Here we organize the field by engineering strategy, identifying five families of levers (junction and built-in-field engineering, doping and defect control, polarization coupling, interface/surface and photoelectrochemical engineering, and architecture and light management) and mapping each onto the metrics it serves and the trade-offs it imposes. A unifying lens is the zero-bias doping paradox: raising carrier density narrows the depletion region that zero-bias collection needs, so the self-powered optimum differs from the biased one. We flag the detectivity, speed, and active-area pitfalls that make zero-bias performance easy to overstate, and condense the synthesis into a decision tree linking target metric to strategy and growth route. The remaining bottlenecks (persistent photoconductivity, p-type ZnO, and reporting consistency) are problems of defect control and rigorous measurement, not of new materials.

papers.title: Area Stability for Largest Small Polygons
papers.abstract: We develop a second order calculus for area maximisation among small polygons of diameter at most one, culminating in rigorous computational proofs of stationarity, spectral stability and strict local maximality modulo orientation preserving Euclidean motions for the polygons $Q_n$, whose diameter graphs consist of a cycle on $n-1$ vertices and one pendant edge, for every even $n$ with $6\le n\le 64$. At a stationary configuration, positive multipliers force first order area decrease along feasible directions that shorten at least one active diameter. Along directions that preserve all active diameters to first order, the reduced Hessian governs second order area change modulo Euclidean motions. Positive multipliers, independent active constraint gradients, and a negative reduced spectrum imply strict local maximality. Outward rounded interval arithmetic establishes existence of strictly convex stationary configurations $Q_n$ with all $n-3$ reduced eigenvalues strictly negative. Together, these results yield explicit neighbourhood radii and rigorous quadratic area decrease bounds for all sufficiently nearby feasible polygons. The reduced spectrum also detects second order degeneracy and instability, as illustrated by an optimal quadrilateral and the regular hexagon.

papers.title: Second Moment Penny Packings via Rolling Spaces
papers.abstract:
We solve the unrestricted minimum second moment problem for six unit disks in the plane by proving that the minimum is \(29/3\) attained uniquely up to isometry and relabelling by one disk together with five of its six neighbours in the triangular lattice.
  The realised contacts themselves define the space of admissible motions, while the directions preserving those contacts to first order define the rolling space consisting of motions whose relative velocities have zero normal component at every realised contact. Together, these spaces lead to an exact tangent cone formula and to a criterion by which a strictly positive centroidal contact balance, combined with rolling rigidity, implies strict local minimality modulo Euclidean motions. Our method recovers the classical five disk minimum \(34/5\) of Graham and Sloane, previously the largest unrestricted case known exactly.
  Geometric reductions and a graph census reduce the global search to finitely many contact graph classes. Exact analysis and validated interval arithmetic then exclude competing configurations, establishing the global bounds and uniqueness. Our method allows us to pass from putative lattice extremisers to unrestricted optimality.

papers.title: The Thue-Morse route to chaos in the open quantum baker map
papers.abstract: We study the resonances of the quantum baker map opened by a window of width $w$ centred at $q_c$. For $q_c=1/2$ the survivor set of the classical doubling map with a hole goes from zero to positive topological entropy along the Thue-Morse route, and we find numerically, for $N$ up to $2^{25}$, that the resonance spectrum follows this route step by step, also where the entropy is zero. Below the threshold $w_c=4a^*-1$, with $a^*$ the Thue-Morse constant, the surviving cycles have periods $2^\nu$ and their thresholds accumulate doubly exponentially. Each cycle gives, as isolated orbits do, a multiplet of resonances close to modulus $2^{-1/2}$, with phases set by its action. Since a cycle is resolved only if its period is shorter than about $\log_2 N$, twice the Ehrenfest time, about $\log_2\log_2 N$ steps are resolved, four at our largest sizes. Near $w_c$ the 16-cycle perturbs the 8-multiplet through a return path that classically opens only at $w_c$. Cutting a few sites of this path removes the perturbation. At $w_c$ the leading resonance jumps within one or two lattice sites, since a window one site wider than the threshold already has an entropy of order $1/\log_2 N$. One site or more above $w_c$ it lies between 0.93 and 1.00 times the value set by the topological pressure, with no free parameter. There the Walsh eigenvalue count grows with the fractal Weyl exponent, and the Fourier count with an exponent a few hundredths smaller at the sizes we reach.

papers.title: Localized Strain Tuning of Second-Harmonic Generation in MoS2 Monolayers and Bilayers
papers.abstract: We investigate the modulation of second-harmonic generation (SHG) in CVD-grown MoS2 monolayers and few-layer flakes through localized mechanical deformation applied by an atomic force microscope (AFM) tip. MoS2 membranes suspended over microstructured Si3N4 substrates allow simultaneous measurements of force and SHG intensity during controlled approach and retraction cycles. Suspended regions exhibit enhanced SHG relative to substrate-supported regions, with pronounced suppression near the clamping boundaries. While the SHG response during compressive loading varies among individual membranes, adhesion-mediated pulling during retraction consistently reduces the SHG intensity until tip detachment, when the signal recovers. By correlating the optical modulation with the measured pull-off force and a phenomenological estimate of effective strain, we obtain a characteristic sensitivity of approximately 12% SHG modulation per 1% effective strain, with comparable behavior in monolayers and bilayers. These findings reveal adhesion-mediated mechanical deformation as a distinct and reversible mechanism for controlling nonlinear optical emission in atomically thin membranes.

papers.title: Identification of Poisson processes through a one-dimensional projection
papers.abstract: We study the identification of stationary Poisson processes in Euclidean space through a single one-dimensional projection. Given a point process and a straight line, each point is retained independently with a probability given by a Gaussian function of its distance to the line; the retained points are projected onto the line. If the process is Poisson, the projection is again Poisson. What a single projection reveals depends on the sign of the second factorial cumulant, which is also the sign of the two-point correlations. Under a Palm domination condition, which holds for positively associated processes, the cumulant is nonnegative. Using a Chen-Stein argument we show that when the cumulant of the projection vanishes, the process is Poisson. Consequently, a single projection identifies non-Poissonianity. The same result holds under negative association. When the cumulant changes sign, a random projection detects a nonzero cumulant with probability one. We propose a test whose rejection region is computed by Monte Carlo. The test, together with a spacings-based variant for repulsive alternatives, rejects determinantal, shot-noise and other classical processes. When applied to lunar impact craters, the test rejects the Poisson hypothesis for craters with diameter below 30 km and does not reject it for craters above 45 km.

papers.title: Cryogenic Luminescence Thermometry of Upconversion Micro- and Nanoparticles via Deep Learning
papers.abstract: Luminescence thermometry with single or optically trapped particles is hampered by weak signals that fluctuate with alignment, collection efficiency, and excitation conditions and, for $\mathrm{Er}^{3+}$-based probes, by the loss of sensitivity of the luminescence intensity ratio (LIR) at cryogenic temperatures. Here we use a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) to predict the temperature directly from single emission spectra of $\mathrm{NaYF}_4{:}\mathrm{Yb}^{3+},\mathrm{Er}^{3+}$ micro- and nanoparticles between $-150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $105\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, and compare it with the standard LIR under adverse conditions deliberately reproduced with particle ensembles. From $-150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the 1D-CNN reduces the single-spectrum mean absolute error from $5.4\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $1.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and keeps its temperature uncertainty nearly constant down to the lowest temperatures, where Stark-component features remain temperature dependent while the LIR loses its sensitivity. Under deliberate optical misalignment, its error increases only from $0.58\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $0.88\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, whereas that of the LIR rises from $1.4\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $3.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The same approach reaches sub-degree accuracy ($0.21\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) over a narrow temperature window and a single calibration valid across different pump powers and wavelengths. These results establish 1D-CNNs as robust single-shot thermometers and a step toward fast thermometry of single and trapped particles.

papers.title: Geometry-controlled clogging and transport mechanisms in confined Y-junctions
papers.abstract: We investigate transport and clogging of hard particles in a confined symmetric Y-junction using off-lattice Monte Carlo simulations. The geometry is controlled by the channel width w and a truncation parameter s that modifies the inner vertex. The flow probability exhibits a sharp sigmoidal crossover, defining a characteristic width wc that depends non-monotonically on s. This non-monotonic behavior persists under variations of the transverse Monte Carlo step, although the absolute values of wc change. Microscopic analysis reveals two distinct blocking mechanisms: single-particle obstruction at small truncations and collective arch-like structures at larger truncations. Residence-time statistics and particle-order inversions provide additional evidence of this change in transport dynamics. Our results demonstrate that local modifications of junction geometry can strongly affect clogging and particle transport, even in a minimal model with excluded-volume interactions only.

papers.title: What Do Co-Folding Models Learn? Insights from Enhanced Transition Path Sampling
papers.abstract: Co-folding models are diffusion-based generative models that sample biomolecular complexes from distributions learned on a large corpus of experimental data. Although these models are powerful for structure prediction, it remains unclear whether the conformational ensembles they learn resemble physically meaningful statistical ensembles. To understand what these models learn, we introduce transition path sampling (TPS), which uses Markov chain Monte Carlo over denoising trajectories to sample the learned distribution. Because its Monte Carlo trajectories resemble biomolecular dynamics, TPS couples directly with enhanced-sampling techniques to recover the full conformational ensemble. Applied to Boltz-2, enhanced TPS reveals physical conformational changes biased toward crystal-like states near the training data, indicating both learned physics and memorization. These results suggest new ways to evaluate and improve co-folding models by jointly assessing structural recovery, proximity to training data, and conformational ensembles.

papers.title: Geometric ergodicity of Gibbs samplers for linear mixed models with several heavy-tailed random-effect components and unknown tail parameters
papers.abstract: Linear mixed models with heavy-tailed random effects are widely used for robust Bayesian analysis of longitudinal data. We study the three-block Gibbs sampler for such models when the random effects are split into several components, such as random intercepts and slopes, each with its own scale and its own scale mixture of normals, when the tail parameters have priors on finite grids and are drawn jointly with the latent weights, and when the random-effects design is rank deficient, as when some subjects contribute a single observation. We give sufficient conditions for geometric ergodicity that attribute the rank deficiency to the components that cause it, and show that, under conditions on the gamma priors on the precision parameters, they hold for Student-t and slash random effects with individual weights, any grid of tail parameters and any design. The result extends to random-effect vectors whose coordinates share a weight, for subject-specific designs with known shape matrices. It justifies Monte Carlo standard errors for regression coefficients, log-scales and posterior probabilities of the tail parameters. Simulations show that the scale and the tail parameter can mix much more slowly than the regression coefficients, and an analysis of beta-HCG data illustrates the methods.

papers.title: Diophantine sets over global function fields
papers.abstract: Let $q\equiv 3\bmod 4$ be a prime power and let $K$ be a finite separable extension of the field of rational functions $\mathbb F_q(t)$, with constant field $\mathbb F_q$. We show that $\mathbb F_q[t]$ is Diophantine in $\mathbb F_q(t)$ and that the latter is Diophantine in $K$. We deduce from work of Demeyer that $K$ has the DPRM property: Diophantine sets over $K$ are the same as listable sets.

papers.title: A filtered basis for Haiman ideals
papers.abstract: Given the polynomial ring $R=\mathbb{C}[x_1, \dots, x_n, y_1, \dots, y_n]$, we consider the Haiman ideal $J(d)$ of polynomials that vanish to order $d$ on the diagonals. We define a rotational order on monomials and use it to construct a filtration on $J(d)$ and a bigraded, homogeneous, free $\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]$-basis compatible with this filtration. This gives a new independent proof that $J(d)$ is free over $y$'s. We also discuss the connections between this filtration and triply-graded link homology.

papers.title: Circle-Pattern Linear Systems for the Twenty Trivalent Delaunay Types of a Genus-Two Surface: Rank, Feasibility and Polytope Dimension
papers.abstract: The hyperelliptic quotient of a closed genus-two Riemann surface is a hyperbolic sphere with six cone points of angle pi. Its Delaunay triangulation T is dual to a trivalent Voronoi graph G of one of twenty combinatorial types. For each type we study the angle system Ax = 1, x >= 0, where A is the vertex-edge incidence matrix of T and pi x_e is the angle subtended at a cone point by the Voronoi edge dual to e, equivalently the intersection angle of the two circumcircles adjacent across e. We prove that rank A = 6 for all twenty types, including the six whose triangulation has a loop, so the affine solution space always has the dimension of Teichmuller space. The polytope P = {Ax = 1, x >= 0} behaves differently. It is six-dimensional for exactly ten types, the ten Delaunay-realizable ones. For nine types it has dimension one, two or three, because non-negativity forces some wedge angles to vanish, and for the type of signature (2,2,2,2,8,8) it is empty. We show that five of the nine and the empty type never occur as Delaunay triangulations, and that the other four occur only as triangulations of non-trivalent Delaunay decompositions. Every vertex of every P is half-integral, as for fractional perfect matching polytopes. For the ten full-dimensional types every facet x_e = 0 lies at an edge where the Whitehead move is admissible, though not conversely, and the move identifies the facets of the two polytopes; these identifications pair the facet orbits of the ten cells under their automorphism groups. The free unfolding of the gluing grows at rate about 7.093. All finite statements are checked by an independent program, and the rank, infeasibility, forced coordinates, dimensions, vertices and facets are verified in Lean 4.

papers.title: Killing Scales for Conformal Killing Tensors of Rank Two and Higher
papers.abstract: We study which metrics in a conformal class admit a Killing tensor with prescribed conformal Killing trace-free part. We call such metrics Killing scales. We also consider whether a given conformal Killing tensor is itself a Killing tensor for some metric in the conformal class, as well as the analogous problem for conformal Killing-Yano forms. Our approach to this problem uses conformal and projective tractors, and the prolongations provided by the BGG splitting operators of the projective and conformal Killing operators. For rank two conformal Killing tensors, we characterise local Killing scales for arbitrary scales on arbitrary conformal manifolds, extending recent results that were restricted to Einstein scales on conformally flat manifolds. The criterion is expressed in terms of the scale tractor and the BGG prolongation of the conformal Killing tensor. We also obtain Killing scale criteria for higher-rank conformal Killing tensors and conformal Killing-Yano forms, under additional hypotheses involving Einstein scales and normal solutions. We describe the tractor geometry of special Einstein products, including Ricci-flat products, and use these constructions to give examples beyond the conformally flat setting.

papers.title: The response field approach to path integral control
papers.abstract: This paper investigates non-linear path integral control problems within the response field formalism of nonequilibrium field theory. The aim of this work is exploratory, based on the identification of correspondences between backward adjoint processes and the response field of non-equilibrium statistical physics, whose properties have not been set out in an optimal control setting. The response field is found to play an analogous role to the backward adjoint process under the stochastic maximum principle. In particular, the gradient of the optimal cost-to-go at the initial time, which is proportional to the optimal control, is given by the average of the response field at the initial time. In contrast to the case of non-equilibrium dynamics, the response function is found to be acausal in the control setting. The linear-quadratic case of path integral control is studied, confirming it as the free theory, meaning that solving the control problem is equivalent to completing the square and determining the propagator for a two point boundary value problem. The developments presented here are a necessary prelude to applications based on field theoretic approximation, for both path integral control and their dual inference problems.

papers.title: Scalability and Performance Trade-offs Between Q-Learning and Parallel Intensified Simulated Annealing in Flexible Job Shop Scheduling
papers.abstract: This article presents a controlled comparison of tabular Q-learning (QL) and Parallelized Simulated Annealing with Intensification (PISA) for the Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem (FJSP).

papers.title: Unlearning Model Identity: Ablating LoRA Weights from Question-Based Identity Tuning
papers.abstract: Large Language Models are trained on diverse corpora containing outputs from proprietary teacher models and provider-curated sources. Models subsequently inherit embedded self-identity traits, persistently asserting specific proprietary names. Service providers of open-weight models frequently require the removal of model identity for downstream applications, such as custom interfaces, without exposing provider affiliations to end-users. Effective identity modification is therefore critical for customized model alignment and deployment. This study proposes a method to localize parameter-level representations of self-identity within low-rank adaptation modules to perform targeted weight ablation. By generating probing questions designed to elicit self-naming outputs and fine-tuning the base model on these responses, the approach identifies and ablates high-magnitude weights within the parameter set. Experimental results demonstrate that distilled identity traits reside within a localized subset of low-rank weights, achieving a complete removal rate in Qwen3.5-2B and a 10% rate in Gemma4-E2B while preserving general task capabilities. These findings confirm that ablating top-tier adaptation weights suppresses distilled self-identification without compromising broader model performance.

papers.title: A complete knot invariant from grid diagrams
papers.abstract: Using grid diagrams, we define an infinite graph associated to each knot type. We prove that the isomorphism class of this grid graph is a complete invariant of the knot, up to mirroring. Even more, we prove that algorithmically determinable finite parts of this graph are enough to determine the knot type.

papers.title: Kleinian groups with tunnel number one
papers.abstract: We give a structural theory for the holonomy groups of hyperbolic links with tunnel number 1 in arbitrary 3-manifolds. This is a first step towards understanding the canonical triangulations of such links, as it generalises the combinatorial structure theory of two-bridge link groups that is an input to the Sakuma--Weeks triangulation.

papers.title: Verifying Declared AI Workloads from GPU Supply Current
papers.abstract: Frontier AI governance agreements require compute verification techniques that allow an external observer to confirm that a hardware operator does not run prohibited workloads. Off-chip, analogue hardware signals, such as power draw, have been proposed as a potential information channel for compute verification. Such signals can be measured externally, without the operator's cooperation. We show that the supply current drawn by a GPU can be used to verify the work declared by the GPU operator, without requiring examples of prohibited workloads or evasion strategies. We record 23.4 h of GPU current with a Rogowski coil under idle, training and inference workloads. We consider five evasion strategies an operator might use to disguise prohibited training. We show that a one-class model fitted to the current draw of permitted, declared work (idle and inference) flags at least 99.9% of windows of prohibited training, including training hidden by the five evasion strategies. As a continuous monitor across successive windows, it detects all 188 episodes of prohibited training hidden by time-sharing with declared inference, with a median delay of 3.0 s, and raises one alarm in 8.8 h of declared work. Incomplete or corrupt recordings of the declared work can undermine verification. An incomplete recording fails loudly; with idle missing, the monitor is in alarm for 99.97% of declared idle. A corrupt recording can fail silently; if the operator runs training during the recording, the monitor can miss hidden training while raising no alarm on declared work. These results suggest that operator declarations together with external analogue sensing might offer a practical route to compute verification.

papers.title: Sharpness of the Brjuno Condition for Hyperbolic Bishop Surfaces
papers.abstract: Let $\mu \in \mathbb{C}$ satisfy $|\mu|=1$, and assume that $\mu$ is not a root of unity and is not Brjuno. Let $Q_\gamma$ denote the Bishop quadric with $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{2+\mu+\mu^{-1}} > 1/2$. Gong and Stolovitch conjectured that there exists a real-analytic surface in $\mathbb{C}^2$ with Moser--Webster invariant $\mu$ that is formally but not holomorphically equivalent to $Q_\gamma$. We prove this conjecture.

papers.title: Superintegrable Systems and the Tractor Connection
papers.abstract: Quadratic constants of motion for natural pseudo-Riemannian Hamiltonians with potential correspond to conformal Killing tensors admitting multiple Killing scales. Taking this correspondence further, we develop a dimension-independent ($n\ge 3$) framework for studying second-order superintegrable systems using conformal tractor calculus, and invariant BGG prolongation of the rank two conformal Killing equation. We apply this framework to classify second-order maximally superintegrable systems within certain natural families of Hamiltonians generated by pairs of conformally related Einstein metrics in arbitrary dimensions. We recover the second-order analogue of Bertrand's theorem as a special case.

papers.title: A Deterministic Polynomial-Query Protocol for Envy-Free Cake Cutting
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic protocol that divides a heterogeneous cake completely and without envy among $n$ agents using $O(n^6\log n)$ Robertson--Webb queries in the worst case. Valuations may be arbitrary nonnegative, nonatomic measures, and bundles may be disconnected. The protocol makes $O(n)$ calls to certified trimming, which uses $O(n^5\log n)$ queries on $n$ pieces. In a certified trim, each agent receives the end part, or suffix, of a different piece without envy, and every shortened piece has a witness tie leading back to a whole piece. At each step, the witness values the shortened suffix exactly as much as her own. For pieces of positive interval length with strictly increasing suffix values, the retained suffix lengths are unique, although their holders may differ. Candidate assignments share a table of value and cut queries. If the coordinatewise median of their value estimates fails a matching test, the test identifies an agent whose value is underestimated, ruling out at least half the remaining assignments. A weighted median of cut marks lets one repair step remove a small envy while allocating almost all of the residue. For complete envy-free chore allocation, the query bound is $O(n^7\log n)$.

papers.title: The Limits of Behavioral Early Warning for Copy-Trading Blow-Ups: A Pre-Registered, Full-Universe On-Chain Study (Hyperliquid)
papers.abstract: A common, rarely-tested assumption behind copy-trading risk controls is that "behavioral monitoring catches blow-ups": that a master trader's conduct drifts before the equity damage that wipes out followers. We test this on real on-chain money over the full public Hyperliquid leaderboard: 37,895 addresses, filtered to 10,395 "master-worth-copying" accounts, yielding 2,621 genuine loss-driven idiosyncratic blow-ups across 48 independent crash-days. On a model-free panel of 2,477 blow-up masters, behavioral drift leads equity for only 9% (216 masters); 69% blow up with no gradual behavioral signal at all, and the overall median lead is negative (-8 days): when conduct moves, it typically lags the equity rather than leading it. A purpose-built three-axis mixture-SPRT detector, pre-registered with its operating point frozen on a disjoint tuning split and read once against a sealed test set, confirms the boundary rather than beating it: it achieves chance-level discrimination (AUC 0.49) at 2% recall. It does post the lowest false-positive rate of any method (0.040, ~1.9x below a leverage tripwire), but at negligible recall that precision is of little practical use. Behavioral early warning is therefore not a viable general safety net for copy-trading blow-ups: most are sudden, a plain equity / drawdown stop fires as early on them, and the residual behavioral signal (gradual over-leveraging) precedes fewer than one blow-up in ten.
papers.intro:
Copy trading and social trading let retail followers mirror a “master” trader’s positions automatically. The arrangement industrializes a single account’s risk: when a master blows up, every follower blows up with them, on the same candle. Regulators have repeatedly flagged this contagion channel and the asymmetry of information it creates: a follower sees a headline return and a leaderboard rank, not the master’s moment-to-moment risk-taking [11, 6, 17]. The implicit promise of every “risk score” and “copy-stop” product layered on top is that watching how the master trades gives an earlier, cleaner warning than watching the equity curve alone.

Copy trading and social trading let retail followers mirror a “master” trader’s positions automatically. The arrangement industrializes a single account’s risk: when a master blows up, every follower blows up with them, on the same candle. Regulators have repeatedly flagged this contagion channel and the asymmetry of information it creates: a follower sees a headline return and a leaderboard rank, not the master’s moment-to-moment risk-taking [11, 6, 17]. The implicit promise of every “risk score” and “copy-stop” product layered on top is that watching how the master trades gives an earlier, cleaner warning than watching the equity curve alone.

That promise rests on a load-bearing empirical assumption that is almost never tested adversarially on real adversarial data: behavioral drift precedes the equity damage. If a master’s conduct degrades gradually—creeping leverage, abandoned stops, averaging into losers—before the account craters, then a behavioral monitor buys followers lead-time the equity itself cannot. If instead most blow-ups are sudden—one oversized trade, a gap, or a master who was always reckless and simply got unlucky—then there is no behavioral runway to detect, and a plain equity threshold is both simpler and earlier.

We put this assumption on real on-chain money. Hyperliquid is a high-volume decentralized perpetual-futures venue whose public info API exposes, with no authentication, the recent fill, order, and ledger history for any address (subject to an ≈\approx10,000-fill cap we return to in Section 3), plus a coarse account-value history [10]. This is an unusually transparent setting: positions and liquidations are settled on-chain, the leaderboard is public, and there is no survivorship curation by a broker. We freeze a leaderboard universe at a fixed date, label blow-ups by a forward-only equity rule, and ask—first model-free, then with a purpose-built detector—when, and for whom, behavior actually leads equity.

1. The boundary (the headline). On 2,477 real idiosyncratic blow-up masters, behavioral drift leads equity for only ≈\approx9%; 69% are sudden; the overall median lead is negative. The popular “behavioral monitoring catches blow-ups” assumption is false as a general law, including in an earlier, scaled-cohort version of this project, whose more favorable numbers this full-universe run overturns. 2. A pre-registered detector that confirms it. A three-axis mixture-SPRT detector, frozen on a disjoint tuning split and read once against a sealed test set, achieves chance-level discrimination (AUC 0.490.49) at 2%2\% recall: the behavioral machinery cannot rank a soon-to-blow-up master above a stable one. It does attain the lowest false-positive rate of any method (≈1.9×\approx 1.9\times below a leverage tripwire), a real but, at this recall, inconsequential property. 3. What little survives is exposure. Among the few masters that do drift early, the trigger is almost always the exposure (leverage) axis, not discipline or tilt—but it precedes fewer than one blow-up in ten, and our on-chain leverage proxy is coarse, so we do not over-read the mechanism.

papers.title: Raynaud and Gruson's flattening techniques in Berkovich geometry
papers.abstract: Raynaud and Gruson introduced a flattening procedure for coherent sheaf in the schemes context that rely on sophisticated techniques of algebra and geometry. These methods were later used by Raynaud, Bosch and L\"utkebohmert in formal geometry, and more recently Ducros has developed analogous tools for Berkovich spaces. However, it should be noted that the expression "flattening by blowing up" is, in this context, a little abusive because the flattening process actually requires a succession of blow up and quasi-\'etale morphisms. The aim of this article is to develop a local flattening technique in Berkovich geometry, in the boundaryless case, which only involves blow up.

papers.title: Foata and Spot Commutation for Parking Functions
papers.abstract: For a parking function $\alpha$, let $\mathrm{spot}(\alpha)$ be the permutation whose $i$th entry is the space occupied by car $i$ and let $\mathrm{foata}(w)$ be Foata's second fundamental transformation on words. Conjecture 6.3 of Celano et al. asserts that $\mathrm{foata}(\mathrm{spot}(\alpha)) = \mathrm{spot}(\mathrm{foata}(\alpha))$ for every unit interval parking function $\alpha$. This paper proves the identity for a larger class: parking functions where each prime component (borrowing Gessel's definition) of $\alpha$ is nondecreasing. Since every unit interval parking function is composed of nondecreasing prime parking functions, the conjecture follows. A key step is showing that $\mathrm{foata}$ preserves the set of parking functions $\alpha$ with $\mathrm{spot}(\alpha) = \mathrm{std}(\alpha)$, where $\mathrm{std}$ denotes standardization. In particular, this proves that inversion count and major index are equidistributed over this larger class.

papers.title: Face-neighbourly polyhedra with eight or nine faces and genus at most three
papers.abstract: A polyhedral surface is face-neighbourly if every pair of faces shares an edge. We classify the combinatorial types of closed orientable face-neighbourly polyhedral surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with eight or nine faces and genus at most three, assuming trivalent vertices, simple planar polygonal faces and distinct supporting planes for adjacent faces. Several common edges between a pair of faces are allowed. The enumeration gives 42,124 candidate maps with eight faces and 203 with nine. SAT certificates exclude all but two maps, both of genus three with eight nonagonal faces. They are realised by Mizhaev's V2 and by the R\"ost--V\'igh polyhedron. With the face-neighbourliness condition removed, the class of genus-three surfaces with eight nonagonal faces has one additional realisable type, Mizhaev's V1.

papers.title: Every friend of 10 has at least eleven distinct prime factors
papers.abstract: A friend of $10$ is a positive integer $N\neq 10$ such that $\sigma(N)/N=\sigma(10)/10=9/5$. Whether one exists is an open problem. Thackeray proved that a friend of $10$ has at least $10$ distinct prime factors. We describe a computer-assisted proof that it has at least $11$. The proof is an exhaustive search over sets of primes, carried out by a recursive certifier written in PARI/GP, which extends the open-source project caioross/solitary10. The new ingredients are a split of ``almost tight'' nodes that avoids enumerating the smallest unknown prime, a treatment of nodes with three or more unknown primes by a saturation dichotomy, a counting rule for unfactored cofactors of cyclotomic values, and the correction of a soundness gap in the earlier closure rule. The certification run for $\omega=10$ visited $157{,}210{,}962$ nodes in $11.4$ hours on $12$ threads. As a consequence, a friend of $10$ would be larger than $10^{38}$.

papers.title: Explicit Error Term in the Chebotarev Density Theorem for Function Fields
papers.abstract: We prove an explicit error term in the Chebotarev Density Theorem for finite generically Galois \'etale morphisms of affine varieties over finite fields, under a mild condition on their size. The error term generalises the known results for curves, and depends only on invariants of the varieties. We present several applications to the explicit error term. We apply it to existence problems, and to the Bateman-Horn conjecture over finite fields.

papers.title: SecretSifter: A Runtime Secret-Detection Engine for Live Web Traffic
papers.abstract: Credentials embedded in client-delivered web artifacts, such as minified JavaScript bundles, webpack chunks, server-side-rendered state objects, and JSON or XML API responses, form a runtime attack surface that repository-time (shift-left) secret scanners do not observe, because the credential enters the served artifact at build time or at runtime, after every source-code gate has passed. This paper presents SecretSifter, an open-source runtime secret-detection engine that inspects live web traffic and reports secret-grade credentials at the point they are delivered to the browser. The engine combines format-anchored and context-gated detection rules, semantic key-name extraction, Shannon-entropy scoring, and dedicated detection of hardcoded CryptoJS/AES material across the full served surface. SecretSifter ships as three editions over one shared detection core: a Burp Suite extension, a Chrome extension, and a standalone Windows and macOS desktop application, with a Bearer-authenticated REST and MCP interface for automation. On a 198-value benchmark of real production client-exposed values (GT-198), the deterministic detection stage reached 79.8% recall at 86.8% precision in default configuration, the highest F1 of any system evaluated. The detection core is released under an open-source (MIT) license, and a de-identified reproducibility bundle and a public synthetic demo target are provided.

papers.title: The Value of Labels in Data Selection for Least Squares
papers.abstract: Suppose a selector sees a finite labelled dataset and chooses $n$ of its rows, with repetition. Ordinary least squares is then fitted to the rows that were chosen, without weights, and the excess loss of the fit on the full dataset is measured in units of the optimal loss. Without further assumptions this ratio does not decay with $n$. We examine the problem for $d$ features and rows of normalized leverage at most $\kappa$, and determine or bound the leading constants. A selector that must establish its rule before seeing the labels has an optimal worst-case ratio of $d\kappa/n$ to leading order, whatever use it makes of the features. With scalar labels, a selector that sees the labels achieves a value between $d\kappa/(2n)$ and $d\kappa\Lambda_d/n$, where $\Lambda_d<1$ is the rounding constant of mean selection. For $d\le4$, the constant is then $d\kappa/2$, so that labels are worth exactly a factor of two there, and for one feature and $m$ outputs it is $\kappa\Lambda_m$. With two or more features the selector can change the proportions of the frequent rows and therefore reshape its own design matrix. We design a simplified optimization problem, which we call a game, that bounds the constant for datasets with exactly fitted frequent rows, then show that its value is at most one half of the gradient energy in several regimes, and that one half is exact along directions in which the frequent rows are rigid, such as an intercept. For grouped designs, in which reshaping amounts to the allocation of a common budget, the constant is $27d/128$ up to an additive constant, compared with $d$ without labels. Nevertheless, one half is not the constant in every dimension: we construct datasets of extremely high dimension and large leverage on which every selection has an excess ratio of at least $(e^{-1/2}-o(1))\,d\kappa/n$, so that labels are worth at most a factor close to $\sqrt e$ there.

papers.title: Measuring Colombia's Informal Output: Relative Earnings and Identification in a Bayesian Two-Sector Model, 1993-2026
papers.abstract: How much of Colombia's measured output is produced by informal work? The answer cannot be read from the labor-informality rate: Colombia combines an informality rate above 50% with a much smaller informal share of output, because informal work is less productive. We estimate a Bayesian two-sector business-cycle model on quarterly national accounts and on reconstructed employment and informality series for 1993-2026. Identification comes from a new quarterly series of informal-to-formal labor earnings built from household-survey microdata for 2007-2026. Formal production uses capital and labor, informal production is labor based, and an accounting relationship maps relative earnings, the informality rate and the formal capital share into the informal output share. We show that aggregate data alone cannot pin down the size of the informal sector, and that relative earnings identify its quarterly path: from 2007 the path is invariant, within 0.3 percentage points, to the model's steady state. The informal share declines from about 30% of GDP in 1993 to 20% in 2026Q2, while labor informality falls from about 69% to 54%. The estimates lie within the range of published shadow-economy series for Colombia, close to the enhanced MIMIC estimates of Asllani, Dell'Anno and Schneider for 2009-2020. Sensitivity analysis quantifies the role of the capital share and of non-wage labor costs.
papers.intro:
An economy can have a high proportion of informal workers without producing an equally high proportion of its output informally. Colombia is a clear case. The national household-survey series used in this paper places labor informality at about 54% of employment in 2026, but work in small, unregistered or own-account activities is much less productive than registered wage employment. Turning a headcount into a share of value added therefore requires information on that productivity gap, as well as a definition of what counts as informal production.

An economy can have a high proportion of informal workers without producing an equally high proportion of its output informally. Colombia is a clear case. The national household-survey series used in this paper places labor informality at about 54% of employment in 2026, but work in small, unregistered or own-account activities is much less productive than registered wage employment. Turning a headcount into a share of value added therefore requires information on that productivity gap, as well as a definition of what counts as informal production.

The indicators available in Colombia measure different things. Labor informality counts workers. DANE’s multidimensional business-informality indicator counts establishments, and it classified 90.2% of microbusinesses as informal in 2024 (DANE, 2025). The statistical office’s estimate of the non-observed economy, 22.4% of gross production in the 2015-base accounts, covers informal, underground and illegal activities together with statistical adjustments (Departamento Administrativo Nacional de Estadística (2021), DANE). This paper estimates something else, namely the share of measured value added produced by informal work in an explicit two-sector production model. Because the units, denominators and coverage differ, none of these figures should be read as an estimate of the others.

Dynamic general equilibrium (DGE) models are a common tool for inferring the size of the informal or shadow economy. Calibrated versions fix its level at an external benchmark and model its dynamics from there (Elgin and Öztunalı, 2012; Solis-Garcia and Xie, 2017), while Bayesian DSGE versions estimate latent sectoral activity jointly with the structural shocks (Orsi et al., 2014). Either way, the level has to be identified, and aggregate data are often not enough to tell a large informal sector from a small one, because different shares can be reconciled with the same aggregates through changes in unobserved sectoral productivity and in the implied steady state. The contribution of this paper is to bring a direct measurement to bear on that problem.

The contribution of this paper is to bring a direct measurement to bear on that problem.

The model is deliberately parsimonious. Competitive formal firms use capital and labor, and informal activity uses labor only, as in a familiar strand of the literature (Ihrig and Moe, 2004; Elgin and Öztunalı, 2012). A representative household divides its work between the two sectors, accumulates capital and chooses consumption, and aggregate shocks, a formality wedge and informal productivity generate fluctuations. We estimate the model by Bayesian methods with a Kalman-filter likelihood. The macroeconomic data are DANE’s 2015-reference national accounts, with reconstructed quarterly observations before 2005, and total employment and labor informality come from the ICML series, which reconstructs the national labor market from 1993 (Vera-Jaramillo, 2025; Vera-Jaramillo, 2026).

The additional source of identification is a quarterly series of relative labor earnings built from DANE’s household-survey microdata since 2007. It distinguishes groups of workers and, on the formal side, is converted from reported wages to labor costs with the statutory non-wage costs of employment. In the model, the ratio of informal to formal output equals the ratio of workers times relative value added per worker, and relative value added per worker can be written in terms of the survey earnings ratio and the formal capital share. The result is a simple link between the data and the quantity of interest (Proposition 1), in which every assumption is explicit and can be changed.

The paper makes four contributions. It provides a quarterly estimate of informal output in Colombia from 1993 to 2026 that uses all the observed and reconstructed information available, together with the other series the model delivers, such as informal and formal GDP, relative productivity and the structural shocks. It shows, with likelihood profiles, prior–posterior comparisons and simulations with known parameters, that aggregate data alone do not determine the size of the informal sector, which helps explain why DGE models in the literature arrive at very different levels for the same country. It then shows that relative earnings resolve the problem for the object of interest: once they are observed, the estimated path of informal output no longer depends on the steady-state share assumed by the model, and simulations recover the true share precisely. Finally, the data and code are public, so the series can be updated every quarter and re-estimated under other definitions, technologies and wage-cost conversions.

The decline mirrors the fall of labor informality from about 69% to 54% of employment, and by the end of the sample informal value added per worker is about one-fifth of its formal counterpart. papers.title: Retracts of well-filtered co-sober spaces are co-sober
papers.abstract: Xu and Zhao asked whether co-sobriety is inherited by the image of a continuous kernel operator, and more generally whether it is inherited by retracts. Both questions have recently been answered in the negative by Xu, Xu, Ji and Qiu. We prove that both questions have positive answers whenever the ambient space is, in addition, well-filtered; in particular they hold for every sober co-sober space. It follows that the ambient space of any counterexample to either question, such as that of Xu, Xu, Ji and Qiu, must be co-sober and not well-filtered. We give an example of a kernel-operator image that is not a direct instance of the inheritance results of Wen and Xu, and we identify the step of the argument that uses well-filteredness.

papers.intro:
Sobriety is arguably the single most useful property of non-Hausdorff topological spaces, and the Hofmann–Mislove theorem describes it through an order isomorphism between the compact saturated sets of a space and the open filters of its lattice of opens. Seeking a dual form of that theorem, Escardó, Lawson and Simpson [1, Definition 8.9] introduced k-irreducible compact saturated sets and the corresponding class of co-sober spaces, and asked whether every sober space is co-sober [1, Problem 9.7]. Wen and Xu [6, Example 2.8] answered this in the negative: Isbell’s complete lattice, equipped with the lower topology, is sober but not co-sober. Shen, Wu, Xi and Zhao [4] subsequently produced a dcpo whose Scott space is sober but not co-sober, and Ji and Xu [3] have shown that the Scott space of a complete Boolean algebra need not be co-sober.

papers.title: Don't Train It, Write It: An AI Agent Writes New Capabilities into Language Model Weights
papers.abstract: We show that an AI agent can write new capabilities into a pretrained language model by adding gated attention heads and MLP neurons inside its existing layers, without backpropagation and without fitting any weight to the answers of task examples. It has a budget of 50 model passes and sees no validation or test instance. Composed in one model, its modules for six BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) subtasks raise the normalized BBH score of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct from 19.95 to 41.05 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: at most 35.01) and that of Gemma-3-1B-it from 10.25 to 32.86. Against the unmodified model at the same precision, both composites leave the next-token distribution on 1,023,000 WikiText tokens unchanged (KL exactly 0), give identical answers on 15,845 items of five other Leaderboard tests and identical scores on the other 18 BBH subtasks. The agent also writes exact multiplication up to 20 digits, running the model only up to 6 (100.0% on the absent lengths of the sealed test in both models; a LoRA with the same budget: at most 2.1%). Sets, rules and report sentences were sealed in git before the first session (manifests timestamped in Bitcoin), with dated amendments listed in Appendix D; a frozen evaluator ran the sealed test once. Verdicts (H5: tracking; H6: composite; H8: one pass vs. chain of thought; H9: fresh and rewritten instances; H10: side effects; H12: multiplication), on the preregistered sealed test, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct: H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H9 success, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success; Gemma-3-1B-it (H7: H5, H6, H8 and H9 in this model): H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H8 (tracking 3) success, H9 partial, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success. Not everything worked: 4 of 45 single modules show small side effects and 5 of 50 sessions hit the 12-hour limit without a module.
papers.intro:
Large language models are improved by training: data, gradients and a loss. A recent line of work asks whether a frontier model can instead read and write the weights of another network directly, much like code [37]. The answer so far is mixed. Weight edits by agents can remove an obstacle that hides an existing skill, for example a failure mode that wastes tokens, and they can teach facts and rules that the model can already use when they are written in its prompt [42]. Whether an edit can give a model an ability it lacks even with help in its prompt was left open [42]; narrow counterexamples have since appeared for addition [35, 29].

Whether an edit can give a model an ability it lacks even with help in its prompt was left open [42]; narrow counterexamples have since appeared for addition [35, 29].

We study this question with a controlled protocol and push it much further. We give a coding agent (Claude Code [3]) tool access to the weights of a small open model and ask it to write a capability that the model does not have. The agent writes the capability as new weights inside the network: attention heads and MLP neurons added to existing layers, behind gates that are exactly zero off their trigger, so that on unrelated text (WikiText) the model computes what the unmodified model computes at the same precision. It never backpropagates through the network and never fits any weight to the answers of task examples. It has a budget of 50 passes (calls to the model, each up to 512 prompts), runs the model only on practice inputs, may request the accuracy of a sealed validation set per length or subtask, and never sees a validation or test instance. Sets, decision rules and the sentences that would report each outcome were sealed before the first session. The agent works from a frozen manual of procedures and lessons from development sessions. For multiplication, tracking and web_of_lies the manual records designs that worked; for navigate and boolean_expressions it states only what to compute, so in two of the five stage-2 tasks the agent designed the circuit without the manual giving it.

Results. The headline result is a composite model. In each host, the official modules for six BBH subtasks [36] are composed, co-resident in one model without interfering, and examined once on a sealed test with the protocol of the Open LLM Leaderboard v2 [11]. The Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct composite scores 41.05 (normalized BBH score), up from 19.95; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct scores 34.89 official, 34.98 with lm-eval-harness and 35.01 with our evaluator, so the 1.5B composite is above all three (Figure 2). The Gemma-3-1B-it composite goes from 10.25 to 32.86. The oracle is the gain that a perfect score on the six subtasks would give (21.37 and 22.52 points, fixed before the exam from the lm-eval baseline): the Qwen gain is close to it and the Gemma gain reaches it. Against its format control, the unmodified model at the same precision (float32), neither composite changes anything else we measured: KL exactly 0 and no change of the top token on 1,023,000 WikiText tokens, the same generation or choice on each of the 15,845 items of IFEval, MATH Level 5, GPQA, MuSR and MMLU-Pro, and identical scores on the other 18 BBH subtasks. The modules add specific capabilities without disturbing the rest; they do not make the model better in general. Module by module, on fresh instances of the sealed test: on tracking_shuffled_objects, which Qwen2.5-1.5B cannot do even with the algorithm in its prompt or with chain of thought (within 5 points of chance), 5 of 5 Qwen sessions reach 90% or more on every absent subtask (median 100.0%), as do 3 of 5 in Gemma (median 98.6%); web_of_lies goes from 52.0% in one pass and 83.6% with chain of thought to 100.0% in Qwen; navigate and boolean_expressions, whose circuits the agent designed without a task manual, score 100.0% and 100.0% in Qwen (means of the 4 and 3 sessions that produced a module; the other 1 and 2 ended at the 12-hour limit and count as 0 in the decision rules) and 100.0% and 100.0% in Gemma; and exact multiplication, which Qwen2.5-1.5B cannot do even with chain of thought, scores 100.0% (Qwen) and 100.0% (Gemma) at the lengths the agent never ran, where a LoRA trained with the same budget scores 1.3% and 2.1% (Figure 1). In stage 1, all 10 official sessions write exact addition that is 100% on the sealed test at every length up to 30 digits, although the agent could run the model only up to 12 digits (Figure 4). Not everything worked: 4 of the 45 single modules show small but measurable side effects, 5 of the 50 stage-2 sessions ended at the 12-hour limit without a module, and some modules lose accuracy on rewritten wording. Section 4 reports every preregistered verdict as it came out, with the sentence fixed for it before the exam.
