papers.title: Shoonya: Zero-Socket In-Process Small Language Models for Graph Databases with Schema-Epoch KV Caching, Live Catalog Logit Masking, and Verifier-Advantage Distillation
papers.abstract: Coupling a property-graph database to an external language-model server imposes a three-part socket tax: serialization overhead dwarfing microsecond graph reads, repeated prefill of verbose schemas, and blind decoding divorced from the live catalog and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) engine. We present Shoonya, from-scratch commercially clean (0.0% non-commercial or share-alike data) tri-modal (Python, Rust, OpenCypher) small language models (16.8M to 1.07B parameters) co-designed with shoonya-infer, a zero-dependency pure-Rust runtime embedded inside the samyama-graph-enterprise address space. Direct GraphStore references unlock three database-native primitives: (1) an epoch-invalidated SchemaPrefixCache over a copy-on-write PagedKvArena accelerating warm CPU time-to-first-token by 4.91x--13.68x with O(1) DDL invalidation; (2) a 36 us columnar catalog and source-span logit mask enforcing valid ontology identifiers and verbatim spans; and (3) a sub-65 us read-only MVCC gate serving Tier-0 queries inside 389.8 MiB INT8 RSS (59.8--67.9 tok/s) with 0.0% hallucination leak. Rank-factorized tied embeddings (-74.5% vocabulary weights), atomic indentation tokens (0/421 indentation errors), 4:1 grouped-query attention with 2:1 cross-layer KV sharing (-93.75% INT8 KV memory), Warmup-Stable-Decay training, KnOTS SVD merging, Step-GRPO, and Rust Jacobi SVD governance keep 100% of layers heavy-tailed ($\alpha \in [1.88, 2.20]$). Finally, we synthesize nine lessons across v0.1--v1.0, resolving a Reverse-Token-Density Distillation Trap via teacher scaling and zero-VRAM Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation (AdvKD), recovering +13.61 MBPP points (33.07%) while reaching 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool planning.
papers.intro:
Modern property-graph databases increasingly embed language-driven workflows alongside declarative query execution: translating natural-language questions into OpenCypher (Francis et al., 2018), synthesizing multi-step agentic tool plans, extracting typed entity-relation triples from unstructured clinical or enterprise text, and enriching domain ontologies (Mandarapu and Kunkunuru, 2026b). Controlled experiments on clinical question answering establish that knowledge-graph grounding helps language models specifically when decisive institutional facts lie outside pretraining corpora (Mandarapu and Kunkunuru, 2026a). Yet in regulated deployments where private subgraphs cannot leave on-premise boundaries, even self-hosting an open-weight model via a separate localhost HTTP or gRPC server introduces a fundamental socket tax: 1. IPC and serialization asymmetry. An in-memory columnar property graph resolves single-hop adjacency and MVCC visibility in 1515–65​μ​s65\,\mu\text{s}, whereas loopback JSON serialization, OS socket scheduling, and Python runtime dispatch cost milliseconds per call—precluding tight per-token or per-candidate database verification. 2. Redundant schema prefill. Enterprise graph schemas span hundreds to thousands of tokens. Stateless socket calls re-prefill the schema prompt on every turn, dominating CPU time-to-first-token (TTFT), while external KV prefix caches (Zheng et al., 2024) lack transactional coherence when database DDL statements mutate labels or properties. 3. Catalog-blind subword decoding. Out-of-process decoders sample tokens without live access to the graph catalog, hallucinating nonexistent edge labels (e.g., :TREATS instead of :TARGETS), inverting edge arrows, or fabricating ungrounded entity strings. External grammar compilers (Willard and Louf, 2023) require tens to hundreds of milliseconds to rebuild static automata upon schema evolution.

papers.title: Legal Is Not Good: A Pre-Registered Benchmark of Low-Cost Language and Decision Models on a New Strategy Game
papers.abstract: Measure Before You Train argued that an agent's decisions should be measured against ground truth, under a protocol fixed in advance, before anyone trains or replaces the model behind them. We carry the method to a second, very different domain, a turn-based strategy game, and ask a deliberately modest question: how well do low-cost agents play under a pre-registered protocol? hexfolk is a minimal two-player 4X game written for this purpose, so no model has seen its rules or positions. A deterministic engine, one agent interface, a referee that never corrects an illegal or late move, and per-decision logs make every game replayable; questions and expected answers were committed before the games, on held-out seeds with mirrored seats and 95% Wilson intervals. Two small open language models (8B and 3B) lose every game to a few-line rule player. Answering in free text they are invalid on 98% of their decisions; constrained to legal moves they never play an invalid one, yet they lose to the uniformly random player (the 8B model wins 10.0 [4.3, 21.4]% of games), refuting our expectation that they would beat it; the result survives a control that shuffles the order of the options. Two native decision models never play an invalid move and both beat random; one loses all 50 games to the rule player, the other is not distinguishable from it in 50 games and beats a one-step search. The paid agents make tens to over a hundred model calls per game; against the same opponents a free 60 ms-per-move search, which makes none, outplays every paid model by the full range of the scale. Two 7-8B models served locally behave the same way. No frontier model is included.
papers.intro:
Agents built on language models are increasingly asked to decide rather than to write: which of a few dozen legal moves to play, which label to assign, whether to act. The companion paper (Lucca, 2026) (MBYT) studied one such agent, a personal inbox router, and found that once ground truth existed a classical baseline beat every zero-shot model. Its method—freeze the inputs, fix the questions and the expected answers before looking, keep a held-out set, report intervals and refuse to rank what the intervals do not separate—is not specific to email, but a single domain cannot show that.

papers.title: KMed-31B Technical Report
papers.abstract: We present KMed-31B, a medical large language model post-trained from an open-weight model for on-premises deployment with limited hardware. Post-training a model for diverse medical tasks remains difficult, because improving one kind of task can lower performance on another. We attribute this to differences between tasks in expected output and available feedback. Medical question answering and diagnosis prediction have reference answers, whereas clinical inquiry has no single correct response and is judged with rubrics. We therefore divide medical training tasks into four categories by these two properties, train one specialist per category with a reward that its feedback supports, and integrate the specialists into a single student with Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD$^2$). For clinical inquiry, we build Synthetic Health Dialogue, a simulated corpus of consultations with lay users and clinicians whose patient cases span common clinical presentations in primary care. Relative to its base model, KMed-31B raises HealthBench Hard from 22.95 to 41.87 and HealthBench Professional from 37.92 to 50.20 in non-thinking mode, and from 23.80 to 51.48 and from 41.97 to 59.18 in thinking mode, while its scores on four multiple-choice medical benchmarks are maintained or slightly improved. KMed-31B has the highest unadjusted HealthBench Hard score among the compared models, including proprietary ones, and scores higher on HealthBench Professional than every open-weight model we compare, including models with more than ten times as many total parameters. Applied to another base model, Qwen3.8-27B, the same training recipe also raises both HealthBench scores. We describe the training recipe, data construction, and settings in detail so that institutions requiring on-premises deployment can develop medical models from open-weight foundations.
papers.intro:
Frontier-level large language models have demonstrated strong performance on medical question answering and health conversations [1, 2]. In real clinical settings, however, services are often not allowed to send patient data outside the institution and must therefore run models on premises with limited hardware resources. This requirement has motivated efforts to develop relatively small open-weight medical models [3, 4]. Despite their small size, these models must still answer knowledge-intensive medical questions, reason about clinical cases, and handle consultations with lay users and clinicians.

Gemma-4-31B-IT is on par with GPT-5.6-sol [5] on MedXpertQA Text but falls far behind it on HealthBench Hard and HealthBench Professional, whereas Muse-Glimmer-30B [6] approaches Qwen3.5-397B [7] on both HealthBench benchmarks while its MedXpertQA Text score falls well below that of Gemma-4-31B-IT (Section 4.2).

Medical question answering has reference answers against which a response can be checked, whereas clinical inquiry covers open-ended requests from lay users and clinicians that have no single correct response. The quality of a clinical response depends on several aspects at once, such as its accuracy, its completeness, and its appropriateness to the user’s context, and its evaluation therefore requires rubrics that specify criteria for each aspect.

Open-ended question answering, multiple-choice question answering, and diagnosis prediction provide reference answers, so their specialists are trained through RL with answer-matching rewards. Clinical inquiry has no single reference answer and relies on rubric-based feedback, so its specialist follows a dedicated recipe that proceeds from SFT to RL with fixed rubrics and then to Diversified ROPD (D-ROPD), our adaptation of rubric-based on-policy distillation (ROPD) [15]. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates separately trained domain specialists into a single student [16, 17], and our MOPD2 adopts the delta signal of on-policy delta distillation (OPD2) [18]. On the student’s own rollouts, the specialist associated with each task category supplies a token-level signal based on its log-probability difference from a fixed reference model (the pretrained Gemma-4-31B checkpoint), so that the signal reflects what each specialist acquired relative to that checkpoint (Section 3.2).

papers.title: Thakaa at AlexandriaX-2026: Who Gets the Final Say? Assigning Output Authority in Dialectal Arabic Machine Translation and Error Detection
papers.abstract: We report first-place systems for all four evaluated AlexandriaX-2026 settings: both English-to-dialect translation tracks, cross-dialect translation, and translation-error detection. In unconstrained translation, our minimum Bayes risk (MBR) selection restricts output authority: four local systems can supply the translation, while seven additional systems contribute only reference evidence. Candidate-constrained MBR beats the strongest complete candidate in all 13 dialects and gains 1.2554 macro spBLEU overall, reaching 33.4891. It also surpasses a retrospective oracle selecting the best whole candidate system per dialect. In the constrained track, country-routed LoRA adapters over a shared NileChat-3B-Base backbone incorporate the released Libyan and Sudanese supervision absent from the training and development splits, raising macro spBLEU from 29.5969 to 30.4233. Post-evaluation, a single adapter trained on all released Alexandria data reaches 30.4733 macro spBLEU; averaging model weights across three training seeds raises this to 30.9726 while retaining one model for inference. For cross-dialect translation, nonparallel target-dialect retrieval guides deliberation, raising Gemma-4-31B-IT without fine-tuning from 24.6898 to 28.4011 spBLEU. For translation-error detection, GPT-5.5 proposes semantic error regions, while MARBERTv2 controls their character boundaries and corroborates additional spans, raising Overall from 0.4691 to 0.4982.

papers.title: Thakaa at StanceEval-2026: Inference-Time Target Grounding for Arabic Stance Detection
papers.abstract: StanceEval-2026 tests Arabic stance classification under target shift, with evaluation targets absent from the labelled task data. We test two ways to supply target information at inference time. For Track 1, we retrieve eight labelled Women Driving demonstrations from the external ArabicStanceX corpus and score the three label tokens with Gemma-4-31B-IT. For the unseen-target track, we prepend cached target context prompted to be factual and non-evaluative, then fuse label predictions and label-token scores from multiple LLMs, with final assignments constrained by published class totals. The systems obtain 85.22 and 91.78 Favg2 on Tracks 1 and 2, ranking sixth and fourth in the final standings. On held-out ArabicStanceX tweets, direct prompting scores 79.45 Favg2; eight random Women Driving demonstrations raise it to 84.78, and similarity retrieval reaches 89.04. Across three target-held-out Mawqif evaluations, a fixed target card raises Gemma-4-31B-IT from 86.54 to 86.93, whereas QLoRA lowers Gemma-4-12B-IT from 84.43 to 83.77. In these separate public evaluations, same-target demonstrations and retrieval improve performance, factual target context provides small, target-dependent gains, and the tested source-only adapter does not improve.
papers.intro:
Stance detection relates a text to a specified target. Sentiment alone is insufficient when a tweet criticises an implementation but supports its goal, or praises an actor without endorsing the target. Arabic social media adds dialectal variation, sarcasm, and implicit reference (Alturayeif et al., 2022; Albalawi et al., 2026b).

StanceEval-2026 (Albalawi et al., 2026a) evaluates this relation under a target shift. Track 1 is nominally the seen-target setting, yet it tests Women Driving after training on Women Empowerment and two other topics. papers.title: ChatGPT Can't Sell (And That's Probably a Good Thing): Buyer-Aligned AI Advice, the Sales-Representative Gap, and Evidence from Commercial Conversations
papers.abstract: AI assistants and merchant sales agents have different objectives: assistants should help buyers compare options and preserve the choice not to purchase, while sales agents also guide qualified buyers toward an authorized next step. We study this sales-representative gap with three evidence streams. In 12,178 historical English GPT-family conversations screened for commercial or transactional intent, a 279-request sample contained recommendation language in 63 first replies (22.6%) and no narrow transactional action wording. In a 56-conversation explicit-buying sample, 24 replies (42.9%) contained recommendation markers, 32 (57.1%) qualification phrases, and none transaction-specific phrases. These lexical measures do not estimate successful selling. A 2026 brand-monitoring cohort of 1,050 GPT-5.4--Gemini answer pairs over 383 purchase-related prompts showed transaction-specific phrases in 0.0% of recommendation-worded prompts, 0.21% of price/comparison prompts, and 9.52% of explicitly transaction-worded prompts. The prompts are selected, not organic shopping sessions. In a prospective pilot across five matched hypothetical product scenarios, sales instructions produced more next-step language than general-assistant instructions (5/5 vs. 2/5), but no increase in clean product choice (3/5 in both); unsupported offers and fit errors also occurred. This pilot cannot establish a population effect. A separate company-affiliated randomized field study reports higher engaged-visitor conversion for Javo, a commercially trained sales agent, than for a frontier-model agent in shared tooling, but does not identify the mechanism. We argue that apparent reluctance to sell can be appropriate for buyer-aligned assistants. Merchant agents should optimize qualified decision progress through catalog grounding, truthful authorization, and safeguards against unsuitable sales.
papers.intro:
ChatGPT can’t sell is an intentionally provocative headline. It does not mean that ChatGPT cannot recommend a product, describe a price, or occasionally make a persuasive case. It names a narrower organizational mismatch: a general-purpose assistant is expected to help the user reach an informed decision, whereas a brand’s on-site representative is expected to help the merchant achieve a legitimate commercial outcome. These goals often align when the product fits. They can diverge when the product does not fit, a term is unfavorable, a cost is uncertain, or an agent invents an action it is not empowered to execute.

A comparison of two laptops may be excellent advice while failing every standard sales-workflow metric. A conversion-maximizing recommendation may increase an order count yet mislead the buyer. Neither follows simply from the number of hedges, disclaimers, or affirmative phrases used by an LLM. The question is whether an assistant recognizes the boundary between advice and selling and whether a specialist can bridge that boundary without compromising consumer welfare.

The persuasion-knowledge literature predicts that buyers notice selling intentions and may react when they infer self-interested recommendations (Friestad and Wright, 1994; Campbell and Kirmani, 2000). Dialogue-based post-training can make models broadly more useful while introducing style or agreeableness incentives that deserve separate evaluation (Ouyang et al., 2022; Sharma et al., 2024). Experimental research on AI sellers also finds that salient profit motives change consumer reactions (Farmer and Harding, 2026; Liu et al., 2025). A user-oriented assistant’s reluctance to close a sale can therefore be socially useful rather than a defect.

papers.title: The Dunford-Pettis property and complemented Hilbert subspaces of Sobolev martingale spaces
papers.abstract: Let $L^1_W$ be the space of integrable terminal values of martingales on a homogeneous tree whose local differences belong to a fixed matrix space $W$. We show that $L^1_W$ has the Dunford-Pettis property if and only if $W$ is spanned by its rank-one matrices. Every complemented reflexive subspace of $L^1_W$ is isomorphic to a Hilbert space. Under the second structural condition of Ayoush, Stolyarov and Wojciechowski, the martingale fractional integral of order $\frac12$ is completely continuous and fails to be absolutely $2$-summing. This gives nonisomorphism with $L^1$ for $W\ne0$. On the $4$-ary tree we exhibit all three possible combinations of the Dunford-Pettis property and the existence of a complemented copy of $\ell^2$. In one example a bounded operator into $\ell^4$ fails to be completely continuous, although every bounded operator into a Hilbert space is completely continuous. We also prove that, for every $n\ge1$, each complemented reflexive subspace of $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{T}^n)$ is isomorphic to a Hilbert space.

papers.title: Plane Curves Whose Curvature Is a Function of the Distance to the Tangent Line: Relations Between Karpenkov's Areal and Angular Densities
papers.abstract: For a plane curve and a point $O$, O. Karpenkov introduced the areal density $A$ and the angular density $B$ as smooth counterparts of the alternating entries of an LLS sequence. Here $A$ is the signed distance from $O$ to the tangent line, and, with the order of the chords in the signed definition fixed here, $A^2B=\kappa$, where $\kappa$ is the signed curvature. A relation between the two densities therefore prescribes the curvature as a function of the distance to the tangent line. Karpenkov asked which curves have $AB$, or $B$ alone, constant. The equation $AB=C$ gives the shrinking, stationary and expanding profiles of planar curve shortening. For constant nonzero $B$, choose the orientation so that $B>0$. Curves with positive support have periodic support or are centred circles. The noncircular closed curves are classified by their turning fractions in $(1/2,1/\sqrt3)$; the centred circle is the only embedded closed solution. Negative support gives smooth open graphs whose two ends approach rays from the origin. On positive support the polar reciprocal is a constant-force orbit, and the original curve is a rotated and scaled velocity curve of that orbit. For $A^3B=C$ we determine which ends extend to infinity, reach a cusp, or spiral into the origin. We describe regularity and the range of turning fractions for the positive-support family $A^pB=C$. Finally, for a general relation $B=\Phi(A)$ the polar reciprocal is an orbit of the central force $L^2/\Phi(1/r)$; we describe the ends of all arcs with $AB<0$ and show that a closed curve with turning fraction $m/n$ has exactly $n(m-1)$ double points. We also describe the curves whose areal or angular density is a linear function of the arclength.

papers.title: When Can a Rewiring Control Test LLM Weight Readers? C2 and an Eligibility Protocol
papers.abstract: Large language models can predict the outputs of small neural networks from raw weights, but success could reflect recognition of weight-space regularities (fingerprints) rather than computation, and function-preserving controls cannot tell these apart. We propose C2, a counterfactual that permutes the columns of a network's final linear readout: every other parameter, and the readout's singular values, norms and entry multiset, are unchanged, and the function can change in an exactly recomputable way; we verify that each evaluated permutation does. C2 separates fingerprinting from computation only under three conditions, which we state as an eligibility protocol: a strategy restricted to C2-invariant summaries must already predict the target; C2 must change a property specific to the rewiring; and the reader's identity must be attested. No natural setting we tested is eligible. On tiny MLPs a frontier reader route followed the rewired function on all 24 networks, but invariant baselines were near chance and its backend could not be attested. In two public CNN zoos the conditions traded off: weight statistics predicted CIFAR-10 accuracy in-distribution, but C2's effect on accuracy was not specific to the swap, while per-image targets were specific but not predictable from invariant summaries. On a constructed population where a planted fingerprint rule works, all conditions hold and C2 separates a rule-following reader from an executor. A self-hosted Qwen3.8-27B followed the rewired function rather than the shortcut, and showed no evidence of using the weights with thinking disabled. A registered replication on fresh networks confirmed both findings (tracking minus stuck 0.875, 95% interval [0.750, 1.000]), and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B also followed the rewiring (tracking minus stuck 0.729 [0.552, 0.885]). The transforms, audits and raw records are available from the authors.

papers.intro:
Language models can identify, describe, and sometimes edit neural networks given only their weights (Takehi et al., 2026; Kabra et al., 2026). Two explanations fit such results. A reader may compute: it executes, approximately or exactly, the forward pass the weights define. Or it may recognise fingerprints: regularities of trained weights, such as norms, spectra, or value distributions, that correlate with what a network does. Several recent evaluations probe readers with function-preserving transformations, such as hidden-unit permutations, sign flips, and positive rescalings (flecart, 2026; Cha et al., 2026; Liu and Yang, 2026). These test whether a reader is consistent, but cannot separate the two explanations, because a fingerprint that survives the transformation predicts the same, correct answer.

The separating experiment needs the opposite edit: one that changes the function while preserving specified within-layer summaries, the statistics a fingerprint can be built from. A reader relying on fingerprints should then answer as if nothing had changed, while a reader that computes should follow the new function. We construct such an edit, C2, and then ask when its outcome actually discriminates. The second question turned out to be the more consequential one. Our contributions are: 1. C2 for any linear readout. Permuting the columns of the final linear layer preserves every within-layer summary of every layer and can change the function in an exactly recomputable way; every permutation we evaluate is selected and verified to change it (Section 3). 2. An eligibility protocol. We state three conditions under which a C2 result is informative about fingerprint use, plus a specificity check we learned we needed (Section 4). 3. Negative eligibility results. In four settings (tiny MLPs with a frontier reader route, tiny MLPs with a self-hosted open-weight reader, and two public CNN zoos), at least one condition fails in every case (Section 5). In particular, the frontier route’s perfect C2 tracking is a feasibility result for the control, not a test of fingerprint use. 4. A positive control with an attested reader. On a constructed population that meets every condition, C2 separates a fingerprint reader from an executor, and a self-hosted open-weight reader follows the rewired function rather than the available shortcut. A registered replication on fresh networks confirms this, adds a second reader family that also follows the rewiring, and confirms that without reasoning the reader does not use the weights (Section 5.4). 5. An auditable artifact. Exact transforms, a deterministic executor, frozen prompt manifests, tool lockdown, free baselines, and script-generated audits.

papers.title: Compared to What? Calibrating Machine-Unlearning Diagnostics with Present, Absent and Suppressed Anchors
papers.abstract: Unlearning methods for language models are judged mainly by behaviour, but a model can stop producing an answer while still encoding it. Internal diagnostics such as linear probes, the logit lens and relearning speed are used to tell removal from suppression, yet none has been checked against cases where the answer is known. We build such cases. A present anchor learned a set of synthetic facts; an absent anchor is a never-taught oracle retrained without them; and suppressed anchors are unlearned with their lower layers frozen, so the facts stay encoded below the frozen block by construction. We compare these anchors with NPO, RMU and gradient difference at a matched operating point on GPT-2 Small and Qwen3-0.6B-Base, scoring every diagnostic per entity with AUROC against the oracle. Behaviour cannot separate the suppressed anchors from the oracle (AUROC 0.51 to 0.58), while probes, the logit lens and relearning gain can (0.65 to 1.00), and the oracle seeds stay near 0.5. Applied to NPO on both models and RMU on Qwen3, the validated diagnostics disagree: probes put the facts at the oracle's level, while the models still relearn them much faster than a never-taught model does. Every unlearned model, anchor or method, also assigns the forgotten answer a far lower log-probability than the oracle does, a black-box signal that flagged all of them. A drift-ratio specificity rule fails on known cases. Code, data and every run are at https://github.com/ArsalanKaleem/unlearning-audit.

papers.intro:
Machine unlearning for language models tries to make a trained model behave as if some part of its training data had never been seen (Cao and Yang, 2015; Bourtoule et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2023). Retraining without the data is the exact answer but is too expensive for large models, so practical methods fine-tune the trained model instead: gradient ascent and gradient difference (Yao et al., 2023), negative preference optimisation (NPO) (Zhang et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2024), and representation misdirection (RMU) (Li et al., 2024). These methods are judged mostly by behaviour. If the model no longer produces the forgotten answers and still does everything else, the method is said to work (Maini et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024; Dorna et al., 2025).

Behaviour cannot settle whether a fact was removed or only hidden. A model that refuses to say an answer may still encode it, and several studies recover “unlearned” knowledge with probes, a few steps of fine-tuning, or adversarial prompts (Patil et al., 2024; Lynch et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2024; Deeb and Roger, 2024; Łucki et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025). So the field now reports a second layer of evidence: linear probes on hidden states (Alain and Bengio, 2016), the logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020), relearning speed, and measures of representation drift. Each of these is read as evidence about removal. None of them has been checked against cases where the answer is known.

This paper does that check. We build models whose internal state is known by construction and use them as anchors: • a present anchor that learned the facts and was never unlearned; • an absent anchor, a never-taught oracle retrained from the base model without the forget facts, at the same number of epochs; • a suppressed anchor that is unlearned with every layer below block kk frozen. Its residual stream below block kk is bit-identical to the present model’s for every input, so the facts are still encoded there however well its output forgets. A diagnostic that cannot tell the suppressed anchor from the absent one cannot certify removal, whatever it says about a real unlearning method. A diagnostic that separates them has earned some trust, and we can then ask where NPO, RMU and gradient difference fall between the anchors. All models are compared at a matched operating point, the earliest training step at which forget accuracy, retain accuracy and perplexity all satisfy a fixed band.

We run the design on synthetic facts injected into GPT-2 Small (Radford et al., 2019) and Qwen3-0.6B-Base (Qwen Team, 2025). The findings are:

1. Behaviour is blind to the difference that matters. At the matched operating point the suppressed anchors and the never-taught oracle answer the forget questions equally rarely (AUROC 0.52 to 0.55 between them, on both models), and paraphrased questions do not separate them either (0.51 to 0.58). 2. Internal diagnostics do separate the anchors. Linear probes, the logit lens at middle depth and the relearning gain all distinguish the suppressed anchors from the oracle (AUROC 0.65 to 1.00), while the other oracle seeds stay near 0.5. 3. The validated diagnostics disagree about real unlearning methods. On both models NPO, and on Qwen3 also RMU, bring linear decodability of the forget facts down to the oracle’s level, so by probes they look removed. The same models relearn the facts much faster than a never-taught model, and they put the correct answer far below the probability a never-taught model gives it. 4. Over-suppression is the one signal that flagged every unlearned model. Every anchor and every method assigns the forgotten answer a much lower log-probability than the never-taught oracle does (AUROC 0.10 to 0.17 against the oracle, on both models). The oracle has no reason to push a city it never learned below the others. This test needs only output probabilities, and it agrees with an independent finding by Yang and Yeung (2026). 5. A drift-ratio gate (forget-set drift at least 1.5 times control-set drift) rejects a LEACE eraser that provably removes linear information (Belrose et al., 2023b), and on Qwen3 it accepts a frozen-trunk anchor whose lower layers still hold the facts.

papers.title: Where Does Personalization Reside in Photo Editing? Evidence from One Photographer's Lightroom History
papers.abstract: Personalized photo-editing systems must infer both a photographer's recurring preferences and the intent of a particular shoot, yet these signals are rarely evaluated separately. We study interpretable Lightroom adjustments in a longitudinal, private dataset of 3,193 edited photographs from 41 catalogs by one professional photographer, with holdouts formed at the batch level. We compare absolute and prior-relative targets, image-conditioned predictors, and estimators that receive a small set of edits from the target batch. Residual prediction improves validation error, but its advantage on held-out batches is small and not significant under a batch-clustered bootstrap (0.592 vs 0.582 EV exposure MAE). In a batch-shared protocol, closed-form shrinkage using 4, 8, or 16 same-batch anchors reaches 0.466, 0.457, or 0.453 EV with the best estimator at each k, compared with 0.586-0.592 EV for the prior-only baseline; the paired reductions are significant under a batch-clustered bootstrap. Learned anchor-conditioned heads do not improve on this closed-form estimator, and a negative-trained prior already yields a low cold-image false-edit rate, leaving little benefit for an additional gate. The recommended estimator is closed-form and auditable, and it requires only a handful of same-batch edits. A render-space check against 383 native Lightroom exports reproduces the ranking: at k=8, online EB lowers Delta E00 against the prior by 0.41 (p=0.042), and the photographer's true parameters lower it by 0.78 (p=0.034). An appendix extends the action space from six to thirteen global controls: a same-batch median look lowers rendered chroma toward the export, while a per-photograph residual head again fails to transfer. The study is limited to one photographer and does not claim that slider accuracy measures aesthetic preference.
papers.intro:
A photographer who edits hundreds of frames from one shoot does not treat each frame independently. After a few corrections, the rest of the shoot tends to receive a similar exposure lift, contrast curve, and color treatment. Commercial tools advertise that they can ‘‘learn your style’’ from an Adobe Lightroom11 1 Adobe and Lightroom are trademarks or registered trademarks of Adobe Inc. This work is independent and not affiliated with or endorsed by Adobe. catalog [1], but the underlying question is rarely decomposed: how much of a predicted adjustment comes from the image itself, how much from the photographer’s long-run history, and how much from the shoot currently being edited?

This paper measures that decomposition on a real editing history. We instrument a private Adobe Lightroom catalog collection from one professional photographer: 41 catalogs, 3,193 edited photographs, six interpretable global adjustments (exposure, contrast, saturation, vibrance, clarity, texture), and batch-level holdouts that mimic the operational workflow “edit a few frames, then apply the result to the rest of the shoot.” The setting is deliberately narrow. The main experiments use six global adjustments; Appendix D extends the action space to highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, eight-band HSL saturation, and dehaze, and shows that a same-batch median look transfers while a per-photograph residual head does not. We do not model local masks or the complete Adobe Lightroom rendering pipeline, and we do not claim that slider accuracy equals aesthetic preference. The narrowness is what makes the signals separable.

papers.title: On the 0-Rotatability of Regular Spider Trees of Leg Length 4
papers.abstract: A tree $T$ on $q$ edges is said to be $0$-rotatable if for every vertex $v \in V(T)$, there exists a graceful labeling $f : V(T) \to \{0, 1, \dots, q\}$ such that $f(v) = 0$. Rofa proved that all regular (symmetric) spider trees with leg length at most $3$ are $0$-rotatable and conjectured that the property holds for every leg length. In this note, we settle the first open case of this conjecture by proving that every regular spider tree $T(k, 4)$ with $k \ge 1$ legs of length $4$ is $0$-rotatable. Our proof combines Rofa's algebraic graceful labeling at the root with complementary labelings, an end-to-end leg-reversal construction placing $0$ at a leaf, and a two-leg reflection permutation placing $0$ at distance $2$ from the root.

papers.title: Certified $p$-adic normal forms: an Eliasson-Vey theorem and zero sets of orbits
papers.abstract: I use the Smith form of the homological operator to construct partial Poincar\'e-Dulac normal forms near an equilibrium of a vector field on $\mathbb {Z}_p^d$ with coefficients divisible by $p$ (by $4$ if $p=2$). Retaining the directions whose removal would cost more than a fixed number of digits gives convergence on an explicit ball for any linear part. For polynomial fields, an exact integer check of the conjugacy defect certifies the computed flow to $K$ digits in rescaled coordinates. When the quadratic parts of an integrable Hamiltonian system at a rank-$0$ point span a Cartan subalgebra, the homological divisors in symplectic eigencoordinates are integers. This lets me use Newton iteration to obtain an exact $p$-adic Eliasson--Vey normal form at every prime and for every Williamson type. In exact linear normal coordinates, a polynomial restricted to an orbit gives a sum of exponentials, to which van der Poorten's bound of $2s-3$ zeros applies for a nonzero sum with $s\ge2$ distinct exponents. For integer orbits of polynomial maps, I combine exact modular orbits, Strassmann bounds and archimedean estimates in an adelic sieve. At every prime, increasing the modular depth eventually excludes a time class exactly when the interpolation along its center-manifold shadow has no zero in $\mathbb {Z}_p$.
papers.intro:
The Poincaré–Dulac construction simplifies a vector field near an equilibrium by solving a homological equation at each degree [1]. For a diagonal linear part this means dividing by numbers of the form ⟨m,λ⟩−λi\langle m,\lambda\rangle-\lambda_{i}, losing as many pp-adic digits as their valuations. In general the eigenvalues can understate the loss. A k×kk\times k Jordan block 3​I+J3I+J over ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3}, for example, has only the eigenvalue 33, yet its Smith exponents are 0,…,0,k0,\ldots,0,k, so inverting it costs kk digits.

Herman and Yoccoz proved a non-Archimedean analog of Siegel’s linearization theorem under a Diophantine condition [13], and Lindahl determines the size of the linearization disk for quadratic maps in one variable [18]. Jenkins and Spallone treat formal and analytic flows and the classification of maps tangent to the identity [14]. papers.title: Dyadic Representation of Fractional Integrals on Spaces of Homogeneous Type and Related Boundedness Phenomena
papers.abstract:
We establish a dyadic representation formula for fractional integral operators in the setting of spaces of homogeneous type. The formula expresses such operators in terms of simpler dyadic model operators, such as so-called paraproducts and shifts, and provides a unified framework that applies to different notions of fractional integrals arising in this general context.
  Motivated by the derivation of this representation, we also investigate the structure of fractional integral operators in spaces of homogeneous type. In this setting, two natural definitions, referred to as volumic and metric, are in general non-equivalent and exhibit markedly different boundedness properties. While the former enjoys well-known $L^p$--$L^q$ estimates, the latter may fail to satisfy any such bounds without additional assumptions; nevertheless, weaker forms of boundedness can still be recovered under suitable conditions.
  The representation formula is intended as a tool for the study of Schatten-type properties of commutators $[b,T]$ of fractional integrals and pointwise multipliers, which will be addressed in a forthcoming companion work by T. Hyt\"onen and the author. Beyond this application, the representation itself may be of independent interest and useful in other contexts.

Dyadic representation formulas have become an important tool in modern harmonic analysis, with numerous developments across a variety of settings and operators. Earlier foundational contributions include [10, 30, 36, 40], while the modern dyadic representation theorem was first established by T. Other notable works include the representation formula for bi-parameter singular integrals in [33], and that for bilinear Calderón–Zygmund operators in [31].

papers.title: One Checkpoint, Four Converters: Per Input Disagreement After On Device Conversion and a Probe Set That Catches It
papers.abstract: A model converted for on device or accelerated inference ships once its top 1 accuracy matches the source model. Accuracy can match while individual decisions change, and the converter, its INT8 recipe and its calibration draw each move them. We convert 5 public checkpoints (four ImageNet classifiers and a sentiment model) with the documented FP32 and INT8 recipes of ExecuTorch, LiteRT, ONNX Runtime and TensorRT and compare every top 1 decision with the PyTorch source on 7,854 images and 1,938 sentences. All 34 strict FP32 conversions reproduce every decision, yet each of the 4 vision INT8 recipes that keeps accuracy equivalent flips more than 1% of decisions: ONNX Runtime static INT8 flips 4.07% (95% CI [3.65, 4.53]) of ResNet 50 decisions while accuracy moves by -0.15 points, and two builds of that recipe from different calibration draws disagree on 3.44% [3.06, 3.88]. Where accuracy is kept, the flipped inputs are the ones the source model barely decides (AUROC of the source margin 0.90 to 0.97 on ResNet 50, every 95% CI inside [0.89, 0.98]), but our preregistered claim that this holds for every recipe fails on the two mobile networks, where INT8 breaks accuracy outright. A probe set of the 200 training inputs with the smallest source margin, chosen before any conversion, flags all 40 vision stacks (recall 95% CI [0.91, 1.00]) and all 6 text stacks that flip at least 0.5% of decisions and none of the exact FP32 conversions, so conversion checks should compare decisions on such a probe set, not accuracy.
papers.intro:
A trained model rarely runs where it was trained. Phones run it through LiteRT, Core ML or ExecuTorch, servers through ONNX Runtime or TensorRT, and the step that gets it there is a converter followed, more often than not, by INT8 post training quantization. Teams accept a converted model when its top 1 accuracy on a held out set matches the source model within a tolerance. That check is cheap and it is what the converters’ own tutorials show.

Teams accept a converted model when its top 1 accuracy on a held out set matches the source model within a tolerance. That check is cheap and it is what the converters’ own tutorials show.

Accuracy can match while the decisions underneath it change. Take one ResNet 50 image from our evaluation set: PyTorch calls it a golden retriever with probability 0.14 against 0.12 for cocker spaniel; the same checkpoint converted with LiteRT’s documented static INT8 recipe calls it a cocker spaniel (0.16 against 0.12). The image is not exotic: it is the median of the 74 such swaps that recipe makes on this model. Every one of them is a user who sees a different answer after the update, and accuracy hides them because swaps in both directions cancel: the ONNX Runtime INT8 build of ResNet 50 fixes 102 source errors and introduces 114.

We measure this per input disagreement for one fixed checkpoint across four converters. The measurement is easy to get wrong in both directions. A harness that is not bitwise reproducible invents flips; on the conversion side, a TF32 default silently changes FP32 numerics and an INT8 build depends on which 256 calibration inputs were drawn. We therefore show first that the instrument reads zero where it should (Section 3), report every rate with an interval next to a calibration redraw floor, and fixed the claims, thresholds and stacks in a preregistration before the main runs.

papers.title: Exact on Paper: Which LLM Serving Shortcuts Flip Graded Answers, Measured Against the Noise of Reordering the Same Requests
papers.abstract: Teams enable serving features such as prefix caching, chunked prefill and speculative decoding after checking that benchmark accuracy is unchanged, because the engine documents them as exact. Accuracy is an aggregate, so a feature can hold it while flipping which requests are answered correctly. We serve one 4B instruction model in vLLM under nine single feature configurations and five replicas of a reference configuration, grade 3,380 requests from five benchmarks in every run, and compare each candidate with a restart floor (fresh process) and a scheduling floor (same requests in a different order). With default kernels every configuration keeps accuracy within one point, and the seven exact features flip the graded outcome of 1.47% (95% CI 1.13 to 1.85) to 1.78% (1.39 to 2.20) of requests, none above the scheduling floor of 1.72%, while the FP8 KV cache flips 3.36% (2.80 to 3.96), as many as FP8 weights. With batch invariant kernels all seven exact features, speculative decoding included, reproduce the reference text on every request, while the FP8 KV cache still flips 3.91% (3.28 to 4.53) of graded outcomes. Floating point arithmetic in a batched engine is not exact. A request’s logits depend on how many other requests share its batch, on how its prompt is split into prefill chunks, and on which kernel the engine picks for the shape at hand (Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Under greedy decoding a change in the last bit of a logit can switch one token, and one switched token can send a math derivation down a different path. A feature can then leave accuracy at the same value while flipping which requests are right. One GSM8K word problem from our runs shows it. All three restarts of the reference configuration answer it correctly with 26. With prefix caching on, the generated text matches the reference for its first 46% of characters, then inserts one word into a restated sentence, and the derivation that follows ends at 13. Other items flip the other way, and accuracy under prefix caching moves by −-0.02 points.

papers.title: Two-term Rogers dilogarithm identities over cubic fields
papers.abstract: We study normalized two-term Rogers dilogarithm relations in cubic fields. For integral, nonunimodular rank-two monomial configurations whose base argument generates a totally real cubic field, finite-prime valuations force the arguments and their complements to be units. Normalization preserves the generated order and reduces the problem to two cubic families without a maximal-order assumption. In the simplest cubic family, an existing unit-equation classification yields exactly ten relations up to simultaneous reflection, with distinct coefficients 2, 3, 7, 13, 19, 31 and 97. Explicit five-term certificates prove all ten evaluations. In the second family, a sharpened lower bound for the height of a solution, together with the two-logarithm theorem of Laurent, Mignotte and Nesterenko, reduces the unit equation to a short certified computation, and the family contributes no relation in this class. A unit-index argument restricts, independently, wedge relations between arbitrary exceptional units of non-Galois totally real cubic fields: any such relation would have a coefficient with no prime factor below 23 and would contradict Ennola's conjecture on fundamental units. In cubic fields with one real embedding, the only five-term certified relation between exceptional units with coefficient greater than one is Lewin's identity. Together, these results give exactly eleven identities in the two classes considered, up to the stated reflections.

papers.title: One machine, three drawings: a didactic analysis of a teaching progression for the function concept from Grade 4 to Grade 10
papers.abstract: The function concept can be entered through a correspondence between sets, a relation that is single-valued, or through a process that turns an input into an output. This paper presents the design rationale and a critical analysis of a source progression for functions (Grades 4-10, nominal ages 9-16, with two levels on relations between quantities), from which French-curriculum and International Baccalaureate chapters published at https://commeunjeu.org are assembled. One schema is presented first and kept throughout: a function is a machine that takes an input, applies a rule and gives exactly one output. Its drawing changes with age (a robot, then a box, then the arrow $f : x \mapsto f(x)$), and each change is shown once, the two drawings side by side; after 15 the box returns only in the lessons, to explain composition and the inverse. The properties that research identifies as difficult (the uniqueness of the output, the constant function, the function without a formula, two rules for one function, preimages) are posed on the machine from Grade 4; the word relation is kept for the link between two quantities, where covariation is taught; the set of ordered pairs comes back as the graph. The choices are related to the function machine as a cognitive root and to its authors' own warnings, to process-object accounts, to studies of concept images and of covariation, and to the French and IB curricula. A block-level audit of the dated source documents found the machine in only 2 of the 177 exercise blocks of Grades 7 to 10, no exercise asking pupils to draw a machine, and public chapters that opened on the relation; the revisions made after the audit are recorded with their counts before and after. No empirical evaluation is reported; hypotheses for one are stated.
papers.intro:
The function is the concept through which school mathematics passes from computing numbers to studying dependences, and it is one of the concepts whose history weighs most on its teaching. Its definitions moved from a quantity composed of a variable and constants to an analytic expression, then to the dependence of one quantity on another, to an arbitrary law of correspondence after Dirichlet, and finally to a set of ordered pairs without any reference to a computation (Kleiner, 1989; Sfard, 1991; Thompson and Carlson, 2017). School definitions of the second half of the twentieth century followed the last steps: two sets and a rule that associates with each element of the first exactly one element of the second, sometimes reached from the relation as a set of pairs (Markovits et al., 1986; Bell and Janvier, 1981). Research on learners has documented the difficulties that remain: definitions recited and contradicted by the concept image (Vinner and Dreyfus, 1989), functions identified with formulas, constant and piecewise functions rejected (Markovits et al., 1986; Oehrtman et al., 2008), and prospective teachers unable to say where the requirement of a single output comes from (Even, 1993).

A curriculum author meets a design problem specific to this concept. The first representation chosen must carry the uniqueness of the output and the arbitrariness of the rule; it must lead to tables, formulas and graphs without being replaced by any of them; and it must not hide that two quantities can vary together. Two entries are available. The first starts from the relation, a set of pairs, and defines a function as a relation in which each first element has one partner. The second starts from a process: a machine receives an input, applies its rule, and gives one output. The second entry has been proposed as a “cognitive root” of the concept by the authors who also named its limits (Tall et al., 2000).

This paper documents and analyses one answer to that problem, a progression written as bilingual (English and French) lessons and exercise sets over seven levels, with two levels on relations between quantities. Its research question is: what becomes of a concept when one schema carries it from age 9 to age 16, and where is that schema not enough? One schema is presented first and kept: a function is a machine that takes an input, applies a rule, and gives exactly one output. The design rests on five principles: (i) the machine is the definition, at every level; later definitions rewrite it, and its drawing lightens with age (Section 4); (ii) the properties of the concept are posed on the machine from Grade 4, with the definition as the argument (Section 5); (iii) the word relation is kept for the link between two quantities, where covariation is taught, and the two meet in “in terms of” (Section 6); (iv) the set of ordered pairs is not the starting point: it comes back as the graph, the set of the points the machine gives (Section 7); (v) f⁡(x)f(x) is read on the machine: the output that the machine ff gives to the input xx (Section 8).

The paper is a design rationale and a curriculum analysis, the companion of a study of a fraction progression by the same author (Tariel-Adam, 2026), whose method it shares. Like a hypothetical learning trajectory (Simon, 1995; Clements and Sarama, 2004), the progression embodies learning goals, an order of activities and hypotheses about learning; the paper makes them explicit and confronts them with the literature and with the documents that implement them. Its method borrows the a priori analysis of didactic engineering (Artigue, 1990; Artigue, 1992) at the level of global choices (the representation, the order of meanings, the drawings) and, in Section 10, at the level of three tasks and their didactic variables. No classroom experiment is reported; statements about learners are taken from the cited literature or presented as design hypotheses. None of the principles is new taken alone: the function machine is classical, and its authors already recommended machines defined by a procedure rather than by a formula (Tall et al., 2000). papers.title: Revisiting RadioGalaxyNET: modern detectors for radio galaxy detection and host identification
papers.abstract: RadioGalaxyNET is the public benchmark for finding extended radio galaxies in EMU pilot-survey images, classifying them and locating their infrared hosts. Its best published results date from 2023: 54.5 box AP (Gal-YOLOv8) and 48.1 host keypoint AP (Gal-DINO). We train three current detectors, D-FINE-seg, YOLO26-pose and RF-DETR, on the same data and score them with the benchmark's own evaluation code, which reproduces the published Gal-DINO numbers exactly. All exceed the published results. D-FINE-seg M reaches 67.1 box AP and 72.4 host AP, 12.6 and 24.3 points above the best published results, and the highest host AP of the detectors we tested; on boxes it is level with YOLO26. Its host lead over YOLO26 comes from host-centered images, which make up most of the benchmark. End to end, D-FINE-seg S is the fastest model at 1.9 ms per image; engine against engine, YOLO26 is faster at the same size. We also report what matters for anyone using the benchmark: its scoring protocol adds 5 to 10 AP, its host labels sit at the image center, its box labels are offset from the image by 1.5 pixels, and its images can be rebuilt from the public survey data, which recovers sky positions and doubles as extra training data. We suggest that future work report host identification F1, as a measure closer to catalog use: D-FINE-seg M 71.8, YOLO26-pose M 70.5, RF-DETR 63.8, Gal-DINO 59.2.
papers.intro:
The Evolutionary Map of the Universe (Norris et al., 2021, EMU;), a survey with the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (Hotan et al., 2021, ASKAP;), will detect millions of extended radio galaxies, and each needs a morphological class and an infrared host galaxy. RadioGalaxyNET (Gupta et al., 2024) made this a computer-vision benchmark: 2,799 images that combine an EMU pilot-survey radio cutout with an infrared cutout of the same field from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (Wright et al., 2010, WISE;) at 3.4 μ\mum, labeled with a box and class (FR-I, FR-II, FR-X or R) for each extended source and a keypoint for its host. The original paper trained several detectors; the best are Gal-YOLOv8 for boxes (54.5 AP) and Gal-DINO, a DINO detection transformer (Zhang et al., 2023) with a keypoint branch, for hosts (48.1 AP). The only later result we found, LARGAL (Anand, 2026), reports 53.5 box AP with its own evaluation script.

papers.abstract: Let $G = *_\lambda G_\lambda$ be a free product of groups and let $g\in G$ be any element not conjugate into any free factor and not conjugate to its inverse. Then $\mathrm{scl}(g) \ge \frac{1}{12}$ and $\mathrm{scl}(g) = \frac{1}{12}$ if and only if $g$ is a product of an element of order $2$ and an element of order $3$. In particular, this classifies all elements in $G = \mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{Z})$ with $\mathrm{scl}_G(g) = \frac{1}{12}$.

papers.title: Computational Strategies for Mixed Logit Estimation Automatic Differentiation, GPU Computing, and Floating-Point Precision
papers.abstract:
Mixed logit estimation can become computationally demanding as sample size and the dimension of preference heterogeneity increase. This study examines how derivative computation, processor choice and floating-point precision affect estimation time and parameter recovery across problem sizes. This paper provides a controlled benchmark, comparing finite differences (FD) with automatic differentiation (AD), central processing unit (CPU) execution with graphics processing unit (GPU) execution, and double-precision (FP64) with single-precision (FP32) arithmetic using Monte Carlo experiments that hold the data-generating process, simulation draws, optimiser, starting values, and objective function fixed across strategies.
  The results show that AD is the dominant source of acceleration. Combining AD with FP32 arithmetic provides further gains, while combining AD, GPU execution, and FP32 arithmetic delivers the largest speed improvements, particularly as sample size and model complexity increase. Our findings indicate substantial computational gains with broadly comparable parameter-recovery performance in the simulated settings considered.An empirical application in health preferences illustrates what extra empirical evidence and statistical benefit on model fit could be achieved, when researchers are made possible to estimate a richer, correlated preference specification.
  We provide an open sourced prototype to for model estimation with AD-FP32 strategy workflow that automatically detect hardware and provide the fastest estimation. Faster estimation can make richer random-coefficient specifications, larger simulation draw counts, bootstrap inference, multi-start optimisation, and robustness checks more feasible in applied choice modelling research.

papers.intro:
Discrete choice models are widely used to analyse individual preferences and predict choice behaviour across transportation, health, marketing, environmental economics, and many other applied fields (Ben-Akiva and Lerman, 1985; McFadden, 1986; Adamowicz et al., 1998; Lancsar and Louviere, 2008). Among these models, mixed logit has become one of the most widely used approaches because it accommodates flexible substitution patterns and rich preference heterogeneity while remaining behaviourally interpretable (McFadden and Train, 2000). In a recent systematic review of health-related discrete choice experiments published between 2018 and 2023, Nouwens et al. (2025) report that 573 of the 1,279 included studies used mixed logit. As empirical applications increasingly seek to estimate willingness to pay (WTP), characterise preference heterogeneity and evaluate complex policy scenarios, mixed logit model has become a standard tool in applied choice modelling.

Applying this model requires researchers to specify how attributes and covariates enter utility, whether their effects are linear or nonlinear, whether higher-order terms or interactions are required, which coefficients vary randomly across individuals, whether random coefficients are correlated, and which mixing distributions are appropriate. These choices can materially affect interpretation: Van Der Pol et al. (2014) show that alternative functional forms for utility can change estimated marginal rates of substitution, while Buckell et al. (2025) show that alternative mixing distributions can change estimated preference distributions and WTP. Further considerations include the covariance structure of random coefficients, the number and type of simulation draws, multi-start optimisation, and bootstrap inference, especially in small samples where asymptotic approximations may be less reliable (Czajkowski and Budziński, 2019; Hole, 2007a). Evaluating whether results are credible, interpretable, behaviourally plausible, and robust to reasonable alternatives requires repeated estimation under competing specifications and computational settings, which can become computationally demanding.

Recent work has sought to reduce the computational cost of mixed logit estimation through improvements in both processor choice and gradient computation. Regarding processor choice, Arteaga et al. (2022) demonstrate that graphics processing unit (GPU)-based computation can substantially accelerate mixed logit estimation in xlogit, which uses analytical gradients for optimisation. For gradient computation, finite differences (FD) remain a common fallback when analytical gradients are unavailable in choice-modelling applications (Hole, 2007b; Hess and Palma, 2019). More recently, Liu et al. (2025) show that automatic differentiation (AD) can reduce the computational cost of gradient evaluation relative to FD. Together, these studies demonstrate the potential of GPU acceleration and AD. However, their practical benefits also depend on researchers’ access to hardware and software, differences in hardware capabilities, and how computational methods are implemented. A further consideration is floating-point precision: how precisely numbers are represented and manipulated during computation. These considerations motivate a joint benchmark of computational strategies that can inform both applied estimation and the development of an accessible estimation tool.

These computational dimensions are closely interdependent. AD changes both the computational cost and the numerical properties of gradient evaluation: unlike FD, it avoids repeated likelihood evaluations at perturbed parameter values and the subtraction of nearby log-likelihood values, the latter of which can be particularly sensitive to round-off error under lower-precision arithmetic (Higham, 2002). Floating-point precision is closely linked to processor choice. Usually known as single-precision, 32-bit floating-point arithmetic (FP32) requires less memory and can provide substantially higher computational throughput than double-precision, 64-bit floating-point arithmetic (FP64) on many GPU architectures, whereas the relative advantage may be smaller on central processing units (CPUs). Some GPU backends also provide limited or no support for FP64 arithmetic. The computational benefit of GPU execution may therefore depend on floating-point precision, while the numerical consequences of lower precision may depend on how gradients are computed. Yet existing evidence provides limited guidance on how the performance of different combinations varies with sample size and model complexity in mixed logit estimation, or whether their computational gains are accompanied by meaningful changes in parameter recovery.

Motivated by this gap, this study addresses two research questions. First, how do selected combinations of gradient computation (FD versus AD), processor choice (CPU versus GPU), and floating-point precision (FP64 versus FP32) affect the runtime of mixed logit estimation? Second, to what extent do these computational choices affect parameter recovery? To answer these questions, we construct a controlled benchmark with precision-specific stopping tolerances in which the dataset, simulation draws, optimisation algorithm, starting values, and objective function are held fixed within each simulation repetition while the computational configuration is varied. We build on and modify the panel data-generating process (DGP) of Cherchi and Guevara (2012). The original parameterisation is well suited to experiments with a fixed random-coefficient dimension, but extending it to higher dimensions increases the variation in deterministic utility differences and makes choices progressively more deterministic. We therefore modify the original design by rescaling the random coefficients as their number increases, so that the variation in systematic utility differences between alternatives remain approximately constant. The motivation and formal justification for this normalisation are provided in the main text and appendix. This controlled DGP allows us to vary both sample size, NN, and model complexity, measured by the number of freely estimated parameters, PP, over a broad range of problem sizes.

papers.title: Where does pancreatic lesion segmentation fail on public CT? An attenuation-stratified analysis of a duct-guided pipeline on PanTS
papers.abstract: Lesion segmentation is a building block of most CT pipelines for pancreatic cancer detection, yet lesion overlap scores stay low. Instead of proposing a new architecture, we report where an end-to-end pipeline fails on a large public dataset. On PanTS we built a three-stage pipeline: pancreas segmentation, maps of the main pancreatic duct (MPD) and common bile duct (CBD), and a lesion model that receives the CT with or without the predicted duct maps. Both lesion models were trained identically on 4007 scans and evaluated once on 737 held-out test scans (127 with a lesion) under a comparison rule fixed before the test run. Lesion Dice was 0.213 with duct maps and 0.209 with CT only (paired difference +0.004, 95% CI -0.011 to +0.019). The duct maps raised the share of lesions touched by a prediction (+0.079, 95% CI +0.024 to +0.134) but also enlarged predictions in lesion-free scans, and lesion-like regions were predicted in all lesion-free test scans. Out of fold, keeping only the predicted components that touched the lesion raised Dice only from 0.285 to 0.309; the loss came mainly from the extent of correctly located predictions. Clearly hypoattenuating lesions, which intensity alone separates from normal pancreas, had the lowest coverage (median 16.6%). From the predicted maps alone, the MPD diameter separated lesion from lesion-free test scans with AUC 0.794 (95% CI 0.747 to 0.839), while the CBD diameter was weak (AUC 0.603) and added nothing. Code for training, inference and evaluation is publicly available.

papers.title: Tracing Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning can increase the success of automated red teaming but it also narrows the attack vector. This study asks where in the attacker-defender-judge learning loop does the narrowing begin and which mechanisms lead to a narrowing attack. Six mechanisms (defender adaptation, success edge, reward reinforcement, row cap, update size, and measurement) are tested across three experiment arms (co-trained, frozen defender, half learning rate) for twenty-four iterations. A frozen defender narrows attack diversity retention (ADR) earlier 0.496 relative to co-trained 0.891 at iteration twelve. Defender updates delay narrowing but dont prevent it. Successful attacks ("winners") have narrower attack diversity than the full set of generated attacks. Attacks closest to previous winners succeed 10-15 percentage points more often than those closest to previous failures. This winner-neighbor advantage holds after a defender update and for a fixed defender too. Attacks with a common opening have a common-opening advantage of 5-16 percentage points. The training row cap and update size account for little impact on ADR, and attack length accounts for only part of the ADR decrease. Narrowing appears to originate from the success only reward through the group-relative training advantage to the attacker update, with a persistent success edge setting the direction.

Red teaming with a trained attacker model extends hand-written test cases to automated scenarios [1, 2], and reinforcement learning allows the attacker to adjust its strategy in response to the defender. Co-training an attacker with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) [3] and a defender with direct preference optimization (DPO) [4] has been reported to reduce attacker diversity [5]. A narrow attack set exposes the defender to a less diverse set of attacks, reducing the coverage that red teaming is meant to provide.

papers.title: Tableau Consequence under Positive Contexts: A Reconstruction of Walukiewicz's Completeness Proof
papers.abstract: We establish a positive-context lifting theorem for tableau consequence in the modal $\mu$-calculus: under explicit syntactic hypotheses, $\mathcal T_B\Rightarrow\mathcal T_C$ induces $\mathcal T_{A(B)}\Rightarrow\mathcal T_{A(C)}$. The proof orders instances of the given relation by birth time and assigns overlapping formula occurrences to the oldest supporting instance. A corollary gives bidirectional replacement by automaton normal form inside positive contexts. Together with a separate unfolding consequence lemma and ANF bisimulation, the lifting theorem yields a self-contained reconstruction of Walukiewicz's completeness proof for Kozen's axiomatisation and makes its least-fixpoint step more transparent. We also give a finite parity-game proof of regular-refutation existence and a two-sided transfer from tableau consequence to thin refutations.

papers.title: What Field Enumeration Costs to Compile in C++26: Native Reflection, Structured-Binding Packs, Reflection Libraries and Hand-Written Serializers on GCC 16
papers.abstract: C++26 adds standard ways to enumerate a struct's fields, among them static reflection (P2996, with P3394 annotations) and structured-binding packs (P1061), alongside hand-written code, X-macros and libraries (Boost.PFR, reflect-cpp, Glaze) that now ship pre-C++26 and C++26 paths. We time each in a struct serializer with byte-identical output on GCC 16.2.0, at the front end and at -O2, in randomized interleaved rounds with code-level checks of every single-factor contrast. At the front end, inline native enumeration in the form used in several of P2996's own examples, an expansion statement over the std::span of define_static_array, costs about as much per struct of 16 scalar fields as Boost.PFR and 7.96x a P1061 pack, itself about as cheap as hand-written code. The same loop over a constant array costs 0.47x as much: about half of the span form's cost comes with the span. The ratio to P1061 shrinks on a heterogeneous type graph and at -O2. In a whole translation unit at the front end the library outweighs the mechanism: 200 structs take 0.59 s with inline native enumeration, 0.56 s with Boost.PFR and 3.86-4.13 s with the C++26 paths of reflect-cpp and Glaze, whose visitors also compute field names. Per type, each library's C++26 path is cheaper than its pre-C++26 path at 16 fields, but Glaze's gain reverses at 128 fields (pinned release v9.1.0); Boost.PFR's C++17 path grows almost quadratically with the number of types. Hand-written serializers sharing one overloaded name grow superlinearly with the number of types. The -freflection flag alone makes reflection-free code up to 1.264x costlier per type on GCC 16.2.0 and up to 2.578x on 16.1.0, so comparisons between mechanisms depend on the point release. Part of the span form's cost grows with the number of structs, which we trace to GCC registering block-scope statics in quadratic time (reported as GCC PR128928).
papers.intro:
Serialization is boilerplate: for every type, code that visits every field. C++ has attacked it with the preprocessor (X-macros), with library “reflection” built on aggregate-initialization probing, structured bindings and parsing of compiler-generated function names (Boost.PFR, reflect-cpp, Glaze), and now with C++26 language features: static reflection (P2996) with annotations (P3394), structured bindings that introduce a pack (P1061), and expansion statements (P1306), which iterate over reflected members and can also destructure a struct directly. For a practitioner the question is concrete: what does each of these cost to compile, and what does each save in source?

Native P2996 compile time has only begun to be measured. Romeo (Romeo, 2026b) times native reflection alone on single translation units; mp-units (Pusz, 2026) runs an in-repo A/B whose author considers the sign of the effect reliable but not its magnitude; simdjson reports, on clang-p2996, a 6% slowdown of its whole build with reflection enabled (Lemire and Geiman Thiesen, 2025); and the field-reflection library (Matsuda, 2026) lists in its README the per-type cost of its std::meta backend next to Boost.PFR’s, as best-of-three numbers. We found no published measurement, as of November 2026, that compares native reflection with each library’s two paths, with P1061, or with hand-written and macro baselines on one serialization task (§5). A tooling vendor’s blog (Soliven, 2026) calls compile-time impact “the biggest open question”.

Research questions.

• RQ1 — mechanisms. Per type, what does field enumeration cost to compile with P2996, with P1061, through a library’s callback API, and by hand; and what does a P3394 annotation query add? • RQ2 — library backends. papers.title: Does the Mixer Matter ? Paired-Seed Ablations of Tiny Bilingual Language Models
papers.abstract: We report paired-seed architecture ablations from the development of Sophea Artemis, our in-house Greek-English model family. Every arm trains on the same 3B targets with a shared tokenizer and recipe; models range from 54M to 759M total parameters and roughly 54M to 124M active parameters. The main finding is that, at this tiny scale, stored capacity matters far more than mixer design. On a fixed held-out test, replacing the dense feed-forward blocks of a recurrent/attention hybrid with sixteen routed experts, at nearly the same approximate active parameters, lowers loss by 0.079 (Greek) and 0.112 (English) nats per target, and doubling to 32 experts lowers it by a further 0.022 and 0.031, at every paired seed. Reusing a four-layer block three times recovers about 40-44% of the gap between a shallow and an independently deep model, consistent with looped-Transformer results. In contrast, the choice among grouped-query attention (GQA), Gated DeltaNet (GDN) hybrids and a Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) hybrid moves loss by only about 0.01-0.02 nats; a 1:1 GDN/GQA hybrid is the one dense variant that improves on GQA in both languages at every held-out seed. In bits per character, Greek and English held-out losses are similar despite a 74.49%/25.51% training split, and synthetic mathematics, which comes from a collection outside the training sources, is the hardest Greek test component and gains least from added experts. Cached decoding needs its own qualification: trained models passed cached-versus-full logit checks only under a fixed-reduction inference policy, which itself changes 1.4-2.8% of next-token argmax choices relative to native evaluation. All results are conditional on one recipe and scale.

Tiny language models can spend their resources in different ways: additional experts increase stored capacity while activating only a subset for each token, reusing a layer block reduces unique weights but repeats computation, and recurrent mixing changes the computation and state needed to process a sequence. Here, tiny means a 768-wide decoder with at most 124M active parameters per token, trained on 3B targets at 2,048-token context; total stored parameters range from 54M to 759M (Table 1).

papers.title: Quantum Variance of Holomorphic Modular Forms and Benjamini-Schramm Convergence
papers.abstract:
We study quantum variance for holomorphic modular forms of fixed weight on sequences of compact hyperbolic surfaces converging to the hyperbolic plane in the sense of Benjamini-Schramm. We first show that quantum ergodicity need not hold for an arbitrary choice of orthonormal basis, even for sequences with a uniform lower bound on the injectivity radius and a uniform spectral gap. The counterexample is constructed using a tower of coverings and arises from the identity contribution in the automorphic kernel.
  We then show that this obstruction is exceptional from the point of view of the choice of basis. For a Haar random orthonormal basis of holomorphic modular forms, the quantum variance converges to zero with probability tending to one uniformly over all observables with bounded supremum norm. The proof combines estimates for the Hilbert-Schmidt norm of a projected multiplication operator with the Haar expectation of the quantum variance, concentration of measure on the special unitary group and a finite-dimensional approximation of the space of observables.

papers.intro:
Quantum ergodicity concerns the asymptotic distribution of eigenfunctions of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on compact Riemannian manifolds whose geodesic flow is ergodic. The classical theorem of Šnirel’man [5], Colin de Verdière [6] and Zelditch [7] asserts that on a compact negatively curved manifold, as one takes Laplace eigenfunctions with eigenvalues tending to infinity, almost all of them become equidistributed. In particular, for compact hyperbolic surfaces, Zelditch proved that as eigenvalue tends to infinity, the mass of most eigenfunctions converges to the uniform measure.

Quantum ergodicity concerns the asymptotic distribution of eigenfunctions of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on compact Riemannian manifolds whose geodesic flow is ergodic. The classical theorem of Šnirel’man [5], Colin de Verdière [6] and Zelditch [7] asserts that on a compact negatively curved manifold, as one takes Laplace eigenfunctions with eigenvalues tending to infinity, almost all of them become equidistributed. In particular, for compact hyperbolic surfaces, Zelditch proved that as eigenvalue tends to infinity, the mass of most eigenfunctions converges to the uniform measure.

A different asymptotic regime was studied by Le Masson and Sahlsten [4], who proved a quantum ergodicity theorem for eigenfunctions in a fixed spectral window along sequences of compact hyperbolic surfaces converging to the hyperbolic plane in the sense of Benjamini and Schramm. Under this geometric convergence, together with a uniform spectral gap and injectivity radius lower bound, they showed that the quantum variance of eigenfunctions in a fixed window tends to zero. Their proof built on a wave propagation approach developed in earlier work of Brooks, Le Masson and Lindenstrauss [14] on discrete graphs. A key step is to bound the quantum variance by the Hilbert-Schmidt norm of an observable which is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. This perspective inspires the first part of our work, where we similarly upper bound the quantum variance for holomorphic modular forms in terms of Hilbert-Schmidt norms of an operator related to the observables.

For the modular surface, the corresponding mass equidistribution theorem in the weight aspect was proved by Holowinsky and Soundararajan [9]. Related equidistribution results in the level aspect were obtained by Nelson [10].
