Random orthonormal bases provide another framework for quantum ergodicity. Zelditch proved that a Haar-random orthonormal basis of spherical harmonics on S2S^{2} is quantum ergodic [11]. He later generalized this to a broad framework for sequences of high-dimensional Hilbert spaces. He showed that a random orthonormal basis obtained by applying a Haar-distributed unitary matrix to a fixed reference basis, is almost surely quantum ergodic. A key ingredient in this framework is the computation of moments of the quantum variance with respect to the Haar measure on the unitary group, which uses the Weingarten formula. Our Proposition 7.1 follows the same approach in computing the expected quantum variance.

papers.title: SignalCount: Approximate Counts with Structured and Semantic Predicates in Seconds
papers.abstract: Many applications store records with structured columns and a text document, and ask how many records in a filtered set meet a criterion that only a reader of the text can judge, such as "How many patients with type 2 diabetes, aged 40 to 70, stopped metformin because their blood sugar stayed high?" An interactive application needs this count in seconds, as the user types the criterion, to decide whether the matching set is worth materializing with a batch pipeline in which an LLM judges the records. Prior approximate query processing over such semantic predicates has an expensive model, the oracle, label a sample at query time, so every query waits for the oracle. We present SignalCount, a production system that answers COUNT queries with structured and semantic predicates and calls no oracle at query time, even for ad-hoc criteria. Its oracle is the production LLM judge, and the judge's logged verdicts calibrate, offline, the fast classifier that already runs in front of the judge. At query time, SignalCount counts the filtered set exactly and draws a uniform sample of at most 1,000 records in one columnar scan, scores the sample with the classifier, and multiplies the average calibrated probability by the exact count. Its 90% interval combines a sampling term with one-sided, rate-dependent margins for calibration error, fitted by split conformal prediction across tenants. In a multi-tenant production deployment, latency has a p99 of 3.8 s and stays flat as the filtered set grows beyond the sample. On tenants held out from fitting, the interval covers the count that the production pipeline returns in 92% of estimates, although estimates run about 15% high in aggregate, because a calibration nearly unbiased per record is still biased per criterion.
papers.intro:
A research hospital is recruiting for a diabetes trial and needs patients whose first-line drug, metformin, failed to control their blood sugar. A coordinator filters the patient records to type 2 diabetes, ages 40 to 70, seen this year and living near a trial site, and 50,000 patients match. The filter is exact, because every part of it is a column. The reason a patient stopped metformin is not a column: it is written in the clinical notes, keyword search cannot separate stopping for side effects from stopping because it stopped working, and no fixed taxonomy anticipates every trial’s criterion. So the coordinator writes the criterion in plain language, and a pipeline of models reads every patient’s notes to find the matches. That pipeline is the right tool for the final list, but it runs over the whole filtered set and takes long enough that nobody wants to run it to find out whether a criterion was worded well.

And a criterion is rarely worded well the first time (Figure 1). “Tried metformin” matches about 9,000 of those patients, and the coordinators can screen only 3,000 charts this quarter. “Stopped metformin” still sweeps in patients who stopped for stomach side effects. “Stopped metformin because blood sugar stayed high” is the cohort the trial wants. The coordinator needs to see, while typing and within seconds, roughly how many patients the criterion selects and how sure that number is, so the cohort is shaped before the slow pipeline runs once. The same loop appears wherever a costly action follows a count over records with text. An insurer asks how many open property claims “describe flood damage, not wind damage” before sending inspectors, and a marketer how many support chats “complain about a problem our new product solves” before paying for a campaign.

SignalCount answers that question: an approximate COUNT over an exactly filtered set with one semantic predicate, returned with a 90% interval within seconds. For the third criterion it estimates about 2,000 matching patients with a 90% interval of 418 to 2,808, in about 2.5 s. Both ends inform the decision: the high end fits the screening capacity, and the low end still leaves enough candidates to fill the trial, so the coordinator saves the cohort and the pipeline finds every match. The example’s numbers are illustrative; Section 5 evaluates the production deployment.

Prior work on aggregates with expensive predicates pairs a cheap model, the proxy, with an expensive model, the oracle, whose answer defines the truth. ABae (Kang et al., 2021) scores every record with the proxy, groups the records into strata by score, and has the oracle label a sample from each stratum at query time. The oracle’s labels give the estimate and its interval, and the proxy only decides where to sample; later systems follow the same pattern (Russo et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2024; Hui et al., 2026). Prediction-powered inference (PPI) (Angelopoulos et al., 2023) instead averages the proxy’s predictions over the records and corrects that average by the proxy’s error on a small sample that the oracle labels. Both intervals hold however poor the proxy is, and both pay for that at query time: each new predicate needs fresh oracle labels, and the proxy runs on every record. In our deployment the oracle is a production LLM judge, and a single call to it has a p50 of 3.7 s and a p90 of 7.7 s. A sample labeled fully in parallel finishes no sooner than its slowest call, which is beyond a budget of 5 s, and the proxy pass grows with the filtered set. We argue this from the judge’s measured latency and did not run either method in production.

SignalCount moves the oracle offline. The production pipeline already runs a fast non-generative classifier in front of its judge (Jev, Section 3), which scores how likely a record’s text is to meet a natural-language criterion, and logs the classifier’s score and the judge’s verdict for every record the judge sees. The classifier is the proxy, and those logs are oracle labels that cost nothing more to collect. Once calibrated to those verdicts, the classifier’s probabilities on a small uniform sample can answer the query directly. The calibration must then transfer to the queried criterion and filtered set, so the interval must account for calibration error. AlloyDB moves proxy training offline for known queries (Chung et al., 2026), and calibrated classifiers measure prevalence with no LLM call for fixed categories in a daily batch (Xu et al., 2026a); SignalCount does so for arbitrary criteria posed at query time, over an exactly counted filtered set, in seconds.

papers.title: Irreducibility of Primitive Special Cycles in Locally Symmetric Spaces of Orthogonal Type
papers.abstract: Let $L$ be an even lattice of signature $(n_1,n_2)$ with $n_1\geq k+1,n_2\geq 2$ and let $X$ denote the quotient of the symmetric space associated to $O(L\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{R})$ by the discriminant kernel of positive spinor norm. We show that primitive special cycles in $X$ of real codimension at most $kn_2$ are irreducible if $L$ splits off $k+1$ hyperbolic planes locally at every prime.

papers.title: Harmonic functions near isolated subanalytic singularities: generalized horns and regular blow-up
papers.abstract:
Let $X\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be a subanalytic set of dimension $d\ge 2$, closed near $0$, with an isolated singularity at $0$ and connected link, whose regular part carries the induced Riemannian metric. We study harmonic functions on $X\setminus\{0\}$ near $0$.
  (i) If $X$ is bi-Lipschitz equivalent, for the intrinsic metric, to a generalized horn $\{(z^\gamma y,z):\ y\in L,\ z\ge 0\}$, with $\gamma\ge 1$ rational and $L$ compact, connected, subanalytic and analytic, then:
  - every bounded harmonic function extends continuously to $0$;
  - every positive harmonic function near $0$ can be written as $qG_X+u_b$, with $q\ge 0$, $u_b$ bounded and $G_X$ a fixed singular profile;
  - a B\^ocher-type theorem holds: a positive harmonic function is either bounded or tends to $+\infty$, and two divergent ones have a nontrivial linear combination that extends continuously.
  The proof relies on a volume doubling and weak Poincar\'e condition on intrinsic balls away from $0$, invariant under bi-Lipschitz homeomorphisms, which together with an annular connectedness condition implies a Harnack inequality on annuli; the decomposition then follows from a Picard-principle argument whose geometric input is the Harnack inequality on the links.
  (ii) If $d\ge 3$ and the spherical blow-up of $X$ at $0$ is a regular manifold with boundary parametrizing $X$ near $0$ (condition (R) of the paper), the singular profile has a polyhomogeneous expansion, which is described and may contain a $\log\rho$ term, $\rho=|x|$.
  (iii) For the rotational cusps $|x|^2=z^m$, $m>2$, $d\ge 3$, whose spherical blow-up is not regular, the profile is radial of order $\rho^{1-m(d-1)/2}$, so that its exponent depends on the rate at which the sections shrink.

papers.title: Probabilistic, facility-specific prioritisation of temperate exoplanets for atmospheric characterisation with JWST and the ELT
papers.abstract: Deciding which temperate exoplanets to observe first matters for JWST transit spectroscopy and for planned ELT reflected-light instruments, yet signal-to-noise metrics ignore habitability and similarity indices ignore observability. We present an open Monte Carlo framework (UHI v6.1) that builds probabilistic priority lists separately for each facility and composition class, never as a single ranking. For each of 6,112 planets in the NASA Exoplanet Archive, 10,000 draws carry catalogue uncertainties through climate, cumulative stellar-XUV atmospheric retention, per-draw rocky, Hycean or gas-rich classes, and a JWST (transiting) or ELT/PCS (non-transiting) detection model, giving each planet a survival probability, a conditional score and a top-N probability. At $5\sigma$, 255 rocky and 71 Hycean candidates remain viable. A Saltelli--Sobol analysis of 32 assumptions ($N = 512$) shows that the location and width of the XUV shoreline dominate the rocky lists, with total-order indices of 0.22 and 0.12 at $5\sigma$ (0.25 and 0.14 at $3\sigma$), and all ten leading indices have 95% bootstrap half-widths below 0.05. For Hycean planets most outputs are degenerate and the analysis does not converge, so that branch is reported as indicative. Membership of these lists is limited mainly by whether a planet survives the habitability vetoes: at $5\sigma$, 3 of the nominal JWST and 4 of the nominal ELT rocky top-10 targets enter the top 10 in at least half of all draws, yet every one of them stays in the top 10 in more than half of the draws in which it survives. Code, per-planet posterior summaries, sensitivity tables and maps are public, so observers can rerun the lists under their own instrument assumptions and see which inputs would most change a target's priority.

Telescope time for the atmospheres of small, temperate planets is scarce and will stay scarce. In both settings a proposer or a committee has to answer the same practical question: of the planets that could be observed, which ones deserve the hours first?

Existing tools address parts of that question. The transmission and emission spectroscopy metrics (TSM and ESM) of Kempton et al. (2018) estimate the signal a transiting planet would give JWST, and they have been used to sort candidates into bins of radius and equilibrium temperature for proposal planning (Hord et al., 2024). These metrics deliberately say nothing about whether a planet is temperate or whether it is likely to have kept an atmosphere. Habitability indices take the opposite view. The Earth Similarity Index (Schulze-Makuch et al., 2011) compares bulk properties with those of the Earth, and the Statistical-likelihood Exo-Planetary Habitability Index, SEPHI (Rodríguez-Mozos & Moya, 2017), combines likelihood functions for several physical criteria. Its recent extension, SEPHI 2.0 (Rodríguez-Mozos & Moya, 2025), adds eccentricity, an updated mass–radius relation, estimated magnetic fields and a combined treatment of thermal (Jeans) and non-thermal (stellar-wind) atmospheric escape, takes the most restrictive criterion as the final index, propagates the input uncertainties with a Monte Carlo loop, and is offered through a public tool intended to help prioritise follow-up observations. Those indices were built to assess habitability potential, and they do that carefully; they do not model atmospheric loss driven by the cumulative XUV fluence, and they are not designed to say whether a given instrument can detect the planet’s atmosphere. Facility-specific star lists, such as the NASA ExEP list of 164 stars for the Habitable Worlds Observatory (Mamajek & Stapelfeldt, 2024), show how a stated observational purpose sharpens target selection. Closest to the present work, Ih et al. (2026) treat the choice of JWST rocky-planet targets as a combinatorial optimisation, a “knapsack” problem, and show how a well-chosen sample can test the cosmic-shoreline hypothesis statistically. Their framework optimises a survey design for a population-level question, whereas the lists presented here rank individual planets and expose the assumptions behind each rank, so the two approaches are complementary.

This paper describes version 6.1 of an open framework, distributed under the name UHI (Unified Habitability Index), that joins these threads into probabilistic priority lists for atmospheric follow-up. An earlier and much simpler version of the code, v5.2, was archived on Zenodo together with a short research note (Viridis, 2026a, v5.2;). Version 6.1 is a different model: it replaces the bolometric shoreline with a cumulative-XUV retention criterion, assigns a composition class in every Monte Carlo draw, and, most importantly for the use of the output, reports lists separately for each facility and each composition class. We never merge JWST-scored and ELT-scored planets into one list, because the two facilities answer different questions and their detection probabilities are not on a common scale. Nor should the scores be read as probabilities of life, and v5.2 and v6.1 numbers should not be compared row by row.

We state the intended uses at the outset, because they determine how the outputs should be read: UC1 JWST shortlist of temperate rocky planets. Proposers and review panels assembling rocky-planet emission or transmission programmes, of the kind recommended by Redfield et al. (2024), can use the JWST rocky list to weigh signal strength against the chance that a target is temperate and has kept an atmosphere (Section 5.2). UC2 ELT preparatory list of non-transiting planets. Teams preparing reflected-light imaging with ELT/PCS can use the ELT rocky list to decide which known radial-velocity planets merit precursor work, such as orbit refinement and stellar characterisation (Section 5.3). UC3 Rocky versus Hycean triage. For temperate planets of intermediate size, the per-draw class probabilities show whether a target belongs in a rocky-atmosphere programme or a Hycean programme, and how strongly that verdict depends on the adopted Hycean climate criterion. This branch is secondary and indicative in v6.1 (Section 5.4). UC4 Which assumption matters most. A global Saltelli–Sobol analysis identifies the model inputs that move the lists the most, and therefore the measurements or theoretical constraints that would most change target priorities. In this paper UC4 is addressed at the global level only; a per-target value-of-information analysis is left for future work (Section 6).
